parts.context: Paul writes from Ephesus, about AD 53–55, to the church he had founded in Corinth, a busy Greek port. Some there doubt that the dead are raised. Paul reminds them of the message he gave them when he first came, around AD 50.

commentary.on: I delivered to you first of all that which I also received
commentary.text: 'Delivered' and 'received' are the technical words Jewish teachers used for passing on tradition carefully, word for word. Paul is signalling that what follows is not his own composition. He is quoting.

commentary.on: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day
commentary.text: Read verses 3 to 5 aloud and you will hear the rhythm of a formula: four short clauses, each beginning 'that'. Scholars across the spectrum, sceptical ones included, think Paul received it within a few years of the crucifixion, most likely when he visited Peter and James in Jerusalem (the next passage). That makes it perhaps the oldest Christian text we have.

commentary.on: he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve
commentary.text: Cephas is Peter's name in Aramaic, the language Jesus spoke. Its appearance here is a fingerprint of the early, Aramaic-speaking church in Jerusalem.

commentary.on: most of whom remain until now
commentary.text: This is the most remarkable line. Paul is in effect saying: if you doubt me, go and ask them. You do not invite people to check with living witnesses unless you are confident of what they will say.

commentary.on: I persecuted the assembly of God
commentary.text: Paul had been a persecutor of the movement. Whatever we make of his experience, his change of side is one of the best-attested facts of early Christianity, and it cost him dearly.

parts.title: Fifteen days with Peter
parts.context: Paul writes to churches in Galatia (central Turkey), around AD 48–55, to insist that his message is not second-hand. He gives a dated account of his contacts with the leaders in Jerusalem.

commentary.on: after three years I went up to Jerusalem to visit Peter, and stayed with him fifteen days
commentary.text: Three years after his conversion, which most date to the early 30s, so this visit is about AD 35–37, within five or six years of the crucifixion. The Greek word for 'visit' (historēsai, from which 'history' comes) can mean to get to know someone and learn from them.

commentary.on: James, the Lord's brother
commentary.text: Paul met Jesus' own brother. James had not followed Jesus in his lifetime (John 7:5) but later led the church in Jerusalem; the creed you just read says the risen Jesus appeared to him. Josephus, the Jewish historian, also mentions 'the brother of Jesus, who was called Christ, whose name was James' (session 5).

commentary.on: before God, I'm not lying
commentary.text: Paul takes an oath, which tells you that his opponents disputed his account. Ancient readers expected witnesses to swear to what mattered.

commentary.on: I laid before them the Good News which I preach
commentary.text: Fourteen years later he checks his message with the leaders in Jerusalem. The earliest Christians cared that what was taught matched what the first witnesses said.

parts.title: We know that his witness is true
parts.context: The last verses of John's Gospel, probably added by the community that published it in the 90s AD.

commentary.on: This is the disciple who testifies about these things, and wrote these things
commentary.text: The Gospel claims to rest on the testimony of 'the disciple whom Jesus loved', an eyewitness who is never named. Tradition identifies him with John, son of Zebedee; some scholars think he was another disciple in Jerusalem.

commentary.on: We know that his witness is true
commentary.text: A group speaks here, vouching for the witness. Whether or not you accept their claim, this is how ancient testimony worked: a named community standing behind a named source.

commentary.on: the world itself wouldn't have room for the books
commentary.text: A deliberate exaggeration, a common ancient way of ending a book. It reminds us again that the Gospels are selective portraits, not complete records.

paras: For we didn’t follow cunningly devised fables when we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but we were eyewitnesses of his majesty.
For he received from God the Father honor and glory when the voice came to him from the Majestic Glory, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.”
We heard this voice come out of heaven when we were with him on the holy mountain.

parts.title: We were eyewitnesses
parts.context: From the Second Letter of Peter, which presents itself as Peter's farewell. It is the New Testament letter whose authorship is most widely doubted: many scholars, including some conservative ones, date it after Peter's death (session 6 explains pseudonymity). Read it as a statement of what the early Church believed about its own message.

commentary.on: we didn't follow cunningly devised fables
commentary.text: The Greek word is mythos, myth. The writer knows the Greek and Roman myths of gods visiting the earth, and insists the Christian story is a different kind of thing: not a tale about the distant past, but a report about a recent man that people saw and heard.

commentary.on: we were eyewitnesses of his majesty
commentary.text: The writer refers to the Transfiguration (Mark 9:2–8), when three disciples saw Jesus shining on a mountain. The claim is extraordinary, and you may doubt it. But notice its form: not 'it is said' but 'we saw'.

commentary.on: We heard this voice come out of heaven when we were with him
commentary.text: Whether this letter is by Peter or by a follower writing in his name, it shows that by the end of the first century Christians defended their faith as testimony, not as myth or philosophy. That is why the historical questions in this journey matter to Christianity in a way they would not to a religion of myths.

compare.why: A short passage that insists the Christian message is not myth but eyewitness testimony. Ancient readers knew the difference between a myth and a report, and so did the first Christians.
compare.title: Not cunningly devised fables

paras: Jesus was crucified around AD 30. Paul's letters, the earliest Christian writings we have, date from about AD 48 to the early 60s. Most scholars date Mark's Gospel around 65–70, Matthew and Luke in the 80s, and John in the 90s; some date them earlier. The Gospels were written while people who had known Jesus, or known those who had, were still alive.
How does that compare? The table sets the main sources for Jesus beside the sources for some other famous ancient figures.

rows: Plutarch (about AD 100) and Arrian (2nd century AD), drawing on lost earlier works
Plato and Xenophon, his own pupils
table.note: The point is not that early sources must be true, but that the Gospels are as close to their subject as the sources historians rely on for most of antiquity, and closer than many.

sections.key: The Gospels were written within living memory, closer to Jesus than many ancient biographies are to their subjects.

paras: The most important passage for historians is the one you read first. Paul wrote in the mid-50s, but he is quoting something earlier, with the marks of an oral formula and an Aramaic name for Peter. His visit to Peter and James in Jerusalem, about three years after his conversion, is the likeliest moment he received it.

Scholars across the spectrum date it to within a few years of the crucifixion. Gerd Lüdemann, an atheist New Testament scholar, put it within three years; Bart Ehrman, an agnostic, agrees it is very early. Whatever one makes of its claim, belief that Jesus had been raised and had appeared to named people was not a legend that grew up over generations. It was there at the start.
sections.key: Paul quotes a summary of the faith that scholars of every view date to within a few years of the crucifixion.

paras: Between Jesus and the written Gospels lie two or three decades of oral tradition: sayings and stories told and retold. How reliable was that stage? In the twentieth century, form critics such as Rudolf Bultmann argued that stories changed freely as communities used them, so that much in the Gospels reflects the early Church more than Jesus.

Other scholars point out that teaching in Jewish and ancient settings was often memorised; that Jesus' sayings are shaped for memory, with parallelism, rhythm and vivid images; and that named people who had known Jesus, Peter, James and John among them, led the communities for decades. Psychologists of memory add a caution on both sides: memory keeps the gist better than the details.
sections.key: Scholars debate whether the oral stage changed the stories freely or kept their substance stable.

paras: The Gospels do not name their authors in the text. The titles 'according to Matthew', 'Mark', 'Luke' and 'John' are attested in the second century, and no rival names were ever attached to them. Around AD 120 Papias, a bishop in Asia Minor, reported that Mark had been Peter's interpreter and wrote down what Peter remembered. Around 180 Irenaeus of Lyons named all four.

Many modern scholars doubt that Matthew and John were written by apostles in their present form, while accepting that they draw on early tradition; others defend the traditional names. Mark and Luke, who were not apostles, are names nobody would invent to give a book authority.
sections.key: The traditional names are attested early and unchallenged; two of them are names nobody would invent.

paras: The Gospels differ. Matthew mentions one angel at the empty tomb, Luke two. Matthew and Luke give different genealogies for Jesus. John places the cleansing of the Temple at the start of Jesus' ministry, the others at the end. Sceptics have long counted these as contradictions.

Historians see them differently. Independent witnesses always differ in detail, and identical accounts suggest copying. Ancient biographers also arranged material by theme rather than strict order, as Plutarch admits. Some differences can be reconciled; some cannot easily be. But none touches the core: that Jesus taught, healed, was crucified under Pilate, and that his followers proclaimed him risen. The early Church had the chance to merge the four into one tidy account (Tatian did so around 170) and chose to keep all four, differences included.
sections.key: The Gospels differ in detail as independent witnesses do; the differences do not touch the core of the story.

paras: How did the Church decide which books belonged in the New Testament? Not by a vote at a single council, but over about three centuries, by recognising books already being read in worship across the churches. The tests, roughly, were apostolic origin (written by an apostle or someone close to one), agreement with the faith handed down, and wide and long use.

The four Gospels and Paul's letters were accepted very early; Irenaeus, around 180, defends the four Gospels against rivals. A few books, such as Hebrews, James, 2 Peter and Revelation, were debated longer. In 367 Athanasius of Alexandria, in his thirty-ninth Festal Letter, listed exactly our twenty-seven books, the first list we have to do so. Councils at Hippo (393) and Carthage (397) in North Africa confirmed the list for the West.
sections.key: The canon was recognised over three centuries from books the churches already read, not chosen by a single decision.

paras: A popular story, repeated by Voltaire and in Dan Brown's novel The Da Vinci Code (2003), says that the Emperor Constantine or the Council of Nicaea in 325 decided which books went into the Bible and suppressed the rest. There is no evidence for this. The Council of Nicaea met to settle the dispute over Arius' teaching about Christ and the date of Easter; none of its surviving decisions mentions the canon.

Constantine did do one thing for the Bible: around 331 he ordered fifty copies of the Scriptures from Eusebius of Caesarea for the churches of his new capital (Eusebius, Life of Constantine IV.36). By then the four Gospels and Paul's letters had been read as Scripture for nearly two centuries.
sections.key: Neither Constantine nor the Council of Nicaea chose the books of the Bible; the core was settled long before.

paras: Other early writings were not accepted. Some were respected but late, like the Shepherd of Hermas, which some churches read for a time. Others, such as the Gospel of Thomas, the Gospel of Peter or the Gospel of Judas, were rejected because they taught a different faith, often the 'gnostic' belief that salvation comes through secret knowledge and that the material world is evil. Most date from the second century or later; a few scholars date parts of Thomas earlier.

Marcion, around 140, accepted only an edited Luke and ten letters of Paul and rejected the Old Testament altogether. The Church's response, insisting on the Jewish Scriptures and on four Gospels, shaped the canon we have.
sections.key: The 'lost gospels' were mostly later, and were left out because they taught a different faith.

sections.h: What this evidence shows, and what it does not
paras: The evidence shows that the claims about Jesus, including the extraordinary claim that he was raised, were made very early, by people who named witnesses, some of them leaders of the movement. It shows that the Gospels were written within living memory, and that the Church kept four distinct accounts rather than one harmonised story.

It does not, by itself, show that every detail is accurate, or that the miracles happened. And so far all our witnesses are Christians. Two more checks follow: whether the text has been copied faithfully since (session 4), and what evidence from outside the Bible says (session 5).
sections.key: The evidence shows early, named testimony and a canon recognised over time; the next checks are the copies and the outside evidence.

debate.question: How close are the Gospels to the eyewitnesses?

positions.name: Very close
positions.who: Richard Bauckham and others
positions.view: The Gospels were written within living memory and rest on the testimony of named eyewitnesses, such as Peter behind Mark, which the authors signal deliberately.
positions.evidence: 1 Corinthians 15 and Galatians 1; Papias on Mark; the naming of minor characters who could be checked.

positions.name: Shaped by communities
positions.who: Rudolf Bultmann and the form critics; Bart Ehrman in a modern form
positions.view: Stories about Jesus circulated orally for decades and changed as they were retold, so the Gospels show us the faith of the early Church more than the facts about Jesus.
positions.evidence: Differences between the Gospels; studies of how memories change in retelling.

positions.name: Remembered Jesus
positions.who: James D. G. Dunn and many others
positions.view: The tradition was flexible in wording but stable in substance, because communities kept and checked the memory of Jesus together. We meet Jesus as he was remembered, which is how we meet any historical figure.
positions.evidence: The mix of stable core and varied detail in the synoptic Gospels.

debate.agree: All agree that Jesus existed, that the Gospels were written in the first century, and that belief in his resurrection goes back to the earliest days.

look.why: Simone Cantarini, in the 1640s, painted the old tradition of Matthew writing his Gospel with an angel's help: the Church's way of saying that inspiration came through a real human author.

His forehead deeply lined; he looks down at the page.
An angel, seen from behind, with braided blond hair tied with a red bow and snowy white wings.
The angel holds a white feather pen and an inkwell, as if handing the writer his tools.

music.why: Bach set Matthew's account of the Passion word for word in Luther's German. In his hands the Gospel is sung as testimony, by an Evangelist who narrates and a crowd that answers.

think.why: How historians weigh the Gospels as sources.

learn.why: Perhaps the oldest words of Christian faith we have, handed on within a few years of the events they describe.

Paul is quoting a formula he received earlier, which takes the evidence back to within a few years of the events

check.q: What is the significance of Paul's remark that 'most' of the five hundred 'remain until now'?
options: It proves the resurrection happened
It invites his readers to check with living witnesses, which a writer confident of his facts would do
It shows the five hundred were all dead
It was added by a later copyist
check.why: It doesn't prove the claim, but it shows Paul expected the witnesses to confirm it.

Independent witnesses always differ in detail, while identical accounts suggest copying
The Church forbade comparing them
One author wrote all four

The traditional names are attested in the second century and never rivalled, though scholars debate how direct the apostolic link is
The names were first given at the Reformation

options: An emperor's decree
A gradual recognition, over about three centuries, of books already read across the churches, judged by apostolic origin, faithfulness and wide use
A single vote at Jerusalem in AD 50
The choice of Martin Luther
check.why: Athanasius' list of 367 and the African councils of 393 and 397 recorded a consensus already largely formed.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: ask an older relative or friend to tell you about an event they witnessed long ago. Notice what stays fixed in their telling and what varies, and thank them for it.
sessions.reflect: Whose testimony do you trust most in your own life, and why?
takeaways: The New Testament was written within living memory; Paul quotes a creed from within a few years of the crucifixion.
The Gospels differ in detail as independent witnesses do; how close they stand to eyewitnesses is debated.
The twenty-seven books were recognised over three centuries; Athanasius first listed them in 367; Constantine and Nicaea did not choose them.
sessions.finding: The New Testament was written within living memory of Jesus, by people who named their witnesses; its books were recognised over time, not picked by an emperor.

background.h: From the Old Testament to the New
paras: Between the last books of the Old Testament and the time of Jesus lie about four centuries. Alexander the Great conquered the region in 332 BC, and Greek became the common language of the eastern Mediterranean. In 63 BC Rome took control. By Jesus' day Judea was ruled by Roman governors and local client kings such as Herod, and many Jews longed for God to free them, perhaps through an anointed king, the 'Messiah' (in Greek, 'Christ').

Jesus was born around 4 BC and crucified in Jerusalem around AD 30. His followers claimed he had been raised from the dead and began to spread the message, first among Jews and then among non-Jews across the Roman Empire.
background.key: Jesus lived under Roman rule, among Jews hoping for a Messiah; his followers spread their message across the Empire.

paras: Paul (also called Saul) was a Jew from Tarsus, in modern Turkey, trained as a strict Pharisee, who at first persecuted the Christians. A few years after Jesus' death he had an experience he describes as seeing the risen Jesus, and he became the movement's most energetic missionary. Between about AD 48 and his execution in Rome in the 60s, he travelled around the eastern Mediterranean founding churches, and wrote them letters.

Thirteen letters in the New Testament carry his name. Scholars agree that at least seven are certainly his, including the two you will read today, 1 Corinthians and Galatians. They are the earliest Christian writings that survive.
background.key: Paul, once a persecutor, became the leading missionary; his letters are the earliest Christian writings.

background.h: Why we read Paul before the Gospels
paras: You might expect a session about the Gospels to start with a Gospel. But the Gospels were written later than Paul's letters, between about AD 65 and 100. If we want to know how close the written record comes to Jesus, the earliest evidence is the place to start.

In 1 Corinthians, Paul quotes a short summary of the faith that he says he had been given, and lists people who saw the risen Jesus. In Galatians he tells us exactly when he met Jesus' closest followers. Then a passage from the end of John's Gospel shows how a Gospel described its own source.
The lecture then asks the other half of the question: how, over the next three centuries, the Church came to recognise these twenty-seven books, and not the 'lost gospels', as its New Testament.
background.key: We start with Paul because his letters are older than the Gospels and take us closest to the events.

sessions.title: Has it been copied faithfully?
sessions.line: No originals survive. So how do we know what was written?
sessions.plain: Before printing, every book was copied by hand, and copies of copies can drift. None of the Bible's original pages survives, and none of any other ancient book. But we have far more, and far older, copies of the Bible than of any other ancient writing, and scholars compare them to work out what was first written. This session shows how that works, what has changed, and what has not.
sessions.why: Sessions 2 and 3 showed where the books came from. But a book written long ago is only useful if what we read today is what was written then. That is the next check.

before: What happens to Jeremiah's scroll, and what happens next?
What does Baruch do, and why does it matter for how Scripture survived?
In the comparison, why do the writers warn against adding or taking away?
sessions.readWhy: The only story in the Bible about a biblical book being written, destroyed and written again. A king cuts up the prophet's scroll and burns it piece by piece; the prophet dictates it again, with more added. It is a parable of how fragile, and how persistent, the written word has been.

paras: In the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah, this word came to Jeremiah from Yahweh, saying,

“Take a scroll of a book, and write in it all the words that I have spoken to you against Israel, and against Judah, and against all the nations, from the day I spoke to you, from the days of Josiah, even to this day.
It may be that the house of Judah will hear all the evil which I intend to do to them; that they may each return from his evil way; that I may forgive their iniquity and their sin.”
Then Jeremiah called Baruch the son of Neriah; and Baruch wrote from the mouth of Jeremiah all Yahweh’s words, which he had spoken to him, on a scroll of a book.
Jeremiah commanded Baruch, saying, “I am restricted. I can’t go into Yahweh’s house.

Therefore you go, and read from the scroll which you have written from my mouth, Yahweh’s words, in the ears of the people in Yahweh’s house on the fast day. Also you shall read them in the ears of all Judah who come out of their cities.
It may be they will present their supplication before Yahweh, and will each return from his evil way; for Yahweh has pronounced great anger and wrath against this people.”
Baruch the son of Neriah did according to all that Jeremiah the prophet commanded him, reading in the book Yahweh’s words in Yahweh’s house.

Now in the fifth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah, in the ninth month, all the people in Jerusalem, and all the people who came from the cities of Judah to Jerusalem, proclaimed a fast before Yahweh.

Then Baruch read the words of Jeremiah from the book in Yahweh’s house, in the room of Gemariah the son of Shaphan, the scribe, in the upper court, at the entry of the new gate of Yahweh’s house, in the ears of all the people.
When Micaiah the son of Gemariah, the son of Shaphan, had heard out of the book all Yahweh’s words,

he went down into the king’s house, into the scribe’s room: and behold, all the princes were sitting there, Elishama the scribe, Delaiah the son of Shemaiah, Elnathan the son of Achbor, Gemariah the son of Shaphan, Zedekiah the son of Hananiah, and all the princes.
Then Micaiah declared to them all the words that he had heard, when Baruch read the book in the ears of the people.

Therefore all the princes sent Jehudi the son of Nethaniah, the son of Shelemiah, the son of Cushi, to Baruch, saying, “Take in your hand the scroll in which you have read in the ears of the people, and come.”
So Baruch the son of Neriah took the scroll in his hand, and came to them.
They said to him, “Sit down now, and read it in our hearing.”
So Baruch read it in their hearing.
Now when they had heard all the words, they turned in fear one toward another, and said to Baruch, “We will surely tell the king of all these words.”
They asked Baruch, saying, “Tell us now, how did you write all these words at his mouth?”
Then Baruch answered them, “He dictated all these words to me with his mouth, and I wrote them with ink in the book.”
Then the princes said to Baruch, “You and Jeremiah go hide. Don’t let anyone know where you are.”
They went in to the king into the court; but they had laid up the scroll in the room of Elishama the scribe. Then they told all the words in the hearing of the king.

So the king sent Jehudi to get the scroll; and he took it out of the room of Elishama the scribe. Jehudi read it in the hearing of the king, and in the hearing of all the princes who stood beside the king.
Now the king was sitting in the winter house in the ninth month; and there was a fire in the brazier burning before him.
When Jehudi had read three or four leaves, the king cut it with the penknife, and cast it into the fire that was in the brazier, until all the scroll was consumed in the fire that was in the brazier.
The king and his servants who heard all these words were not afraid, and didn’t tear their garments.
Moreover Elnathan and Delaiah and Gemariah had made intercession to the king that he would not burn the scroll; but he would not listen to them.
The king commanded Jerahmeel the king’s son, and Seraiah the son of Azriel, and Shelemiah the son of Abdeel, to arrest Baruch the scribe and Jeremiah the prophet; but Yahweh hid them.
Then Yahweh’s word came to Jeremiah, after the king had burned the scroll, and the words which Baruch wrote at the mouth of Jeremiah, saying,
“Take again another scroll, and write in it all the former words that were in the first scroll, which Jehoiakim the king of Judah has burned.

Concerning Jehoiakim king of Judah you shall say, ‘Yahweh says: “You have burned this scroll, saying, “Why have you written therein, saying, ‘The king of Babylon will certainly come and destroy this land, and will cause to cease from there man and animal?’ ” ’
Therefore Yahweh says concerning Jehoiakim king of Judah: “He will have no one to sit on David’s throne. His dead body will be cast out in the day to the heat, and in the night to the frost.

I will punish him, his offspring, and his servants for their iniquity. I will bring on them, on the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and on the men of Judah, all the evil that I have pronounced against them, but they didn’t listen.” ’ ”

Then took Jeremiah another scroll, and gave it to Baruch the scribe, the son of Neriah, who wrote therein from the mouth of Jeremiah all the words of the book which Jehoiakim king of Judah had burned in the fire; and many similar words were added to them.

parts.title: The prophet dictates a scroll
parts.context: Jerusalem, 605–604 BC, the fourth year of King Jehoiakim. Babylon has just defeated Egypt at Carchemish and is about to become master of the region. Jeremiah has been warning for twenty years that disaster is coming.

commentary.on: Take a scroll of a book, and write in it all the words that I have spoken to you
commentary.text: Here is the moment spoken prophecy becomes a written book. Jeremiah had preached for over twenty years; now his words are collected on a scroll so they can be read where he cannot go.

commentary.on: Baruch wrote from the mouth of Jeremiah
commentary.text: Baruch son of Neriah is a professional scribe, and the first named 'secretary' of a biblical book. Many books of the Bible came into being like this: a prophet or teacher speaking, a scribe writing. That is why it makes sense to speak of human authors and editors without denying that the words are, as believers say, God's.

commentary.on: I am restricted. I can't go into Yahweh's house
commentary.text: Jeremiah has been banned from the Temple for his preaching. The written word goes where the prophet cannot. That is one reason books matter: they outlive bans, prisons and deaths.

parts.title: The scroll is read in the Temple
parts.context: A year later, on a public fast day, Baruch reads the scroll aloud in the Temple. The royal officials hear of it.

commentary.on: in the room of Gemariah the son of Shaphan, the scribe
commentary.text: A detail worth noticing: a clay seal impression reading 'Gemaryahu son of Shaphan' was found in the City of David in Jerusalem in the 1980s, in a layer burned in the Babylonian destruction of 587 BC. Whether it belonged to this very man cannot be proved, but the name, the father's name and the period fit.

commentary.on: how did you write all these words at his mouth?
commentary.text: The officials ask about the process of writing. Baruch's answer, 'He dictated ... and I wrote them with ink in the book', is the clearest description in the Bible of how one of its books was made.

commentary.on: You and Jeremiah go hide
commentary.text: The officials know the king will be furious. Writing that challenges power has always been dangerous.

parts.title: The king burns it
parts.context: Winter, in the palace. The scroll is read to King Jehoiakim beside a brazier.

commentary.on: When Jehudi had read three or four leaves, the king cut it with the penknife
commentary.text: A scribe's penknife was used for trimming reed pens. The king uses the tool of writing to destroy writing, column by column, as it is read. It is a calculated act of contempt.

commentary.on: were not afraid, and didn't tear their garments
commentary.text: Compare the people in Nehemiah 8, who wept when they heard the Law. Tearing one's garments was a sign of grief and repentance; the king and his servants show none. The writer wants us to notice the contrast.

commentary.on: but Yahweh hid them
commentary.text: The writer's comment. The prophet and the scribe survive, and so will the words.

parts.title: Written again, with more
parts.context: After the burning, Jeremiah is told to write the scroll again.

commentary.on: Take again another scroll, and write in it all the former words
commentary.text: The destroyed text is restored, from memory and dictation. This is how ancient texts survived disaster: through people who knew them and copied them again.

commentary.on: many similar words were added to them
commentary.text: Honest and important. The book grew, under the prophet's own direction. Ancient books were often expanded and re-edited. In fact the Greek translation of Jeremiah is about one-eighth shorter than the Hebrew and arranged differently, and the Dead Sea Scrolls contain copies of both forms. Textual scholars study exactly this kind of growth.

paras: Now, Israel, listen to the statutes and to the ordinances which I teach you, to do them; that you may live, and go in and possess the land which Yahweh, the God of your fathers, gives you.
You shall not add to the word which I command you, neither shall you take away from it, that you may keep the commandments of Yahweh your God which I command you.
I testify to everyone who hears the words of the prophecy of this book, if anyone adds to them, may God add to him the plagues which are written in this book.
If anyone takes away from the words of the book of this prophecy, may God take away his part from the tree of life, and out of the holy city, which are written in this book.

parts.title: Moses' warning
parts.context: From Deuteronomy, presented as Moses' farewell speeches to Israel before they enter the promised land.

commentary.on: You shall not add to the word which I command you, neither shall you take away from it
commentary.text: Ancient law codes and treaties often ended with curses on anyone who altered them; the Babylonian Code of Hammurabi does. Here the warning protects the commandments themselves. It shows how seriously the text's integrity was taken, and also, by implication, that people knew texts could be tampered with.

parts.title: John's warning
parts.context: The last verses of the last book of the Bible, the Revelation to John, written in the 90s AD.

commentary.on: if anyone adds to them ... If anyone takes away from the words of the book of this prophecy
commentary.text: The warning applies to 'this book', the Revelation, not to the whole Bible, which had not yet been collected. It is a copyist's curse, aimed at scribes who might change a text as they copied it. It is a fitting end to the Bible all the same: a reminder that every generation receives the text from those before it, and is responsible for handing it on intact.

compare.why: The first and last books of the Bible to say it warn against adding to or taking from the words. Such warnings were common in the ancient world; they show that copyists were expected to be faithful, and also that people knew texts could be changed.
compare.title: Do not add, do not take away

paras: No original manuscript of any biblical book survives, nor of any classical book: not Plato, not Caesar, not Virgil. Ancient texts were written on papyrus or parchment, which decay, and were copied by hand. What we have are copies of copies, and copyists make mistakes: they skip a line, misread a letter, or 'correct' what they think is an error.

The question is not whether the copies differ (they do) but whether we can recover what was written. That is the work of textual criticism, a discipline developed first for the Greek and Latin classics and then applied to the Bible. How does the Bible compare?

Over a thousand, mostly papyrus fragments

Dead Sea Scrolls, 3rd century BC to 1st century AD; complete codices about AD 930 and 1008
Hundreds of scrolls and thousands of medieval manuscripts
table.note: Manuscript counts for classical works are approximate and change as catalogues are revised.

sections.key: No ancient book survives in its original, but the Bible is far better attested than any other.

paras: Because there are so many manuscripts, there are also very many variants, places where the manuscripts differ: hundreds of thousands, more than the number of words in the New Testament. Bart Ehrman made this point famous in Misquoting Jesus (2005).

Most variants are trivial: spelling, word order (which matters little in Greek), obvious slips. A small number matter. The longer ending of Mark (16:9–20) and the story of the woman caught in adultery (John 7:53–8:11) are absent from the earliest manuscripts, as is the angel stirring the pool in John 5:4, which you will meet in session 5. A verse on the Trinity in some older English Bibles (1 John 5:7) is a late addition. Modern Bibles mark all of these. Ehrman himself has said that no essential Christian belief depends on a disputed reading; his argument is about what the variants show of the copyists, not that the text is lost.
sections.key: There are many variants, but most are trivial and the significant ones are known and marked in modern Bibles.

sections.h: How scholars work out the original
paras: Imagine a letter copied by hand a hundred times, by different people in different towns, and each copy copied again. Every copy has a few slips, but different slips in different places. If you gather many copies and lay them side by side, the mistakes stand out, because most copies agree where one goes wrong. That, in essence, is textual criticism.

Scholars also use a few rules of thumb. Older copies are usually closer to the original. A reading found in copies from several different regions is more likely original than one found in only one region. And where copies differ, the harder or shorter reading is often the original, because copyists tended to smooth out difficulties and add explanations, as with the angel in John 5:4.
sections.key: Lay many copies side by side, and the slips stand out; older, widespread and harder readings are usually original.

sections.h: Check it in your own Bible
paras: You do not have to take any of this on trust. Open almost any modern Bible at Mark 16:9 or John 7:53 and you will find a note or brackets saying the passage is missing from the earliest manuscripts. Many Bibles add footnotes elsewhere saying 'some manuscripts read…'. Those notes are the work of textual critics, shown openly to every reader.
A tradition that wanted to hide changes in its book would not print them on the page. The openness of modern Bibles about their own text is itself part of the answer to the question of this session.
sections.key: Modern Bibles show their doubtful passages openly in notes and brackets: you can check them yourself.

paras: For the Old Testament, the great discovery came in 1947, when Bedouin shepherds found jars of scrolls in caves near Qumran by the Dead Sea. Over the next decade, around 900 manuscripts were recovered, including parts of every book of the Hebrew Bible except Esther, most of them copied between about 250 BC and AD 68.

The most famous, the Great Isaiah Scroll, was copied around 125 BC, about a thousand years earlier than the oldest Hebrew manuscript of Isaiah known before. Comparing them showed two things at once. Some books circulated in more than one form, as Jeremiah did. And yet the text of Isaiah had been copied with remarkable faithfulness across a millennium: the differences are overwhelmingly matters of spelling and small wording.
sections.key: The Dead Sea Scrolls showed the Hebrew text copied with remarkable care across a thousand years, alongside some variety of editions.

paras: A common claim is that today's Bible is like a game of Chinese whispers: Hebrew into Greek into Latin into English, changing at every step. This is simply not how modern Bibles are made. Since the Reformation, translators have worked directly from the Hebrew, Aramaic and Greek, using the best manuscripts available. Today's translations draw on the Dead Sea Scrolls and on Greek manuscripts that the King James translators of 1611 never saw.

Translations do differ, in method rather than in text. Some aim to follow the original word for word (the King James, the English Standard Version); others aim to render the meaning in natural modern English (the New International Version, the New Living Translation). Comparing two of them is one of the best ways to see where the original is difficult.
sections.key: Modern Bibles are translated directly from the Hebrew and Greek, from better manuscripts than ever before.

refs: Manuscript figures: Institute for New Testament Textual Research (INTF), Münster; Bruce M. Metzger and Bart D. Ehrman, The Text of the New Testament (4th ed., 2005); for classical texts, L. D. Reynolds (ed.), Texts and Transmission (1983).
Bart D. Ehrman, Misquoting Jesus (2005), and the interview in the 2007 paperback edition.
Dead Sea Scrolls: James C. VanderKam, The Dead Sea Scrolls Today (2nd ed., 2010); the Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsaᵃ), Israel Museum.
Jeremiah's two editions: Emanuel Tov, Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible (3rd ed., 2012). The Gemaryahu bulla: Yigal Shiloh, City of David excavations (1982).

debate.question: Can we trust the copies?

positions.name: The text is uncertain
positions.who: Bart Ehrman
positions.view: The copyists changed the text, sometimes deliberately for theological reasons, and since we lack the originals we cannot be sure we have the words the authors wrote, especially for the earliest decades.
positions.evidence: Hundreds of thousands of variants; the gap between the originals and the earliest full manuscripts; known additions such as Mark 16:9–20.

positions.name: The text is secure
positions.who: Bruce Metzger, Daniel Wallace and most textual scholars
positions.view: The number and age of the manuscripts let us reconstruct the original text with a very high degree of confidence; the uncertain readings are few, known and affect no central belief.
positions.evidence: Early papyri; agreement across independent families of manuscripts; quotations in early writers.

positions.name: The question is mistaken
positions.who: Some recent scholars, such as David Parker
positions.view: For the earliest period it may make more sense to speak of a living text used by communities than of one fixed original; the variants are themselves evidence of how the first Christians read.
positions.evidence: Multiple editions of some Old Testament books at Qumran; early variety in the Gospel texts.

debate.agree: All agree that we have more and earlier copies of the New Testament than of any other ancient work, and that the doubtful passages are known.

look.why: Zurbarán and his workshop, around 1640–1650, painted Jerome with Paula and Eustochium, the two Roman women who studied the Scriptures with him in Bethlehem and helped him make the Latin Bible. Jerome compared Hebrew and Greek manuscripts and complained about copyists' errors: textual criticism is as old as the Church.
points: On the right, an old man with a white beard in a light red cloak over a white robe: Jerome, holding a book.
He gestures towards the two women on the left, dressed in black habits over white robes; one of them holds a book.
A red hat hangs on the wall behind him: a cardinal's hat, an anachronism, since there were no cardinals in Jerome's day, but the usual sign of him in painting.
To the left, a pale cityscape under a cloudy sky.

music.why: Charles Jennens compiled the words of Handel's Messiah entirely from the King James Bible, Old and New Testaments together: the canon as one story, set to music in 1741.

think.why: Christians have trusted the Bible not only by arguing about it but by living with it. This depth asks what practices do to us.

learn.why: A line from the Isaiah scroll that survived a thousand years in a cave: the grass withers, the word stands.

check.q: Bart Ehrman says there are more variants than words in the New Testament. What is the best response?
options: Deny that there are variants
Most are trivial; the large number exists because there are so many manuscripts; the significant ones are known and marked
Agree that the original text is lost
Say that only the King James text matters
check.why: More manuscripts mean more variants, but also more evidence for recovering the original.

check.q: What did the Great Isaiah Scroll show when compared with medieval Hebrew manuscripts copied a thousand years later?
options: That Isaiah had been completely rewritten
That the text had been copied with remarkable faithfulness, the differences mostly small
That Isaiah was written by Christians
That the scroll was a forgery
check.why: At the same time, other scrolls showed that books such as Jeremiah circulated in more than one form.

check.q: Why is it wrong to call a modern Bible 'a translation of a translation of a translation'?
options: Because modern Bibles are not translations
Because modern translators work directly from the Hebrew, Aramaic and Greek, using the earliest manuscripts available
Because the Latin Vulgate was never translated
Because English Bibles are copied from the King James
check.why: Modern translations go back to the original languages and draw on better manuscripts than ever before.

check.q: Why do scholars know that John 5:4 (the angel stirring the pool) was probably added later?
options: A pope removed it
It is missing from the oldest manuscripts, which can be compared because so many survive
It contradicts Genesis
It is written in Latin
check.why: Comparing many manuscripts is how additions are spotted and marked.

check.q: In Jeremiah 36, the burned scroll is rewritten 'and many similar words were added'. What does this teach about ancient books?
options: That Jeremiah's book is a forgery
That books could grow and be re-edited, which is why scholars study different editions, such as the shorter Greek Jeremiah
That kings wrote the Bible
That nothing was ever written down
check.why: Growth under the prophet's own direction is different from later corruption, and scholars can see both.

tutorial.question: 'We don't have the originals, and it's been copied and translated so often that it must have changed.' Assess this claim.
tutorial.approach: Explain why no ancient book survives in its original. Set out the manuscript evidence for both Testaments, including the Dead Sea Scrolls, with the comparison to classical texts. Explain variants with real examples. Explain how modern translations are made. Conclude with what we can and cannot know.
strong: Notes that no ancient book survives in its original manuscript.
Gives the scale and age of the evidence, with the comparison to classical texts.
Explains what variants are and gives real examples of significant ones.
Uses the Dead Sea Scrolls accurately, including the evidence of different editions.
Explains that modern translations work from the original languages.
Distinguishes certainty about the text from belief in its truth.

reading.author: Bart D. Ehrman
reading.title: Misquoting Jesus
reading.why: The best-selling sceptical account of how the text was changed.

reading.author: Peter J. Williams
reading.title: Can We Trust the Gospels?
reading.why: A short reply, with a good chapter on the manuscripts.

reading.author: Bruce M. Metzger and Bart D. Ehrman
reading.title: The Text of the New Testament
reading.why: The standard textbook, written jointly by a believer and a sceptic.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: copy out by hand one short passage you love (a psalm, a few lines of a Gospel) slowly and carefully, as scribes once did. Give it to someone who might need it.
sessions.reflect: Jehoiakim burned the scroll; Jeremiah wrote it again. What words in your life have you had to write, or say, again?
takeaways: No ancient original survives, but the Bible is far better attested than any other ancient book.
Variants are many but mostly trivial; the significant ones, such as Mark 16:9–20 and John 5:4, are known and marked.
The Dead Sea Scrolls showed the text copied faithfully across a thousand years; modern Bibles translate directly from the Hebrew and Greek.
sessions.finding: The copies are remarkably faithful: there are more and older copies of the Bible than of any other ancient book, and the doubtful passages are known.

paras: So far we have seen that the Old Testament is genuinely ancient and that the New Testament was written within living memory of Jesus. But that only helps if the Bible we read today says what was written then. Think again of the family story: it may have started with an eyewitness, but if it was retold carelessly for generations, it may have changed along the way. That is today's check.
background.key: Today's check: has the text been passed down without being changed?

paras: Until printing was invented in Europe around 1450, every copy of every book was written by hand. In biblical times people wrote on scrolls of papyrus (made from reeds) or parchment (made from animal skin), with reed pens and ink. Professional scribes did most of the writing. Copying was slow, and every copy could introduce mistakes.

No original manuscript of any biblical book survives, and none of any other ancient book. What we have are copies of copies. The question of this session is whether we can know what was originally written, and also who decided which books belonged in the Bible.
background.key: Every ancient book survives only in hand-made copies; the question is how faithful they are.

paras: Jeremiah was a prophet in Jerusalem from about 627 BC until after the city fell to the Babylonians in 587 BC. For forty years he warned the kings of Judah that their injustice and worship of other gods would bring disaster, and that Babylon would conquer them. He was unpopular, imprisoned and threatened with death. His book, one of the longest in the Bible, collects his sayings and stories about him.
Our passage comes from 605–604 BC, the year Babylon defeated Egypt at the battle of Carchemish and became the great power of the region. Jeremiah's warnings were about to come true.
background.key: Jeremiah warned Jerusalem for forty years before Babylon destroyed it.

paras: It is the only story in the Bible about one of its own books being written, destroyed and written again. It shows a prophet dictating to a scribe, the scroll being read aloud, a king burning it, and the book being rewritten with more added. In a few pages it shows how fragile written texts were, and how they survived.
The two short passages in the comparison, from the first and last books of the Bible to warn about it, show that ancient writers knew texts could be changed and wanted them copied faithfully.
background.key: Jeremiah 36 is the Bible's own story of a book written, destroyed and written again.

sessions.title: The evidence outside the Bible
sessions.line: What archaeology and Roman and Jewish writers confirm, and where they are silent.
sessions.plain: So far all our witnesses have been inside the Bible. This session looks outside: at inscriptions, tunnels, coins, ossuaries and royal records dug up over the last two centuries, and at what Roman and Jewish writers said about Jesus and the first Christians. It also shows honestly where the evidence is thin, silent or against the Bible.
sessions.why: Sessions 2 to 4 showed that the books are ancient, close to the events and faithfully copied. But a sceptic will rightly say a book cannot vouch for itself. Here we test the Bible against evidence that no Christian controlled.
answers: Does archaeology support the Bible?
Do non-Christian writers of the time mention Jesus?
Where is the evidence silent, or against the Bible?
What can archaeology prove, and what can it never prove?
before: Each passage mentions a real person, place or event. Which details could an archaeologist test?
Which of these details would a writer living far away, centuries later, be likely to get wrong?
In the comparison, what do the Roman and Jewish writers say, and what is their attitude to the Christians?
sessions.readWhy: Five short passages chosen because they make specific, checkable claims: a king's tribute and an Assyrian siege, a tunnel, five rulers named in one sentence, a pool with five porches, and a Roman governor in Corinth. Each has been tested by archaeology. Read them first; the commentary after each tells you what was found.

paras: Now in the fourteenth year of king Hezekiah, Sennacherib king of Assyria came up against all the fortified cities of Judah, and took them.

Hezekiah king of Judah sent to the king of Assyria to Lachish, saying, “I have offended you. Return from me. That which you put on me, I will bear.” The king of Assyria appointed to Hezekiah king of Judah three hundred talents of silver and thirty talents of gold.
Hezekiah gave him all the silver that was found in Yahweh’s house, and in the treasures of the king’s house.
At that time, Hezekiah cut off the gold from the doors of Yahweh’s temple, and from the pillars which Hezekiah king of Judah had overlaid, and gave it to the king of Assyria.

The king of Assyria sent Tartan and Rabsaris and Rabshakeh from Lachish to king Hezekiah with a great army to Jerusalem. They went up and came to Jerusalem. When they had come up, they came and stood by the conduit of the upper pool, which is in the highway of the fuller’s field.

Now the rest of the acts of Hezekiah, and all his might, and how he made the pool, and the conduit, and brought water into the city, aren’t they written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah?
When Hezekiah saw that Sennacherib had come, and that he was planning to fight against Jerusalem,
he took counsel with his princes and his mighty men to stop the waters of the springs which were outside of the city, and they helped him.
So, many people gathered together and they stopped all the springs and the brook that flowed through the middle of the land, saying, “Why should the kings of Assyria come, and find abundant water?”
This same Hezekiah also stopped the upper spring of the waters of Gihon, and brought them straight down on the west side of David’s city. Hezekiah prospered in all his works.

Now in the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, Pontius Pilate being governor of Judea, and Herod being tetrarch of Galilee, and his brother Philip tetrarch of the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis, and Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene,
in the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas, the word of God came to John, the son of Zacharias, in the wilderness.
After these things, there was a feast of the Jews, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem.
Now in Jerusalem by the sheep gate, there is a pool, which is called in Hebrew, “Bethesda”, having five porches.
In these lay a great multitude of those who were sick, blind, lame, or paralyzed, waiting for the moving of the water;
for an angel went down at certain times into the pool and stirred up the water. Whoever stepped in first after the stirring of the water was healed of whatever disease he had.
A certain man was there who had been sick for thirty-eight years.
When Jesus saw him lying there, and knew that he had been sick for a long time, he asked him, “Do you want to be made well?”
The sick man answered him, “Sir, I have no one to put me into the pool when the water is stirred up, but while I’m coming, another steps down before me.”
Jesus said to him, “Arise, take up your mat, and walk.”
Immediately, the man was made well, and took up his mat and walked.
Now it was the Sabbath on that day.
But when Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, the Jews with one accord rose up against Paul and brought him before the judgment seat,
saying, “This man persuades men to worship God contrary to the law.”
But when Paul was about to open his mouth, Gallio said to the Jews, “If indeed it were a matter of wrong or of wicked crime, you Jews, it would be reasonable that I should bear with you;
but if they are questions about words and names and your own law, look to it yourselves. For I don’t want to be a judge of these matters.”
So he drove them from the judgment seat.
Then all the Greeks seized Sosthenes, the ruler of the synagogue, and beat him before the judgment seat. Gallio didn’t care about any of these things.

parts.title: Sennacherib invades Judah
parts.context: The book of Kings, compiled during or after the exile from older royal records, describes the Assyrian invasion of Judah in 701 BC, in the reign of King Hezekiah.

commentary.on: Sennacherib king of Assyria came up against all the fortified cities of Judah, and took them
commentary.text: Sennacherib's own account survives. On clay prisms found at Nineveh (one, the Taylor Prism, is in the British Museum) he boasts that he took forty-six of Hezekiah's walled cities and shut Hezekiah up in Jerusalem 'like a bird in a cage'. Notice that he does not claim to have taken Jerusalem, which fits the Bible's account that the city was spared (2 Kings 19).

commentary.on: sent to the king of Assyria to Lachish
commentary.text: Lachish was Judah's second city. Sennacherib was so proud of capturing it that he lined a room of his palace at Nineveh with carved reliefs of the siege: battering rams, archers, and families led into exile. The reliefs are in the British Museum. Excavations at Lachish have found the Assyrian siege ramp, arrowheads and sling stones.

commentary.on: three hundred talents of silver and thirty talents of gold
commentary.text: Sennacherib's prism also records the tribute: thirty talents of gold, exactly as here, and eight hundred talents of silver rather than three hundred. Scholars suggest different counting or the inclusion of other goods. Two independent records of the same payment, from enemies on opposite sides, agreeing on the gold, is a rare thing in ancient history.

parts.title: Hezekiah's tunnel
parts.context: Two brief notes from Kings and Chronicles about Hezekiah's preparations for that same Assyrian siege: securing Jerusalem's water supply.

commentary.on: how he made the pool, and the conduit, and brought water into the city
commentary.text: The tunnel exists. It runs 533 metres through the rock under Jerusalem from the Gihon spring to the Pool of Siloam, and you can still wade through it. In 1880 a boy found an inscription near its end, in which the tunnellers describe how two teams, cutting from each end, heard each other's picks and broke through. The Siloam inscription, in the Hebrew script of about 700 BC, is now in Istanbul.

commentary.on: to stop the waters of the springs which were outside of the city
commentary.text: The purpose matches the Bible: to deny water to the besiegers and bring it inside the walls. Archaeologists debate whether every part of the tunnel was Hezekiah's work, but the inscription's script and the city's expansion at this time fit his reign.

parts.title: Five rulers in one sentence
parts.context: Luke dates the start of John the Baptist's preaching the way ancient historians dated events: by who was ruling. In two verses he names an emperor, a governor, three local rulers and two high priests.

commentary.on: the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar
commentary.text: Tiberius succeeded Augustus in AD 14, so his fifteenth year is about AD 28–29. Luke is anchoring his story in Roman time.

commentary.on: Pontius Pilate being governor of Judea
commentary.text: Until 1961, Pilate was known only from the Gospels, Josephus, Philo and Tacitus. That year, Italian archaeologists at Caesarea found a limestone block reused in a theatre, inscribed with the words 'Pontius Pilatus, prefect of Judaea', from a building he dedicated to Tiberius.

commentary.on: Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene
commentary.text: Critics once accused Luke of a blunder here, because the best-known Lysanias was killed in 36 BC. But an inscription from Abila in Syria, from the reign of Tiberius, mentions 'Lysanias the tetrarch', showing there was a later ruler of that name, as Luke says.

commentary.on: in the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas
commentary.text: Caiaphas was high priest from about AD 18 to 36; Annas, his father-in-law, had been deposed but kept great influence. In 1990 workers building a park in Jerusalem broke into a family tomb holding an ornate bone box inscribed 'Joseph son of Caiaphas'. Many scholars think it held the high priest's bones.

parts.title: A pool with five porches
parts.context: From John's Gospel, written in the 90s AD, after the Romans had destroyed Jerusalem in AD 70. The writer describes a pool by the Sheep Gate.

commentary.on: there is a pool, which is called in Hebrew, “Bethesda”, having five porches
commentary.text: A pool with five porches seemed an odd shape, and some critics took John's details as symbolic rather than real. Excavations near the Church of St Anne, from the late nineteenth century onwards, uncovered two large pools separated by a central wall, with colonnades on four sides and one across the middle: five porches. John knew Jerusalem as it was before the Romans destroyed it.

commentary.on: for an angel went down at certain times into the pool and stirred up the water
commentary.text: You met this in the last session. This verse is missing from the oldest manuscripts of John, and most modern translations put it in a footnote; the World English Bible keeps it. It was probably a copyist's note explaining verse 7 that slipped into the text. Scholars know about it precisely because there are so many manuscripts to compare.

commentary.on: Arise, take up your mat, and walk
commentary.text: Archaeology can confirm that the pool existed, with its porches, where John says. It cannot confirm that a paralysed man walked. That is the limit of what it can do, and the lecture will say more.

parts.title: Paul before Gallio
parts.context: From the Acts of the Apostles, Luke's second volume. Paul has spent eighteen months in Corinth when he is hauled before the Roman governor.

commentary.on: when Gallio was proconsul of Achaia
commentary.text: Lucius Junius Gallio was the elder brother of the philosopher Seneca. Fragments of a letter from the Emperor Claudius, carved in stone at Delphi and published in 1905, name Gallio as proconsul and can be dated to AD 52. Proconsuls usually served a single year, so Paul's trial falls around AD 51–52. This inscription is the fixed point from which the whole chronology of Paul's life is calculated.

commentary.on: if they are questions about words and names and your own law, look to it yourselves
commentary.text: Gallio speaks exactly as a Roman governor would: Rome did not judge disputes about Jewish religion. The scene has the feel of first-hand knowledge of how Roman provinces worked.

commentary.on: Gallio didn't care about any of these things
commentary.text: Luke's portrait of a bored, aloof aristocrat fits what we know of Gallio from his brother's writings. Small touches like this are why many classical historians, not only Christians, have rated Acts highly as a source for the Roman world.

read.ref: 2 Kings 18:13–17; 2 Kings 20:20; 2 Chronicles 32:2–4; 2 Chronicles 32:30; Luke 3:1–2; John 5:1–9; Acts 18:12–17

paras: Such indeed were the precautions of human wisdom. The next thing was to seek means of propitiating the gods, and recourse was had to the Sibylline books, by the direction of which prayers were offered to Vulcanus, Ceres, and Proserpina. Juno, too, was entreated by the matrons, first, in the Capitol, then on the nearest part of the coast, whence water was procured to sprinkle the fane and image of the goddess. And there were sacred banquets and nightly vigils celebrated by married women. But all human efforts, all the lavish gifts of the emperor, and the propitiations of the gods, did not banish the sinister belief that the conflagration was the result of an order. Consequently, to get rid of the report, Nero fastened the guilt and inflicted the most exquisite tortures on a class hated for their abominations, called Christians by the populace. Christus, from whom the name had its origin, suffered the extreme penalty during the reign of Tiberius at the hands of one of our procurators, Pontius Pilatus, and a most mischievous superstition, thus checked for the moment, again broke out not only in Judæa, the first source of the evil, but even in Rome, where all things hideous and shameful from every part of the world find their centre and become popular. Accordingly, an arrest was first made of all who pleaded guilty; then, upon their information, an immense multitude was convicted, not so much of the crime of firing the city, as of hatred against mankind. Mockery of every sort was added to their deaths. Covered with the skins of beasts, they were torn by dogs and perished, or were nailed to crosses, or were doomed to the flames and burnt, to serve as a nightly illumination, when daylight had expired.

Nero offered his gardens for the spectacle, and was exhibiting a show in the circus, while he mingled with the people in the dress of a charioteer or stood aloft on a car. Hence, even for criminals who deserved extreme and exemplary punishment, there arose a feeling of compassion; for it was not, as it seemed, for the public good, but to glut one man's cruelty, that they were being destroyed.

3. Now there was about this time Jesus, a wise man, if it be lawful to call him a man; for he was a doer of wonderful works, a teacher of such men as receive the truth with pleasure. He drew over to him both many of the Jews and many of the Gentiles. He was [the] Christ. And when Pilate, at the suggestion of the principal men amongst us, had condemned him to the cross, those that loved him at the first did not forsake him; for he appeared to them alive again the third day; as the divine prophets had foretold these and ten thousand other wonderful things concerning him. And the tribe of Christians, so named from him, are not extinct at this day.

Festus was now dead, and Albinus was but upon the road; so he assembled the sanhedrim of judges, and brought before them the brother of Jesus, who was called Christ, whose name was James, and some others, [or, some of his companions]; and when he had formed an accusation against them as breakers of the law, he delivered them to be stoned

parts.title: Nero blames the Christians
parts.context: Cornelius Tacitus (about 56–120), senator and consul, was the greatest Roman historian. He wrote the Annals around 116. Here he describes the great fire of Rome in AD 64 and how Nero, rumoured to have started it, shifted the blame.
parts.author: Tacitus
parts.translator: Alfred John Church and William Jackson Brodribb (1876)

commentary.on: a class hated for their abominations, called Christians by the populace
commentary.text: Tacitus has no sympathy for the Christians at all. That is what makes his testimony valuable: a hostile witness has no reason to invent the founder of a movement he despises.

commentary.on: Christus, from whom the name had its origin, suffered the extreme penalty during the reign of Tiberius at the hands of one of our procurators, Pontius Pilatus
commentary.text: In one sentence a Roman senator confirms the founder's title (Christus), the manner of his death (the 'extreme penalty' meant crucifixion), the emperor (Tiberius) and the governor (Pilate), all as the Gospels say. Tacitus probably drew on Roman records or common knowledge among officials; he does not seem to be repeating Christian sources. (He calls Pilate 'procurator', the title of his own day; the Caesarea stone shows Pilate was officially 'prefect'.)

commentary.on: again broke out not only in Judæa, the first source of the evil, but even in Rome
commentary.text: The movement began in Judaea, was 'checked' by the execution, and then spread to Rome within about thirty years. That is the same outline as the book of Acts.

commentary.on: an immense multitude was convicted
commentary.text: By AD 64 there were enough Christians in Rome to be called an 'immense multitude', and they died rather than deny their faith. Christian tradition places the deaths of Peter and Paul in Rome in these years.

parts.plain: Tacitus says: after the great fire of Rome in AD 64, people blamed the Emperor Nero. To shift the blame, Nero accused the Christians, a group people already disliked. Their name comes from Christus, who was executed by the governor Pontius Pilate when Tiberius was emperor. The movement started in Judea and spread to Rome. Nero had a huge number of them killed in cruel ways, so cruel that people began to feel sorry for them.

parts.ref: Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews XVIII.3.3
parts.title: The famous passage about Jesus
parts.context: Josephus, whom you met in session 2, wrote his great history of the Jewish people, the Antiquities, in Rome around 93–94. In the middle of his account of Pilate's governorship comes this paragraph, the most debated passage in ancient history.
parts.author: Flavius Josephus

commentary.on: if it be lawful to call him a man
commentary.text: Read this paragraph carefully, because it has been tampered with. Josephus was a Jew who did not become a Christian, so he would not have written 'He was [the] Christ' or that Jesus rose 'as the divine prophets had foretold'. Almost all scholars think Christian copyists added these phrases.

commentary.on: a wise man
commentary.text: But most scholars, Jewish, Christian and secular, think a shorter original lies underneath: a neutral note that Jesus was a wise man and a doer of 'wonderful works', who won followers, was condemned to the cross by Pilate at the instigation of Jewish leaders, and whose followers, the Christians, still existed. A tenth-century Arabic version quoted by the Christian historian Agapius gives something close to that shorter form.

commentary.on: the tribe of Christians, so named from him, are not extinct at this day
commentary.text: The tone of this closing line sounds like Josephus, not a Christian: a little surprised that the movement had survived. Notice how textual criticism, comparing manuscripts and styles, lets us separate the original from the additions, the same method used on the Bible itself.

parts.plain: Josephus says: around this time lived Jesus, a wise man who did remarkable deeds and taught many people, Jews and non-Jews. When Pilate had him crucified, after leading Jews accused him, his followers did not abandon him, and the Christians, named after him, still exist. (Some phrases, such as 'He was [the] Christ', were almost certainly added later by Christian copyists; the commentary explains.)

parts.ref: Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews XX.9.1
parts.title: The brother of Jesus
parts.context: Later in the Antiquities, Josephus describes how in AD 62, between two Roman governors, the high priest Ananus took the chance to execute some of his enemies.
parts.author: Flavius Josephus

commentary.on: the brother of Jesus, who was called Christ, whose name was James
commentary.text: This passage is almost universally accepted as genuine. It is a passing remark, not a Christian phrase, and it identifies James by his famous brother. It is the same James whom Paul met in Jerusalem (session 3).

commentary.on: he delivered them to be stoned
commentary.text: Josephus tells us James died for his faith around AD 62, killed by the high priest. A man who had not believed in his brother during his lifetime died as a leader of his brother's followers. Christians have long asked what could explain that change; the creed in 1 Corinthians 15 gives their answer.

parts.plain: Josephus says: in AD 62, while there was no Roman governor in Judea, the high priest Ananus put on trial 'the brother of Jesus, who was called Christ, whose name was James', with some others, and had them stoned to death.

compare.author: Tacitus and Flavius Josephus
compare.work: A Roman and a Jew on Jesus
compare.translator: Alfred John Church and William Jackson Brodribb (1876)
compare.why: Two historians who were not Christians and had no reason to flatter them. Tacitus, a Roman senator, despised the Christians; Josephus, a Jewish priest, did not follow Jesus. What they say, and how they say it, is some of the most important evidence we have.
compare.title: A Roman and a Jew on Jesus

sections.h: What archaeology can and cannot do
paras: Archaeology tests a text's setting: whether its people, places, customs and events fit what we can dig up. A writer who invents a story far away and long afterwards usually gets the setting wrong. A writer close to the events usually gets it right.

But archaeology has limits. Most of what happened in the ancient world left no trace. Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence, though it can count when we would expect to find something. And archaeology can never confirm a miracle or prove that God spoke. It can tell us whether the Bible's world is real, not whether its theology is true.
sections.key: Archaeology can test the Bible's setting, never its miracles or its theology.

paras: For the Old Testament, the evidence grows stronger as we move forward in time. From the ninth century BC onwards, kings of Israel and Judah appear in the records of their neighbours, and Hebrew inscriptions begin to survive. The table lists the most important finds.

rows: The earliest mention of 'Israel' outside the Bible, as a people in Canaan
King Mesha of Moab tells of his revolt against Israel and names Omri, king of Israel, and Yahweh
An Aramaean king boasts of killing kings of Israel and of the 'House of David': the first mention of David outside the Bible
The tunnellers' own record of Hezekiah's water tunnel
Sennacherib's prisms and the Lachish reliefs
Assyria's account of the invasion of Judah, the siege of Lachish and Hezekiah's tribute
Two tiny rolled amulets inscribed with the priestly blessing: the oldest surviving words of the Bible
Oil rations for 'Jehoiachin, king of Judah' and his sons in exile
Cyrus's policy of returning displaced peoples and restoring their sanctuaries (it does not name the Jews)

sections.key: From the ninth century BC, Israel's kings appear in their neighbours' records, and finds repeatedly fit the Bible's account.

paras: For the New Testament, the setting is very well attested. The table lists finds that touch the people and places named in the Gospels and Acts. None proves the faith; all show that the writers knew the world they described.

rows: Pontius Pilate, 'prefect of Judaea', in a dedication to Tiberius
A bone box inscribed 'Joseph son of Caiaphas', probably the high priest's family tomb
A 'Lysanias the tetrarch' in Tiberius's reign, as Luke says
Twin pools with colonnades, the 'five porches'
The large stepped pool of Jesus' day
Gallio proconsul of Achaia in AD 51–52, dating Paul in Corinth
A paving stone laid by an Erastus, a city official; possibly the man Paul names
A fishing boat of the first century, of the kind the disciples used

sections.key: The people, places and officials of the Gospels and Acts are repeatedly confirmed by finds.

sections.h: Roman and Jewish witnesses to Jesus
paras: Several writers who were not Christians mention Jesus or his followers within a century of his death. Tacitus (about 116) and Josephus (about 93), whom you have just read, are the most important. Pliny the Younger, governor of Bithynia, wrote to the Emperor Trajan around 112 that Christians met before dawn to sing 'a hymn to Christ as to a god'. Suetonius (about 121) says the Emperor Claudius expelled Jews from Rome because of disturbances 'at the instigation of Chrestus', probably a garbled reference to Christ; Acts 18:2 mentions the same expulsion. The Syrian Stoic Mara bar Serapion, after AD 73, speaks of the Jews killing their 'wise king'.

None of these adds much detail, and none was written by an eyewitness. But they are independent, some are hostile, and together they confirm the outline: a Jewish teacher called Christ, executed under Pilate in Tiberius' reign, whose followers spread rapidly and worshipped him. That is why almost no professional historian, believer or not, doubts that Jesus existed and was crucified.
sections.key: Tacitus, Josephus, Pliny and others independently confirm that Jesus lived, was executed under Pilate and was soon worshipped.

sections.h: Where the evidence is silent or against
paras: Honesty requires the other side. The further back the Bible goes, the thinner the outside evidence. There is no direct archaeological trace of the Hebrew slaves in Egypt or of a great Exodus through Sinai, and Egyptian records do not mention it. Excavations at Jericho in the 1950s by Kathleen Kenyon found no walls standing at the time most scholars date Joshua's conquest, and the same is true of Ai; others dispute her dating. The patriarchs, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, cannot be tested at all.

In the New Testament, Luke's census under Quirinius (Luke 2:2) is a known puzzle: Quirinius' census in Judaea was in AD 6, but Jesus was born before Herod died in 4 BC. Scholars have proposed solutions, none universally accepted. Archaeologists also argue fiercely about how large the kingdom of David and Solomon was. These are real difficulties, and a thinking person should know them.
sections.key: The Exodus, the conquest and the patriarchs lack outside confirmation, and some puzzles remain, such as the census of Quirinius.

paras: A pattern emerges. Where the Bible describes events from the ninth century BC onwards, outside evidence often confirms its kings, wars and places, sometimes in remarkable detail. For earlier periods, the evidence is largely silent, and scholars divide over how to read that silence. For the New Testament, the setting is confirmed again and again, and hostile outside writers confirm the core facts about Jesus.

This does not prove the Bible's theological claims, and nothing could. But it does rule out one popular view: that the Bible is a collection of tales invented long after, by people who did not know the world they wrote about. On the whole, its writers knew their world. Whether their witness to God is true is the question no spade can answer.
sections.key: The Bible's writers generally knew their world; the further back, the thinner the outside evidence.

Pilate Stone (Israel Museum); Caiaphas ossuary (Israel Museum); Gallio inscription: Jerome Murphy-O'Connor, St. Paul's Corinth (3rd ed. 2002); Pool of Siloam: Ronny Reich and Eli Shukron (2004).

On the Testimonium: John P. Meier, A Marginal Jew, vol. 1 (1991), ch. 3; Shlomo Pines, An Arabic Version of the Testimonium Flavianum (1971).
