debate.question: How far does archaeology support the Bible?

positions.name: Broadly reliable
positions.who: Kenneth Kitchen and others
positions.view: Where it can be tested, the Bible's history is repeatedly confirmed; where evidence is lacking, that is what we should expect for small, mobile peoples, and it is no reason to doubt the text.
positions.evidence: The finds from the ninth century onwards; Egyptian and Near Eastern parallels to earlier periods.

positions.name: Late and largely invented
positions.who: Thomas L. Thompson, Niels Peter Lemche (the 'minimalists')
positions.view: The Old Testament was written mostly in the Persian or Hellenistic period, and its stories of early Israel tell us about the writers' own time, not about the past.
positions.evidence: The lack of evidence for the patriarchs, Exodus and conquest; the late date of many manuscripts.

positions.name: A historical core, later shaping
positions.who: William Dever, Israel Finkelstein and many others
positions.view: The Bible preserves genuine memories, especially from the monarchy onwards, shaped by later writers with religious aims. Each story must be weighed on its evidence.
positions.evidence: Strong confirmation for the later kings; weaker or contrary evidence for earlier periods.

debate.agree: All agree that from the ninth century BC the Bible names real kings and events attested elsewhere, and that archaeology cannot settle questions of faith.

look.why: Giorgio Vasari, painter and the first great historian of art, painted Luke around 1570: the evangelist who presents himself as a careful researcher, shown at work. The bull beside him is Luke's traditional symbol.
points: A bearded man in profile, hunched over a tablet propped on his raised knee, drawing with a feather quill.
He holds an inkwell and steadies the tablet with the same hand.
A grey bull lies at his feet, looking away to our right.
In the top left corner, a glimpse of a picture of a woman holding a baby.

music.why: An African American spiritual that asks the listener the eyewitness question directly: 'Were you there when they crucified my Lord?'

think.why: What almost all historians, Christian or not, agree about Jesus.

learn.why: Luke's own statement of method: research, order, and the certainty it is meant to give.

listen.why: Two historians discuss what can be known about Jesus from the sources, Christian and otherwise.

check.q: Why does Tacitus's mention of Christ carry particular weight with historians?
options: He was a Christian bishop
He was a hostile Roman senator with no reason to invent the founder of a movement he despised
He met Jesus personally
He quotes the Gospel of Mark
check.why: Hostile witnesses who confirm a fact are especially valuable.

check.q: What is the scholarly consensus on Josephus's passage about Jesus in Antiquities XVIII?
options: It is entirely genuine
It is an entirely Christian forgery
Christian copyists added phrases, but a shorter original by Josephus probably lies underneath
It was written by Tacitus
check.why: The second passage, on James 'the brother of Jesus', is almost universally accepted.

check.q: Which of these is the strongest outside evidence for the Bible's account of Hezekiah?
options: The Cyrus Cylinder
Sennacherib's own prism, which records his siege of Judah, Hezekiah shut up in Jerusalem and thirty talents of gold
The Merneptah Stele
The Galilee boat
check.why: Two enemies' records of the same events, agreeing on the tribute in gold.

check.q: Which statement about archaeology and the Exodus is fair?
options: Archaeology has proved the Exodus happened exactly as described
There is no direct archaeological or Egyptian evidence for it; scholars divide over how to read that silence
Archaeology has proved there was never an Israel
The Merneptah Stele describes the Exodus
check.why: Absence of evidence counts most where evidence would be expected; how much to expect here is the debate.

check.q: The Gallio inscription at Delphi matters chiefly because:
options: It mentions Jesus
It dates Gallio's year as proconsul to about AD 51–52, giving a fixed point for Paul's life
It proves the resurrection
It was written by Paul
check.why: Acts 18:12 puts Paul before Gallio; the inscription anchors the whole chronology of Paul.

check.q: What can archaeology never do?
options: Confirm the names of kings
Show that a writer knew the places he described
Confirm that a miracle happened or that God spoke
Date an inscription
check.why: It tests the setting, not the theology.

tutorial.question: 'You can't trust the Bible: it's just a book vouching for itself.' How far does evidence from outside the Bible answer this?
tutorial.approach: Explain what archaeology can and cannot do. Give three Old Testament and three New Testament finds and what they show. Use Tacitus and Josephus. Then give the strongest counter-evidence honestly (the Exodus, Jericho, Quirinius). Conclude with what outside evidence establishes and what it cannot.
strong: Explains the limits of archaeology (setting, not theology; absence of evidence).
Uses specific finds accurately, with dates (e.g. Tel Dan, Siloam, Sennacherib, Pilate Stone, Gallio).
Uses Tacitus and Josephus, noting the interpolation in Josephus.
Faces the counter-evidence fairly: the Exodus, Jericho, Quirinius.
Identifies the pattern: stronger evidence for later periods and for the New Testament setting.
Concludes proportionately, neither 'archaeology proves the Bible' nor 'archaeology disproves it'.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: visit a museum with objects from the biblical world, or look up one of the finds in this session in a museum's online collection (the British Museum's Lachish reliefs, the Israel Museum's Pilate Stone), and show it to someone.
sessions.reflect: What kind of evidence would you need before you trusted an ancient book? Is it the same kind you use for trusting people today?
takeaways: From the ninth century BC, Israel's kings appear in outside records, and many places and people in the Gospels and Acts are confirmed by finds.
Tacitus and Josephus, neither of them Christian, confirm that Jesus lived and was executed under Pilate, and that his followers spread.
The Exodus, the conquest and the patriarchs lack outside confirmation; archaeology tests the setting, never the miracles.
sessions.finding: Outside evidence often backs up the Bible's people and places, especially from about 850 BC onwards and in the New Testament; some early stories have no outside support.

paras: Four checks so far: what the Bible is, where both Testaments came from, and whether it has been copied faithfully. All of the evidence so far has come from the Bible itself and the people who kept it. Now we look outside: at what has been dug up, and at what non-Christian writers said.
background.key: Today's check: does anything outside the Bible back it up?

background.h: Two empires and a small kingdom
paras: The first two passages in this session take us back to about 700 BC. Judah, the southern kingdom with Jerusalem as its capital, was small and caught between great powers. The most terrifying was Assyria, centred on Nineveh in modern northern Iraq, whose armies had already destroyed the northern kingdom of Israel in 722 BC.

In 701 BC the Assyrian king Sennacherib invaded Judah. King Hezekiah of Judah prepared Jerusalem for a siege. This is one of the best documented moments in the whole Old Testament, because the Assyrians recorded it too.
background.key: In 701 BC Assyria invaded Judah; both sides left records.

paras: The other three passages come from the New Testament, set in the Roman Empire of the first century AD. Judea was governed by a Roman prefect, Pontius Pilate from AD 26 to 36, alongside local rulers and the Jewish high priests in Jerusalem. Greece, where Paul preached in the city of Corinth, was the Roman province of Achaia, governed by a proconsul.
These names, rulers, places and titles are exactly the kind of details a writer far away or long afterwards would tend to get wrong.
background.key: The New Testament names Roman and Jewish officials whose existence and titles can be checked.

paras: So far in this journey every witness has been inside the Bible. A sceptic will rightly say that a book cannot vouch for itself. So this session chooses passages that make specific claims that can be checked against evidence no Christian controlled: inscriptions, buildings, royal records and the writings of Roman and Jewish historians.

Read each passage and its commentary, which tells you what has been found. Then, in the comparison, you will read two ancient historians, one Roman and one Jewish, neither of them Christian, on Jesus and his followers.
background.key: We test the Bible against evidence that no Christian controlled.

sessions.title: The sceptic's case
sessions.line: Spinoza's argument that Moses did not write the books of Moses, and the modern case against the Bible, at full strength.
sessions.plain: In 1670 the philosopher Baruch Spinoza argued that the books traditionally ascribed to Moses were written centuries later, and that the Bible must be studied like any other old book. Modern biblical criticism grew from arguments like his. This session lets the sceptic speak first and fully, before any reply.
sessions.why: Four checks have mostly gone the Bible's way, with honest gaps. Now we hear the strongest case against the traditional view, in the words of the man who started the modern critical study of the Bible, and then in its modern form.
answers: Did Moses write the first five books of the Bible?
Where did modern biblical criticism come from?
What is the strongest modern case against trusting the Bible?
What does that case prove, and what does it not?
before: What evidence does Spinoza give that Moses did not write the Pentateuch?
Whom does Spinoza credit with first noticing the problem?
Which of his arguments do you find strongest, and which weakest?
sessions.readWhy: This is the founding text of the modern case that the Bible's books were not written by the people tradition names. Spinoza argues carefully, from the text itself, and openly builds on a medieval Jewish scholar. It deserves to be read in full rather than in summary.

paras: (1) In the former chapter we treated of the foundations and principles of Scriptural knowledge, and showed that it consists solely in a trustworthy history of the sacred writings; such a history, in spite of its indispensability, the ancients neglected, or at any rate, whatever they may have written or handed down has perished in the lapse of time, consequently the groundwork for such an investigation is to a great extent, cut from under us. (2) This might be put up with if succeeding generations had confined themselves within the limits of truth, and had handed down conscientiously what few particulars they had received or discovered without any additions from their own brains: as it is, the history of the Bible is not so much imperfect as untrustworthy: the foundations are not only too scanty for building upon, but are also unsound. (3) It is part of my purpose to remedy these defects, and to remove common theological prejudices. (4) But I fear that I am attempting my task too late, for men have arrived at the pitch of not suffering contradiction, but defending obstinately whatever they have adopted under the name of religion. (5) So widely have these prejudices taken possession of men's minds, that very few, comparatively speaking, will listen to reason. (6) However, I will make the attempt, and spare no efforts, for there is no positive reason for despairing of success.

(7) In order to treat the subject methodically, I will begin with the received opinions concerning the true authors of the sacred books, and in the first place, speak of the author of the Pentateuch, who is almost universally supposed to have been Moses. (8) The Pharisees are so firmly convinced of his identity, that they account as a heretic anyone who differs from them on the subject. (9) Wherefore, Aben Ezra, a man of enlightened intelligence, and no small learning, who was the first, so far as I know, to treat of this opinion, dared not express his meaning openly, but confined himself to dark hints which I shall not scruple to elucidate, thus throwing, full light on the subject.

(10) The words of Aben Ezra which occur in his commentary on Deuteronomy are as follows: "Beyond Jordan, &c . . . If so be that thou understandest the mystery of the twelve . . . moreover Moses wrote the law . . . The Canaanite was then in the land . . . . it shall be revealed on the mount of God . . . . then also behold his bed, his iron bed, then shalt thou know the truth." (11) In these few words he hints, and also shows that it was not Moses who wrote the Pentateuch, but someone who lived long after him, and further, that the book which Moses wrote was something different from any now extant.
(12) To prove this, I say, he draws attention to the facts:
(13) 1. That the preface to Deuteronomy could not have been written by Moses, inasmuch as he ad never crossed the Jordan.

(14) II. That the whole book of Moses was written at full length on the circumference of a single altar (Deut. xxvii, and Josh. viii:37), which altar, according to the Rabbis, consisted of only twelve stones: therefore the book of Moses must have been of far less extent than the Pentateuch. (15) This is what our author means, I think, by the mystery of the twelve, unless he is referring to the twelve curses contained in the chapter of Deuteronomy above cited, which he thought could not have been contained in the law, because Moses bade the Levites read them after the recital of the law, and so bind the people to its observance. (16) Or again, he may have had in his mind the last chapter of Deuteronomy which treats of the death of Moses, and which contains twelve verses. (17) But there is no need to dwell further on these and similar conjectures.

(18) III. That in Deut. xxxi:9, the expression occurs, "and Moses wrote the law:" words that cannot be ascribed to Moses, but must be those of some other writer narrating the deeds and writings of Moses.

(19) IV. That in Genesis xii:6, the historian, after narrating that Abraham journeyed through the and of Canaan, adds, "and the Canaanite was then in the land," thus clearly excluding the time at which he wrote. (20) So that this passage must have been written after the death of Moses, when the Canaanites had been driven out, and no longer possessed the land.

(21) Aben Ezra, in his commentary on the passage, alludes to the difficulty as follows:- "And the Canaanite was then in the land: it appears that Canaan, the grandson of Noah, took from another the land which bears his name; if this be not the true meaning, there lurks some mystery in the passage, and let him who understands it keep silence." (22) That is, if Canaan invaded those regions, the sense will be, the Canaanite was then in the land, in contradistinction to the time when it had been held by another: but if, as follows from Gen. chap. x. Canaan was the first to inhabit the land, the text must mean to exclude the time present, that is the time at which it was written; therefore it cannot be the work of Moses, in whose time the Canaanites still possessed those territories: this is the mystery concerning which silence is recommended.

(23) V. That in Genesis xxii:14 Mount Moriah is called the mount of God, a name which it did not acquire till after the building of the Temple; the choice of the mountain was not made in the time of Moses, for Moses does not point out any spot as chosen by God; on the contrary, he foretells that God will at some future time choose a spot to which this name will be given.

(24) VI. Lastly, that in Deut. chap. iii., in the passage relating to Og, king of Bashan, these words are inserted: "For only Og king of Bashan remained of the remnant of giants: behold, his bedstead was a bedstead of iron: is it not in Rabbath of the children of Ammon? nine cubits was the length thereof, and four cubits the breadth of it, after the cubit of a man." (25) This parenthesis most plainly shows that its writer lived long after Moses; for this mode of speaking is only employed by one treating of things long past, and pointing to relics for the sake of gaining credence: moreover, this bed was almost certainly first discovered by David, who conquered the city of Rabbath (2 Sam. xii:30.) (26) Again, the historian a little further on inserts after the words of Moses, "Jair, the son of Manasseh, took all the country of Argob unto the coasts of Geshuri and Maachathi; and called them after his own name, Bashan-havoth-jair, unto this day." (27) This passage, I say, is inserted to explain the words of Moses which precede it. (28) "And the rest of Gilead, and all Bashan, being the kingdom of Og, gave I unto the half tribe of Manasseh; all the region of Argob, with all Bashan, which is called the land of the giants." (29) The Hebrews in the time of the writer indisputably knew what territories belonged to the tribe of Judah, but did not know them under the name of the jurisdiction of Argob, or the land of the giants. (30) Therefore the writer is compelled to explain what these places were which were anciently so styled, and at the same time to point out why they were at the time of his writing known by the name of Jair, who was of the tribe of Manasseh, not of Judah.

(31) We have thus made clear the meaning of Aben Ezra and also the passages of the Pentateuch which he cites in proof of his contention. (32) However, Aben Ezra does not call attention to every instance, or even the chief ones; there remain many of greater importance, which may be cited. (33) Namely (I.), that the writer of the books in question not only speaks of Moses in the third person, but also bears witness to many details concerning him; for instance, "Moses talked with God;" "The Lord spoke with Moses face to face;" "Moses was the meekest of men" (Numb. xii:3); "Moses was wrath with the captains of the host; "Moses, the man of God, "Moses, the servant of the Lord, died;" "There was never a prophet in Israel like unto Moses," &c. (34) On the other hand, in Deuteronomy, where the law which Moses had expounded to the people and written is set forth, Moses speaks and declares what he has done in the first person: "God spake with me" (Deut. ii:1, 17, &c.), "I prayed to the Lord," &c. (35) Except at the end of the book, when the historian, after relating the words of Moses, begins again to speak in the third person, and to tell how Moses handed over the law which he had expounded to the people in writing, again admonishing them, and further, how Moses ended his life. (36) All these details, the manner of narration, the testimony, and the context of the whole story lead to the plain conclusion that these books were written by another, and not by Moses in person.

(37) III. We must also remark that the history relates not only the manner of Moses' death and burial, and the thirty days' mourning of the Hebrews, but further compares him with all the prophets who came after him, and states that he surpassed them all. (38) "There was never a prophet in Israel like unto Moses, whom the Lord knew face to face." (39) Such testimony cannot have been given of Moses by, himself, nor by any who immediately succeeded him, but it must come from someone who lived centuries afterwards, especially, as the historian speaks of past times. (40) "There was never a prophet," &c. (41) And of the place of burial, "No one knows it to this day."

(42) III. We must note that some places are not styled by the names they bore during Moses' lifetime, but by others which they obtained subsequently. (43) For instance, Abraham is said to have pursued his enemies even unto Dan, a name not bestowed on the city till long after the death of Joshua (Gen. xiv:14, Judges xviii:29).

(101) The historian whom we already know to be but one individual brings his history down to the liberation of Jehoiakim, and adds that he himself sat at the king's table all his life - that is, at the table either of Jehoiakim, or of the son of Nebuchadnezzar, for the sense of the passage is ambiguous: hence it follows that he did not live before the time of Ezra. (102) But Scripture does not testify of any except of Ezra (Ezra vii:10), that he "prepared his heart to seek the law of the Lord, and to set it forth, and further that he was a ready scribe in the law of Moses." (103) Therefore, I can not find anyone, save Ezra, to whom to attribute the sacred books.

(104) Further, from this testimony concerning Ezra, we see that he prepared his heart, not only to seek the law of the Lord, but also to set it forth; and, in Nehemiah viii:8, we read that "they read in the book of the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading."

parts.title: Why he writes
parts.context: Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677), a Dutch Jewish philosopher expelled from Amsterdam's synagogue at 23, published his Theologico-Political Treatise anonymously in 1670. In the previous chapter he argued that the Bible must be interpreted from its own history and language, as one studies nature. Here he begins to apply that method.
parts.author: Baruch Spinoza

commentary.on: a trustworthy history of the sacred writings
commentary.text: This is Spinoza's key idea. To understand a text you must know who wrote it, when, for whom and in what language. Today this sounds obvious; in 1670 it was revolutionary to apply it to the Bible.

commentary.on: the history of the Bible is not so much imperfect as untrustworthy
commentary.text: Spinoza is not only saying information is lost. He is saying the traditions about who wrote the Bible are positively unreliable, because later generations added their own guesses.

commentary.on: men have arrived at the pitch of not suffering contradiction
commentary.text: He expects to be attacked, and he was. Notice the tone: he presents himself as reason against prejudice. Whether or not he is right about the Bible, this stance, follow the evidence wherever it leads, became one of the founding attitudes of the modern West.

parts.plain: Spinoza says: to understand the Bible we need to know its history: who wrote each book, and when. But that history has been lost, and what people believe about it is unreliable. I will try to put this right, though people hate being contradicted about religion.

parts.title: A medieval rabbi's hints
parts.context: Spinoza turns to the Pentateuch, the five books traditionally ascribed to Moses, and to the clues left by Abraham ibn Ezra (about 1089–1167), the great Spanish Jewish commentator.
parts.author: Baruch Spinoza

commentary.on: Aben Ezra, a man of enlightened intelligence, and no small learning
commentary.text: Ibn Ezra noticed problems five hundred years before Spinoza but, Spinoza says, dared only to hint at them. The point matters: the difficulties were not invented by modern sceptics. Careful believing readers saw them first.

commentary.on: If so be that thou understandest the mystery of the twelve
commentary.text: Ibn Ezra's cryptic phrases, quoted from his commentary on Deuteronomy. Spinoza is about to decode them one by one.

commentary.on: it was not Moses who wrote the Pentateuch, but someone who lived long after him
commentary.text: Spinoza's thesis, stated plainly. Notice that he also says Moses did write something, 'the book which Moses wrote was something different from any now extant'. He is not claiming Moses never existed.

parts.plain: Spinoza says: almost everyone thinks Moses wrote the first five books of the Bible. But a famous medieval rabbi, Ibn Ezra, dropped hints that he didn't, and was afraid to say so openly. I will explain his hints.

parts.title: Five clues
parts.context: Spinoza sets out the clues one by one. Keep a Bible beside you if you can, or simply follow the argument.
parts.author: Baruch Spinoza

commentary.on: the preface to Deuteronomy could not have been written by Moses, inasmuch as he ad never crossed the Jordan
commentary.text: Deuteronomy opens by saying Moses spoke 'beyond the Jordan', that is, east of it. That phrase only makes sense for someone writing west of the Jordan, in the land Moses never entered. (The 'ad' is a misprint for 'had' in the Gutenberg text; we have kept it as printed.)

commentary.on: and Moses wrote the law
commentary.text: Deuteronomy 31:9 describes Moses writing, in the third person. Spinoza says this is someone narrating what Moses did.

commentary.on: and the Canaanite was then in the land
commentary.text: Genesis 12:6. The word 'then' implies that, when the writer lived, the Canaanites were no longer in the land, which would place him after the conquest under Joshua, after Moses' death. This is perhaps his strongest single clue.

commentary.on: Mount Moriah is called the mount of God
commentary.text: Genesis 22:14 refers to the mountain where the Temple was later built, centuries after Moses. Defenders reply that a place can be named prophetically or that a later editor updated a name.

commentary.on: let him who understands it keep silence
commentary.text: Ibn Ezra's caution, as Spinoza reads it, was fear of being called a heretic. That is a reminder that free inquiry was dangerous for Jews and Christians alike in the Middle Ages.

parts.plain: Spinoza lists clues. Deuteronomy describes Moses as speaking 'beyond the Jordan', as if written from the other side of the river, where Moses never went. It says 'Moses wrote the law', as if someone else were describing him. Genesis says 'the Canaanite was then in the land', as if they had gone by the writer's day. And a mountain is called by a name it only got centuries later.

parts.title: The iron bed, and Moses in the third person
parts.context: Spinoza's sixth clue, then his own additions, which he regards as decisive.
parts.author: Baruch Spinoza

commentary.on: his bedstead was a bedstead of iron: is it not in Rabbath of the children of Ammon?
commentary.text: Deuteronomy 3:11 points readers to a relic they can go and see, the giant king's bed, as something from the distant past. Spinoza says only a writer living long after Moses would talk like this.

commentary.on: unto this day
commentary.text: A phrase that appears often in the Pentateuch. Each time, it implies a gap between the events and the time of writing.

commentary.on: Moses was the meekest of men
commentary.text: Numbers 12:3. Spinoza's point: would the humblest man on earth write that about himself? Defenders reply that a later editor could add such a note to a book substantially by Moses; critics reply that the notes are too many and too woven in.

commentary.on: these books were written by another, and not by Moses in person
commentary.text: His conclusion from the way the books speak of Moses: in the third person, with praise and with details he could not record of himself.

parts.plain: Spinoza says: the text points to a giant king's iron bed as an old relic you can still go and see, and keeps saying things are so 'unto this day'. It speaks of Moses as 'he', and praises him as the humblest of men. All this, he argues, shows someone else wrote these books, long after Moses.

parts.title: The death of Moses, and later names
parts.context: Spinoza adds two more arguments: the account of Moses' death, and place names that came into use only later.
parts.author: Baruch Spinoza

commentary.on: There was never a prophet in Israel like unto Moses
commentary.text: Deuteronomy 34:10. This compares Moses with 'all the prophets who came after him', which, as Spinoza says, implies a writer looking back over centuries. You will read the chapter itself in the comparison.

commentary.on: No one knows it to this day
commentary.text: Moses' grave is unknown 'to this day' (Deuteronomy 34:6). Even the ancient rabbis agreed Moses could not have written the account of his own death; a Talmudic tradition says Joshua wrote the last eight verses.

commentary.on: Abraham is said to have pursued his enemies even unto Dan, a name not bestowed on the city till long after the death of Joshua
commentary.text: Genesis 14:14 calls a city Dan, but Judges 18:29 says it was renamed Dan much later. An anachronism like this is the kind of evidence historians use to date documents of every kind.

parts.plain: Spinoza says: the books describe Moses' death and burial, say that no prophet since has been like him, and use place names, like Dan, that came into use long after his death.

parts.title: His candidate: Ezra
parts.context: After arguing that the books from Genesis to Kings are the work of one historian, Spinoza names a candidate. (The cut marked '…' skips his discussion of the other historical books.)
parts.author: Baruch Spinoza

commentary.on: anyone, save Ezra, to whom to attribute the sacred books
commentary.text: Spinoza thinks Ezra, the scribe you met reading the Law in session 2, compiled these books from older sources after the exile.

commentary.on: gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading
commentary.text: He quotes Nehemiah 8:8, the very passage you read in session 2, as evidence that Ezra expounded and edited the Law. The same verse that showed a people reverently hearing the Law is, for Spinoza, a clue that the Law was being shaped. Hold both readings in mind.

parts.plain: Spinoza says: one historian seems to have put all these books together, and the best candidate is Ezra, the scribe who read and explained the Law to the people.

read.author: Baruch Spinoza
read.who: Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677), a Dutch Jewish philosopher expelled from Amsterdam's synagogue at 23, published his Theologico-Political Treatise anonymously in 1670.

paras: Moses went up from the plains of Moab to Mount Nebo, to the top of Pisgah, that is opposite Jericho. Yahweh showed him all the land of Gilead to Dan,
and all Naphtali, and the land of Ephraim and Manasseh, and all the land of Judah, to the Western Sea,
and the south, and the Plain of the valley of Jericho the city of palm trees, to Zoar.

Yahweh said to him, “This is the land which I swore to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, saying, ‘I will give it to your offspring.’ I have caused you to see it with your eyes, but you shall not go over there.”
So Moses the servant of Yahweh died there in the land of Moab, according to Yahweh’s word.
He buried him in the valley in the land of Moab opposite Beth Peor, but no man knows where his tomb is to this day.
Moses was one hundred twenty years old when he died. His eye was not dim, nor his strength gone.
The children of Israel wept for Moses in the plains of Moab thirty days, until the days of weeping in the mourning for Moses were ended.
Joshua the son of Nun was full of the spirit of wisdom, for Moses had laid his hands on him. The children of Israel listened to him, and did as Yahweh commanded Moses.
Since then, there has not arisen a prophet in Israel like Moses, whom Yahweh knew face to face,
in all the signs and the wonders which Yahweh sent him to do in the land of Egypt, to Pharaoh, and to all his servants, and to all his land,
and in all the mighty hand, and in all the awesome deeds, which Moses did in the sight of all Israel.
Abram passed through the land to the place of Shechem, to the oak of Moreh. At that time, Canaanites were in the land.
These are the kings who reigned in the land of Edom, before any king reigned over the children of Israel.

parts.title: The death of Moses
parts.context: The last chapter of the five books of Moses.

commentary.on: no man knows where his tomb is to this day
commentary.text: 'To this day' looks back from a later time. Almost every reader, ancient and modern, agrees that at least this chapter was written after Moses.

commentary.on: Since then, there has not arisen a prophet in Israel like Moses
commentary.text: Written, it seems, after many prophets had come and gone. The question is not whether this chapter is later, which nearly everyone accepts, but how much of the rest is.

parts.title: At that time, Canaanites were in the land
parts.context: Abraham's arrival in Canaan, centuries before Moses. Spinoza's older translation reads 'the Canaanite was then in the land'.

commentary.on: At that time, Canaanites were in the land
commentary.text: Read it slowly. 'At that time' does seem to assume a later reader for whom the Canaanites were gone. Defenders of Moses' authorship suggest a later editor's note; critics say the explanation is simpler if the whole was written later.

parts.title: Before any king reigned over Israel
parts.context: A list of the kings of Edom, Israel's neighbour.

commentary.on: before any king reigned over the children of Israel
commentary.text: This phrase seems to presuppose that Israel already had kings, which it did not until Saul, around 1000 BC, long after Moses. Spinoza uses it later in the same chapter.

compare.why: Three short passages that Spinoza cites. Read them and judge for yourself how strong his clues are.
compare.title: Test his evidence yourself

paras: Spinoza was born in Amsterdam in 1632 to a family of Portuguese Jews who had fled the Inquisition. In 1656, aged 23, he was expelled from the synagogue with an unusually harsh curse, for opinions we can only partly reconstruct. He earned a modest living grinding lenses and wrote philosophy that scandalised Jews and Christians alike.

The Theologico-Political Treatise, published anonymously in 1670 with a false place of printing, argued for freedom of thought and for reading the Bible as a historical document. It was banned in Holland in 1674. It is now seen as a founding text of modern biblical criticism, and of the liberal idea of free speech: its title page promises to show that 'freedom of philosophising' does no harm to religion or the state.
sections.key: Spinoza's treatise of 1670 was banned and reviled, and became a founding text of both biblical criticism and free speech.

paras: Spinoza did not invent his evidence. Some of it had been noticed for centuries. The Talmud discusses who wrote the last eight verses of Deuteronomy. Abraham ibn Ezra in the twelfth century hinted at the problems. In Spinoza's own century Thomas Hobbes in Leviathan (1651) and the French Protestant Isaac La Peyrère made similar points.

What was new in Spinoza was his principle: the Bible should be read with the same methods as any other ancient text, by asking who wrote it, when, for whom and in what language, without assuming in advance that it is divine. This is historical criticism.
sections.key: Spinoza's evidence was partly old; his new principle was to read the Bible like any other book.

paras: In the following two centuries scholars developed Spinoza's insight. They noticed that the Pentateuch seems to combine sources: different names for God (Yahweh in some passages, Elohim in others), doublets (two accounts of creation in Genesis 1 and 2, two versions of the flood woven together), and different styles and concerns.

In 1878 the German scholar Julius Wellhausen gave this its classic form, the documentary hypothesis: four sources, called J (Yahwist), E (Elohist), D (Deuteronomist) and P (Priestly), written between the tenth and fifth centuries BC and combined after the exile. For a century this was the standard view in universities.
sections.key: Wellhausen's theory of four sources, J, E, D and P, was the standard view for a century.

paras: The critical method was soon applied to everything. Hermann Samuel Reimarus, published after his death (1774–78), argued that Jesus was a failed political messiah and the disciples invented the resurrection. David Friedrich Strauss's Life of Jesus (1835) treated the Gospel miracles as myth; George Eliot translated it in 1846. Today Bart Ehrman argues that several New Testament letters were written by others in the apostles' names (Forged, 2011).

Put at its strongest, the modern case runs like this. The Bible's books were written, edited and re-edited by many anonymous hands, often long after the events. Some carry false names. They contradict each other in details. For the earliest periods archaeology is silent or against them. Their writers had religious purposes. And the miracles they report are just what legend produces. So whatever its value, the Bible cannot be trusted as a record of what God did and said.
sections.key: At its strongest, the sceptic's case says the Bible is late, edited, partly pseudonymous, contradictory and legendary.

paras: Scholars who defend earlier origins or substantial reliability point to other evidence. The covenant form of Deuteronomy has parallels with ancient Near Eastern treaties. Egyptian names and details appear in the Joseph and Exodus stories. Ancient authors often wrote of themselves in the third person; Julius Caesar did so throughout his account of the Gallic war. And Wellhausen's four-document theory has itself broken down in its classic form: scholars now disagree widely about how the Pentateuch was composed.

On the New Testament, writing in someone's name (pseudonymity) is debated: some think it was an accepted practice in a teacher's school, others that the early Church rejected known forgeries. The traditional authorship of most of Paul's letters, and of the core of the Gospel tradition, is widely accepted.
sections.key: Defenders point to ancient treaty forms, Egyptian detail, third-person writing, and the collapse of the classic four-source theory.

paras: This is a serious case, and it should be faced rather than waved away. Several of its points are now accepted by many believing scholars: that the Pentateuch contains material from after Moses' time, that its books were edited over centuries, and that the Gospel writers shaped their material.

But it does not follow that the books are untrustworthy. Ancient histories were routinely compiled from sources; that does not make them fiction. Session 4 showed how often the Bible's setting is confirmed. And the sceptic's assumption that miracles cannot happen is a philosophical claim, not a historical finding: no study of manuscripts can settle it, which is why Hall IV takes it up. Spinoza showed that the Bible must be read honestly. The last session asks how a believer can read it so.
sections.key: Some of the case is now widely accepted; its conclusion that the Bible is untrustworthy does not follow from it.

debate.question: Who wrote the Torah?

positions.name: Moses
positions.who: Traditional Jewish and Christian teaching
positions.view: Moses wrote the five books, apart from a few later notes such as the account of his death, as Jesus and the New Testament assume.
positions.evidence: The books' own statements that Moses wrote (Exodus 24:4, Deuteronomy 31:9); the unanimous ancient tradition.

positions.name: Four documents
positions.who: Julius Wellhausen and the classical critics
positions.view: The Pentateuch combines four sources (J, E, D, P) written over five centuries and joined after the exile; Moses wrote none of it.
positions.evidence: Different divine names, doublets and styles; later place names and perspectives.

positions.name: A long growth
positions.who: Most scholars today, believing and not
positions.view: The Pentateuch grew over centuries from older traditions, perhaps around an ancient core linked to Moses, and reached its final form in or after the exile. The details are hotly debated.
positions.evidence: The breakdown of the four-source theory; comparisons with other ancient Near Eastern texts.

debate.agree: All agree that the Pentateuch contains some material from after Moses and that it was edited over time; they disagree on how much, when and by whom.

look.why: Painted in Rembrandt's workshop in Amsterdam around 1653, possibly by his pupil Willem Drost, in the same city and decade in which the young Spinoza was expelled from the synagogue. It shows not a scholar at his books but a man thinking.
points: A gaunt man with a trimmed brown beard and a large, soft brown beret.
His hands are folded at the bottom of the picture; he leans over them.
His head turns to our left; his deep-set eyes look away, as if at a thought.
A robe banded with rust red and gold, and a heavy gold chain across his chest.

music.why: Brahms chose his own texts from Luther's Bible for this Requiem, leaving out the creeds and even the name of Christ: an honest, searching reading of Scripture by a man unsure what he believed.

think.why: Underneath the argument about the Bible lies the argument about God. This depth sets out the strongest cases on both sides.

listen.why: Bart Ehrman, the best-known sceptical scholar of the New Testament, explains his case. Listen for what he accepts as well as what he rejects.

check.q: Which of Spinoza's clues is strongest against Moses writing the whole Pentateuch?
options: That Moses could not write
Passages such as 'the Canaanite was then in the land' and 'to this day', which look back from a later time
That the Pentateuch is in Greek
That Moses never existed
check.why: Spinoza never denies Moses existed or wrote something; his clues are later perspectives in the text.

check.q: What was genuinely new in Spinoza's approach?
options: Noticing that Moses' death is described in Deuteronomy
The principle that the Bible should be studied with the same historical methods as any other book
Translating the Bible into Dutch
Denying that the Bible was ever read in synagogues
check.why: The Talmud and ibn Ezra had noticed some problems; the method was Spinoza's contribution.

check.q: Which of these is a philosophical assumption rather than a historical finding?
options: That ancient writers used sources
That the Pentateuch was edited over time
That miracles cannot happen
That Deuteronomy 34 was written after Moses' death
check.why: No study of texts can settle whether miracles are possible.

check.q: What is the state of Wellhausen's documentary hypothesis today?
options: Universally accepted in its 1878 form
Its classic four-source form has broken down; scholars agree on growth over time but disagree widely on how
Disproved by the Dead Sea Scrolls
Never taken seriously
check.why: Many now speak of fragments, supplements or a long process of editing.

check.q: Spinoza cites Nehemiah 8:8 ('gave the sense') as evidence. For what?
options: That Ezra was illiterate
That Ezra expounded and, he thinks, compiled and edited the books
That Nehemiah wrote Genesis
That the people could not understand Hebrew
check.why: The same verse can be read as reverent explanation or as a clue to editing.

tutorial.question: Does the critical case against the traditional authorship of the Bible show that it cannot be trusted?
tutorial.approach: First state Spinoza's evidence fully and fairly. Then show how his method developed into the documentary hypothesis and the modern sceptic's case. Then separate the questions: who wrote the books, how they were composed, whether they are historically reliable, and whether they are true. Say which points are now widely accepted and which conclusions do not follow.
strong: States Spinoza's evidence accurately (third person, death of Moses, 'then', 'to this day', later names).
Notes his debt to ibn Ezra and the Talmud.
Explains historical criticism, the documentary hypothesis and its later breakdown.
States the modern case at full strength, including pseudonymity and archaeology.
Separates authorship, composition, reliability and truth.
Identifies the philosophical assumptions in the strongest sceptical case.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: find someone who doubts the Bible and ask them why, then listen without arguing until you could state their case so well that they would agree with your summary.
sessions.reflect: Which part of the sceptic's case unsettled you most? What would you need to know to answer it?
takeaways: Spinoza argued from the text that Moses did not write the Pentateuch, and that the Bible must be studied like any other book.
His method led to historical criticism, the documentary hypothesis and the modern sceptic's case.
Some of the case is widely accepted; that the Bible cannot be trusted does not follow from it.
sessions.finding: The sceptic's best case is serious: the books were written and edited over time by many hands. But that does not make them untrustworthy, and its strongest step rests on an assumption, not evidence.

paras: The first five books of the Bible, Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers and Deuteronomy, are called the Torah (Hebrew for 'teaching' or 'law') or the Pentateuch (Greek for 'five scrolls'). They run from the creation of the world to the death of Moses, just before the Israelites enter the promised land. Jewish and Christian tradition held for two thousand years that Moses himself wrote them.
This session examines the most famous challenge to that tradition, and through it the whole modern critical approach to the Bible.
background.key: Tradition held that Moses wrote the first five books; this session tests that belief.

paras: Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677) was born in Amsterdam to a family of Portuguese Jews who had fled persecution. Amsterdam was then the freest city in Europe, a refuge for religious minorities and a centre of printing. At 23 Spinoza was expelled from his synagogue for his opinions. He lived quietly, grinding lenses for a living, and became one of the great philosophers of the modern age.

Europe in his lifetime had just been through decades of wars between Catholics and Protestants. Spinoza believed that if people read the Bible as a historical book, they would stop killing each other over it. In 1670 he published his argument anonymously.
background.key: Spinoza wrote in the freest city in Europe, after decades of religious war, to argue for freedom of thought.

paras: Every journey on Rose Window includes the strongest objection at full strength, before any reply. For the Bible, the strongest objection is that its books were not written by the people tradition names, were edited long after the events, and must be read like any other ancient book. Spinoza's treatise is where that case was first made openly and in detail, and he makes it from the text itself.
You will read his chapter in six short passages, each with a commentary. Then you can test three of his key verses yourself in the comparison.
background.key: Spinoza's chapter is the founding statement of the case against the traditional view, made from the text itself.

sessions.title: The verdict, and how to read it
sessions.line: So, can I trust it? And how should I read it?
sessions.plain: If the Bible was written by many people over centuries and handed down through fallible copies, how should a thinking person read it? Augustine, who knew its difficulties well, argued that a text may hold more than one true meaning and that the test of a good reading is love. The road to Emmaus shows the Christian key to the whole library.
sessions.why: We have weighed the evidence and heard the sceptic. The last question is practical: not only whether the Bible can be trusted, but how to read it so that trust is honest.
answers: So, can a thinking person trust the Bible?
How should it be read today?
Does a passage have one meaning or many?
What, for Christians, is the key to the whole Bible?
before: What does Augustine say when someone insists, 'Moses meant what I say'?
What rule does Augustine give for deciding between readings?
In Luke 24, what makes the two disciples' hearts burn?
sessions.readWhy: At the end of the Confessions Augustine argues with readers who insist that only their interpretation of Genesis is right. His answer is a short masterpiece on interpretation: humble about our grasp of an author's mind, confident that truth is shared, and governed by love.

paras: But which of us shall, among those so many truths, which occur to enquirers in those words, as they are differently understood, so discover that one meaning, as to affirm, "this Moses thought," and "this would he have understood in that history"; with the same confidence as he would, "this is true," whether Moses thought this or that? For behold, O my God, I Thy servant, who have in this book vowed a sacrifice of confession unto Thee, and pray, that by Thy mercy I may pay my vows unto Thee, can I, with the same confidence wherewith I affirm, that in Thy incommutable world Thou createdst all things visible and invisible, affirm also, that Moses meant no other than this, when he wrote, In the Beginning God made heaven and earth? No. Because I see not in his mind, that he thought of this when he wrote these things, as I do see it in Thy truth to be certain. For he might have his thoughts upon God's commencement of creating, when he said In the beginning; and by heaven and earth, in this place he might intend no formed and perfected nature whether spiritual or corporeal, but both of them inchoate and as yet formless. For I perceive, that whichsoever of the two had been said, it might have been truly said; but which of the two he thought of in these words, I do not so perceive. Although, whether it were either of these, or any sense beside (that I have not here mentioned), which this so great man saw in his mind, when he uttered these words, I doubt not but that he saw it truly, and expressed it aptly.

Let no man harass me then, by saying, Moses thought not as you say, but as I say: for if he should ask me, "How know you that Moses thought that which you infer out of his words?" I ought to take it in good part, and would answer perchance as I have above, or something more at large, if he were unyielding. But when he saith, "Moses meant not what you say, but what I say," yet denieth not that what each of us say, may both be true, O my God, life of the poor, in Whose bosom is no contradiction, pour down a softening dew into my heart, that I may patiently bear with such as say this to me, not because they have a divine Spirit, and have seen in the heart of Thy servant what they speak, but because they be proud; not knowing Moses' opinion, but loving their own, not because it is truth, but because it is theirs. Otherwise they would equally love another true opinion, as I love what they say, when they say true: not because it is theirs, but because it is true;

and on that very ground not theirs because it is true. But if they therefore love it, because it is true, then is it both theirs, and mine; as being in common to all lovers of truth. But whereas they contend that Moses did not mean what I say, but what they say, this I like not, love not: for though it were so, yet that their rashness belongs not to knowledge, but to overboldness, and not insight but vanity was its parent. And therefore, O Lord, are Thy judgements terrible; seeing Thy truth is neither mine, nor his, nor another's; but belonging to us all, whom Thou callest publicly to partake of it, warning us terribly, not to account it private to ourselves, lest we be deprived of it. For whosoever challenges that as proper to himself, which Thou propoundest to all to enjoy, and would have that his own which belongs to all, is driven from what is in common to his own; that is, from truth, to a lie. For he that speaketh a lie, speaketh it of his own.

Hearken, O God, Thou best judge; Truth Itself, hearken to what I shall say to this gainsayer, hearken, for before Thee do I speak, and before my brethren, who employ Thy law lawfully, to the end of charity: hearken and behold, if it please Thee, what I shall say to him. For this brotherly and peaceful word do I return unto Him: "If we both see that to be true that Thou sayest, and both see that to be true that I say, where, I pray Thee, do we see it? Neither I in thee, nor thou in me; but both in the unchangeable Truth itself, which is above our souls." Seeing then we strive not about the very light of the Lord God, why strive we about the thoughts of our neighbour which we cannot so see, as the unchangeable Truth is seen: for that, if Moses himself had appeared to us and said, "This I meant"; neither so should we see it, but should believe it. Let us not then be puffed up for one against another, above that which is written: let us love the Lord our God with all our heart, with all our soul, and with all our mind: and our neighbour as ourself. With a view to which two precepts of charity, unless we believe that Moses meant, whatsoever in those books he did mean, we shall make God a liar, imagining otherwise of our fellow servant's mind, than he hath taught us. Behold now, how foolish it is, in such abundance of most true meanings, as may be extracted out of those words, rashly to affirm, which of them Moses principally meant; and with pernicious contentions to offend charity itself, for whose sake he spake every thing, whose words we go about to expound.

parts.title: Can we know what Moses meant?
parts.context: The last books of the Confessions (about 397–400) are a meditation on the first verse of Genesis, 'In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth.' Augustine has set out several possible meanings and now asks whether anyone can be sure which one Moses intended. The whole book is addressed to God.
parts.author: Augustine of Hippo

commentary.on: this Moses thought
commentary.text: Augustine distinguishes two claims: 'this is true' and 'this is what Moses meant'. He thinks we can often be sure of the first and rarely of the second. That distinction is the beginning of humility in reading any text.

commentary.on: Because I see not in his mind
commentary.text: We cannot see into another person's mind, least of all one who lived long ago. Modern scholars say the same about 'authorial intention'. Augustine reached it in 400.

commentary.on: I doubt not but that he saw it truly, and expressed it aptly
commentary.text: But he is no sceptic. He trusts that Moses saw truly, even if we cannot be sure exactly what Moses saw. Trust in the author and humility about our interpretation go together.

parts.plain: Augustine says: the first verse of Genesis can be understood in several true ways. I can be sure what is true, but I can't see inside Moses' mind to know which meaning he intended, though I'm sure he meant something true.

parts.title: Not mine, not yours, but the truth's
parts.context: Augustine turns to readers who say, 'Moses meant what I say, not what you say.'
parts.author: Augustine of Hippo

commentary.on: not because it is truth, but because it is theirs
commentary.text: Augustine's diagnosis of quarrels over the Bible: people love their own interpretation because it is theirs, not because it is true. Anyone who has watched a religious argument, or an argument about anything, will recognise this.

commentary.on: as being in common to all lovers of truth
commentary.text: Truth belongs to no one. If a reading is true, it is yours and mine alike. This is one of the deepest ideas in Western thought about inquiry: truth is a common good, not private property.

commentary.on: For he that speaketh a lie, speaketh it of his own
commentary.text: An echo of John 8:44. The person who claims truth as his own possession has already turned it into a lie, because he has made it about himself.

parts.plain: Augustine says: people who insist 'Moses meant what I say, not what you say' are often proud. They love their opinion because it is theirs, not because it is true. But truth belongs to everyone who loves it, not to any one person.

parts.title: The rule of love
parts.context: Augustine ends the argument by appealing to the two great commandments.
parts.author: Augustine of Hippo

commentary.on: but both in the unchangeable Truth itself, which is above our souls
commentary.text: When two people both see that something is true, where do they see it? Not in each other's minds, says Augustine, but in the truth itself, which stands above both of them. That is why argument can be peaceful: both parties are looking at the same thing.

commentary.on: let us love the Lord our God with all our heart, with all our soul, and with all our mind: and our neighbour as ourself
commentary.text: Jesus' summary of the Law (Matthew 22:37–40). For Augustine this is the purpose of all Scripture. In another book, On Christian Doctrine, he says that anyone whose reading builds up this double love is not dangerously mistaken, even if he misses the author's exact meaning; and anyone whose reading does not build it up has not yet understood the Bible.

commentary.on: with pernicious contentions to offend charity itself, for whose sake he spake every thing
commentary.text: The final irony: to fight bitterly over what the Bible means is to defeat the very purpose for which it was written. A reading that leads to hatred is wrong, however clever or literal.

parts.plain: Augustine says: if we both see that something is true, we see it in the truth itself, not in each other's minds. So let us not quarrel. The whole point of the Bible is love of God and of our neighbour, and fighting over its meaning betrays that point.

read.author: Augustine of Hippo
read.who: The last books of the Confessions (about 397–400) are a meditation on the first verse of Genesis, 'In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth.

paras: Behold, two of them were going that very day to a village named Emmaus, which was sixty stadia from Jerusalem.
They talked with each other about all of these things which had happened.
While they talked and questioned together, Jesus himself came near, and went with them.
But their eyes were kept from recognizing him.
He said to them, “What are you talking about as you walk, and are sad?”
One of them, named Cleopas, answered him, “Are you the only stranger in Jerusalem who doesn’t know the things which have happened there in these days?”
He said to them, “What things?”
They said to him, “The things concerning Jesus, the Nazarene, who was a prophet mighty in deed and word before God and all the people;
and how the chief priests and our rulers delivered him up to be condemned to death, and crucified him.
But we were hoping that it was he who would redeem Israel. Yes, and besides all this, it is now the third day since these things happened.
Also, certain women of our company amazed us, having arrived early at the tomb;
and when they didn’t find his body, they came saying that they had also seen a vision of angels, who said that he was alive.
Some of us went to the tomb, and found it just like the women had said, but they didn’t see him.”
He said to them, “Foolish men, and slow of heart to believe in all that the prophets have spoken!
Didn’t the Christ have to suffer these things and to enter into his glory?”
Beginning from Moses and from all the prophets, he explained to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself.
They came near to the village where they were going, and he acted like he would go further.
They urged him, saying, “Stay with us, for it is almost evening, and the day is almost over.”
He went in to stay with them.
When he had sat down at the table with them, he took the bread and gave thanks. Breaking it, he gave it to them.
Their eyes were opened and they recognized him, then he vanished out of their sight.
They said to one another, “Weren’t our hearts burning within us, while he spoke to us along the way, and while he opened the Scriptures to us?”
They rose up that very hour, returned to Jerusalem, and found the eleven gathered together, and those who were with them,
saying, “The Lord is risen indeed, and has appeared to Simon!”
They related the things that happened along the way, and how he was recognized by them in the breaking of the bread.
He said to them, “This is what I told you, while I was still with you, that all things which are written in the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms, concerning me must be fulfilled.”
Then he opened their minds, that they might understand the Scriptures.

parts.title: A stranger on the road
parts.context: The evening of the first Easter Sunday. Two followers of Jesus, one named Cleopas, are walking from Jerusalem to Emmaus, a village about seven miles away, after the crucifixion.

commentary.on: But we were hoping that it was he who would redeem Israel
commentary.text: The saddest line in the Gospels. They had hoped Jesus would free Israel; his death ended their hope. They know the facts, even the report of the empty tomb, but cannot make sense of them.

commentary.on: Beginning from Moses and from all the prophets, he explained to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself
commentary.text: The stranger gives them a Bible study. The facts make sense only when they are read within the whole story of Scripture. This is how Christians have read the Old Testament ever since: as a long story leading to Christ.

parts.title: Recognised in the breaking of bread
parts.context: They reach the village at evening and invite the stranger in.

commentary.on: Their eyes were opened and they recognized him
commentary.text: They recognise him at a meal, as he breaks bread. Christians have always seen here the pattern of their worship: the Scriptures explained, then the bread broken.

commentary.on: Weren't our hearts burning within us, while he spoke to us along the way, and while he opened the Scriptures to us?
commentary.text: The verse you will learn by heart. Reading the Bible well, Luke suggests, is not only an intellectual exercise; it is an encounter. Even before they knew who he was, something in them responded.

parts.title: The law, the prophets and the psalms
parts.context: Later that night, Jesus appears to the gathered disciples in Jerusalem.

commentary.on: the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms
commentary.text: The three parts of the Hebrew Bible, named by their largest books, exactly as you met them in session 2. Jesus claims the whole collection points to him.

commentary.on: Then he opened their minds, that they might understand the Scriptures
commentary.text: Luke's last word on reading the Bible: understanding is a gift as well as an achievement. That is the believer's claim. A thinking person can test the evidence, as this journey has done; trusting the God it speaks of is a further step.

compare.why: The risen Jesus walks with two disciples and explains 'in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself'. This is the key with which Christians have read the whole library: the story finds its centre in Christ.
compare.title: The key on the road

paras: Put the six checks together. The Bible is a library, read for what each book is. Its Old Testament is genuinely ancient and its New Testament was written within living memory. Its text has been copied more faithfully, and is better attested, than any other ancient book. Outside evidence often confirms its people and places, though some early stories have none. And the strongest case against it shows that its books grew and were edited, not that they are untrustworthy.

So a thinking person can trust the Bible as a collection of ancient writings, close to what they describe and faithfully handed down. Whether to trust what it says about God is a different kind of question. History can show that the witnesses were in a position to know; it cannot make you believe them. That last step, as the two disciples found on the road to Emmaus, is taken another way.
sections.key: The Bible can be trusted as ancient, close and faithfully copied; trusting its God is a further step.

paras: You met Augustine in the first session, disappointed by the Bible's plain style. By the time he wrote these chapters, about twenty years later, he was a bishop who preached on the Scriptures several times a week and had spent years on the first chapters of Genesis alone.

He had come to think that the Bible's plainness was deliberate: it is 'lowly in access, in its recesses lofty', open to the simplest reader and deep enough for the cleverest. And he had come to think its difficulties are part of its purpose, because they make us search, and humble us.
sections.key: Augustine came to see the Bible's plainness as deliberate and its difficulties as part of its purpose.

paras: We cannot see into another person's mind, Augustine says, so we should be slow to claim we know exactly what Moses intended. But we can know whether a reading is true. If two readings are both true, why fight over which one Moses had in mind? Perhaps he meant both, or God, who inspired him, did.

This is not relativism. Augustine thinks some readings are false, and that truth is one. But he thinks a great text can hold more truth than any single reader can see, and that arrogance about interpretation is itself a failure to read rightly.
sections.key: We cannot see an author's mind, but we can ask whether a reading is true; a great text holds more than one truth.

paras: What, then, is the test? Augustine's answer, here and at length in On Christian Doctrine, is the double commandment: love of God and of neighbour. The whole of Scripture, he says, aims at this. Whoever reads it in a way that builds up love, even if he misses the author's meaning, is mistaken in a good direction, like a traveller who leaves the road but still reaches the destination; but he should be corrected, lest he get used to leaving the road.
It is a principle with consequences. A reading that leads to hatred of others is wrong, however literal.
sections.key: For Augustine a reading that does not build up love of God and neighbour has not yet understood the Bible.

paras: Christians developed a rich method from this. The early theologian Origen, and later the Middle Ages, spoke of four senses of Scripture: the literal (what happened, what the words say), the allegorical (what it shows about Christ and the Church), the moral (how we should live) and the anagogical (what it shows of our final hope). Jerusalem was the standard example: literally a city, allegorically the Church, morally the soul, anagogically heaven.

But the literal sense came first. Augustine warned in his Literal Meaning of Genesis that Christians who talk nonsense about the natural world, claiming the Bible's authority, bring the Scriptures into contempt among educated unbelievers. Thomas Aquinas held that all the other senses rest on the literal one.
sections.key: The four senses rest on the literal sense, which must not be twisted into nonsense.

paras: You saw in session 1 that the churches differ on the Bible's authority. They also differ in how they read it, though less than they once did.

Protestants, following Luther and Tyndale, stress the plain sense of the text and the right of every believer to read it, with preaching at the centre of worship. Catholics, following the Second Vatican Council's Dei Verbum (1965), read Scripture together with Tradition and the Church's teaching, and encourage both historical study and spiritual reading; since 1943 they have embraced modern scholarship. The Orthodox read the Bible above all in worship, through the Fathers and the liturgy, where most of the Psalter is sung every week. In practice all three now share much of the same scholarship, and many of the same translations.
sections.key: Protestants stress the plain sense and personal reading; Catholics, Scripture with Tradition; the Orthodox, Scripture in worship and the Fathers.

paras: For most Christians the Bible has never been mainly a private book. It is read aloud in worship, often in a lectionary, a pattern of readings that in many churches takes people through much of the Bible every few years. The psalms are sung. The Gospel is often carried in procession, and people stand to hear it, as the people stood for Ezra.

Reading this way teaches something that private study can miss: the Bible was written to be heard by a community, and much of it was first spoken. Paul's letters were read to whole churches. To hear it read well, in a quiet church, is still one of the best ways to meet it.
sections.key: The Bible was written to be heard, and most Christians still meet it read aloud in worship.

paras: So how can a thinking person read the Bible well? Some practical rules follow from this journey. Read each book for what it is. Read it whole, not in fragments. Learn what scholars know of its history and text, without fear; truth cannot contradict truth. Hear the sceptic out, and know which of his claims are evidence and which are assumptions. Read it with others, past and present. And read it, as Augustine did, with the double love he thought was its purpose.

Can you trust the Bible? You now know that its writers were close to the events, that outside evidence often confirms their world, that the text has reached us faithfully to a remarkable degree, that the hard questions are real, and that the Church's best readers knew them. Whether you trust the God it speaks of is a further step, which no history can take for you.
sections.key: Read by genre, read whole, learn the scholarship without fear, hear the sceptic, read with others and with love.

refs: Augustine, Confessions III.5 and XII.18–32; On Christian Doctrine I.35–36 (the rule of love; the traveller, I.36.41); The Literal Meaning of Genesis I.19.39.
Origen, On First Principles IV; the four senses with Jerusalem as example: John Cassian, Conferences XIV.8; Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I, q. 1, a. 10.
Pius XII, Divino Afflante Spiritu (1943); Dei Verbum (1965), §§12, 21–25.
Henri de Lubac, Medieval Exegesis (1959–64); John Barton, The Nature of Biblical Criticism (2007).

debate.question: How should the Bible be read?

positions.name: The plain sense
positions.who: The Reformers, and many Protestants since
positions.view: Scripture interprets Scripture, and its plain meaning is clear enough for any reader to grasp what is needed for salvation; it is the final authority.
positions.evidence: Luther's and Tyndale's insistence on the literal sense and on Bibles in the people's language.

positions.name: With the Church's tradition
positions.who: Catholic and Orthodox teaching
positions.view: The Bible was written, collected and recognised within the Church, and is best read within its living tradition, which keeps the spiritual senses alongside the literal.
positions.evidence: The canon itself was recognised by the Church; the Fathers' four senses; the liturgy.

positions.name: Historically first
positions.who: Modern historical critics
positions.view: The first task is to recover what each text meant in its own time, using every tool of history and language; later theological meanings must not be read back into it.
positions.evidence: The gains of textual and historical study since Spinoza.

debate.agree: All agree that the literal and historical sense matters and that the Bible should be read whole and with care. Most now accept that the three approaches can learn from one another.

look.why: An American painter of the 1720s shows the road itself: the moment before recognition, while the stranger is still explaining the Scriptures and the travellers' hearts are burning.

The central figure, long-haired and bearded, in a pink robe.

music.why: An old Irish prayer, put into English verse in the early twentieth century: a reader asking that the Word become the light he sees by.

think.why: Augustine's warning about Christians talking nonsense on nature is still the best starting point for faith and science.

learn.why: The disciples' words on the road to Emmaus: the experience Christians hope for when they read.

check.q: Augustine distinguishes 'this is true' from 'this is what Moses meant'. Why?
options: Because Moses was often wrong
Because we can often know whether a reading is true, but cannot see into the author's mind to be sure what he intended
Because only bishops can know what Moses meant
Because Genesis has no meaning
check.why: Humility about intention, confidence about truth: that is his principle.

check.q: What does Augustine say about a reader who misses the author's meaning but builds up love of God and neighbour?

He is mistaken in a good direction, like a traveller who leaves the road but reaches the destination, though he should be corrected
He has understood perfectly
He should stop reading

Because it brings the Scriptures into contempt among educated unbelievers and misreads what the Bible is for
Because science is forbidden

check.q: In Luke 24, why are the facts not enough for the two disciples?

They know the facts but cannot make sense of them until they are read within the whole story of Scripture

check.q: Which describes a real difference between how Catholics and Orthodox, on the one hand, and many Protestants, on the other, read the Bible?

Catholics and Orthodox read it within the Church's Tradition and worship; many Protestants stress its plain sense and every believer's right to interpret it
Protestants reject the literal sense
Only Protestants use the four senses

Then give your own rules for reading, using Augustine and Luke 24, and say what trust in the Bible can and cannot rest on.
