sections.key: For nearly three centuries Christians had no sacred buildings: the people themselves were the temple.

paras: The Temple Solomon built was destroyed by the Babylonians in 587 BC, rebuilt after the exile, magnificently enlarged by Herod the Great, and destroyed again by the Romans in AD 70. Jesus prayed in it and taught in its courts. After its fall, Jewish life gathered round the synagogue, the 'assembly', a place not of sacrifice but of reading, prayer and teaching, and Jews prayed facing the place where the Temple had stood.

The early Church inherited both. From the Temple it took the idea of a holy place and of sacrifice, now understood as Christ's once-for-all offering, remembered at the altar. From the synagogue it took the gathering to read Scripture, sing psalms and pray. A cathedral holds both inheritances in one building: the altar at the east end, the pulpit and the lectern in the nave. When you see them, you are seeing the Temple and the synagogue side by side.
sections.key: A church holds two inheritances side by side: the Temple's altar and the synagogue's reading and prayer.

sections.h: The basilica: borrowing Rome's public hall
paras: That changed with the Emperor Constantine, who ended the persecution in 313 and began to build churches on an imperial scale: the Lateran in Rome, and in the 320s and 330s the great church over the tomb of St Peter. Christians did not copy pagan temples, which were small houses for a god's statue, with the worship outside. They needed room for a crowd inside. So they borrowed the basilica, the Roman public hall used for law courts and business.

A basilica is a long rectangle: a tall central space, the nave, lit by windows high up, with lower aisles on either side behind rows of columns, and at the far end a rounded recess, the apse, where a magistrate once sat. In the Christian basilica the bishop sat there, with the altar in front of him. Almost every great church in Europe, including every Gothic cathedral, is a descendant of this plan. When you walk up a nave towards an altar, you are walking up a Roman hall of justice.
sections.key: Christians copied the Roman public hall, not the pagan temple, because they needed room for a crowd inside.

paras: Once Christians had buildings, they needed to say what they were. The answer they gave, again and again, came from the last book of the Bible: the church is an image of the heavenly Jerusalem, the city of God that comes down out of heaven in Revelation 21. When a church was consecrated, the service read that chapter, and from about the seventh century the hymn sung at a dedication began 'Urbs beata Ierusalem', 'Blessed city, heavenly Jerusalem'.

The other text read at a dedication was Jacob's cry when he woke from his dream of the ladder: 'How awesome this place is! This is none other than God's house, and this is the gate of heaven' (Genesis 28:17). Its Latin opens the chant for the anniversary of a church's dedication, 'Terribilis est locus iste', and a related chant, 'Locus iste', 'This place was made by God', is the text of the music in this session.

Notice what has happened. Paul said the people are the temple. The dedication rites keep that, but add something: the building is a sign of the people, and of the city they are travelling towards. It is a picture of heaven you can walk into.
sections.key: Once Christians had buildings, they explained them as pictures of the heavenly Jerusalem.

paras: Around the year 1000 Europe began building churches in stone on a scale not seen since Rome. A Burgundian monk, Rodulfus Glaber, writing around 1030, said it was as though the whole world were throwing off its old age and clothing itself in a white robe of churches. Historians call the style Romanesque, 'Roman-like', because it used the round arch and heavy masonry of Roman building.

Romanesque churches were often vast, built for monks and for pilgrims coming to see the relics of saints. But round arches and stone vaults are heavy. They push outwards as well as down, so the walls had to be thick and the windows small. The light inside a great Romanesque church is dim, solemn and beautiful, rather like the 'thick darkness' of Solomon's inner room.
That is where we will leave the story until the next session, when an abbot near Paris decided that a house of God should be full of light.
sections.key: Romanesque churches were massive and dim, because round stone arches need thick walls.

paras: Christians are not alone in setting places apart. The Greeks had the temenos, a piece of land 'cut off' for a god; many peoples have mountains, groves or springs that are holy. The historian of religion Mircea Eliade argued that human beings everywhere mark out a sacred centre, a place where heaven and earth are joined, and build their world around it. Jacob's 'gate of heaven' at Bethel is a perfect example.

What is distinctive in the Christian story is the movement you have seen in this session: from a holy place, to a holy people, and then back to holy places understood as signs of that people. Christianity never quite decided that buildings do not matter, and never quite decided that they do. The cathedrals are the most magnificent result of that indecision.
sections.key: All peoples set holy places apart; Christianity keeps moving between holy places and a holy people.

paras: By now you can see the question that runs through this journey. Is a church a house for God, a place made holy, where heaven touches earth? Or is it a house for God's people, a shelter for the real temple, which is the community? Or is it a sign, made of stone and glass, that points beyond itself?

Christians have given all three answers, sometimes in the same building. The medieval builders believed the first and the third. The Reformers, as we will see, often insisted on the second. Keep your own answer open. By the end of the journey you will have been inside a cathedral in every sense but the physical one, and you will be able to judge.
sections.key: Is a church a house for God, a shelter for God's people, or a sign pointing beyond itself? Keep the question open.

refs: 1 Kings 8; 2 Chronicles 5–7 (the parallel account).
1 Corinthians 3:9–17; John 4:21–24; Acts 7:48–50.
Dura-Europos house church: Carl H. Kraeling, The Christian Building (The Excavations at Dura-Europos, Final Report VIII.2, 1967); L. Michael White, Building God's House in the Roman World (1990).
Constantine's churches: Richard Krautheimer, Early Christian and Byzantine Architecture (1965; 4th ed. 1986).
The dedication hymn 'Urbs beata Ierusalem' and the chants 'Terribilis est locus iste' and 'Locus iste': the Roman rite for the dedication of a church.
Rodulfus Glaber, Histories III.13 (written about 1030).

debate.question: Is a church a house for God, or a house for God's people?

positions.name: A house for God
positions.who: The Catholic and Orthodox traditions; historians of religion such as Mircea Eliade
positions.view: Places really can be made holy. A consecrated church is set apart, like the Temple, a place where heaven and earth meet, and the building itself is an offering to God.
positions.evidence: Solomon's dedication, Jacob at Bethel, and rites of consecration that go back at least to the fourth century.

positions.name: A house for God's people
positions.who: Many of the Protestant Reformers; Paul, as they read him
positions.view: God does not live in buildings but in people. The church is the assembly (the Greek ekklesia), and a building is only a useful shelter for it. To treat stone as holy risks idolatry.
positions.evidence: Christians had no special buildings for nearly three centuries; 'the Most High doesn't dwell in temples made with hands' (Acts 7:48).

positions.name: A sign that points beyond itself
positions.who: Many medieval writers, and many theologians today
positions.view: The building is neither God's container nor a mere shelter. It is a sign, even a kind of sacrament: made of 'living stones', it shows what the people are meant to become, the city of God.
positions.evidence: The dedication rites, which read both Revelation 21 and the 'living stones' of 1 Peter 2:5.

debate.agree: All three agree that no building can contain God, and that a church without a living community is only a museum. They disagree about what stone and glass can add.

look.why: Peeter Neeffs spent his life in Antwerp painting the insides of great churches. This one shows a church in use: not a monument but a busy house of prayer, where the whole building leads the eye one way.
points: The long view down the nave to the altar in the distance: everything is arranged to lead your eye one way.
Light coming in through the arched windows on the left, falling in patches on the wall, the floor and the ceiling.
People doing different things at once: walking, sitting, kneeling at the smaller altars along the sides.
How small the people are against the columns and the vaults.

music.why: Bruckner wrote this short motet in 1869 for the dedication of a chapel in the new cathedral at Linz. Its Latin words come from the old rite for dedicating a church: 'This place was made by God, a priceless mystery, beyond reproach.'

think.why: John says the Word 'lived among us'; the Greek means he pitched his tent among us, the word used for the tabernacle. God's dwelling moves from a building to a person.

learn.why: A pilgrim's song about longing for God's house, and the best answer to the question whether a building can matter: 'a day in your courts is better than a thousand'.

check.q: In 1 Kings 8:27, what does Solomon say about the house he has built?
options: It is where God will live for ever
Even the heavens cannot contain God, so this house cannot either
It is a copy of God's house in heaven
It is for the king's use only
check.why: Solomon's prayer is the paradox at the heart of every church: the house is real and dedicated, yet it cannot hold God. It is a place to pray towards, where God promises to hear.

check.q: Where did most of the earliest Christians meet for worship?
options: In the Temple in Jerusalem
In purpose-built basilicas
In private houses
In Roman law courts
check.why: For nearly three centuries Christians met mainly in homes. The house church at Dura-Europos, adapted around AD 232, is the best surviving example.

check.q: What was a basilica before it became the model for churches?
options: A Greek temple
A Roman public hall for law courts and business
A Jewish synagogue
A monastery
check.why: Christians needed room for a crowd inside, so they borrowed the Roman public hall, not the temple, which was a small house for a god's statue.

check.q: What does Paul say is God's temple in 1 Corinthians 3?
options: The Temple in Jerusalem
The church building in Corinth
The believers themselves
The heavens
check.why: 'You are a temple of God.' Paul was writing to a church with no building at all.

tutorial.question: 'Heaven cannot contain you; how much less this house.' If that is true, why build churches at all?
tutorial.approach: Begin with the paradox in Solomon's prayer and his own answer to it. Set Paul's 'you are God's building' beside it. Then use one piece of history from the lecture, the house church, the basilica or the dedication rite, to show how Christians actually answered. End with your own view, and give a reason for it.
strong: States the paradox clearly: God is everywhere, yet people set places apart.
Uses Solomon's own answer: the house is a place to pray towards, where God promises to hear, not a container.
Brings in Paul: the people themselves are the temple.
Notes that Christians managed without special buildings for nearly three centuries.
Distinguishes a building as a dwelling for God from a building as a meeting place or a sign.
Reaches a view of its own and defends it against the strongest alternative.

reading.author: Simon Jenkins
reading.title: England's Cathedrals
reading.why: A lively tour of every English cathedral by a writer who loves them without claiming to believe.

reading.author: Mircea Eliade
reading.title: The Sacred and the Profane
reading.why: A historian of religion on why people everywhere set holy places apart.

reading.author: L. Michael White
reading.title: Building God's House in the Roman World
reading.why: How Christians and others moved from houses to buildings of their own.

reading.author: Richard Krautheimer
reading.title: Early Christian and Byzantine Architecture
reading.why: The classic account of how the first churches came to look as they do.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: go into a church on a weekday when nothing is happening, and if you can, take someone with you. Sit at the back for ten minutes and notice how the building is arranged: where it leads your eye, and where the light falls.
sessions.reflect: Is there anywhere you go that feels set apart, as if it asks something of you? What makes it so?
takeaways: Solomon's prayer holds the paradox: God cannot be contained, yet people set places apart to meet him.
The first Christians were the temple; when they built, they borrowed the Roman basilica.
Churches came to be explained as pictures of the heavenly Jerusalem.

sessions.title: The new light
sessions.line: An abbot near Paris rebuilds his church to be almost all window, and Gothic is born.
sessions.plain: In the 1140s Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis near Paris, rebuilt the east end of his church so that it was ringed with tall coloured windows. He believed light could lift the mind to God. Historians usually call this the birth of Gothic. This session asks what he was really doing.
sessions.why: Session 1 left us in the dim, thick-walled churches of the eleventh century, where God was met in solemn darkness. Now the darkness breaks. To see why, we read the chapter of the Bible that the builders of cathedrals had always in mind: the city made of light.
before: The city in Revelation has no sun and no temple. What does it have instead?
Count the precious stones and the kinds of light. Why might an abbot in love with coloured glass read this chapter again and again?
Notice who is inside the city and who is outside it.

paras: I saw a new heaven and a new earth: for the first heaven and the first earth have passed away, and the sea is no more.
I saw the holy city, New Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared like a bride adorned for her husband.
I heard a loud voice out of heaven saying, “Behold, God’s dwelling is with people, and he will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God.
He will wipe away every tear from their eyes. Death will be no more; neither will there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain, any more. The first things have passed away.”
He who sits on the throne said, “Behold, I am making all things new.” He said, “Write, for these words of God are faithful and true.”
He said to me, “I have become the Alpha and the Omega, the Beginning and the End. I will give freely to him who is thirsty from the spring of the water of life.
He who overcomes, I will give him these things. I will be his God, and he will be my son.

But for the cowardly, unbelieving, sinners, abominable, murderers, sexually immoral, sorcerers, idolaters, and all liars, their part is in the lake that burns with fire and sulfur, which is the second death.”
One of the seven angels who had the seven bowls, who were loaded with the seven last plagues came, and he spoke with me, saying, “Come here. I will show you the wife, the Lamb’s bride.”
He carried me away in the Spirit to a great and high mountain, and showed me the holy city, Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God,
having the glory of God. Her light was like a most precious stone, as if it were a jasper stone, clear as crystal;
having a great and high wall; having twelve gates, and at the gates twelve angels; and names written on them, which are the names of the twelve tribes of the children of Israel.
On the east were three gates; and on the north three gates; and on the south three gates; and on the west three gates.
The wall of the city had twelve foundations, and on them twelve names of the twelve Apostles of the Lamb.
He who spoke with me had for a measure a golden reed to measure the city, its gates, and its walls.
The city is square, and its length is as great as its width. He measured the city with the reed, twelve thousand twelve stadia. Its length, width, and height are equal.
Its wall is one hundred forty-four cubits, by the measure of a man, that is, of an angel.
The construction of its wall was jasper. The city was pure gold, like pure glass.
The foundations of the city’s wall were adorned with all kinds of precious stones. The first foundation was jasper; the second, sapphire; the third, chalcedony; the fourth, emerald;
the fifth, sardonyx; the sixth, sardius; the seventh, chrysolite; the eighth, beryl; the ninth, topaz; the tenth, chrysoprase; the eleventh, jacinth; and the twelfth, amethyst.
The twelve gates were twelve pearls. Each one of the gates was made of one pearl. The street of the city was pure gold, like transparent glass.
I saw no temple in it, for the Lord God, the Almighty, and the Lamb, are its temple.
The city has no need for the sun or moon to shine, for the very glory of God illuminated it, and its lamp is the Lamb.
The nations will walk in its light. The kings of the earth bring the glory and honor of the nations into it.
Its gates will in no way be shut by day (for there will be no night there),
and they shall bring the glory and the honor of the nations into it so that they may enter.
There will in no way enter into it anything profane, or one who causes an abomination or a lie, but only those who are written in the Lamb’s book of life.
He showed me a river of water of life, clear as crystal, proceeding out of the throne of God and of the Lamb,

in the middle of its street. On this side of the river and on that was the tree of life, bearing twelve kinds of fruits, yielding its fruit every month. The leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations.
There will be no curse any more. The throne of God and of the Lamb will be in it, and his servants will serve him.
They will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads.
There will be no night, and they need no lamp light or sun light; for the Lord God will illuminate them. They will reign forever and ever.

notes.text: 'The holy city, New Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven': the words that opened the reading at the dedication of a church.
Light like a precious stone, clear as crystal. Suger wrote that gazing on the gems of his altar carried his mind from material things to immaterial ones.
The twelve foundation stones echo the twelve stones on the breastplate of Israel's high priest (Exodus 28:17–21). Medieval writers wrote whole books on what each stone meant.
The surprise of the chapter: 'I saw no temple in it.' In the end there is no building, because God is present everywhere. The cathedral is a picture of a city that will not need one.
The light of the city is the glory of God, and its lamp is the Lamb, that is, Christ.

sessions.readWhy: This vision of the new Jerusalem was read at the dedication of churches, and every Gothic cathedral is in some sense an attempt to build it: a city of jewels and light coming down from heaven to earth.

paras: This is the message which we have heard from him and announce to you, that God is light, and in him is no darkness at all.
If we say that we have fellowship with him and walk in the darkness, we lie, and don’t tell the truth.
But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus Christ, his Son, cleanses us from all sin.
Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom can be no variation, nor turning shadow.
compare.why: Two short sayings that gave the Middle Ages its theology of light: 'God is light', and God is 'the Father of lights', the source from which every good gift comes down. The writer known as Dionysius opens his book on the heavenly hierarchy with the second of these.

paras: Suger was born around 1081 to a family of no importance and given as a boy to the abbey of Saint-Denis, a few miles north of Paris. There he was schooled alongside the future King Louis VI. He became abbot in 1122 and ruled the abbey until his death in January 1151, and he was one of the most powerful men in France: adviser to two kings and, while Louis VII was away on the Second Crusade (1147–1149), regent of the kingdom.

Saint-Denis was no ordinary abbey. It held the relics of St Denis, the first bishop of Paris and the patron saint of France, and it was the burial place of French kings. Its old church, from the eighth century, was too small for the crowds who came on feast days. Suger wrote that people were crushed in the doorways and that women had to be carried out over the heads of the men. He resolved to rebuild.
sections.key: Suger was a powerful abbot with a crowded, ancient church and the will to rebuild it.

paras: He began at the west end, with a new front of three great doorways, consecrated in 1140. Then he turned to the east end, the choir, where the altar and the relics were. Between 1140 and 1144 his masons built something new: a semicircle of slender columns, a double walkway around the altar (an ambulatory), and beyond it a ring of shallow chapels, each with two large windows of coloured glass. Because the chapels were so shallow, their windows seemed to join into one wall of light around the altar.

The new choir was consecrated on 11 June 1144, with the king and queen and about twenty archbishops and bishops present. Suger wrote two short books about the work, on his administration of the abbey and on the consecration, and in them he says what he wanted: that the whole church should shine with the wonderful, unbroken light of its brightest windows, flooding the beauty within.

Only part of Suger's choir survives (the upper parts were rebuilt in the thirteenth century), and only fragments of his glass. But visitors who walk round the ambulatory today still see his columns, his ribbed vaults and the shallow chapels with their windows.
sections.key: Between 1140 and 1144 Suger's masons built a choir whose walls seemed to turn into coloured light.

paras: Suger had verses carved and painted around his building, and they tell us how he thought. On the gilded doors of the west front he wrote, in Latin, that the noble work shines, and that its brightness should brighten minds so that they travel through true lights to the true light, where Christ is the true door. The most quoted line is short: the dull mind rises to truth through material things.

He also describes sitting in his church and looking at the jewels on the great altar cross. The beauty of the stones, he says, called him away from outward cares, and he seemed to find himself in some strange region of the universe, neither wholly in the mud of earth nor wholly in the purity of heaven, and to be carried from this lower world to the higher in an 'anagogical' way. 'Anagogical' means 'leading upward'. One of his windows at Saint-Denis, which still partly survives, is known as the Anagogical Window.

So for Suger, beauty is a ladder. Gold, gems and above all coloured light are not distractions from God; they are the way a slow human mind, which learns through the senses, is drawn upward towards him.
sections.key: For Suger, beauty and light were a ladder: the mind rises to God through material things.

sections.h: Denis, Dionysius and the light of God
paras: Here a strange story of mistaken identity matters. In Acts 17, when Paul preaches in Athens, one of the few who believe is 'Dionysius the Areopagite'. Around AD 500 an unknown Christian writer, probably a monk in Syria who had absorbed the Greek philosophy of Plato's later followers, wrote a series of books under that name. They describe a universe in which God's light pours down through ranks of angels and of the Church, and in which every created thing, rightly seen, is a light that leads back to its source.

In the ninth century the abbey of Saint-Denis came to identify three people as one: Paul's convert in Athens, the author of these mystical books, and their own St Denis, martyr and first bishop of Paris. The abbey owned a Greek manuscript of the writings, sent to the Frankish king in 827, and they were translated into Latin there and later by the Irish scholar John Scotus Eriugena. So the patron saint of Suger's abbey was, as Suger believed, the great teacher of the theology of light.

Whether Suger actually read and built from these books is the question in this session's debate. What is certain is that the identification of Denis with Dionysius gave his abbey, and him, a reason to think that light was holy.
sections.key: A case of mistaken identity linked Suger's abbey to a great Christian theology of light.

sections.h: How it was done: arches, ribs and buttresses
paras: None of the techniques at Saint-Denis was new on its own. Pointed arches had been used in Burgundy (they came originally from the Islamic world), and rib vaults in Normandy and England (Durham Cathedral has them from about 1100). What was new was combining them so that the walls could almost disappear.

A round arch can only be as high as half its width. A pointed arch can be made taller or narrower at will, and it pushes its weight more downwards and less outwards. A rib vault gathers the weight of the stone ceiling onto a few points, like the ribs of an umbrella onto its frame, so that between those points the wall no longer carries anything and can be opened up. And buttresses, piers of stone set against the outside wall, take the remaining outward push. A generation later, at Notre-Dame in Paris and elsewhere, builders began to throw these buttresses out as 'flying' arches over the side aisles, so that the upper walls too could become glass.
Put simply: the Gothic builders turned a church from a heavy box with holes in it into a stone skeleton with glass between the bones.
sections.key: Pointed arches, rib vaults and buttresses together turned the wall into a stone skeleton with glass between the bones.

paras: We know the patrons' names far better than the builders'. Gothic churches were built by master masons who learned their craft by apprenticeship, moved from site to site, and worked with carpenters, quarrymen, smiths and glaziers. They drew their designs full-size on plaster floors and boards, and passed on rules of geometry by which a whole building could be laid out with a cord and a set square.

Suger tells a story about one problem. His roof needed beams of great length, and his carpenters told him that no trees so tall could be found near Paris. One morning he went into the forest of Yveline himself with his foresters, who laughed at him, and by the end of the day had found the twelve great trees he needed. The story is told to show God's favour, but it also shows how much a cathedral depended on materials, labour and luck, and on a patron who would not give up.
sections.key: Cathedrals depended on skilled masons, materials, luck and a patron who would not give up.

paras: Imagine coming to Saint-Denis on a feast day in 1150, from a village of wooden houses lit by fires. You pass under the carved doors of the west front, through the dim older nave, and then, at the far end, the choir opens like a lantern: columns as thin as reeds, and beyond them a ring of windows glowing red and blue, with candles burning before the gilded shrines of the saints. Nothing in your life has looked like this.

That experience, more than any theory, is what made the new style spread. Bishops and abbots who saw Saint-Denis wanted the same for their own churches, and within a century the cathedrals of northern France had been rebuilt in the new way.
sections.key: The experience of walking into the new light, more than any theory, is what made Gothic spread.

sections.h: A word with a bad name
paras: Nobody at the time called it Gothic. Contemporaries called it 'the French work', opus francigenum. The word 'Gothic' was coined by Italian writers of the Renaissance as an insult: in their view this was the barbarous building of the Goths who had destroyed Rome, as opposed to the noble style of the ancients. Only in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, with the Gothic Revival, did the word become a compliment.

The style spread with astonishing speed: Sens, Noyon, Laon, Paris (Notre-Dame was begun in 1163), and to England, where a French mason, William of Sens, rebuilt the choir of Canterbury after a fire in 1174. In the next session we go to the most complete of all the Gothic cathedrals, built in the generation after Suger: Chartres.
sections.key: 'Gothic' began as an insult; the style spread across France and to England within a generation.

refs: Suger, De administratione (On What Was Done during His Administration) and De consecratione (On the Consecration), written about 1144–1149; Latin text and English translation in Erwin Panofsky, Abbot Suger on the Abbey Church of St.-Denis and Its Art Treasures (1946; 2nd ed. 1979).
Suger's door inscription ('Mens hebes ad verum per materialia surgit') and his account of the altar gems: De administratione XXVII and XXXIII.
The consecration of 11 June 1144: De consecratione.

Pseudo-Dionysius, The Celestial Hierarchy I.1 (opening with James 1:17); the Greek manuscript given to Louis the Pious in 827 (now Paris, BnF gr. 437); translations by Hilduin of Saint-Denis and John Scotus Eriugena.
Durham Cathedral rib vaults (begun 1093): Christopher Wilson, The Gothic Cathedral (1990).
'Opus francigenum': the chronicle of Burchard of Hall (about 1280), describing the church at Wimpfen; the Renaissance term in Giorgio Vasari, Lives (1550).
Canterbury: Gervase of Canterbury's account of the fire of 1174 and the rebuilding.

debate.question: Was Gothic light a theology, or mainly a feat of engineering and fashion?

positions.name: A theology in stone and glass
positions.who: Erwin Panofsky (1946); Otto von Simson, The Gothic Cathedral (1956)
positions.view: Suger, steeped in the writings of Dionysius that his abbey treasured, set out to build their vision: light pouring down from God, and the mind rising through light back to God. Gothic architecture is this theology made visible.
positions.evidence: Suger's verse inscriptions, his 'anagogical' language, and the identification of St Denis with Dionysius at that very abbey.

positions.name: Mostly not
positions.who: Peter Kidson, 'Panofsky, Suger and St Denis' (1987), and many architectural historians since
positions.view: Suger never quotes Dionysius directly, and his language about light is the common coin of medieval writing. The building's forms came from masons solving practical problems with techniques already in use. To read it as a treatise in stone is to project a modern scholar's ideas onto the past.
positions.evidence: The absence of direct quotation; the separate histories of the pointed arch and the rib vault.

positions.name: A defence against critics
positions.who: Conrad Rudolph, Artistic Change at St-Denis (1990)
positions.view: Suger did have a theory of art, but he developed it to defend costly art against reforming monks such as Bernard of Clairvaux. His writings, which come after the building, justify what he had done, drawing on Hugh of Saint-Victor and others.
positions.evidence: The defensive tone of Suger's books, written in the 1140s at the height of the controversy over monastic art.

debate.agree: All agree that Saint-Denis was a turning point, that Suger loved light, colour and precious things and wrote about them as few patrons did, and that the building made a new kind of church possible.

look.why: Antwerp's cathedral was built over the fourteenth to sixteenth centuries, the late flowering of the style that began at Saint-Denis. In Neeffs's painting you can see what all the engineering was for: height and light.
points: The tall, cream-coloured arches and the ribbed vaults: the stone skeleton of a Gothic building.
The tall windows, through which you can see light-blue sky.
Dark statues set high on the walls, and framed paintings above wooden pulpits with lit candles.
People in bright clothes crossing the black-and-white floor, or kneeling by the altars.

music.why: James MacMillan sets the ancient Advent antiphon 'O Oriens': 'O radiant dawn, splendour of eternal light'. It is the theology of this session in four minutes of music.

think.why: Gregory of Nyssa's 'light so bright it seems like darkness' and Suger's coloured light are two Christian ways of meeting God through what overwhelms the senses.

learn.why: 'The life was the light of men. The light shines in the darkness.' The lines behind every Christian building that reaches for light.

check.q: Which part of Saint-Denis did Suger rebuild between 1140 and 1144 to be filled with light?
options: The crypt
The east end, the choir
The bell tower
The cloister
check.why: The new choir, with its ring of shallow chapels and their windows, was consecrated on 11 June 1144.

check.q: Who was the author of the books of 'Dionysius the Areopagite', as scholars now think?
options: The first bishop of Paris
Paul's convert in Athens (Acts 17)
An unknown Christian writer of around AD 500 who used that name
Abbot Suger himself
check.why: The writings date from around 500, probably from Syria. Saint-Denis came to believe their author, Paul's convert and their own patron saint were one person.

check.q: What does a rib vault do?
options: Hides the roof timbers
Gathers the weight of the stone ceiling onto a few points, so the walls between can open up
Makes the building lower and safer
Stops sound echoing
check.why: Like the ribs of an umbrella, the ribs carry the vault down to a few points. Between them the wall can become window.

check.q: In Revelation 21, what does the city not have?
options: Walls
Gates
A temple
Precious stones
check.why: 'I saw no temple in it, for the Lord God, the Almighty, and the Lamb, are its temple.' The cathedral pictures a city that will not need a cathedral.

tutorial.question: Was Gothic architecture a theology in stone?
tutorial.approach: Set out Panofsky's case first, using Suger's own words about light and 'leading upward'. Then give Kidson's objection fairly. Ask yourself whether a building has to be designed from a theology in order to express one, and decide.
strong: Explains what was new at Saint-Denis: the combination of pointed arches, rib vaults and buttresses that let the walls become glass.
Quotes or paraphrases Suger: the dull mind rising to truth through material things.
Explains the Denis–Dionysius identification and why it mattered.
Gives Kidson's objection at its strongest: no direct quotation, and practical origins for the forms.
Considers Rudolph's middle view: theory as defence, written after the building.
Distinguishes what Suger intended from what the building can mean to those who use it.

reading.author: Philip Ball
reading.title: Universe of Stone: Chartres Cathedral and the Triumph of the Medieval Mind
reading.why: A science writer's clear and enthusiastic account of how and why the Gothic cathedrals were built.

reading.author: Christopher Wilson
reading.title: The Gothic Cathedral: The Architecture of the Great Church 1130–1530
reading.why: The best single-volume history of the buildings themselves.

reading.author: Erwin Panofsky
reading.title: Abbot Suger on the Abbey Church of St.-Denis and Its Art Treasures
reading.why: Suger's own writings in Latin and English, with the essay that started the debate.

reading.author: Conrad Rudolph
reading.title: Artistic Change at St-Denis
reading.why: Reads Suger's programme as a response to the twelfth-century argument about art.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: bring some light into a dark place in someone else's life. Visit or ring someone who is ill, grieving or alone, and stay long enough to really listen.
sessions.reflect: Has something beautiful ever lifted your mind above itself? What happened, and what did it lead you to?
takeaways: At Saint-Denis in 1140–1144 Suger built a choir ringed with coloured light.
Pointed arches, rib vaults and buttresses let the walls become glass.
Scholars still argue whether Gothic light was a theology, a feat of engineering, or a defence of art.

sessions.title: Reading the glass
sessions.line: Inside Chartres with a sharp-eyed American, learning to read stories told in light.
sessions.plain: Medieval windows were not decoration. They were stories told in light, and people learned to read them. This session takes you inside Chartres Cathedral with Henry Adams, an American historian who loved it, and teaches you to read a window pane by pane.
sessions.why: Suger's choir at Saint-Denis survives only in part. Chartres, rebuilt in the generation after him, still has almost all its glass. If Saint-Denis was the idea, Chartres is the idea complete, and the glass is where to begin.
before: Adams says blue is the key to the windows. Watch for why.
He insists that the windows are flat, 'like a rug hung on the wall'. What does he think would ruin them?
Notice how often he admits what he does not know, and what he does instead.

read.author: Henry Adams
read.who: American historian and writer (1838–1918), grandson and great-grandson of presidents, who fell in love with the French cathedrals in middle age.
paras: At last we are face to face with the crowning glory of Chartres. Other churches have glass,—quantities of it, and very fine,—but we have been trying to catch a glimpse of the glory which stands behind the glass of Chartres, and gives it quality and feeling of its own. For once the architect is useless and his explanations are pitiable; the painter helps still less; and the decorator, unless he works in glass, is the poorest guide of all, while, if he works in glass, he is sure to lead wrong; and all of them may toil until Pierre Mauclerc's stone Christ comes to life, and condemns them among the unpardonable sinners on the southern portal, but neither they nor any other artist will ever create another Chartres. You had better stop here, once for all, unless you are willing to feel that Chartres was made what it is, not by artist, but by the Virgin.

If this imperial presence is stamped on the architecture and the sculpture with an energy not to be mistaken, it radiates through the glass with a light and colour that actually blind the true servant of Mary. One becomes, sometimes, a little incoherent in talking about it; one is ashamed to be as extravagant as one wants to be; one has no business to labour painfully to explain and prove to one's self what is as clear as the sun in the sky; one loses temper in reasoning about what can only be felt, and what ought to be felt instantly, as it was in the twelfth century, even by the truie qui file and the ane qui vielle. Any one should feel it that wishes; any one who does not wish to feel it can let it alone. Still, it may be that not one tourist in a hundred—perhaps not one in a thousand of the English-speaking race—does feel it, or can feel it even when explained to him, for we have lost many senses.

Therefore, let us plod on, laboriously proving God, although, even to Saint Bernard and Pascal, God was incapable of proof; and using such material as the books furnish for help. It is not much. The French have been shockingly negligent of their greatest artistic glory. One knows not even where to seek. One must go to the National Library and beg as a special favour permission to look at the monumental work of M. Lasteyrie, if one wishes to make even a beginning of the study of French glass. Fortunately there exists a fragment of a great work which the Government began, but never completed, upon Chartres; and another, quite indispensable, but not official, upon Bourges; while Viollet-le-Duc's article "Vitrail" serves as guide to the whole. Ottin's book "Le Vitrail" is convenient. Male's volume "L'Art Religieux" is essential. In English, Westlake's "History of Design" is helpful. Perhaps, after reading all that is readable, the best hope will be to provide the best glasses with the largest possible field; and, choosing an hour when the church is empty, take seat about halfway up the nave, facing toward the western entrance with a morning light, so that the glass of the western windows shall not stand in direct sun.

The glass of the three lancets is the oldest in the cathedral. If the portal beneath it, with the sculpture, was built in the twenty or thirty years before 1150, the glass could not be much later. It goes with the Abbe Suger's glass at Saint-Denis, which was surely made as early as 1140-50, since the Abbe was a long time at work on it, before he died in 1152. Their perfection proves, what his biographer asserted, that the Abbe Suger spent many years as well as much money on his windows at Saint-Denis, and the specialists affirm that the three lancets at Chartres are quite as good as what remains of Suger's work. Viollet-le-Duc and M. Paul Durand, the Government expert, are positive that this glass is the finest ever made, as far as record exists; and that the northern lancet representing the Tree of Jesse stands at the head of all glasswork whatever. The windows claim, therefore, to be the most splendid colour decoration the world ever saw, since no other material, neither silk nor gold, and no opaque colour laid on with a brush, can compare with translucent glass, and even the Ravenna mosaics or Chinese porcelains are darkness beside them.

The claim may not be modest, but it is none of ours. Viollet-le-Duc must answer for his own sins, and he chose the lancet window of the Tree of Jesse for the subject of his lecture on glass in general, as the most complete and perfect example of this greatest decorative art. Once more, in following him, one is dragged, in spite of one's self, into technique, and, what is worse, into a colour world whose technique was forgotten five hundred years ago. Viollet-le-Duc tried to recover it. "After studying our best French windows," he cautiously suggests that "one might maintain," as their secret of harmony, that "the first condition for an artist in glass is to know how to manage blue. The blue is the light in windows, and light has value only by opposition." The radiating power of blue is, therefore, the starting-point, and on this matter Viollet-le-Duc has much to say which a student would need to master; but a tourist never should study, or he ceases to be a tourist; and it is enough for us if we know that, to get the value they wanted, the artists hatched their blues with lines, covered their surface with figures as though with screens, and tied their blue within its own field with narrow circlets of white or yellow, which, in their turn, were beaded to fasten the blue still more firmly in its place. We have chiefly to remember the law that blue is light:—

But also it is that luminous colour which gives value to all others. If you compose a window in which there shall be no blue, you will get a dirty or dull (blafard) or crude surface which the eye will instantly avoid; but if you put a few touches of blue among all these tones, you will immediately get striking effects if not skilfully conceived harmony. So the composition of blue glass singularly preoccupied the glassworkers of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. If there is only one red, two yellows, two or three purples, and two or three greens at the most, there are infinite shades of blue, ... and these blues are placed with a very delicate observation of the effects they should produce on other tones, and other tones on them.

Viollet-le-Duc took the window of the Tree of Jesse as his first illustration of the rule, for the reason that its blue ground is one continuous strip from top to bottom, with the subordinate red on either side, and a border uniting the whole so plainly that no one can fail to see its object or its method.

The blue tone of the principal subject [that is to say, the ground of the Tree of Jesse] has commanded the tonality of all the rest. This medium was necessary to enable the luminous splendour to display its energy. This primary condition had dictated the red ground for the prophets, and the return to the blue on reaching the outside semicircular band. To give full value both to the vigour of the red, and to the radiating transparency of the blue, the ground of the corners is put in emerald green; but then, in the corners themselves, the blue is recalled and is given an additional solidity of value by the delicate ornamentation of the squares.

This translation is very free, but one who wants to know these windows must read the whole article, and read it here in the church, the Dictionary in one hand, and binocle in the other, for the binocle is more important than the Dictionary when it reaches the complicated border which repeats in detail the colour-scheme of the centre:—

The border repeats all the tones allotted to the principal subjects, but by small fragments, so that this border, with an effect both solid and powerful, shall not enter into rivalry with the large arrangements of the central parts.

One would think this simple enough; easily tested on any illuminated manuscript, Arab, Persian, or Byzantine; verified by any Oriental rug, old or new; freely illustrated by any Chinese pattern on a Ming jar, or cloisonne vase; and offering a kind of alphabet for the shop-window of a Paris modiste. A strong red; a strong and a weak yellow; a strong and a weak purple; a strong and a weak green, are all to be tied together, given their values, and held in their places by blue. The thing seems simpler still when it appears that perspective is forbidden, and that these glass windows of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, like Oriental rugs, imply a flat surface, a wall which must not be treated as open. The twelfth- century glassworker would sooner have worn a landscape on his back than have costumed his church with it; he would as soon have decorated his floors with painted holes as his walls. He wanted to keep the coloured window flat, like a rug hung on the wall.

The radiation of translucent colours in windows cannot be modified by the artist; all his talent consists in profiting by it, according to a given harmonic scheme on a single plane, like a rug, but not according to an effect of aerial perspective. Do what you like, a glass window never does and never can represent anything but a plane surface; its real virtues even exist only on that condition. Every attempt to present several planes to the eye is fatal to the harmony of colour, without producing any illusion in the spectator ... Translucid painting can propose as its object only a design supporting as energetically as possible a harmony of colours.

Whether this law is absolute you can tell best by looking at modern glass which is mostly perspective; but, whether you like it or not, the matter of perspective does not enter into a twelfth-century window more than into a Japanese picture, and may be ignored. The decoration of the twelfth century, as far as concerns us, was intended only for one plane, and a window was another form of rug or embroidery or mosaic, hung on the wall for colour,—simple decoration to be seen as a whole. If the Tree of Jesse teaches anything at all, it is that the artist thought first of controlling his light, but he wanted to do it not in order to dim the colours; on the contrary, he toiled, like a jeweller setting diamonds and rubies, to increase their splendour. If his use of blue teaches this lesson, his use of green proves it. The outside border of the Tree of Jesse is a sort of sample which our schoolmaster Viollet-le-Duc sets, from which he requires us to study out the scheme, beginning with the treatment of light, and ending with the value of the emerald green ground in the corners.

Complicated as the border of the Tree of Jesse is, it has its mates in the borders of the two other twelfth-century windows, and a few of the thirteenth-century in the side aisles; but the southern of the three lancets shows how the artists dealt with a difficulty that upset their rule. The border of the southern window does not count as it should; something is wrong with it and a little study shows that the builder, and not the glassworker, was to blame. Owing to his miscalculation—if it was really a miscalculation—in the width of the southern tower, the builder economized six or eight inches in the southern door and lancet, which was enough to destroy the balance between the colour-values, as masses, of the south and north windows. The artist was obliged to choose whether he would sacrifice the centre or the border of his southern window, and decided that the windows could not be made to balance if he narrowed the centre, but that he must balance them by enriching the centre, and sacrificing the border. He has filled the centre with medallions as rich as he could make them, and these he has surrounded with borders, which are also enriched to the utmost; but these medallions with their borders spread across the whole window, and when you search with the binocle for the outside border, you see its pattern clearly only at the top and bottom. On the sides, at intervals of about two feet, the medallions cover and interrupt it; but this is partly corrected by making the border, where it is seen, so rich as to surpass any other in the cathedral, even that of the Tree of Jesse. Whether the artist has succeeded or not is a question for other artists—or for you, if you please—to decide; but apparently he did succeed, since no one has ever noticed the difficulty or the device.

The southern lancet represents the Passion of Christ. Granting to Viollet-le-Duc that the unbroken vertical colour-scheme of the Tree of Jesse made the more effective window, one might still ask whether the medallion-scheme is not the more interesting. Once past the workshop, there can be no question about it; the Tree of Jesse has the least interest of all the three windows. A genealogical tree has little value, artistic or other, except to those who belong in its branches, and the Tree of Jesse was put there, not to please us, but to please the Virgin. The Passion window was also put there to please her, but it tells a story, and does it in a way that has more novelty than the subject. The draughtsman who chalked out the design on the whitened table that served for his sketch-board was either a Greek, or had before him a Byzantine missal, or enamel or ivory. The first medallion on these legendary windows is the lower left-hand one, which begins the story or legend; here it represents Christ after the manner of the Greek Church. In the next medallion is the Last Supper; the fish on the dish is Greek. In the middle of the window, with the help of the binocle, you will see a Crucifixion, or even two, for on the left is Christ on the Cross, and on the right a Descent from the Cross; in this is the figure of man pulling out with pincers the nails which fasten Christ's feet; a figure unknown to Western religious art. The Noli Me Tangere, on the right, near the top, has a sort of Greek character. All the critics, especially M. Paul Durand, have noticed this Byzantine look, which is even more marked in the Suger window at Saint-Denis, so as to suggest that both are by the same hand, and that the hand of a Greek. If the artist was really a Greek, he has done work more beautiful than any left at Byzantium, and very far finer than anything in the beautiful work at Cairo, but although the figures and subjects are more or less Greek, like the sculptures on the portal, the art seems to be French.

Look at the central window! Naturally, there sits the Virgin, with her genealogical tree on her left, and her Son's testimony on her right to prove her double divinity. She is seated in the long halo; as, on the western portal, directly beneath her, her Son is represented in stone, Her crown and head, as well as that of the Child, are fourteenth-century restorations more or less like the original; but her cushioned throne and her robes of imperial state, as well as the flowered sceptre in either hand, are as old as the sculpture of the portal, and redolent of the first crusade. On either side of her, the Sun and the Moon offer praise; her two Archangels, Michael and Gabriel, with resplendent wings, offer not incense as in later times, but the two sceptres of spiritual and temporal power; while the Child in her lap repeats His Mother's action and even her features and expression. At first sight, one would take for granted that all this was pure Byzantium, and perhaps it is; but it has rather the look of Byzantium gallicized, and carried up to a poetic French ideal. At Saint-Denis the little figure of the Abbe Suger at the feet of the Virgin has a very Oriental look, and in the twin medallion the Virgin resembles greatly the Virgin of Chartres, yet, for us, until some specialist shows us the Byzantine original, the work is as thoroughly French as the fleches of the churches.

Byzantine art is altogether another chapter, and, if we could but take a season to study it in Byzantium, we might get great amusement; but the art of Chartres, even in 1100, was French and perfectly French, as the architecture shows, and the glass is even more French than the architecture, as you can detect in many other ways. Perhaps the surest evidence is the glass itself. The men who made it were not professionals but amateurs, who may have had some knowledge of enamelling, but who worked like jewellers, unused to glass, and with the refinement that a reliquary or a crozier required. The cost of these windows must have been extravagant; one is almost surprised that they are not set in gold rather than in lead. The Abbe Suger shirked neither trouble nor expense, and the only serious piece of evidence that this artist was a Greek is given by his biographer who unconsciously shows that the artist cheated him: "He sought carefully for makers of windows and workmen in glass of exquisite quality, especially in that made of sapphires in great abundance that were pulverized and melted up in the glass to give it the blue colour which he delighted to admire." The "materia saphirorum" was evidently something precious,—as precious as crude sapphires would have been,—and the words imply beyond question that the artist asked for sapphires and that Suger paid for them; yet all specialists agree that the stone known as sapphire, if ground, could not produce translucent colour at all. The blue which Suger loved, and which is probably the same as that of these Chartres windows, cannot be made out of sapphires. Probably the "materia saphirorum" means cobalt only, but whatever it was, the glassmakers seem to agree that this glass of 1140-50 is the best ever made. M. Paul Durand in his official report of 1881 said that these windows, both artistically and mechanically, were of the highest class: "I will also call attention to the fact that the glass and the execution of the painting are, materially speaking, of a quality much superior to windows of the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. Having passed several months in contact with these precious works when I copied them, I was able to convince myself of their superiority in every particular, especially in the upper parts of the three windows." He said that they were perfect and irreproachable. The true enthusiast in glass would in the depths of his heart like to say outright that these three windows are worth more than all that the French have since done in colour, from that day to this; but the matter concerns us chiefly because it shows how French the experiment was, and how Suger's taste and wealth made it possible.

Certain it is, too, that the southern window—the Passion—was made on the spot, or near by, and fitted for the particular space with care proportionate to its cost. All are marked by the hand of the Chartres Virgin. They are executed not merely for her, but by her. At Saint-Denis the Abbe Suger appeared,—it is true that he was prostrate at her feet, but still he appeared. At Chartres no one—no suggestion of a human agency—was allowed to appear; the Virgin permitted no one to approach her, even to adore. She is enthroned above, as Queen and Empress and Mother, with the symbols of exclusive and universal power. Below her, she permitted the world to see the glories of her earthly life;—the Annunciation, Visitation, and Nativity; the Magi; King Herod; the Journey to Egypt; and the single medallion, which shows the gods of Egypt falling from their pedestals at her coming, is more entertaining than a whole picture- gallery of oil paintings.

notes.text: Chartres is dedicated to Mary (Notre-Dame), and Adams writes throughout as if she herself were the patron who commissioned the building. It is his way of saying that it was made for her. The 'stone Christ' of Pierre Mauclerc is the figure of Christ at the Last Judgement on the south porch, which Mauclerc (Peter of Dreux, Duke of Brittany) paid for.
'Truie qui file' and 'ane qui vielle': a sow spinning and a donkey playing the hurdy-gurdy, comic carvings at Chartres. Adams means that even the humblest pilgrim felt what tourists now miss.
The three lancets: three tall windows in the west front, under the great rose, made around 1145–1155 and saved from the fire of 1194. Adams says Suger died in 1152; it was in January 1151.

Eugène Viollet-le-Duc (1814–1879) restored many French cathedrals and wrote a ten-volume dictionary of medieval architecture; 'Vitrail' is its article on stained glass. The indented paragraphs that follow are Adams's own, very free, translation of him. The Tree of Jesse window shows Christ's family tree growing from Jesse, father of King David (Isaiah 11:1).
By 'modern glass' Adams means the pictorial glass of his own day, painted like an oil painting with depth and perspective. Medieval glass is flat on purpose.

'Her double divinity' is Adams's own phrase, not the teaching of any church: Christians honour Mary but do not hold her to be divine. He writes as a fascinated outsider, half in love with the cult he describes.

Adams says the words about 'sapphire' glass come from Suger's biographer. Most scholars take them from Suger's own account of his work. Medieval blue glass was coloured with cobalt, not ground sapphires.

sessions.readWhy: Adams was not a believer, and he says so; but no one in English has written about Chartres glass with more love or a sharper eye. Read him as a guide standing beside you in the nave, enthusiastic, opinionated, sometimes wrong, and always looking.

compare.author: George Herbert
compare.who: Poet and parish priest at Bemerton near Salisbury (1593–1633).
paras:
Lord, how can man preach thy eternall word?
He is a brittle crazie glasse:
Yet in thy temple thou dost him afford
This glorious and transcendent place,
To be a window, through thy grace.

But when thou dost anneal in glasse thy storie,
Making thy life to shine within
The holy Preachers; then the light and glorie
More rev'rend grows, & more doth win:
Which else shows watrish, bleak, & thin.

Doctrine and life, colours and light, in one
When they combine and mingle, bring
A strong regard and aw: but speech alone
Doth vanish like a flaring thing,
And in the eare, not conscience ring.

notes.text: 'Crazie' means cracked or flawed, as in 'crazed' glass.
To anneal is to fire paint into glass in a kiln so that it becomes part of it, exactly as medieval glass-painters did.

compare.why: A country parson, a century after the Reformation, turns the church window into a picture of the preacher: a 'brittle crazie glasse' that only shines when God's story is 'annealed', fired, into it. 'Anneal' is the glass-painter's word.

paras: On the night of 10 June 1194 the cathedral of Chartres burned. The town's great treasure was a tunic believed to have been worn by Mary, given to the cathedral in 876, and for three days it was thought lost. Then it was found safe in the crypt, where priests had carried it and sheltered from the flames. The people took this as a sign that Mary wanted a new and greater church.

It was built with remarkable speed. Most of the new cathedral stood within about twenty-five years, though it was not consecrated until 1260. The west front with its three doorways and the three lancet windows above them had survived the fire, and the builders kept them, fitting the new church behind the old front.

Chartres has more than 150 windows, most of them made between about 1200 and 1235, and it has kept more of its original glass than any other great cathedral. Much of that is luck: it escaped the iconoclasm of the Reformation and the violence of the French Revolution, and in both World Wars the glass was taken out and stored in safety.
sections.key: Chartres burned in 1194, rose again in about twenty-five years, and has kept most of its medieval glass.

paras: Medieval glass was made from sand melted with the ash of burnt wood or ferns, which supplied potash. Colour came from metal oxides added to the melt: cobalt for blue, copper for red and green, manganese for purple. Red glass was so dark that it was usually made as a thin layer of red over clear glass.

The molten glass was blown into a bubble, swung into a cylinder, cut open and flattened into a sheet. The glazier laid out the design full-size on a whitewashed table, cut pieces of coloured glass to shape with a hot iron, and painted on the details, faces, folds and lettering, with a dark paint made of ground glass and iron or copper oxide. The pieces were fired in a kiln so that the paint fused into the glass. Then they were joined with strips of lead, called cames, and the panels fixed into the stone on an iron frame.

We know this from a remarkable book, On Divers Arts, written around the 1120s by a German monk who called himself Theophilus. It is a practical manual for making glass, painting it and setting it, and the methods it describes were used, with little change, for centuries.
sections.key: Coloured glass, painted detail fired in a kiln, and lead strips: the method barely changed for centuries.

sections.h: Blue, red and the colour of light
paras: Adams's great lesson, taken from Viollet-le-Duc, is that 'blue is light'. In a window the blue does not sit still: it seems to spread, to glow and to advance, while red recedes and can turn murky. The masters of Chartres balanced the two, holding the blue in place with borders of other colours.

Because the glass was made by hand, it is uneven: thicker and thinner, full of tiny bubbles and streaks. This is why old glass sparkles and changes with the hour and the weather, as no machine-made glass can. The famous 'blue of Chartres' is not one colour but many, shifting through the day.
sections.key: Blue carries the light and holds the colours together; handmade glass sparkles because it is uneven.

paras: Did the colours mean something? Sometimes. Medieval writers gave colours symbolic values, and the association of blue with Mary, now so familiar, grew precisely in these centuries, as the French historian Michel Pastoureau has shown: blue rose from a minor colour to the colour of the Virgin and of the French kings in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, partly because of the new blue glass. Red often goes with martyrs and with Christ's Passion, white with purity and resurrection.

But there was no fixed code, and most colour choices in a window are made for the reasons Adams gives: balance, contrast and the behaviour of light. It is a good rule to look for meaning only where the window itself gives a clue, such as a figure who always wears the same colour.
sections.key: Colours sometimes carry meaning, but there was no fixed code; look for meaning only where the window gives a clue.

paras: The great narrative windows at Chartres are built of medallions, circles, squares and quatrefoils, each holding one scene, set against a background of patterned glass and surrounded by a border. To read one, start at the bottom, usually on the left, and work upwards, row by row, as if climbing towards heaven. The story generally ends at the top.

Look at the bottom panels first, because that is often where the givers are. Dozens of the Chartres windows show the trades that are said to have paid for them: bakers with their loaves, butchers with an ox, wine merchants with their barrels, money-changers at their tables. These are not advertisements; they are offerings, the town's work brought into the church.

Then look for pairs. Medieval Christians read the Old Testament as foreshadowing the New, and windows often set the two side by side. This is called typology. In the Good Samaritan window at Chartres, the parable is told alongside the story of Adam and Eve: humanity wounded on the road, and the Samaritan, who stands for Christ, bringing it home.
Finally, step back. A window is meant to be seen from a distance as a single field of colour, as well as read close up. Both kinds of looking belong to it.
sections.key: Start at the bottom, look for the givers, look for Old and New Testament pairs, then step back.

paras: Around the year 600, Pope Gregory the Great wrote to Serenus, bishop of Marseilles, who had smashed the images in his churches to stop people worshipping them. Gregory rebuked him: to adore a picture is one thing, he wrote, but to learn through a picture what is to be adored is another, for what writing is to those who can read, a picture is to the unlearned. The phrase 'the Bible of the poor' grew out of this idea, and it is often used of medieval glass.

It is partly true. Windows did tell the stories of Scripture and the saints to people who could not read. But many windows are fifteen or twenty metres up; their scenes are small, and their typology is subtle enough to puzzle experts. Most people would have needed someone, a preacher, a guide or a parent, to explain them. That is the debate in this session.
sections.key: Windows did teach, but many are too high and subtle to read without a guide.

sections.h: How to look at a window today
paras: A few practical things help. Take binoculars, as Adams did with his 'binocle': many scenes are too high to see clearly with the naked eye. Choose the time of day. East windows glow in the morning, west windows and roses in the late afternoon, and south windows at midday; a window in full sun can be too bright to read, so Adams advises sitting with the light behind the glass but not shining straight through it.

Find the guidebook or the panel that numbers the scenes, and start at the bottom. Look for the givers. Then put the guide away and simply look for a few minutes at the whole window, letting the colour do what it was made to do.
sections.key: Take binoculars, choose the time of day, follow the numbered scenes, then simply look.

paras: In the 1240s Louis IX of France built the Sainte-Chapelle in Paris to house the relics of Christ's Passion he had bought, a chapel whose walls are almost entirely glass. In England, Canterbury Cathedral kept some of the oldest glass in the country, from the late twelfth century, and York Minster's Great East Window, glazed by John Thornton between 1405 and 1408, is one of the largest areas of medieval stained glass in the world.

Much was lost. The Reformation in England, and above all the Civil War of the 1640s, saw windows smashed as idolatrous; later, clear glass was often preferred for light to read by. The Victorians revived the craft, and many churches you visit will have nineteenth-century glass made with the old methods. Herbert's poem, written in the 1630s between these two worlds, keeps the medieval idea alive in a Protestant key: the window is still a place where God's story shines, but now it is the preacher's life that must be the glass.
sections.key: Glass reached its height in the thirteenth century, was smashed at the Reformation, and was revived by the Victorians.

refs: The fire of 1194 and the tunic: the Miracles of the Blessed Virgin Mary of Chartres (Latin, around 1210); see Philip Ball, Universe of Stone (2008), and Malcolm Miller, Chartres Cathedral (1985).
Dates of the glass: Claudine Lautier and the Corpus Vitrearum France; consecration of 1260.
Theophilus, On Divers Arts (De diversis artibus), Book II; English translation by J. G. Hawthorne and C. S. Smith (1963).
The trade windows: Jane Welch Williams, Bread, Wine and Money: The Windows of the Trades at Chartres Cathedral (1993), which questions whether the guilds actually paid.
The Good Samaritan window (north aisle, about 1205–1215): Wolfgang Kemp, The Narratives of Gothic Stained Glass (1997).
Gregory the Great, Letters, Book XI, letter 10 (to Serenus of Marseilles, 600).
York Minster Great East Window (1405–1408): York Glaziers Trust.

debate.question: Were the windows read, or simply seen?

positions.name: Books for those who cannot read
positions.who: Gregory the Great (around 600); Émile Mâle, The Gothic Image (1898)
positions.view: Images taught the faith to people who had no books. Mâle called the cathedral a book in stone and glass in which every part has a meaning, laid out with the order of an encyclopedia.
positions.evidence: Gregory's letter; the clear narrative order of medallion windows; the use of familiar stories.

positions.name: Too high and too subtle to read
positions.who: Many modern historians of glass, such as Wolfgang Kemp and Madeline Caviness
positions.view: Most windows are hard to see from the floor and their schemes are learned, made by clergy for clergy as much as for the people. Their first work was to make the church a place of holy light and to honour the saints and the givers.
positions.evidence: The height and small scale of many scenes; typology that needs a commentary; the prominence of donors.

positions.name: Read together, out loud
positions.who: Historians of preaching and pilgrimage
positions.view: People did not read windows alone like books. They learned them from sermons, feast-day processions and guides, and a window reminded them of a story they had already heard. Reading was shared.
positions.evidence: Sermons that point to images in the church; the use of windows on the feast days of the saints they show.

debate.agree: All agree that the windows were meant to be looked at with understanding, and that they did far more than decorate: they turned light itself into something holy.

look.why: Jan van Eyck painted the Annunciation, the moment the angel tells Mary she will bear a son, inside a church, and made it a lesson in light. Some scholars, following Erwin Panofsky, read the three windows behind Mary as the Trinity and the single coloured window above as God, with the old round-arched building standing for the old covenant into which the new light now enters.
points: Behind Mary, three tall windows of clear glass made of little round panes (bull's-eye glass).
High above, a single window of coloured glass with one standing figure, between figures painted on the wall.
Gold lines of light coming in from a window at the upper left, with a white dove flying down them towards Mary.
The angel's greeting and Mary's answer painted in gold letters. Mary's answer is upside down.
The floor, set with tiles drawn with scenes and figures.

music.why: Hildegard of Bingen was writing music and visions of light in the Rhineland while the first great windows were being made in France. Her chant is the sound of the same century.

think.why: Because in Christ God took a body, Christians believed that matter, even sand, ash and metal, could carry holiness. Stained glass is that belief made visible.

learn.why: Hopkins's world 'charged with the grandeur of God', flaming out 'like shining from shook foil', is the world seen as the glaziers saw it: shot through with light.

check.q: Where do you usually start reading a medieval medallion window?
options: At the top
At the bottom, usually on the left
In the middle
Anywhere you like
check.why: Most narrative windows read from the bottom upwards, row by row, climbing towards heaven.

check.q: What did glass-painters use to draw faces and folds on coloured glass?
options: Oil paint
Gold leaf
A dark paint of ground glass and metal oxide, fired in a kiln
Ink
check.why: The paint was fired so that it fused into the glass. Herbert's word 'anneal' comes from this.

check.q: Why does Adams say blue matters so much?
options: It was the cheapest colour
It carries the light and holds the other colours together
It was the only colour allowed for Mary
It never fades
check.why: 'Blue is light', as Viollet-le-Duc put it: it glows and seems to spread, giving value to the other colours.

check.q: What does 'typology' mean in a window?
options: Labelling scenes with letters
Setting Old Testament scenes beside the New Testament events they were thought to foreshadow
Showing the trades that paid for the window
Repeating patterns in the border
check.why: The Good Samaritan window at Chartres, for instance, tells the parable alongside the story of Adam and Eve.

tutorial.question: 'What writing is to those who can read, a picture is to the unlearned.' Does Gregory's claim fit the windows of Chartres?
tutorial.approach: Explain what Gregory meant and why he wrote it. Then test it against what you have learned about the windows: their height, their order, their typology, their givers. Use Adams as a witness, and Herbert as a different answer to what a window is for.
strong: Places Gregory's letter in context: a bishop destroying images, and Gregory distinguishing learning from worship.
Shows where the claim fits: windows do tell biblical and saints' stories in order.
Shows where it does not: height, small scale, learned typology, the need for a guide.
Notes that windows also do something other than teach: they make light holy and honour saints and givers.
Uses Herbert to show a Protestant reworking: the window as the preacher's life.
Reaches a balanced judgement of its own.

reading.author: Malcolm Miller
reading.title: Chartres Cathedral
reading.why: A short guide by the Englishman who led visitors round Chartres for more than fifty years.

reading.author: Virginia Chieffo Raguin
reading.title: Stained Glass: From Its Origins to the Present
reading.why: A clear, well-illustrated history of the craft.

reading.author: Émile Mâle
reading.title: The Gothic Image
reading.why: The classic reading of the cathedral as a book of meanings (French original 1898).

reading.author: Wolfgang Kemp
reading.title: The Narratives of Gothic Stained Glass
reading.why: How the windows actually tell their stories, and for whom.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: take someone with you, a child or a friend, to look at one stained-glass window near you, in a church or a museum. Work out its story together from the bottom up, and tell them what you have learned.
sessions.reflect: Herbert says words alone 'vanish like a flaring thing'. Whose life has preached to you more than their words?
takeaways: Chartres kept most of its medieval glass: stories told in light, made from sand, ash and metal.
Read a window from the bottom up, find the givers and the Old and New Testament pairs, then step back.
Windows taught, but they also made light holy; most people needed a guide to read them.

sessions.title: Why this waste?
sessions.line: The case against the cathedrals, at full strength.
sessions.plain: Not everyone loved the new splendour. Its fiercest critic was a monk, Bernard of Clairvaux, who said the church was dressing its stones in gold while its poor went naked. This session gives his case at full strength, beside Augustine's honest struggle with beauty and a scene from the Gospels where the same question is asked of Jesus.
sessions.why: So far we have walked through the cathedrals as their makers hoped we would. Now we must hear the strongest objection, made in the twelfth century by a man who had seen the new splendour and wanted none of it. It has never gone away.
before: Augustine both loves beauty and fears it. Find the sentence where he says both at once.
Who does he blame: the craftsmen, the beautiful things, or himself?
In the Gospel, who complains about the waste, and what exactly does Jesus answer?

read.author: Augustine of Hippo
read.who: North African bishop and theologian (354–430), whose Confessions, written in his forties, is the first great autobiography of the inner life.
paras: There remains the pleasure of these eyes of my flesh, on which to make my confessions in the hearing of the ears of Thy temple, those brotherly and devout ears; and so to conclude the temptations of the lust of the flesh, which yet assail me, groaning earnestly, and desiring to be clothed upon with my house from heaven. The eyes love fair and varied forms, and bright and soft colours. Let not these occupy my soul; let God rather occupy it, who made these things, very good indeed, yet is He my good, not they. And these affect me, waking, the whole day, nor is any rest given me from them, as there is from musical, sometimes in silence, from all voices. For this queen of colours, the light, bathing all which we behold, wherever I am through the day, gliding by me in varied forms, soothes me when engaged on other things, and not observing it. And so strongly doth it entwine itself, that if it be suddenly withdrawn, it is with longing sought for, and if absent long, saddeneth the mind.

O Thou Light, which Tobias saw, when, these eyes closed, he taught his son the way of life; and himself went before with the feet of charity, never swerving. Or which Isaac saw, when his fleshly eyes being heavy and closed by old age, it was vouchsafed him, not knowingly, to bless his sons, but by blessing to know them. Or which Jacob saw, when he also, blind through great age, with illumined heart, in the persons of his sons shed light on the different races of the future people, in them foresignified; and laid his hands, mystically crossed, upon his grandchildren by Joseph, not as their father by his outward eye corrected them, but as himself inwardly discerned. This is the light, it is one, and all are one, who see and love it. But that corporeal light whereof I spake, it seasoneth the life of this world for her blind lovers, with an enticing and dangerous sweetness. But they who know how to praise Thee for it, "O all-creating Lord," take it up in Thy hymns, and are not taken up with it in their sleep. Such would I be. These seductions of the eyes I resist, lest my feet wherewith I walk upon Thy way be ensnared; and I lift up mine invisible eyes to Thee, that Thou wouldest pluck my feet out of the snare. Thou dost ever and anon pluck them out, for they are ensnared. Thou ceasest not to pluck them out, while I often entangle myself in the snares on all sides laid; because Thou that keepest Israel shalt neither slumber nor sleep.

What innumerable toys, made by divers arts and manufactures, in our apparel, shoes, utensils and all sorts of works, in pictures also and divers images, and these far exceeding all necessary and moderate use and all pious meaning, have men added to tempt their own eyes withal; outwardly following what themselves make, inwardly forsaking Him by whom themselves were made, and destroying that which themselves have been made!
