positions.name: Yes, and we should accept it
positions.who: Carl Sagan, Pale Blue Dot (1994); Sigmund Freud on the 'blows' to human self-love (1917)
positions.view: The universe is vast and we are not at its centre or the purpose of it. Facing this honestly is humbling and grown-up, and it gives us our responsibility: to be kind to one another and to care for the only home we have.
positions.evidence: The scale of the cosmos; the Voyager photograph; common descent; the history of human self-importance corrected by science.

positions.name: Yes, and it is a loss
positions.who: Max Weber, 'Science as a Vocation' (1917); in a religious key, symbolic readers such as Matthieu Pageau
positions.view: The scientific way of seeing, by itself, strips the world of meaning: a 'disenchantment'. We gain power over matter and lose our place in an ordered whole. That is the fruit of Genesis 3 again, and it leaves people exposed and adrift.
positions.evidence: The modern experience of meaninglessness; the gap between what science explains and what people need to live by.

positions.name: No: greatness was never size or place
positions.who: Psalm 8; Boethius (about 524); Augustine; today, historians such as Dennis Danielson
positions.view: The ancients knew the earth was tiny and the universe vast, and were not crushed by it. Human dignity never rested on being in the middle. It rests on being the creature who can know and name the world and be known by God. Pascal put it most sharply (you will meet him in Hall VI): the universe can crush a human being, but the human being knows it and the universe does not.
positions.evidence: Ptolemy's 'point'; Psalm 8, read in full in Human dignity, which looks at the stars and asks 'what is man?'; Danielson's history; the fact that the knower of the cosmos is part of what is to be explained.

debate.agree: All agree that we are physically tiny in a vast universe, and that how we live in the face of it is the real question.

look.why: Thomas Moran painted the Green River cliffs of Wyoming in 1881, in the decades when geologists were reading the earth's great age in such rocks; the Green River country is famous for its fossil beds. Look at the size of the riders beside the cliffs.
points: Sheer, towering cliffs lit cream-white and rust-orange by a low sun.
A long line of riders on horseback, Native Americans in feathered headdresses, winding into the distance.
A crystal-blue river, and a row of tiny tepees on the far horizon.
A pale yellow sun low over rose-pink, flat-topped cliffs.
The artist's signature in the lower right corner: 'TYMoran 1881'.

music.why: 'I see the stars, I hear the rolling thunder': a Swedish hymn of 1885, the year of Huxley's essay. Its singer looks at the vastness of the universe and is not made small, but moved to praise.

think.why: The modern debate about science and faith, in depth.

learn.why: 'The heavens declare the glory of God': the same sky that makes us feel small, read as speech. The heavens have meaning as well as matter.

listen.why: A Christian mathematician and an atheist biologist debate whether science has buried God. Listen for where they agree on the science and disagree on what follows.

check.q: What exactly did Huxley argue against Gladstone?
options: That evolution proves atheism
That Genesis was written by Babylonians
That the order of creation in Genesis 1, read as natural history, contradicts the fossil record; whether Gladstone read Genesis rightly he left open
That God does not exist
check.why: Huxley attacked the reading of Genesis as a scientific timetable.

check.q: Dennis Danielson argued that the 'Copernican demotion' is a cliché. Why?
options: Because Galileo was never tried
Because Copernicus was wrong
Because in medieval cosmology the centre was the lowest, least honoured place, so moving the earth from it was not felt as a demotion
Because the earth really is at the centre
check.why: Galileo even said the earth was not the 'sump' of the universe.

check.q: How does this session suggest the historians' correction and this course's frame fit together?
options: The frame proves the historians wrong
They are about different subjects
The correction shows the lost 'centre' was never a place in space; what modern people lost was the meeting of meaning and matter, which keeps the frame's point in a corrected form
The correction proves the frame entirely false
check.why: Neither cancels the other: history corrected, point deepened.

check.q: The sceptic says the 'two ways of seeing' is a retreat invented after science won. What is the best reply from this course?
options: Science has not won
Genesis was written after Darwin
Augustine and Origen read 'heaven' and 'earth' as two orders long before modern science, so it is not a late invention, though it must still earn its place
Meaning can be measured
check.why: The reading is ancient; whether it is true is a further question.

check.q: Which is the hardest problem for reconciling Genesis with evolution?
options: The length of the ark
Animal death and suffering over hundreds of millions of years before humans, given Paul's link between sin and death
The name of Adam's third son
That birds appear on day five
check.why: Christians answer it in different ways; it remains debated.

check.q: What does the step from 'Genesis is not science' to 'Genesis is untrue' depend on?
options: The age of the universe
The philosophical assumption that only matter, and what science can measure, is real
Genetics
Fossil evidence
check.why: That assumption is not itself a scientific finding.

tutorial.question: Does science disprove Genesis, and does modern knowledge diminish us?
tutorial.approach: State the scientific picture and the sceptic's case at full strength, using Huxley. Set out the claim that modern knowledge re-enacts the fruit of Genesis 3, with Copernicus, Freud and Sagan, then the historians' correction (Danielson), and say how the two fit. Face the hardest problems honestly. Conclude by distinguishing what science shows from what it cannot test.
strong: States the scientific picture accurately, with dates.
States the sceptic's case at full strength, including the charge that 'meaning' is a retreat.
Uses Huxley accurately, including his distinction between Genesis-as-science and religion.
Explains the 'fruit again' parallel and Danielson's correction fairly, without letting either cancel the other.
Faces genetics and death before the fall honestly.
Distinguishes scientific findings from the assumption that only matter is real.

reading.author: Francis Collins
reading.title: The Language of God
reading.why: The head of the Human Genome Project on why he believes.

reading.author: Carl Sagan
reading.title: Pale Blue Dot
reading.why: The modern case for cosmic humility, beautifully written.

reading.author: Richard Dawkins
reading.title: The Greatest Show on Earth
reading.why: The evidence for evolution, by its best-known atheist advocate.

reading.author: C. S. Lewis
reading.title: The Discarded Image
reading.why: The medieval picture of the universe, and why it did not make people feel small.

reading.author: Dennis Danielson
reading.title: 'The Great Copernican Cliché', American Journal of Physics 69
reading.why: The short paper that corrects the 'demotion' story.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: on a clear night, go out and look at the stars for ten minutes. Learn the name of one star or constellation, and then say Psalm 19:1 under it. Let the science deepen your wonder rather than replace it.
sessions.reflect: When you think of the size of the universe, do you feel smaller, or more astonished that you can know it? Which of the three positions in the debate is closest to yours?
takeaways: Science shows that Genesis is not a scientific timetable; it cannot show that Genesis is false about God and humanity.
Knowledge of matter alone re-enacts the fruit, leaving us exposed and off-centre; the historians correct the 'demotion' story but deepen its point.
The way back is not to reject science but to join it to meaning.

sessions.title: Babel and the Word: the centre restored
sessions.line: A tower built from below, one man called, and 'In the beginning was the Word'.
sessions.plain: The last story in Genesis 1–11 is the tower of Babel: people trying to reach heaven from below, with bricks, and losing the one language that held them together. Then God calls one man, Abraham. Centuries later John's Gospel opens with the first words of Genesis, 'In the beginning', and says that the Word through whom all things were made 'became flesh'. This session reads both, and gives the verdict.
sessions.why: Session 6 asked whether science leaves us small and off-centre, and found that what was lost was never a place but the meeting of meaning and matter. So how is that meeting restored? Babel shows the wrong way; John shows the answer.
answers: Why are there so many peoples and languages?
What does John mean by 'the Word'?
Why does John begin 'In the beginning'?
How do we get back to the centre?
sessions.finding: At Babel people try to reach heaven from below, by matter alone, and their one language is scattered. John answers Genesis: the Word through whom all things were made, meaning itself, became flesh, so heaven and earth meet in a person. The centre was never a place in space; it is that meeting, offered to each person.

paras: Six sessions: heaven and earth, meaning and matter (1); Eden, the centre where they meet, with the human being as the link (2); the opened eyes and the exile east (3); violence spreading further out (4); the waters returning and the world ordered again (5); and the modern eye that sees only matter, which leaves us exposed and off-centre (6). One story of Genesis 1–11 remains, and then a page from the New Testament that answers the whole.
background.key: Meaning and matter, the centre, exile, violence, flood and the modern fruit.

paras: The tower of Babel is set in 'the land of Shinar', the old name for Babylonia. Babylon had a great stepped temple tower, a ziggurat called Etemenanki, 'the house of the foundation of heaven and earth', dedicated to Marduk. The Greek historian Herodotus described it in the fifth century BC: eight storeys, with a temple at the top. A ziggurat was a man-made mountain, a centre built by human hands where the gods were meant to come down.
So the first and last stories of Genesis 1–11 both face Babylon: its creation myth at the beginning, its great tower at the end.
background.key: Babel is Babylon, whose ziggurat was called 'the house of the foundation of heaven and earth'.

paras: The Gospel of John is the fourth account of Jesus in the New Testament. Christian tradition holds that it was written by John, one of the twelve disciples, in Ephesus near the end of the first century; many scholars think it comes from a community that looked to him as its founding witness. It was written in Greek for readers who knew both the Jewish Scriptures, in their Greek translation, and the ideas of Greek philosophy.

Its opening, John 1:1–18, is often called the Prologue. Notice its first words. 'In the beginning' is exactly how the Greek translation of Genesis begins (en archē). Genesis 1:1 says 'In the beginning, God created'; John 1:1 says 'In the beginning was the Word'. The famous line is John's, not Genesis's, and John chose its first words on purpose.
background.key: John's Gospel, written in Greek late in the first century, opens with the first words of Genesis on purpose.

paras: The main reading has three parts: the tower of Babel (Genesis 11:1–9); the call of Abraham (12:1–3), the hinge between the story of everyone and the story of one family; and the opening of John's Gospel (John 1:1–14), which reads Genesis 1 again from the other end.
The comparison returns to Augustine's Confessions, this time Book XI, where he asks how God 'spoke' the world into being, and what kind of word that was. It brings the course back to where it began.
background.key: Babel, Abraham, John 1, and Augustine on the Word.

before: What are the builders of Babel trying to do, and with what?
In Genesis 12, what does God promise Abraham, and for whose sake?
Which words in John 1 echo Genesis 1? What does John say the Word became?
sessions.readWhy: The last story of Genesis 1–11, the call of Abraham, and the Gospel that answers Genesis.

paras: The whole earth was of one language and of one speech.
As they traveled from the east, they found a plain in the land of Shinar, and they lived there.
They said to one another, “Come, let’s make bricks, and burn them thoroughly.” They had brick for stone, and they used tar for mortar.
They said, “Come, let’s build ourselves a city, and a tower whose top reaches to the sky, and let’s make a name for ourselves, lest we be scattered abroad on the surface of the whole earth.”
Yahweh came down to see the city and the tower, which the children of men built.
Yahweh said, “Behold, they are one people, and they all have one language, and this is what they begin to do. Now nothing will be withheld from them, which they intend to do.
Come, let’s go down, and there confuse their language, that they may not understand one another’s speech.”
So Yahweh scattered them abroad from there on the surface of all the earth. They stopped building the city.
Therefore its name was called Babel, because there Yahweh confused the language of all the earth. From there, Yahweh scattered them abroad on the surface of all the earth.
Now Yahweh said to Abram, “Leave your country, and your relatives, and your father’s house, and go to the land that I will show you.
I will make of you a great nation. I will bless you and make your name great. You will be a blessing.
I will bless those who bless you, and I will curse him who treats you with contempt. All the families of the earth will be blessed through you.”
In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
The same was in the beginning with God.
All things were made through him. Without him, nothing was made that has been made.
In him was life, and the life was the light of men.
The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness hasn’t overcome it.
There came a man, sent from God, whose name was John.
The same came as a witness, that he might testify about the light, that all might believe through him.
He was not the light, but was sent that he might testify about the light.
The true light that enlightens everyone was coming into the world.
He was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world didn’t recognize him.
He came to his own, and those who were his own didn’t receive him.
But as many as received him, to them he gave the right to become God’s children, to those who believe in his name:
who were born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God.
The Word became flesh, and lived among us. We saw his glory, such glory as of the one and only Son of the Father, full of grace and truth.

parts.title: The tower of Babel
parts.context: After the flood, Noah's descendants spread out (Genesis 10 lists seventy nations). This story steps back to tell how they came to speak different languages.

commentary.on: The whole earth was of one language and of one speech.
commentary.text: One language: one way of joining words to meanings, shared by everyone. Language is where heaven and earth meet in daily life: a sound, which is matter, carrying a meaning. Hold that thought.

commentary.on: As they traveled from the east, they found a plain in the land of Shinar
commentary.text: The Hebrew can mean 'from the east' or 'eastward'; either way, they are still on the move, far from Eden, and they settle on a flat plain. There is no mountain here. They will make one.

commentary.on: They had brick for stone, and they used tar for mortar.
commentary.text: A precise detail: in Mesopotamia there was little stone, so builders used baked mud bricks and bitumen. Stone is given; bricks are made. The tower is built entirely of human-made matter.

commentary.on: let’s build ourselves a city, and a tower whose top reaches to the sky, and let’s make a name for ourselves
commentary.text: A city, as Cain built; a tower to the sky, a mountain of their own; and a name. They want a centre where heaven and earth meet, but built from below, by their own technique, to their own glory. It is the fruit again: reaching for heaven by matter alone.

commentary.on: lest we be scattered abroad on the surface of the whole earth
commentary.text: They fear being scattered, and so resist the command to 'fill the earth' (Genesis 1:28; 9:1). Uniformity and control instead of filling the world God made.

commentary.on: Yahweh came down to see the city and the tower
commentary.text: Gentle irony: the tower meant to reach heaven is so small that God has to 'come down' to see it. Heaven cannot be reached from below. It can only come down.

commentary.on: Therefore its name was called Babel, because there Yahweh confused the language of all the earth.
commentary.text: A pun. The Babylonians said Bab-ili meant 'gate of god'. Genesis connects it with the Hebrew balal, 'to confuse'. Not the gate of heaven, but the place where words lose their shared meaning. The scattering is a judgement, and also a mercy: it breaks the power of one proud empire and sends people out to fill the earth.

parts.title: The call of Abraham
parts.context: Genesis 11 ends with the generations from Noah's son Shem to Abram (later Abraham), who lived in Ur in Mesopotamia and then in Haran. Then God speaks.

commentary.on: Leave your country, and your relatives, and your father’s house
commentary.text: After eleven chapters about all humanity, the story narrows to one man. God's answer to Babel is not a better tower but a call: leave, and trust. The way back to the centre does not begin with building upwards. It begins with listening to a word from above.

commentary.on: I will make of you a great nation. I will bless you and make your name great.
commentary.text: The builders of Babel wanted to 'make a name for ourselves'. God gives Abraham a great name as a gift. Greatness grasped, or greatness received: the difference between Babel and Abraham, and between Genesis 3 and the way back.

commentary.on: All the families of the earth will be blessed through you.
commentary.text: God chooses one family, not instead of the scattered nations, but for their sake. Christians read the rest of the Bible, and the coming of Jesus, as this promise kept. The next course in this hall follows Abraham.

parts.title: In the beginning was the Word
parts.context: The opening of John's Gospel, written in Greek late in the first century. 'Word' translates the Greek logos, which means a word, a speech, and also the reason or meaning behind something. The 'John' of verse 6 is John the Baptist, a prophet who prepared the way for Jesus.

commentary.on: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
commentary.text: John 1:1, not Genesis. John starts with the very words that start the Bible, 'In the beginning', and makes the link explicit. Genesis 1 told how God created by speaking: 'God said', ten times. John says that what God spoke was not a sound that passed away, but the Word, who was with God and was God.

commentary.on: All things were made through him. Without him, nothing was made that has been made.
commentary.text: Genesis 1 again: everything made by God's word. Now the Word is 'him', a person. The meaning through which the world was ordered, heaven giving form to earth, is personal.

commentary.on: The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness hasn’t overcome it.
commentary.text: 'Let there be light' (Genesis 1:3), and darkness on the face of the deep. John reads the first day as a picture of what the Word does always: light that the dark cannot master.

commentary.on: He was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world didn’t recognize him.
commentary.text: The tragedy of Genesis 3 in a sentence. The world made through the Word did not know him: eyes opened, but not to this.

commentary.on: The Word became flesh, and lived among us.
commentary.text: The centre of John's Gospel, and the answer to this course. In Genesis meaning comes down to give matter its form. Here meaning itself becomes matter: 'flesh', a human body. Heaven and earth meet, not in a garden or a tower, but in a person. 'Lived among us' is literally 'pitched his tent among us', the word for Israel's tabernacle, the movable Eden where God dwelt.

commentary.on: We saw his glory
commentary.text: The glory that filled the tabernacle and the Temple is now seen in a human face. The way to the tree of life, guarded since Genesis 3, has opened from the other side.

paras: But how didst Thou speak? In the way that the voice came out of the cloud, saying, This is my beloved Son? For that voice passed by and passed away, began and ended; the syllables sounded and passed away, the second after the first, the third after the second, and so forth in order, until the last after the rest, and silence after the last. Whence it is abundantly clear and plain that the motion of a creature expressed it, itself temporal, serving Thy eternal will. And these Thy words, created for a time, the outward ear reported to the intelligent soul, whose inward ear lay listening to Thy Eternal Word. But she compared these words sounding in time, with that Thy Eternal Word in silence, and said "It is different, far different. These words are far beneath me, nor are they, because they flee and pass away; but the Word of my Lord abideth above me for ever." If then in sounding and passing words Thou saidst that heaven and earth should be made, and so madest heaven and earth, there was a corporeal creature before heaven and earth, by whose motions in time that voice might take his course in time. But there was nought corporeal before heaven and earth; or if there were, surely Thou hadst, without such a passing voice, created that, whereof to make this passing voice, by which to say, Let the heaven and the earth be made. For whatsoever that were, whereof such a voice were made, unless by Thee it were made, it could not be at all. By what Word then didst Thou speak, that a body might be made, whereby these words again might be made?

Why, I beseech Thee, O Lord my God? I see it in a way; but how to express it, I know not, unless it be, that whatsoever begins to be, and leaves off to be, begins then, and leaves off then, when in Thy eternal Reason it is known, that it ought to begin or leave off; in which Reason nothing beginneth or leaveth off. This is Thy Word, which is also "the Beginning, because also It speaketh unto us." Thus in the Gospel He speaketh through the flesh; and this sounded outwardly in the ears of men; that it might be believed and sought inwardly, and found in the eternal Verity; where the good and only Master teacheth all His disciples. There, Lord, hear I Thy voice speaking unto me; because He speaketh us, who teacheth us; but He that teacheth us not, though He speaketh, to us He speaketh not. Who now teacheth us, but the unchangeable Truth? for even when we are admonished through a changeable creature; we are but led to the unchangeable Truth; where we learn truly, while we stand and hear Him, and rejoice greatly because of the Bridegroom's voice, restoring us to Him, from Whom we are. And therefore the Beginning, because unless It abided, there should not, when we went astray, be whither to return. But when we return from error, it is through knowing; and that we may know, He teacheth us, because He is the Beginning, and speaking unto us.

In this Beginning, O God, hast Thou made heaven and earth, in Thy Word, in Thy Son, in Thy Power, in Thy Wisdom, in Thy Truth; wondrously speaking, and wondrously making. Who shall comprehend? Who declare it? What is that which gleams through me, and strikes my heart without hurting it; and I shudder and kindle? I shudder, inasmuch as I am unlike it; I kindle, inasmuch as I am like it. It is Wisdom, Wisdom's self which gleameth through me; severing my cloudiness which yet again mantles over me, fainting from it, through the darkness which for my punishment gathers upon me. For my strength is brought down in need, so that I cannot support my blessings, till Thou, Lord, Who hast been gracious to all mine iniquities, shalt heal all my infirmities. For Thou shalt also redeem my life from corruption, and crown me with loving kindness and tender mercies, and shalt satisfy my desire with good things, because my youth shall be renewed like an eagle's. For in hope we are saved, wherefore we through patience wait for Thy promises. Let him that is able, hear Thee inwardly discoursing out of Thy oracle: I will boldly cry out, How wonderful are Thy works, O Lord, in Wisdom hast Thou made them all; and this Wisdom is the Beginning, and in that Beginning didst Thou make heaven and earth.

parts.author: Augustine of Hippo
parts.title: How did you speak?
parts.context: Augustine thinks of the voice from heaven at Jesus' baptism, 'This is my beloved Son' (Matthew 3:17). That voice was real sound: air moving, syllables one after another.
parts.plain: Augustine says: when God spoke from the cloud, the words were sounds made by something created, passing away one syllable after another. My soul heard them and said: these are far beneath me; they pass, but the Word of God lasts for ever. And God could not have made heaven and earth with such passing sounds, because before heaven and earth there was nothing physical to make a sound with. So by what Word did God speak?

commentary.on: For that voice passed by and passed away, began and ended
commentary.text: Here is what a word is, as we know it: a sound, a piece of matter, moving air, that comes and goes. And yet it carries a meaning that does not pass when the sound does. Every word joins earth and heaven in a small way.

commentary.on: the motion of a creature expressed it, itself temporal, serving Thy eternal will
commentary.text: The sound is earth; the meaning it serves is heaven. Augustine sees the two orders of Genesis 1 in every sentence spoken.

commentary.on: By what Word then didst Thou speak, that a body might be made
commentary.text: The question that leads to John 1. God's creating Word cannot be a sound, because sound needs a body and there were no bodies yet. It must be the eternal Word himself.

parts.author: Augustine of Hippo
parts.title: He speaks through the flesh
parts.context: Augustine leaves out a chapter (XI.7, marked '…') on how the eternal Word speaks all things at once. He calls the Word 'the Beginning', reading John 1:1 and Genesis 1:1 together: God made heaven and earth 'in the Beginning', that is, in the Word.
parts.plain: Augustine says: the Word is the eternal Reason of God, in which it is known when each thing should begin and end. In the Gospel this Word speaks through the flesh, so that people hear him outwardly and then find the truth within. He is called the Beginning because, unless he remained, there would be nowhere to return to when we went astray. In this Beginning God made heaven and earth. When this Wisdom shines in me I shudder, because I am unlike it, and I glow, because I am like it.

commentary.on: Thus in the Gospel He speaketh through the flesh; and this sounded outwardly in the ears of men
commentary.text: The Word became flesh, so the eternal meaning spoke in a human voice. Heaven used earth to reach us, as every word does, but here completely.

commentary.on: unless It abided, there should not, when we went astray, be whither to return
commentary.text: The whole course in a sentence. We went astray, east, from the centre. The way back exists because the Word, the Beginning, has not moved. The centre is not a place we left behind on a map; it is the Word who remains.

commentary.on: I shudder, inasmuch as I am unlike it; I kindle, inasmuch as I am like it.
commentary.text: Augustine stands where Adam stood: dust and breath, unlike God and like him. Unlikeness makes him tremble; likeness, the image of God, makes him burn. Remember his line in session 1: nearness to God 'is not farness of place'.

commentary.on: In this Beginning, O God, hast Thou made heaven and earth, in Thy Word
commentary.text: Augustine joins Genesis 1:1 and John 1:1 into one sentence: 'In the beginning God made heaven and earth' means God made them in the Word. The first line of the Bible already pointed to Christ.

compare.author: Augustine of Hippo
compare.why: In Book XI of the Confessions, just before the chapters on time, Augustine asks how God 'spoke' heaven and earth into being. Not, he says, as we speak, with sounds that pass. Read three short chapters: they explain what a word is, and why the Word became flesh.
compare.title: Augustine: the Word that does not pass away

paras: What does Genesis say about the world and about us? It says the world has two sides, heaven and earth, meaning and matter, and that God orders them by his word, so that the world is good. It says that the human being, dust and breath, was set at the centre where the two meet, to tend it. It says that knowledge grasped apart from God opened our eyes to ourselves, exposed, and sent us from the centre to the edge, where violence spread until the world nearly went back to chaos. And it says that God did not give up.

Is Genesis 1 science, myth or something else? It is not a scientific account: session 6 showed that, and most Christians agree. Nor is it myth in the sense of a false story: it answers the myths around it with a radically different picture of God and humanity. It is something else: true stories about what the world is and what we are, told in the forms of their time, which the oldest readers read with both eyes open.
sections.key: Genesis 1–11 is neither science nor mere myth: true stories about meaning and matter, the centre, exile and God's faithfulness.

paras: Babel is the last and largest attempt in Genesis to make a centre without God. A ziggurat was a man-made mountain, built so that heaven would come down to it. Its name in Babylon, 'the house of the foundation of heaven and earth', says exactly what it was for. Genesis notes that it was built of brick, not stone: matter made and stacked by human technique. The builders' aim is to 'make a name for ourselves'.

What happens is that their language breaks. Language was the thing that held their world together, sounds joined to shared meanings. At Babel the link between word and meaning comes apart. That is the logic of the story: when matter is gathered without meaning, people stop understanding one another. The judgement is also a mercy. No single empire, with one language and one will, gets to rule everyone.
sections.key: Babel tries to reach heaven from below with matter alone; the link between word and meaning breaks and the people scatter.

paras: A word is a strange thing. Physically it is almost nothing: a breath of air shaped by the mouth, or a few marks of ink. Yet it can carry a meaning that gathers countless things into one. The word 'tree' covers every oak and ash and apple that ever grew. A word is matter and meaning together, earth and heaven in a single sound. That is why language is where heaven and earth meet in ordinary life, and why Genesis 1 says God made the world by speaking.

Augustine saw this in the passage you have read. The voice from the cloud was real sound, which 'passed by and passed away'. What it meant did not pass. Every word we speak is a small likeness of creation: meaning given a body.
sections.key: A word is matter carrying meaning; language is where heaven and earth meet in daily life, a small likeness of creation.

paras: John wrote 'Word' in Greek: logos. For Greek readers it was a large word. It meant speech, but also reason, account, the meaning or order of something. Around 500 BC the philosopher Heraclitus taught that a logos, a rational order, runs through all things. The Stoic philosophers later called the divine reason that orders the universe the logos. The Jewish thinker Philo of Alexandria, a contemporary of Jesus, used the word for God's instrument in making the world. You will meet these thinkers properly in the Athens hall.

So when John wrote 'In the beginning was the Logos', Jewish readers heard Genesis, 'God said', and Greek readers heard the reason behind the universe. John claimed both, and then said something neither had said: that this Logos 'became flesh'.
sections.key: Logos means word, reason and meaning; John's readers heard both Genesis and Greek philosophy, and John said the Logos became flesh.

paras: John's opening is a deliberate rereading of Genesis 1. The famous words are John 1:1, not Genesis. But John begins where Genesis begins, and walks through its first day.

Genesis tells how meaning came down to order matter. John tells how meaning itself came down and became matter. That is the restoration of the centre: the meeting of heaven and earth is no longer only a place, a garden, a tent or a temple. It is a person.

sections.key: John 1 rereads Genesis 1 on purpose: the Word through whom all was made became flesh.

paras: Put the course together and the shape is clear. In Eden heaven and earth met, and the human being was the link. At the fall the link broke and humanity went east. At Babel people tried to rebuild the meeting from below, and failed. In the Word made flesh the meeting is restored from above: in Christ, Christians believe, God and humanity, meaning and matter, are joined in one person.

Later in the same chapter Jesus tells a new disciple, 'you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man' (John 1:51), recalling Jacob's dream of a stairway between earth and heaven, which the next course in this hall reads. Jesus himself is the stairway. And at Pentecost, as you saw in The whole story, many languages carried one message: Babel reversed. So the centre we lost was never a place in space. It is the meeting of heaven and earth, offered now in you.
sections.key: In the Word made flesh heaven and earth meet in a person; the lost centre was never a place but that meeting, now offered to each person.

paras: Between Babel and John stands Abraham. Genesis 11 ends with humanity scattered and proud. Genesis 12 begins God's answer: not a tower, but a call. 'Leave your country… I will make your name great… all the families of the earth will be blessed through you.' The name the Babel builders tried to make is given to Abraham as a gift. The blessing is for everyone.

That is why Genesis 1–11 matters for the whole Bible. Everything that follows, Abraham, the Exodus, the tabernacle and Temple, the kings and prophets, Jesus, the first Christians and the vision of a new creation, is the long way back to the centre.
sections.key: God's answer to Babel is a call, not a tower: Abraham's family, blessed for the sake of all.

sections.h: How the traditions read Genesis today
paras: Jews and Christians of every tradition hold Genesis to be Scripture. They differ in how they read its opening chapters.

debate.question: What kind of truth does Genesis 1–11 tell?

positions.name: Historical truth
positions.who: Traditional readers; young-earth creationists
positions.view: Genesis 1–11 records what actually happened, in order, and its theological truth depends on its historical accuracy.

positions.name: Theological history
positions.who: Many evangelical and Catholic scholars
positions.view: Genesis 1–11 refers to real events and people, such as a real fall, but tells them in a stylised, symbolic way suited to its time.

positions.name: Symbolic truth
positions.who: Origen and Augustine in their spiritual readings; modern symbolic readers such as Matthieu Pageau; many modern theologians
positions.view: Genesis 1–11 is above all about the structure of reality, heaven and earth, centre and edge, and the human place in it. Whether or not each event is historical, the stories show what is always true of the world and of us.
positions.evidence: The two heavens of Genesis 1; the sanctuary pattern of Eden; the movement east; John's rereading of Genesis 1.

closing.title: Your answer
closing.prompt: What does Genesis say about the world and about us? In about 300 words, make the case for what you think Genesis 1–11 truly teaches, using the frame of heaven and earth if it helps you, and answer the strongest objection to it.
closing.practice: Read the whole of Genesis 1–11 in one sitting, aloud if you can, and then John 1:1–14. Over the next week read Genesis again, a chapter a day, asking each time: where is the centre here, and who is moving towards it or away from it?
synthesis: This course asked what the Bible's first eleven chapters say about the world and about us. It read them as their oldest interpreters did, with two eyes open: one on matter, what things are made of, and one on meaning, what they are and what they are for. Here are the short answers, in order.

What do 'the heavens and the earth' mean? Everything; and, as Augustine saw, two orders of reality. 'Heaven' is the invisible order that gives things their meaning; 'earth', 'formless and empty', is matter waiting to receive it. God puts them in order by speaking, dividing and naming, and calls the result good. Is Genesis 1 a science lesson? No. It uses the ancient picture of the world, answers the Babylonian myths around it, and tells us what the world is and what it is for. Rashi, Augustine and Calvin all said it was not written to teach physics.

What is Eden? The centre of the world: the high place where heaven and earth meet, with its tree in the middle and its river flowing out to the four corners. It is described in the language of Israel's sanctuary, and Ezekiel calls it the holy mountain of God. What am I? Dust and breath: made from below, alive from above, the link between earth and heaven, God's image set at the centre to tend it and to name things truly.

What went wrong? A creature from the wild edge offered knowledge, and the man and woman took it apart from the one who gives things their meaning. 'Their eyes were opened': they saw themselves from outside, exposed, and were ashamed. They hid, blamed and were sent east, from the centre to the edge. Christians differ about what we inherit from that first wrong: inherited loss, inherited mortality, or inherited guilt; Jews reject original sin altogether. All agree that God came looking: 'Where are you?'

Why do people hurt each other? Because, away from the centre, violence spreads. Cain goes further east, builds a city with his own name on it, and his descendant Lamech sings of seventy-sevenfold revenge. Yet no one is fated: God warns Cain that he can master sin, and marks him for protection. Will God give up on us? No. The flood is creation undone, the waters God divided pouring back; then his wind moves over the deep as at the beginning, the world is ordered again, and he binds himself never to undo it. Geology finds no worldwide flood, and Christians read the story as global, local or theological.

Doesn't science say otherwise? Science rules out reading Genesis as a scientific timetable, as Huxley showed in 1885. It does not show that Genesis is false about what it was written to say. But knowledge of matter alone re-enacts the fruit: studying the world only from outside, we found ourselves small, exposed and off-centre. The historians add a correction: in the medieval picture the centre was the lowest place, and the first Copernicans did not feel demoted. Both are true. What modern people lost was never a place in space. It was the meeting of meaning and matter.

Why so many peoples? At Babel humanity tried to reach heaven from below, with bricks and a tower, to make a name for itself; and its one language, the meeting of sound and meaning, broke apart. Then God called Abraham and gave him a name as a gift, for the blessing of every family on earth.

And the Word? 'In the beginning was the Word' is John 1:1, not Genesis. John begins with Genesis's first words on purpose. Genesis showed meaning coming down to order matter; John says that meaning itself, the Word through whom all things were made, 'became flesh, and lived among us'. A word is a sound that carries a meaning, earth and heaven together; in Christ, Christians believe, heaven and earth meet in a person. So the centre we lost was never a point on a map. It is that meeting, restored, and offered to each person.

So what is Genesis 1–11? Neither science nor mere myth, but true stories about the shape of reality and our place in it, told in the forms of their time. Its picture of us is realistic and hopeful: dust and breath, made for the centre, exiled by our own grasping, never abandoned. It is worth counting how much of the West grew from these pages: the goodness of the material world, which made it worth studying; the dignity of every person as God's image; the weekly day of rest; the conviction that we are our brothers' keepers; the unity of the human family; even the dove with an olive leaf. Whatever you conclude, you cannot understand the West without them, or, perhaps, yourself.

title: Abraham and the promise
question: Why does the story turn on one family?
line: Seven sessions following one family for four generations, from Abraham leaving home to Joseph forgiving his brothers, asking at each step why God would choose them, what it meant for everyone else, and whether the hardest story, the binding of Isaac, can be answered.
why: Half the people on earth call Abraham their father. From Genesis 12 the Bible narrows from all humanity to one family, and the Christian, Jewish and Muslim faiths all grew from what happened next: a promise, a covenant, a son nearly sacrificed, a cheat renamed Israel, and brothers reconciled. This journey reads Genesis 12–50 with the New Testament, the Qur'an, Jewish legend, Ovid and the sceptics, and asks the obvious question: why them? It is written at the depth of a first-year university course, for anyone.
follows: A first-year theology paper on the patriarchal narratives of Genesis 12–50, with elements of papers on the Abrahamic faiths, the doctrine of justification and the philosophy of religion (Kierkegaard and Kant on Genesis 22).

Weigh the historical and archaeological evidence for the patriarchs, including the anachronisms.
Explain the covenant ceremony of Genesis 15 and how Paul and James use Genesis 15:6, and set out Catholic, Protestant, Orthodox and Jewish views of faith and works.
Read the stories of Hagar and Ishmael from several sides, including Paul's allegory and their place in Islam.
Explain Abraham's argument for Sodom, what it shows about God's justice, and the debate about Sodom's sin.
State the objection to the binding of Isaac at full strength (Kant, Ingersoll) and compare Jewish, Christian, Islamic and Kierkegaardian readings.
Trace Jacob's change from Bethel to the Jabbok, and compare the traditions' views of election.
Explain Joseph's forgiveness and the idea of providence in Genesis 50:20, and give a reasoned answer to the scandal of particularity.

sessions.title: Would you leave everything?
sessions.line: One man is told to leave his country, his family and his gods, and he goes.
sessions.plain: God tells Abram (later called Abraham) to leave his home and his gods and go to a land he has never seen, and promises that through him every family on earth will be blessed. He goes. Then, almost at once, he lies to save his own skin. This session reads the call that turns the whole Bible, and asks what kind of man was chosen.

background.h: Where we are, and the question
paras: Genesis 1 to 11 is everyone's story: a good creation, the fall, the flood, and the tower of Babel, where humanity was scattered. At chapter 12 the story changes and follows one family for four generations: Abraham, his son Isaac, his grandson Jacob, and Jacob's twelve sons, above all Joseph.

So the question of this journey is simple: why does the story turn on one family? If God cares about the whole world, why choose one man? We follow the family in order, hear the strongest objection (the binding of Isaac) in session 5, still to come, and give a verdict at the end.

background.key: From chapter 12 the Bible follows one family. Why them? That is the question of the journey.

paras: Abraham is called Abram at first, and his wife Sarah is Sarai; God will rename them in session 2. Lot is his nephew. Yahweh is God's personal name in the Hebrew Bible, printed 'the LORD' in many English Bibles.

If Genesis's numbers are added up, Abraham lived around 2000 to 1800 BC. His family starts in Ur, near the mouth of the Euphrates in today's southern Iraq, moves about 1,000 kilometres north-west to Haran in today's south-eastern Turkey, and from there Abraham goes south into Canaan, roughly modern Israel and the Palestinian territories. Ur and Haran were both centres of the worship of the moon god, Sin.

timeline.text: Ur at its height; its great ziggurat is built for the moon god

background.key: Abram and Sarai, later Abraham and Sarah, around 2000–1800 BC: from Ur to Haran to Canaan.

paras: Genesis does not say who wrote it. Jewish and Christian tradition held that Moses wrote the first five books of the Bible. From the Middle Ages on, careful readers noticed clues pointing to later hands: Genesis 36:31 lists 'the kings who reigned in the land of Edom, before any king reigned over the children of Israel', which sounds like someone writing after Israel had kings. Most scholars think Genesis was put together over centuries from older stories and reached its final form around 600 to 400 BC. Many believers accept this and still read it as inspired; others hold to the traditional view. ('What is the Bible?' weighs the evidence; whether Abraham himself existed is in this session's lecture.)

Abraham's world already had cities, writing and stories of its own, and Genesis shares much with it: lists of ancestors, a great flood, customs found in Hammurabi's laws. What is new is the God: one God, not many, who speaks to one man and makes him a promise for the sake of the whole world.
background.key: Tradition says Moses; most scholars say many hands, finished around 600–400 BC. The setting is ancient; the God is new.

paras: The reading has four parts: the family's background, with a verse from Joshua saying they 'served other gods'; the call itself (12:1–9); Abraham at his worst, straight afterwards (12:10–20); and a New Testament view of what he did (Hebrews 11). The comparison is the Jewish and Muslim story of Abraham and the idols, which answers what Genesis leaves out: why did he leave his father's gods?
background.key: The call, Abraham's failure, a New Testament view, and the story of Abraham and the idols.

before: What exactly does God ask Abraham to leave, and what does he promise in return?
Who is the promise for? Look for the word 'all'.
In Egypt, what does Abraham do, and who comes out of the story looking better?
sessions.readWhy: The call of Abraham, the hinge of the whole Bible, read in four parts: his family, the call, his first failure, and how the New Testament saw it.

paras: Now this is the history of the generations of Terah. Terah became the father of Abram, Nahor, and Haran. Haran became the father of Lot.
Haran died in the land of his birth, in Ur of the Chaldees, while his father Terah was still alive.
Abram and Nahor married wives. The name of Abram’s wife was Sarai, and the name of Nahor’s wife was Milcah, the daughter of Haran, who was also the father of Iscah.
Sarai was barren. She had no child.

Terah took Abram his son, Lot the son of Haran, his son’s son, and Sarai his daughter-in-law, his son Abram’s wife. They went from Ur of the Chaldees, to go into the land of Canaan. They came to Haran and lived there.
The days of Terah were two hundred five years. Terah died in Haran.
Joshua said to all the people, “Yahweh, the God of Israel, says, ‘Your fathers lived of old time beyond the River, even Terah, the father of Abraham, and the father of Nahor. They served other gods.
I took your father Abraham from beyond the River, and led him throughout all the land of Canaan, and multiplied his offspring, and gave him Isaac.
Now Yahweh said to Abram, “Leave your country, and your relatives, and your father’s house, and go to the land that I will show you.
I will make of you a great nation. I will bless you and make your name great. You will be a blessing.
I will bless those who bless you, and I will curse him who treats you with contempt. All the families of the earth will be blessed through you.”
So Abram went, as Yahweh had told him. Lot went with him. Abram was seventy-five years old when he departed from Haran.

Abram took Sarai his wife, Lot his brother’s son, all their possessions that they had gathered, and the people whom they had acquired in Haran, and they went to go into the land of Canaan. They entered into the land of Canaan.
Abram passed through the land to the place of Shechem, to the oak of Moreh. At that time, Canaanites were in the land.
Yahweh appeared to Abram and said, “I will give this land to your offspring.”
He built an altar there to Yahweh, who had appeared to him.
He left from there to go to the mountain on the east of Bethel and pitched his tent, having Bethel on the west, and Ai on the east. There he built an altar to Yahweh and called on Yahweh’s name.
Abram traveled, still going on toward the South.
There was a famine in the land. Abram went down into Egypt to live as a foreigner there, for the famine was severe in the land.
When he had come near to enter Egypt, he said to Sarai his wife, “See now, I know that you are a beautiful woman to look at.
It will happen, when the Egyptians see you, that they will say, ‘This is his wife.’ They will kill me, but they will save you alive.
Please say that you are my sister, that it may be well with me for your sake, and that my soul may live because of you.”
When Abram had come into Egypt, Egyptians saw that the woman was very beautiful.
The princes of Pharaoh saw her, and praised her to Pharaoh; and the woman was taken into Pharaoh’s house.
He dealt well with Abram for her sake. He had sheep, cattle, male donkeys, male servants, female servants, female donkeys, and camels.
Yahweh afflicted Pharaoh and his house with great plagues because of Sarai, Abram’s wife.
Pharaoh called Abram and said, “What is this that you have done to me? Why didn’t you tell me that she was your wife?
Why did you say, ‘She is my sister,’ so that I took her to be my wife? Now therefore, see your wife, take her, and go your way.”
Pharaoh commanded men concerning him, and they escorted him away with his wife and all that he had.
By faith, Abraham, when he was called, obeyed to go out to the place which he was to receive for an inheritance. He went out, not knowing where he went.
By faith, he lived as an alien in the land of promise, as in a land not his own, dwelling in tents with Isaac and Jacob, the heirs with him of the same promise.
For he looked for the city which has the foundations, whose builder and maker is God.
By faith, even Sarah herself received power to conceive, and she bore a child when she was past age, since she counted him faithful who had promised.
Therefore as many as the stars of the sky in multitude, and as innumerable as the sand which is by the sea shore, were fathered by one man, and him as good as dead.
These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them and embraced them from afar, and having confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth.
For those who say such things make it clear that they are seeking a country of their own.
If indeed they had been thinking of that country from which they went out, they would have had enough time to return.
But now they desire a better country, that is, a heavenly one. Therefore God is not ashamed of them, to be called their God, for he has prepared a city for them.

parts.title: A family from Ur
parts.context: The last verses of Genesis 11 introduce Abraham's family. With them we read two verses from the book of Joshua, written about Israel's later history: Joshua, Moses' successor, reminds the people where they came from.

commentary.on: Now this is the history of the generations of Terah.
commentary.text: Genesis is organised by these 'generations' (in Hebrew, toledot): 'this is the history of…'. Each one opens a new chapter of the family story. This one introduces Terah, Abraham's father, and it will run all the way to Abraham's death.

commentary.on: Haran died in the land of his birth, in Ur of the Chaldees
commentary.text: Ur was one of the oldest and richest cities in the world. Do not confuse Haran, Abraham's brother, with Haran the city where the family later settles: in Hebrew they are spelt differently. 'Of the Chaldees' is a detail worth noticing: the Chaldeans are first mentioned in records of the ninth century BC, so this phrase was probably added by a later writer to tell readers which Ur was meant.

commentary.on: Sarai was barren. She had no child.
commentary.text: Five words, and the whole story hangs on them. Everything God is about to promise depends on children, and Sarai cannot have them. The Bible often begins its greatest stories with an impossibility.

commentary.on: They went from Ur of the Chaldees, to go into the land of Canaan. They came to Haran and lived there.
commentary.text: The journey starts before God speaks, with Terah, and stalls halfway. Abraham's call in the next chapter is to finish a journey his father did not.

commentary.on: Your fathers lived of old time beyond the River, even Terah, the father of Abraham, and the father of Nahor. They served other gods.
commentary.text: Genesis never says so, but this verse does: Abraham's family worshipped other gods. 'The River' is the Euphrates. So the call is not only to a new place. It is out of a whole world of gods, into trust in one God. That is the gap the comparison readings fill in.

parts.title: The call
parts.context: The family has settled in Haran. Then God speaks to Abram: the first words God says to him, and the turning point of the whole Bible.

commentary.on: Leave your country, and your relatives, and your father’s house
commentary.text: Three circles, each closer than the last: his country, his clan, his own father's household. In the ancient world these were everything: your safety, your identity, your inheritance, your gods. He is asked to give up all three, for a land God has not yet named: 'the land that I will show you'.

commentary.on: I will make of you a great nation. I will bless you and make your name great.
commentary.text: Remember Babel, just one chapter earlier, where people said 'let's make a name for ourselves'. Here God says 'I will make your name great'. What the builders tried to seize, God gives as a gift.

commentary.on: You will be a blessing.
commentary.text: The blessing is not only for Abram. He is blessed in order to be a blessing. That is the first answer this journey will find to its question: the family is chosen for the sake of others.

commentary.on: All the families of the earth will be blessed through you.
commentary.text: The most important sentence in the passage. The scattered 'families of the earth' from Genesis 10–11 are not forgotten. God chooses one family as the way to reach every family. The New Testament will quote this sentence as the first announcement of the gospel (Galatians 3:8).

commentary.on: So Abram went, as Yahweh had told him.
commentary.text: No argument, no questions, no reply recorded at all. He simply goes. He is seventy-five years old. This is what the Bible will later call faith: trusting God enough to act.

commentary.on: At that time, Canaanites were in the land.
commentary.text: The promised land is not empty. Other peoples live there. The promise will take generations to come true, and Abraham will die owning only a grave (Genesis 23).

commentary.on: There he built an altar to Yahweh and called on Yahweh’s name.
commentary.text: Wherever Abraham stops, he builds an altar: a pile of stones on which to offer sacrifices. He claims no land, but he marks it out for God. Shechem and Bethel will become two of Israel's holiest places.

parts.title: Straight away, a lie
parts.context: Immediately after the call, famine strikes Canaan, and Abram goes down to Egypt, which had the Nile and grain when other lands did not. Genesis tells this story straight after the promise, and it tells a similar one twice more (Genesis 20 and 26).

commentary.on: Please say that you are my sister, that it may be well with me for your sake
commentary.text: The man who has just trusted God with his whole future does not trust God with this. Afraid of being killed for his beautiful wife, he asks her to pretend to be his sister. (She was in fact his half-sister, Genesis 20:12 says; a half-truth is still a lie.) He saves himself by putting her at risk.

commentary.on: the woman was taken into Pharaoh’s house
commentary.text: Sarai is taken into the king's household as a wife, and Abram is paid handsomely. It is a shocking story, told without comment. The promised mother of the promised family is lost to a foreign king within a page of the promise.

commentary.on: He had sheep, cattle, male donkeys, male servants, female servants, female donkeys, and camels.
commentary.text: Notice 'camels': this detail matters for the lecture. Domesticated camels are not found in Canaan's archaeology until the tenth century BC, so many scholars think the storyteller has described Abraham's wealth in the terms of a later age.

commentary.on: Yahweh afflicted Pharaoh and his house with great plagues because of Sarai, Abram’s wife.
commentary.text: God protects Sarai, and so his own promise, when Abram does not. The plagues on Pharaoh look forward to the plagues of Egypt in Exodus, when Abraham's descendants are rescued from another Pharaoh.

commentary.on: What is this that you have done to me? Why didn’t you tell me that she was your wife?
commentary.text: The pagan king behaves more honourably than the man of faith, and rebukes him. Genesis does not hide this. Its heroes are not chosen because they are good. That will be true of every generation of this family.

parts.title: How the New Testament saw it
parts.context: The Letter to the Hebrews, written in the first century AD by an unknown early Christian, has a famous chapter on faith which lists the heroes of Israel's story. This is its section on Abraham and Sarah.

commentary.on: He went out, not knowing where he went.
commentary.text: Hebrews sums up the call in one line. Faith, here, is not believing something without evidence; it is setting out on someone's word without knowing the destination.

commentary.on: dwelling in tents with Isaac and Jacob
commentary.text: Abraham never builds a house in the promised land. He lives in tents, like a nomad, and so do his son and grandson. He is a resident foreigner in the land he was promised.

commentary.on: For he looked for the city which has the foundations, whose builder and maker is God.
commentary.text: Hebrews reads the tents as a sign: Abraham was looking for something more than a piece of land. Compare Babel again: there, people built a city to reach heaven; Abraham waits for a city God builds.

commentary.on: These all died in faith, not having received the promises
commentary.text: An honest line. Abraham died without seeing the promise come true: he had one son of the promise, not a nation, and a grave, not a land. Faith in the Bible often means living towards a promise you will not see fulfilled.

commentary.on: they desire a better country, that is, a heavenly one
commentary.text: This is a Christian reading: the earthly land points to a heavenly one. Jewish readers keep the promise of the land itself in view, as you will see in the next session.

paras: When Abraham attained the age of twenty years, his father Terah fell ill. He spoke as follows to his sons Haran and Abraham, "I adjure you by your lives, my sons, sell these two idols for me, for I have not enough money to meet our expenses." Haran executed the wish of his father, but if any one accosted Abraham, to buy an idol from him, and asked him the price, he would answer, "Three manehs," and then question in turn, "How old art thou?" "Thirty years," the reply would be. "Thou art thirty years of age, and yet thou wouldst worship this idol which I made but to-day?" The man would depart and go his way, and another would approach Abraham, and ask, "How much is this idol?" and "Five manehs" would be the reply, and again Abraham would put the question, "How old art thou?"--"Fifty years."--"And dost thou who art fifty years of age bow down before this idol which was made but to-day?" Thereupon the man would depart and go his way. Abraham then took two idols, put a rope about their necks, and, with their faces turned downward, he dragged them along the ground, crying aloud all the time: "Who will buy an idol wherein there is no profit, either unto itself or unto him that buys it in order to worship it? It has a mouth, but it speaketh not; eyes, but it seeth not; feet, but it walketh not; ears, but it heareth not."

Alone with the idols, and while he repeated the words, "The Eternal He is God, the Eternal He is God!" he struck the king's idols from their thrones, and began to belabor them with an axe. With the biggest he started, and with the smallest he ended. He hacked off the feet of one, and the other he beheaded. This one had his eyes struck out, the other had his hands crushed. After all were mutilated, he went away, having first put the axe into the hand of the largest idol.

The feast ended, the king returned, and when he saw all his idols shivered in pieces, he inquired who had perpetrated the mischief. Abraham was named as the one who had been guilty of the outrage, and the king summoned him and questioned him as to his motive for the deed. Abraham replied: "I did not do it; it was the largest of the idols who shattered all the rest. Seest thou not that he still has the axe in his hand? And if thou wilt not believe my words, ask him and he will tell thee."

Of old we gave unto Abraham his direction, for we knew him worthy.
When he said to his Father and to his people, "What are these images to which ye are devoted?"
They said, "We found our fathers worshipping them."
He said, "Truly ye and your fathers have been in a plain mistake."
They said, "Hast thou come unto us in earnest? or art thou of those who jest?"
He said, "Nay, your Lord is Lord of the Heavens and of the Earth, who hath created them both; and to this am I one of those who witness:
-And, by God, I will certainly lay a plot against your idols, after ye shall have retired and turned your backs."
So, he broke them all in pieces, except the chief of them, that to it they might return, inquiring.
They said, "Who hath done this to our gods? Verily he is one of the unjust."
They said, "We heard a youth make mention of them: they call him Abraham."
They said, "Then bring him before the people's eyes, that they may witness against him."
They said, "Hast thou done this to our gods, O Abraham?"
He said, "Nay, that their chief hath done it: but ask ye them, if they can speak."
So they turned their thoughts upon themselves, and said, "Ye truly are the impious persons:"
Then became headstrong in their former error and exclaimed,"Thou knowest that these speak not."
He said, "What! do ye then worship, instead of God, that which doth not profit you at all, nor injure you? Fie on you and on that ye worship instead of God! What! do ye not then understand?"
They said: "Burn him, and come to the succour of your gods: if ye will do anything at all."
We said, "O fire! be thou cold, and to Abraham a safety!"

parts.author: Louis Ginzberg
parts.work: The Legends of the Jews, volume I
parts.ref: Legends of the Jews: Abraham and the idols
parts.title: The idol-seller's son
parts.context: Louis Ginzberg (1873–1953), a great Jewish scholar, gathered the stories that rabbis told about the Bible's characters over many centuries, from the Midrash (Jewish commentary in story form) and the Talmud, and retold them in seven volumes (1909–38). This story is first found in Genesis Rabbah 38:13, a Jewish commentary on Genesis from about AD 400–500. In Ginzberg's version Terah makes idols; in the second scene, Abraham is in the palace of King Nimrod, the 'mighty hunter' of Genesis 10, whom legend made Abraham's persecutor. The '…' marks a cut.
parts.plain: The legend says: Abraham's father Terah made and sold idols. When Abraham was sent to sell them, he asked the customers how a grown man could worship something made yesterday, and dragged the idols through the street. Later, left alone with the king's idols, he smashed them all and put the axe in the hand of the biggest. When the king asked who had done it, Abraham said: ask the big idol, he did it.

commentary.on: Thou art thirty years of age, and yet thou wouldst worship this idol which I made but to-day?
commentary.text: The argument is simple, and deep: how can something you made be your god? It is the same argument the Hebrew prophets use (Isaiah 44:9–20).

commentary.on: It has a mouth, but it speaketh not; eyes, but it seeth not
commentary.text: These words come almost exactly from Psalm 115:5–6. The legend puts the psalm's mockery of idols into Abraham's mouth, making him the first to see what the psalm would later say.

commentary.on: having first put the axe into the hand of the largest idol
commentary.text: A joke with a point. Abraham does not argue; he sets a trap. If the idols are gods, the big one could have done it. If they are not, the king must admit it.

commentary.on: ask him and he will tell thee.
commentary.text: The punchline: the king cannot ask the idol, because it cannot speak, and to say so is to admit that it is no god. In the rest of the legend, as in the Qur'an, the king throws Abraham into a furnace and God saves him.

parts.author: The Qur'an
parts.title: Abraham breaks the idols
parts.context: The Qur'an is the holy book of Islam, revealed, Muslims believe, to the Prophet Muhammad between about AD 610 and 632. It tells many stories of Abraham (Ibrahim in Arabic), whom it calls a prophet and the 'friend of God'. This translation is by J. M. Rodwell, an English clergyman (1861). The one-line breaks follow the verses.
parts.plain: The Qur'an says: God gave Abraham true guidance. Abraham asked his father and his people why they worshipped statues, broke them all except the biggest, and told the people to ask the big one who had done it. They had to admit that the idols could not speak. So they tried to burn him, and God made the fire cool.

commentary.on: They said, "We found our fathers worshipping them."
commentary.text: The people's only defence of their gods is custom: it is what our fathers did. Abraham's call is, precisely, to leave his father's house. Both the Jewish and the Islamic stories make him the first person to think the question through.

commentary.on: So, he broke them all in pieces, except the chief of them
commentary.text: The same story as the Jewish legend, almost detail for detail: the idols smashed, the biggest left, the challenge to ask it. The two traditions shared many stories about Abraham, told and retold in the centuries around Muhammad's time.

commentary.on: We said, "O fire! be thou cold, and to Abraham a safety!"
commentary.text: God rescues Abraham from the fire, as in the Jewish legend. In Islam, Abraham is the great example of the hanif: a person who turned from idols to the one God by his own clear sight, before Judaism or Christianity existed (the Qur'an says he 'was neither Jew nor Christian', Sura 3:67).

compare.author: Louis Ginzberg and The Qur'an
compare.work: The Legends of the Jews, volume I
compare.ref: Legends of the Jews: Abraham and the idols
compare.why: Genesis does not say why Abraham left his father's gods. Later Jews and Muslims told a famous story to explain it. Read the Jewish version, from a collection of ancient Jewish legends, and the Qur'an's version, which is remarkably similar.
compare.title: Abraham and the idols

paras: After Babel the question left hanging is: what will God do about the whole world now? Genesis 12 gives a surprising answer. Not a new flood, and not a message to everyone at once, but one man and a promise. Five times in three verses comes the word 'bless'. The story narrows so that the blessing can widen: one family, for the sake of 'all the families of the earth'. Hold on to that pattern. It is the Bible's first answer to the question of this journey.
sections.key: After Babel, God answers the world's problem through one family, blessed in order to bless every family on earth.

paras: There is no archaeological evidence of Abraham himself: no inscription, no grave that can be tested. We should not expect one; nomads leave little behind. So the question is whether the stories fit the world they describe.

In the mid-twentieth century many scholars, led by the American archaeologist William F. Albright, thought they did. Names like Abram and Jacob are found in documents of the early second millennium BC; tablets from Mari, on the Euphrates, describe semi-nomadic herders moving between towns; and customs in the stories, such as a childless wife giving her servant to her husband, appear in ancient laws and contracts. From the 1970s Thomas L. Thompson and John Van Seters argued that the parallels were weak or fitted later periods just as well, and that the stories were written in the first millennium BC. The camels and 'Ur of the Chaldees' point the same way.

Where things stand now: most scholars think the stories as we have them were shaped centuries after the time they describe, and that they cannot be proved or disproved as history. Some, such as the Egyptologist Kenneth Kitchen, argue that details fit the early second millennium well. Many think they keep real memories of the family's origins. The honest answer is that we do not know, and that the stories' importance never depended on archaeology: their power is in what they say about God and people.
