sections.key: Nothing in archaeology proves or disproves Abraham; most scholars think the stories were shaped later, while some argue they fit an earlier age.

paras: About half the people on earth belong to a religion that calls Abraham its father: Judaism, Christianity and Islam are often called the 'Abrahamic' faiths. In all three he has the same title, the friend of God (Isaiah 41:8; James 2:23; Qur'an 4:125). His traditional tomb, the Cave of Machpelah in Hebron, is holy to Jews and Muslims alike; the Arabic name of Hebron, al-Khalil, means 'the friend'.
But each faith claims him differently, and the differences matter for the whole journey.

rows: Avraham Avinu, 'Abraham our father', the first Jew, who made God known in the world
Being born into, or joining, the people of the covenant, and keeping it
The 'father of all those who believe' (Romans 4:11), Jew and Gentile
Isaac; and Jesus as Abraham's promised offspring (Matthew 1:1; Galatians 3:16)
Ibrahim, a prophet, the hanif who turned from idols; 'neither Jew nor Christian' (Sura 3:67)
Ismail (Ishmael), ancestor of the Arabs and of Muhammad, and Ishaq (Isaac)
Submitting to God as Abraham did; 'Muslim' means 'one who submits'

sections.key: Jews, Christians and Muslims all call Abraham father and 'friend of God', but each claims him through a different son or a different kind of family.

paras: The surprising thing about Abraham is how little Genesis praises him. It never says he was chosen because he was good, wise or devout. God simply calls him. Then, within a page, he lies, endangers his wife, and is scolded by a pagan king. He does it again in Genesis 20. His son Isaac does the same thing in Genesis 26.

This is deliberate, and it is the second clue to the journey's question. If God chose the best family, the story would be about them. Because he chooses an ordinary, flawed family and keeps his promise in spite of them, the story is about him. Genesis gives its own reason later, and it looks forward, not back: God has chosen Abraham 'that he may command his children and his household after him… to do righteousness and justice' (Genesis 18:19, which you will read in session 4).
sections.key: Genesis shows Abraham's failures straight after his call: the family is chosen by grace, not for being good.

paras: What did Abraham actually do? He left. That is the first picture of faith in the Bible: not a feeling, not a theory, but a journey on the strength of a promise. Hebrews calls it going out 'not knowing where he went'.

Ancient people usually belonged to a place and its gods. Abraham's God is not tied to a place: he speaks in Haran, appears at Shechem, rescues in Egypt. This is part of what made Abraham's faith new. The God who calls him is the God of the whole earth, who goes with his people wherever they go.
sections.key: Abraham's faith is first of all action: leaving on the strength of a promise, following a God not tied to any one place.

refs: Genesis 11:27–12:20; Genesis 20; 26:6–11; Joshua 24:2–3; Hebrews 11:8–16; Acts 7:2–4.

Archaeology: W. F. Albright, The Archaeology of Palestine (1949); Thomas L. Thompson, The Historicity of the Patriarchal Narratives (1974); John Van Seters, Abraham in History and Tradition (1975); Kenneth Kitchen, On the Reliability of the Old Testament (2003), chapter 7.
Camels: Lidar Sapir-Hen and Erez Ben-Yosef, 'The Introduction of Domestic Camels to the Southern Levant', Tel Aviv 40 (2013): 277–285.
Ur and Haran as centres of the moon god Sin: Leonard Woolley, Ur of the Chaldees (1929); Ur was excavated 1922–34.
The idols story: Genesis Rabbah 38:13; Louis Ginzberg, The Legends of the Jews I (1909); Qur'an 21:51–71, 6:74–83, 3:67, 4:125.
Friend of God: Isaiah 41:8; 2 Chronicles 20:7; James 2:23; Qur'an 4:125.

debate.question: How much history is in the Abraham stories?

positions.name: Substantially historical
positions.who: Kenneth Kitchen; many conservative scholars
positions.view: Abraham was a real man of the early second millennium BC, and the stories preserve reliable memories of his life, with some details updated by later scribes.
positions.evidence: Names, customs and ways of life that fit the Middle Bronze Age; the unflattering honesty of the stories, which no one would invent about a national founder.

positions.name: Memories retold
positions.who: Many mainstream scholars
positions.view: There may be real ancestral memories behind the stories, but they were shaped and written down centuries later to speak to Israel's own time, so we cannot recover the history behind them.
positions.evidence: Anachronisms such as camels and the Chaldeans; the stories' focus on later concerns such as the land and neighbouring peoples.

positions.name: Later literature
positions.who: Thomas L. Thompson, John Van Seters
positions.view: The stories were composed in the first millennium BC, perhaps during or after the exile in Babylon, as a founding story for the people; they are not history in any useful sense.
positions.evidence: The weakness of the Bronze Age parallels; the many features that fit the first millennium better.

debate.agree: All agree that there is no direct archaeological evidence of Abraham, and that the stories reached their present form long after the time they describe.

look.why: George Catlin, an American painter who travelled among the native peoples of North America, painted this camp of skin tents between 1855 and 1869. It has nothing to do with Abraham, but it shows the way of life Hebrews describes: a people 'dwelling in tents', moving with their herds, at home in the land without owning it.
points: A camp seen from above, with tents scattered across open land.
Small figures busy among the tents.
Low hills in the background, and a glowing sky at sunrise or sunset.
Green land stretching into the distance, with a river or water on the right.

music.why: 'Precious Lord, take my hand, lead me on': Thomas A. Dorsey's gospel song is the prayer of someone walking a road they cannot see the end of, which is Abraham's road.

think.why: Abraham is the first person in the Bible to be called out alone, by name, from his family and its gods. The idea of the individual person before God starts here.

learn.why: The New Testament's summary of Abraham's faith: going out, not knowing where.

check.q: Genesis tells the story of Abraham lying in Egypt straight after God's promise. What is the best explanation of why?
options: To show from the start that God chose Abraham by grace, not because he was good, and keeps his promise in spite of him
To show that Abraham was punished for lying
To explain why Abraham's descendants later had to go down to Egypt
To show that Abraham's faith was already complete before the covenant
check.why: Abraham is not punished; Pharaoh is. The story shows God protecting his promise when Abraham fails it.

check.q: God says 'I will make your name great'. Which earlier story is this deliberately answering?
options: The creation of Adam
Cain and Abel
The flood
The tower of Babel, where people said 'let's make a name for ourselves'
check.why: What the builders tried to seize, God gives as a gift.

check.q: Why do many scholars think the camels in Genesis 12:16 tell us something about when the story was written?
options: Because camels could not have crossed the desert from Haran to Canaan
Because domestic camels are not found in Canaan's archaeology until the tenth century BC, so the detail may reflect a later age
Because Genesis elsewhere says Abraham travelled only with donkeys
Because the Hebrew word may mean donkeys, so it is a mistranslation
check.why: It may be a later storyteller's updating; it does not by itself show the story is invented.

check.q: What does Joshua 24:2 add to Genesis's account of Abraham?
options: That Abraham's family 'served other gods' beyond the Euphrates
That Abraham smashed his father's idols
That God first called Abraham while he was still in Ur
That Terah refused to leave Ur
check.why: So the call is out of a world of many gods, which is the gap the idol stories fill.

check.q: A Jew, a Christian and a Muslim all call Abraham 'father'. Which statement is accurate?
options: They agree that his heir was Isaac
Muslims, like Jews, claim him chiefly through Isaac
Christians claim him through faith, Jews through the covenant people descended from Isaac and Jacob, and Muslims chiefly through Ishmael and his submission to God
Only Christians call him 'friend of God'
check.why: All three call him 'friend of God'; they differ over the line and the meaning of being his child.

check.q: What is the most accurate summary of the archaeological evidence for Abraham?
options: There is no direct evidence either way; scholars debate how well the stories fit the early second millennium BC
Inscriptions from Ur name him
Tablets from Mari mention Abraham by name
Archaeology has disproved his existence
check.why: Nothing proves or disproves him; the debate is about how well the stories fit their setting.

tutorial.question: Why does the Bible's story turn, at Genesis 12, from the whole world to one man?
tutorial.approach: Start with the problem left at the end of Genesis 1–11 (Babel). Then read the promise of 12:1–3 closely: what is promised, and for whom. Use the story of the lie in Egypt to say what kind of man Abraham is, and what that shows about why he was chosen. Finish with what Jews, Christians and Muslims each make of him.
strong: Connects Genesis 12 with Babel: the scattered nations and the 'name'.
Notices that the blessing is for 'all the families of the earth'.
Uses the lie in Egypt to show that Abraham was chosen by grace, not merit.
Explains what Abraham left behind, including his family's gods (Joshua 24:2).
Is honest about the historical evidence: no proof either way.
Distinguishes how Judaism, Christianity and Islam claim Abraham.

reading.author: Bruce Feiler
reading.title: Abraham: A Journey to the Heart of Three Faiths
reading.why: A journalist's lively journey through Abraham's lands and the three faiths.

reading.author: Jon D. Levenson
reading.title: Inheriting Abraham
reading.why: A leading Jewish scholar on how Judaism, Christianity and Islam each claim Abraham, and why the differences matter.

reading.author: John Van Seters
reading.title: Abraham in History and Tradition
reading.why: The classic argument that the stories are late; read with Kitchen's reply.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: do one thing you have been putting off because you cannot see how it will turn out, a conversation, an apology, an offer of help, trusting that it is right even without knowing the outcome.
sessions.reflect: What would you find hardest to leave: your country, your family, or the way your family has always done things?
takeaways: At Genesis 12 the story narrows from all humanity to one family, so that 'all the families of the earth' may be blessed.
Abraham leaves his country, his family and its gods; straight away he fails, and God keeps his promise anyway.
There is no direct evidence of Abraham; Jews, Christians and Muslims all call him father, through different sons and in different ways.

sessions.title: When God makes a promise
sessions.line: Stars, a strange ceremony at sunset, and the sentence that divided the Reformation.
sessions.plain: Years pass and Abram still has no child. God tells him to look at the stars: that is how many descendants he will have. Abram believes him, and Genesis says God 'credited it to him for righteousness'. That one sentence became one of the most argued-over in history. This session reads the two great promises of Genesis 15 and 17, explains the ancient ceremony God performs, and shows how Jews and the different churches understand faith and good works.
sessions.why: Session 1 showed God choosing Abraham by grace and promising a blessing for every family. But a promise is only as good as the one who makes it. Now we ask what binds God to it, and what Abraham has to do.
answers: What is a covenant, and what happens in the strange ceremony of Genesis 15?
What does it mean that Abraham's faith was 'credited to him for righteousness'?
Are we saved by faith or by good works? How do Catholics, Protestants, Orthodox and Jews answer?
Why circumcision, and why does God change Abram's and Sarai's names?
sessions.finding: God binds himself to Abraham by covenant, taking the whole risk of the promise on himself, and Abraham's trust in it, not his merit, is what Genesis calls righteousness; Christians and Jews still debate what that means for faith and works.

paras: In session 1 God called Abram out of Ur and Haran and promised him a land, a great nation, and a blessing for all the families of the earth. Abram went, and almost at once failed. The finding: the family is chosen by grace, for the sake of everyone else.
background.key: Chosen by grace, for everyone's sake.

paras: Between the last session's reading and this one, Genesis tells how Abram and his nephew Lot separate (chapter 13), and how Abram rescues Lot from raiding kings and is blessed by Melchizedek, a mysterious priest-king of Salem, probably Jerusalem (chapter 14). Then comes chapter 15.

By now Abram has lived in Canaan for about ten years. He has wealth and servants, but no son, and he and Sarai are old. The promise of 'a great nation' must look like a joke. So the question of this session is the obvious one: can God's promise be trusted, and what makes it sure?

timeline.text: The call; Abram aged 75
Abram and Lot part; Melchizedek blesses Abram
The stars and the covenant ceremony
Hagar bears Ishmael; Abram aged 86 (session 3)
New names and circumcision; Abraham aged 99
Isaac is born; Abraham aged 100

background.key: Ten years in Canaan, still no son: can the promise be trusted?

paras: A covenant is a binding agreement with promises and obligations, like a treaty or a marriage. Ancient kings made covenants with weaker kings: I will protect you, you will be loyal to me. They were sealed with oaths and ceremonies, and they called down curses on whoever broke them.
In Hebrew you do not 'make' a covenant, you 'cut' one (karat berit). This session shows why.
background.key: A covenant is a binding agreement sealed with an oath; in Hebrew you 'cut' one.

paras: The main reading has three parts: the promise of the stars (15:1–6), the covenant ceremony (15:7–21) and the covenant of circumcision with new names (17:1–14).

The comparison is three short New Testament passages that argue about Genesis 15:6, 'he believed in Yahweh, who credited it to him for righteousness'. Paul uses it to say we are made right with God by faith; James uses it to say faith without works is dead. Their apparent disagreement split Western Christianity in the sixteenth century. Reading them side by side is the best way to understand that argument.
background.key: The promise, the ceremony and the sign; then Paul and James on what Abraham's faith means.

before: What is Abram's complaint, and how does God answer it?
In the ceremony, who walks between the cut animals, and who doesn't?
In the comparison, do Paul and James really disagree? What does each mean by 'works'?
sessions.readWhy: The two great covenant chapters, in three parts: the stars, the ceremony, and the sign.

paras: After these things Yahweh’s word came to Abram in a vision, saying, “Don’t be afraid, Abram. I am your shield, your exceedingly great reward.”
Abram said, “Lord Yahweh, what will you give me, since I go childless, and he who will inherit my estate is Eliezer of Damascus?”
Abram said, “Behold, you have given no children to me: and, behold, one born in my house is my heir.”
Behold, Yahweh’s word came to him, saying, “This man will not be your heir, but he who will come out of your own body will be your heir.”
Yahweh brought him outside, and said, “Look now toward the sky, and count the stars, if you are able to count them.” He said to Abram, “So your offspring will be.”
He believed in Yahweh, who credited it to him for righteousness.
He said to Abram, “I am Yahweh who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldees, to give you this land to inherit it.”
He said, “Lord Yahweh, how will I know that I will inherit it?”
He said to him, “Bring me a heifer three years old, a female goat three years old, a ram three years old, a turtledove, and a young pigeon.”
He brought him all these, and divided them in the middle, and laid each half opposite the other; but he didn’t divide the birds.
The birds of prey came down on the carcasses, and Abram drove them away.
When the sun was going down, a deep sleep fell on Abram. Now terror and great darkness fell on him.
He said to Abram, “Know for sure that your offspring will live as foreigners in a land that is not theirs, and will serve them. They will afflict them four hundred years.
I will also judge that nation, whom they will serve. Afterward they will come out with great wealth;
but you will go to your fathers in peace. You will be buried at a good old age.
In the fourth generation they will come here again, for the iniquity of the Amorite is not yet full.”
It came to pass that, when the sun went down, and it was dark, behold, a smoking furnace and a flaming torch passed between these pieces.
In that day Yahweh made a covenant with Abram, saying, “I have given this land to your offspring, from the river of Egypt to the great river, the river Euphrates:
the land of the Kenites, the Kenizzites, the Kadmonites,
the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Rephaim,
the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Girgashites, and the Jebusites.”
When Abram was ninety-nine years old, Yahweh appeared to Abram and said to him, “I am God Almighty. Walk before me and be blameless.
I will make my covenant between me and you, and will multiply you exceedingly.”
Abram fell on his face. God talked with him, saying,
“As for me, behold, my covenant is with you. You will be the father of a multitude of nations.
Your name will no more be called Abram, but your name will be Abraham; for I have made you the father of a multitude of nations.
I will make you exceedingly fruitful, and I will make nations of you. Kings will come out of you.
I will establish my covenant between me and you and your offspring after you throughout their generations for an everlasting covenant, to be a God to you and to your offspring after you.
I will give to you, and to your offspring after you, the land where you are traveling, all the land of Canaan, for an everlasting possession. I will be their God.”
God said to Abraham, “As for you, you will keep my covenant, you and your offspring after you throughout their generations.
This is my covenant, which you shall keep, between me and you and your offspring after you. Every male among you shall be circumcised.
You shall be circumcised in the flesh of your foreskin. It will be a token of the covenant between me and you.
He who is eight days old will be circumcised among you, every male throughout your generations, he who is born in the house, or bought with money from any foreigner who is not of your offspring.
He who is born in your house, and he who is bought with your money, must be circumcised. My covenant will be in your flesh for an everlasting covenant.
The uncircumcised male who is not circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin, that soul shall be cut off from his people. He has broken my covenant.”

parts.title: Count the stars
parts.context: Some time after Abram's rescue of Lot, God speaks to him in a vision. It is the first time in the story that Abram speaks back.

commentary.on: Don’t be afraid, Abram. I am your shield, your exceedingly great reward.
commentary.text: 'Don't be afraid' is the first thing God says. Abram has just fought kings and refused their spoils (Genesis 14:22–23). God says: I am your protection and your reward. Not the land, not the wealth: God himself.

commentary.on: Lord Yahweh, what will you give me, since I go childless
commentary.text: Abram answers with an honest complaint. What use is a reward without a son? The heir of his estate will be his steward, Eliezer. The Bible lets its people argue with God; the next session but one is about exactly that.

commentary.on: Look now toward the sky, and count the stars, if you are able to count them.
commentary.text: God answers the complaint not with an explanation but with a sight. Without city lights the desert sky shows thousands of stars. 'So your offspring will be.' One old man, no children, and a promise as big as the sky.

commentary.on: He believed in Yahweh, who credited it to him for righteousness.
commentary.text: The most important verse in the chapter. 'Believed' (in Hebrew he'emin, from the same root as 'Amen') means to trust, to rely on, to count something firm. 'Righteousness' means being in the right with God. God counts Abram's trust as putting him right. He has done nothing yet: no law, no circumcision, no sacrifice. He simply trusts the promise. Paul, Luther and the Council of Trent will all argue over this verse.

parts.title: The ceremony at sunset
parts.context: Abram asks for a sign. What follows is an ancient ceremony for making a covenant, strange to us but clear to its first hearers. Jeremiah 34:18 describes the same ceremony: people 'cut the calf in two and passed between its parts'.

commentary.on: Lord Yahweh, how will I know that I will inherit it?
commentary.text: Abram believed about the son; now he asks for assurance about the land. Faith in the Bible is not the absence of questions.

commentary.on: and divided them in the middle, and laid each half opposite the other
commentary.text: This is what 'cutting' a covenant meant. The animals were cut in two and the halves laid in two rows. Each party walked between them, saying in effect: may I be cut in pieces like these animals if I break my word. It was a self-curse.

commentary.on: Now terror and great darkness fell on him.
commentary.text: Abram falls into a deep sleep and is overwhelmed. Then God tells him the future: his descendants will be foreigners and slaves for four hundred years, and then will come out with great wealth. This is the story of Exodus, foretold. The promise will be kept, but slowly and through suffering.

commentary.on: for the iniquity of the Amorite is not yet full
commentary.text: A striking phrase. The land will not be given yet, because its people have not yet sinned enough to lose it. God's gift to Abraham is not a licence to take others' land unjustly; it waits on God's justice towards those people too.

commentary.on: a smoking furnace and a flaming torch passed between these pieces
commentary.text: The climax. Fire and smoke, signs of God's presence (as in the burning bush and the pillar of fire), pass between the pieces. But Abram does not. Only God walks the path of the self-curse. God takes the whole risk of the covenant on himself: may I be torn apart if I fail. Christian readers have seen here a hint of the cross, where God bears the cost of his own promise.

commentary.on: I have given this land to your offspring, from the river of Egypt to the great river, the river Euphrates
commentary.text: The promise of the land, given as already done: 'I have given'. Its borders are ideal rather than surveyed. The promise of the land remains central to Judaism; Christians have usually read it as fulfilled in, or pointing beyond to, a wider inheritance (Romans 4:13 speaks of Abraham inheriting 'the world').

parts.title: New names and a sign
parts.context: Thirteen more years have passed. Ishmael, Abram's son by Sarai's servant Hagar, has been born (you will read that story in session 3). Now God appears again, renews the covenant, and gives it a sign.

commentary.on: I am God Almighty. Walk before me and be blameless.
commentary.text: 'God Almighty' translates El Shaddai, an ancient name of God whose meaning is debated. This time the covenant includes a call on Abram: walk before me, live your whole life in my sight. Genesis 15 was God's promise; Genesis 17 adds the human answer.

commentary.on: Your name will no more be called Abram, but your name will be Abraham
commentary.text: Abram means 'exalted father'; Abraham sounds like 'father of a multitude' (av hamon). In the ancient world a new name meant a new identity, given by a superior. Sarai becomes Sarah (17:15); both forms mean 'princess'. The names announce the promise before there is any child to show for it.

commentary.on: an everlasting covenant, to be a God to you and to your offspring after you
commentary.text: This is the heart of every covenant in the Bible: 'I will be your God, and you will be my people'. It is about a relationship, not only land and children.

commentary.on: Every male among you shall be circumcised.
commentary.text: Circumcision, the removal of the foreskin, was practised by Egyptians and other neighbours, usually at puberty or marriage. Here it is done to every boy at eight days old, before he can choose anything, as a sign that he belongs to the covenant by God's gift. Jews have kept it ever since as the covenant of Abraham (brit milah). Christians, after a great debate (Acts 15), did not require it of non-Jewish believers, and see baptism as the sign of the new covenant (Colossians 2:11–12). Muslims practise it as a custom of Abraham.

commentary.on: he who is born in the house, or bought with money from any foreigner
commentary.text: Even slaves and foreigners in Abraham's household were included in the covenant sign. The family was never only a bloodline.

paras: What then will we say that Abraham, our forefather, has found according to the flesh?
For if Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast about, but not toward God.
For what does the Scripture say? “Abraham believed God, and it was accounted to him for righteousness.”
Now to him who works, the reward is not counted as grace, but as something owed.
But to him who doesn’t work, but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is accounted for righteousness.
Even as Abraham “believed God, and it was counted to him for righteousness.”
Know therefore that those who are of faith are children of Abraham.
The Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, preached the Good News beforehand to Abraham, saying, “In you all the nations will be blessed.”
So then, those who are of faith are blessed with the faithful Abraham.
For you are all children of God, through faith in Christ Jesus.
For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ.
There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free man, there is neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus.
If you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring and heirs according to promise.
Wasn’t Abraham our father justified by works, in that he offered up Isaac his son on the altar?
You see that faith worked with his works, and by works faith was perfected.
So the Scripture was fulfilled which says, “Abraham believed God, and it was accounted to him as righteousness,” and he was called the friend of God.
You see then that by works, a man is justified, and not only by faith.

parts.title: Paul: credited, not earned
parts.context: Paul's Letter to the Romans, about AD 57, written to Christians in Rome, both Jews and non-Jews (Gentiles). Paul argues that Gentiles do not need to become Jews, by being circumcised and keeping the law of Moses, to belong to God's people. His proof is Abraham.

commentary.on: For if Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast about, but not toward God.
commentary.text: 'Justified' means declared or made right with God, the courtroom word for being acquitted. By 'works' Paul means here the deeds that the law of Moses commands. If Abraham earned God's approval, he could boast; but he didn't.

commentary.on: Now to him who works, the reward is not counted as grace, but as something owed.
commentary.text: A wage is earned; a gift is not. Paul's point is that God's acceptance of Abraham was a gift ('grace'), received by trusting, not a wage. That is why it is open to anyone.

commentary.on: believes in him who justifies the ungodly
commentary.text: A startling phrase: God puts right 'the ungodly'. Paul's opponents would have said God justifies the godly. Paul says Abraham was an idol-worshipper's son when God called him.

parts.title: Paul: Abraham's children
parts.context: Paul's Letter to the Galatians, written a few years earlier to churches in what is now Turkey. Teachers had told the Gentile Christians there that they must be circumcised. Paul is furious.

commentary.on: Know therefore that those who are of faith are children of Abraham.
commentary.text: Here is Paul's whole argument in a sentence. Abraham's true family is not defined by blood or by circumcision but by sharing his trust in God. That is how 'all the families of the earth' can be blessed through him.

commentary.on: preached the Good News beforehand to Abraham, saying, “In you all the nations will be blessed.”
commentary.text: Paul quotes Genesis 12:3 and calls it the gospel, the 'good news', announced in advance. For him, the promise to Abraham was always meant to reach the Gentiles.

commentary.on: There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free man, there is neither male nor female
commentary.text: One of the most influential sentences in history. In Abraham's family, the deepest divisions of the ancient world, race, status and sex, no longer decide who belongs. Abraham's household, which included slaves and foreigners, was a first sketch of this.

parts.title: James: faith that works
parts.context: The Letter of James, traditionally by James, the brother of Jesus and leader of the church in Jerusalem, who was killed in AD 62. James writes to Christians whose faith had become talk without action: 'faith, if it has no works, is dead' (2:17).

commentary.on: Wasn’t Abraham our father justified by works, in that he offered up Isaac his son on the altar?
commentary.text: James points to the later story of Abraham offering Isaac, which you will read in session 5. For James, Abraham's trust in Genesis 15 was proved, and completed, by what he did.

commentary.on: You see that faith worked with his works, and by works faith was perfected.
commentary.text: James is not saying works instead of faith. He is saying faith and works belong together, like a body and its breath (2:26). Faith that never acts is not real faith.

commentary.on: You see then that by works, a man is justified, and not only by faith.
commentary.text: This sentence seems to contradict Paul directly, and Martin Luther thought it did: in 1522 he called James 'an epistle of straw' compared with Paul's letters. Most interpreters think the two use 'works' and 'faith' differently: Paul is attacking the idea that keeping the law earns God's acceptance; James is attacking a 'faith' that is only words.

compare.why: Genesis 15:6 became the centre of a great argument. Paul uses it to show that we are put right with God by trusting him, not by keeping the law. James, writing to Christians who said they believed but did nothing, uses the same verse to insist that real faith acts. Read all three passages, then the lecture shows how the churches have argued over them.
compare.title: Paul and James on Abraham's faith

paras: The ceremony of Genesis 15 is the key to the whole chapter. In an ancient covenant both parties would walk between the cut animals, calling down death on themselves if they broke faith. Here only God, as fire and smoke, passes through. Abram is asleep.

That means the covenant does not depend on Abram keeping his side. It depends on God. Scholars call this a 'covenant of grant' or a promissory covenant: a king's free gift to a loyal servant, guaranteed by the king's own oath. It is why the promise survives Abraham's failures, and his son's, and his grandson's. It answers the question this session started with: the promise can be trusted because God has bound himself to it.
sections.key: Only God passes between the pieces: he binds himself to the promise, so it does not depend on Abraham's success.

paras: Genesis 15:6 is short, but every word matters. Abram 'believed', or trusted, God's promise when there was no evidence of a son. God 'credited' that trust to him, a bookkeeping word: entered it on his account. As 'righteousness': as being in the right, in a right relationship with God.

Jewish interpreters have read the verse in more than one way. The great medieval commentator Rashi took it as Christians do: God counted Abram's faith as merit. Nachmanides suggested the opposite subject: Abram counted God's promise as an act of God's righteousness. Either way, Judaism has always joined faith to faithfulness: the Mishnah (about AD 200) says that Abraham kept the whole law even before it was given, citing Genesis 26:5.
sections.key: Abram trusted the promise with no evidence, and God counted that trust as putting him right with him.

sections.h: Faith and works: how the traditions answer
paras: In 1517 a German monk, Martin Luther, began the Protestant Reformation, and at its heart was this question: how is a sinner made right with God? Luther's answer, drawn from Paul's reading of Abraham, was 'by faith alone' (sola fide): God counts Christ's righteousness to the one who trusts him, as he counted Abraham's trust; good works follow as the fruit, not the root. The Catholic Church answered at the Council of Trent, in its Decree on Justification of 1547. Trent agreed that justification is God's free gift and that faith is 'the beginning of human salvation, the foundation and root of all justification'; but it taught that God's grace truly makes a person righteous within, and that this grows through faith working in love and good works.

The argument lasted four centuries. Then, in 1999, the Lutheran World Federation and the Catholic Church signed a Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification, agreeing in substance that we are accepted by God by grace alone, through faith in Christ, not because of any merit, and that the Holy Spirit renews the heart and calls us to good works. Methodists, Anglicans and Reformed churches later joined it. Differences of emphasis remain.

cols: How we are put right with God
rows: By God's grace, received in faith and baptism, which really makes the person righteous within
Faith working through love; good works done in grace help us grow in justification
Abraham's faith was real and living, and it showed itself in obedience (Trent, Session VI, 1547)
By grace alone, through faith alone: Christ's righteousness counted to the believer
The fruit and evidence of faith, never the ground of acceptance
Abraham was counted righteous before he had done anything (Romans 4)
Salvation is union with God (theosis), a lifelong healing of the whole person, not chiefly a legal verdict
Grace and human freedom work together (synergy); faith and works are inseparable
Abraham's faith and his obedience are one journey towards God
God's covenant with Israel is a gift; repentance and God's mercy restore the relationship
Keeping the commandments is the faithful response to the covenant, not a way to earn it
Abraham trusted and obeyed; he 'kept my commandments' (Genesis 26:5)

sections.key: Protestants say 'faith alone', Catholics 'faith working through love', the Orthodox 'faith and works together towards union with God'; since 1999 Lutherans and Catholics agree that acceptance is by grace through faith.

paras: Since the 1970s many scholars, notably E. P. Sanders, James Dunn and N. T. Wright, have argued that the Reformation read Paul too much through its own question. They point out that first-century Judaism did not teach that people earn God's favour; it taught that God graciously chose Israel, and that keeping the law was the response. Paul's real argument, they say, was about who belongs to Abraham's family: must non-Jews become Jews, by circumcision and the food laws, to be God's people? His answer was no: Abraham himself was counted righteous before he was circumcised (Romans 4:10–11).

This view, called the New Perspective on Paul, is itself debated; many Protestant scholars think it underplays the human problem of sin that Paul also addresses. But it has helped Christians read Judaism more fairly, and it puts Genesis 12:3 at the centre: the point of Abraham's family is that it should one day include all nations.
sections.key: The 'New Perspective' says Paul's main point was that Gentiles join Abraham's family by faith, without becoming Jews; it is debated.

paras: Genesis 17 adds a sign: circumcision, on the eighth day. It marks the covenant on the body of every male in the household, son or slave, native or foreigner. It comes after Abraham's faith and does not create it; it seals what God has already promised.

The three Abrahamic faiths handle the sign differently. Judaism keeps it as the covenant of Abraham, with the naming of the child. The early Church decided at the Council of Jerusalem (about AD 49, Acts 15) that Gentile believers need not be circumcised, and came to see baptism, given to infants in most churches, as the sign of belonging. Islam keeps circumcision as part of the way of Abraham, though the Qur'an does not command it.
sections.key: Circumcision seals a covenant already given; Judaism keeps it, Christianity replaced it with baptism, Islam keeps it as Abraham's custom.

refs: Genesis 15; 17; 26:5; Jeremiah 34:18–20; Romans 4; Galatians 3; James 2:14–26; Acts 15.

Covenant ritual: Gordon Wenham, Genesis 16–50 and Genesis 1–15 (1987, 1994); Moshe Weinfeld, 'The Covenant of Grant in the Old Testament and in the Ancient Near East', Journal of the American Oriental Society 90 (1970).
Rashi and Nachmanides on Genesis 15:6; Mishnah Kiddushin 4:14.

Martin Luther, Preface to the New Testament (1522), on James; Council of Trent, Session VI, Decree on Justification (1547), chapter 8; Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification (1999), §15; World Methodist Council (2006), Anglican Consultative Council (2016) and World Communion of Reformed Churches (2017) associations.
E. P. Sanders, Paul and Palestinian Judaism (1977); James D. G. Dunn, 'The New Perspective on Paul' (1983); N. T. Wright, Paul and the Faithfulness of God (2013).
Circumcision in Egypt: Herodotus, Histories II.104; the tomb relief of Ankhmahor at Saqqara (about 2300 BC).

debate.question: Is Abraham the father of faith alone, or of faith that obeys?

positions.name: Faith alone
positions.who: Martin Luther; John Calvin; most evangelical Protestants
positions.view: Abraham was counted righteous simply by trusting God's promise, before any work or sign. His later obedience was the fruit of that faith, not part of the reason God accepted him.
positions.evidence: Genesis 15:6 comes before circumcision (Genesis 17) and before the offering of Isaac (Genesis 22); Romans 4:3–5, 10–11.

positions.name: Faith working through love
positions.who: The Council of Trent; Catholic and many Anglican theologians
positions.view: God's grace is a free gift, received by faith, but it really changes the person, and faith that lives shows itself in obedience; James is right that faith is completed by works.
positions.evidence: James 2:21–24; Galatians 5:6, 'faith working through love'; Abraham's whole life of obedience.

positions.name: Faithfulness
positions.who: Jewish tradition; many Orthodox theologians; some New Perspective scholars
positions.view: The question 'faith or works' is a false choice. Abraham's trust and his obedience are one thing: faithfulness to God, within a relationship God began.
positions.evidence: Genesis 26:5, 'Abraham obeyed my voice, and kept my requirements'; the Hebrew word emunah means both faith and faithfulness.

debate.agree: All agree that God began the relationship, that Abraham's trust was real, and that true faith does not stay idle.

look.why: Peter Paul Rubens painted this in about 1626 as a design for a great tapestry. It shows the scene just before this session's reading (Genesis 14:18–20): Melchizedek, priest-king of Salem, brings out bread and wine to bless Abram. Christians have long seen in it a picture of the Eucharist, and Hebrews 7 calls Christ a priest 'after the order of Melchizedek'.
points: The whole scene is painted as a tapestry being unrolled by winged infants (putti) against grey and gold columns.
Abraham, in armour and a crimson cape, leans forward from the left.
Melchizedek, white-bearded, in a gold cape with a fur collar and a red cap wreathed with leaves, meets him in the centre.
Behind Melchizedek, a man carries a basket of bread across his shoulders.
In the lower right corner, men hold huge silver and gold vessels.

music.why: Mary's song, the Magnificat (Luke 1:46–55), ends: 'as he spoke to our fathers, to Abraham and his offspring forever'. The promise of Genesis 15 is still being sung over in the New Testament, and Bach set it in 1723 with trumpets and drums.

think.why: Abraham's faith is trust in a God who speaks and keeps promises. Ask what reasons people give for believing that such a God is real.

learn.why: Count the stars: the promise, and the verse that Paul, Luther and Trent argued over.

check.q: In the covenant ceremony of Genesis 15, why does it matter that only the smoking furnace and flaming torch pass between the pieces?
options: It shows that God alone takes on the self-curse, so the covenant depends on God keeping his word, not on Abram
It shows the ceremony was a sacrifice to atone for Abram's sins
It shows that Abram was not yet worthy to take part, because he had asked for a sign
It shows that Abram would have to keep the law before he could share in the covenant
check.why: Passing between the pieces meant 'may I be torn apart if I fail'. Only God does it.

check.q: Paul argues from the order of events in Genesis. Which is his point in Romans 4:10–11?
options: Abraham was counted righteous before he was circumcised, so he can be the father of uncircumcised believers too
Abraham was counted righteous because he was circumcised
Gentiles must be circumcised to share Abraham's faith
Abraham was circumcised before he believed
check.why: Genesis 15:6 comes before Genesis 17; Paul uses that to include Gentiles.

check.q: Which is the best account of how Paul and James can both cite Genesis 15:6?
options: James is speaking of Isaac's faith, not Abraham's
They use 'works' differently: Paul rejects works of the law as a way to earn acceptance, James rejects a 'faith' that never acts
Paul wrote to Jews and James to Gentiles, so different rules apply
One of them misquoted it
check.why: Most interpreters, including the Joint Declaration of 1999, read them as complementary.

check.q: What did the Joint Declaration of 1999 agree?
options: That we are justified by works, which complete faith
That Lutherans and Catholics agree in substance that we are accepted by God by grace alone through faith in Christ, not by merit, while differences of emphasis remain
That the Catholic Church accepts all of Luther's teaching
That Catholic, Lutheran and Orthodox teaching are now identical
check.why: It was a real but limited agreement, later joined by Methodists, Anglicans and Reformed churches.

check.q: What does 'the iniquity of the Amorite is not yet full' (Genesis 15:16) suggest about the promise of the land?
options: That the Amorites were to be destroyed at once
That the land would go to Abraham's descendants because they were more righteous than its people
That the promise of the land had been withdrawn
That the land would be given only when its inhabitants had forfeited it by their own wrongdoing, in God's time and justice
check.why: The gift waits on God's justice towards the land's people too.

check.q: According to the 'New Perspective on Paul', what was Paul's main concern in Romans and Galatians?
options: Whether Gentiles must become Jews, by circumcision and the law, to belong to Abraham's family
Whether Christians should keep the Sabbath on Saturday
Whether Christians must give up every Jewish custom
How an individual sinner can find a gracious God
check.why: The question of who belongs to Abraham's family; the view is debated.

tutorial.question: What does Genesis 15 teach about God's promise and Abraham's faith, and how have Christians and Jews understood it?
tutorial.approach: Explain the promise of the stars and Genesis 15:6. Then explain the covenant ceremony and why it matters that only God passes through. Set Paul and James side by side. End with the main views of faith and works, and say which you find most convincing and why.
strong: Explains what 'believed' and 'credited… for righteousness' mean.
Explains the covenant ceremony and its self-curse, and the significance of God alone passing through.
Shows how Paul uses the order of Genesis 15 and 17.
Reconciles, or fairly sets out the tension between, Paul and James.
Distinguishes Catholic, Protestant, Orthodox and Jewish views, and mentions the 1999 Joint Declaration.
Mentions circumcision as a sign and how the traditions treat it.

reading.author: Gordon Wenham
reading.title: Genesis 16–50 (Word Biblical Commentary)
reading.why: A careful scholarly commentary on the Abraham stories.

reading.author: Alister McGrath
reading.title: Iustitia Dei: A History of the Christian Doctrine of Justification
reading.why: The standard history of the faith and works debate.

reading.author: N. T. Wright
reading.title: Justification: God's Plan and Paul's Vision
reading.why: A readable statement of the New Perspective, written in answer to its critics.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: keep one promise that costs you something, and make it a promise you could easily have got out of.
sessions.reflect: Is there a promise of God, or a hope, that you find hard to believe because you cannot yet see any sign of it?
takeaways: In the covenant ceremony only God passes between the pieces: he binds himself to the promise.
Abram trusted God's promise with no evidence, and God credited it to him as righteousness.
Paul and James both use Abraham; the churches still differ on faith and works, though Lutherans and Catholics agreed much in 1999.

sessions.title: The other son
sessions.line: A slave woman, a boy in the desert, and the God who sees.
sessions.plain: Sarai cannot have children, so she gives her Egyptian slave, Hagar, to Abram to bear a child for her. Hagar has a son, Ishmael, but is driven out, twice. Both times, God finds her in the desert. This session asks the obvious question about choosing: what about the ones who are not chosen? It is also the beginning of the story of Islam, which traces itself to Ishmael.
sessions.why: Sessions 1 and 2 showed God choosing one family and binding himself to his promise. But choosing one means not choosing others. Here, for the first time, we meet someone outside the line of the promise, and see how God treats her.
answers: Who were Hagar and Ishmael, and why were they sent away?
If God chose Isaac, did he abandon Ishmael?
How do Islam and Christianity each read the story of Hagar?
How should we read a story that includes slavery and cruelty?
sessions.finding: Choosing one family does not mean abandoning others: the God of Abraham sees the slave woman, hears her son, and blesses him too, and the story makes us feel for the one who was not chosen.

paras: God chose Abraham by grace, for the sake of every family on earth (session 1), and bound himself to his promise by covenant: Abraham's trust, not his merit, was counted as righteousness (session 2). But there is still no son.
background.key: Chosen by grace; a promise God guarantees; still no son.

paras: This session's story happens between the stars of Genesis 15 and the new names of Genesis 17. Abram is 85, Sarai is 75, and they have waited ten years in Canaan. Sarai decides to help the promise along.

In the ancient Near East a childless wife could give her slave woman to her husband to bear a child that would legally count as the wife's. The Laws of Hammurabi, from Babylon about 1750 BC, regulate exactly this situation (laws 144–147), including what happens if the slave then puts on airs and claims equality with her mistress: she may be returned to slavery but not sold. Marriage contracts found at Nuzi, in northern Iraq, from the fifteenth century BC, also require it. To Abram and Sarai's neighbours, nothing about the plan was strange.
background.key: A childless wife giving her slave to bear a child was a known custom, regulated in Hammurabi's laws.

paras: Hagar is an Egyptian, perhaps acquired during the visit to Egypt in Genesis 12, though Genesis doesn't say. She is a slave: she has no say in what is done with her body. Slavery in the ancient world was usually through debt, war or purchase, and it was everywhere; the Bible's own laws later regulate and limit it, and its stories, like this one, show its cruelty.
Hagar matters far beyond Genesis. In Islam she is Hajar, the mother of Ishmael (Ismail), and every pilgrim to Mecca re-enacts her search for water.
background.key: Hagar is an Egyptian slave with no say over her body; in Islam she is Hajar, honoured mother of Ishmael.

paras: The main reading has four parts: Hagar's first flight (16), the birth of Isaac (21:1–7), Hagar and Ishmael driven out (21:8–21), and Paul's reading of the story (Galatians 4), which shows how differently a story can be used.

The comparison is from the Qur'an: Abraham's prayer for the son he settled 'in an unfruitful valley, nigh to thy holy house', and Abraham and Ishmael building the Kaaba in Mecca. They show how the story continues for a quarter of the world's people.
background.key: Hagar's two flights, Isaac's birth, Paul's allegory, and the Qur'an's Ishmael.

before: Who acts in this story, and who is acted on? Notice who speaks and who doesn't.
What does God promise Hagar and her son?
In the comparison, where does the Qur'an place Ishmael?
sessions.readWhy: The story of the son who was not chosen, in four parts: Hagar's first flight, Isaac's birth, Hagar and Ishmael driven out, and how Paul read it.

paras: Now Sarai, Abram’s wife, bore him no children. She had a servant, an Egyptian, whose name was Hagar.
Sarai said to Abram, “See now, Yahweh has restrained me from bearing. Please go in to my servant. It may be that I will obtain children by her.” Abram listened to the voice of Sarai.
Sarai, Abram’s wife, took Hagar the Egyptian, her servant, after Abram had lived ten years in the land of Canaan, and gave her to Abram her husband to be his wife.
He went in to Hagar, and she conceived. When she saw that she had conceived, her mistress was despised in her eyes.
Sarai said to Abram, “This wrong is your fault. I gave my servant into your bosom, and when she saw that she had conceived, she despised me. May Yahweh judge between me and you.”
But Abram said to Sarai, “Behold, your maid is in your hand. Do to her whatever is good in your eyes.” Sarai dealt harshly with her, and she fled from her face.
Yahweh’s angel found her by a fountain of water in the wilderness, by the fountain on the way to Shur.
He said, “Hagar, Sarai’s servant, where did you come from? Where are you going?”
She said, “I am fleeing from the face of my mistress Sarai.”
Yahweh’s angel said to her, “Return to your mistress, and submit yourself under her hands.”
Yahweh’s angel said to her, “I will greatly multiply your offspring, that they will not be counted for multitude.”
Yahweh’s angel said to her, “Behold, you are with child, and will bear a son. You shall call his name Ishmael, because Yahweh has heard your affliction.
He will be like a wild donkey among men. His hand will be against every man, and every man’s hand against him. He will live opposed to all of his brothers.”
She called the name of Yahweh who spoke to her, “You are a God who sees,” for she said, “Have I even stayed alive after seeing him?”
Therefore the well was called Beer Lahai Roi. Behold, it is between Kadesh and Bered.
Hagar bore a son for Abram. Abram called the name of his son, whom Hagar bore, Ishmael.
Abram was eighty-six years old when Hagar bore Ishmael to Abram.
Yahweh visited Sarah as he had said, and Yahweh did to Sarah as he had spoken.
Sarah conceived, and bore Abraham a son in his old age, at the set time of which God had spoken to him.
Abraham called his son who was born to him, whom Sarah bore to him, Isaac.
Abraham circumcised his son, Isaac, when he was eight days old, as God had commanded him.
Abraham was one hundred years old when his son, Isaac, was born to him.
Sarah said, “God has made me laugh. Everyone who hears will laugh with me.”
She said, “Who would have said to Abraham that Sarah would nurse children? For I have borne him a son in his old age.”
The child grew and was weaned. Abraham made a great feast on the day that Isaac was weaned.
Sarah saw the son of Hagar the Egyptian, whom she had borne to Abraham, mocking.
Therefore she said to Abraham, “Cast out this servant and her son! For the son of this servant will not be heir with my son, Isaac.”
The thing was very grievous in Abraham’s sight on account of his son.

God said to Abraham, “Don’t let it be grievous in your sight because of the boy, and because of your servant. In all that Sarah says to you, listen to her voice. For your offspring will be named through Isaac.
I will also make a nation of the son of the servant, because he is your child.”

Abraham rose up early in the morning, and took bread and a container of water, and gave it to Hagar, putting it on her shoulder; and gave her the child, and sent her away. She departed, and wandered in the wilderness of Beersheba.
The water in the container was spent, and she put the child under one of the shrubs.
She went and sat down opposite him, a good way off, about a bow shot away. For she said, “Don’t let me see the death of the child.” She sat opposite him, and lifted up her voice, and wept.
God heard the voice of the boy.
The angel of God called to Hagar out of the sky, and said to her, “What troubles you, Hagar? Don’t be afraid. For God has heard the voice of the boy where he is.
Get up, lift up the boy, and hold him with your hand. For I will make him a great nation.”
God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water. She went, filled the container with water, and gave the boy a drink.
God was with the boy, and he grew. He lived in the wilderness, and as he grew up, became an archer.
He lived in the wilderness of Paran. His mother got a wife for him out of the land of Egypt.
Tell me, you that desire to be under the law, don’t you listen to the law?
For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by the servant, and one by the free woman.
However, the son by the servant was born according to the flesh, but the son by the free woman was born through promise.
These things contain an allegory, for these are two covenants. One is from Mount Sinai, bearing children to bondage, which is Hagar.
For this Hagar is Mount Sinai in Arabia, and answers to the Jerusalem that exists now, for she is in bondage with her children.
But the Jerusalem that is above is free, which is the mother of us all.
For it is written,

“Rejoice, you barren who don’t bear.
Break out and shout, you who don’t travail.
For the desolate have more children than her who has a husband.”
Now we, brothers, as Isaac was, are children of promise.
But as then, he who was born according to the flesh persecuted him who was born according to the Spirit, so also it is now.
However what does the Scripture say? “Throw out the servant and her son, for the son of the servant will not inherit with the son of the free woman.”
So then, brothers, we are not children of a servant, but of the free woman.

parts.title: The God who sees
parts.context: Abram has lived in Canaan for ten years. Sarai, still childless, makes a plan.

commentary.on: Please go in to my servant. It may be that I will obtain children by her.
commentary.text: Sarai's plan was legal and normal. Notice that it repeats an old pattern: in Genesis 3, a woman takes and gives to her husband, and he listens to her voice. Here 'Abram listened to the voice of Sarai'. Human beings trying to secure God's promise their own way.

commentary.on: When she saw that she had conceived, her mistress was despised in her eyes.
commentary.text: Exactly what Hammurabi's laws foresaw. The slave who can bear a child feels herself above the free woman who can't. Everyone in this triangle behaves badly.

commentary.on: Behold, your maid is in your hand. Do to her whatever is good in your eyes.
commentary.text: Abram washes his hands of the woman carrying his child. Sarai 'dealt harshly with her', using a Hebrew verb later used for Egypt's oppression of the Israelites (Exodus 1:11–12). The irony is deliberate: the ancestors of Israel oppress an Egyptian slave, before Egyptians oppress Israel.

commentary.on: Hagar, Sarai’s servant, where did you come from? Where are you going?
commentary.text: The first time in the Bible that 'the angel of Yahweh' appears, it is not to Abram but to a runaway Egyptian slave in the desert. He calls her by name. No one else in the story has.

commentary.on: Return to your mistress, and submit yourself under her hands.
commentary.text: A hard command, and readers have always found it so. Why send her back? The likeliest answer in the story is survival: a pregnant woman alone in the desert would die. The promises that follow are the reason to return.

commentary.on: You shall call his name Ishmael, because Yahweh has heard your affliction.
commentary.text: Ishmael means 'God hears'. The boy's very name tells the story: God heard a slave woman's misery. Hagar receives a promise of countless descendants, like Abram's.

commentary.on: She called the name of Yahweh who spoke to her, “You are a God who sees,”
commentary.text: Hagar is the only person in the whole Bible who gives God a name. 'El Roi': the God who sees me. The one person in the story whom nobody sees, a foreign slave, is the one who sees God and is seen by him.

parts.title: Isaac: laughter
parts.context: Fourteen years later, after God has renewed the covenant and given new names (Genesis 17) and promised a son to Sarah (Genesis 18, which you will read in the next session), the promise is kept.

commentary.on: Yahweh visited Sarah as he had said, and Yahweh did to Sarah as he had spoken.
commentary.text: The sentence says the same thing twice, on purpose: 'as he had said… as he had spoken'. After twenty-five years, God keeps his word exactly.

commentary.on: Abraham was one hundred years old when his son, Isaac, was born to him.
commentary.text: The age is the point. This child is not the product of planning or custom, like Ishmael, but of a promise. Paul will call Isaac the son 'born through promise' (Galatians 4:23).

commentary.on: God has made me laugh. Everyone who hears will laugh with me.
commentary.text: Isaac's name, Yitzhak, means 'he laughs'. Both Abraham and Sarah had laughed in disbelief when the son was promised (17:17; 18:12). Now the laughter of disbelief becomes the laughter of joy.

parts.title: Driven out
parts.context: A few years later, when Isaac is weaned, perhaps aged two or three, Ishmael is about sixteen.

commentary.on: Sarah saw the son of Hagar the Egyptian, whom she had borne to Abraham, mocking.
commentary.text: The Hebrew word, metzahek, is a play on Isaac's name: 'laughing' or 'playing'. It may mean that Ishmael mocked Isaac, or only that he was playing, or 'Isaac-ing', acting as an heir. Sarah does not even name him: he is 'the son of Hagar the Egyptian'.

commentary.on: Cast out this servant and her son!
commentary.text: Sarah wants Ishmael removed as a rival heir. Under ancient law, a slave's son freed with his mother lost his claim to inherit, so this may also be an act of freeing them. But it is a freedom that drives them into the desert.

commentary.on: The thing was very grievous in Abraham’s sight on account of his son.
commentary.text: Abraham loves Ishmael. Genesis says so plainly: 'his son'. God tells him to do as Sarah says, but adds a promise: Ishmael too will be a nation, 'because he is your child'.

commentary.on: Don’t let me see the death of the child.
commentary.text: One of the most painful moments in the Bible. The water is gone. A mother puts her son under a bush and sits a bowshot away so she will not have to watch him die.

commentary.on: God heard the voice of the boy.
commentary.text: Ishmael's name again: 'God hears'. The boy is not part of the covenant line, and God hears him anyway. Hagar weeps, but it is the boy's voice God answers.

commentary.on: God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water.
commentary.text: The well was there; she could not see it. The God who sees opens her eyes. Ishmael grows up in the wilderness of Paran, an archer, and his mother finds him a wife from her own country, Egypt. Genesis 25:9 adds a moving detail: when Abraham died, 'Isaac and Ishmael, his sons, buried him' together.

parts.title: Paul's allegory
parts.context: Paul again, writing to Gentile Christians who were being told to be circumcised and keep the law of Moses. He turns the story of Hagar and Sarah into an allegory, a story in which each figure stands for something else, to make his argument.

commentary.on: These things contain an allegory, for these are two covenants.
commentary.text: Paul says openly that he is reading the story as an allegory. Hagar, the slave, stands for the covenant made at Mount Sinai and the law; Sarah, the free woman, for the new covenant of the promise.

commentary.on: For this Hagar is Mount Sinai in Arabia
commentary.text: A surprising move. Paul links Hagar with Sinai, where the law was given, and with Arabia, where Ishmael's descendants lived. In ordinary Jewish thinking, the Jews were Sarah's children and the law their glory. Paul reverses it, to argue that those who rely on the law are, in his allegory, slaves.

commentary.on: Now we, brothers, as Isaac was, are children of promise.
commentary.text: Paul's point: Gentile believers, who were never part of Abraham's bloodline, are like Isaac, born by God's promise, not by human effort.

commentary.on: Throw out the servant and her son, for the son of the servant will not inherit with the son of the free woman.
commentary.text: Paul quotes Sarah's words as Scripture. Many readers today are uneasy: the allegory takes no notice of Hagar's suffering or of God's care for her and Ishmael, and it was later used against Jews. Paul's purpose was to defend the freedom of Gentile Christians; but his reading is one use of the story, not the whole of it.

paras:
ABRAHAM said, "O Lord make this land secure, and turn aside me and my children from serving idols:
For many men, O my Lord, have they led astray. But whosoever shall follow me, he truly shall be of me; and whosoever shall disobey me. . . . Thou truly art Gracious, Merciful.
O our Lord! verily I have settled some of my offspring in an unfruitful valley, nigh to thy holy house; O our Lord, that they may strictly observe prayer! Make thou therefore the hearts of men to yearn toward them, and supply them with fruits that they may be thankful.
O our Lord! thou truly knowest what we hide and what we bring to light; nought on earth or in heaven is hidden from God. Praise be to God who hath given me, in my old age, Ismael and Isaac! My Lord is the hearer of prayer.

And when Abraham, with Ismael, raised the foundations of the House, they said, "O our Lord! accept it from us; for thou art the Hearer, the Knower.
O our Lord! make us also Muslims, and our posterity a Muslim people; and teach us our holy rites, and be turned towards us, for thou art He who turneth, the Merciful.

parts.author: The Qur'an
parts.title: Abraham's prayer for the valley
parts.context: This sura is named after Abraham. Here he prays for Mecca, the 'land' he asks God to make secure, and for the son he left there. The 'holy house' is the Kaaba, the cube-shaped shrine at the centre of Mecca, towards which Muslims pray. Muslim tradition tells that Abraham left Hagar and the baby Ishmael in this valley; Hagar ran seven times between two hills, Safa and Marwa, looking for water, until the spring of Zamzam burst out.
parts.plain: Abraham prays: make this land safe, and keep me and my children from serving idols. I have settled some of my children in a barren valley near your holy house, so that they may pray; make people's hearts love them, and give them food. Praise God who gave me, in my old age, Ishmael and Isaac.

commentary.on: turn aside me and my children from serving idols
commentary.text: Abraham's first prayer is the one you met in session 1: no idols. In Islam, Mecca was founded as a place of pure worship of the one God, which later generations corrupted with idols until Muhammad cleansed it.

commentary.on: verily I have settled some of my offspring in an unfruitful valley, nigh to thy holy house
commentary.text: Here the desert where Hagar and Ishmael were sent becomes the valley of Mecca. What Genesis tells as an expulsion, the Islamic tradition tells as a settling, by God's command, at the place of his house. Every year, pilgrims on the Hajj walk seven times between Safa and Marwa, remembering Hagar's search for water, and drink from the well of Zamzam.

commentary.on: Praise be to God who hath given me, in my old age, Ismael and Isaac!
commentary.text: Both sons, named together, with thanks. Notice that Ishmael comes first, as the elder. In the Qur'an, both are prophets.

parts.author: The Qur'an
parts.title: Building the House
parts.context: The Qur'an's longest sura. These verses describe Abraham and Ishmael raising the foundations of the Kaaba together.
parts.plain: Abraham and Ishmael built the foundations of God's house, and prayed: accept this from us; make us people who submit to you, and our descendants too; teach us how to worship, and forgive us.

commentary.on: And when Abraham, with Ismael, raised the foundations of the House
commentary.text: Father and son, together, building God's house. The son Genesis sends away is, in the Qur'an, his father's partner in founding the central shrine of the faith.

commentary.on: O our Lord! make us also Muslims, and our posterity a Muslim people
commentary.text: 'Muslim' means 'one who submits' to God. For Islam, Abraham and Ishmael were Muslims in this original sense, long before Muhammad. So Islam does not see itself as a new religion, but as a return to the faith of Abraham.

compare.author: The Qur'an
compare.why: In Islam, the son who was sent away is not a side character. Ishmael, Ismail in Arabic, is a prophet and the ancestor of the Arabs and of Muhammad. Read two short passages from the Qur'an: Abraham's prayer for the son he settled in the desert, and Abraham and Ishmael building the Kaaba, the shrine at Mecca.
compare.title: Ishmael in the Qur'an

paras: Read the Hagar stories again and count who sees whom. Sarai and Abram look at Hagar as a means to an end: a womb, then a problem. No one in the household calls her by her name; she is 'my servant', 'your maid', 'this servant'. Then, in the desert, the angel calls her 'Hagar', asks where she is going, and listens to her answer. She names God 'the God who sees me'.

This is the first thing the story says about the unchosen: God sees them. The covenant goes through Isaac, but God's care does not stop at the covenant's edge. Ishmael's name, 'God hears', says the same. The story was told and kept by Abraham's descendants through Isaac, and they told it with sympathy for the son who was sent away.
sections.key: The household sees Hagar as a means; God sees her as a person, and hears her son.

paras: Does God's choice of Isaac mean the rejection of Ishmael? Genesis says no. Ishmael receives promises almost as large as Isaac's: a great nation, countless descendants, twelve princes (17:20). He is circumcised with Abraham (17:23–26), so he bears the covenant's sign. God is 'with the boy' (21:20). What he does not receive is the covenant role: to be the line through which the promise to all nations is carried.

That distinction, between being loved and being given a particular task, is one of the keys to the whole journey. The Jewish scholar Jon Levenson puts it this way: in Genesis, chosenness is real and often painful, but the unchosen are not damned; they are part of the story, and frequently treated with great tenderness.
sections.key: Ishmael is loved, blessed and protected; what he is not given is the covenant role of carrying the promise.

paras: The same story is read in remarkably different ways. Paul used it as an allegory of law and freedom. Jewish tradition identified Ishmael with the Arabs, and later rabbis were sometimes hostile, sometimes sympathetic; one midrash says Abraham secretly visited Ishmael in the desert. Islam places Hagar and Ishmael at the centre of its holiest rites.

In recent decades many Christian readers, especially women, have read the story from Hagar's side. The American theologian Delores Williams, in Sisters in the Wilderness (1993), saw in Hagar the experience of Black women in America: enslaved, used for their bodies, driven out, and met by God in the wilderness, who gave them not freedom at once but survival and a future.

A story of chosen and unchosen, both under God's care
An Egyptian slave who sees God and is seen
Ancestor of the Arab peoples; sometimes a rival, sometimes a penitent (some rabbis said he repented)
Explains Israel's relation to its neighbours
Some rabbis identified her with Keturah, whom Abraham later married (Genesis 25:1)
In Paul, the son 'born according to the flesh'
Paul's allegory of law and promise (Galatians 4); modern readers from Hagar's side
In Paul, the covenant of slavery; for many today, the God who sees the oppressed

The founding of Mecca and the Hajj
Hajar, honoured mother; her search for water is re-enacted by every pilgrim

sections.key: Paul made Hagar an allegory; the rabbis linked Ishmael with the Arabs; Islam honours Hajar and Ismail at Mecca; many readers today read from Hagar's side.

paras: This story contains slavery, sexual use of a woman who could not refuse, jealousy and expulsion. Genesis does not approve of what Abram and Sarai do; it simply tells it, and lets the reader see the cost. Its sympathy is plainly with Hagar and the boy.

We should also say what the story does not settle. It does not tell us whether God approved of the slavery that frames it; later biblical law limits slavery and commands care for the foreigner and the runaway slave (Deuteronomy 23:15–16), and the New Testament's 'neither slave nor free' (Galatians 3:28) became, in time, part of the case against it. It is fair to ask why God tells Hagar to return and later tells Abraham to listen to Sarah. Readers have answered: for survival, for the promise's sake, or as the hard limits of a world God works within rather than approves. The question deserves to be held, not hurried.
sections.key: Genesis tells Hagar's story without approving its cruelty; its sympathy is with her, and the hard questions remain fair ones.

paras: The story of the two sons does not end with the expulsion. When Abraham dies 'at a good old age', Genesis records: 'Isaac and Ishmael, his sons, buried him in the cave of Machpelah' (25:9). The two half-brothers, separated as boys, stand together at their father's grave.

Today that grave, in Hebron, is one of the most contested places on earth, divided between a synagogue and a mosque. The one image Genesis leaves us of the two sons together is of them burying their father in peace.
sections.key: Isaac and Ishmael bury Abraham together: the story ends with the brothers side by side.

refs: Laws of Hammurabi §§144–147, trans. L. W. King (1910); the Nuzi marriage contract (HSS 5 67), in J. B. Pritchard, Ancient Near Eastern Texts (3rd ed. 1969).
Qur'an 14:35–41; 2:124–129; 37:100–101. Hajar, Safa and Marwa, and Zamzam: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of the Prophets (hadith 3364).
Jon D. Levenson, The Death and Resurrection of the Beloved Son (1993) and Inheriting Abraham (2012).
Rabbinic traditions: Genesis Rabbah 61:4 (Hagar as Keturah); Pirke de-Rabbi Eliezer 30 (Abraham visits Ishmael).

debate.question: How should we read the story of Hagar and Ishmael?

positions.name: A story of the promise
positions.who: Most traditional Jewish and Christian readers
positions.view: The story's main point is that God keeps his promise his own way, through Isaac, not through human schemes; Ishmael is blessed, but the covenant line is Isaac's.
positions.evidence: Genesis 17:19–21; 21:12; the contrast between the planned son and the promised son.

positions.name: A story of the God who sees
positions.who: Phyllis Trible; Delores Williams; many readers today
positions.view: The story's heart is Hagar: used, abused and driven out by the family of promise, and met by God in the wilderness. It judges the chosen family and shows God's care for the oppressed.
positions.evidence: Hagar alone names God; God appears to her first; the angel calls her by name; Ishmael means 'God hears'.

positions.name: A story of two peoples
positions.who: Islamic tradition; many historians of religion
positions.view: The story is the founding of two lines of Abraham's descendants, both blessed; Ishmael's line is not a footnote but its own great story, centred on Mecca.

debate.agree: All agree that God hears Ishmael and blesses him, and that the story does not hide the suffering of Hagar.

look.why: Hagar was an Egyptian, and when she found her son a wife, she went back to Egypt for her (Genesis 21:21). Sanford Robinson Gifford, an American landscape painter, saw this Egyptian town on the Nile in 1869 and painted it in 1874, in hazy desert light.
points: A dirt path winds through gold-green grass towards a town on low hills.
Tiny people walk on the path, and one rides a horse.
In the town, flat-topped buildings and one domed building with two slender minarets, among palm trees.
A low sun blazes over rocky mountains on the left.
To the right, people sit near a white tent, with horses and smaller animals grazing.

music.why: John Newton, once a slave-ship captain, wrote 'Amazing Grace' after his conversion: 'I once was lost, but now am found, was blind, but now I see'. Hagar's God opens blind eyes; Newton's song came out of the slave trade.

think.why: Hagar was a slave. Ask how the Bible that contains her story became, over centuries, part of the case against slavery.

learn.why: The only time in the Bible a person names God: the God who sees.

check.q: Why might Sarai's plan to have a child through Hagar have seemed reasonable to her neighbours?
options: Because Hagar had asked to become Abram's wife
Because Hagar was Abram's first wife
Because God had told her to
Because ancient laws and contracts, such as Hammurabi's, recognised a childless wife giving her slave to bear a child that counted as hers
check.why: It was a known and regulated custom.

check.q: What is the significance of Hagar naming God 'El Roi'?
options: It means 'God of Abraham'
It was the usual Egyptian name for God
It shows Hagar worshipped another god
It is the only time a person in the Bible gives God a name, and it is a foreign slave whom no one else in the story sees
check.why: The unseen woman is the one who sees God and is seen.

check.q: Which statement about Ishmael in Genesis is accurate?
options: God rejects him and promises him nothing
He never meets Isaac again
He becomes the covenant heir instead of Isaac
He is blessed, promised a great nation and twelve princes, and circumcised, but the covenant line passes through Isaac
check.why: He is loved and blessed; what he is not given is the covenant role. He buries Abraham with Isaac.

check.q: In Galatians 4, Paul links Hagar with Mount Sinai. Why is this surprising?
options: Because Hagar is never mentioned again after Genesis
Because Sinai is where Abraham bound Isaac
Because Paul identifies Hagar with the Gentile Christians he is defending
Because Sinai, where the law was given, was the glory of the Jews, Sarah's descendants; Paul reverses the usual identification to argue for Gentile freedom
check.why: Paul's allegory turns the expected reading upside down for his argument.

check.q: What does Hagar's search for water mean in Islam?
options: Pilgrims on the Hajj walk seven times between the hills of Safa and Marwa in memory of it, and drink from the well of Zamzam
Pilgrims drink from the wells of Beersheba
It is remembered by fasting during Ramadan
It explains why Muslims pray five times a day
check.why: Hajar's search is part of the central pilgrimage of Islam.

check.q: Why does the Hebrew word for what Ishmael was doing (Genesis 21:9) matter?
options: It is a play on Hagar's name
It shows Ishmael was mocking Sarah's old age
It proves he was attacking Isaac
It is a play on Isaac's name ('laughing' or 'playing') and may mean only that he was playing, or acting as an heir, so the reason for the expulsion is ambiguous
check.why: Metzahek echoes Yitzhak; translators differ between 'mocking' and 'playing'.

tutorial.question: What does the story of Hagar and Ishmael show about God's choosing?
tutorial.approach: Tell the two stories (Genesis 16 and 21) briefly. Then ask what God does for Hagar and Ishmael, and what he does not give them. Compare Paul's allegory with the Islamic tradition and with readings from Hagar's side. End by saying how the story answers the question 'what about the ones not chosen?'
strong: Explains the ancient custom behind Sarai's plan.
Notices that God appears first to Hagar, calls her by name, and that she names God.
Distinguishes between being blessed and being given the covenant role.
Explains Paul's allegory and its limits.
Describes Hagar and Ishmael's place in Islam.
Faces the story's troubling elements honestly.
