closing.title: Your answer
closing.prompt: Why does the Bible's story turn on one family? In about 300 words, give your answer, using at least three generations of the family, and answer the strongest objection to it.
closing.practice: Read the whole of Genesis 12–50 over the next fortnight, three or four chapters a day. Each day, ask: who is chosen here, who is not, and how does God treat each of them?
synthesis: This journey asked why the Bible's story turns, at Genesis 12, from all humanity to one family. Here are the short answers to its questions.

Who was Abraham? A man from Ur, whose family 'served other gods', called in about 2000 to 1800 BC, if Genesis's numbers are taken at face value, to leave his country, his clan and his father's house for a land God would show him. Did he exist? Archaeology cannot say: there is no direct evidence either way, and most scholars think the stories were shaped centuries later, while some argue they fit the early second millennium well. Jews, Christians and Muslims all call him father and 'friend of God', through different sons and in different ways.

What did God promise, and how could it be trusted? A land, a great nation, and a blessing for 'all the families of the earth'. God bound himself by covenant: in the ancient ceremony of Genesis 15, only God passed between the pieces, taking the whole risk of the promise on himself. Abraham trusted it with no evidence, and God 'credited it to him for righteousness'. Paul read this as faith, not works of the law; James as faith that acts; Catholics, Protestants, Orthodox and Jews still frame faith and works differently, though Lutherans and Catholics agreed much in 1999.

What about those who were not chosen? God saw Hagar, the Egyptian slave whom the household used and drove out; she is the only person in the Bible to name God, 'the God who sees'. He heard Ishmael and blessed him; Isaac and Ishmael buried their father together. In Islam, Hajar and Ismail stand at the heart of the pilgrimage to Mecca. Later, Esau, passed over for Jacob, is the one who runs to forgive.

What was the family chosen for? God said it himself: 'to do righteousness and justice' (18:19). Abraham welcomed strangers, who turned out to be God and angels, and pleaded for Sodom: 'Shouldn't the Judge of all the earth do right?' God welcomed the argument, because his justice is real and can be appealed to.

How can God ask Abraham to sacrifice his son? This is the strongest objection, and it is real: Kant argued that we can never be surer a voice is God's than that killing a child is wrong; Ingersoll that 'the boy was not consulted'. The story is told as a test, and it ends with the knife stopped and a ram given instead; in a world that knew child sacrifice, that was a 'no', though it transforms more than it rejects the idea that a child belongs to God. Jews remember Isaac's binding at Rosh Hashanah, Christians see a figure of Christ, Muslims celebrate a consenting son at Eid al-Adha; Kierkegaard insisted that faith is not easy. All agree no one may use the story to harm another.

Why does God choose flawed people? Because the choosing is by grace. Abraham lied, Sarah drove out Hagar, Jacob cheated his brother, Joseph's brothers sold him. But being chosen did not leave them as they were: Jacob, wrestling at the Jabbok, stopped grabbing and asked, admitted his name, was renamed Israel, and was reconciled with Esau. 'Esau I hated' means 'not chosen', and the churches read election very differently.

Can people who hurt each other be reconciled? Joseph tested his brothers, Judah offered himself in Benjamin's place, and Joseph forgave: 'you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to save many people alive'. It is the Bible's clearest picture of providence: God bringing good out of evil without making evil good.

So why does the story turn on one family? Not because they were better than others, nor to keep the blessing for themselves, nor at the expense of others, but so that, through one real family in history, chosen by grace and held by God's promise, every family on earth might be blessed. The objection that this is favouritism, or that universal truths cannot hang on one people's story, is serious. Genesis's answer is to show it happening: Joseph, the son sold by his brothers, feeds 'all countries'. Christians believe the promise is fulfilled in Jesus, 'the son of Abraham', through whom Abraham's family is opened to every nation; Jews, that it continues in the covenant people; Muslims, that it was renewed in Muhammad, descendant of Ishmael.

One more thing. Count how much of the West comes from these chapters. The idea of a calling, a life lived towards a promise rather than repeating the past, begins with Abraham's leaving. Hospitality to strangers as a sacred duty, the right to argue for justice even with the highest authority, the dignity of the slave whom God sees, the conviction that forgiveness can break a cycle of revenge between brothers: all are here. So is the hardest question about obedience and conscience, which Kant and Kierkegaard turned into modern philosophy. And the word for a people defined by their struggle with God, Israel, comes from one night by a river.
exam: 'The family is chosen for the sake of all the families of the earth.' Discuss with reference to Genesis 12:1–3 and 18:19.

title: Exodus and the law
question: What are freedom and law for?
line: Seven sessions from slavery in Egypt to the mountain of Sinai: the God who hears the cry of slaves, the name from the burning bush, the night of Passover, the sea and the desert, the Ten Commandments beside the laws of Babylon, the question whether it happened, and the promise of a new covenant written on the heart.
why: No story has shaped the West's idea of freedom more than the Exodus, and no law has shaped its idea of justice more than the law given at Sinai. Jews retell it every Passover; Christians read Jesus's death through it; slaves in America sang it; revolutionaries and civil rights leaders preached it. This journey reads Exodus with the Talmud, Hammurabi, Frederick Douglass and Tacitus, faces the archaeology honestly, and asks what freedom and law are for. It is written at the depth of a first-year university course, for anyone.
follows: A first-year theology paper on the Pentateuch (Exodus, the law and covenant) in its ancient Near Eastern setting, with elements of papers on biblical archaeology and on law and ethics.

Explain the Sinai covenant and the Ten Commandments, compare the law of Moses with Hammurabi's, and assess its treatment of slavery.
State the case against the historicity of the Exodus at full strength, and the evidence and scholarly positions on the other side.
Explain the love command, Jeremiah's new covenant, the meaning of 'Old' and 'New Testament', and how Jews and the churches relate to the law.

sessions.title: Slaves in Egypt
sessions.line: A king afraid of foreigners, two midwives who say no, and a God who hears.
sessions.plain: Genesis ended with Jacob's family safe in Egypt. Exodus begins centuries later: a new king who fears them, forced labour, and an order to kill every baby boy. Two midwives refuse. A baby is hidden in a basket on the Nile and raised by Pharaoh's own daughter. He grows up, kills a slave-driver, and runs away. Then, at the end of the chapter, God hears the slaves' cry. This session asks why Israel's story begins in slavery, and what it tells us about God.
sessions.why: This is the first session. 'Abraham and the promise' ended with Joseph's family saved in Egypt and his bones waiting to go home. Exodus asks the next question: what happens when the family becomes a people, and the people become slaves?
answers: How did Abraham's descendants become slaves in Egypt?
Who were the midwives, and why does the Bible honour them?
Who was Moses, and why does his story start with a crime and an escape?
Does God notice injustice, and what does he do about it?
How have enslaved people read this story?
sessions.finding: Israel's story begins in slavery, and its God is the one who hears the cry of slaves; the first resistance comes not from heroes but from two midwives who fear God more than Pharaoh.

paras: If you have taken 'Abraham and the promise', you have followed one family for four generations: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Jacob's twelve sons. God promised Abraham descendants, a land, and that through him 'all the families of the earth' would be blessed. Genesis ended with the whole family living in Egypt, where Joseph had saved them from famine, and with Joseph's last words: 'God will surely visit you, and bring you up out of this land'.

Exodus, the second book of the Bible, picks up the story. Its name is Greek for 'the way out'. It tells how the family became a nation of slaves, how God brought them out, and what happened at the mountain of Sinai, where they received the law. It is the founding story of the Jewish people, and Jews still retell it every year at Passover.
background.key: Genesis ended with Jacob's family in Egypt; Exodus, 'the way out', tells how they became slaves and were set free.

paras: Exodus is the Bible's great story of freedom. But it is a strange kind of freedom story: the slaves walk out of Egypt and, within three months, they are standing at a mountain receiving laws. That raises the question of this journey: what are freedom and law for? Is law the opposite of freedom, or what freedom is for?

We will follow the story in order: slavery, God's name, the night of Passover, the sea and the desert, the Ten Commandments. One session gives the strongest objection its full weight: did any of this happen? The last session gives a verdict, and explains why Christians call the two halves of their Bible the Old and New 'Testaments'.

background.key: What are freedom and law for? We follow the story from slavery to Sinai, hear the case against, then give a verdict.

paras: Moses is the central human figure of the Hebrew Bible: the man who led Israel out of Egypt, spoke with God on the mountain of Sinai and gave Israel its law. Jews call him Moshe Rabbenu, 'Moses our teacher', and count him the greatest of the prophets: 'there has not arisen a prophet in Israel like Moses, whom Yahweh knew face to face' (Deuteronomy 34:10). Christians see him as the giver of the old covenant, which Jesus fulfils; in the Gospels Moses appears beside Jesus on a mountain, at the Transfiguration. Muslims honour him as Musa, the prophet named more often in the Qur'an than anyone else.

His name is probably Egyptian. The Bible explains it with a Hebrew pun, 'Because I drew him out of the water' (Exodus 2:10), but '-mose', meaning 'born of', is also the ending of Egyptian names like Thutmose and Ahmose, 'born of Thoth' and 'born of the moon'. No Egyptian record mentions him: everything we know comes from the Bible, from Exodus to Deuteronomy. How much of his story is history is the question of session 6, still to come.
background.key: Moses: Judaism's lawgiver and greatest prophet, honoured by Christians and Muslims; his name is probably Egyptian.

paras: The Bible does not name the Pharaoh, and that makes dating hard. It says the slaves built 'storage cities' named Pithom and Raamses (Exodus 1:11). Pi-Ramesses, 'the house of Ramesses', was the great Delta capital built by Ramesses II, who reigned from about 1279 to 1213 BC. So many scholars who think there is history here place the Exodus in his reign. Another date, about 1446 BC, comes from adding up the Bible's own numbers (1 Kings 6:1 says Solomon began the Temple 480 years after the Exodus).

Egypt was the greatest power of the ancient world: a land of pharaohs who were worshipped as gods, monumental building projects and huge forced-labour gangs. Semitic people from Canaan, like Jacob's family, had lived in the eastern Nile Delta for centuries. Session 6, still to come, weighs what archaeology can and cannot tell us.

background.key: Exodus names no Pharaoh; the city of Raamses points to Ramesses II, in the thirteenth century BC, though the Bible's own numbers suggest earlier.

background.h: Who wrote Exodus, and where did Moses get his ideas?
paras: Exodus does not say who wrote the whole book, though it says Moses wrote some things down: a record of a battle, 'all Yahweh's words' at Sinai, and the words of the covenant (Exodus 17:14; 24:4; 34:27). Tradition held that Moses wrote all five books of the Torah. Most scholars today think they were gathered and edited over centuries from older traditions and finished around 600 to 400 BC, though some passages, like the song Miriam and Moses sing at the sea, may be among the oldest writing in the Bible. Many believers accept this account and still read Exodus as inspired; others hold to the traditional view.

Where did the ideas come from? The Bible's own answer is: from God, on the mountain. But it also says Moses grew up as the son of Pharaoh's daughter (Exodus 2:10), and the New Testament adds that he 'was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians' (Acts 7:22). Israel's law also looks like other ancient laws in some ways. Hammurabi, king of Babylon, had issued a famous law code centuries before, and the covenant at Sinai follows the pattern of ancient treaties between a great king and a lesser one. You will compare the two law codes in session 5. What scholars find new is what the law says: a God who takes the side of slaves, a day of rest for everyone, servants and animals included, and one law for rich and poor.
background.key: Tradition says Moses; most scholars say many hands over centuries. Moses' world had Egyptian wisdom, Babylonian law and royal treaties; a God who frees slaves is new.

paras: The main reading has three parts: the slavery and the midwives (1:8–22), the baby in the basket (2:1–10), and Moses' first attempt at justice, his flight, and God's response (2:11–25).

The comparison has two parts. First, the escaped slave and abolitionist Frederick Douglass describes how he and his friends sang about 'Canaan' while planning to run away: enslaved Americans read Exodus as their own story. Second, a Jewish legend about the midwives, which shows how the rabbis honoured them.

paras: Now there arose a new king over Egypt, who didn’t know Joseph.
He said to his people, “Behold, the people of the children of Israel are more and mightier than we.
Come, let’s deal wisely with them, lest they multiply, and it happen that when any war breaks out, they also join themselves to our enemies and fight against us, and escape out of the land.”
Therefore they set taskmasters over them to afflict them with their burdens. They built storage cities for Pharaoh: Pithom and Raamses.
But the more they afflicted them, the more they multiplied and the more they spread out. They started to dread the children of Israel.
The Egyptians ruthlessly made the children of Israel serve,
and they made their lives bitter with hard service in mortar and in brick, and in all kinds of service in the field, all their service, in which they ruthlessly made them serve.
The king of Egypt spoke to the Hebrew midwives, of whom the name of the one was Shiphrah, and the name of the other Puah,
and he said, “When you perform the duty of a midwife to the Hebrew women, and see them on the birth stool, if it is a son, then you shall kill him; but if it is a daughter, then she shall live.”
But the midwives feared God, and didn’t do what the king of Egypt commanded them, but saved the baby boys alive.
The king of Egypt called for the midwives, and said to them, “Why have you done this thing and saved the boys alive?”
The midwives said to Pharaoh, “Because the Hebrew women aren’t like the Egyptian women; for they are vigorous and give birth before the midwife comes to them.”
God dealt well with the midwives, and the people multiplied, and grew very mighty.
Because the midwives feared God, he gave them families.
Pharaoh commanded all his people, saying, “You shall cast every son who is born into the river, and every daughter you shall save alive.”
A man of the house of Levi went and took a daughter of Levi as his wife.
The woman conceived and bore a son. When she saw that he was a fine child, she hid him three months.
When she could no longer hide him, she took a papyrus basket for him, and coated it with tar and with pitch. She put the child in it, and laid it in the reeds by the river’s bank.
His sister stood far off, to see what would be done to him.
Pharaoh’s daughter came down to bathe at the river. Her maidens walked along by the riverside. She saw the basket among the reeds, and sent her servant to get it.
She opened it, and saw the child, and behold, the baby cried. She had compassion on him, and said, “This is one of the Hebrews’ children.”
Then his sister said to Pharaoh’s daughter, “Should I go and call a nurse for you from the Hebrew women, that she may nurse the child for you?”
Pharaoh’s daughter said to her, “Go.”
The young woman went and called the child’s mother.
Pharaoh’s daughter said to her, “Take this child away, and nurse him for me, and I will give you your wages.”
The woman took the child, and nursed it.
The child grew, and she brought him to Pharaoh’s daughter, and he became her son. She named him Moses, and said, “Because I drew him out of the water.”
In those days, when Moses had grown up, he went out to his brothers and saw their burdens. He saw an Egyptian striking a Hebrew, one of his brothers.
He looked this way and that way, and when he saw that there was no one, he killed the Egyptian, and hid him in the sand.
He went out the second day, and behold, two men of the Hebrews were fighting with each other. He said to him who did the wrong, “Why do you strike your fellow?”
He said, “Who made you a prince and a judge over us? Do you plan to kill me, as you killed the Egyptian?”
Moses was afraid, and said, “Surely this thing is known.”
Now when Pharaoh heard this thing, he sought to kill Moses. But Moses fled from the face of Pharaoh, and lived in the land of Midian, and he sat down by a well.
Now the priest of Midian had seven daughters. They came and drew water, and filled the troughs to water their father’s flock.
The shepherds came and drove them away; but Moses stood up and helped them, and watered their flock.
When they came to Reuel, their father, he said, “How is it that you have returned so early today?”
They said, “An Egyptian delivered us out of the hand of the shepherds, and moreover he drew water for us, and watered the flock.”
He said to his daughters, “Where is he? Why is it that you have left the man? Call him, that he may eat bread.”
Moses was content to dwell with the man. He gave Moses Zipporah, his daughter.
She bore a son, and he named him Gershom, for he said, “I have lived as a foreigner in a foreign land.”
In the course of those many days, the king of Egypt died, and the children of Israel sighed because of the bondage, and they cried, and their cry came up to God because of the bondage.
God heard their groaning, and God remembered his covenant with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob.
God saw the children of Israel, and God was concerned about them.

parts.title: A king afraid
parts.context: Some centuries after Joseph. Jacob's descendants, the 'children of Israel', have multiplied in Egypt, as God promised Abraham. A new Pharaoh sees them as a threat.

commentary.on: Now there arose a new king over Egypt, who didn’t know Joseph.
commentary.text: A whole history of injustice begins with forgetting. The new king does not know, or chooses not to remember, that a Hebrew once saved Egypt from famine. Without that memory the Israelites are simply foreigners, and dangerous ones.

commentary.on: Come, let’s deal wisely with them, lest they multiply
commentary.text: This is the logic of every persecution: they are many, they might side with our enemies, we must 'deal wisely' with them. The king's fear is political, and his remedy is to turn a people into a labour force.

commentary.on: They built storage cities for Pharaoh: Pithom and Raamses.
commentary.text: A detail that can be checked. Pi-Ramesses was the capital built by Ramesses II in the thirteenth century BC; Egyptian texts describe foreign workers hauling stone and making bricks. Session 6 will ask how far details like this take us.

commentary.on: But the more they afflicted them, the more they multiplied
commentary.text: The oppression backfires. The promise to Abraham, 'I will multiply your offspring', cannot be stopped by a king.

commentary.on: But the midwives feared God, and didn’t do what the king of Egypt commanded them
commentary.text: The first act of resistance in the Bible's story of freedom is by two women, Shiphrah and Puah, who are named while the mighty Pharaoh is not. They refuse an order to murder because they 'feared God'. This is the oldest recorded act of civil disobedience: obeying God rather than the state when the state commands evil.

commentary.on: Because the Hebrew women aren’t like the Egyptian women
commentary.text: They lie to Pharaoh, cleverly, and God blesses them for it. The Bible does not pretend that protecting the innocent from a murderer is always tidy.

commentary.on: You shall cast every son who is born into the river
commentary.text: The king's last order makes the whole of Egypt complicit. The Nile, source of Egypt's life, is to become a grave. Remember the river: the next passage happens on its bank.

parts.title: A basket among the reeds
parts.context: A couple from the tribe of Levi have a son. Their names are given later: Amram and Jochebed (Exodus 6:20). His sister, unnamed here, is Miriam.

commentary.on: she took a papyrus basket for him, and coated it with tar and with pitch
commentary.text: The Hebrew word for 'basket' is tevah. It is used in only one other story in the Bible: Noah's ark. Like Noah, this baby is saved from the waters in a little ark, and he will save his people.

commentary.on: His sister stood far off, to see what would be done to him.
commentary.text: A girl watching from the reeds. She will become Miriam the prophetess, who leads the women in song at the Red Sea (session 4).

commentary.on: She had compassion on him, and said, “This is one of the Hebrews’ children.”
commentary.text: Pharaoh's own daughter knows exactly whose child it is, and disobeys her father's decree. Compassion crosses the line between oppressor and oppressed. Jewish tradition calls her Bithiah, 'daughter of God'.

commentary.on: She named him Moses, and said, “Because I drew him out of the water.”
commentary.text: A double pun. In Hebrew Mosheh sounds like 'drawing out'; in Egyptian, mose means 'son' or 'born of', as in the name Ramesses, 'Ra is the one who bore him'. The boy who will lead Israel has an Egyptian name and grows up in Pharaoh's palace. Acts 7:22 says he was 'instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians'.

parts.title: A failed rescue, and a God who hears
parts.context: The story skips Moses' childhood. Now he is a grown man, a prince of Egypt, who knows he is a Hebrew.

commentary.on: He saw an Egyptian striking a Hebrew, one of his brothers.
commentary.text: Moses calls the slaves his 'brothers'. He chooses his people. Hebrews 11:24–25 praises this: he 'refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter'.

commentary.on: He looked this way and that way, and when he saw that there was no one, he killed the Egyptian
commentary.text: Moses' first attempt at justice is a secret killing. Jewish commentators have argued about it ever since: was it justified defence of a slave, or a crime? Notice that it achieves nothing. Freedom will not come through one man's violence.

commentary.on: Who made you a prince and a judge over us?
commentary.text: The people he tried to help do not want him. The question is a fair one, and the rest of Exodus answers it: God will make him their leader, not his own anger.

commentary.on: but Moses stood up and helped them, and watered their flock
commentary.text: In exile, Moses still cannot bear to see the weak bullied. The same instinct, rescuing shepherd girls at a well, without violence this time. Like Jacob, he meets his wife at a well.

commentary.on: I have lived as a foreigner in a foreign land.
commentary.text: He names his son Gershom, which sounds like 'a stranger there'. Moses knows what it is to be a foreigner. Israel's law will later say again and again: 'you know the heart of a foreigner, for you were foreigners in Egypt'.

commentary.on: God heard their groaning, and God remembered his covenant with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob.
commentary.text: Four verbs, in the last two verses: God heard, God remembered, God saw, God knew (the Hebrew of 'was concerned' is literally 'knew'). This is the turning point. The God of Exodus is the God who hears the cry of slaves. That is the first thing the book says about him, and it shaped everything after it.

paras: I am the more inclined to think that he suspected us, because, prudent as we were, as I now look back, I can see that we did many silly things, very well calculated to awaken suspicion. We were, at times, remarkably buoyant, singing hymns and making joyous exclamations, almost as triumphant in their tone as if we reached a land of freedom and safety. A keen observer might have detected in our repeated singing of
O Canaan, sweet Canaan, I am bound for the land of Canaan,
something more than a hope of reaching heaven. We meant to reach the north--and the north was our Canaan.
I thought I heard them say, There were lions in the way, I don't expect to Star Much longer here.
Run to Jesus--shun the danger-- I don't expect to stay Much longer here.

was a favorite air, and had a double meaning. In the lips of some, it meant the expectation of a speedy summons to a world of spirits; but, in the lips of our company, it simply meant, a speedy pilgrimage toward a free state, and deliverance from all the evils and dangers of slavery.

The two Hebrew midwives were Jochebed, the mother of Moses, and Miriam, his sister. When they appeared before Pharaoh, Miriam exclaimed: "Woe be to this man when God visits retribution upon him for his evil deeds." The king would have killed her for these audacious words, had not Jochebed allayed his wrath by saying: "Why dost thou pay heed to her words? She is but a child, and knows not what she speaks." Yet, although Miriam was but five years old at the time, she nevertheless accompanied her mother, and helped her with her offices to the Hebrew women, giving food to the new-born babes while Jochebed washed and bathed them.

The king used all sorts of devices to render the midwives amenable to his wishes. He approached them with amorous proposals, which they both repelled, and then he threatened them with death by fire. But they said within themselves: "Our father Abraham opened an inn, that he might feed the wayfarers, though they were heathen, and we should neglect the children, nay, kill them? No, we shall have a care to keep them alive." Thus they failed to execute what Pharaoh had commanded. Instead of murdering the babes, they supplied all their needs. If a mother that had given birth to a child lacked food and drink, the midwives went to well-to-do women, and took up a collection, that the infant might not suffer want. They did still more for the little ones. They made supplication to God, praying: "Thou knowest that we are not fulfilling the words of Pharaoh, but it is our aim to fulfil Thy words. O that it be Thy will, our Lord, to let the child come into the world safe and sound, lest we fall under the suspicion that we tried to slay it, and maimed it in the attempt." The Lord hearkened to their prayer, and no child born under the ministrations of Shiphrah and Puah, or Jochebed and Miriam, as the midwives are also called, came into the world lame or blind or afflicted with any other blemish.

parts.author: Frederick Douglass
parts.ref: Frederick Douglass, My Bondage and My Freedom (1855)
parts.title: The north was our Canaan
parts.context: Frederick Douglass (1818–1895) was born into slavery in Maryland, escaped in 1838, and became the most famous abolitionist and orator in America. In this chapter of his second autobiography he describes a failed escape plot of 1835 with five friends. 'Mr. Freeland' was the farmer to whom they were hired out. Canaan was the promised land of Exodus; the songs are spirituals of the kind the enslaved sang. The line 'I don't expect to Star' is a misprint for 'stay' in the original.
parts.plain: Douglass says: we were so excited about our escape plan that we sang hymns almost as if we were already free. When we sang about being 'bound for the land of Canaan', we didn't only mean heaven. We meant the North, where we could be free. Some sang these songs about dying and going to heaven; for us they meant running away from slavery.

commentary.on: something more than a hope of reaching heaven. We meant to reach the north--and the north was our Canaan.
commentary.text: This is the key sentence. Slaveholders taught the enslaved Christianity in the hope that it would make them content with heaven later. The enslaved heard something else in the Bible: a God who brought slaves out of Egypt. 'Canaan' meant the free North, or Canada.

commentary.on: was a favorite air, and had a double meaning.
commentary.text: The spirituals had two meanings at once: heaven, and escape. 'Go down, Moses, way down in Egypt land, tell old Pharaoh, let my people go' was sung by enslaved people throughout the American South. Harriet Tubman, who led dozens of slaves to freedom, was called 'Moses'.

commentary.on: a speedy pilgrimage toward a free state, and deliverance from all the evils and dangers of slavery.
commentary.text: Exodus gave enslaved people a language of hope that their owners could not forbid, because it was in the owners' own Bible. Douglass's plot failed, and he was jailed; three years later he escaped alone.

parts.author: Louis Ginzberg
parts.work: The Legends of the Jews, volume II
parts.ref: Legends of the Jews: the midwives
parts.title: Abraham opened an inn
parts.context: Louis Ginzberg's retelling of the rabbis' legends (see 'Abraham and the promise'), drawn here mainly from the Talmud (Sotah 11b) and the Midrash on Exodus. The rabbis identified the midwives Shiphrah and Puah with Moses' mother Jochebed and sister Miriam.
parts.plain: The legend says: the two midwives were Moses' mother and sister. Miriam, only five, warned Pharaoh that God would punish him. Pharaoh tried to win the midwives over and threatened them, but they reasoned: our ancestor Abraham fed even foreign strangers, so how could we kill children? So instead they collected food for poor mothers and prayed for every baby, and God rewarded them.

commentary.on: Our father Abraham opened an inn, that he might feed the wayfarers, though they were heathen, and we should neglect the children, nay, kill them?
commentary.text: The midwives' reasoning comes from the family story: Abraham welcomed strangers (you met him at his tent door in 'Abraham and the promise'). His descendants could not murder children. Their moral memory is their resistance.

commentary.on: If a mother that had given birth to a child lacked food and drink, the midwives went to well-to-do women, and took up a collection
commentary.text: The legend turns refusal into something more: active care. Not only did they not kill, they fed the poor. Disobeying an evil law is only half of goodness.

commentary.on: The Lord hearkened to their prayer, and no child born under the ministrations of Shiphrah and Puah
commentary.text: God answers the midwives' prayer. The Bible says the same more briefly: 'he gave them families' (Exodus 1:21). The rabbis went further and said that from these women came Israel's priests and kings. The lowliest act of courage is honoured most.

compare.author: Frederick Douglass and Louis Ginzberg
compare.ref: Frederick Douglass, My Bondage and My Freedom (1855)
compare.why: For people in slavery, Exodus was not ancient history. Read two short extracts: an American slave planning his escape in 1835, and a Jewish legend about the midwives who said no.
compare.title: How the enslaved read Exodus

paras: Most peoples tell founding stories about heroes, kings or gods. Rome traced itself to Aeneas, a prince of Troy; Egypt's pharaohs claimed descent from the gods. Israel's founding story is unique in the ancient world: we were slaves. Every year at Passover, Jews still say it aloud, and the law repeats it like a refrain: 'remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt' (Deuteronomy 15:15).

That memory became the basis of an ethic. Because you were slaves, rest your servants on the Sabbath. Because you were foreigners, love the foreigner. Because you were oppressed, do not oppress. A people that remembers being at the bottom is meant to look after those at the bottom.
sections.key: Israel's founding story is unique: 'we were slaves'. The memory of slavery became the basis of its ethics.

paras: The most important verses in these chapters are the last ones: God heard, remembered, saw, knew. In the ancient world gods were usually on the side of kings; Pharaoh himself was worshipped as a god. The God of Exodus takes the side of the slaves against the god-king.

This is not a passing idea. It runs through the whole Bible: God 'executes justice for the fatherless and widow and loves the foreigner' (Deuteronomy 10:18); Mary sings that God 'has put down princes from their thrones, and has exalted the lowly' (Luke 1:52). Catholic teaching calls it God's 'preferential option for the poor'; Latin American liberation theology, from the 1970s, made Exodus its central text.
sections.key: The God of Exodus hears the cry of slaves and takes their side against a god-king: a theme that runs through the whole Bible.

paras: Shiphrah and Puah are the first people in history recorded as refusing an unjust order out of conscience. Their example echoes through the West: the apostles telling the authorities 'We must obey God rather than men' (Acts 5:29); Thomas More refusing Henry VIII; Christians who hid Jews under the Nazis.

The story does not make civil disobedience simple. The midwives lie; Moses kills. The Bible honours the midwives and lets Moses' violence fail. The difference is worth noticing: they protect life, he takes it. Where the line falls between legitimate resistance and violence is a question the West has argued over ever since, from Augustine to Martin Luther King.
sections.key: The midwives are history's first recorded conscientious objectors; the story honours their protection of life and lets Moses' violence fail.

paras: Moses grows up between two worlds: born a Hebrew slave, raised an Egyptian prince, with an Egyptian name. He belongs fully to neither, and he flees to a third, Midian, in the desert of Arabia, where he marries the daughter of a foreign priest. Many Israelite names in the story are Egyptian too: Phinehas, Hophni, Merari.

Christians have always seen in Moses a figure of Christ: a baby threatened by a king's massacre, who escapes, grows up to deliver his people, and gives the law on a mountain. Matthew's Gospel tells Jesus's birth with exactly these echoes (Matthew 2:13–16).
sections.key: Moses belongs fully to no world: a Hebrew with an Egyptian name and education. Christians see him as a figure of Christ.

paras: No book of the Bible has mattered more to oppressed people. Enslaved Africans in America sang 'Go Down, Moses' and called Harriet Tubman their Moses. Martin Luther King's last speech, the night before he was murdered in 1968, ended on the mountain where Moses saw the promised land.

There is a hard irony here. Slaveholders read the same Bible, and the same law of Moses regulated slavery rather than abolishing it (session 5 will face this). The enslaved heard the deeper current: a God who brings slaves out. Douglass himself wrote that between the Christianity of Christ and the slaveholding Christianity of America he recognised 'the widest possible difference'.
sections.key: Enslaved Americans read Exodus as their own story; the irony is that their owners read the same book.

refs: Exodus 1–2; 6:20; Deuteronomy 10:18; 15:15; Acts 5:29; 7:22; Hebrews 11:24–26; Matthew 2:13–16; Luke 1:52.
Pi-Ramesses (Qantir): Edgar Pusch and others, excavations from 1980; the Leiden Papyrus 348 on 'Apiru hauling stone; James Hoffmeier, Israel in Egypt (1997).
The midwives as Jochebed and Miriam: Talmud, Sotah 11b; Exodus Rabbah 1:13. Bithiah: 1 Chronicles 4:18 and Leviticus Rabbah 1:3.
Frederick Douglass, My Bondage and My Freedom (1855), ch. XIX; Narrative of the Life (1845), appendix; Sarah Bradford, Scenes in the Life of Harriet Tubman (1869).
Gustavo Gutiérrez, A Theology of Liberation (1971); Catechism of the Catholic Church 2448 ('preferential love'); Martin Luther King, 'I've Been to the Mountaintop' (3 April 1968).

debate.question: Was Moses right to kill the Egyptian?

positions.name: Justified defence
positions.who: Some rabbis (Exodus Rabbah 1:29); many modern readers
positions.view: Moses killed a man who was beating, perhaps killing, a defenceless slave. Defending the innocent against deadly violence is just.
positions.evidence: 'He saw an Egyptian striking a Hebrew'; Acts 7:24 says Moses 'defended him, and avenged him who was oppressed'.

positions.name: A wrong, and a lesson
positions.who: Other Jewish and Christian commentators
positions.view: Moses acted in secret and in anger, on his own authority. The story shows that freedom cannot come by one man's violence: it fails, and Moses must flee and wait forty years for God's call.
positions.evidence: 'He looked this way and that way'; the Hebrews reject him; he flees; God, not Moses, finally sets them free.

positions.name: Neither simply
positions.who: Many readers today
positions.view: The story deliberately leaves it unresolved. It shows Moses' passion for justice, which God later uses, and its danger when it acts alone.
positions.evidence: The narrator makes no judgement; the same instinct, without violence, helps the shepherd girls at the well.

debate.agree: All agree that Moses' sympathy for the oppressed was right, and that his act did not bring freedom: God did.

look.why: Sébastien Bourdon, a French painter, painted the moment Pharaoh's daughter finds the baby Moses in the 1650s, as an elegant procession by a river.
points: A smiling, blond infant lies in a basket held by a bare-chested, bearded man by the riverbank.
The tallest woman, in a gold diadem and a golden-yellow gown, reaches out her arm towards the baby.
Two women stoop to reach for the basket.
A procession of women and girls in bright robes follows behind; the last girl offers a tiny bouquet.
Trees line the far bank under a brilliant blue sky.

music.why: 'Were You There' is one of the spirituals created by enslaved African Americans, who sang their own suffering into the Bible's stories. 'Go Down, Moses' comes from the same tradition.

think.why: Exodus is the Bible's great story of slaves set free. Ask how the West moved from accepting slavery to abolishing it.

learn.why: The turning point of Exodus: God hears, remembers, sees and knows.

check.q: Why does the new Pharaoh enslave the Israelites, according to Exodus 1?
options: Because he feared that a growing foreign people might side with Egypt's enemies
Because God told him to
Because Joseph had wronged Egypt
Because they had broken Egyptian law
check.why: 'Lest they multiply, and… join themselves to our enemies': the logic of persecution.

check.q: What is unusual about how Exodus 1 names people?
options: It names every Pharaoh
It names the two midwives, Shiphrah and Puah, but not the mighty Pharaoh
It names Moses' parents first
It names no women
check.why: The humble resisters are remembered by name; the god-king is not.

check.q: The Hebrew word for Moses' basket, tevah, is used in only one other story in the Bible. Which?
options: The tower of Babel
Noah's ark
The burning bush
Jacob's ladder
check.why: Both are saved from the waters in an 'ark' to save others.

check.q: What does Moses' first attempt to help the slaves show, in the story's own logic?
options: That the Hebrews were ungrateful and should stay slaves
That violence is the way to freedom
That Pharaoh was just
That one man's secret violence achieves nothing; freedom must come from God
check.why: He is rejected, flees, and waits forty years; God, not Moses' anger, brings freedom.

check.q: What did 'Canaan' mean in the songs Douglass and his friends sang?
options: Their owner's farm
The land of Israel today
Both heaven and, secretly, the free North they meant to escape to
Only heaven after death
check.why: 'The north was our Canaan': the songs had a double meaning.

check.q: What makes Israel's founding story unusual among ancient peoples?
options: It begins with a great king
It claims descent from the gods
It has no founder
It begins in slavery, and the memory of slavery becomes the basis of its ethics
check.why: 'Remember that you were a slave in Egypt' is the refrain of Israel's law.

tutorial.question: What does Exodus 1–2 say about God, power and the people who resist it?
tutorial.approach: Describe Pharaoh's fear and policy. Then look at those who resist: the midwives, Moses' mother and sister, Pharaoh's daughter, Moses himself. Compare their methods and how the story judges them. End with what the last verses of chapter 2 say about God, and how enslaved people later read the story.
strong: Explains Pharaoh's fear and the logic of his oppression.
Notices that the resisters are mostly women, and the midwives are named.
Contrasts the midwives' protection of life with Moses' killing and its failure.
Explains the four verbs of 2:24–25 and why they matter.
Uses Douglass to show how the enslaved read Exodus.
Notes the unusual fact that Israel's founding story is one of slavery.

reading.author: Jonathan Sacks
reading.title: Covenant and Conversation: Exodus
reading.why: A former Chief Rabbi's essays on each week's reading from Exodus; wise and readable.

reading.author: Albert J. Raboteau
reading.title: Slave Religion
reading.why: How enslaved Africans in America made Christianity, and Exodus, their own.

reading.author: Brevard Childs
reading.title: The Book of Exodus: A Critical, Theological Commentary
reading.why: The classic theological commentary.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: find out about one place where people are held in forced labour or modern slavery today, and do one concrete thing: give, write, or change what you buy.
sessions.reflect: Who are the people around you whose cry is easy not to hear?
takeaways: A new king who forgot Joseph turns Israel into slaves; the oppression backfires, as the promise to Abraham keeps working.
The first resisters are two midwives who fear God more than Pharaoh; Moses' own violence fails.
The God of Exodus hears, remembers, sees and knows the slaves' suffering; the enslaved in America read it as their own story.

sessions.title: What is your name?
sessions.line: A shepherd, a bush that burns and is not consumed, and the most mysterious name of God.
sessions.plain: Moses is a fugitive shepherd in the desert when he sees a bush on fire that does not burn up. God speaks from it, tells him to go back to Egypt and set the slaves free, and Moses asks the obvious question: who are you? The answer, 'I AM WHO I AM', has puzzled and fascinated readers for three thousand years. This session asks who the God of Exodus is, what his name means, and why Moses didn't want the job.
sessions.why: Session 1 ended with God hearing the slaves' cry. Now he acts, and the first thing he does is reveal who he is. Before the slaves can be freed, they need to know who is freeing them.
answers: What happened at the burning bush?
What does God's name, 'I AM WHO I AM', mean?
Why do Jews not say the name of God, and why do English Bibles print 'the LORD'?
Why did Moses refuse, and why did God choose him anyway?
Is the God of Exodus the same God Christians worship?
sessions.finding: The God who frees Israel is not a force of nature or a god of one place but a personal God who has a name, keeps his promises to Abraham, and says 'I will be with you'; his name points to a being beyond all our categories.

paras: In session 1, a new Pharaoh enslaved Abraham's descendants; two midwives refused to kill the babies; Moses was saved in a basket, raised as an Egyptian prince, killed a slave-driver and fled. At the end God heard the slaves' cry. Finding: Israel's story begins in slavery, and its God hears the cry of slaves.
background.key: Slavery, resistance, flight; and a God who hears.

paras: By Jewish tradition Moses was forty when he fled and spent forty years in Midian (Acts 7:23, 30 has the same numbers). He has become a shepherd for his father-in-law Jethro, a priest of Midian, in the deserts east of Egypt. The prince of Egypt now spends his days with sheep.

He leads the flock to 'God's mountain', called Horeb here and Sinai elsewhere. Where exactly it is no one knows: the traditional site, Jebel Musa in the south of the Sinai peninsula, where St Catherine's Monastery has stood since the sixth century, is one of about a dozen candidates, some of them in Arabia, where Midian was.
background.key: Forty years on, Moses is a shepherd in the desert, at the mountain of God.

paras: In the ancient world, every god had a name, and knowing a god's name gave you a way to call on him, and sometimes a kind of power over him. Egypt had hundreds of gods: Ra the sun, Osiris of the dead, Hapi the Nile. Pharaoh himself was 'son of Ra'. Each god had a place, a function, a temple.
So Moses' question, 'What is his name?', is the question any slave in Egypt would ask: which god are you, and what can you do? The answer is like no other god's.
background.key: Ancient gods had names, places and functions; Moses asks which god this is.

paras: The main reading has three parts: the bush (3:1–6), the call and the name (3:7–15), and two short passages where Pharaoh asks 'Who is Yahweh?' and God answers with seven promises (5:1–2; 6:2–8).
The comparison is from Jewish legend again: why God chose a shepherd, and why he spoke from a thorn-bush.
background.key: The bush, the name, Pharaoh's question and God's seven promises; then Jewish legends of the shepherd and the thorn-bush.

before: What does Moses have to do before God speaks? What does God tell him to do next?
How many objections does Moses raise? Which one gets the strangest answer?
In 6:6–8, count the things God says 'I will' do.
sessions.readWhy: The burning bush and God's name, in three parts.

paras: Now Moses was keeping the flock of Jethro, his father-in-law, the priest of Midian, and he led the flock to the back of the wilderness, and came to God’s mountain, to Horeb.
Yahweh’s angel appeared to him in a flame of fire out of the middle of a bush. He looked, and behold, the bush burned with fire, and the bush was not consumed.
Moses said, “I will go now, and see this great sight, why the bush is not burned.”
When Yahweh saw that he came over to see, God called to him out of the middle of the bush, and said, “Moses! Moses!”
He said, “Here I am.”
He said, “Don’t come close. Take off your sandals, for the place you are standing on is holy ground.”
Moreover he said, “I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.”
Moses hid his face because he was afraid to look at God.
Yahweh said, “I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt, and have heard their cry because of their taskmasters, for I know their sorrows.

I have come down to deliver them out of the hand of the Egyptians, and to bring them up out of that land to a good and large land, to a land flowing with milk and honey; to the place of the Canaanite, the Hittite, the Amorite, the Perizzite, the Hivite, and the Jebusite.
Now, behold, the cry of the children of Israel has come to me. Moreover I have seen the oppression with which the Egyptians oppress them.
Come now therefore, and I will send you to Pharaoh, that you may bring my people, the children of Israel, out of Egypt.”
Moses said to God, “Who am I, that I should go to Pharaoh, and that I should bring the children of Israel out of Egypt?”
He said, “Certainly I will be with you. This will be the token to you, that I have sent you: when you have brought the people out of Egypt, you shall serve God on this mountain.”
Moses said to God, “Behold, when I come to the children of Israel, and tell them, ‘The God of your fathers has sent me to you,’ and they ask me, ‘What is his name?’ what should I tell them?”
God said to Moses, “I AM WHO I AM,” and he said, “You shall tell the children of Israel this: ‘I AM has sent me to you.’ ”

God said moreover to Moses, “You shall tell the children of Israel this, ‘Yahweh, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you.’ This is my name forever, and this is my memorial to all generations.
Afterward Moses and Aaron came, and said to Pharaoh, “This is what Yahweh, the God of Israel, says, ‘Let my people go, that they may hold a feast to me in the wilderness.’ ”
Pharaoh said, “Who is Yahweh, that I should listen to his voice to let Israel go? I don’t know Yahweh, and moreover I will not let Israel go.”
God spoke to Moses, and said to him, “I am Yahweh.
I appeared to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, as God Almighty; but by my name Yahweh I was not known to them.
I have also established my covenant with them, to give them the land of Canaan, the land of their travels, in which they lived as aliens.
Moreover I have heard the groaning of the children of Israel, whom the Egyptians keep in bondage, and I have remembered my covenant.

Therefore tell the children of Israel, ‘I am Yahweh, and I will bring you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians, and I will rid you out of their bondage, and I will redeem you with an outstretched arm, and with great judgments.
I will take you to myself for a people. I will be your God; and you shall know that I am Yahweh your God, who brings you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians.
I will bring you into the land which I swore to give to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob; and I will give it to you for a heritage: I am Yahweh.’ ”

parts.title: A bush that burns
parts.context: Moses is in the desert with Jethro's flock, at Horeb, 'the mountain of God'.

commentary.on: the bush burned with fire, and the bush was not consumed
commentary.text: Fire that does not destroy. Jewish readers have seen in it Israel, burning in the furnace of slavery but not consumed; Christians, in the Orthodox tradition especially, have seen Mary, who bore God without being consumed, or the incarnation itself: God's presence in a creature that is not destroyed by it.

commentary.on: I will go now, and see this great sight
commentary.text: Moses turns aside. The call comes only when he stops to look. A rabbinic saying holds that God waited to see whether Moses would turn aside before he spoke.

commentary.on: He said, “Here I am.”
commentary.text: Hineni, the same answer Abraham gave on the way to Moriah. Moses' readiness comes before he knows what will be asked.

commentary.on: Take off your sandals, for the place you are standing on is holy ground.
commentary.text: The first time the word 'holy' appears in Exodus. The ground is holy not in itself but because God is present. Muslims, Hindus and many Eastern Christians still remove their shoes to pray; the practice goes back to this verse.

commentary.on: I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.
commentary.text: God introduces himself by his history with a family. Not a god of the sun or of the Nile, but the God of persons, who made promises. Jesus quotes this verse to argue for the resurrection: God 'is not the God of the dead, but of the living' (Mark 12:26–27).

parts.title: I AM WHO I AM
parts.context: God tells Moses why he has come, and gives him a mission.

commentary.on: I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt, and have heard their cry
commentary.text: The verbs of 2:24–25 again, now in God's own mouth: seen, heard, known. Then a new one: 'I have come down to deliver them'. The God who hears also acts.

commentary.on: Come now therefore, and I will send you to Pharaoh
commentary.text: God will deliver them, and he will do it through Moses. That is the pattern of the whole Bible: God acts through people.

commentary.on: Who am I, that I should go to Pharaoh
commentary.text: The first of five objections (3:11; 3:13; 4:1; 4:10; 4:13). Moses, who once acted on his own, now refuses to act at all. God's answer is not 'you are able' but 'I will be with you'.

commentary.on: Certainly I will be with you.
commentary.text: In Hebrew, ehyeh immach: 'I will be with you'. Hold on to the word ehyeh, 'I will be' or 'I am'. It comes back two verses later as God's name.

commentary.on: I AM WHO I AM
commentary.text: In Hebrew, ehyeh asher ehyeh. It can be translated 'I am who I am', 'I will be what I will be', or 'I am the one who is'. It is a name and also a refusal to be named like other gods: God cannot be pinned down, used or controlled. But the context gives it warmth: two verses earlier, ehyeh meant 'I will be with you'.

commentary.on: This is my name forever, and this is my memorial to all generations.
commentary.text: The name is YHWH, from the same verb 'to be'. It is written in Hebrew with four consonants (the 'Tetragrammaton', the 'four letters') and appears about 6,800 times in the Hebrew Bible. Because it was later thought too holy to pronounce, its original vowels are uncertain; 'Yahweh' is scholars' best reconstruction.

parts.title: Who is Yahweh?
parts.context: Moses and his brother Aaron go to Pharaoh. The first meeting goes badly: Pharaoh doubles the slaves' work (5:6–23). Then God speaks to Moses again.

commentary.on: Who is Yahweh, that I should listen to his voice to let Israel go?
commentary.text: Pharaoh's question is the question of the whole story. He thinks he is a god; he has never heard of a slave-god called Yahweh. The plagues, in the next session, are God's answer: 'that you may know that I am Yahweh' is repeated again and again.

commentary.on: I appeared to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, as God Almighty; but by my name Yahweh I was not known to them.
commentary.text: A puzzling sentence, since the name Yahweh appears many times in Genesis. Some scholars see here a sign of different sources woven together; Jewish and Christian readers have often taken it to mean that the patriarchs knew the name but not its full meaning, which would now be shown in action.

commentary.on: I will bring you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians, and I will rid you out of their bondage, and I will redeem you with an outstretched arm
commentary.text: Seven 'I will's in three verses: bring out, rid, redeem, take, be your God, bring in, give. 'Redeem' means to buy back a relative from slavery, the duty of the nearest kinsman. God acts as Israel's family.

commentary.on: I will take you to myself for a people. I will be your God
commentary.text: The heart of the covenant, 'I will be your God, you will be my people', which you met with Abraham. Freedom is not just from Egypt; it is for a relationship. The rest of Exodus explains what that means. At the Passover meal, Jews drink four cups of wine for the first four of these promises.

paras: Moses watched over the flocks with loving care. He led the young animals to pasture first, that they might have the tender, juicy grass for their food; the somewhat older animals he led forth next, and allowed them to graze off the herbs suitable for them; and finally came the vigorous ones that had attained their full growth, and to them he gave the hard grass that was left, which the others could not eat, but which afforded good food for them. Then spake God, "He that understandeth how to pasture sheep, providing for each what is good for it, he shall pasture My people."

Once a kid escaped from the flock, and when Moses followed it, he saw how it stopped at all the water courses, and he said to it: "Poor kid, I knew not that thou wast thirsty, and wast running after water! Thou art weary, I ween," and he carried it back to the herd on his shoulder. Then said God: "Thou hast compassion with a flock belonging to a man of flesh and blood! As thou livest, thou shalt pasture Israel, My flock."

There were good reasons for selecting the thorn-bush as the vessel for a Divine vision. It was "clean," for the heathen could not use it to make idols. God's choosing to dwell in the stunted thorn-bush conveyed the knowledge to Moses that He suffers along with Israel. Furthermore, Moses was taught that there is nothing in nature, not even the insignificant thorn-bush, that can exist without the presence of the Shekinah. Besides, the thorn-bush may be taken as the symbol for Israel in several respects. As the thorn- bush is the lowliest of all species of trees, so the condition of Israel in the exile is the lowliest as compared with that of all the other nations, but as the thorn-bush releases no bird that alights upon it without lacerating its wings, so the nations that subjugate Israel will be punished. Also, as a garden hedge is made of the thorn-bush, so Israel forms the hedge for the world, the garden of God, for without Israel the world could not endure.

Furthermore, as the thorn- bush bears thorns and roses alike, so Israel has pious and impious members, and as the thorn-bush requires ample water for its growth, so Israel can prosper only through the Torah, the celestial water. And the thorn-bush, the leaf of which consists of five leaflets, was to indicate to Moses that God had resolved to redeem Israel only for the sake of the merits of five pious men, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Aaron, and Moses. The numbers represented by the letters composing the Hebrew word for thorn-bush, Seneh, add up to one hundred and twenty, to convey that Moses would reach the age of one hundred and twenty years, and that the Shekinah would rest on Mount Horeb for one hundred and twenty days. Finally, in order to give Moses an illustration of His modesty, God descended from the exalted heavens and spake to him from a lowly thorn-bush instead of the summit of a lofty mountain or the top of a stately cedar tree.

parts.author: Louis Ginzberg
parts.work: The Legends of the Jews, volume II
parts.ref: Legends of the Jews: the shepherd and the thorn-bush
parts.title: He shall pasture My people
parts.context: Ginzberg's retelling of rabbinic legends, here chiefly from the Midrash on Exodus (Exodus Rabbah 2:2 and 2:5). The '…' marks a cut. 'Shekinah' is the rabbis' word for God's presence dwelling in the world.
parts.plain: The legend says: Moses was a caring shepherd who gave each animal the grass it needed, so God said he would shepherd Israel. Once he followed a runaway young goat, found it was only thirsty, and carried it back on his shoulder; God said, if you care like this for a man's flock, you shall shepherd mine. And God spoke from a thorn-bush, the lowliest plant, to show that he suffers with his people, and that nothing in the world is without his presence.

commentary.on: He that understandeth how to pasture sheep, providing for each what is good for it, he shall pasture My people.
commentary.text: The rabbis' answer to 'why Moses?': not his princely education but his care for the weakest. The young get the tender grass. Leadership is shepherding.

commentary.on: Poor kid, I knew not that thou wast thirsty
commentary.text: A 'kid' here is a young goat. Moses does not punish the runaway; he understands it. Christians will hear Jesus's parable of the shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine to find the one lost sheep and carries it home on his shoulders (Luke 15:4–5).

commentary.on: God's choosing to dwell in the stunted thorn-bush conveyed the knowledge to Moses that He suffers along with Israel.
commentary.text: A remarkable idea: God shares his people's suffering. He does not watch the slaves from a palace in the sky; he is in the thorn. Christians will see the idea taken to its furthest point in the cross.

commentary.on: there is nothing in nature, not even the insignificant thorn-bush, that can exist without the presence of the Shekinah.
commentary.text: If God can speak from a thorn-bush, no place is too ordinary for God. That is why the ground was holy.

compare.author: Louis Ginzberg
compare.work: The Legends of the Jews, volume II
compare.ref: Legends of the Jews: the shepherd and the thorn-bush
compare.why: Jewish teachers asked questions of every detail. Why did God choose Moses? Why speak from a lowly thorn-bush and not a great tree? Read their answers, as Ginzberg retold them.
compare.title: Why a shepherd? Why a thorn-bush?

paras: The name God gives Moses is built from the Hebrew verb 'to be'. 'I AM WHO I AM' has been read in two main ways, both of which may be intended. One stresses presence and faithfulness: 'I will be with you; I will be who I will be for you' (many Jewish interpreters, and modern scholars). The other stresses being: God is not one being among others but Being itself, the one who simply is.

The second reading came through the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, the Septuagint (third century BC), which rendered it ego eimi ho on, 'I am the one who is'. Philosophers who knew Plato heard in it the eternal, unchanging reality behind all things. Augustine, Maimonides and Thomas Aquinas all took it this way; Aquinas called 'He who is' the most proper name of God, because God's very nature is to exist.
sections.key: 'I AM' means both 'I will be with you' and 'I am the one who simply is': faithful presence and Being itself.

paras: Out of reverence, and to avoid breaking the commandment 'You shall not misuse the name', Jews stopped pronouncing the name YHWH, probably in the last centuries before Christ. When reading aloud they say Adonai, 'my Lord', or in conversation HaShem, 'the Name'. Only the high priest spoke it, once a year, in the Temple; after the Temple's destruction in AD 70, its pronunciation was lost.

This is why most English Bibles print 'the LORD' in small capitals where the Hebrew has YHWH. 'Jehovah' is a sixteenth-century mistake: the consonants of YHWH combined with the vowels of Adonai, which scribes had written in as a reminder to say 'Adonai'. The World English Bible used in Rose Window prints 'Yahweh', as many scholars do; the Catholic Church in 2008 asked that the name not be spoken or sung in its worship, out of respect for Jewish practice.

paras: Moses raises five objections: who am I? what is your name? what if they don't believe me? I'm not eloquent. Please send someone else. The last one makes God angry, but God still does not choose someone else; he sends Aaron to speak for him.

The pattern recurs throughout the Bible. Jeremiah says 'I am a child'; Isaiah says 'I am a man of unclean lips'; Jonah runs away. God's chosen are rarely volunteers. The one who once acted on his own strength must now act on God's promise: 'I will be with you'.
sections.key: Moses raises five objections; the Bible's prophets are rarely volunteers, and God's answer is 'I will be with you'.

paras: Is the God of Exodus the God of Christians and Muslims? All three faiths say they worship the God who spoke to Moses. Jesus calls him Father and quotes the bush. John's Gospel has Jesus say 'before Abraham came into existence, I AM' (John 8:58), using the very words of Exodus 3:14 in Greek; his hearers take up stones, because they understand him to be claiming the divine name. The Qur'an tells the story of the bush too (Sura 20:9–14), where God tells Moses that there is no god but him.

So the three faiths agree on who God is in this story, and disagree over what God did next: Christians believe the I AM of the bush became a man in Jesus; Jews and Muslims believe that God has no partner and no incarnation.
sections.key: Jews, Christians and Muslims all claim the God of the bush; Christians hear Jesus claiming the name I AM, which Jews and Muslims reject.

debate.question: What does 'I AM WHO I AM' mean?

positions.name: I will be with you
positions.who: Many Jewish interpreters (Rashi); Martin Buber; many modern scholars
positions.view: The name is a promise of presence and faithfulness: 'I will be there as I will be there'. God is known by what he does for his people, not by a definition.
positions.evidence: 'Certainly I will be with you' (3:12) uses the same verb; the context is rescue, not philosophy.

positions.name: The one who is
positions.who: The Septuagint; Augustine; Maimonides; Aquinas
positions.view: The name reveals that God's nature is simply to be: he is not one being among others but the source of all being, eternal and unchanging.
positions.evidence: The verb 'to be'; the Greek 'I am the one who is'; Malachi 3:6, 'I, Yahweh, don't change'.

positions.name: A refusal to be named
positions.who: Some modern theologians
positions.view: God gives no name that could be used to control him, as names of gods were used in magic. 'I am who I am' means: you will not pin me down.
positions.evidence: The ancient use of divine names in spells; the commandment against misusing the name.

debate.agree: All agree the name comes from the verb 'to be' and marks the God of Exodus off from the gods of Egypt.

look.why: Moses was keeping his father-in-law's flock in the wilderness when God called him. This seventeenth- or eighteenth-century landscape, by a follower of the French painter Claude Lorrain, is not of Moses, but it shows a herdsman at rest with his animals under a golden sky.

music.why: 'Thou changest not, thy compassions they fail not; as thou hast been, thou forever wilt be.' Thomas Chisholm's hymn (1923) is a meditation on the God whose name is 'I will be who I will be'.

think.why: The God of the bush is not one thing among others but 'the one who is'. Ask what philosophers mean when they say God is not a being but Being itself.

learn.why: The name of God from the burning bush.

Both are titles of Egyptian gods

Because the Hebrew is unclear

check.q: Where does the form 'Jehovah' come from?

It is the original pronunciation
It is the Greek form of the name

check.q: Why did John 8:58, 'before Abraham came into existence, I AM', provoke Jesus's hearers to pick up stones?

Because he claimed to be older than Abraham
Because he insulted Abraham
Because he spoke Greek
check.why: Using the divine name of Exodus 3:14 of himself was heard as blasphemy.

It means to pay a fine

sessions.practice: Live it this week: 'turn aside' once a day. Stop for five minutes somewhere ordinary, a kitchen, a bus, a park bench, and treat it as holy ground: notice what is there, and pray if you can.

sessions.title: Let my people go
sessions.line: Plagues on Egypt, a lamb's blood on the door, and the night that every generation remembers.
sessions.plain: Pharaoh refuses to free the slaves. Ten plagues strike Egypt, from the Nile turned to blood to the death of the firstborn. On the last night the Israelites eat a meal in haste, a lamb with bitter herbs and bread without yeast, and mark their doors with its blood so that death 'passes over' them. Then they go. This session asks what the plagues mean, whether they were fair, and why that meal is still eaten, by Jews at Passover and, in another form, by Christians every Sunday.
sessions.why: Session 2 showed God revealing his name and promising 'I will bring you out'. Pharaoh answered: 'Who is Yahweh?' This session is God's answer, and the night of freedom itself.
answers: What were the plagues, and why ten?
Was it fair for God to 'harden Pharaoh's heart' and kill Egypt's firstborn?
What is Passover, and how do Jews keep it today?
How is Passover connected to the Last Supper and Easter?
Can the plagues be explained naturally?
sessions.finding: Liberation comes through judgement on a power that made itself a god, and it is remembered in a meal: Passover makes every generation part of the story, and Christians read Jesus's death and the Eucharist in its light; the death of the firstborn remains a hard question.

paras: Israel's story begins in slavery, and its God hears the cry of slaves (session 1). That God revealed his name to Moses at the burning bush, 'I AM', and promised 'I will be with you' and 'I will bring you out' (session 2). Pharaoh replied: 'Who is Yahweh? I will not let Israel go.'
background.key: The God who hears has named himself and promised to act; Pharaoh refuses.

paras: Between the last session and this one, chapters 7 to 11 tell of ten plagues: the Nile turned to blood, frogs, gnats, flies, the death of livestock, boils, hail, locusts, darkness, and finally the death of the firstborn. Each time Pharaoh relents, then changes his mind.

Many of the plagues strike at Egypt's gods. The Nile was worshipped as Hapi; the frog-headed goddess Heqet watched over birth; darkness defeated Ra, the sun god; and Pharaoh's own firstborn was heir to a god-king. God says it plainly: 'I will execute judgments against all the gods of Egypt' (12:12).

Locusts, darkness

paras: The main reading has three parts: the first plague (7:14–24), the instructions for the Passover meal (12:1–14), and the night of the exodus itself (12:29–42).

The comparison is from the New Testament: the Last Supper, which was a Passover meal, and Paul's words 'Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed'. Together they show why Christians cannot understand Easter, or Communion, without this chapter.
background.key: The first plague, the Passover meal and the night of the exodus; then the Last Supper.

What must every household do on Passover night, and why?
