paras: Yahweh said to Moses, “Pharaoh’s heart is stubborn. He refuses to let the people go.
Go to Pharaoh in the morning. Behold, he is going out to the water. You shall stand by the river’s bank to meet him. You shall take the rod which was turned to a serpent in your hand.
You shall tell him, ‘Yahweh, the God of the Hebrews, has sent me to you, saying, “Let my people go, that they may serve me in the wilderness. Behold, until now you haven’t listened.”
Yahweh says, “In this you shall know that I am Yahweh. Behold: I will strike with the rod that is in my hand on the waters which are in the river, and they shall be turned to blood.
The fish that are in the river will die and the river will become foul. The Egyptians will loathe to drink water from the river.” ’ ”

Yahweh said to Moses, “Tell Aaron, ‘Take your rod, and stretch out your hand over the waters of Egypt, over their rivers, over their streams, and over their pools, and over all their ponds of water, that they may become blood. There will be blood throughout all the land of Egypt, both in vessels of wood and in vessels of stone.’ ”

Moses and Aaron did so, as Yahweh commanded; and he lifted up the rod, and struck the waters that were in the river, in the sight of Pharaoh, and in the sight of his servants; and all the waters that were in the river were turned to blood.
The fish that were in the river died. The river became foul. The Egyptians couldn’t drink water from the river. The blood was throughout all the land of Egypt.
The magicians of Egypt did the same thing with their enchantments. So Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and he didn’t listen to them, as Yahweh had spoken.
Pharaoh turned and went into his house, and he didn’t even take this to heart.
All the Egyptians dug around the river for water to drink; for they couldn’t drink the river water.
Yahweh spoke to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt, saying,
“This month shall be to you the beginning of months. It shall be the first month of the year to you.
Speak to all the congregation of Israel, saying, ‘On the tenth day of this month, they shall take to them every man a lamb, according to their fathers’ houses, a lamb for a household;

and if the household is too little for a lamb, then he and his neighbor next to his house shall take one according to the number of the souls. You shall make your count for the lamb according to what everyone can eat.
Your lamb shall be without defect, a male a year old. You shall take it from the sheep, or from the goats.
You shall keep it until the fourteenth day of the same month; and the whole assembly of the congregation of Israel shall kill it at evening.
They shall take some of the blood, and put it on the two door posts and on the lintel, on the houses in which they shall eat it.
They shall eat the meat in that night, roasted with fire, and unleavened bread. They shall eat it with bitter herbs.
Don’t eat it raw, nor boiled at all with water, but roasted with fire; with its head, its legs and its inner parts.
You shall let nothing of it remain until the morning; but that which remains of it until the morning you shall burn with fire.
This is how you shall eat it: with your belt on your waist, your sandals on your feet, and your staff in your hand; and you shall eat it in haste: it is Yahweh’s Passover.

For I will go through the land of Egypt in that night, and will strike all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, both man and animal. I will execute judgments against all the gods of Egypt. I am Yahweh.
The blood shall be to you for a token on the houses where you are. When I see the blood, I will pass over you, and no plague will be on you to destroy you when I strike the land of Egypt.
This day shall be a memorial for you. You shall keep it as a feast to Yahweh. You shall keep it as a feast throughout your generations by an ordinance forever.

At midnight, Yahweh struck all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh who sat on his throne to the firstborn of the captive who was in the dungeon, and all the firstborn of livestock.
Pharaoh rose up in the night, he, and all his servants, and all the Egyptians; and there was a great cry in Egypt, for there was not a house where there was not one dead.
He called for Moses and Aaron by night, and said, “Rise up, get out from among my people, both you and the children of Israel; and go, serve Yahweh, as you have said!
Take both your flocks and your herds, as you have said, and be gone; and bless me also!”
The Egyptians were urgent with the people, to send them out of the land in haste, for they said, “We are all dead men.”
The people took their dough before it was leavened, their kneading troughs being bound up in their clothes on their shoulders.
The children of Israel did according to the word of Moses; and they asked of the Egyptians jewels of silver, and jewels of gold, and clothing.
Yahweh gave the people favor in the sight of the Egyptians, so that they let them have what they asked. They plundered the Egyptians.
The children of Israel traveled from Rameses to Succoth, about six hundred thousand on foot who were men, in addition to children.
A mixed multitude went up also with them, with flocks, herds, and even very much livestock.

They baked unleavened cakes of the dough which they brought out of Egypt; for it wasn’t leavened, because they were thrust out of Egypt, and couldn’t wait, and they had not prepared any food for themselves.
Now the time that the children of Israel lived in Egypt was four hundred thirty years.
At the end of four hundred thirty years, to the day, all of Yahweh’s armies went out from the land of Egypt.
It is a night to be much observed to Yahweh for bringing them out from the land of Egypt. This is that night of Yahweh, to be much observed by all the children of Israel throughout their generations.

parts.title: The Nile turned to blood
parts.context: Moses and Aaron have performed a sign before Pharaoh: Aaron's staff became a serpent, and Pharaoh's magicians did the same (7:8–13). Now the plagues begin, at the river where Hebrew babies were drowned.

commentary.on: Pharaoh’s heart is stubborn. He refuses to let the people go.
commentary.text: The 'heart' in Hebrew is the seat of will and decision, not just feeling. A 'heavy' or 'hard' heart is a will that refuses to change. Watch who hardens it: sometimes Pharaoh (8:15), sometimes God (9:12), sometimes it is simply 'hardened'.

commentary.on: Behold, he is going out to the water.
commentary.text: Moses meets Pharaoh at the Nile in the morning, perhaps as he goes to the river to worship. The river was Egypt's life and a god. It was also where Pharaoh had ordered the Hebrew boys drowned. The first plague strikes there.

commentary.on: In this you shall know that I am Yahweh.
commentary.text: The answer to Pharaoh's 'Who is Yahweh?' The plagues are a lesson in who God is, for Egypt as well as Israel: the phrase recurs throughout (7:5; 8:22; 9:29; 14:4).

commentary.on: The magicians of Egypt did the same thing with their enchantments.
commentary.text: Egypt's magicians can copy the first plagues, but only by making things worse. They can turn water to blood; they cannot turn it back. By the third plague they give up: 'This is God's finger' (8:19).

commentary.on: So Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and he didn’t listen to them, as Yahweh had spoken.
commentary.text: The passive 'was hardened' leaves open who did it. The lecture sets out how Jews and Christians have read it.

parts.title: A lamb for every house
parts.context: Before the last plague, God gives instructions for a meal. It is the only command in Exodus given before the people are free, and it is to be repeated every year 'throughout your generations'.

commentary.on: This month shall be to you the beginning of months.
commentary.text: Freedom resets the calendar. The year begins with the month of the exodus (in spring, called Nisan). Israel's time will be counted from its liberation.

commentary.on: a lamb for a household; and if the household is too little for a lamb, then he and his neighbor next to his house shall take one
commentary.text: Freedom is celebrated by households and neighbours, around a table. No one is to eat alone, and no lamb is to be wasted.

commentary.on: They shall take some of the blood, and put it on the two door posts and on the lintel
commentary.text: The blood on the door marks a household that has trusted God's word. It is the first great sign of 'substitution' in the Bible after the ram that took Isaac's place: a lamb's death in place of the firstborn's.

commentary.on: They shall eat it with bitter herbs.
commentary.text: Every detail is a memory. Bitter herbs for the bitterness of slavery; unleavened bread because there was no time for dough to rise. At the Passover table today, Jews still eat bitter herbs (maror) and flat bread (matzah).

commentary.on: with your belt on your waist, your sandals on your feet, and your staff in your hand; and you shall eat it in haste
commentary.text: A meal eaten standing up, ready to leave. Freedom requires being ready to go.

commentary.on: When I see the blood, I will pass over you
commentary.text: 'Pass over' is pesach in Hebrew, which gives the festival its name. In Greek it became pascha, and Pascha is the name for Easter in most of the world's languages to this day.

commentary.on: This day shall be a memorial for you.
commentary.text: A memorial (zikkaron) is more than remembering. At the Passover meal, the Seder, Jews say: 'In every generation each person must see himself as if he himself came out of Egypt' (Mishnah Pesachim 10:5). The past is made present.

parts.title: The night of freedom
parts.context: Midnight. The tenth plague.

commentary.on: At midnight, Yahweh struck all the firstborn in the land of Egypt
commentary.text: The hardest verse in the story. Pharaoh had killed Israel's sons; now Egypt's sons die, from the palace to the dungeon. God had warned: 'Israel is my son, my firstborn… Let my son go… Behold, I will kill your firstborn son' (4:22–23). The lecture faces the moral question directly.

commentary.on: there was a great cry in Egypt, for there was not a house where there was not one dead.
commentary.text: The 'great cry' uses the same word as Israel's cry under slavery (3:7). Now Egypt cries. The story does not hide the grief. Jewish tradition remembers it: at the Seder, a drop of wine is removed from the cup for each plague, so the cup of joy is less full for the suffering of Egypt.

commentary.on: Rise up, get out from among my people
commentary.text: The god-king gives in. Pharaoh, who asked 'Who is Yahweh?', now says 'go, serve Yahweh' and even 'bless me also'.

commentary.on: They plundered the Egyptians.
commentary.text: The slaves leave with silver and gold, as God told Abraham they would (Genesis 15:14). Rabbis called it back wages for centuries of unpaid labour. It will later be melted down for the golden calf (session 5).

commentary.on: A mixed multitude went up also with them
commentary.text: A small phrase with a large meaning. Not only Israelites leave Egypt, but 'a mixed multitude' of other people, probably other slaves and foreigners. The people of God are, from the start, not a single bloodline.

commentary.on: It is a night to be much observed to Yahweh
commentary.text: Literally 'a night of watching': God watched over them, so they keep watch for him. Jews keep it every spring at Passover, and Christians keep the Easter Vigil, the night before Easter, with the reading of this chapter.

paras: The day of unleavened bread came, on which the Passover must be sacrificed.
Jesus sent Peter and John, saying, “Go and prepare the Passover for us, that we may eat.”
They said to him, “Where do you want us to prepare?”
He said to them, “Behold, when you have entered into the city, a man carrying a pitcher of water will meet you. Follow him into the house which he enters.
Tell the master of the house, ‘The Teacher says to you, “Where is the guest room, where I may eat the Passover with my disciples?” ’
He will show you a large, furnished upper room. Make preparations there.”
They went, found things as Jesus had told them, and they prepared the Passover.
When the hour had come, he sat down with the twelve apostles.
He said to them, “I have earnestly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer,
for I tell you, I will no longer by any means eat of it until it is fulfilled in God’s Kingdom.”
He received a cup, and when he had given thanks, he said, “Take this, and share it among yourselves,
for I tell you, I will not drink at all again from the fruit of the vine, until God’s Kingdom comes.”
He took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke, and gave it to them, saying, “This is my body which is given for you. Do this in memory of me.”
Likewise, he took the cup after supper, saying, “This cup is the new covenant in my blood, which is poured out for you.
Purge out the old yeast, that you may be a new lump, even as you are unleavened. For indeed Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed in our place.
Therefore let’s keep the feast, not with old yeast, neither with the yeast of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.

parts.title: The Last Supper
parts.context: Luke's Gospel, written in the later first century. Jesus and his disciples are in Jerusalem for Passover, the festival that brought crowds of pilgrims to the city every spring.

commentary.on: The day of unleavened bread came, on which the Passover must be sacrificed.
commentary.text: Luke sets the scene carefully: this is the day the Passover lambs were sacrificed in the Temple. (John's Gospel dates the meal a day earlier, so that Jesus dies at the very hour the lambs are killed; scholars still debate which dating is right.)

commentary.on: I have earnestly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer
commentary.text: Jesus chooses Passover, the meal of liberation from slavery, for his last meal and to explain his coming death.

commentary.on: This is my body which is given for you. Do this in memory of me.
commentary.text: Jesus takes the unleavened bread of Passover and gives it a new meaning. 'In memory' is the language of Exodus 12:14: a memorial that makes the past present. Christians have done this every week since, at the Eucharist, Mass, Holy Communion or Lord's Supper.

commentary.on: This cup is the new covenant in my blood, which is poured out for you.
commentary.text: Two echoes at once: the Passover lamb's blood on the doorposts, and the 'blood of the covenant' Moses sprinkled at Sinai (Exodus 24:8, which you will meet in session 5). 'New covenant' is Jeremiah's phrase (Jeremiah 31:31; you will read it in session 7). In Latin, 'covenant' is testamentum: this is why the Christian Scriptures are called the New Testament.

parts.title: Christ, our Passover
parts.context: Paul writing to the church in Corinth about AD 54, about twenty years after Jesus's death, using the customs of Passover, when all yeast was cleared out of Jewish homes.

commentary.on: For indeed Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed in our place.
commentary.text: Paul calls Jesus the Passover lamb. As the lamb's blood meant death passed over the house, Christians believe Christ's death means that death and sin pass over those who trust him. John the Baptist calls him 'the Lamb of God' (John 1:29).

commentary.on: not with old yeast, neither with the yeast of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth
commentary.text: As Jewish families cleared their homes of yeast before Passover, Christians are to clear their lives of malice. The festival becomes a way of living.

compare.why: Jesus died at Passover. The first Christians could not explain his death without this chapter. Read the account of his last meal with his disciples, and Paul's words to the Corinthians.
compare.title: Christ our Passover

paras: The phrase troubles readers: if God hardened Pharaoh's heart, how can Pharaoh be blamed? Look at the text closely. In the first five plagues, Pharaoh hardens his own heart, or it 'was hardened'. Only from the sixth plague does the text say 'Yahweh hardened Pharaoh's heart' (9:12).

Jewish and Christian readers have seen a pattern here. Maimonides argued that a person can sin so deeply and repeatedly that he loses the power to repent: God's 'hardening' is the confirmation of what Pharaoh chose. Origen and later Christian writers made a similar point: the same sun melts wax and hardens clay; God's actions reveal what is already in a heart. Paul, in Romans 9:17, uses Pharaoh to argue that God is free in his mercy, which Calvinists read strongly and others more gently (you met that debate with Jacob and Esau).
sections.key: Pharaoh hardens his own heart five times before God 'hardens' it; many read God's hardening as confirming Pharaoh's own choice.

paras: The death of Egypt's firstborn is one of the hardest passages in the Bible. The firstborn children of slaves and prisoners died too, and they had enslaved no one. No reading removes the difficulty, and readers should not pretend it does.

Several things can be said. The story frames it as a measure-for-measure judgement on a nation that killed Israel's sons, after nine warnings. Jewish tradition refused to gloat: the Talmud tells that when the angels wanted to sing as the Egyptians drowned, God rebuked them: 'The work of my hands is drowning in the sea, and you would sing?' (Megillah 10b). At the Seder, the cup is diminished for every plague. Christians have read the story as pointing beyond itself to a God who, in the end, gives his own firstborn Son (Romans 8:32). Critics say this is still a God who kills children, and that the story reflects an ancient people's understanding of God rather than God himself; that question will come back in session 6.
sections.key: The death of the firstborn is a real moral difficulty; Jewish tradition refused to gloat, and Christians read it in the light of the cross.

paras: Passover (Pesach) is the oldest continuously kept festival in the world: Jews have celebrated it for at least two and a half thousand years. Today it lasts seven or eight days in spring, and begins with the Seder ('order'), a family meal following the Haggadah ('telling'), the book of readings, songs and questions.

The youngest child asks four questions, beginning 'Why is this night different from all other nights?' The family tells the story, eats matzah and bitter herbs, dips greens in salt water for the slaves' tears, drinks four cups of wine for the four promises of Exodus 6, and opens the door for the prophet Elijah. It ends with the hope: 'Next year in Jerusalem'.
sections.key: Passover is the world's oldest continuously kept festival; at the Seder every generation tells the story as its own.

paras: Jesus died at Passover, and the first Christians understood his death through it. He was the lamb; his blood marked those who would be spared; his last meal was a Passover meal, which became the Christian Eucharist; his rising was a new exodus, from death to life. That is why Easter falls near Passover every year, why its name in most languages is Pascha, and why the Easter Vigil reads Exodus 14.
The churches differ on what happens at the Eucharist, but all keep it as the memorial Jesus commanded.

rows: The Mass: the one sacrifice of Christ made present
Truly, the bread and wine becoming his body and blood (transubstantiation)
The Divine Liturgy: heaven and earth joined
Truly, a mystery not defined philosophically
Truly, 'in, with and under' the bread and wine
Truly, though Anglicans hold a range of views on how
The Lord's Supper: a memorial and a spiritual feeding
Spiritually, by faith (Calvin); or as a memorial (Zwingli)

sections.key: Christians read Jesus's death as the true Passover; the Last Supper became the Eucharist, understood differently by each church.

paras: Some have tried to explain the plagues naturally: a red algae or volcanic dust turning the Nile red, which killed fish, drove frogs onto land, bred insects and spread disease. Others have linked them to the eruption of Thera (Santorini) in about 1600 BC, or compared an Egyptian text, the Admonitions of Ipuwer, which laments that 'the river is blood'.

Most scholars are cautious. Ipuwer is a poem about social chaos, probably older and not describing plagues; Thera's date does not fit. And the story itself is not interested in mechanism. Even where a natural process might be involved, the claim is about timing, purpose and who is Lord: 'that you may know that I am Yahweh'.
sections.key: Natural explanations have been proposed, but most scholars are cautious, and the story's claim is about who is Lord, not how.

refs: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Laws of Repentance 6:3; Origen, On First Principles III.1.10–11.
Talmud, Megillah 10b and Sanhedrin 39b ('the work of my hands is drowning'); Mishnah Pesachim 10:5; the Passover Haggadah.
Catechism of the Catholic Church 1340, 1376; Martin Luther, Small Catechism (1529); Thirty-Nine Articles 28 (1571); John Calvin, Institutes IV.17.
The Admonitions of Ipuwer (Papyrus Leiden I 344), in Miriam Lichtheim, Ancient Egyptian Literature I (1973); Greta Hort, 'The Plagues of Egypt', ZAW 69–70 (1957–58).

debate.question: How should we read the hardening of Pharaoh's heart?

positions.name: Pharaoh chose, God confirmed
positions.who: Maimonides; Origen; many Jewish and Catholic readers
positions.view: Pharaoh hardened himself first, five times. God's hardening confirmed his choice and removed his freedom to repent, as a just punishment.
positions.evidence: The order of the verbs: Pharaoh hardens his own heart (8:15, 32) before God hardens it (9:12).

positions.name: God's sovereign purpose
positions.who: Augustine in his later writings; Calvin; Reformed theology
positions.view: God hardened Pharaoh to display his power and make his name known, as Paul says; God is free to show mercy or not, and Pharaoh remained guilty.
positions.evidence: Exodus 4:21 (before any plague); 9:16; Romans 9:17–18.

positions.name: A way of speaking
positions.who: Many modern scholars
positions.view: Hebrew often attributes everything to God, the first cause, without denying human choice. The phrase expresses God's control of the story, not a mechanism overriding Pharaoh's will.
positions.evidence: Both kinds of statement stand side by side; similar language elsewhere (1 Samuel 2:25; Isaiah 6:10).

debate.agree: All agree that Pharaoh is held responsible, and that the story's point is God's lordship over the god-king.

look.why: Jesus's last meal with his disciples was a Passover meal, and Christians remember it every time they share bread and wine. Sebastiano Ricci, a Venetian painter, painted it in 1713–14 as a banquet seen through a stone arch.
points: Seventeen people and a dog gather around a long table set with plates of food, seen through a wide stone arch.
At the centre of the far side sits Jesus, with light radiating from his head, pointing upward with one finger.
The other men converse in pairs and threes, or look towards him.
A gold candelabra hangs over the white tablecloth; an arched doorway on the left opens to blue sky.
On the near side a balding man with a long grey beard sits with his back half turned.

music.why: Bach's St Matthew Passion (1727) tells the story of Jesus's last Passover and death. Its opening chorus calls the listener to 'see the Bridegroom, see him as a lamb'.

think.why: Jesus chose Passover to explain his death. Ask what his followers believed about who he was, and why.

learn.why: The command to keep Passover 'throughout your generations', the root of both the Seder and the Eucharist.

check.q: In the first five plagues, who is said to harden Pharaoh's heart?
options: Moses
The magicians
Always God
Pharaoh himself, or it 'was hardened'; God is first said to harden it at the sixth plague
check.why: The order matters to many interpreters: Pharaoh chose first.

check.q: What is the significance of the first plague striking the Nile?
options: Pharaoh lived on a boat
The Nile was the only water in Egypt
It was the easiest plague
The Nile was Egypt's life and a god, and the river where Hebrew boys had been drowned
check.why: Judgement begins where Egypt's crime and its trust both lay.

check.q: What does 'memorial' mean at the Passover Seder, according to the Mishnah?
options: A gravestone
Remembering a sad event
A list of names
Making the past present: each person must see himself as if he came out of Egypt
check.why: Mishnah Pesachim 10:5.

check.q: Why does Easter have the name 'Pascha' in most languages?
options: It comes from pesach, 'Passover', because Jesus died and rose at Passover
It is the name of a Greek goddess
It is Latin for 'resurrection'
It means 'spring'
check.why: Hebrew pesach, Greek pascha.

check.q: What do Jews do at the Seder to remember the suffering of Egypt?
options: Nothing; they celebrate only
They remove a drop of wine from the cup for each plague
They fast
They break a plate
check.why: Joy is diminished for others' suffering, as in the Talmud's rebuke of the singing angels.

check.q: Why does 'the new covenant in my blood' (Luke 22:20) give the New Testament its name?
options: Because the phrase appears on its first page
Because 'covenant' in Latin is testamentum, and Christians called the scriptures of the new covenant the New Testament
Because Jesus wrote a will
Because Luke wrote the first book
check.why: Old and New Testament mean old and new covenant.

tutorial.question: What does the Passover mean, for Israel and for Christians?
tutorial.approach: Explain the plagues as a judgement on Egypt and its gods, and face the moral question of the tenth. Describe the Passover meal and how each element remembers the exodus. Explain how Jews keep it today. Then show how the Last Supper and Paul reinterpret it, and how the churches understand the Eucharist.
strong: Explains the plagues as an answer to 'Who is Yahweh?' and a judgement on Egypt's gods.
Discusses the hardening of Pharaoh's heart, using the text's order.
Faces the death of the firstborn honestly, with Jewish and Christian responses.
Explains the Passover meal and the Seder.
Explains the Last Supper and 'Christ our Passover'.
Explains the link between 'covenant' and 'Testament'.

reading.why: The Passover service with a former Chief Rabbi's commentary.

reading.title: Jesus and the Jewish Roots of the Eucharist
reading.why: A Catholic scholar on the Last Supper as Passover.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: share a meal deliberately with someone who would otherwise eat alone, as the Passover command asks households to share with their neighbours.
sessions.reflect: What would you need to be 'ready to leave', belt on and staff in hand, if God called you out of something?
takeaways: The plagues answer Pharaoh's question 'Who is Yahweh?' and strike Egypt's gods; Pharaoh hardens his own heart before God hardens it.
The Passover meal makes every generation part of the exodus; the death of the firstborn remains a real moral difficulty.
Jesus died at Passover; the Last Supper became the Eucharist, and 'new covenant' gave the New Testament its name.

sessions.title: Through the sea
sessions.line: Trapped between an army and the water, a way through, a song, and the long, thirsty road of freedom.
sessions.plain: The slaves leave Egypt, but Pharaoh changes his mind and sends his chariots after them. Trapped against the sea, the people panic: it would have been better to stay slaves. Then the sea opens, they cross, and the chariots are drowned. They sing. A few days later they are thirsty and furious again. This session asks what freedom is really like, and how the story of the sea became the West's great story of liberation.
sessions.why: Session 3 brought the night of freedom: Passover, and the slaves walking out of Egypt. But walking out is not the same as being free. This session follows them to the sea and into the desert, and asks what freedom asks of the people who receive it.
answers: What happened at the sea, and where was it?
Why did the freed slaves keep wanting to go back to Egypt?
What is freedom for: freedom from, or freedom for?
How has the Exodus shaped movements for freedom in the West?
Is God only the liberator of Israel?
sessions.finding: Freedom is not the end but the beginning: the freed slaves are saved at the sea by God, not by their own strength, yet they long to go back to Egypt; the story became the West's pattern for liberation, and the prophets insisted God frees other peoples too.

paras: God heard the cry of Israel's slaves (session 1), revealed his name, 'I AM', and promised to bring them out (session 2). After the plagues and the Passover night, Pharaoh let them go, with a 'mixed multitude' (session 3).
background.key: Heard, named, and brought out on Passover night.

paras: The shortest route from Egypt to Canaan ran along the coast, the 'way of the Philistines', guarded by Egyptian forts. Exodus says God led them the long way, 'by the way of the wilderness by the Red Sea… lest perhaps the people change their minds when they see war, and they return to Egypt' (13:17–18). They are led by a pillar of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night.
They carry Joseph's bones with them (13:19), keeping the promise made at the end of Genesis.
background.key: God leads them the long way, by cloud and fire, carrying Joseph's bones.

paras: English Bibles say 'the Red Sea', following the Greek translation. The Hebrew is yam suph, which most scholars translate 'Sea of Reeds'. Reeds grow in fresh or brackish water, which suggests one of the marshy lakes along what is now the Suez Canal, such as Lake Timsah or the Bitter Lakes, rather than the deep Gulf of Suez. Others defend the Gulf of Suez, or even the Gulf of Aqaba. No one knows for certain.

The text says God drove the sea back 'by a strong east wind all night'. In 2010 two American scientists, Carl Drews and Weiqing Han, used computer models to show that a strong wind blowing for twelve hours over a shallow lagoon in the eastern Nile Delta could push the water back and open a land bridge for a few hours. The Bible's point, either way, is that God did it, at the right moment.
background.key: The Hebrew says 'Sea of Reeds', probably a marshy lake near today's Suez Canal; the text speaks of a strong east wind.

paras: The main reading has four parts: trapped at the sea (14:10–22), the crossing (14:23–31), the song of Moses and Miriam (15:1–3, 20–21), and, only weeks later, a quarrel over water in the desert (17:1–7).

The comparison is three short passages from later in the Bible, showing how Israel remembered the sea: a psalm, a prophet's appeal, and a startling claim by the prophet Amos that God has brought other nations out of other lands.
background.key: Trapped, crossing, singing, quarrelling; then how the psalms and prophets remembered the Exodus.

before: What do the people say when they see the Egyptians coming? What does Moses say? What does God say?
Who sings after the crossing, and what do they sing about?
In chapter 17, what question are the people really asking?
sessions.readWhy: The crossing of the sea and the first weeks of freedom, in four parts.

paras: When Pharaoh came near, the children of Israel lifted up their eyes, and behold, the Egyptians were marching after them; and they were very afraid. The children of Israel cried out to Yahweh.
They said to Moses, “Because there were no graves in Egypt, have you taken us away to die in the wilderness? Why have you treated us this way, to bring us out of Egypt?

Isn’t this the word that we spoke to you in Egypt, saying, ‘Leave us alone, that we may serve the Egyptians?’ For it would have been better for us to serve the Egyptians than to die in the wilderness.”
Moses said to the people, “Don’t be afraid. Stand still, and see the salvation of Yahweh, which he will work for you today; for you will never again see the Egyptians whom you have seen today.
Yahweh will fight for you, and you shall be still.”
Yahweh said to Moses, “Why do you cry to me? Speak to the children of Israel, that they go forward.
Lift up your rod, and stretch out your hand over the sea and divide it. Then the children of Israel shall go into the middle of the sea on dry ground.
Behold, I myself will harden the hearts of the Egyptians, and they will go in after them. I will get myself honor over Pharaoh, and over all his armies, over his chariots, and over his horsemen.
The Egyptians shall know that I am Yahweh when I have gotten myself honor over Pharaoh, over his chariots, and over his horsemen.”
The angel of God, who went before the camp of Israel, moved and went behind them; and the pillar of cloud moved from before them, and stood behind them.
It came between the camp of Egypt and the camp of Israel. There was the cloud and the darkness, yet gave it light by night. One didn’t come near the other all night.
Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and Yahweh caused the sea to go back by a strong east wind all night, and made the sea dry land, and the waters were divided.
The children of Israel went into the middle of the sea on the dry ground, and the waters were a wall to them on their right hand, and on their left.
The Egyptians pursued, and went in after them into the middle of the sea: all of Pharaoh’s horses, his chariots, and his horsemen.
In the morning watch, Yahweh looked out on the Egyptian army through the pillar of fire and of cloud, and confused the Egyptian army.
He took off their chariot wheels, and they drove them heavily; so that the Egyptians said, “Let’s flee from the face of Israel, for Yahweh fights for them against the Egyptians!”
Yahweh said to Moses, “Stretch out your hand over the sea, that the waters may come again on the Egyptians, on their chariots, and on their horsemen.”
Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and the sea returned to its strength when the morning appeared; and the Egyptians fled against it. Yahweh overthrew the Egyptians in the middle of the sea.
The waters returned, and covered the chariots and the horsemen, even all Pharaoh’s army that went in after them into the sea. There remained not so much as one of them.
But the children of Israel walked on dry land in the middle of the sea, and the waters were a wall to them on their right hand, and on their left.
Thus Yahweh saved Israel that day out of the hand of the Egyptians; and Israel saw the Egyptians dead on the seashore.
Israel saw the great work which Yahweh did to the Egyptians, and the people feared Yahweh; and they believed in Yahweh and in his servant Moses.
Then Moses and the children of Israel sang this song to Yahweh, and said,

“I will sing to Yahweh, for he has triumphed gloriously.
He has thrown the horse and his rider into the sea.

Yah is my strength and song.
He has become my salvation.
This is my God, and I will praise him;
my father’s God, and I will exalt him.

Yahweh is a man of war.
Yahweh is his name.
Miriam the prophetess, the sister of Aaron, took a tambourine in her hand; and all the women went out after her with tambourines and with dances.
Miriam answered them,

“Sing to Yahweh, for he has triumphed gloriously.
The horse and his rider he has thrown into the sea.”

All the congregation of the children of Israel traveled from the wilderness of Sin, starting according to Yahweh’s commandment, and encamped in Rephidim; but there was no water for the people to drink.
Therefore the people quarreled with Moses, and said, “Give us water to drink.”
Moses said to them, “Why do you quarrel with me? Why do you test Yahweh?”
The people were thirsty for water there; so the people murmured against Moses, and said, “Why have you brought us up out of Egypt, to kill us, our children, and our livestock with thirst?”
Moses cried to Yahweh, saying, “What shall I do with these people? They are almost ready to stone me.”
Yahweh said to Moses, “Walk on before the people, and take the elders of Israel with you, and take the rod in your hand with which you struck the Nile, and go.
Behold, I will stand before you there on the rock in Horeb. You shall strike the rock, and water will come out of it, that the people may drink.” Moses did so in the sight of the elders of Israel.
He called the name of the place Massah, and Meribah, because the children of Israel quarreled, and because they tested Yahweh, saying, “Is Yahweh among us, or not?”

parts.title: Trapped
parts.context: The Israelites are camped by the sea. Pharaoh has regretted letting his workforce go, and his chariots are coming.

commentary.on: Because there were no graves in Egypt, have you taken us away to die in the wilderness?
commentary.text: Bitter sarcasm: Egypt, land of pyramids and tombs, had no graves? The freed slaves' first reaction to danger is to wish they were slaves again.

commentary.on: For it would have been better for us to serve the Egyptians than to die in the wilderness.
commentary.text: This is the deepest problem of freedom. Slavery was terrible, but it was safe and familiar. Freedom is frightening. The same complaint will return again and again (16:3; 17:3; Numbers 14:4).

commentary.on: Don’t be afraid. Stand still, and see the salvation of Yahweh
commentary.text: Moses' answer: do nothing; God will act. 'Salvation' here means rescue, deliverance from a real enemy. It is the first time the word appears in Exodus.

commentary.on: Why do you cry to me? Speak to the children of Israel, that they go forward.
commentary.text: But God's answer is different: stop praying and walk. Jewish commentators loved this verse: there is a time for prayer and a time to move. The sea does not open until someone steps forward. One midrash says it opened only when a man named Nahshon walked into the water up to his neck.

commentary.on: Yahweh caused the sea to go back by a strong east wind all night
commentary.text: A natural means, a wind, used at the right time. The Bible is not embarrassed by natural processes; for its writers, God works through the wind as easily as without it.

commentary.on: the waters were a wall to them on their right hand, and on their left
commentary.text: The waters that once drowned Hebrew babies now protect them. Remember the first chapter of Genesis: God divided the waters and made dry land appear. The crossing is a new creation: a people born out of the water.

parts.title: The crossing
parts.context: Before dawn, the Egyptians follow the Israelites into the dry seabed.

commentary.on: He took off their chariot wheels, and they drove them heavily
commentary.text: Egypt's chariots were the most advanced military technology of the age. Their wheels clog in the mud. The superpower is undone by the ground under its wheels.

commentary.on: Let’s flee from the face of Israel, for Yahweh fights for them against the Egyptians!
commentary.text: The Egyptians themselves confess what Pharaoh refused to: Yahweh is God. Pharaoh's question, 'Who is Yahweh?', is answered.

commentary.on: Israel saw the Egyptians dead on the seashore.
commentary.text: The story does not look away. The people who chased them are dead. You met the Jewish tradition's refusal to rejoice at this in the last session.

commentary.on: and they believed in Yahweh and in his servant Moses.
commentary.text: The crossing ends in faith: they 'believed', the same verb used of Abraham under the stars (Genesis 15:6). But, as the next passages show, belief born of a miracle does not last long.

parts.title: The first song
parts.context: The Song of the Sea, one of the oldest poems in the Bible. Many scholars date its language to the twelfth or eleventh century BC, older than most of the prose around it.

commentary.on: I will sing to Yahweh, for he has triumphed gloriously.
commentary.text: The first song in the Bible. Freedom bursts into poetry. Jews sing it every morning in synagogue, and Christians sing it at the Easter Vigil.

commentary.on: Yah is my strength and song. He has become my salvation.
commentary.text: 'Yah' is a short form of the divine name, as in 'Hallelu-jah', 'praise Yah'. The verse is repeated in Psalm 118:14 and Isaiah 12:2.

commentary.on: Yahweh is a man of war.
commentary.text: A line that troubles modern readers. Its first hearers heard it as good news: their God fights for slaves against an empire. The whole Bible will wrestle with this image, as you will see in the next journey, on Joshua and the kings.

commentary.on: Miriam the prophetess, the sister of Aaron, took a tambourine in her hand
commentary.text: Miriam, the girl who watched the basket from the reeds, now leads the women in song. She is the first woman in the Bible called a prophet. Micah 6:4 names her with Moses and Aaron as Israel's three leaders.

parts.title: Is Yahweh among us?
parts.context: A few weeks later. The people have already complained about bitter water (15:22–25) and about hunger, when God sent manna, the 'bread from heaven' (chapter 16). Now there is no water at all.

commentary.on: Why have you brought us up out of Egypt, to kill us, our children, and our livestock with thirst?
commentary.text: The same complaint as at the sea. Freedom keeps feeling like a trap. The people are not wicked; they are thirsty, frightened, and used to having their lives run for them.

commentary.on: What shall I do with these people? They are almost ready to stone me.
commentary.text: The burden of leading free people. Moses cries to God as the slaves once cried in Egypt.

commentary.on: You shall strike the rock, and water will come out of it
commentary.text: God provides again: water from a rock in the desert. Paul later read the rock as a figure of Christ (1 Corinthians 10:4).

commentary.on: Is Yahweh among us, or not?
commentary.text: The real question behind every complaint. After the plagues and the sea, they still doubt that God is with them. The name of the place, Massah ('testing') and Meribah ('quarrel'), becomes a byword: 'Don't harden your heart, as at Meribah' (Psalm 95:8). The slaves are out of Egypt; Egypt is not yet out of the slaves.

paras:
When Israel went out of Egypt,
the house of Jacob from a people of foreign language,

Judah became his sanctuary,
Israel his dominion.

The sea saw it, and fled.
The Jordan was driven back.

The mountains skipped like rams,
the little hills like lambs.

What was it, you sea, that you fled?
You Jordan, that you turned back?

You mountains, that you skipped like rams;
you little hills, like lambs?

Tremble, you earth, at the presence of the Lord,
at the presence of the God of Jacob,

who turned the rock into a pool of water,
the flint into a spring of waters.

My people, what have I done to you?
How have I burdened you?
Answer me!

For I brought you up out of the land of Egypt,
and redeemed you out of the house of bondage.
I sent before you Moses, Aaron, and Miriam.

My people, remember now what Balak king of Moab devised,
and what Balaam the son of Beor answered him from Shittim to Gilgal,
that you may know the righteous acts of Yahweh.”

Are you not like the children of the Ethiopians to me, children of Israel?” says Yahweh. “Haven’t I brought up Israel out of the land of Egypt, and the Philistines from Caphtor, and the Syrians from Kir?

parts.title: The sea saw it, and fled
parts.context: A short psalm sung at Passover, part of the Hallel ('praise') psalms (113–118). Jesus and his disciples probably sang the Hallel at the Last Supper ('when they had sung a hymn', Mark 14:26).

commentary.on: When Israel went out of Egypt, the house of Jacob from a people of foreign language
commentary.text: The psalm compresses the whole Exodus into one line. Israel was strangers in Egypt, among a people whose language they did not speak.

commentary.on: The sea saw it, and fled. The Jordan was driven back.
commentary.text: Two crossings in one breath: the sea at the start of the journey and the river Jordan at its end (Joshua 3). The whole of nature makes way.

commentary.on: who turned the rock into a pool of water
commentary.text: The water from the rock at Meribah, remembered as God's gift, not the people's quarrel.

parts.title: What have I done to you?
parts.context: The prophet Micah, in the eighth century BC, imagines God bringing a case against his people for their injustice.

commentary.on: My people, what have I done to you? How have I burdened you? Answer me!
commentary.text: God speaks like a wronged friend. The Exodus is the evidence of his love: he set them free; why have they forgotten? The verse is sung in the Reproaches of the Good Friday liturgy.

commentary.on: I sent before you Moses, Aaron, and Miriam.
commentary.text: Miriam named with her brothers as one of the leaders God gave his people.

parts.title: Other exoduses
parts.context: Amos, the earliest of the written prophets (about 760 BC), attacking Israel's complacency.

commentary.on: Are you not like the children of the Ethiopians to me, children of Israel?
commentary.text: A shocking question to people who thought the Exodus made them God's favourites. The Ethiopians, distant and dark-skinned to Amos's hearers, are just as much God's children.

commentary.on: Haven’t I brought up Israel out of the land of Egypt, and the Philistines from Caphtor, and the Syrians from Kir?
commentary.text: God has had other exoduses: he brought Israel's enemies from their homelands too. The God of Exodus is the God of all nations. Being freed is a gift and a calling, not a sign of superiority.

compare.why: The Exodus became the story Israel told about itself, and the prophets used it to call the people back. Read a psalm, a prophet's appeal, and one surprising verse from Amos.
compare.title: How Israel remembered the sea

sections.h: Out of Egypt, Egypt not out of them
paras: The most realistic thing about the Exodus story is that the freed slaves keep wanting to go back. 'It would have been better for us to serve the Egyptians'; 'We wish that we had died… in Egypt, when we sat by the meat pots' (16:3); 'Let's choose a leader, and let's return into Egypt' (Numbers 14:4). In the end the generation that left Egypt dies in the desert, and only their children enter the promised land, forty years later.

A saying often quoted puts it well: it took one night to take Israel out of Egypt, and forty years to take Egypt out of Israel. Slavery shapes the mind: dependence, fear, the habit of being told what to do. Freedom has to be learned.
sections.key: The freed slaves keep wanting to go back: it took one night to take Israel out of Egypt and forty years to take Egypt out of Israel.

paras: The philosopher Isaiah Berlin, in a famous lecture of 1958, distinguished two ideas of liberty. Negative liberty is freedom from: no one stopping you doing what you want. Positive liberty is freedom for: the power to live a good life, to govern yourself well. Berlin warned that positive liberty can be twisted by tyrants who claim to know what is good for you.

Exodus has both, and holds them together. God brings Israel out from under Pharaoh: freedom from. But the purpose, repeated throughout, is 'that they may serve me': freedom for. The Hebrew word for 'serve' (avad) is the same word as 'slave' in Egypt. Israel moves not from service to no service, but from serving Pharaoh to serving God, from a master who works you to death to one who gives you a day of rest. That is the bridge to the next session, at Sinai.
sections.key: Exodus is freedom from Pharaoh and freedom for serving God: the same Hebrew word, avad, means both 'serve' and 'be a slave'.

paras: No other story has shaped Western movements for liberty so deeply. The political philosopher Michael Walzer, in Exodus and Revolution (1985), argued that it gave the West its pattern of political hope: oppression, liberation, a covenant, a long march, a promised land.

Its uses have not all been good. The same story that inspired the enslaved also inspired settlers who saw themselves as a new Israel taking a new Canaan from its inhabitants. The story contains its own corrective: Amos's reminder that God frees other peoples too, and the law's command to love the foreigner 'for you were foreigners in Egypt'.

rows: Saw their crossing to New England as a flight from a Pharaoh-like king to a promised land
Benjamin Franklin and Thomas Jefferson proposed a Great Seal showing Pharaoh drowning in the Red Sea, with the motto 'Rebellion to tyrants is obedience to God'
Inscribed with Leviticus 25:10: 'Proclaim liberty throughout the land'
Spirituals ('Go Down, Moses'); Harriet Tubman called 'Moses'
Martin Luther King's sermons on the Exodus and his last speech, 'I've been to the mountaintop'
Latin American Catholics read Exodus as God's option for the poor
Settler movements, including the Afrikaner 'Great Trek'
Saw themselves as a chosen people entering a promised land, often at the expense of its inhabitants

sections.key: The Exodus became the West's pattern of liberation, used by Puritans, founders, the enslaved and the civil rights movement, and also, darkly, by settlers.

paras: At the sea, the people are helpless. They do not fight; the Egyptians are defeated by the mud and the water. This is central to the story: freedom is a gift before it is an achievement. Israel did not liberate itself.

Christians have read the crossing as a picture of baptism, passing through water from slavery to freedom (1 Corinthians 10:1–2): the early Church baptised at the Easter Vigil, after reading Exodus 14. Jewish tradition sees the crossing as the moment the people were born. In both, freedom is received before it is used.
sections.key: At the sea Israel does nothing; freedom is a gift before it is an achievement. Christians read the crossing as baptism.

refs: Exodus 13:17–17:7; Numbers 14:1–4; Psalm 95:8; Psalm 114; Micah 6:3–5; Amos 9:7; 1 Corinthians 10:1–4; Mark 14:26.

The date of the Song of the Sea: Frank Moore Cross and David Noel Freedman, Studies in Ancient Yahwistic Poetry (1950/1975).
Nahshon: Talmud, Sotah 37a; Mekhilta on Exodus 14:15.
Isaiah Berlin, 'Two Concepts of Liberty' (Oxford inaugural lecture, 1958); Michael Walzer, Exodus and Revolution (1985).
The Great Seal proposal: report of the committee (Franklin, Jefferson, Adams), 20 August 1776; the Liberty Bell, cast 1752.

debate.question: What is the freedom the Exodus gives?

positions.name: Political liberation
positions.who: Liberation theologians; Michael Walzer; the civil rights tradition
positions.view: The Exodus is about real slaves freed from a real empire. It shows that God sides with the oppressed and that political liberation is part of salvation.
positions.evidence: The slavery, the cry, the plagues on a king; Israel's laws protecting slaves and foreigners; the story's use by the enslaved.

positions.name: Freedom for God
positions.who: Much Jewish tradition; most Christian theology
positions.view: The goal of the Exodus is not independence but covenant: freedom from Pharaoh in order to serve God and live by his law. Political freedom without that becomes a new slavery.
positions.evidence: 'Let my people go, that they may serve me' (8:1); the march leads to Sinai; the people's longing for Egypt.

positions.name: A spiritual pattern
positions.who: Origen; much Christian devotion; Gregory of Nyssa, The Life of Moses
positions.view: The Exodus is a picture of the soul's journey from sin to God: Egypt is sin, the sea is baptism, the desert is the testing of faith, Canaan is heaven.
positions.evidence: 1 Corinthians 10:1–11 ('these things happened to them as examples'); the spirituals' double meaning.

debate.agree: All agree that freedom in the Exodus is God's gift, and that it is more than the absence of a master.

look.why: An unknown American painter made this picture in or after 1863, the year of Abraham Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation. It is not of the Exodus, but it belongs to the story the Exodus inspired: a man holding a broken chain.
points: In the centre right, a man in a blue uniform with a red belt faces us, holding broken pieces of a chain in either hand.
Behind him a woman in a red dress and a child in a black suit face an American flag on a flagpole.
To the left, a rider on horseback holds up another flag, and lets a third, red and white, drag on the ground.
In the background, a tall white monument on the left, and an arched stone structure on the right with a large grey bird on top.
Distant hills and a body of water with small red rowing boats.

music.why: Aretha Franklin recorded this gospel album live in a Los Angeles church in 1972, the music that grew from the spirituals of the enslaved. It is still the best-selling live gospel album ever made.

think.why: The Exodus insists slaves are people God hears. Ask where the equal worth of every person comes from.

learn.why: Moses' words at the sea, for any moment when you are trapped.

check.q: Why did God lead the Israelites 'the long way', according to Exodus 13:17?

Lest they see war and change their minds and return to Egypt
To find water

Sea of Reeds, suggesting a marshy lake rather than the deep Red Sea
The Dead Sea

check.q: At the sea, Moses says 'stand still', but God says 'go forward'. What did Jewish commentators take from this?

That Moses disobeyed God
That the people should fight

It is the name of Moses' father
It means both 'serve' and 'be a slave': Israel goes from serving Pharaoh to serving God

That Israel should return to Egypt

check.q: Which of these is a fair statement about the Exodus in Western history?
options: It was used only by Jews
It was used only by the oppressed
It was never used politically

tutorial.question: What does the story of the sea and the desert teach about freedom?
tutorial.approach: Tell the story from the trap at the sea to the quarrel at Meribah. Show how the people react to danger and hardship, and what God does. Use Berlin's distinction between freedom from and freedom for, and the word avad. Then describe the Exodus in Western history, honestly, and end with what Amos 9:7 adds.
strong: Notices the people's repeated longing for Egypt and explains it.
Explains that freedom at the sea is God's gift, not Israel's achievement.
Uses the distinction between freedom from and freedom for, with avad.
Explains Miriam's role and the Song of the Sea.
Describes the Exodus in Western liberation movements, including its misuse.
Uses Amos 9:7 to show the universal reach of the story.

reading.why: A short, brilliant book on how the Exodus shaped Western politics.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: name one 'Egypt' you keep wanting to go back to, a habit, a resentment, a way of being told what to do, and take one step forward away from it.
sessions.reflect: Where in your life would you rather be safely unfree than frighteningly free?
takeaways: At the sea the people are helpless and want to go back; God saves them, by a strong east wind, and they sing.
Freedom has to be learned: the generation that left Egypt keeps longing for it; freedom from Pharaoh is freedom for serving God.
The Exodus became the West's freedom story, used for good and ill; Amos insists God frees other peoples too.

sessions.title: Ten words at Sinai
sessions.line: A freed people at a mountain, a covenant, ten commandments, and the oldest law code in the world beside them.
sessions.plain: Three months after leaving Egypt, the Israelites camp at Mount Sinai. God offers them a covenant: 'you shall be my own possession… a kingdom of priests'. They agree. Then, amid thunder and smoke, God speaks the Ten Commandments, followed by laws for daily life, and the covenant is sealed with blood. This session asks why a freed people receives law at once, what the Ten Commandments mean, and how Israel's law compares with the law of Babylon.
sessions.why: Session 4 showed that freedom is fragile and has to be learned. The answer Exodus gives is Sinai: freedom is given a shape, in a covenant and a law. This is the heart of the journey's question.
answers: Why does God give laws straight after setting the people free?
What is a covenant, and what happened at Sinai?
What do the Ten Commandments say, and why do the churches number them differently?
How does the law of Moses compare with other ancient law, such as Hammurabi's?
Did the law of Moses approve of slavery?
sessions.finding: Freedom is for covenant: the law given at Sinai binds a freed people to God and to each other, begins with grace, protects the weak and limits power, and, unlike Hammurabi's, gives one law for rich and poor alike, though it still regulated slavery rather than abolishing it.

paras: God heard the slaves (1), named himself 'I AM' (2), brought them out on Passover night (3), and saved them at the sea; but the freed slaves keep longing for Egypt, and freedom has to be learned (4).
background.key: Heard, named, freed, saved; but freedom has to be learned.

paras: You met covenants with Abraham: binding agreements, sealed with oaths and ceremonies. In the ancient Near East the great kings, especially the Hittites of what is now Turkey, made treaties with lesser kings. These treaties followed a pattern: the great king introduced himself, recalled what he had done for the lesser king, laid down conditions, required the treaty to be kept in a temple and read aloud, called witnesses, and listed blessings and curses.

In 1954 the American scholar George Mendenhall pointed out that the Sinai covenant follows this pattern closely: 'I am Yahweh your God' (introduction), 'who brought you out of Egypt' (history), the commandments (conditions), the tablets kept in the Ark (deposit), and blessings and curses (Deuteronomy 28). Israel's relationship with God was modelled on a treaty with a king, but the king was God, and the people were former slaves.

rows: What he has done for the lesser king
'who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage' (20:2)
The Ten Commandments and the laws that follow (20–23)
Kept in a temple and read aloud
The tablets in the Ark; 'the book of the covenant' read to the people (24:7)

background.key: The Sinai covenant follows the pattern of ancient treaties between a great king and a lesser one.

paras: The main reading has four parts: God's offer of the covenant (19:1–8), the Ten Commandments (20:1–17), a sample of the laws that follow (21:2, 23–25; 22:21–27; 23:9), and the sealing of the covenant in blood (24:3–8).

The comparison is from the Code of Hammurabi, the most famous law code of the ancient world, written in Babylon about 1750 BC, several centuries before Moses. Reading the two side by side shows what Israel's law shared with its neighbours, and where it was new.
background.key: The offer, the Ten Commandments, the case laws and the sealing; then Hammurabi's laws.

before: What does God say he has done before he gives any commands?
Which commandments are about God, and which about other people?
In the laws that follow, who is protected?
sessions.readWhy: The covenant at Sinai, in four parts: the offer, the Ten Commandments, the laws for daily life, and the sealing.

paras: In the third month after the children of Israel had gone out of the land of Egypt, on that same day they came into the wilderness of Sinai.
When they had departed from Rephidim, and had come to the wilderness of Sinai, they encamped in the wilderness; and there Israel encamped before the mountain.
Moses went up to God, and Yahweh called to him out of the mountain, saying, “This is what you shall tell the house of Jacob, and tell the children of Israel:
‘You have seen what I did to the Egyptians, and how I bore you on eagles’ wings, and brought you to myself.
Now therefore, if you will indeed obey my voice, and keep my covenant, then you shall be my own possession from among all peoples; for all the earth is mine;
and you shall be to me a kingdom of priests, and a holy nation.’ These are the words which you shall speak to the children of Israel.”
Moses came and called for the elders of the people, and set before them all these words which Yahweh commanded him.
All the people answered together, and said, “All that Yahweh has spoken we will do.”
Moses reported the words of the people to Yahweh.
God spoke all these words, saying,
“I am Yahweh your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage.
“You shall have no other gods before me.
“You shall not make for yourselves an idol, nor any image of anything that is in the heavens above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth:

you shall not bow yourself down to them, nor serve them, for I, Yahweh your God, am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children, on the third and on the fourth generation of those who hate me,
and showing loving kindness to thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments.
“You shall not misuse the name of Yahweh your God, for Yahweh will not hold him guiltless who misuses his name.
“Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy.
You shall labor six days, and do all your work,

but the seventh day is a Sabbath to Yahweh your God. You shall not do any work in it, you, nor your son, nor your daughter, your male servant, nor your female servant, nor your livestock, nor your stranger who is within your gates;
for in six days Yahweh made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them, and rested the seventh day; therefore Yahweh blessed the Sabbath day, and made it holy.
“Honor your father and your mother, that your days may be long in the land which Yahweh your God gives you.
“You shall not murder.
“You shall not commit adultery.
“You shall not steal.
“You shall not give false testimony against your neighbor.
“You shall not covet your neighbor’s house. You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife, nor his male servant, nor his female servant, nor his ox, nor his donkey, nor anything that is your neighbor’s.”
“If you buy a Hebrew servant, he shall serve six years, and in the seventh he shall go out free without paying anything.
But if any harm follows, then you must take life for life,
eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot,
burning for burning, wound for wound, and bruise for bruise.
“You shall not wrong an alien or oppress him, for you were aliens in the land of Egypt.
“You shall not take advantage of any widow or fatherless child.
If you take advantage of them at all, and they cry at all to me, I will surely hear their cry;
and my wrath will grow hot, and I will kill you with the sword; and your wives shall be widows, and your children fatherless.
“If you lend money to any of my people with you who is poor, you shall not be to him as a creditor. You shall not charge him interest.
If you take your neighbor’s garment as collateral, you shall restore it to him before the sun goes down,
for that is his only covering, it is his garment for his skin. What would he sleep in? It will happen, when he cries to me, that I will hear, for I am gracious.
“You shall not oppress an alien, for you know the heart of an alien, since you were aliens in the land of Egypt.
Moses came and told the people all Yahweh’s words, and all the ordinances; and all the people answered with one voice, and said, “All the words which Yahweh has spoken will we do.”
Moses wrote all Yahweh’s words, then rose up early in the morning and built an altar at the base of the mountain, with twelve pillars for the twelve tribes of Israel.
He sent young men of the children of Israel, who offered burnt offerings and sacrificed peace offerings of cattle to Yahweh.
Moses took half of the blood and put it in basins, and half of the blood he sprinkled on the altar.
He took the book of the covenant and read it in the hearing of the people, and they said, “We will do all that Yahweh has said, and be obedient.”
Moses took the blood, and sprinkled it on the people, and said, “Look, this is the blood of the covenant, which Yahweh has made with you concerning all these words.”

parts.title: On eagles' wings
parts.context: The third month after leaving Egypt. The people camp at the foot of Sinai, the mountain where God spoke to Moses from the bush.

commentary.on: how I bore you on eagles’ wings, and brought you to myself
commentary.text: God begins with what he has done, not what they must do. The goal of the Exodus is put in one phrase: 'brought you to myself'. Not to a land first, but to God.

commentary.on: if you will indeed obey my voice, and keep my covenant, then you shall be my own possession from among all peoples
commentary.text: 'Own possession' (segullah) is a king's personal treasure. The covenant is an offer, with a condition: Israel can say no.

commentary.on: for all the earth is mine
commentary.text: Israel is chosen, but not because God cares only for Israel: all the earth is his. The chosen people is chosen within the whole world, for its sake.

commentary.on: you shall be to me a kingdom of priests, and a holy nation
commentary.text: A priest stands between God and people. Israel is to be a whole nation of priests, standing between God and the world. That is the purpose of the choosing, as with Abraham: to be a blessing. Christians later applied the phrase to the Church (1 Peter 2:9).

commentary.on: All that Yahweh has spoken we will do.
commentary.text: The people accept the covenant before they hear its terms. The rabbis praised this trust: 'we will do', and only then 'we will understand'.

parts.title: The ten words
parts.context: On the third day, amid thunder, lightning, smoke and a trumpet blast (19:16–19), God speaks to the whole people. The Bible itself calls these 'the ten words' (Exodus 34:28; Deuteronomy 4:13), Decalogue in Greek.

commentary.on: I am Yahweh your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage.
commentary.text: The first 'word' is not a command but a statement of grace: I freed you. Every command that follows rests on it. Jews count this as the first of the ten. Law in the Bible is a response to rescue, not a way of earning it.

commentary.on: You shall have no other gods before me.
commentary.text: The foundation of everything: one God alone. In a world of many gods, this was revolutionary. It also limits every human power: no Pharaoh can be a god again.

commentary.on: You shall not make for yourselves an idol, nor any image
commentary.text: God is not to be made into a thing that can be seen, carried and controlled. The churches have differed over whether this forbids religious art: Orthodox and Catholics hold that after God became visible in Christ, images of him are allowed; some Protestants removed images from churches.

commentary.on: Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy.
commentary.text: The longest commandment. One day in seven, no one works: 'you, nor your son, nor your daughter, your male servant, nor your female servant, nor your livestock, nor your stranger'. A weekly day of rest for slaves and animals was unheard of in the ancient world. In Deuteronomy's version the reason given is: 'remember that you were a servant in the land of Egypt'.

commentary.on: Honor your father and your mother
commentary.text: The hinge between duties to God and duties to others. Parents stand in a sense for God; the family is the first school of the covenant.

commentary.on: You shall not murder.
commentary.text: Not 'kill', as older Bibles had it: the Hebrew word ratsach means unlawful killing. The same law allowed war and capital punishment, which is why Jews and Christians have argued about both.

commentary.on: You shall not covet your neighbor’s house.
commentary.text: The last commandment reaches inside: it forbids not an act but a desire. No human court can enforce it. The law of Sinai is not only about behaviour but about the heart, as the prophets will insist.

parts.title: Laws for daily life
parts.context: After the Ten Commandments come three chapters of case laws, called 'the book of the covenant' (21–23), on slaves, injuries, property, loans, justice and festivals. Here are four short samples.

commentary.on: If you buy a Hebrew servant, he shall serve six years, and in the seventh he shall go out free without paying anything.
commentary.text: The first law after the Ten Commandments is about slaves, and it limits slavery. A Hebrew bonded for debt goes free in the seventh year. The law of Moses regulated slavery rather than abolishing it, as the lecture explains.

commentary.on: eye for eye, tooth for tooth
commentary.text: The famous lex talionis. It sounds cruel, but its purpose was to limit revenge: no more than an eye for an eye, and the same for everyone. Jewish courts interpreted it as monetary compensation (Talmud, Bava Kamma 84a).

commentary.on: You shall not wrong an alien or oppress him, for you were aliens in the land of Egypt.
commentary.text: The memory of Egypt becomes law. Rabbis counted that the Torah commands care for the stranger thirty-six times, more than any other command.

commentary.on: If you take your neighbor’s garment as collateral, you shall restore it to him before the sun goes down
commentary.text: A poor man's cloak is his blanket. You may take it as security for a loan by day, but must return it at night. 'When he cries to me, I will hear, for I am gracious': the God who heard the slaves in Egypt hears the poor debtor too.

commentary.on: you know the heart of an alien, since you were aliens in the land of Egypt
commentary.text: Ethics grounded in memory and empathy: you know what it feels like. This is the reason given most often in the whole law.

parts.title: The blood of the covenant
parts.context: Moses writes down the laws, builds an altar, and seals the covenant.

commentary.on: with twelve pillars for the twelve tribes of Israel
commentary.text: Every tribe is represented. The covenant is made with the whole people together.

commentary.on: He took the book of the covenant and read it in the hearing of the people
commentary.text: The law is not secret, kept by priests. It is read aloud to everyone. A people governed by a written law that all can hear is one of Israel's great gifts to the West.

commentary.on: Look, this is the blood of the covenant
commentary.text: Half the blood on the altar, half on the people: God and Israel bound by one life. Jesus echoes these words at the Last Supper: 'This cup is the new covenant in my blood' (Luke 22:20), which you read in session 3.
