paras: section 15. If a man has caused either a palace slave or palace maid, or a slave of a poor man or a poor man's maid, to go out of the gate, he shall be put to death.

section 16. If a man has harboured in his house a manservant or a maidservant, fugitive from the palace, or a poor man, and has not produced them at the demand of the commandant, the owner of that house shall be put to death.

section 117. If a man a debt has seized him, and he has given his wife, his son, his daughter for the money, or has handed over to work off the debt, for three years they shall work in the house of their buyer or exploiter, in the fourth year he shall fix their liberty.
section 196. If a man has caused the loss of a gentleman's eye, his eye one shall cause to be lost.
section 197. If he has shattered a gentleman's limb, one shall shatter his limb.
section 198. If he has caused a poor man to lose his eye or shattered a poor man's limb, he shall pay one mina of silver.
section 199. If he has caused the loss of the eye of a gentleman's servant or has shattered the limb of a gentleman's servant, he shall pay half his price.
section 200. If a man has made the tooth of a man that is his equal to fall out, one shall make his tooth fall out.
section 201. If he has made the tooth of a poor man to fall out, he shall pay one-third of a mina of silver.
section 282. If a slave has said to his master 'Thou art not my master,' as his slave one shall put him to account and his master shall cut off his ear.

parts.author: The Code of Hammurabi
parts.work: The Oldest Code of Laws in the World
parts.title: An eye for a gentleman's eye
parts.context: Hammurabi was king of Babylon about 1792–1750 BC. His code, introduced by a prologue in which the gods call him 'to cause justice to prevail in the land… that the strong should not oppress the weak', has 282 laws. This translation, by the Cambridge scholar C. H. W. Johns, appeared in 1903, two years after the stone was found; Johns dated Hammurabi earlier than scholars do now. 'Gentleman' means a free citizen of the upper class; 'poor man' a lower-class freeman; a 'mina' is a weight of silver.
parts.plain: Hammurabi's laws say: anyone who helps a palace slave escape, or hides a runaway slave and does not hand him over, shall be put to death. A man who sells his family to pay a debt gets them back after three years. If you destroy a gentleman's eye, your eye is destroyed; if a poor man's, you pay a fine; if a slave's, you pay his owner half his price. A slave who denies his master has his ear cut off.

commentary.on: the owner of that house shall be put to death
commentary.text: In Babylon, hiding a runaway slave is a capital crime. Compare Deuteronomy 23:15–16: 'You shall not deliver to his master a servant who has escaped from his master to you… You shall not oppress him.' The law of Moses protects the runaway.

commentary.on: for three years they shall work in the house of their buyer or exploiter, in the fourth year he shall fix their liberty.
commentary.text: Be fair to Hammurabi: on debt-slavery his law is more generous than Exodus 21:2, freeing family members after three years, not six. Israel's law is not better at every point.

commentary.on: If a man has caused the loss of a gentleman's eye, his eye one shall cause to be lost.
commentary.text: Here is 'eye for eye', several centuries before Moses. But notice: it applies only to a 'gentleman'. The next laws set lesser penalties for harming a poor man, and a payment to the owner for a slave.

commentary.on: If he has caused a poor man to lose his eye or shattered a poor man's limb, he shall pay one mina of silver.
commentary.text: In Babylon, the punishment depends on the class of the victim. An upper-class eye is worth an eye; a poor man's eye is worth silver. In Israel, 'eye for eye' applies to everyone, and the law says 'You shall have one kind of law for the foreigner as well as the native-born' (Leviticus 24:22).

commentary.on: If a slave has said to his master 'Thou art not my master,' as his slave one shall put him to account and his master shall cut off his ear.
commentary.text: The last law of the code protects the master. Exodus 21:26–27 points the other way: a master who destroys his slave's eye or tooth must set the slave free. The direction of Israel's law, even where it allowed slavery, was towards the slave.

compare.author: The Code of Hammurabi
compare.work: The Oldest Code of Laws in the World
compare.why: The Code of Hammurabi, carved on a black stone pillar about 1750 BC, is the most famous law code of the ancient world. It was found in 1901 at Susa in Iran and is now in the Louvre. Read ten of its 282 laws, on runaway slaves, debt, and injuries, and compare them with what you have just read.
compare.title: The law of Babylon

paras: The order at Sinai matters. God does not say 'keep these laws and I will free you'. He says 'I brought you out; now live like free people'. The Ten Commandments begin with what God has done. In Jewish thought, the Torah is a gift, and the festival of its giving, Shavuot (Pentecost), is a joyful one. Psalm 119 says: 'I will walk in liberty, for I have sought your precepts.'

This is the answer the journey has been looking for. Law is not the opposite of freedom. It is freedom's shape: how a people who have been slaves live together so that no one enslaves anyone again. A Pharaoh rules by whim; a covenant people lives by a law that binds even its rulers (Deuteronomy 17:18–20 orders the king to copy out the law and read it every day, 'that his heart not be lifted up above his brothers').
sections.key: The law comes after the rescue, as its response: law is freedom's shape, binding even kings.

sections.h: The Ten Commandments, numbered three ways
paras: Everyone agrees there are ten 'words'; they disagree about where to divide them. Jews count 'I am Yahweh your God' as the first word. Catholics and Lutherans, following Augustine, combine 'no other gods' and 'no images' as one commandment and split the last into two (not coveting a neighbour's wife; not coveting his goods). The Orthodox and most Protestants, following Philo, Josephus and the early Church, make 'no images' a separate second commandment.

The difference is not trivial. Where images are a separate commandment, some Protestants removed paintings and statues from churches at the Reformation; Catholics and the Orthodox held that the commandment forbids worshipping images, not making them.

rows: I am Yahweh your God who brought you out

sections.key: The Ten Commandments are numbered three ways; the dispute over images shaped how churches look.

paras: When the Code of Hammurabi was found in 1901, some concluded that Moses had simply copied Babylon. Scholars now see a shared legal tradition, like a common language: 'eye for eye', laws about goring oxen, debts and theft appear in both. Some of the case laws of Exodus are almost word for word like Babylonian ones.

The differences are as striking as the similarities. Hammurabi's law comes from the king, under the gods; Moses' comes from God, and binds the king too. Hammurabi's penalties depend on class; Israel has one law for all, citizen and foreigner. Hammurabi executes those who shelter runaway slaves; Deuteronomy forbids returning them. Hammurabi has nothing like the Sabbath, the care for the stranger 'because you were strangers', or a command against coveting. And in Hammurabi property crimes could be punished by death, while in Israel, with one exception (kidnapping, 21:16), they were punished by restitution.
sections.key: Hammurabi and Moses share a legal tradition; Moses' law binds kings, applies to all classes and protects the runaway slave.

sections.h: Did the law of Moses approve of slavery?
paras: This question must be faced honestly. The law of Moses did not abolish slavery. It regulated it: Hebrew debt-slaves went free after six years; foreign slaves could be held permanently (Leviticus 25:44–46); a master who beat a slave to death was to be punished, but one whose slave survived 'a day or two' was not, 'for the servant is his property' (21:21). Defenders of American slavery quoted these verses.

Yet the law also pointed beyond slavery. Kidnapping a person to sell was a capital crime (21:16), which abolitionists used against the slave trade. Slaves rested on the Sabbath, went free if injured, and could not be returned if they ran away. The whole law rested on the memory 'you were slaves in Egypt'. Over centuries Jews and Christians drew from that memory the conclusion the law itself had not reached: that no human being should own another. Session 7 will ask how the law's deepest principle, love of neighbour, judges its own compromises.
sections.key: The law regulated slavery rather than abolishing it, but its memory of Egypt and its protections pointed beyond it.

paras: The story does not end at Exodus 24. Moses goes up the mountain for forty days to receive the stone tablets. Below, the people grow impatient and ask Aaron to make them gods; he melts their gold, the gold they took from Egypt, into a calf, and they worship it: 'These are your gods, Israel, which brought you up out of the land of Egypt' (32:4). Moses comes down and smashes the tablets.

The covenant is broken almost as soon as it is made. What saves it is Moses' prayer, 'forgive their sin, and if not, please blot me out of your book' (32:32), and God's mercy: he renews the covenant and reveals himself as 'merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness' (34:6). The law could not by itself make the people faithful. That is the problem session 7 will take up.
sections.key: The people break the covenant at once with the golden calf; it survives only by Moses' intercession and God's mercy.

The Code of Hammurabi, trans. C. H. W. Johns (1903); Martha Roth, Law Collections from Mesopotamia and Asia Minor (1995); the stele: Louvre, Sb 8.
Numbering: Augustine, Questions on Exodus 71; Philo, On the Decalogue; Josephus, Antiquities III.91–92; Catechism of the Catholic Church 2066; Westminster Shorter Catechism Q. 45–81.

debate.question: Is law the opposite of freedom?

positions.name: Law is freedom's shape
positions.who: Jewish tradition; Thomas Aquinas; many Christian thinkers
positions.view: Law given by a good God is what makes freedom possible: it protects the weak, binds the powerful and forms people who can live freely together. Without it, freedom collapses into a new slavery.
positions.evidence: The order of Exodus: rescue, then Sinai; Psalm 119:45; Deuteronomy 17 binding the king; the Sabbath as freedom from endless work.

positions.name: Law prepares for freedom
positions.who: Paul; Martin Luther
positions.view: The law is good, but it cannot make anyone good; it shows us our failure, as the golden calf shows Israel's, and so leads us to the grace that frees from within. It was 'a tutor to bring us to Christ' (Galatians 3:24).
positions.evidence: The calf within forty days; Romans 7:12, 'the law is holy'; Jeremiah 31's promise of a law written on the heart.

positions.name: Freedom is the absence of law
positions.who: Some modern liberal and libertarian thinkers
positions.view: Every law limits liberty; the best law is the least law, protecting only against harm to others. Religious law, especially, should not bind people who do not share the faith.
positions.evidence: John Stuart Mill's harm principle (On Liberty, 1859); the dangers of states that claim to know what is good for people.

debate.agree: All agree that law can protect the weak against the powerful, and that no law alone can make people good.

look.why: While Moses was on Sinai receiving the law, the people made a golden calf. This late sixteenth-century painting from Tintoretto's workshop in Venice shows the people gathered, with the calf and a mountain in the distance.

Further back, to the left, a crowd surrounds a tall structure supporting a gold-coloured calf, with four women kneeling in front playing instruments.
To the right in the distance, people sit around a cloth-covered table under a canopy.

tutorial.question: Why does a freed people receive law at Sinai, and what kind of law is it?
tutorial.approach: Explain the covenant and its treaty pattern. Walk through the Ten Commandments, noting the first word and the Sabbath. Use the case laws and Hammurabi to show what is shared and what is new. Face the question of slavery honestly. End with the golden calf and what it shows.

Explains the covenant and its treaty pattern.
Discusses specific commandments and the numbering dispute.
Compares Hammurabi fairly, including where Hammurabi is more generous.
Faces the law's regulation of slavery honestly, with its protections.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: keep one real Sabbath: twenty-four hours without paid work or shopping, and make sure someone who works for you, or serves you, gets rest too.
sessions.reflect: Which of the ten 'words' would most change your life if you kept it completely?
takeaways: At Sinai a freed people receives a covenant modelled on ancient treaties; it begins with grace: 'I brought you out'.
The Ten Commandments are numbered three ways; the law protects the weak and binds kings, and unlike Hammurabi has one law for all.
The law regulated slavery rather than abolishing it, and was broken within forty days at the golden calf: law alone could not make the people faithful.

sessions.title: The case against: did it happen?
sessions.line: Two million people, forty years in the desert, and no trace in the sand. The sceptic's case at full strength.
sessions.plain: Exodus says that about 600,000 men, with women and children perhaps two million people, left Egypt and lived forty years in the Sinai desert. Egypt kept detailed records; archaeologists have searched the desert for a century. They have found nothing. Many scholars conclude that the Exodus, as told, never happened. This session sets out that case at full strength, then the evidence on the other side, then what is at stake.
sessions.why: Sessions 1 to 5 read the story as its tellers meant it, from slavery to Sinai. Now we ask the question a modern reader asks: did it happen? It comes here, once you know the story well enough to see what history would have to show.
answers: Is there any evidence outside the Bible for the Exodus?
What is the strongest case that it did not happen as told?
What evidence suggests a real memory behind the story?
What do Jewish and Christian scholars make of the debate?
Does it matter whether the Exodus happened?
sessions.finding: No outside evidence confirms the Exodus as told, and the numbers cannot be literal; but the story has real Egyptian roots, most scholars think a smaller historical core lies behind it, some that it is a founding myth, and its meaning for Jews and Christians never rested on the numbers.

paras: God heard the slaves (1), revealed his name (2), freed them on Passover night (3) and at the sea, though freedom had to be learned (4), and gave them a covenant and law at Sinai (5). Each session read the story as its tellers meant it. Now the doubter speaks.
background.key: Five sessions read the story; now the doubter.

background.h: What history would have to show
paras: If the Exodus happened as Exodus and Numbers describe it, we might expect to find three kinds of evidence: Egyptian records of a slave people, plagues, a disaster to the army and a mass departure; traces of a vast population camping in Sinai for forty years; and signs of a newly arrived people conquering Canaan, as the book of Joshua describes, around the same time.
You met the method in 'What is the Bible?': test old stories against outside evidence, and say plainly where it is silent or against. Here the silence is loud.
background.key: Three kinds of evidence would be expected: Egyptian records, traces in Sinai, and a conquest of Canaan.

paras: The main reading gathers the Bible's own claims: the census of 603,550 fighting men (Numbers 1), its dates (1 Kings 6:1 and Genesis 15:13), its claim of a written itinerary (Numbers 33), and the short creed every Israelite farmer recited when bringing his first harvest to the Temple (Deuteronomy 26).

The comparison is the oldest surviving account of the Exodus by an outsider: the Roman historian Tacitus, writing about AD 100. It is hostile and garbled, but it shows that ancient writers knew a story of people expelled from Egypt led by Moses.
background.key: The Bible's own numbers and dates, its creed; then a hostile Roman account.

before: If 603,550 men were 'able to go out to war', how many people would that make in all?
What do the dates in 1 Kings 6:1 and Genesis 15:13 suggest about when the Exodus happened?
In Deuteronomy 26, what is the story that every Israelite was to tell, and what is missing from it?
sessions.readWhy: The Bible's own claims about the Exodus: its numbers, its dates, its records and its creed.

paras: These are those who were counted, whom Moses and Aaron counted, and the twelve men who were princes of Israel, each one for his fathers’ house.
So all those who were counted of the children of Israel by their fathers’ houses, from twenty years old and upward, all who were able to go out to war in Israel—
all those who were counted were six hundred three thousand five hundred fifty.

In the four hundred and eightieth year after the children of Israel had come out of the land of Egypt, in the fourth year of Solomon’s reign over Israel, in the month Ziv, which is the second month, he began to build Yahweh’s house.
He said to Abram, “Know for sure that your offspring will live as foreigners in a land that is not theirs, and will serve them. They will afflict them four hundred years.
These are the journeys of the children of Israel, when they went out of the land of Egypt by their armies under the hand of Moses and Aaron.
Moses wrote the starting points of their journeys by the commandment of Yahweh. These are their journeys according to their starting points.

You shall answer and say before Yahweh your God, “My father was a Syrian ready to perish. He went down into Egypt, and lived there, few in number. There he became a great, mighty, and populous nation.
The Egyptians mistreated us, afflicted us, and imposed hard labor on us.
Then we cried to Yahweh, the God of our fathers. Yahweh heard our voice, and saw our affliction, our toil, and our oppression.
Yahweh brought us out of Egypt with a mighty hand, with an outstretched arm, with great terror, with signs, and with wonders;
and he has brought us into this place, and has given us this land, a land flowing with milk and honey.

parts.title: How many?
parts.context: The book of Numbers is named after the census with which it opens, taken in the second year after leaving Egypt.

commentary.on: from twenty years old and upward, all who were able to go out to war in Israel
commentary.text: The census counts only men of fighting age. Add women, children and the elderly, and the total is usually estimated at two to three million: more than the entire population of Egypt at the time, by most estimates, and a column that would stretch hundreds of kilometres.

commentary.on: all those who were counted were six hundred three thousand five hundred fifty.
commentary.text: A precise number, 603,550, which matches Exodus 12:37's 'about six hundred thousand'. Its precision is part of the problem: how could such a host leave no trace? The lecture sets out the main proposals, including that the Hebrew word for 'thousand' may originally have meant a clan or military unit.

parts.title: When?
parts.context: Two dating clues. Solomon began the Temple in about 966 BC. And God told Abraham that his descendants would be oppressed in a foreign land for four hundred years.

commentary.on: In the four hundred and eightieth year after the children of Israel had come out of the land of Egypt
commentary.text: Counting back 480 years from about 966 BC gives about 1446 BC. But 480 is 12 times 40, and 40 is the Bible's round number for a generation, so many scholars read it as 'twelve generations' rather than a precise count. The city of Raamses (Exodus 1:11) points instead to the 1200s BC.

commentary.on: They will afflict them four hundred years.
commentary.text: Exodus 12:40 gives 430 years in Egypt. Another round number, or nearly so; and the genealogy of Moses (four generations from Levi, Exodus 6:16–20) seems to allow far less. The Bible's own chronology does not fit together neatly.

parts.title: A written record?
parts.context: Numbers 33 lists forty-two places where Israel camped between Egypt and the Jordan.

commentary.on: Moses wrote the starting points of their journeys by the commandment of Yahweh.
commentary.text: The text claims a written record. Some of the place names can be identified (Rameses, Succoth, the Sea, Kadesh, Dibon); most cannot. Scholars debate whether the list preserves an ancient itinerary or was composed later from known routes.

parts.title: What every farmer said
parts.context: When an Israelite farmer brought the first fruits of his harvest to the sanctuary, he was to recite this short history. Many scholars think it is one of the oldest summaries of Israel's story.

commentary.on: My father was a Syrian ready to perish. He went down into Egypt, and lived there, few in number.
commentary.text: 'Syrian' is Aramean: the ancestor is Jacob, whose family came from Aram, around Haran. The creed starts small: a wandering ancestor, a family 'few in number'.

commentary.on: The Egyptians mistreated us, afflicted us, and imposed hard labor on us.
commentary.text: 'Us', not 'them'. Every farmer, centuries later, says that he was a slave in Egypt. This is how Israel kept the story: not as distant history but as its own identity, recited at every harvest.

commentary.on: Yahweh brought us out of Egypt with a mighty hand, with an outstretched arm
commentary.text: Notice what the creed contains and what it leaves out: slavery, a cry, rescue, the land. No numbers, no forty years, no Sinai. Some scholars think this simpler memory came first, and the great account in Exodus grew around it.

paras: Most writers, however, agree in stating that once a disease, which horribly disfigured the body, broke out over Egypt; that king Bocchoris, seeking a remedy, consulted the oracle of Hammon, and was bidden to cleanse his realm, and to convey into some foreign land this race detested by the gods. The people, who had been collected after diligent search, finding themselves left in a desert, sat for the most part in a stupor of grief, till one of the exiles, Moyses by name, warned them not to look for any relief from God or man, forsaken as they were of both, but to trust to themselves, taking for their heaven-sent leader that man who should first help them to be quit of their present misery. They agreed, and in utter ignorance began to advance at random. Nothing, however, distressed them so much as the scarcity of water, and they had sunk ready to perish in all directions over the plain, when a herd of wild asses was seen to retire from their pasture to a rock shaded by trees. Moyses followed them, and, guided by the appearance of a grassy spot, discovered an abundant spring of water. This furnished relief. After a continuous journey for six days, on the seventh they possessed themselves of a country, from which they expelled the inhabitants, and in which they founded a city and a temple.

parts.author: Tacitus
parts.translator: Alfred John Church and William Jackson Brodribb (1873)
parts.title: Moyses, by name
parts.context: Publius Cornelius Tacitus (about AD 56–120) was Rome's greatest historian, and no friend of the Jews: the next chapters of his Histories call their customs 'perverse and disgusting'. Here he reports what 'most writers' say about Jewish origins. Bocchoris was a real Egyptian king of the eighth century BC; Hammon is the Egyptian god Amun. The Egyptian priest Manetho, in the third century BC, had told a similar story of 'lepers' expelled from Egypt led by a priest who took the name Moses. This is the Church and Brodribb translation of 1873.
parts.plain: Tacitus says: most writers agree that when a disfiguring disease broke out in Egypt, King Bocchoris was told by an oracle to drive out this race, hated by the gods. Left in the desert, the exiles despaired, until one of them, called Moses, told them to rely on themselves. Dying of thirst, they followed a herd of wild donkeys to a spring. After six days of travel, on the seventh they seized a land, drove out its people, and built a city and a temple.

commentary.on: once a disease, which horribly disfigured the body, broke out over Egypt
commentary.text: In the Egyptian and Greek versions the story is turned upside down: the Israelites are not slaves freed by God but diseased outcasts expelled by Pharaoh. This 'leper' slander, which goes back to Manetho, is one of the oldest anti-Jewish myths. The Jewish historian Josephus wrote a whole book, Against Apion (about AD 95), to refute it.

commentary.on: Moyses by name, warned them not to look for any relief from God or man
commentary.text: Tacitus knows the name Moses and a story of departure from Egypt, a desert, thirst and a spring of water. But in his version Moses teaches self-reliance, not trust in God: the opposite of the biblical story.

commentary.on: After a continuous journey for six days, on the seventh they possessed themselves of a country
commentary.text: A garbled echo of the Sabbath, which Romans thought was laziness. As evidence, this passage shows that an Exodus story with Moses was widely known by AD 100; it does not show that the events happened, because Tacitus is reporting what others said, more than a thousand years later.

compare.author: Tacitus
compare.translator: Alfred John Church and William Jackson Brodribb (1873)
compare.why: The Exodus was known outside Israel, but in garbled and hostile forms. The fullest surviving account by a pagan writer is by the Roman historian Tacitus, writing about AD 100 as a preface to the Roman siege of Jerusalem. Read it as evidence of what ancient non-Jews believed, and of the hostility Jews faced.
compare.title: A Roman view

sections.h: The case against, at full strength
paras: Here is the sceptic's case, as made by the Israeli archaeologist Israel Finkelstein and the historian Neil Asher Silberman in The Bible Unearthed (2001), and by many others.

First, Egypt is silent. Egyptian records of the New Kingdom are abundant, yet no text mentions Israelite slaves, Moses, plagues, a drowned army or a mass escape. Second, Sinai is silent. Archaeologists have surveyed the Sinai peninsula and dug at Kadesh-barnea, where Israel is said to have camped for decades, and found no trace of a large population in the late second millennium BC. Two million people for forty years would leave something. Third, Canaan contradicts the conquest: Jericho and Ai, the first cities Joshua takes, were unoccupied or unwalled at the likely time. Fourth, Israel seems to have emerged from within Canaan: around 1200 BC hundreds of new villages appear in the central hills, with pottery and houses like the Canaanites', distinguished mainly by the absence of pig bones. Fifth, some details fit a later age: place names and geography in the story match the seventh century BC better than the thirteenth. Their conclusion: the Exodus is a powerful founding myth, shaped largely in the seventh century BC, when Judah was facing a new Egypt.
sections.key: The sceptic's case: Egypt and Sinai are silent, Jericho and Ai contradict the conquest, Israel seems to emerge from within Canaan, and some details fit the seventh century.

sections.h: The case for a historical core
paras: The other side is not nothing. Semitic people from Canaan really did live in the Nile Delta, and some were labourers; an Egyptian papyrus (Leiden 348) mentions 'Apiru' hauling stones for Ramesses II's city, Pi-Ramesses, the city Exodus calls Raamses. Several names in the story are Egyptian: Moses, Phinehas, Hophni, Merari. The Merneptah Stele (about 1208 BC) shows that a people called 'Israel' existed in Canaan by then.

And there is the argument from embarrassment. No people invents a founding story in which its ancestors were slaves. Many scholars, such as Richard Elliott Friedman and Ronald Hendel, think a smaller group, perhaps the tribe of Levi (whose members bear the Egyptian names), did come out of Egypt, brought the worship of Yahweh with them, and joined the people forming in Canaan, whose whole nation then took the story as its own, as the farmer's creed says, 'us'. On the numbers, many scholars note that the Hebrew elef, 'thousand', can mean a clan or a military unit, which would reduce 603 'thousand' to some thousands of people.
sections.key: Semites in the Delta, Egyptian names, the Merneptah Stele and the embarrassment of slave ancestors suggest a smaller real exodus behind the story.

paras: Scholars today fall broadly into three groups. Most professional historians and archaeologists hold the middle position in some form; many evangelical and Orthodox Jewish scholars hold the first; a significant minority, the second.

In 2001 Rabbi David Wolpe, of a large synagogue in Los Angeles, told his congregation at Passover that the Exodus as told probably did not happen, and that it did not matter to their faith. The sermon caused an uproar, and showed how much was felt to be at stake.

rows: A large exodus under Moses in the 15th or 13th century BC; the numbers explained or taken as written
Kenneth Kitchen, James Hoffmeier; many evangelical and Orthodox Jewish scholars
The authentic Egyptian background; the absence of evidence in a desert is not evidence of absence
A smaller group escaped Egypt, perhaps the Levites, and their story became all Israel's
Richard Elliott Friedman, Ronald Hendel, William Dever (in part), most historians
Egyptian names; slave ancestors are not invented; the old creed
No exodus; Israel emerged from Canaan, and the story was composed later
Israel Finkelstein (largely), Thomas L. Thompson, John Van Seters
The silence of Egypt and Sinai; the archaeology of Jericho and the hill villages

sections.key: Scholars hold three positions: historical as told, a historical core, or founding myth; most historians hold a version of the middle one.

paras: For Jews, the Exodus is the centre of the faith: the first commandment grounds itself in it. Some Jewish thinkers say the story's truth is in its meaning and in the people who live by it; others, that a God who did not act in history is not the God of the Bible. For Christians, the question is less central than the resurrection, but not unimportant: Jesus and Paul speak of the Exodus as real, and Christian faith is a faith in a God who acts in history.

Two things are clear. The story's moral and religious claims, that God hears the oppressed, that freedom is for covenant, that the stranger is to be loved, do not depend on the number 603,550. And the evidence does not prove the story false: it shows that the account as we have it is not a modern historical report. That is the conclusion 'What is the Bible?' reached about Genesis too: test, weigh, and read each book as what it is.
sections.key: The story's claims about God and justice do not hang on the numbers; the evidence does not prove it false, but shows it is not a modern historical report.

paras: Whatever your view, three things are worth holding together. The evidence against a large Exodus in the form described is strong, and should not be waved away. The evidence for a real Egyptian background is real, and should not be dismissed either. And the story, whatever its origin, became true in another sense: for three thousand years a people has told it as its own, and slaves in America found their own freedom in it.

A Christian reader might add one more point. The Bible itself treats the Exodus as a story that keeps happening: Isaiah promises a new exodus from Babylon ('I will even make a way in the wilderness', 43:19), and the Gospels tell Jesus's death and resurrection as the greatest exodus of all (Luke 9:31 literally calls his coming death his 'exodus'). The question 'did it happen?' and the question 'is it happening?' belong together.
sections.key: Hold together: strong evidence against the numbers, real Egyptian roots, and a story that kept coming true; the Bible itself tells of new exoduses.

refs: Numbers 1:44–46; 33; 1 Kings 6:1; Genesis 15:13; Exodus 6:16–20; 12:37–41; Deuteronomy 26:5–9; Isaiah 43:16–19; Luke 9:31.

debate.question: Did the Exodus happen?

positions.name: Yes, essentially as told
positions.who: Kenneth Kitchen; James Hoffmeier; many traditional Jews and Christians
positions.view: The Exodus happened under Moses in the second millennium BC. Its Egyptian background is authentic; desert nomads leave little trace; the numbers can be explained by the meaning of elef or taken on trust.
positions.evidence: Pi-Ramesses; Semitic labourers in Egypt; Egyptian names; the absence of evidence in a desert is not evidence of absence.

positions.name: A real escape, a growing story
positions.who: Richard Elliott Friedman; Ronald Hendel; most historians
positions.view: A smaller group, perhaps the Levites, escaped Egypt and brought the worship of Yahweh; their story became the founding memory of all Israel and grew in the telling.
positions.evidence: The Egyptian names of Levites; the embarrassment of slave ancestors; the simple early creed of Deuteronomy 26.

positions.name: A founding myth
positions.who: Israel Finkelstein (largely); Thomas L. Thompson
positions.view: There was no exodus. Israel emerged from the people of Canaan, and the story was composed centuries later to give the nation an identity and a God who had freed it.
positions.evidence: The silence of Egyptian records and of Sinai; Jericho and Ai; the Canaanite character of the first Israelite villages.

debate.agree: All agree that the account in its present form is not a modern historical report, that no Egyptian record mentions the events, and that the story shaped Israel's identity more than any other.

look.why: In the desert God fed the people with manna, 'bread from heaven', every morning for forty years (Exodus 16). Bachiacca, a Florentine painter, imagined the scene in the 1540s and 50s as a crowd across a fantastic landscape, with animals no Israelite would have seen.
points: About fifty men, women and children gather in groups across a hilly landscape, in pink, orange, blue, red, green and brown.
In the lower left, a crowd follows a man who points to the right with a stick.
Others sit on rocks, stand by large urns, or bend to the ground to gather.
Along the foreground are a porcupine, a white rabbit, a black bear, a cow and cheetah-like animals, and a giraffe.
A path leads to buildings on a jagged coastline beneath craggy aquamarine mountains.

music.why: Psalm 23 in the Scottish metrical version, sung to Crimond: 'He leadeth me the quiet waters by… In death's dark vale I fear no ill'. The psalm of a God who leads his people through the wilderness.

think.why: The Exodus claims that God acts in history. Ask how evidence and faith relate when history is silent.

learn.why: The oldest short creed of Israel, recited by every farmer at harvest: we were slaves, and God brought us out.

check.q: Which of these is part of the strongest case against the Exodus as told?
options: The Bible contradicts itself about Moses' name
The Egyptians had no slaves
The Red Sea is too deep
No Egyptian record mentions it, no trace of a large population has been found in Sinai, and Jericho and Ai were not occupied at the likely time

check.q: What does the Merneptah Stele (about 1208 BC) show?
options: That the plagues happened
That a people called 'Israel' existed in Canaan by then
That Moses was an Egyptian prince
That the Exodus happened under Merneptah

check.q: What is the 'argument from embarrassment' for a historical core?
options: That the Bible is embarrassed by the plagues
That Egypt was embarrassed and hid the records
That Moses was embarrassed to speak
That no people would invent a founding story in which its ancestors were slaves
check.why: Founding myths usually flatter; this one does not.

check.q: How do some scholars explain the number 603,550?
options: By the Hebrew elef, 'thousand', possibly meaning a clan or military unit, which would greatly reduce the total
As the population of Canaan
As including the Egyptians
As a copying error for 6,035
check.why: Mendenhall, Humphreys and others; still debated.

check.q: What is notable about the creed in Deuteronomy 26:5–9?
options: It was written in Egypt
It denies the Exodus
It gives the exact numbers
Each later farmer says 'the Egyptians mistreated us', and it contains slavery, rescue and land but no numbers or forty years
check.why: A simple, early-seeming memory told as each Israelite's own story.

check.q: What does Tacitus's account (Histories V.3) best show?
options: That the Exodus happened exactly as in the Bible
That Moses was Roman
That an Exodus story with Moses was widely known by AD 100, in a hostile, garbled form going back to Egyptian anti-Jewish slander
That Jews invented the Sabbath in Rome
check.why: Evidence of the story's spread and of ancient hostility, not of the events.

tutorial.question: Did the Exodus happen, and does it matter?
tutorial.approach: Set out the sceptic's case at full strength (Egypt, Sinai, the conquest, Israel's emergence in Canaan). Then the evidence for an Egyptian background and a historical core. Describe the three scholarly positions fairly. End with your judgement on what the evidence shows, and on what, for Jews and Christians, depends on it.
strong: States the case against fairly and specifically.
Gives the evidence for an Egyptian background, including names and Pi-Ramesses.
Explains the problem of the numbers and the elef proposal.
Sets out the three positions with named scholars.
Distinguishes what the evidence shows from what it does not.
Reflects on what is at stake for Jews and Christians.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: tell someone the story of where your family came from, the hard parts too, and ask them about theirs.
sessions.reflect: If the Exodus did not happen as told, what, if anything, would you lose? If it did, what would it ask of you?
takeaways: The case against is strong: Egypt and Sinai are silent, the conquest does not fit the archaeology, and Israel seems to emerge from Canaan.
There is a real Egyptian background, and many scholars think a smaller group escaped; the numbers cannot be literal.
The story's claims about God and justice do not hang on the numbers; scholars hold three positions, and the Bible itself tells of new exoduses.

sessions.title: The law of love, and a new covenant
sessions.line: Love your neighbour, love the stranger, a law written on the heart, and why the Bible has two Testaments.
sessions.plain: The law of Moses contains one sentence that became the most famous moral command in the world: 'you shall love your neighbour as yourself'. Next to it is another: love the foreigner as yourself, 'for you were foreigners in Egypt'. Centuries later, after the covenant had been broken again and again, the prophet Jeremiah promised a 'new covenant', written not on stone but on the heart. This session gathers the journey's answer: what are freedom and law for? And it explains why Christians call the two halves of their Bible the Old and New Testaments.
sessions.why: Session 6 weighed whether the Exodus happened. This last session asks what it was all for, and where the law of Sinai leads: to love, and to a promise of a new covenant.
answers: What is the heart of the law of Moses?
Who is my neighbour, and what does the law say about foreigners?
What did Jeremiah mean by a 'new covenant'?
Why do Christians call their scriptures the Old and New Testaments?
Do Christians still keep the law of Moses? How do Jews and the churches differ?
So, what are freedom and law for?
sessions.finding: The law's aim is love of God and neighbour, including the stranger; when the covenant was broken the prophets promised a new covenant written on the heart, which is why Christians call their scriptures the Old and New Testaments; freedom is for love, and law is its shape.

paras: The God of Exodus hears the cry of slaves (1), has a name that means 'I will be with you' (2), sets his people free on Passover night (3), saves them at the sea though freedom has to be learned (4), and gives them a covenant and law at Sinai, which they break at once (5). Whether it happened as told is debated; its meaning does not hang on the numbers (6).
background.key: Heard, named, freed, saved, given law, unfaithful; and the history weighed.

paras: Leviticus, the third book of the Torah, is mostly about priests, sacrifices and purity, and most readers skip it. But at its centre, in chapter 19, is a chapter of laws that sum up the whole Torah: 'You shall be holy; for I, Yahweh your God, am holy.' Holiness turns out to mean honest weights, fair wages, care for the deaf and blind, food left for the poor, and love.

Centuries later, after the kingdom of Judah had broken the covenant again and again and faced destruction by Babylon in 587 BC, the prophet Jeremiah promised something new. You will meet the kings and prophets properly in the next journey; here we read his most famous promise.

timeline.text: The Exodus and Sinai, by many scholars' dating
King David
A 'book of the law' found in the Temple under King Josiah
Babylon destroys Jerusalem; Jeremiah promises a new covenant
Jesus: 'This cup is the new covenant in my blood'
Christians begin to speak of the 'Old' and 'New' covenant books

background.key: Leviticus 19 sums up the law; Jeremiah promised a new covenant when the old was broken.

paras: The main reading has four parts: holiness in daily life (Leviticus 19:1–4, 9–18), the foreigner (19:33–37), Jeremiah's new covenant (Jeremiah 31:31–34), and Jesus's answer to 'which commandment is the greatest?' (Mark 12:28–34).

The comparison is two short stories from the Talmud: Rabbi Akiva dying with the Shema on his lips, and Hillel summing up the whole law while a stranger stands on one leg. Together they are the Jewish answer to the scribe's question, a generation either side of Jesus.
background.key: Holiness, the stranger, the new covenant and the greatest commandment; then Akiva and Hillel on the heart of the law.

before: In Leviticus 19, what does 'be holy' turn out to mean in practice?
What reason does the law give for loving the foreigner?
In Jeremiah, what is new about the new covenant? What stays the same?
sessions.readWhy: The heart of the law, the prophets' promise, and Jesus's summary, in four parts.

paras: Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying,
“Speak to all the congregation of the children of Israel, and tell them, ‘You shall be holy; for I, Yahweh your God, am holy.
“ ‘Each one of you shall respect his mother and his father. You shall keep my Sabbaths. I am Yahweh your God.
“ ‘Don’t turn to idols, nor make molten gods for yourselves. I am Yahweh your God.
“ ‘When you reap the harvest of your land, you shall not wholly reap the corners of your field, neither shall you gather the gleanings of your harvest.
You shall not glean your vineyard, neither shall you gather the fallen grapes of your vineyard. You shall leave them for the poor and for the foreigner. I am Yahweh your God.
“ ‘You shall not steal.
“ ‘You shall not lie.
“ ‘You shall not deceive one another.
“ ‘You shall not swear by my name falsely, and profane the name of your God. I am Yahweh.
“ ‘You shall not oppress your neighbor, nor rob him.
“ ‘The wages of a hired servant shall not remain with you all night until the morning.
“ ‘You shall not curse the deaf, nor put a stumbling block before the blind; but you shall fear your God. I am Yahweh.
“ ‘You shall do no injustice in judgment. You shall not be partial to the poor, nor show favoritism to the great; but you shall judge your neighbor in righteousness.
“ ‘You shall not go around as a slanderer among your people.
“ ‘You shall not endanger the life of your neighbor. I am Yahweh.
“ ‘You shall not hate your brother in your heart. You shall surely rebuke your neighbor, and not bear sin because of him.
“ ‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.
“ ‘If a stranger lives as a foreigner with you in your land, you shall not do him wrong.

The stranger who lives as a foreigner with you shall be to you as the native-born among you, and you shall love him as yourself; for you lived as foreigners in the land of Egypt. I am Yahweh your God.
“ ‘You shall do no unrighteousness in judgment, in measures of length, of weight, or of quantity.
You shall have just balances, just weights, a just ephah, and a just hin. I am Yahweh your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.
“ ‘You shall observe all my statutes and all my ordinances, and do them. I am Yahweh.’ ”

“Behold, the days come,” says Yahweh,
“that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel,
and with the house of Judah:

“But this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days,”
says Yahweh:
“I will put my law in their inward parts,
and I will write it in their heart.
I will be their God,
and they shall be my people.
One of the scribes came, and heard them questioning together, and knowing that he had answered them well, asked him, “Which commandment is the greatest of all?”
Jesus answered, “The greatest is, ‘Hear, Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one:
you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind, and with all your strength.’ This is the first commandment.
The second is like this, ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ There is no other commandment greater than these.”
The scribe said to him, “Truly, teacher, you have said well that he is one, and there is none other but he,

and to love him with all the heart, and with all the understanding, with all the soul, and with all the strength, and to love his neighbor as himself, is more important than all whole burnt offerings and sacrifices.”
When Jesus saw that he answered wisely, he said to him, “You are not far from God’s Kingdom.”
No one dared ask him any question after that.

parts.title: You shall be holy
parts.context: Leviticus 19, the 'holiness code', addressed to 'all the congregation', not only priests.

commentary.on: You shall be holy; for I, Yahweh your God, am holy.
commentary.text: The whole chapter hangs on this. To be holy is to be set apart for God, and to be like him. And what God is like turns out, in the verses that follow, to be just and kind.

commentary.on: You shall leave them for the poor and for the foreigner.
commentary.text: Leave the edges of your field unharvested and the dropped grapes on the ground. Welfare built into farming: the poor gather what is left, with dignity, by their own work. The book of Ruth is a story about this law.

commentary.on: The wages of a hired servant shall not remain with you all night until the morning.
commentary.text: Pay workers the same day. A day labourer lived from hand to mouth; a delayed wage meant a hungry family.

commentary.on: You shall not curse the deaf, nor put a stumbling block before the blind
commentary.text: Laws protecting those who cannot defend themselves: the deaf cannot hear the curse, the blind cannot see the stumbling block, but God sees and hears. 'You shall fear your God' means: you will answer to him even when no one else can catch you.

commentary.on: You shall not be partial to the poor, nor show favoritism to the great
commentary.text: Justice is blind both ways: no bribe for the rich, but no rigged verdict for the poor either. Equality before the law.

commentary.on: you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.
commentary.text: Here, in the middle of a list of laws, is the sentence Jesus will call the second greatest commandment, and Rabbi Akiva 'the great principle of the Torah'. In context, 'neighbour' first means a fellow Israelite. But read on.

parts.title: Love the stranger
parts.context: The same chapter, a few verses later.

commentary.on: The stranger who lives as a foreigner with you shall be to you as the native-born among you, and you shall love him as yourself
commentary.text: The command to love is extended, in the same words, to the foreigner. 'As yourself' twice in one chapter: the neighbour, and the stranger. Jesus's parable of the Good Samaritan, in which the 'neighbour' is a despised foreigner, grows from this verse.

commentary.on: for you lived as foreigners in the land of Egypt.
commentary.text: The reason is the memory of Egypt. The whole journey comes together here: the slavery of session 1 becomes the ethic of the law. You know what it is to be a stranger; never treat a stranger as you were treated.

commentary.on: You shall have just balances, just weights
commentary.text: Love includes honest business. Cheating with weights is cheating the poor, who cannot check. Love of neighbour is not only a feeling but fair measures.

commentary.on: I am Yahweh your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.
commentary.text: The same words that opened the Ten Commandments close this passage. Every law rests on the rescue.

parts.title: A new covenant
parts.context: Jeremiah prophesied in Jerusalem from about 627 BC until its destruction by Babylon in 587 BC. He watched the covenant fail. In the middle of his darkest book comes a 'book of consolation' (chapters 30–33), with this promise.

commentary.on: I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah
commentary.text: The only place in the Hebrew Bible where the phrase 'new covenant' appears. It is made with Israel and Judah, God's own people.

commentary.on: not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers in the day that I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt
commentary.text: The Sinai covenant is the old one. God took them 'by the hand', like a father leading a child. The problem was not the law but the people: 'which covenant of mine they broke'.

commentary.on: I will put my law in their inward parts, and I will write it in their heart.
commentary.text: This is what is new. Not a new law, but the same law written in a new place: not on stone tablets, which can be smashed as Moses smashed them, but on the heart. The command against coveting, which no court could enforce, will be kept from within.

commentary.on: I will be their God, and they shall be my people.
commentary.text: The old covenant formula, unchanged. The relationship is the same; only its depth is new.

commentary.on: for I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more.
commentary.text: The new covenant rests on forgiveness, as the old was renewed by mercy after the golden calf. Christians hear this promise fulfilled in Jesus, whose words at the Last Supper, 'the new covenant in my blood', quote this verse (Luke 22:20; Hebrews 8:8–12). Jews read it as a promise to Israel still to be fully kept.

parts.title: The greatest commandment
parts.context: Jerusalem, in the last week of Jesus's life. A scribe, an expert in the law, asks a question rabbis often debated: which commandment is the greatest?

commentary.on: The greatest is, ‘Hear, Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one
commentary.text: Jesus answers with the Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4–5), the prayer every Jew said morning and evening, and still does. He does not invent a new commandment; he names the oldest.

commentary.on: The second is like this, ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’
commentary.text: Jesus joins Deuteronomy 6:5 and Leviticus 19:18: love of God and love of neighbour, inseparable. Jewish teachers before and after him gave similar summaries, as the comparison shows.

commentary.on: is more important than all whole burnt offerings and sacrifices
commentary.text: The scribe agrees, and goes further, echoing the prophets (Hosea 6:6; Micah 6:6–8). Jesus and this Jewish teacher of the law are in complete agreement about the heart of the Torah.

commentary.on: You are not far from God’s Kingdom.
commentary.text: A rare moment of warmth between Jesus and a scribe. The summary of the law is common ground between Jews and Christians.

paras: Once, as the Rabbis tell us, the Roman Government issued a decree forbidding Israel to study the law. Whereupon Pappus, the son of Yehudah, one day found Rabbi Akiva teaching it openly to multitudes, whom he had gathered round him to hear it. "Akiva," said he, "art thou not afraid of the Government?" "List," was the reply, "and I will tell thee how it is by a parable. It is with me as with the fishes whom a fox, walking once by a river's side, saw darting distractedly to and fro in the stream; and, addressing, inquired, 'From what, pray, are ye fleeing?' 'From the nets,' they replied, 'which the children of men have set to ensnare us.' 'Why, then,' rejoined the fox, 'not try the dry land with me, where you and I can live together, as our fathers managed to do before us?' 'Surely,' exclaimed they, 'thou art not he of whom we have heard so much as the most cunning of animals, for herein thou art not wise, but foolish.

For if we have cause to fear where it is natural for us to live, how much more reason have we to do so where we needs must die!' Just so," continued Akiva, "is it with us who study the law, in which (Deut. xxx. 20) it is written, 'He is thy life and the length of thy days;' for if we suffer while we study the law, how much more shall we if we neglect it?" Not many days after, it is related, this Rabbi Akiva was apprehended and thrown into prison. As it happened, they led him out for execution just at the time when "Hear, O Israel!" fell to be repeated, and as they tore his flesh with currycombs, and as he was with long-drawn breath sounding forth the word one, his soul departed from him. Then came forth a voice from heaven which said, "Blessed art thou, Rabbi Akiva, for thy soul and the word one left thy body together."

Once a Gentile came to Shamai, and said, "Proselytize me, but on condition that thou teach me the whole law, even the whole of it, while I stand upon one leg." Shamai drove him off with the builder's rod which he held in his hand. When he came to Hillel with the same challenge, Hillel converted him by answering him on the spot, "That which is hateful to thyself, do not do to thy neighbor. This is the whole law, and the rest is its commentary." (Tobit, iv. 15; Matt. vii. 12.)

parts.author: The Talmud
parts.ref: The Talmud: Akiva and Hillel (Berakhot 61b; Shabbat 31a)
parts.title: Hear, O Israel
parts.context: The Talmud gathers the teaching of the rabbis from about 200 BC to AD 500. Rabbi Akiva (about 50–135) was the greatest teacher of his age; he was executed by the Romans after the second Jewish revolt, when they banned the teaching of the Torah. Hillel, a generation before Jesus, and Shammai (spelled 'Shamai' here) led the two great schools of Jewish law. These translations are from P. I. Hershon's Talmudic Miscellany (1880), reprinted in a 1901 anthology. The references in brackets after Hillel's saying were added by the translator, to the book of Tobit and to Jesus's Golden Rule.
parts.plain: The first story says: when Rome banned the study of the law, Akiva went on teaching it in public. He explained with a parable: fish in danger in the river would be in far worse danger on dry land; the law is our life, as water is the fishes'. He was arrested and tortured to death, and died saying the Shema, 'Hear, O Israel', on the word 'one'. The second says: a non-Jew asked to be taught the whole law while standing on one leg. Shammai drove him away; Hillel said: 'What is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbour. That is the whole law; the rest is commentary.'

commentary.on: 'He is thy life and the length of thy days;'
commentary.text: Akiva's parable answers the journey's question from the inside: the law is not a cage but water to a fish, the element a free people lives in. To give it up for safety would be to die.

commentary.on: as he was with long-drawn breath sounding forth the word one, his soul departed from him.
commentary.text: Akiva dies saying the Shema, 'Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one', the first half of Jesus's greatest commandment. The Talmud tells that he said he had always wondered how he could love God 'with all your soul', that is, even if God takes your life, and now he could. Jews still recite the Shema at the moment of death.

commentary.on: That which is hateful to thyself, do not do to thy neighbor. This is the whole law, and the rest is its commentary.
commentary.text: Hillel's summary is Leviticus 19:18 in negative form, a generation before Jesus gave it in positive form: 'Whatever you desire for men to do to you, you shall also do to them; for this is the law and the prophets' (Matthew 7:12). The full saying ends: 'Go and learn it.' The summary does not replace the law; it tells you what the law is for.

commentary.on: Shamai drove him off with the builder's rod which he held in his hand.
commentary.text: The story contrasts two kinds of teacher: one who guards the law against the outsider, one who opens it to him. Hillel's patience with the stranger is itself the law of love in action.

compare.author: The Talmud
compare.ref: The Talmud: Akiva and Hillel (Berakhot 61b; Shabbat 31a)
compare.why: The rabbis of the first and second centuries asked the same question as the scribe in Mark: what is the heart of the law? Read two short stories from the Talmud, the great collection of rabbinic teaching: one about loving God with your whole life, one about loving your neighbour.
compare.title: The whole law on one leg

paras: Jewish tradition counts 613 commandments in the Torah (Talmud, Makkot 23b). Over the centuries teachers tried to sum them up. The Talmud records a series of summaries: David in eleven (Psalm 15), Isaiah in six (33:15), Micah in three: 'act justly, love mercy, walk humbly with your God' (6:8), Habakkuk in one: 'the righteous shall live by his faith' (2:4). Rabbi Akiva called 'love your neighbour as yourself' the great principle; Hillel, 'what is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbour'.

Jesus's answer, love of God and love of neighbour, stands in this Jewish tradition. Paul draws the conclusion: 'love is the fulfilment of the law' (Romans 13:10). Jews and Christians differ on much, but not on this: the heart of the law is love.
sections.key: Jewish teachers and Jesus alike summed up the 613 commandments as love of God and neighbour.

paras: The Torah commands care for the stranger more than any other single thing; the Talmud counts thirty-six times (Bava Metzia 59b). 'Stranger' (ger) means a resident foreigner: someone living among Israel without land or family, the most vulnerable person in an ancient society. The reason given, again and again, is Egypt: 'you know the heart of a stranger'.

This has had a long history. Christians in the early centuries were known for caring for strangers and the sick; the Emperor Julian complained in about 362 that Christians 'support not only their own poor but ours as well'. How nations should treat migrants and refugees is fiercely debated today, and the Bible does not settle every question of policy. But it is clear about the principle: the stranger is a neighbour, to be loved 'as yourself'.
sections.key: The Torah commands love of the stranger more than any other thing, grounded in the memory of Egypt.

paras: Here is the answer to a question many people ask. 'Testament' comes from the Latin testamentum, which translated the Greek diathēkē, which translated the Hebrew berit: 'covenant'. The 'Old Testament' means the books of the old covenant, the one made at Sinai; the 'New Testament' means the books of the new covenant Jeremiah promised, which Christians believe Jesus made at the Last Supper ('this cup is the new covenant in my blood').

The names go back to the late second century, to writers like Irenaeus, Tertullian and Melito of Sardis. Jews, naturally, do not call their scriptures 'old': for them it is the Tanakh, the whole Hebrew Bible. Many Christian scholars today use 'Hebrew Bible' or 'First Testament' out of respect, and because 'old' can wrongly suggest 'out of date'. In Christian teaching the Old Testament is not replaced: Jesus said 'I didn't come to destroy, but to fulfil' (Matthew 5:17), and the Church rejected Marcion, who wanted to throw it out, in the second century.
sections.key: 'Testament' means covenant: the Old Testament is the books of the Sinai covenant, the New of the new covenant Jeremiah promised.

sections.h: Do Christians keep the law of Moses?
paras: Christians do not keep most of the 613 commandments: they do not keep kosher, circumcise boys as a religious duty, or offer sacrifices. Yet they keep the Ten Commandments and call the law 'holy, righteous and good' (Romans 7:12). How does that fit? The early Church settled one part at the Council of Jerusalem (Acts 15): Gentile believers need not become Jews. Later theologians explained the rest in different ways.

Thomas Aquinas set out the classic Catholic account: the law has moral precepts (like the Ten Commandments), which are part of natural law and bind everyone forever; ceremonial precepts (sacrifices, food laws), which pointed to Christ and are fulfilled; and judicial precepts (Israel's civil law), which applied to Israel as a nation. Most Protestants and the Orthodox hold something similar. Lutherans stress that the law shows us our sin and drives us to Christ; Reformed Christians add a 'third use': the law as a guide for grateful living.

rows: All 613 commandments bind Jews, as interpreted by the rabbis; non-Jews are bound by the seven laws of Noah
Israel's covenant way of life; a light to the nations
The moral law (summed up in the Ten Commandments) binds all; the ceremonial law is fulfilled in Christ
Natural law made clear; a teacher pointing to Christ (Aquinas)
The commandments are fulfilled in Christ and kept in the life of the Spirit
Healing and transformation of the person (theosis)
The moral law still speaks, but no one is saved by keeping it
To show sin and drive us to Christ; to order society
The moral law is the Christian's guide; ceremonial and civil laws have ended
The 'third use': a rule of grateful living (Calvin)

sections.key: Christians keep the moral law, summed up in the Ten Commandments, but not the ceremonial law; Jews keep the 613 commandments; the churches explain this differently.

sections.h: The verdict: what are freedom and law for?
paras: This journey asked what freedom and law are for. Exodus answers in a story. Freedom begins with a God who hears the cry of slaves and acts. It is a gift before it is an achievement, and it has to be learned: the freed slaves long for Egypt. It is not freedom from all service, but freedom from Pharaoh for the service of God, whose first gift is a day of rest.

Law is not freedom's opposite but its shape: a covenant that binds the powerful, protects the weak, gives one law for rich and poor, and turns the memory of slavery into love of the stranger. Its heart is love of God and neighbour. But law written on stone could not make people faithful; it was broken at once. So the prophets promised a new covenant written on the heart, which Christians believe Jesus made, and from which their 'New Testament' takes its name. Freedom is for love, and law is the shape love takes among people who have been slaves.
sections.key: Freedom is God's gift, from Pharaoh for God; law is freedom's shape, and its heart is love; the new covenant writes it on the heart.

debate.question: How should Christians relate to the law of Moses?

positions.name: Fulfilled, not abolished
positions.who: Catholic, Orthodox and Reformed traditions; Aquinas; Calvin
positions.view: The moral law, summed up in the Ten Commandments and the two great commandments, still binds everyone and guides Christian life; the ceremonial and civil laws pointed to Christ and are fulfilled in him.
positions.evidence: Matthew 5:17–18; Romans 13:8–10; Acts 15; Jeremiah 31: the same law, written on the heart.

positions.name: Law and gospel
positions.who: Luther and the Lutheran tradition
positions.view: The law is holy but cannot save: it shows us our sin and drives us to Christ, who frees us; Christians do good out of gratitude and love, not under the law's command.
positions.evidence: Galatians 3:24; Romans 7; the golden calf; Paul's 'you are not under law, but under grace' (Romans 6:14).

positions.name: Torah still for Israel
positions.who: Jewish tradition; some Christian scholars ('Paul within Judaism')
positions.view: The Torah remains Israel's covenant way of life, binding on Jews; Paul objected only to forcing it on Gentiles. The new covenant does not cancel God's covenant with Israel.
positions.evidence: Romans 11:29, 'the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable'; Acts 21:20–24, where Paul keeps the law; Jeremiah 31 made 'with the house of Israel'.

debate.agree: All agree that the heart of the law is love of God and neighbour, and that God's covenant with Israel was not a mistake.

look.why: The heart of the law is love. Andrea del Sarto, a Florentine painter, painted Charity in the 1520s: in Christian tradition charity, love, is the greatest of the virtues and 'the fulfilment of the law'.
points: A young woman in a carnation-pink gown, her auburn hair bound with a blue ribbon, holds a standing infant close.

music.why: 'Ubi caritas et amor, Deus ibi est': where charity and love are, God is there. An ancient chant sung at the washing of feet on Maundy Thursday, set by Maurice Duruflé in 1960.

think.why: Jeremiah promised a law written on the heart. Ask how practices and habits form a person from within.

learn.why: The promise of the new covenant, from which the New Testament takes its name.

Then use Leviticus 19 and Jeremiah 31 to say what the law is for and why a new covenant was promised. Explain 'Old' and 'New Testament', and how Jews and the churches relate to the law. End with your own answer.

Uses the Exodus story to show freedom as gift, learned, and 'for' service.

takeaways: Leviticus 19 turns holiness into everyday justice and love, of the neighbour and of the stranger 'for you were strangers in Egypt'.
Jeremiah promised a new covenant: the same law written on the heart; 'Testament' means covenant.

closing.title: Your answer
closing.prompt: What are freedom and law for? In about 300 words, answer from the story of Exodus, using at least three of its episodes, and answer the strongest objection to your view.
closing.practice: Read the whole of Exodus 1–20 over the next week, three chapters a day. Then, if you can, ask a Jewish friend or synagogue whether you might join a Passover Seder, or read a Haggadah at home.
synthesis: This journey asked what freedom and law are for, following Israel from slavery in Egypt to the mountain of Sinai. Here are the short answers to its questions.

How did Abraham's family become slaves? A new king who 'didn't know Joseph' feared them as foreigners and turned them into forced labour, building cities like Raamses. The first to resist were two midwives who 'feared God' more than Pharaoh. Moses' own attempt at justice, a secret killing, failed. Then 'God heard their groaning', remembered, saw and knew. Israel's founding story is unique: we were slaves. The enslaved in America read it as their own.

Who is the God of Exodus? He speaks from a bush that burns and is not consumed, as the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and gives his name: 'I AM WHO I AM', meaning both 'I will be with you' and 'I am the one who simply is'. Jews do not speak the name; English Bibles print 'the LORD'; Christians hear Jesus claim it ('before Abraham was, I AM').

Why the plagues and the Passover? The plagues answer Pharaoh's 'Who is Yahweh?' and judge Egypt's gods; Pharaoh hardened his own heart before God hardened it. The death of the firstborn is a real moral difficulty, which Jewish tradition refused to celebrate. The Passover meal makes every generation part of the story; Jesus died at Passover, his last supper became the Eucharist, and 'the new covenant in my blood' gave the New Testament its name.

What is freedom like? At the sea the people were helpless; freedom was a gift before it was an achievement. Then they longed for Egypt again and again: it took one night to take Israel out of Egypt and forty years to take Egypt out of Israel. Freedom from Pharaoh was freedom for serving God; the same Hebrew word means 'serve' and 'slave'. The story became the West's pattern of liberation, used by the enslaved and by revolutionaries, and sometimes by conquerors; Amos insisted God frees other peoples too.

What is the law for? At Sinai a freed people received a covenant that begins with grace: 'I brought you out'. The Ten Commandments bind kings, give a day of rest to slaves and animals, and forbid even coveting. Beside Hammurabi's law, Israel's has one law for rich and poor and protects the runaway slave, though it regulated slavery rather than abolishing it, and Hammurabi was kinder to debt-slaves. The people broke the covenant at once with the golden calf; it survived by mercy.

Did it happen? No Egyptian record or Sinai excavation confirms it, the numbers cannot be literal, and the conquest does not fit the archaeology. But the story has real Egyptian roots, slave ancestors are not invented, and most historians think a smaller exodus lies behind it, while some think it a founding myth. Its claims about God and justice do not hang on the numbers.

So what are freedom and law for? Freedom is God's gift to slaves, for love; law is freedom's shape. Its heart is love of God and of neighbour, including the stranger, 'for you were strangers in Egypt'. Because law on stone could not make people faithful, Jeremiah promised a new covenant written on the heart, which Christians believe Jesus made; that is why their Bible has an Old and a New Testament. Jews keep the Torah as their covenant way of life; the churches keep its moral law in different ways; all agree that its heart is love.

One more thing. Count how much of the West comes from these chapters: the weekly day of rest; the idea that even rulers are under law; one law for rich and poor; the right to refuse an unjust order; care for the stranger; a calendar that remembers liberation; and the story every movement for freedom has told, from the American founders to Martin Luther King. When people in the West say that no one should be a slave, they are, knowingly or not, retelling Exodus.

title: Kings and prophets
question: What happens when power forgets justice?
line: Six sessions from the day Israel asked for a king to the fall of Jerusalem and beyond: a prophet's warning, David and Nathan, Ahab and Elijah, Amos's cry for justice, the exile in Babylon, the God of war, and the servant who suffers.
why: Every society must decide who holds power and what stops them abusing it. Israel's answer, a king under God's law with prophets beside him to say 'you are the man', became one of the roots of the West's belief that no ruler is above the law and that the poor have a claim on justice. This journey reads Samuel, Kings and the prophets with Aristotle, Plato, Hesiod and Thomas Paine, looks at what archaeology has found, faces the hardest objection, the wars of Joshua, and ends with Isaiah's servant who gives his life instead of taking others'. It is written at the depth of a first-year university course, for anyone.
follows: A first-year theology paper on the historical books and the prophets of the Hebrew Bible, with elements of papers on biblical archaeology, political theology and the problem of violence in Scripture.
before: exodus

sessions.title: Give us a king
sessions.line: A people asks for a king like everyone else's, a prophet warns them what kings do, and a shepherd boy is chosen.
sessions.plain: Israel has lived in its land for generations without a king, led by 'judges' in times of crisis. Now the people demand a king 'like all the nations'. The old prophet Samuel warns them what kings do: they take. God lets them have one anyway, but Israel's law puts the king under God's law, and the prophets keep watch. Then God sends Samuel to choose a new king, and he passes over seven tall brothers for the youngest, out with the sheep: David. This session asks why people want strong rulers, and what Israel believed power is for.
sessions.why: This is the first session. 'Exodus and the law' ended with a freed people bound to God by covenant at Sinai, with a law for rich and poor alike. Now that people has a land, and it wants what every other nation has: a king. Before we can ask what happens when power forgets justice, we need to see what power was meant to be.
answers: Why did Israel want a king, and why was Samuel against it?
What did Samuel warn that kings would do?
What limits did Israel's law put on its kings?
Why was David chosen, and what does 'anointed' mean?
Did David really exist?
sessions.finding: Israel got its king, but its law put the king under God's law and its prophets kept watch: power was allowed, but never absolute.

paras: If you have taken 'Exodus and the law', you followed Israel out of slavery to the mountain of Sinai, where God gave them his law and made a covenant with them. The Bible then tells how, under Moses' successor Joshua, the tribes entered Canaan, the land promised to Abraham. (How they took it is the hardest story in the Bible; session 5, still to come, faces it head on.)

For about two centuries after that, Israel had no king. It was a loose alliance of twelve tribes. When enemies attacked, God raised up leaders called 'judges', such as Deborah, Gideon and Samson, who rescued the people and then went home. The book of Judges ends with the people falling apart, and a refrain: 'In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did that which was right in his own eyes' (Judges 21:25). The last and greatest of the judges was Samuel, who was also a prophet. Our story begins when he is old.
background.key: After Sinai and the settlement of Canaan, Israel lived for about two centuries without a king, led by 'judges' in crises; Samuel was the last.

paras: Every society has to decide who holds power and what stops them abusing it. The books of Samuel and Kings tell the story of Israel's kings over about four hundred years, from the first king to the destruction of Jerusalem. Running beside the kings, all the way through, are the prophets, who told them, often at great risk, that they too were under God's law.

That raises the question of this journey: what happens when power forgets justice? We will follow the story in order: why Israel wanted a king, how its greatest king abused his power, what the prophets demanded, how the kingdom fell, and what hope was left. One session gives the strongest objection its full weight: Israel's own God commanded war against the Canaanites. The last session gives a verdict.

background.key: What happens when power forgets justice? We follow Israel's kings and the prophets who confronted them, hear the case against, then give a verdict.

background.h: Who were the kings and the prophets?
paras: Israel had three kings over the whole nation: Saul, David and Solomon, from about 1030 to 930 BC. David made Jerusalem his capital; his son Solomon built the Temple there. After Solomon the kingdom split in two: Israel in the north, with its capital at Samaria, and Judah in the south, around Jerusalem, ruled by David's descendants. In 722 BC the Assyrian empire destroyed the northern kingdom. In 587 BC the Babylonians destroyed Jerusalem and the Temple.

A prophet, in the Bible, is not mainly someone who predicts the future. A prophet is someone who speaks God's word to the present, usually to people who do not want to hear it, kings above all. Some are famous: Nathan, Elijah, Amos, Isaiah, Jeremiah. Women were among them too: Deborah, and Huldah, whom the king's own officials consulted (2 Kings 22:14). Jews, Christians and Muslims all honour these prophets; several, like Elijah (Ilyas) and David (Dawud), are named in the Qur'an.
background.key: Three kings over all Israel (Saul, David, Solomon), then two kingdoms, destroyed in 722 and 587 BC. Prophets spoke God's word to the present, especially to kings.

background.h: Who wrote these books, and is it history?
paras: The books of Samuel and Kings do not name their authors. Jewish tradition (the Talmud, Bava Batra 15a) credits Samuel with the books that bear his name, and Jeremiah with Kings. Most scholars today think Joshua, Judges, Samuel and Kings form one long history, put together in Judah in the late 600s BC and finished during the exile in Babylon after 587 BC. Its authors used older written sources, which they name, such as 'the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel' (1 Kings 14:19), and they wrote to explain a catastrophe: why the kingdoms fell.

Can any of it be checked? Some of it can. In 1993 archaeologists at Tel Dan, in northern Israel, found an inscription set up by an Aramean king in the 800s BC, boasting of victory over the 'king of Israel' and the 'house of David'. Most scholars take this as the earliest mention of David outside the Bible, about 150 years after his time. How big David's kingdom really was is hotly debated: some archaeologists, such as Israel Finkelstein, think it was a small hill-country chiefdom; others, such as Yosef Garfinkel, point to a fortified town of about 1000 BC at Khirbet Qeiyafa as a sign of an organised kingdom.
background.key: Samuel and Kings are part of one history finished in the exile from older sources. The Tel Dan inscription (found 1993) names the 'house of David'; the size of his kingdom is debated.

paras: Israel was a small country on the land bridge between Egypt and Mesopotamia, the two great centres of ancient power. Its kings were minor players compared with the pharaohs and the emperors of Assyria and Babylon, who ruled as gods or as the chosen of gods. That is the background to everything in this journey: in the ancient world, the king usually was the law.

paras: The main reading has three parts: the people demand a king and Samuel warns them (1 Samuel 8); the law of the king in Deuteronomy, which puts limits on him (Deuteronomy 17); and the choosing of David (1 Samuel 16).

The comparison is from Aristotle, the Greek philosopher who studied the governments of many cities. He asks the same question as Samuel from a different angle: what is the difference between a king and a tyrant?
background.key: The demand for a king, the law that limits him, and the choice of David; then Aristotle on kings and tyrants.
