sessions.readWhy: Three passages: the people demand a king, the law that limits him, and the choosing of the youngest son.

paras: When Samuel was old, he made his sons judges over Israel.
Now the name of his firstborn was Joel; and the name of his second, Abijah. They were judges in Beersheba.
His sons didn’t walk in his ways, but turned away after dishonest gain, took bribes, and perverted justice.
Then all the elders of Israel gathered themselves together and came to Samuel to Ramah.
They said to him, “Behold, you are old, and your sons don’t walk in your ways. Now make us a king to judge us like all the nations.”
But the thing displeased Samuel, when they said, “Give us a king to judge us.”
Samuel prayed to Yahweh.
Yahweh said to Samuel, “Listen to the voice of the people in all that they tell you; for they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me as the king over them.
According to all the works which they have done since the day that I brought them up out of Egypt even to this day, in that they have forsaken me, and served other gods, so they also do to you.
Now therefore listen to their voice. However you shall protest solemnly to them, and shall show them the way of the king who will reign over them.”
Samuel told all Yahweh’s words to the people who asked him for a king.

He said, “This will be the way of the king who shall reign over you: he will take your sons, and appoint them as his servants, for his chariots, and to be his horsemen; and they will run before his chariots.

He will appoint them to him for captains of thousands, and captains of fifties; and he will assign some to plow his ground, and to reap his harvest, and to make his instruments of war, and the instruments of his chariots.
He will take your daughters to be perfumers, to be cooks, and to be bakers.
He will take your fields, your vineyards, and your olive groves, even their best, and give them to his servants.
He will take one tenth of your seed, and of your vineyards, and give it to his officers, and to his servants.
He will take your male servants, your female servants, your best young men, and your donkeys, and assign them to his own work.
He will take one tenth of your flocks; and you will be his servants.
You will cry out in that day because of your king whom you will have chosen for yourselves; and Yahweh will not answer you in that day.”
But the people refused to listen to the voice of Samuel; and they said, “No; but we will have a king over us,
that we also may be like all the nations, and that our king may judge us, and go out before us, and fight our battles.”
Samuel heard all the words of the people, and he rehearsed them in the ears of Yahweh.
Yahweh said to Samuel, “Listen to their voice, and make them a king.”
Samuel said to the men of Israel, “Everyone go to your own city.”
When you have come to the land which Yahweh your God gives you, and possess it and dwell in it, and say, “I will set a king over me, like all the nations that are around me,”

you shall surely set him whom Yahweh your God chooses as king over yourselves. You shall set as king over you one from among your brothers. You may not put a foreigner over you, who is not your brother.
Only he shall not multiply horses to himself, nor cause the people to return to Egypt, to the end that he may multiply horses; because Yahweh has said to you, “You shall not go back that way again.”
He shall not multiply wives to himself, that his heart not turn away. He shall not greatly multiply to himself silver and gold.
It shall be, when he sits on the throne of his kingdom, that he shall write himself a copy of this law in a book, out of that which is before the Levitical priests.
It shall be with him, and he shall read from it all the days of his life, that he may learn to fear Yahweh his God, to keep all the words of this law and these statutes, to do them;

that his heart not be lifted up above his brothers, and that he not turn away from the commandment to the right hand, or to the left, to the end that he may prolong his days in his kingdom, he and his children, in the middle of Israel.

Yahweh said to Samuel, “How long will you mourn for Saul, since I have rejected him from being king over Israel? Fill your horn with oil, and go. I will send you to Jesse the Bethlehemite; for I have provided a king for myself among his sons.”
Samuel said, “How can I go? If Saul hears it, he will kill me.”
Yahweh said, “Take a heifer with you, and say, I have come to sacrifice to Yahweh.
Call Jesse to the sacrifice, and I will show you what you shall do. You shall anoint to me him whom I name to you.”
Samuel did that which Yahweh spoke, and came to Bethlehem. The elders of the city came to meet him trembling, and said, “Do you come peaceably?”
He said, “Peaceably; I have come to sacrifice to Yahweh. Sanctify yourselves, and come with me to the sacrifice.” He sanctified Jesse and his sons, and called them to the sacrifice.
When they had come, he looked at Eliab, and said, “Surely Yahweh’s anointed is before him.”

But Yahweh said to Samuel, “Don’t look on his face, or on the height of his stature, because I have rejected him; for I don’t see as man sees. For man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.”
Then Jesse called Abinadab, and made him pass before Samuel. He said, “Yahweh has not chosen this one, either.”
Then Jesse made Shammah to pass by. He said, “Yahweh has not chosen this one, either.”
Jesse made seven of his sons to pass before Samuel. Samuel said to Jesse, “Yahweh has not chosen these.”
Samuel said to Jesse, “Are all your children here?”
He said, “There remains yet the youngest. Behold, he is keeping the sheep.”
Samuel said to Jesse, “Send and get him, for we will not sit down until he comes here.”
He sent, and brought him in. Now he was ruddy, with a handsome face and good appearance. Yahweh said, “Arise! Anoint him, for this is he.”
Then Samuel took the horn of oil, and anointed him in the middle of his brothers. Then Yahweh’s Spirit came mightily on David from that day forward. So Samuel rose up and went to Ramah.

parts.title: Give us a king
parts.context: About 1050 BC. Samuel has led Israel for many years as judge and prophet. He is old, and his sons, whom he has made judges, are corrupt. The elders come to him at his home town, Ramah.

commentary.on: His sons didn’t walk in his ways, but turned away after dishonest gain, took bribes, and perverted justice.
commentary.text: The crisis starts with corrupt judges. The people's complaint is real: power without justice. But notice their answer: not better judges, but more power in one man's hands.

commentary.on: Now make us a king to judge us like all the nations.
commentary.text: 'Like all the nations' is the key phrase. Israel was meant to be different, a people ruled directly by God through his law. Now it wants to be normal.

commentary.on: for they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me as the king over them.
commentary.text: God takes it personally. In Israel's faith, God was the true king. Asking for a human king 'like all the nations' meant trusting a man with the power to save them instead of God.

commentary.on: This will be the way of the king who shall reign over you: he will take your sons
commentary.text: Samuel's warning is one of the sharpest descriptions of state power in ancient literature. Read it as a list: he will take your sons, your daughters, your fields, a tenth of your grain, your servants, your flocks. Six times in the Hebrew: 'he will take'.

commentary.on: He will take one tenth of your flocks; and you will be his servants.
commentary.text: The end of the list is the sting. The people freed from slavery in Egypt will become 'servants', the same Hebrew word as 'slaves', to their own king. They are walking back into Pharaoh's house by the front door.

commentary.on: that we also may be like all the nations, and that our king may judge us, and go out before us, and fight our battles.
commentary.text: The people want security: someone to judge and someone to fight. It is a very human wish, and every age has felt it when things fall apart.

commentary.on: Yahweh said to Samuel, “Listen to their voice, and make them a king.”
commentary.text: God gives them what they ask for. The Bible does not forbid kings; it lets the people learn what power does. The rest of the story is that lesson.

parts.title: The law of the king
parts.context: Deuteronomy, the fifth book of the Torah, is presented as Moses' last speeches before Israel enters the land. Here Moses anticipates the day when Israel will want a king, and lays down rules for him. Scholars debate when this law was written; many think it reached its final form in the 600s BC.

commentary.on: you shall surely set him whom Yahweh your God chooses as king over yourselves.
commentary.text: The king is chosen by God, not seized by force and not born to the job by right. His authority is borrowed.

commentary.on: Only he shall not multiply horses to himself
commentary.text: Horses meant chariots: military power. Wives meant foreign alliances and a royal harem. Silver and gold meant wealth. Each is limited. No other law code of the ancient Near East known to us limits the king in this way; in Egypt and Babylon the king made the law.

commentary.on: he shall write himself a copy of this law in a book
commentary.text: The king must copy out the law by hand and read it 'all the days of his life'. He is not above the law; he is its first student.

commentary.on: that his heart not be lifted up above his brothers
commentary.text: The king is still a 'brother' to his people, not a god. This one phrase contains a whole theory of government: rulers are fellow citizens under the same law. Later readers in the West, from medieval lawyers to the English Puritans, quoted it against kings who claimed to be above the law.

parts.title: The youngest son
parts.context: Saul became the first king, but he disobeyed God and lost his favour. Now God sends Samuel secretly to Bethlehem, to the family of a man called Jesse, to anoint a new king while Saul is still on the throne.

commentary.on: Fill your horn with oil, and go.
commentary.text: Kings were 'anointed': oil was poured on their heads as a sign that God had chosen them. The Hebrew for 'anointed one' is mashiach, Messiah; in Greek it is christos, Christ. Every time you hear 'Christ', you are hearing this ceremony.

commentary.on: For man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.
commentary.text: Saul had been chosen partly because he was tall and handsome (1 Samuel 9:2). Now God refuses to judge by height. It is one of the most quoted lines in the Bible.

commentary.on: There remains yet the youngest. Behold, he is keeping the sheep.
commentary.text: Again and again in the Bible God chooses the younger son: Abel, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, now David. And the shepherd: the king of Israel is to be a shepherd of his people, not their owner.

commentary.on: Then Yahweh’s Spirit came mightily on David from that day forward.
commentary.text: David is anointed in secret, years before he becomes king. He will spend those years as Saul's servant, then as a fugitive. Power in this story is a gift and a trust, not a prize.

paras: Now the corruptions attending each of these governments are these; a kingdom may degenerate into a tyranny, an aristocracy into an oligarchy, and a state into a democracy. Now a tyranny is a monarchy where the good of one man only is the object of government, an oligarchy considers only the rich, and a democracy only the poor; but neither of them have a common good in view.

A kingdom, as we have said, partakes much of the nature of an aristocracy, and is bestowed according to worth, as either virtue, family, beneficent actions, or these joined with power; for those who have been benefactors to cities and states, or have it in their powers to be so, have acquired this honour, and those who have prevented a people from falling into slavery by war, as Codrus, or those who have freed them from it, as Cyrus, or the founders of cities, or settlers of colonies, as the kings of Sparta, Macedon, and Molossus. A king desires to be the guardian of his people, that those who have property may be secure in the possession of it, and that the people in general meet with no injury; but a tyrant, as has been often said, has no regard to the common good, except for his own advantage; his only object is pleasure, but a king's is virtue: what a tyrant therefore is ambitious of engrossing is wealth, but a king rather honour. The guards too of a king are citizens, a tyrant's foreigners.

parts.author: Aristotle
parts.title: For the common good, or his own?
parts.context: Aristotle (384–322 BC) was a student of Plato and the tutor of Alexander the Great. His Politics, written in Athens around 330 BC, sorts governments into good forms and their corrupt versions. This is William Ellis's English translation of 1776; 'a state' in the first paragraph is Ellis's word for what we would call a constitutional government. The cut is marked '…'.
parts.plain: Aristotle says: every good form of government can go bad. A kingdom goes bad when it becomes a tyranny: rule by one man for his own good, not the common good. A true king is chosen for his virtue or his service, and he guards his people and their property. A tyrant cares only for his own pleasure and wealth. You can tell them apart by their guards: a king is protected by his own citizens, a tyrant by foreign mercenaries.

commentary.on: a kingdom may degenerate into a tyranny
commentary.text: For Aristotle, as for Samuel, the danger is built in: one-man rule easily turns bad. The difference is the remedy. Aristotle relies on the ruler's virtue and the right constitution. Israel added something else: a law above the king, and prophets to say so.

commentary.on: a tyranny is a monarchy where the good of one man only is the object of government
commentary.text: This is Aristotle's test: whose good does the ruler serve? Samuel's warning describes the same thing from below: 'he will take'.

commentary.on: A king desires to be the guardian of his people, that those who have property may be secure in the possession of it
commentary.text: Remember this line when you read about Naboth's vineyard in the next session, still to come: the king who wants a poor man's land is exactly what Aristotle calls a tyrant.

commentary.on: The guards too of a king are citizens, a tyrant's foreigners.
commentary.text: A memorable detail: a tyrant cannot trust his own people. Aristotle and the Bible agree that a ruler who must be protected from his people has already betrayed them.

compare.author: Aristotle
compare.why: Aristotle studied the constitutions of more than a hundred Greek cities. Read how he tells a king from a tyrant: the same question Samuel's warning raises.
compare.title: A king or a tyrant?

paras: Israel's elders had good reasons. Samuel's sons were corrupt; the tribes were divided; the Philistines, a powerful people on the coast with iron weapons, were pressing in. They wanted order, justice and someone to fight their battles. Every society in crisis feels the same pull towards a strong ruler.

The Bible takes the wish seriously and still calls it a rejection of God. Its point is not that order is bad, but that the people looked for salvation in power itself. Samuel's warning lists what that power costs: your children, your land, your harvest, your freedom. Whoever holds power will be tempted to take.
sections.key: Israel wanted a king for real reasons: corruption, division and war. The Bible's warning is that power, once given, takes.

paras: In Egypt the pharaoh was a god. In Babylon, Hammurabi received his laws from the sun god and then issued them himself; the king stood at the top of the law. Deuteronomy 17 turns this upside down: Israel's king must copy out the law and obey it, must not hoard horses, wives or gold, and must not think himself above his 'brothers'.

The Jewish scholar Joshua Berman has argued that this is one of the first attempts in history to limit a ruler by law. Its echoes run through Western history: Magna Carta (1215) put the English king under the law; the Scottish minister Samuel Rutherford's Lex, Rex (1644), 'the law is king', quoted Deuteronomy 17 against Charles I; and Thomas Paine's Common Sense (1776), the pamphlet that pushed America towards independence, used 1 Samuel 8 to argue that monarchy itself was a mistake.
sections.key: Unlike Egypt and Babylon, Israel put its king under the law. Magna Carta, Rutherford's Lex, Rex and Paine's Common Sense all drew on these chapters.

paras: From the start, Israel's kings had a prophet at their side who was not their servant. Samuel anoints Saul and later rebukes him; he anoints David; Nathan will confront David; Elijah will confront Ahab. The prophet speaks for God, and God is above the king.

Historians sometimes call this an early form of the separation of powers. It is not a constitution in the modern sense: the prophets had no army and often paid for their words with exile or death. But it established a principle the West never quite forgot: there is a voice that can say to the most powerful person in the land, 'you are wrong'.
sections.key: Israel's kings had prophets beside them who answered to God, not the king: an early form of the idea that power must be checked.

paras: The ceremony in 1 Samuel 16 gave the West one of its most important words. An anointed king was the 'Lord's anointed': in Hebrew mashiach, in Greek christos. After the kingdom fell, Israel's prophets promised a future anointed king from David's line who would reign with justice. That hope is where the words Messiah and Christ come from.

Anointing is still part of the British coronation. At the coronation of Charles III in 2023, as at every coronation since 1727, the choir sang Handel's 'Zadok the Priest', whose words come from the anointing of Solomon in 1 Kings 1. The king was anointed behind a screen, the most sacred moment of the service.
sections.key: 'Anointed' is mashiach in Hebrew and christos in Greek: Messiah and Christ. British monarchs are still anointed, to Handel's 'Zadok the Priest'.

paras: For a time in the 1980s and early 1990s, some scholars argued that David was a legend, like King Arthur. Then, in 1993 and 1994, fragments of a stone inscription were found at Tel Dan in northern Israel. Written in Aramaic in the 800s BC by a king of Damascus, it boasts of killing a 'king of the house of David'. Most scholars now accept that David was a real founder of a dynasty.

What remains debated is the size and splendour of his kingdom. The Bible describes an empire; some archaeologists find little building in Jerusalem around 1000 BC and think David ruled a modest hill-country chiefdom. Others point to the fortified town of Khirbet Qeiyafa, dated to about 1000 BC, and to large stone structures in Jerusalem, as signs of a real kingdom. Both sides agree the evidence is limited, and each new excavation shifts the debate.
sections.key: The Tel Dan inscription (1993–94) mentions the 'house of David'; most scholars accept David existed. How large his kingdom was is still debated.

refs: Aristotle, Politics III.7 (1279b) and V.10 (1310b–1311a), tr. William Ellis (1776).
Joshua Berman, Created Equal: How the Bible Broke with Ancient Political Thought (2008); Samuel Rutherford, Lex, Rex (1644); Thomas Paine, Common Sense (1776).

The Tel Dan stele: A. Biran and J. Naveh, Israel Exploration Journal 43 (1993) and 45 (1995). Khirbet Qeiyafa: Y. Garfinkel and others, excavations 2007–2013. Israel Finkelstein and Neil Asher Silberman, David and Solomon (2006).
Talmud, Bava Batra 14b–15a (authorship); Sanhedrin 20b (the debate on kingship); Don Isaac Abravanel, commentary on Deuteronomy 17 and 1 Samuel 8.

debate.question: Was asking for a king a sin?

positions.name: Yes: God alone was king
positions.who: Gideon (Judges 8:23); Rabbi Nehorai in the Talmud; Don Isaac Abravanel (1437–1508); Thomas Paine
positions.view: God was Israel's king. Asking for a human one 'like all the nations' was a lack of trust, and monarchy itself breeds tyranny. Abravanel, a Jewish statesman who served kings, argued that Israel never needed one.
positions.evidence: 'They have rejected me as the king over them' (8:7); Gideon: 'Yahweh shall rule over you'; the long list of bad kings that follows.

positions.name: No: kingship was planned, under conditions
positions.who: Rabbi Judah in the Talmud (Sanhedrin 20b); Maimonides; most Christian readers
positions.view: God had already promised Abraham that 'kings will come out of you' (Genesis 17:6) and given a law for kings in Deuteronomy 17. The sin was the people's motive, to be 'like all the nations', not kingship itself.
positions.evidence: Deuteronomy 17 assumes a king; God chooses David 'a man after his own heart' (1 Samuel 13:14); the Messiah will be a king from David's line.

positions.name: Both: a concession that God uses
positions.who: Many modern scholars and theologians
positions.view: The books of Samuel deliberately keep both views side by side. Kingship is a concession to human weakness, like divorce in Jesus's teaching, which God nonetheless uses for his purposes.
positions.evidence: Chapters 8 and 12 are against the king; chapters 9 and 10 tell of God choosing Saul; the text preserves the tension.

debate.agree: All agree that the king must be under God's law, and that the people looked to power for a safety it could not give.

look.why: Andrea del Castagno painted the young David, the shepherd Samuel anointed, on a leather parade shield in Florence around 1450. The city saw itself in David: a small republic standing up to giants.
points: The painting is shaped like a shield, wider at the top and narrowing towards the base.
A young man with curling brown hair, David, stands astride a severed head at his feet.
He holds the end of a long red sling, weighted by a stone, swinging behind him.
A stone is embedded in the forehead of the head on the ground.
Behind him are grey boulders, a winding river and low trees, under a blue sky with white clouds.

music.why: Handel's 'Zadok the Priest' sets the words of Solomon's anointing as king (1 Kings 1). It has been sung at every British coronation since 1727.

think.why: Aristotle and Samuel ask the same question about power from two traditions. See how Athens and Jerusalem together shaped the West.

learn.why: God's answer to judging by appearances: one of the most quoted lines in the Bible.

check.q: What problem led Israel's elders to ask for a king?
options: Samuel had become a tyrant
The Egyptians had invaded
God had told them to choose one
Samuel's sons, the judges, were corrupt, and the people wanted to be 'like all the nations'
check.why: Corrupt judges took bribes; the people's answer was a king like other nations had.

check.q: What is the main point of Samuel's warning in 1 Samuel 8?
options: That kings must be descended from Moses
That kings are always chosen by God
That a king will take: their children, land, harvest and freedom, until they are his servants
That the Philistines would defeat them
check.why: 'He will take' is repeated; the freed slaves would become servants of their own king.

check.q: What makes the law of the king in Deuteronomy 17 unusual in the ancient world?
options: It lets the king change the law
It forbids kings altogether
It makes the king a god
It puts the king under the law: he must copy it, read it daily and not exalt himself above his brothers
check.why: In Egypt and Babylon the king was the source of law; in Israel he was its first student.

check.q: Why does God reject David's tall eldest brother Eliab?
options: Because he was too young
Because God looks at the heart, not the outward appearance
Because he was not from Bethlehem
Because Saul had already chosen him
check.why: 'Man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart' (16:7).

check.q: The Hebrew mashiach and the Greek christos both mean:
options: Anointed one
Shepherd
King of kings
Son of David
check.why: Kings were anointed with oil; 'Messiah' and 'Christ' both mean 'the anointed one'.

check.q: According to Aristotle, how can you tell a king from a tyrant?
options: A tyrant is always elected
A king rules for the common good and is guarded by citizens; a tyrant rules for himself and is guarded by foreigners
A king is always descended from a king
There is no real difference
check.why: Whose good the ruler serves is Aristotle's test, and the guards give it away.

tutorial.question: Is the Bible for or against kings?
tutorial.approach: Set out the case against (1 Samuel 8, Judges 8:23) and the case for (Deuteronomy 17, the choice of David). Then ask what the conditions are: what must a king be and do? Compare with Aristotle's king and tyrant. End with what this tradition gave Western ideas about limited government.
strong: Explains why the people asked for a king and why Samuel objected.
Uses the 'he will take' list as a description of state power.
Explains how Deuteronomy 17 limits the king, and why that was unusual.
Compares Israel's answer with Aristotle's king and tyrant.
Mentions at least one later use: Magna Carta, Lex, Rex or Common Sense.
Notes that the Bible keeps both views in tension.

reading.why: A brilliant literary translation of 1 and 2 Samuel, with notes on how the story is told.

reading.author: Joshua Berman

reading.why: How the Torah's politics differed from Egypt's and Babylon's.

reading.why: The sceptical archaeological case for a smaller kingdom, to read alongside its critics.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: think of one place where you have power over someone (at work, at home, as a customer). Use it once this week deliberately for their good rather than your own convenience.
sessions.reflect: Where do you look for security: to a strong leader, to money, to God? What would it cost you?
takeaways: Israel asked for a king 'like all the nations'; Samuel warned that a king would take their children, land and freedom.
Deuteronomy 17 put the king under God's law: he must copy and obey it and not exalt himself above his brothers.
God chose David, the youngest shepherd, looking at the heart; 'anointed' gives us the words Messiah and Christ.

sessions.title: You are the man
sessions.line: A king takes another man's wife and his life; a prophet tells him a story. Another king takes a vineyard, and Elijah meets him in it.
sessions.plain: David, now king, sees a woman bathing, takes her, and when she becomes pregnant he arranges for her husband to be killed in battle. No one dares to say anything, until the prophet Nathan tells him a story about a rich man who stole a poor man's only lamb. David is furious with the rich man, and Nathan says: 'You are the man.' David repents. A century later King Ahab wants his neighbour's vineyard; his wife Jezebel has the owner killed with false witnesses, and the prophet Elijah meets Ahab in the stolen vineyard. This session asks what power does when no one is watching, and who can hold it to account.
sessions.why: Session 1 showed power given, under God's law, with prophets watching. Now we see what happens when kings forget it, and what the prophets did about it.
answers: What did David do to Bathsheba and Uriah?
How did Nathan confront the king, and why did it work?
Why is this story so unusual for an ancient kingdom?
What happened in Naboth's vineyard, and who was Elijah?
Does power corrupt everyone?
sessions.finding: Even Israel's greatest king abused his power in secret; but in Israel even a king could be accused, and the prophets spoke God's law to power.

paras: Session 1 ended with David anointed in secret. Years followed in which he fought Goliath, served and then fled from the jealous King Saul, and finally became king, first of Judah and then of all Israel, around 1010 BC. He captured Jerusalem and made it his capital, brought the ark of the covenant there, and God promised him through the prophet Nathan that his 'house', his dynasty, would last for ever (2 Samuel 7:16).

David is the hero of the Hebrew Bible: a warrior, a poet to whom many psalms are credited, 'a man after his own heart', as God calls him (1 Samuel 13:14). That is what makes the story you are about to read so shocking. The Bible tells its greatest king's worst crime in full.
background.key: David became king around 1010 BC, made Jerusalem his capital and was promised a lasting dynasty. The Bible still tells his worst crime in full.

paras: Nathan was a prophet at David's court. He brought God's promise of a dynasty, and he brought God's judgement on David's sin. Later he helped make sure Solomon became king. He is the model of the court prophet who will not flatter.

Elijah lived about a century later, in the northern kingdom of Israel. He was a wild figure from Tishbe, east of the Jordan, who challenged King Ahab and Queen Jezebel for leading Israel to worship Baal, the Canaanite storm god. Jews still set a place for Elijah at the Passover meal, and the New Testament presents John the Baptist as coming 'in the spirit and power of Elijah' (Luke 1:17).
background.key: Nathan was David's court prophet, who would not flatter. Elijah challenged Ahab and Jezebel in the north a century later; Jews still set a place for him at Passover.

background.h: Ahab and Jezebel: what outside sources say
paras: Ahab ruled the northern kingdom from about 874 to 853 BC. Here outside evidence is unusually strong. An Assyrian inscription, the Kurkh Monolith, records that 'Ahab the Israelite' brought 2,000 chariots and 10,000 soldiers to the battle of Qarqar in 853 BC against the Assyrian king Shalmaneser III: one of the largest chariot forces on the field. The Mesha Stele, found in Jordan in 1868, names Ahab's father Omri as a king of Israel who oppressed Moab.
So Ahab was a powerful, internationally important king. The Bible is not interested in that. It remembers him for one stolen vineyard. That choice is itself a judgement about what matters in a ruler.
background.key: Assyrian and Moabite inscriptions confirm Ahab and his father Omri as powerful kings; the Bible remembers Ahab for a stolen vineyard.

paras: The main reading has three parts: David's crime (2 Samuel 11), Nathan's parable (2 Samuel 12), and Naboth's vineyard (1 Kings 21).

The comparison is from Plato's Republic, the most famous work of Greek philosophy. A character tells the story of a shepherd who finds a ring that makes him invisible, and asks: if you could never be caught, would you still be just? David's crime is that question lived out.
background.key: David's crime, Nathan's parable, Naboth's vineyard; then Plato's ring of invisibility.

before: Where should David have been, according to the first verse?
How does Uriah behave, compared with the king?
In both stories, who knows what the king has done, and who speaks up?
sessions.readWhy: Two kings who took what was not theirs, and two prophets who told them so.

paras: At the return of the year, at the time when kings go out, David sent Joab, and his servants with him, and all Israel; and they destroyed the children of Ammon, and besieged Rabbah. But David stayed at Jerusalem.
At evening, David arose from his bed and walked on the roof of the king’s house. From the roof, he saw a woman bathing, and the woman was very beautiful to look at.
David sent and inquired after the woman. One said, “Isn’t this Bathsheba, the daughter of Eliam, Uriah the Hittite’s wife?”
David sent messengers, and took her; and she came in to him, and he lay with her (for she was purified from her uncleanness); and she returned to her house.
The woman conceived; and she sent and told David, and said, “I am with child.”
David sent to Joab, “Send me Uriah the Hittite.” Joab sent Uriah to David.
When Uriah had come to him, David asked him how Joab did, and how the people fared, and how the war prospered.
David said to Uriah, “Go down to your house and wash your feet.” Uriah departed out of the king’s house, and a gift from the king was sent after him.
But Uriah slept at the door of the king’s house with all the servants of his lord, and didn’t go down to his house.
When they had told David, saying, “Uriah didn’t go down to his house,” David said to Uriah, “Haven’t you come from a journey? Why didn’t you go down to your house?”

Uriah said to David, “The ark, Israel, and Judah, are staying in tents; and my lord Joab and the servants of my lord, are encamped in the open field. Shall I then go into my house to eat and to drink, and to lie with my wife? As you live, and as your soul lives, I will not do this thing!”
David said to Uriah, “Stay here today also, and tomorrow I will let you depart.” So Uriah stayed in Jerusalem that day, and the next day.
When David had called him, he ate and drank before him; and he made him drunk. At evening, he went out to lie on his bed with the servants of his lord, but didn’t go down to his house.
In the morning, David wrote a letter to Joab, and sent it by the hand of Uriah.
He wrote in the letter, saying, “Send Uriah to the forefront of the hottest battle, and retreat from him, that he may be struck, and die.”
When Joab kept watch on the city, he assigned Uriah to the place where he knew that valiant men were.
The men of the city went out, and fought with Joab. Some of the people fell, even of David’s servants; and Uriah the Hittite died also.
When Uriah’s wife heard that Uriah her husband was dead, she mourned for her husband.
When the mourning was past, David sent and took her home to his house, and she became his wife, and bore him a son. But the thing that David had done displeased Yahweh.
Yahweh sent Nathan to David. He came to him, and said to him, “There were two men in one city; the one rich, and the other poor.
The rich man had very many flocks and herds,

but the poor man had nothing, except one little ewe lamb, which he had bought and raised. It grew up together with him, and with his children. It ate of his own food, drank of his own cup, and lay in his bosom, and was like a daughter to him.

A traveler came to the rich man, and he spared to take of his own flock and of his own herd, to prepare for the wayfaring man who had come to him, but took the poor man’s lamb, and prepared it for the man who had come to him.”
David’s anger burned hot against the man, and he said to Nathan, “As Yahweh lives, the man who has done this deserves to die!
He must restore the lamb fourfold, because he did this thing, and because he had no pity!”
Nathan said to David, “You are the man. This is what Yahweh, the God of Israel, says: ‘I anointed you king over Israel, and I delivered you out of the hand of Saul.

I gave you your master’s house, and your master’s wives into your bosom, and gave you the house of Israel and of Judah; and if that would have been too little, I would have added to you many more such things.

Why have you despised Yahweh’s word, to do that which is evil in his sight? You have struck Uriah the Hittite with the sword, and have taken his wife to be your wife, and have slain him with the sword of the children of Ammon.
Now therefore the sword will never depart from your house, because you have despised me, and have taken Uriah the Hittite’s wife to be your wife.’

“This is what Yahweh says: ‘Behold, I will raise up evil against you out of your own house; and I will take your wives before your eyes, and give them to your neighbor, and he will lie with your wives in the sight of this sun.
For you did this secretly, but I will do this thing before all Israel, and before the sun.’ ”
David said to Nathan, “I have sinned against Yahweh.”
Nathan said to David, “Yahweh also has put away your sin. You will not die.
However, because by this deed you have given great occasion to Yahweh’s enemies to blaspheme, the child also who is born to you will surely die.”
After these things, Naboth the Jezreelite had a vineyard, which was in Jezreel, next to the palace of Ahab king of Samaria.

Ahab spoke to Naboth, saying, “Give me your vineyard, that I may have it for a garden of herbs, because it is near my house; and I will give you for it a better vineyard than it. Or, if it seems good to you, I will give you its worth in money.”
Naboth said to Ahab, “May Yahweh forbid me, that I should give the inheritance of my fathers to you!”

Ahab came into his house sullen and angry because of the word which Naboth the Jezreelite had spoken to him; for he had said, “I will not give you the inheritance of my fathers.” He laid himself down on his bed, and turned away his face, and would eat no bread.
But Jezebel his wife came to him, and said to him, “Why is your spirit so sad, that you eat no bread?”

He said to her, “Because I spoke to Naboth the Jezreelite, and said to him, ‘Give me your vineyard for money; or else, if it pleases you, I will give you another vineyard for it.’ He answered, ‘I will not give you my vineyard.’ ”
Jezebel his wife said to him, “Do you now govern the kingdom of Israel? Arise, and eat bread, and let your heart be merry. I will give you the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite.”
So she wrote letters in Ahab’s name, and sealed them with his seal, and sent the letters to the elders and to the nobles who were in his city, who lived with Naboth.
She wrote in the letters, saying, “Proclaim a fast, and set Naboth on high among the people.
Set two men, wicked fellows, before him, and let them testify against him, saying, ‘You cursed God and the king!’ Then carry him out, and stone him to death.”
The men of his city, even the elders and the nobles who lived in his city, did as Jezebel had instructed them in the letters which she had written and sent to them.
They proclaimed a fast, and set Naboth on high among the people.

The two men, the wicked fellows, came in and sat before him. The wicked fellows testified against him, even against Naboth, in the presence of the people, saying, “Naboth cursed God and the king!” Then they carried him out of the city and stoned him to death with stones.
Then they sent to Jezebel, saying, “Naboth has been stoned, and is dead.”

When Jezebel heard that Naboth had been stoned, and was dead, Jezebel said to Ahab, “Arise, take possession of the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite, which he refused to give you for money; for Naboth is not alive, but dead.”
When Ahab heard that Naboth was dead, Ahab rose up to go down to the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite, to take possession of it.
Yahweh’s word came to Elijah the Tishbite, saying,
“Arise, go down to meet Ahab king of Israel, who dwells in Samaria. Behold, he is in the vineyard of Naboth, where he has gone down to take possession of it.

You shall speak to him, saying, ‘Yahweh says, “Have you killed and also taken possession?” ’ You shall speak to him, saying, ‘Yahweh says, “In the place where dogs licked the blood of Naboth, dogs will lick your blood, even yours.” ’ ”

parts.title: A king who stayed at home
parts.context: Around 1000 BC. Israel is at war with the Ammonites, east of the Jordan, and has besieged their capital, Rabbah (modern Amman). David is in Jerusalem.

commentary.on: At the return of the year, at the time when kings go out
commentary.text: The first sentence is already a judgement. Spring was the season for war, and kings led their armies. 'But David stayed at Jerusalem.' The king is not where he should be.

commentary.on: David sent and inquired after the woman.
commentary.text: Notice the verbs: David saw, sent, inquired, sent, took. They are the verbs of power. Samuel had warned, 'he will take'.

commentary.on: Isn’t this Bathsheba, the daughter of Eliam, Uriah the Hittite’s wife?
commentary.text: The servant's answer is a warning in itself: she has a father and a husband, and her husband is one of David's own soldiers. David knows exactly who she is.

commentary.on: The ark, Israel, and Judah, are staying in tents
commentary.text: Uriah, a foreigner (a Hittite), is more loyal to Israel's God and army than Israel's king. He will not sleep at home while his comrades are in the field. His integrity becomes his death warrant.

commentary.on: and sent it by the hand of Uriah.
commentary.text: The cruellest detail: Uriah carries his own death sentence to his commander.

commentary.on: But the thing that David had done displeased Yahweh.
commentary.text: Up to here God has not been mentioned. Everything has been done in secret, by a king who seems to have got away with it. Then this sentence: someone was watching.

parts.title: You are the man
parts.context: Some months later. The child has been born. No one at court has said a word. God sends the prophet Nathan to the king.

commentary.on: There were two men in one city; the one rich, and the other poor.
commentary.text: Nathan does not accuse David directly. He tells a story, and David, who as king was also chief judge, hears it as a legal case. It is the most famous parable in the Old Testament.

commentary.on: It ate of his own food, drank of his own cup, and lay in his bosom, and was like a daughter to him.
commentary.text: The lamb 'lay in his bosom': the same words used of a wife. Nathan's story makes David feel the poor man's loss before he sees himself in it.

commentary.on: As Yahweh lives, the man who has done this deserves to die!
commentary.text: David passes sentence on himself. His sense of justice is still alive; he has simply not applied it to himself. That is how power usually blinds.

commentary.on: You are the man.
commentary.text: Two words in Hebrew, atta ha'ish. A prophet with no army says to the most powerful man in the land: you. In most kingdoms of the ancient world, Nathan would have been killed.

commentary.on: You have struck Uriah the Hittite with the sword
commentary.text: God holds David guilty of the murder, though Ammonites did the killing. Arranging a death through others does not make a ruler innocent.

commentary.on: David said to Nathan, “I have sinned against Yahweh.”
commentary.text: The king makes no excuse. Jewish and Christian tradition both link Psalm 51, 'Have mercy on me, God', to this moment; its heading says so. David is forgiven, but the consequences remain, and the rest of his life is darkened by violence in his own family.

parts.title: Naboth's vineyard
parts.context: About 860 BC, in the northern kingdom of Israel. Ahab, the king, has a palace at Jezreel. Next to it is a vineyard belonging to a man named Naboth.

commentary.on: Give me your vineyard, that I may have it for a garden of herbs
commentary.text: Ahab offers a fair price. In most ancient kingdoms that would end the matter, or the king would simply take it. Notice what he wants it for: a vegetable garden.

commentary.on: May Yahweh forbid me, that I should give the inheritance of my fathers to you!
commentary.text: Naboth's land is not just property. In Israel's law the land belonged to God, who gave each family its share for ever: 'the land is mine' (Leviticus 25:23). Naboth will not sell his family's inheritance, even to the king.

commentary.on: Do you now govern the kingdom of Israel?
commentary.text: Jezebel was a princess from Sidon, in Phoenicia, where kings did as they pleased. She mocks Ahab for respecting a law that limits him. Two ideas of kingship collide.

commentary.on: So she wrote letters in Ahab’s name, and sealed them with his seal
commentary.text: The murder is done legally: a fast, a trial, two witnesses (the Torah's requirement), a charge of blasphemy. Injustice dressed in the forms of justice is the most dangerous kind.

commentary.on: Have you killed and also taken possession?
commentary.text: Elijah's question has two verbs, and the second is the point. Ahab did not throw a stone, but he took the vineyard. The prophet holds the king responsible for the injustice he profited from.

paras: Now that those who practise justice do so involuntarily and because they have not the power to be unjust will best appear if we imagine something of this kind: having given both to the just and the unjust power to do what they will, let us watch and see whither desire will lead them; then we shall discover in the very act the just and unjust man to be proceeding along the same road, following their interest, which all natures deem to be their good, and are only diverted into the path of justice by the force of law. The liberty which we are supposing may be most completely given to them in the form of such a power as is said to have been possessed by Gyges, the ancestor of Croesus the Lydian. According to the tradition, Gyges was a shepherd in the service of the king of Lydia; there was a great storm, and an earthquake made an opening in the earth at the place where he was feeding his flock. Amazed at the sight, he descended into the opening, where, among other marvels, he beheld a hollow brazen horse, having doors, at which he stooping and looking in saw a dead body of stature, as appeared to him, more than human, and having nothing on but a gold ring; this he took from the finger of the dead and reascended. Now the shepherds met together, according to custom, that they might send their monthly report about the flocks to the king; into their assembly he came having the ring on his finger, and as he was sitting among them he chanced to turn the collet of the ring inside his hand, when instantly he became invisible to the rest of the company and they began to speak of him as if he were no longer present. He was astonished at this, and again touching the ring he turned the collet outwards and reappeared;

he made several trials of the ring, and always with the same result--when he turned the collet inwards he became invisible, when outwards he reappeared. Whereupon he contrived to be chosen one of the messengers who were sent to the court; whereas soon as he arrived he seduced the queen, and with her help conspired against the king and slew him, and took the kingdom. Suppose now that there were two such magic rings, and the just put on one of them and the unjust the other; no man can be imagined to be of such an iron nature that he would stand fast in justice. No man would keep his hands off what was not his own when he could safely take what he liked out of the market, or go into houses and lie with any one at his pleasure, or kill or release from prison whom he would, and in all respects be like a God among men. Then the actions of the just would be as the actions of the unjust; they would both come at last to the same point. And this we may truly affirm to be a great proof that a man is just, not willingly or because he thinks that justice is any good to him individually, but of necessity, for wherever any one thinks that he can safely be unjust, there he is unjust. For all men believe in their hearts that injustice is far more profitable to the individual than justice, and he who argues as I have been supposing, will say that they are right. If you could imagine any one obtaining this power of becoming invisible, and never doing any wrong or touching what was another's, he would be thought by the lookers-on to be a most wretched idiot, although they would praise him to one another's faces, and keep up appearances with one another from a fear that they too might suffer injustice. Enough of this.

parts.author: Plato
parts.title: The ring of Gyges
parts.context: Plato (c. 428–348 BC) wrote the Republic in Athens around 375 BC, as a conversation led by his teacher Socrates. Here Plato's brother Glaucon, playing devil's advocate, tells an old Lydian legend to argue that people are only just because they fear being caught. Lydia was a kingdom in what is now western Turkey; 'collet' means the setting of the ring's stone. Translated by Benjamin Jowett (1871).
parts.plain: Glaucon says: imagine giving both a just man and an unjust man the power to do anything they like without consequences. Take the story of Gyges, a shepherd who found a gold ring that made him invisible. As soon as he discovered its power, he got himself sent to court, seduced the queen, killed the king and took the kingdom. Give the same ring to a just man, says Glaucon, and he would do the same. People are only just because they cannot get away with injustice.

commentary.on: he seduced the queen, and with her help conspired against the king and slew him, and took the kingdom
commentary.text: The parallel with David is striking: a shepherd who becomes king, a stolen wife, a murdered husband. Gyges had a magic ring; David had the power of a king. In both cases the crime is possible because no one can stop them.

commentary.on: wherever any one thinks that he can safely be unjust, there he is unjust.
commentary.text: This is Glaucon's challenge, and the rest of the Republic tries to answer it. Plato's Socrates argues that injustice destroys the soul of the one who does it, whether he is caught or not.

commentary.on: he would be thought by the lookers-on to be a most wretched idiot
commentary.text: A sharp observation: people praise justice in public and privately think the honest man a fool. The Bible's answer to the ring is not only that injustice harms you. It is that no one is invisible: 'the thing that David had done displeased Yahweh'.

compare.author: Plato
compare.why: Plato asks David's question in its purest form: if you could do anything without being seen, would you still be just?
compare.title: The ring of invisibility

paras: David's crime and Gyges' ring describe the same danger: power that no one can see or stop. David did everything 'secretly', as God says through Nathan (12:12). He used messengers, letters and his army commander. No one at court objected; they were all his servants.

Plato's answer, through Socrates, is that injustice damages the soul of the one who does it. The Bible's answer adds a witness: God sees, and God sends a prophet. Both agree on the danger. In 1887 the English historian Lord Acton put it in words that have become proverbial: 'Power tends to corrupt, and absolute power corrupts absolutely.'
sections.key: David and Gyges both act unseen. Plato says injustice harms the soul; the Bible adds that God sees and sends a prophet. Lord Acton: 'Power tends to corrupt.'

paras: Nathan's method is a lesson in itself. He does not lecture the king. He tells a story about a poor man and a lamb, and lets David's own sense of justice catch fire. Only then does he turn it round: 'You are the man.' Jesus would later teach the same way, in parables that make the hearer judge himself.

The courage is as remarkable as the skill. David had just arranged one murder to cover his tracks. Nathan had no army, no office that protected him, nothing but the conviction that the king was under God's law.
sections.key: Nathan tells a story that lets David condemn himself, then turns it on him: a method Jesus's parables would use. It took great courage.

paras: David's reply is three words in Hebrew: 'I have sinned against Yahweh.' Compare Saul, who when confronted by Samuel made excuses and blamed the people (1 Samuel 15:20–24). The Bible's judgement on its kings rests less on whether they sinned (they all did) than on whether they turned back.

Even Ahab, the worst of the northern kings, humbled himself after Elijah's words, and God noticed (1 Kings 21:27–29). Repentance did not erase the consequences: violence haunted David's family for the rest of his life. But it kept him within the covenant. Psalm 51, traditionally his prayer after Nathan's visit, became the great prayer of repentance for Jews and Christians alike, and is still sung in churches every Lent.
sections.key: David confesses without excuse; Saul made excuses. Repentance does not erase consequences, but it is what the Bible judges. Psalm 51 became the great prayer of repentance.

paras: Naboth's vineyard shows what a king under God's law could not do: take a citizen's land. In Israel, each family's land was an inheritance from God, not the king's to redistribute. Jezebel's world was different: Phoenician and Canaanite kings could take what they wanted. Her contempt, 'Do you now govern the kingdom of Israel?', is the voice of absolute power.

The story also shows how injustice works through institutions. The elders, the nobles, the judges and the witnesses all go along with the queen's letters. No one refuses. The only voice raised is Elijah's, after the fact. That is why the prophets kept saying that justice is everyone's business, not only the king's.
sections.key: In Israel, land was a family's inheritance from God, not the king's. Naboth's murder was done through the courts; only the prophet spoke.

sections.h: Speaking truth to power in the West
paras: Nathan and Elijah became models for the Christian West. In AD 390 the emperor Theodosius ordered a massacre at Thessalonica. Ambrose, bishop of Milan, refused him communion until he did public penance, and wrote to him citing David and Nathan. The most powerful man in the Roman world knelt in church.

The pattern recurs: Thomas Becket against Henry II, Thomas More against Henry VIII, Dietrich Bonhoeffer against Hitler, churches in communist Poland and East Germany. Not all were prophets, and churches have often flattered power instead. But the idea that a ruler can be told 'you are the man' by someone with no power at all comes straight from these chapters.
sections.key: Ambrose confronted the emperor Theodosius in 390, citing Nathan. From Becket to Bonhoeffer, the idea that power can be called to account comes from these chapters.

refs: 2 Samuel 7; 11–12; 1 Samuel 13:14; 15:20–24; 1 Kings 21; Leviticus 25:23; Psalm 51 (heading); Luke 1:17.
Plato, Republic II, 359c–360d, tr. Benjamin Jowett (1871).
The Kurkh Monolith of Shalmaneser III (British Museum); the Mesha Stele (Louvre), found at Dhiban in 1868.
Ambrose, Letter 51 to Theodosius (AD 390); Theodoret, Church History V.17.
