debate.question: Does power corrupt everyone?

positions.name: Yes: people are only just when watched
positions.who: Glaucon in Plato's Republic; Thomas Hobbes
positions.view: Give anyone the ring and they will use it. Justice is a bargain we make because we fear each other; take away the fear, and the bargain collapses.
positions.evidence: Gyges; David, the best of Israel's kings; Lord Acton's dictum; much of history.

positions.name: No: the just person stays just
positions.who: Plato's Socrates; Aristotle; the Stoics
positions.view: Injustice damages the soul of the one who does it. A truly just person would not use the ring, because they would be harming themselves.
positions.evidence: Socrates' life and death; the long argument of the Republic.

positions.name: Everyone is tempted, so power needs witnesses
positions.who: The biblical writers; James Madison and the American founders
positions.view: Even the best person can fall, as David did. So power must be limited by law and watched by others: prophets, courts, a free press. 'If men were angels, no government would be necessary' (Madison, Federalist 51).
positions.evidence: David's fall and repentance; Deuteronomy 17; Nathan and Elijah.

debate.agree: All agree that unseen, unchecked power is dangerous; they differ on whether the cure is character, law, or both.

look.why: Rubens painted another moment when David was stopped from abusing his power. Before he became king, David set out to kill a rich man, Nabal, who had insulted him. Nabal's wife Abigail met him on the road with food and talked him out of it (1 Samuel 25). Like Nathan, she stopped David with words.
points: A woman, Abigail, kneels in the middle of a crowd, in a white veil, slate-blue dress and pearls.
She points down to a basket of bread held by a man in the lower left corner.
David, in a breastplate with crimson cloth over his shoulders, bends towards her and cups her elbow.
Armed men and horses stand behind David on the right; women, men and a donkey with baskets of bread stand behind Abigail on the left.
Dark grey and amber clouds fill the sky above a wooded hill.

music.why: Allegri's 'Miserere', written for the Sistine Chapel in the 1630s, sets Psalm 51, traditionally David's prayer after Nathan said 'You are the man'.

think.why: Glaucon says people are only good when watched; the Bible says someone always is. Ask whether morality needs God.

learn.why: The heart of the prayer traditionally linked to David's repentance after Nathan's visit.

check.q: Why does the story of David and Bathsheba begin by saying it was 'the time when kings go out'?
options: To date it to spring
To explain why Uriah was in Jerusalem
To praise David's wisdom in staying safe
To show that David was not where a king should be: he had stayed at home while his army fought
check.why: 'But David stayed at Jerusalem': the first hint of a king who has stopped doing his duty.

check.q: Why did Nathan tell David a story instead of accusing him directly?
options: So that David, as judge, would condemn the injustice before seeing that it was his own
Because he was afraid to speak plainly
Because prophets were forbidden to accuse kings
To entertain the court
check.why: David passes sentence on the rich man, and so on himself: 'You are the man.'

check.q: How does God judge David's part in Uriah's death?
options: As Joab's fault alone
As an accident of war
As innocent, since Ammonites killed Uriah
As murder: 'You have struck Uriah the Hittite with the sword'
check.why: Arranging a death through others does not make a ruler innocent.

check.q: Why did Naboth refuse to sell his vineyard to the king, even at a fair price?
options: He wanted more money
It was his family's inheritance from God, which Israel's law said should not be sold away
He hated Ahab personally
Jezebel had forbidden it
check.why: 'The inheritance of my fathers': in Israel the land was God's, given to each family.

check.q: What makes Jezebel's plot especially dangerous, as the story tells it?
options: She murders Naboth through a fake legal process, with a fast, a trial and two witnesses
She acts openly
She asks Elijah's permission
She uses an army
check.why: Injustice dressed as justice: the elders and nobles all go along with it.

check.q: In Plato's Republic, what is Glaucon's point in telling the story of the ring of Gyges?
options: That kings should wear rings
That magic is real
That Socrates is wrong about the gods
That people are just only because they fear being caught; give them invisibility and they will do wrong
check.why: 'Wherever any one thinks that he can safely be unjust, there he is unjust.'

tutorial.question: Compare the stories of David and Uriah and of Ahab and Naboth. What do they show about power, and how are they answered?
tutorial.approach: Describe each crime and how it was carried out. Notice what each king took, and how secrecy or legal forms hid it. Then compare how each was confronted (Nathan, Elijah) and how each responded. Bring in Plato's ring of Gyges. End with the principle these stories gave the West.
strong: Describes both crimes precisely, with the verbs of taking.
Notices secrecy in David's case and false legal process in Ahab's.
Explains Nathan's method and the risk he took.
Explains why Naboth would not sell (the land as God's inheritance).
Compares Glaucon's challenge with the Bible's answer.
Notes David's repentance and its limits.

reading.author: Robert Alter
reading.title: The David Story
reading.why: Alter's notes on 2 Samuel 11–12 show how much the narrator says in few words.

reading.author: Walter Brueggemann
reading.title: The Prophetic Imagination
reading.why: A classic short book on the prophets as critics of royal power.

reading.author: Baruch Halpern
reading.title: David's Secret Demons
reading.why: A historian's sceptical portrait of David as a ruthless Iron Age ruler.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: is there something you have done that you would not want seen? Name it honestly to God, and, if it hurt someone, put it right.
sessions.reflect: If you had the ring of Gyges for a day, what would you be tempted to do? What does that tell you?
takeaways: David took Bathsheba and arranged Uriah's death in secret; the prophet Nathan exposed him with a parable: 'You are the man.'
Ahab and Jezebel took Naboth's vineyard through a fake trial; Elijah confronted the king in the stolen field.
Plato's ring of Gyges asks whether anyone stays just unseen; the Bible answers that no one is unseen, and power must be called to account.

sessions.title: Let justice roll on
sessions.line: A shepherd from the south walks into a rich kingdom's temple and says God hates its worship. Three prophets ask what God really wants.
sessions.plain: Around 760 BC the northern kingdom of Israel was rich and religious. Its temples were full and its festivals splendid. A shepherd called Amos came up from the south and told them that God hated their worship, because the same people who sang the hymns were selling the poor for a pair of sandals. Micah and Isaiah said the same in Judah. Their message: what God wants is not more religion but justice, mercy and humility. These words, especially 'let justice roll on like rivers', became the motto of the American civil rights movement. This session asks what religion is for, if it does not make people just.
sessions.why: Session 2 showed prophets confronting single kings for single crimes. Now the prophets go further: they accuse a whole society, its courts, its markets and even its worship. The question of this journey widens: what happens when not only a king but a whole people forgets justice?
answers: Who was Amos, and why was his message so shocking?
Did the prophets reject worship and sacrifice?
What does Micah 6:8 say God requires?
How does Hesiod's justice compare with the prophets'?
How did these words shape the civil rights movement?
sessions.finding: The prophets said that worship without justice is worthless to God; what he requires is to act justly, love mercy and walk humbly with him.

paras: After Solomon died, about 930 BC, the kingdom split. The north, called Israel, had ten tribes, the richer land and a series of royal families that often overthrew one another; Ahab, from session 2, was one of its kings. The south, called Judah, had Jerusalem, the Temple and David's descendants on the throne.

By about 760 BC both kingdoms were enjoying a rare time of peace and wealth. The great empires were weak for the moment. In the north King Jeroboam II had won back lost territory. The rich had a winter house and a summer house, and 'houses of ivory' (Amos 3:15), decorated with carved ivory; archaeologists digging at Samaria, the northern capital, in the 1930s found hundreds of pieces of exactly such ivory. But wealth was flowing upwards. Small farmers fell into debt, lost their land and were sold into slavery for what they owed.
background.key: Around 760 BC both kingdoms were rich and at peace; in the north, wealth flowed to the few while poor farmers lost their land and freedom.

background.h: Who were Amos, Micah and Isaiah?
paras: Amos was not a professional prophet. He came from Tekoa, a village in the hills south of Bethlehem, in Judah, and he said of himself: 'I was a herdsman, and a farmer of sycamore figs' (Amos 7:14). God sent him north, to Bethel, the royal temple of the northern kingdom. The priest there told him to go home (Amos 7:12–13).

Isaiah lived in Jerusalem from about 740 to 700 BC; he seems to have had access to the royal court and advised several kings. Micah, his younger contemporary, came from Moresheth, a country town south-west of Jerusalem, and spoke for the farmers whose land was being swallowed. These three, with Hosea, are the first prophets whose words were collected into books of their own. They are called the 'writing prophets'.
background.key: Amos was a herdsman from Judah sent to the north's royal temple; Isaiah a Jerusalem prophet close to the court; Micah a countryman. They are the first 'writing prophets'.

paras: The main reading gathers four short oracles, the prophets' word for a message from God: Amos's charge against Israel (Amos 2), Amos on worship (Amos 5), Micah's question about what God wants (Micah 6), and Isaiah on worship and justice (Isaiah 1). They were spoken within about forty years of one another.

The comparison is from Hesiod, a Greek farmer-poet who lived about the same time as Amos, around 700 BC. In his Works and Days he warns the 'princes' who take bribes that Justice, the daughter of Zeus, sees what they do. It is one of the closest things in Greek literature to a prophet.
background.key: Four oracles from Amos, Micah and Isaiah, all around 760–700 BC; then Hesiod, a Greek poet of the same time, on bribe-taking princes.

before: List the crimes Amos names in chapter 2. Who is being hurt?
What does God say he hates, and what does he want instead?
Micah asks a series of questions. How do they get bigger, and what is the answer?
sessions.readWhy: Four short oracles from three prophets: the charge, the rejection of worship without justice, and what God requires.

paras: Yahweh says:

and they lay themselves down beside every altar on clothes taken in pledge;
and in the house of their God they drink the wine of those who have been fined.

I hate, I despise your feasts,
and I can’t stand your solemn assemblies.

Take away from me the noise of your songs!
I will not listen to the music of your harps.

But let justice roll on like rivers,
and righteousness like a mighty stream.

How shall I come before Yahweh,
and bow myself before the exalted God?
Shall I come before him with burnt offerings,
with calves a year old?

Will Yahweh be pleased with thousands of rams?
With tens of thousands of rivers of oil?
Shall I give my firstborn for my disobedience?
The fruit of my body for the sin of my soul?

He has shown you, O man, what is good.
What does Yahweh require of you, but to act justly,
to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?

“What are the multitude of your sacrifices to me?”, says Yahweh.
“I have had enough of the burnt offerings of rams
and the fat of fed animals.
I don’t delight in the blood of bulls,
or of lambs,
or of male goats.

When you come to appear before me,
who has required this at your hand, to trample my courts?

Bring no more vain offerings.
Incense is an abomination to me.
New moons, Sabbaths, and convocations:
I can’t stand evil assemblies.

My soul hates your New Moons and your appointed feasts.
They are a burden to me.
I am weary of bearing them.

When you spread out your hands, I will hide my eyes from you.
Yes, when you make many prayers, I will not hear.
Your hands are full of blood.

Wash yourselves. Make yourself clean.
Put away the evil of your doings from before my eyes.
Cease to do evil.

Learn to do well.
Seek justice.
Relieve the oppressed.
Defend the fatherless.
Plead for the widow.”

parts.title: Sold for a pair of sandals
parts.context: Amos begins (1:3–2:5) by condemning Israel's neighbours, Damascus, Gaza, Tyre, Edom, Ammon, Moab and even Judah, for their crimes. His northern audience would have cheered. Then he turns on them.

commentary.on: For three transgressions of Israel, yes, for four
commentary.text: The same formula Amos used for the foreign nations. The listeners expected Israel to be spared, as God's people. Instead they get the longest charge of all.

commentary.on: because they have sold the righteous for silver, and the needy for a pair of sandals
commentary.text: People sold into slavery for small debts, perhaps the price of a pair of sandals. The law of Moses allowed debt-servitude but limited it (Exodus 21:2). Amos says the rich have turned it into a trade in human beings.

commentary.on: They trample on the dust of the earth on the head of the poor
commentary.text: A violent image: the rich grind the poor into the ground. Notice that all of Amos's charges are economic and legal, not ritual. He is not accusing them of forgetting the festivals.

commentary.on: they lay themselves down beside every altar on clothes taken in pledge
commentary.text: The law said that a poor man's cloak taken as a pledge for a loan must be returned by sunset, because it was his only blanket (Exodus 22:26–27). The rich were lying on those cloaks at the altar: worship and robbery in the same place.

parts.title: I hate your feasts
parts.context: The same prophet, later in the book. The northern kingdom's temples at Bethel and Gilgal are busy with festivals and sacrifices.

commentary.on: I hate, I despise your feasts
commentary.text: God speaks in the first person, and the language is as strong as Hebrew allows. These are the festivals commanded in the law. The problem is not the feasts but the people keeping them.

commentary.on: Take away from me the noise of your songs!
commentary.text: Their hymns are 'noise' to God. A sobering line for anyone who loves church music, as this app does: beautiful worship is no substitute for justice.

commentary.on: But let justice roll on like rivers, and righteousness like a mighty stream.
commentary.text: The climax. In the dry hills of Israel most streams vanished in summer; Amos asks for justice like a river that never dries up. Martin Luther King quoted this verse in his 'I have a dream' speech in 1963, in the older translation 'roll down like waters'.

parts.title: What does the Lord require?
parts.context: Micah imagines God bringing a lawsuit against his people (6:1–5). Here a worshipper, stung by the charge, asks what would satisfy God.

commentary.on: Shall I come before him with burnt offerings, with calves a year old?
commentary.text: The questions grow: a calf, then thousands of rams, then rivers of oil, then a child. The worshipper thinks God wants more and more costly religion.

commentary.on: Shall I give my firstborn for my disobedience?
commentary.text: The last question names child sacrifice, which some neighbouring peoples practised and which Israel's law forbade (Deuteronomy 12:31). It is the logical end of thinking you can buy God off.

commentary.on: He has shown you, O man, what is good.
commentary.text: The answer is not new: 'he has shown you'. God has already said what he wants, in the law and the covenant.

commentary.on: to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God
commentary.text: Many call this the summary of the whole Old Testament. Justice (mishpat): fair dealing, especially for the weak. Mercy (chesed): loyal, faithful love. Humility before God. The Talmud (Makkot 24a) says that the 613 commandments of the Torah were summed up by David in eleven, by Isaiah in six, and by Micah in three: these three.

parts.title: Your hands are full of blood
parts.context: The opening chapter of Isaiah, spoken in Jerusalem, probably in the late 700s BC. The Temple is the setting: crowds coming to sacrifice and pray.

commentary.on: I don’t delight in the blood of bulls
commentary.text: Isaiah, the most Temple-centred of the prophets, says it too. The prophets are not outsiders attacking religion; they are insiders saying what religion is for.

commentary.on: When you spread out your hands, I will hide my eyes from you.
commentary.text: Even prayer is refused. The reason follows at once: the hands raised in prayer are the hands that have done harm.

commentary.on: Your hands are full of blood.
commentary.text: Not literal murder, but the blood of the poor and powerless, drained by corrupt courts and unjust dealing.

commentary.on: Seek justice. Relieve the oppressed. Defend the fatherless. Plead for the widow.
commentary.text: Four short commands. The fatherless and the widow had no man to speak for them in court in a society where only men usually did. God asks his people to be their advocates.

paras: And now I will tell a fable for princes who themselves understand. Thus said the hawk to the nightingale with speckled neck, while he carried her high up among the clouds, gripped fast in his talons, and she, pierced by his crooked talons, cried pitifully. To her he spoke disdainfully: 'Miserable thing, why do you cry out? One far stronger than you now holds you fast, and you must go wherever I take you, songstress as you are. And if I please I will make my meal of you, or let you go. He is a fool who tries to withstand the stronger, for he does not get the mastery and suffers pain besides his shame.' So said the swiftly flying hawk, the long-winged bird.

But you, Perses, listen to right and do not foster violence; for violence is bad for a poor man. Even the prosperous cannot easily bear its burden, but is weighed down under it when he has fallen into delusion. The better path is to go by on the other side towards justice; for Justice beats Outrage when she comes at length to the end of the race. But only when he has suffered does the fool learn this. For Oath keeps pace with wrong judgements. There is a noise when Justice is being dragged in the way where those who devour bribes and give sentence with crooked judgements, take her. And she, wrapped in mist, follows to the city and haunts of the people, weeping, and bringing mischief to men, even to such as have driven her forth in that they did not deal straightly with her.

But they who give straight judgements to strangers and to the men of the land, and go not aside from what is just, their city flourishes, and the people prosper in it: Peace, the nurse of children, is abroad in their land, and all-seeing Zeus never decrees cruel war against them. Neither famine nor disaster ever haunt men who do true justice; but light-heartedly they tend the fields which are all their care. The earth bears them victual in plenty, and on the mountains the oak bears acorns upon the top and bees in the midst. Their woolly sheep are laden with fleeces; their women bear children like their parents. They flourish continually with good things, and do not travel on ships, for the grain-giving earth bears them fruit.

You princes, mark well this punishment you also; for the deathless gods are near among men and mark all those who oppress their fellows with crooked judgements, and reck not the anger of the gods. For upon the bounteous earth Zeus has thrice ten thousand spirits, watchers of mortal men, and these keep watch on judgements and deeds of wrong as they roam, clothed in mist, all over the earth. And there is virgin Justice, the daughter of Zeus, who is honoured and reverenced among the gods who dwell on Olympus, and whenever anyone hurts her with lying slander, she sits beside her father, Zeus the son of Cronos, and tells him of men's wicked heart, until the people pay for the mad folly of their princes who, evilly minded, pervert judgement and give sentence crookedly. Keep watch against this, you princes, and make straight your judgements, you who devour bribes; put crooked judgements altogether from your thoughts.

parts.author: Hesiod
parts.title: Justice, the daughter of Zeus
parts.context: Hesiod was a farmer in Boeotia, in central Greece, around 700 BC. Works and Days is a long poem addressed to his brother Perses, who, Hesiod says, cheated him of his share of their father's land by bribing the local 'princes', the nobles who acted as judges. Translated by Hugh G. Evelyn-White (1914). 'Reck not' means 'do not care about'.
parts.plain: Hesiod tells the judges a fable: a hawk carries off a nightingale and says, 'I am stronger than you; I will do as I like.' That is the law of the strong. But Hesiod tells Perses to choose justice instead. When judges take bribes, Justice is dragged through the city weeping. Where judges are fair to everyone, the city flourishes in peace and plenty. The gods have thousands of invisible watchers, and Justice herself, daughter of Zeus, tells her father about every crooked judgement, until the whole people pays for their rulers' crimes.

commentary.on: He is a fool who tries to withstand the stronger
commentary.text: The hawk states the philosophy of might makes right: the same one Jezebel lived by. Both Hesiod and the prophets were writing against it.

commentary.on: those who devour bribes and give sentence with crooked judgements
commentary.text: Hesiod and Amos accuse the same people: judges who take bribes. 'you who afflict the just, who take a bribe, and who turn away the needy in the courts' (Amos 5:12). Corruption in the courts was the injustice both men had seen with their own eyes.

commentary.on: they who give straight judgements to strangers and to the men of the land
commentary.text: Notice 'strangers': like the law of Moses, Hesiod says justice must be the same for foreigners and locals.

commentary.on: the deathless gods are near among men and mark all those who oppress their fellows with crooked judgements
commentary.text: The likeness to the prophets is striking: the powerful are watched. The difference is worth noticing too. Hesiod's Justice protects the city's prosperity; the prophets' God takes the side of the poor, even against his own people and his own Temple.

compare.author: Hesiod
compare.why: Hesiod, a Greek farmer-poet who lived about the same time as Amos, warns corrupt judges that Justice is watching. Read him beside the prophets.
compare.title: The hawk and the nightingale

sections.h: Religion that does not make people just
paras: The prophets' charge is easy to misread. They did not say that worship, sacrifice and festivals were wrong; those were commanded in the law, and Isaiah received his own call in the Temple (Isaiah 6). They said that worship by people who exploit the poor is worthless, even offensive, to God. In their eyes, justice is not an extra beside religion: it is part of worship.

That idea has been one of the most powerful in Western history, and one of the most uncomfortable. It means that a society's piety can be judged by how it treats its weakest members. Jesus quoted the prophet Hosea twice, 'I desire mercy, and not sacrifice' (Matthew 9:13; 12:7), and his parable of the sheep and the goats (Matthew 25) makes care for the hungry, the stranger and the prisoner the test of the last judgement.
sections.key: The prophets did not reject worship but said that worship by people who exploit the poor is worthless. Jesus took up the theme: 'I desire mercy, and not sacrifice.'

paras: Two Hebrew words run through these passages. Mishpat, 'justice', means fair judgement in the courts and fair dealing in the market, especially for those with no power. Tsedaqah, 'righteousness', means right relationships, living as the covenant requires. The prophets nearly always use them together, as Amos does.

Neither word means private virtue alone. Both are social. In Israel's law the land belonged to God, debts were to be cancelled every seventh year (Deuteronomy 15), and the widow, the orphan and the stranger were under God's special protection. When the prophets demanded justice, they were demanding that Israel keep its own covenant.
sections.key: Mishpat (justice) and tsedaqah (righteousness) are social words: fair courts, fair dealing and right relationships, as the covenant required.

paras: Hesiod and Amos lived within a few decades of each other, about 700 miles apart, and probably never heard of each other. Both were men of the land; both saw powerful men take bribes and the poor lose their farms; both said the powerful were watched by a higher justice. The parallel suggests something common in the human sense of justice.

The differences are as important. Hesiod's gods were themselves violent and unjust in the old myths he tells elsewhere (Theogony). Justice is one goddess among many, and Hesiod's chief argument is prudential: justice pays, injustice brings famine and war. The prophets' God is one, and he is just in his own nature. He does not merely reward the just city; he takes the side of the weak against his own people. Amos even says God's choice of Israel makes its guilt greater: 'I have only chosen you of all the families of the earth. Therefore I will punish you for all of your sins' (Amos 3:2).
sections.key: Hesiod and Amos saw the same corruption and both said the powerful were watched. But Hesiod argues that justice pays; the prophets' one just God sides with the weak even against his own people.

paras: The northern kingdom did not listen. Within forty years of Amos's preaching, the Assyrian empire had swept down from what is now northern Iraq. In 722 BC it captured Samaria and deported much of the population; the ten northern tribes vanished from history, the 'lost tribes' of later legend. Assyrian records of King Sargon II boast of carrying off about 27,000 people from Samaria.

The prophets' words were remembered in Judah, which survived for another century and a half. Their followers collected the oracles, and because events seemed to have proved them right, the books were kept and read. That is how the words of a herdsman from Tekoa came to us.
sections.key: Assyria destroyed the northern kingdom in 722 BC, deporting its people. Judah kept the prophets' words because events had proved them right.

paras: Martin Luther King quoted Amos 5:24 again and again: in his first speech of the Montgomery bus boycott in 1955, in his 'Letter from Birmingham Jail' in 1963, where he called Amos an 'extremist for justice', and in 'I have a dream' at the March on Washington the same year. Today the verse is carved on the Civil Rights Memorial in Montgomery, Alabama, designed by Maya Lin in 1989, with water flowing over the names of those who died in the movement.

Micah 6:8 has had a similar life. Jimmy Carter swore his oath as American president in 1977 on a Bible open at it, and it is one of the most quoted verses in the world. Abraham Joshua Heschel, the Jewish scholar who marched with King at Selma in 1965, argued in his book The Prophets (1962) that what most of us treat as a small, everyday injustice, the prophets treated as a catastrophe, because they felt the sufferings of ordinary people as God feels them.
sections.key: King quoted Amos 5:24 from Montgomery (1955) to 'I have a dream' (1963); it is carved on the Civil Rights Memorial. Heschel, who marched with King, explained the prophets' outrage.

refs: Hesiod, Works and Days 202–264, tr. Hugh G. Evelyn-White (1914).
Talmud, Makkot 24a (the commandments summed up). The Samaria ivories: J. W. Crowfoot and Grace M. Crowfoot, Early Ivories from Samaria (1938). Sargon II's annals on the capture of Samaria.
Martin Luther King Jr., Holt Street Baptist Church address (5 December 1955); 'Letter from Birmingham Jail' (16 April 1963); 'I Have a Dream' (28 August 1963).
Abraham Joshua Heschel, The Prophets (1962); Walter Brueggemann, The Prophetic Imagination (1978).

debate.question: Were the prophets preaching politics?

positions.name: Yes: they demanded a just society
positions.who: Walter Rauschenbusch and the Social Gospel (c. 1900); Gustavo Gutiérrez and liberation theology (1971); Martin Luther King
positions.view: The prophets attacked courts, markets, land-grabbing and debt slavery. Their message is about structures, not just private sins, and churches that keep it private have tamed it.
positions.evidence: Amos's charges are economic and legal; Isaiah 1:17; the land and debt laws of the covenant.

positions.name: No: they called Israel back to God
positions.who: Many traditional Jewish and Christian readers
positions.view: The prophets were not reformers with a programme but messengers calling a covenant people back to its God. Injustice was the symptom; unfaithfulness to God was the disease. Reading them as political activists flattens them.
positions.evidence: The prophets attack idolatry as fiercely as injustice; 'walk humbly with your God'; their hope is in God's action, not policy.

positions.name: Both: justice is how you worship
positions.who: Abraham Joshua Heschel; many modern scholars
positions.view: The division between religion and politics is modern. For the prophets, knowing God and doing justice were the same thing: 'He judged the cause of the poor and needy... Wasn't this to know me?' (Jeremiah 22:16).
positions.evidence: Jeremiah 22:16; Micah 6:8 joins justice, mercy and humility before God.

debate.agree: All agree that, for the prophets, a people that worships God while exploiting the poor has not understood him.

look.why: The prophets told Israel to 'plead for the widow'. Cornelis van Poelenburch painted the prophet Elijah meeting a poor widow at Zarephath, on the coast north of Israel, during a famine (1 Kings 17). She was a foreigner, gathering sticks to cook a last meal for herself and her son, and God sent the prophet to her.
points: In the lower right, an old bearded man, Elijah, in a red cloak over a grey-blue robe, stands barefoot and reaches out a hand.
A young woman in a blue dress kneels before him, one hand stretched towards him.
Behind her a boy carries a bundle of sticks on his back.
To the left, a broken column with a heavy stone beam rises from the ground, overgrown with plants.
Behind them stand the crumbling walls of ruined buildings; further off, people walk and ride across the plain under a blue sky with large clouds.

music.why: Thomas Dorsey's gospel song was Martin Luther King's favourite. Mahalia Jackson sang it at his funeral in 1968; she had sung at the March on Washington, where he quoted Amos: 'let justice roll down'.

think.why: The prophets said the poor, the widow and the stranger matter to God. See where the idea of human rights comes from.

learn.why: The prophets' message in a single line, carved on the Civil Rights Memorial in Montgomery.

check.q: Why would Amos's audience have been shocked by Amos 2:6?
options: Because Amos was a priest
Because he forbade them to worship
Because Amos praised Israel's enemies
Because after condemning the surrounding nations, he condemned Israel at greater length than any of them
check.why: They expected Israel to be spared; instead it received the longest charge.

check.q: What kinds of sin does Amos condemn in chapter 2?
options: Mainly breaking the Sabbath
Mainly mistakes in ritual
Mainly worshipping foreign gods
Mainly economic and legal injustice: selling the poor, perverting justice, keeping pledged cloaks
check.why: All the charges concern how the rich treat the poor.

check.q: What is the prophets' point about worship and sacrifice?
options: That worship offered by people who exploit the poor is worthless to God
That God had abolished the Temple
That music has no place in worship
That only prophets may offer sacrifice
check.why: They do not reject worship as such, but worship without justice.

check.q: According to Micah 6:8, what does God require?
options: To act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God
Your firstborn child
Thousands of rams and rivers of oil
To go up to Jerusalem three times a year
check.why: The Talmud says Micah summed up the Torah in these three.

check.q: How does Hesiod's view of justice differ most from the prophets'?
options: Hesiod thought bribes were acceptable
Hesiod argues mainly that justice pays and brings prosperity; the prophets' one God sides with the poor even against his own people
There is no difference
Hesiod does not mention judges
check.why: Both see the same corruption; the prophets' God is just in his own nature and takes the side of the weak.

check.q: Where is Amos 5:24 carved today?
options: On the Lincoln Memorial
On the Liberty Bell
On the Statue of Liberty
On the Civil Rights Memorial in Montgomery, Alabama
check.why: Maya Lin's memorial (1989) has water flowing over the names of those who died in the movement.

tutorial.question: 'I hate, I despise your feasts.' Did the prophets reject religion?
tutorial.approach: Read Amos 5, Micah 6 and Isaiah 1 closely. What exactly do they condemn, and what do they ask for? Show that the same prophets valued the Temple and the law. Compare Hesiod's justice. End with how Jesus and the civil rights movement took up the prophets' message.
strong: Distinguishes between rejecting worship and rejecting worship without justice.
Explains mishpat and tsedaqah as social words.
Uses specific charges from Amos 2 (sandals, pledged cloaks).
Compares Hesiod fairly, noting likeness and difference.
Mentions Jesus's use of Hosea, or Matthew 25.
Mentions King's use of Amos 5:24.

reading.author: Abraham Joshua Heschel
reading.title: The Prophets
reading.why: The classic book on what it was like to be a prophet, by a rabbi who marched at Selma.

reading.author: Martin Luther King Jr.
reading.title: Letter from Birmingham Jail
reading.why: A modern prophetic text that draws directly on Amos.

reading.author: Walter Brueggemann

reading.why: How the prophets imagined an alternative to royal power.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: before your next act of worship or prayer, do one concrete act of justice or mercy for someone who cannot repay you: pay a bill you have been putting off, give to a food bank, or speak up for someone being treated unfairly.
sessions.reflect: If a prophet looked at your week, what would he say about the gap between what you believe and how you treat people with less power than you?
takeaways: Amos, a herdsman from Judah, condemned rich Israel for selling the poor and corrupting justice while keeping lavish festivals.
The prophets did not reject worship but said worship without justice is worthless: 'act justly, love mercy, and walk humbly with your God'.
Hesiod, at the same time, warned Greek judges that Justice was watching; the prophets' God takes the side of the poor. King made Amos 5:24 the motto of civil rights.

sessions.title: By the rivers of Babylon
sessions.line: Jerusalem burns, the Temple falls, and the people are marched into exile. A prophet writes to them: build houses, and pray for the city of your enemies.
sessions.plain: In 587 BC the Babylonian army destroyed Jerusalem, burned Solomon's Temple and took the leading people into exile in Babylon, in what is now Iraq. It was the end of everything Israel had trusted: the land, the king, the Temple. The Bible explains the disaster as God's judgement on centuries of injustice and unfaithfulness. But in exile something unexpected happened. The prophet Jeremiah wrote to the exiles telling them to settle down and pray for Babylon. The people learned to live as a faithful minority in a foreign land, and much of the Hebrew Bible took its final shape there. This session asks what is left when everything you trusted is gone.
sessions.why: Session 3 heard the prophets warn that a people that forgets justice will fall. The north fell in 722 BC. Now we see the south fall, and ask what faith becomes after the king, the land and the Temple are gone.
answers: Why did Jerusalem fall, and what does outside evidence show?
How did the Bible explain the disaster?
What did Jeremiah tell the exiles to do?
What does Psalm 137 teach about grief and anger?
What did the exile give Judaism and the West?
sessions.finding: When the king, the land and the Temple were lost, Israel found that God was still with them in exile, and learned to seek the good of the city where they lived.

paras: After the northern kingdom fell to Assyria in 722 BC, Judah survived alone for 135 years. It had good kings and bad. Hezekiah survived an Assyrian siege of Jerusalem in 701 BC; the Assyrian king Sennacherib's own account says he shut Hezekiah up 'like a bird in a cage' but does not claim to have taken the city. Josiah, around 622 BC, found 'the book of the law' in the Temple and led a great reform (2 Kings 22–23). But he was killed in battle in 609 BC, and his successors were weak.

Meanwhile Babylon, under its king Nebuchadnezzar II, replaced Assyria as the great power. Judah's kings swung between submission and revolt, hoping Egypt would save them. The prophet Jeremiah told them to submit to Babylon and was imprisoned as a traitor for saying so (Jeremiah 37–38).
background.key: Judah survived Assyria, but Babylon became the new empire; Judah's kings rebelled, and Jeremiah, who urged submission, was jailed as a traitor.

paras: Jeremiah was a priest's son from Anathoth, a village just north of Jerusalem, who prophesied for about forty years, from around 627 BC until after the fall of the city. He is the prophet we know best as a person: his book includes his complaints to God, his arrests, a scroll of his words that the king cut up and burned, and his time at the bottom of a muddy cistern (Jeremiah 36; 38).

He is often called the 'weeping prophet'. Jewish tradition credits him with Lamentations, the five poems of grief over Jerusalem; most scholars think they were written by others soon after the fall. Jeremiah also promised the new covenant written on the heart (Jeremiah 31), which you met if you took 'Exodus and the law'.
background.key: Jeremiah prophesied in Jerusalem for forty years up to its fall; he was arrested, his scroll burned, and he was thrown into a cistern. Tradition credits him with Lamentations.

paras: The fall of Jerusalem is one of the best documented events in the Bible. The Babylonian Chronicle, a cuneiform tablet in the British Museum, records that Nebuchadnezzar captured 'the city of Judah' in 597 BC, seized its king and appointed one of his own choosing; this matches 2 Kings 24. Clay tablets from Babylon list oil rations for 'Jehoiachin, king of Judah' and his sons in exile, the king of 2 Kings 25:27–30.

At Lachish, a fortress south-west of Jerusalem, archaeologists in 1935 found letters written on pieces of pottery during the Babylonian attack. One officer writes that they are watching for the fire signals of Lachish, 'for we cannot see Azekah'. Jeremiah 34:7 says that Lachish and Azekah were the last fortified cities left. In Jerusalem, burned layers, arrowheads and collapsed houses from the destruction have been excavated in the City of David.
background.key: The Babylonian Chronicle records the capture of Jerusalem in 597 BC; ration tablets name the exiled king Jehoiachin; the Lachish letters were written during the final siege.

paras: The main reading has two parts: the fall of Jerusalem (2 Kings 25) and Jeremiah's letter to the exiles (Jeremiah 29).
The comparison this time comes from inside the Bible: two poems written by people who lived through the disaster, Psalm 137 and Lamentations 3. They show how faith sounded in the ruins.
background.key: The fall of Jerusalem and Jeremiah's letter; then two poems of grief from the exile, Psalm 137 and Lamentations 3.

before: What happens to the king, the Temple and the people in 2 Kings 25?
What surprising things does Jeremiah tell the exiles to do?
In Psalm 137, what are the exiles asked to do, and why can't they?
sessions.readWhy: The catastrophe, and a prophet's letter to the survivors telling them how to live.

paras: In the ninth year of his reign, in the tenth month, in the tenth day of the month, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came, he and all his army, against Jerusalem, and encamped against it; and they built forts against it around it.
So the city was besieged until the eleventh year of king Zedekiah.
On the ninth day of the fourth month, the famine was severe in the city, so that there was no bread for the people of the land.

Then a breach was made in the city, and all the men of war fled by night by the way of the gate between the two walls, which was by the king’s garden (now the Chaldeans were against the city around it); and the king went by the way of the Arabah.
But the Chaldean army pursued the king, and overtook him in the plains of Jericho; and all his army was scattered from him.
Then they captured the king, and carried him up to the king of Babylon to Riblah; and they passed judgment on him.
They killed Zedekiah’s sons before his eyes, then put out Zedekiah’s eyes, bound him in fetters, and carried him to Babylon.

Now in the fifth month, on the seventh day of the month, which was the nineteenth year of king Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard, a servant of the king of Babylon, came to Jerusalem.
He burned Yahweh’s house, the king’s house, and all the houses of Jerusalem, even every great house, he burned with fire.
All the army of the Chaldeans, who were with the captain of the guard, broke down the walls around Jerusalem.

Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard carried away captive the residue of the people who were left in the city, and those who fell away, who fell to the king of Babylon, and the residue of the multitude.
But the captain of the guard left some of the poorest of the land to work the vineyards and fields.

Now these are the words of the letter that Jeremiah the prophet sent from Jerusalem to the residue of the elders of the captivity, and to the priests, to the prophets, and to all the people whom Nebuchadnezzar had carried away captive from Jerusalem to Babylon,
(after Jeconiah the king, the queen mother, the eunuchs, the princes of Judah and Jerusalem, the craftsmen, and the smiths, had departed from Jerusalem),
by the hand of Elasah the son of Shaphan, and Gemariah the son of Hilkiah, (whom Zedekiah king of Judah sent to Babylon to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon). It said:
Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel, says to all the captives whom I have caused to be carried away captive from Jerusalem to Babylon:
“Build houses and dwell in them. Plant gardens and eat their fruit.
Take wives and father sons and daughters. Take wives for your sons, and give your daughters to husbands, that they may bear sons and daughters. Multiply there, and don’t be diminished.
Seek the peace of the city where I have caused you to be carried away captive, and pray to Yahweh for it; for in its peace you will have peace.”
For Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel says: “Don’t let your prophets who are among you and your diviners deceive you. Don’t listen to your dreams which you cause to be dreamed.
For they prophesy falsely to you in my name. I have not sent them,” says Yahweh.
For Yahweh says, “After seventy years are accomplished for Babylon, I will visit you and perform my good word toward you, in causing you to return to this place.
For I know the thoughts that I think toward you,” says Yahweh, “thoughts of peace, and not of evil, to give you hope and a future.
You shall call on me, and you shall go and pray to me, and I will listen to you.
You shall seek me, and find me, when you search for me with all your heart.

I will be found by you,” says Yahweh, “and I will turn again your captivity, and I will gather you from all the nations, and from all the places where I have driven you, says Yahweh. I will bring you again to the place from where I caused you to be carried away captive.”

parts.title: The fall of Jerusalem
parts.context: The final siege began in January 588 BC (by our calendar). King Zedekiah, whom Nebuchadnezzar had put on the throne in 597 BC, had rebelled against Babylon, against Jeremiah's advice.

commentary.on: the famine was severe in the city, so that there was no bread for the people of the land
commentary.text: The siege lasted about eighteen months. Lamentations describes what famine did inside the walls in images too terrible to repeat here (Lamentations 4:10).

commentary.on: They killed Zedekiah’s sons before his eyes, then put out Zedekiah’s eyes
commentary.text: The last thing the last king of Judah saw was the death of his sons. The end of David's royal line seemed to have come; the promise of 2 Samuel 7, that David's house would last for ever, seemed broken.

commentary.on: He burned Yahweh’s house, the king’s house, and all the houses of Jerusalem
commentary.text: The Temple Solomon built had stood for nearly four hundred years. Jews still mourn its destruction, and the later destruction of the Second Temple by Rome in AD 70, on the fast of Tisha B'Av, the ninth day of the month of Av.

commentary.on: But the captain of the guard left some of the poorest of the land to work the vineyards and fields.
commentary.text: A quiet irony. The rich who had seized the poor man's land were carried off; the poor were left to farm it. The prophets had warned of exactly this reversal.

parts.title: Seek the peace of the city
parts.context: Written about 594 BC, after the first deportation of 597 BC, to the exiles already in Babylon. Some prophets were telling them the exile would be over in two years (Jeremiah 28). Jeremiah sends a different message.

commentary.on: Build houses and dwell in them. Plant gardens and eat their fruit.
commentary.text: Jeremiah tells them to stop waiting to go home and start living. This is a long exile, not a short one.

commentary.on: Seek the peace of the city where I have caused you to be carried away captive, and pray to Yahweh for it
commentary.text: One of the most remarkable verses in the Bible: pray for Babylon, the city that destroyed yours. The Hebrew for 'peace' is shalom: wholeness, welfare, flourishing. Jews in the diaspora have prayed for the government of the land they live in ever since; many synagogues still say such a prayer every Sabbath.

commentary.on: After seventy years are accomplished for Babylon
commentary.text: Seventy years is a lifetime: none of the adults who heard this would go home. In fact Babylon fell to Cyrus of Persia in 539 BC, 66 years after its first conquests in Judah in 605 BC, and Cyrus let the exiles return.

commentary.on: to give you hope and a future
commentary.text: Jeremiah 29:11 is one of the most popular verses in the world, printed on cards and mugs as a personal promise. In context it is a promise to a whole people in exile, that God has not given up on them. The promise is real, but it comes after seventy years, not before.

commentary.on: You shall seek me, and find me, when you search for me with all your heart.
commentary.text: The heart of the letter. Without a Temple, far from the land, they can still find God. That discovery changed Judaism for ever: God was not tied to one place.

paras:
By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down.
Yes, we wept, when we remembered Zion.

On the willows in that land,
we hung up our harps.

For there, those who led us captive asked us for songs.
Those who tormented us demanded songs of joy:
“Sing us one of the songs of Zion!”
How can we sing Yahweh’s song in a foreign land?

If I forget you, Jerusalem,
let my right hand forget its skill.

Let my tongue stick to the roof of my mouth if I don’t remember you,
if I don’t prefer Jerusalem above my chief joy.

Remember my affliction and my misery,
the wormwood and the bitterness.

My soul still remembers them,
and is bowed down within me.

This I recall to my mind;
therefore I have hope.

It is because of Yahweh’s loving kindnesses that we are not consumed,
because his compassion doesn’t fail.

They are new every morning.
Great is your faithfulness.

“Yahweh is my portion,” says my soul.
“Therefore I will hope in him.”

Yahweh is good to those who wait for him,
to the soul who seeks him.

It is good that a man should hope
and quietly wait for the salvation of Yahweh.

parts.title: By the rivers of Babylon
parts.context: Written by an exile in Babylon, or soon after the return. Babylon was laced with canals from the Euphrates. The psalm ends (verses 7–9) with a terrible curse on Babylon's children, which we have not printed here; the lecture discusses it.

commentary.on: By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down. Yes, we wept, when we remembered Zion.
commentary.text: Zion is the hill of Jerusalem, and a name for the city itself. This line has been set to music more than almost any other in the Bible, from Renaissance motets to Verdi's opera Nabucco (1842) and the reggae hit 'Rivers of Babylon' (1970).

commentary.on: How can we sing Yahweh’s song in a foreign land?
commentary.text: The exiles' captors want entertainment, Jerusalem's songs as a curiosity. The exiles' question is the question of every refugee and every believer in a hostile place: can faith survive away from home?

commentary.on: If I forget you, Jerusalem, let my right hand forget its skill.
commentary.text: A harpist's oath: if I forget, let my playing hand wither. Jews still recall this verse at weddings, when a glass is broken in memory of Jerusalem.

parts.title: New every morning
parts.context: Lamentations is five poems of grief over the fallen city, each an alphabetical acrostic in Hebrew, as if to say: this is grief from A to Z. This passage sits at the exact centre of the book.

commentary.on: Remember my affliction and my misery, the wormwood and the bitterness.
commentary.text: The poet does not pretend. Wormwood is a bitter plant; the whole chapter so far has been a cry of pain.

commentary.on: This I recall to my mind; therefore I have hope.
commentary.text: The turn. Hope here is not a feeling but a choice to remember something. The poet's circumstances have not changed at all.

commentary.on: They are new every morning. Great is your faithfulness.
commentary.text: In the middle of the worst disaster in Israel's history, the most famous words of hope in the book. The hymn 'Great is thy faithfulness' (1923) is built on them.

commentary.on: It is good that a man should hope and quietly wait for the salvation of Yahweh.
commentary.text: Waiting is the posture of exile, and of Advent. The church sings 'O come, O come, Emmanuel, and ransom captive Israel' in the same spirit.

compare.why: Two poems from the exile, one of grief and anger, one of hope found at the bottom of grief. They are how faith sounded in the ruins.
compare.title: Songs in a strange land

paras: A historian's answer is straightforward. Judah was a small state between Egypt and Babylon. Its kings bet on Egypt and rebelled against Babylon, twice, and Babylon punished rebellion by destroying cities and deporting their leaders. Jeremiah's advice to submit was politically realistic, and it was ignored.

The Bible's own answer is theological. The authors of Kings say Judah fell because it had broken the covenant: worshipping other gods, and shedding 'innocent blood' (2 Kings 24:3–4). Their whole history, from Joshua to Kings, was written or completed to explain this catastrophe. They do not blame Babylon's gods for being stronger. They blame their own people. That is unusual: defeated nations in the ancient world usually concluded that their god had lost.
sections.key: Historically, a small state rebelled against an empire. The Bible says Judah fell for breaking the covenant: defeated peoples usually decided their god had lost, but Israel blamed itself.

paras: The exile should have been the end of Israel's faith. The land, the king and the Temple, the three things God had promised, were gone. Instead the exile became one of the most creative periods in its history. The prophet Ezekiel, among the exiles, saw a vision of God's glory leaving the Temple and appearing in Babylon (Ezekiel 1; 10). God was not tied to one place.

Many scholars think that in the exile, without sacrifice, the Jews began to gather to read Scripture and pray: the roots of the synagogue. Much of the Hebrew Bible was collected, edited and completed in these years. The Sabbath, circumcision and the food laws became marks of identity for a people living among others. The Jewish people learned to be a faithful minority in a foreign land, and has been one for most of its history since.
sections.key: Without land, king or Temple, the exiles found God was still with them. The synagogue, much of the Hebrew Bible and the life of a faithful minority grew from the exile.

paras: Psalm 137 does not end with verse 6. Verses 7–9 curse Edom, which had helped Babylon, and then Babylon itself, ending with a blessing on whoever dashes its infants against the rock. It is one of the most shocking verses in Scripture.

Readers have handled it in different ways. Some churches simply leave it out when the psalm is sung. Augustine and the medieval monks read the 'little ones' as sins to be killed while still small. Many modern readers say the psalm is honest: it shows what grief and rage feel like in people who have seen their own children killed, and it takes that rage to God in prayer rather than acting on it. The Bible does not say this curse is right; it records that people prayed it. C. S. Lewis's Reflections on the Psalms (1958) is a famous discussion of these 'cursing psalms'.
sections.key: Psalm 137 ends with a curse on Babylon's children. Readers have omitted it, allegorised it, or read it as honest rage taken to God instead of acted on.

paras: In 539 BC Cyrus the Great of Persia captured Babylon. His policy was to let deported peoples go home and rebuild their temples. The Cyrus Cylinder, a clay inscription found in Babylon in 1879 and now in the British Museum, announces this policy in general terms (it does not mention the Jews). The Bible remembers Cyrus with startling warmth: the book of Isaiah even calls him God's 'anointed' (Isaiah 45:1).

Some exiles returned to Jerusalem and rebuilt the Temple, finished in 515 BC. Many stayed in Babylon, which remained a great centre of Jewish life for fifteen hundred years; the Babylonian Talmud was compiled there. The exile is the beginning of the diaspora, the scattering of the Jewish people across the world.
sections.key: Cyrus of Persia took Babylon in 539 BC and let the exiles return; the Temple was rebuilt by 515 BC, but many stayed: the start of the diaspora.

paras: Exile became one of the great images of the human condition. Augustine's City of God (426) describes Christians as pilgrims in the earthly city, using Jeremiah's letter: they should seek its peace while their true home is elsewhere. The church's prayer 'Hail, holy Queen' calls this life a 'valley of tears' where we are 'poor banished children of Eve'.

Others heard Psalm 137 as their own song: enslaved Africans in America and the Caribbean, Verdi's Italians under Austrian rule, whose chorus 'Va, pensiero' became an unofficial national anthem. The exile gave the West a way to speak of displacement, longing and faithfulness far from home.
sections.key: Augustine read Jeremiah's letter as the Christian's calling in the earthly city. Exile became the West's language for displacement and longing, from 'banished children of Eve' to Verdi.

debate.question: Was the exile God's punishment?

positions.name: Yes: the covenant curses came true
positions.who: The authors of Kings; Jeremiah; much traditional Jewish and Christian reading
positions.view: Israel had been warned for centuries by the prophets. The exile was the consequence the covenant itself had named (Deuteronomy 28). Accepting this was the way back to God.
positions.evidence: 2 Kings 17 and 24:3–4; Jeremiah 25; Lamentations 1:18: 'Yahweh is righteous; for I have rebelled'.

positions.name: No: it was politics and empire
positions.who: Most secular historians
positions.view: Babylon destroyed many small states; Judah was one of them. The theological explanation was written after the event by people trying to make sense of disaster.
positions.evidence: Babylonian records; the fate of neighbouring kingdoms; the late composition of the history.

positions.name: Not only: the suffering was more than the sin
positions.who: Psalm 44; parts of Lamentations; the book of Job; many Jewish thinkers after the Holocaust
positions.view: The Bible itself protests that the suffering went beyond any guilt, and that children suffered for their parents' sins. Ezekiel rejects the proverb that 'the fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge' (Ezekiel 18:2).
positions.evidence: Psalm 44:17–22; Lamentations 5:7; Ezekiel 18.

debate.agree: All agree that Judah fell to Babylon in 587 BC, and that the faith that survived the exile was deeper, not shallower, for it.

look.why: The book of Daniel is set among the exiles in Babylon and Persia. Daniel, a young man from Judah taken to Babylon, rises at court but keeps praying towards Jerusalem three times a day, and is thrown to the lions for it (Daniel 6). Rubens painted him in the den.
points: A young man, Daniel, with long dark hair, sits on a rock in a cave, his legs crossed, wearing only a white cloth and a red cloak.
His hands are clasped at his chest and his head is tipped back as he looks up towards the light.
Lions surround him on every side: some lie down, one opens its jaws wide, one looks straight out at us.
Bones and a skull lie on the floor of the cave.
High above, through an opening in the rock, there is a patch of blue sky and green leaves.

takeaways: Babylon destroyed Jerusalem and the Temple in 587 BC, as outside records confirm; the Bible blamed Judah's unfaithfulness, not its God's weakness.
Jeremiah told the exiles to build houses and seek the peace of Babylon: God could be found without a Temple.
