sessions.title: The case against: the God of war
sessions.line: Before Israel had kings, it had a land, and the Bible says God told them to take it by killing everyone in it. The sceptic's case at full strength.
sessions.plain: The book of Joshua tells how Israel entered Canaan and destroyed its cities, killing 'both man and woman, both young and old', and says God commanded it. Later, God tells King Saul to wipe out the Amalekites, 'infant and nursing baby'. Thomas Paine, in 1795, said that no one could believe God commanded such things without giving up their sense of justice; Richard Dawkins and many others say the same today. This journey has been about power that forgets justice. Here the charge is against God himself. This session puts the case at full strength, then the best answers given by Jews and Christians, and leaves you to weigh them.
sessions.why: Sessions 1 to 4 followed the prophets as they held kings to God's justice. But a reader who takes that justice seriously will ask: what about God's own commands in Joshua? It comes here, once you have seen how high the Bible sets the standard of justice, because the objection uses that very standard.
answers: What do Joshua and Deuteronomy actually command?
What is the strongest case against the God of the Old Testament?
What did 'devoted to destruction' mean in the ancient world?
Did the conquest happen as described?
How have Jews and Christians answered the charge?
sessions.finding: The texts are as hard as the critics say; the main answers are that they use the exaggerated language of ancient war, that they were never a licence for later killing, and that Christians read them in the light of Jesus. Whether those answers are enough is the question.

paras: This session steps back in the story, to before Saul and David. If you took 'Exodus and the law', you followed Israel to Sinai and the edge of the promised land. Moses died within sight of it, and his assistant Joshua led the people across the river Jordan. The book of Joshua tells how they captured the city of Jericho, whose walls fell when the priests blew their trumpets, and then conquered the cities of Canaan one after another.

The Canaanites were the peoples who already lived there, in city-states with their own kings and gods, chief among them Baal. The Bible says God gave Israel the land because of the Canaanites' wickedness, naming child sacrifice among their practices (Deuteronomy 9:5; 12:31), and that Israel would lose the land in turn if it did the same. That, as you saw in session 4, is how the Bible explains the exile.
background.key: Joshua led Israel into Canaan after Moses' death. The Bible says God gave them the land because of the Canaanites' wickedness, and that Israel would lose it for the same.

background.h: Why this is the hardest objection
paras: Most objections to the Bible are about whether things happened. This one is about whether God is good. The texts do not merely describe slaughter, as history books describe many wars. They say God commanded it, and they include children.

Christians and Jews cannot dismiss the question as an outsider's attack, because the Bible itself taught them to ask it. Abraham asked God over Sodom, 'Shouldn't the Judge of all the earth do right?' (Genesis 18:25). The prophets you met in sessions 2 and 3 condemned kings for shedding innocent blood. The objection judges the God of Joshua by the standard of the God of Amos.
background.key: The texts say God commanded the killing, including children. The objection judges them by the Bible's own standard of justice.

background.h: Who were Thomas Paine and Richard Dawkins?
paras: Thomas Paine (1737–1809) was an English-born writer whose pamphlet Common Sense (1776), as you saw in session 1, helped spark the American Revolution. He went to France to support its revolution and was imprisoned in Paris during the Terror. The Age of Reason (1794–1807), written partly in prison, attacked the Bible as a book of human invention. Paine was not an atheist; he believed in one God, but thought the God of Joshua could not be him. It made him one of the most hated men in America.

Richard Dawkins (born 1941) is an Oxford biologist whose book The God Delusion (2006) became the best-known statement of the 'new atheism'. He makes the same charge in our own time, with less restraint.
background.key: Paine, author of Common Sense, attacked the Bible in The Age of Reason (1790s) as a believer in God; Dawkins renewed the charge in The God Delusion (2006).

paras: The main reading has three parts: the fall of Jericho (Joshua 6), the law of war in Deuteronomy (Deuteronomy 20), and God's command to Saul about the Amalekites (1 Samuel 15). Read them slowly. Don't soften them.
The comparison is Paine's own charge, in his own words.
background.key: Jericho, the law of war, and the command to Saul; then Paine's charge.

before: Who is spared at Jericho, and why?
Deuteronomy 20 has two rules for two kinds of city. What is the difference?
What reason does God give for the command against Amalek?
sessions.readWhy: Three passages, read without softening: the hardest commands in the Bible.

paras: On the seventh day, they rose early at the dawning of the day, and marched around the city in the same way seven times. On this day only they marched around the city seven times.
At the seventh time, when the priests blew the trumpets, Joshua said to the people, “Shout, for Yahweh has given you the city!
The city shall be devoted, even it and all that is in it, to Yahweh. Only Rahab the prostitute shall live, she and all who are with her in the house, because she hid the messengers that we sent.
But as for you, only keep yourselves from what is devoted to destruction, lest when you have devoted it, you take of the devoted thing; so you would make the camp of Israel accursed and trouble it.
But all the silver, gold, and vessels of bronze and iron are holy to Yahweh. They shall come into Yahweh’s treasury.”

So the people shouted and the priests blew the trumpets. When the people heard the sound of the trumpet, the people shouted with a great shout, and the wall fell down flat, so that the people went up into the city, every man straight in front of him, and they took the city.
They utterly destroyed all that was in the city, both man and woman, both young and old, and ox, sheep, and donkey, with the edge of the sword.
When you draw near to a city to fight against it, then proclaim peace to it.
It shall be, if it gives you answer of peace and opens to you, then it shall be that all the people who are found therein shall become forced laborers to you, and shall serve you.
If it will make no peace with you, but will make war against you, then you shall besiege it.
When Yahweh your God delivers it into your hand, you shall strike every male of it with the edge of the sword;

but the women, the little ones, the livestock, and all that is in the city, even all its plunder, you shall take for plunder for yourself. You may use the plunder of your enemies, which Yahweh your God has given you.
Thus you shall do to all the cities which are very far off from you, which are not of the cities of these nations.
But of the cities of these peoples that Yahweh your God gives you for an inheritance, you shall save alive nothing that breathes;
but you shall utterly destroy them: the Hittite, the Amorite, the Canaanite, the Perizzite, the Hivite, and the Jebusite, as Yahweh your God has commanded you;
that they not teach you to follow all their abominations, which they have done for their gods; so would you sin against Yahweh your God.
Samuel said to Saul, “Yahweh sent me to anoint you to be king over his people, over Israel. Now therefore listen to the voice of Yahweh’s words.
Yahweh of Armies says, ‘I remember what Amalek did to Israel, how he set himself against him on the way, when he came up out of Egypt.
Now go and strike Amalek, and utterly destroy all that they have, and don’t spare them; but kill both man and woman, infant and nursing baby, ox and sheep, camel and donkey.’ ”

parts.title: The walls of Jericho
parts.context: Israel has crossed the Jordan. For six days the army and the priests with the ark of the covenant have marched once around Jericho in silence. Now it is the seventh day.

commentary.on: The city shall be devoted, even it and all that is in it, to Yahweh.
commentary.text: 'Devoted' translates the Hebrew herem: something given over entirely to God, which no one may keep. In war, it meant total destruction: nothing taken as plunder, no one taken as a slave.

commentary.on: Only Rahab the prostitute shall live, she and all who are with her in the house, because she hid the messengers
commentary.text: In the middle of the slaughter, a Canaanite woman and her family are saved because she sheltered Israel's spies and confessed faith in their God (Joshua 2:9–11). The New Testament lists her among Jesus's ancestors (Matthew 1:5). The text itself breaks its own rule of 'no survivors'.

commentary.on: the wall fell down flat
commentary.text: The victory is God's, not Israel's. That is the point of the strange liturgy of trumpets and marching: Israel did not take Jericho by its own strength.

commentary.on: They utterly destroyed all that was in the city, both man and woman, both young and old, and ox, sheep, and donkey, with the edge of the sword.
commentary.text: This is the sentence the objection rests on. Read it plainly: it describes the killing of everyone, including the old and the young, and presents it as obedience to God.

parts.title: The law of war
parts.context: Deuteronomy 20 is a law for Israel's wars. It begins (20:1–9) by sending home anyone who has just built a house, planted a vineyard or become engaged, or who is afraid.

commentary.on: When you draw near to a city to fight against it, then proclaim peace to it.
commentary.text: The first rule is to offer peace. For distant cities, the law restricts war: peace must be offered first, and if there is fighting, the women and children are spared. By modern standards it is still harsh: those who surrender become forced labourers.

commentary.on: But of the cities of these peoples that Yahweh your God gives you for an inheritance, you shall save alive nothing that breathes
commentary.text: The second rule is the one at the heart of the objection. For the cities of Canaan itself, no one is to be left alive.

commentary.on: that they not teach you to follow all their abominations, which they have done for their gods
commentary.text: The stated reason is religious, not ethnic: to stop Israel adopting Canaanite worship, which the law says included burning children (Deuteronomy 12:31). The critics reply that no reason could justify killing children.

parts.title: Remember Amalek
parts.context: Saul is now king. The Amalekites were a nomadic people of the southern desert who, Exodus says, attacked the weakest stragglers at the back of Israel's column as they came out of Egypt (Deuteronomy 25:17–18).

commentary.on: I remember what Amalek did to Israel
commentary.text: The command is presented as punishment for an attack centuries before. Notice that the people punished are not the people who attacked.

commentary.on: kill both man and woman, infant and nursing baby
commentary.text: The most explicit command of all. Saul obeys only in part, sparing the king and the best animals, and for this God rejects him as king (15:9–23). The story condemns Saul for being too merciful, or rather for keeping the plunder: 'to obey is better than sacrifice' (15:22).

paras: There are matters in that book, said to be done by the express command of God, that are as shocking to humanity, and to every idea we have of moral justice, as any thing done by Robespierre, by Carrier, by Joseph le Bon, in France, by the English government in the East Indies, or by any other assassin in modern times. When we read in the books ascribed to Moses, Joshua, etc., that they (the Israelites) came by stealth upon whole nations of people, who, as the history itself shews, had given them no offence; that they put all those nations to the sword; that they spared neither age nor infancy; that they utterly destroyed men, women and children; that they left not a soul to breathe; expressions that are repeated over and over again in those books, and that too with exulting ferocity; are we sure these things are facts? are we sure that the Creator of man commissioned those things to be done? Are we sure that the books that tell us so were written by his authority?

To charger the commission of things upon the Almighty, which in their own nature, and by every rule of moral justice, are crimes, as all assassination is, and more especially the assassination of infants, is matter of serious concern. The Bible tells us, that those assassinations were done by the express command of God. To believe therefore the Bible to be true, we must unbelieve all our belief in the moral justice of God; for wherein could crying or smiling infants offend? And to read the Bible without horror, we must undo every thing that is tender, sympathising, and benevolent in the heart of man. Speaking for myself, if I had no other evidence that the Bible is fabulous, than the sacrifice I must make to believe it to be true, that alone would be sufficient to determine my choice.

parts.author: Thomas Paine
parts.work: The Age of Reason, Part II
parts.ref: Thomas Paine, The Age of Reason, Part II, chapter 1
parts.title: Are we sure the Creator commissioned these things?
parts.context: Thomas Paine (1737–1809) wrote The Age of Reason in three parts; Part II appeared in 1795. Robespierre, Carrier and Joseph le Bon were leaders of the Terror in France in 1793–94, when thousands were executed; Paine himself narrowly escaped the guillotine. 'The English government in the East Indies' refers to British rule in India. 'To charger' is a printer's error in the original for 'to charge'.
parts.plain: Paine says: the books of Moses and Joshua describe acts as shocking as the worst crimes of the French Terror or of the British in India: whole peoples, who had done Israel no harm, killed with no mercy for age or infancy. And they say God commanded it. Paine asks whether we can be sure these things happened, that God ordered them, or that God inspired the books. To believe the Bible, he says, you would have to stop believing that God is just, and silence every tender feeling in the human heart. He would rather believe the Bible is a human book.

commentary.on: as shocking to humanity, and to every idea we have of moral justice, as any thing done by Robespierre
commentary.text: Paine compares the Bible's wars with the political killings he had just seen. His argument is moral, not scientific: he does not say miracles are impossible; he says these commands are evil.

commentary.on: that they spared neither age nor infancy
commentary.text: Paine fixes on the children, as every serious critic since has done. This is the strongest point of the case.

commentary.on: are we sure these things are facts? are we sure that the Creator of man commissioned those things to be done?
commentary.text: Notice that Paine asks three different questions: did it happen, did God command it, and is the book inspired? The answers you will meet below take up each in turn.

commentary.on: To believe therefore the Bible to be true, we must unbelieve all our belief in the moral justice of God
commentary.text: The heart of the argument. Paine, a believer in God, uses God's justice against the Bible. If our moral sense comes from God, he says, it cannot be right to override it in God's name.

compare.author: Thomas Paine
compare.work: The Age of Reason, Part II
compare.ref: Thomas Paine, The Age of Reason, Part II, chapter 1
compare.why: Thomas Paine wrote this in the 1790s, after living through the Terror in France. Read his charge in full, then decide what you think of the answers.
compare.title: The case against

paras: Put most sharply, the case runs like this. The Bible says God commanded Israel to kill every man, woman and child in the cities of Canaan, and later every Amalekite infant. Killing children is wrong; no one seriously disputes this. So either God commanded something wrong, and is not good, or he did not command it, and the Bible is wrong about what God said. Either way, the Bible cannot be a reliable guide to a good God.

Richard Dawkins pressed the charge in The God Delusion (2006). In our words: he calls the God of the Old Testament jealous, vindictive and genocidal, among many other things, and argues that people who claim to take their morals from the Bible in fact pick and choose by a moral sense that comes from somewhere else. He cites a study by the Israeli psychologist Georges Tamarin (1966), who asked over a thousand Israeli schoolchildren whether Joshua was right to destroy Jericho. Most approved. When the same story was told of an invented Chinese general, most disapproved. Dawkins's point is that sacred texts can make good people approve of atrocity. History offers examples: in 1638 the English soldier John Underhill defended the burning of a Pequot village in New England, women and children included, by appealing to David's wars.
sections.key: Either God commanded something wrong, or the Bible misreports God. Dawkins adds that sacred texts can make people approve of atrocity, and history shows it has happened.

paras: The first answer is historical. In 1868 a stone was found in Jordan on which Mesha, king of Moab, around 840 BC, boasts of capturing a town from Israel and killing all its people, seven thousand of them, because he had 'devoted' them to his god. He uses the same word as Joshua: herem. Assyrian and Egyptian kings boasted in the same way of wiping out enemies who in fact survived. The Merneptah Stele, which you met in 'Exodus and the law', declares that 'Israel is laid waste, its seed is not'.

The Bible itself seems to use the language like this. Joshua 10:40 says Joshua 'left no one remaining'; yet the next book, Judges, begins with the same Canaanites still living in the land, and Israel failing to drive them out (Judges 1:21–33). After 1 Samuel 15 wipes out the Amalekites, Amalekites raid David's town in 1 Samuel 30. Scholars such as Paul Copan and Matthew Flannagan (Did God Really Command Genocide?, 2014) argue that 'utterly destroy' was the stock exaggeration of ancient war reports, like a football fan saying his team 'slaughtered' the other side, and that the actual command was to drive out and defeat. Critics answer that the texts still present killing children as God's will, whatever happened.
sections.key: Mesha of Moab (c. 840 BC) uses the same word, 'devoted', of his own massacre; ancient kings boasted of total victories. The Bible's own later chapters show the Canaanites still there.

paras: The second answer is archaeological, and it cuts both ways. In the 1950s the British archaeologist Kathleen Kenyon excavated Jericho and concluded that its great walls had fallen around 1550 BC, and that there was little or no walled city there in the 1200s BC, when most scholars date Israel's arrival. Other excavators disagree about the dates, but most archaeologists now think the conquest did not happen as Joshua describes. Israel seems to have emerged mostly within Canaan, in new hill-country villages around 1200 BC, as you saw in 'Exodus and the law'.

If so, the massacres may never have taken place. But that does not settle the objection. The question is not only what happened; it is what the Bible says God wanted. And if the stories are later accounts written to warn Israel against foreign gods, a critic can still ask why the warning was written in blood.
sections.key: Kenyon found no walled Jericho in the 1200s BC; most archaeologists think the conquest did not happen as told. But the objection is about what the Bible says God wanted.

sections.h: How the traditions read these texts
paras: Neither Jews nor Christians have treated these commands as a standing order. The Mishnah (Yadayim 4:4) records that the Assyrian king Sennacherib had long ago 'mixed up the nations', so that the Canaanites and Amalekites could no longer be identified; the commands could never be carried out again. The great Jewish philosopher Maimonides (1138–1204) ruled that even the Canaanite cities had to be offered peace first. Many rabbis read 'Amalek' as a name for evil itself, not for a people.

Christians read them through Jesus, who told his followers to love their enemies (Matthew 5:44) and rebuked his disciples when they wanted to call down fire on a village (Luke 9:54–55). The great early scholar Origen, in his Homilies on Joshua (around 240), read Joshua's wars as the soul's battle against sin: the enemies to be destroyed are the vices within. Augustine and Aquinas developed a theory of just war that ruled out deliberately killing the innocent. And the prophets themselves looked forward to a day when nations 'shall beat their swords into plowshares' (Isaiah 2:4).
sections.key: The Mishnah ruled the commands could never be carried out again; Maimonides required peace to be offered. Christians read them through Jesus's 'love your enemies' and Origen's allegory.

paras: Christian thinkers today give three main answers. Some say God, as the giver of life, has the right to take it, and that the judgement on Canaan was unique and unrepeatable; the American philosopher William Lane Craig has defended this view, and it has been fiercely criticised, including by other Christians. Others, like Copan and Flannagan, say the commands were limited and the language exaggerated, aimed at driving out and destroying Canaanite religion, not people.

A third group, including the theologians Eric Seibert and Gregory Boyd, says the Bible records Israel's understanding of God, which was real but incomplete; that understanding grew, through the prophets, to its fullness in Jesus. On this view the conquest stories show how God bore with his people's violent picture of him, and Jesus shows God as he truly is: one who dies for his enemies rather than killing them. Critics of this view ask how we know which parts of the Bible to trust. You will have to weigh these for yourself; none of them makes the texts easy.
sections.key: Some say God may take life and Canaan was unique (Craig); some say the language is exaggerated (Copan); some say Israel's picture of God grew towards Jesus (Seibert, Boyd). None makes the texts easy.

debate.question: Did God command the destruction of the Canaanites?

positions.name: No, and the Bible is wrong to say he did
positions.who: Thomas Paine; Richard Dawkins; many modern readers
positions.view: Killing children is always wrong. A book that says God commanded it cannot be God's word, and people who follow such texts can be led to approve of atrocity.
positions.evidence: Joshua 6:21; Deuteronomy 20:16; 1 Samuel 15:3; Tamarin's study; Underhill and other later uses.

positions.name: Yes, but less than it sounds, and never again
positions.who: Paul Copan and Matthew Flannagan; William Lane Craig (in a stronger form); much traditional reading
positions.view: The language is the exaggeration of ancient war reports; the command was to drive out a people whose religion included child sacrifice, after long patience (Genesis 15:16). It was unique to that moment and gives no licence to anyone since.
positions.evidence: The Mesha Stele; Rahab; Judges 1; Deuteronomy 12:31; the Mishnah and Maimonides on the commands as ended.

positions.name: Israel heard God through its own time
positions.who: Origen (in his own way); Eric Seibert; Gregory Boyd; many modern theologians
positions.view: These texts record Israel's real but limited understanding of God, which grew through the prophets and was fulfilled in Jesus, who loved his enemies. Christians read every part of Scripture in his light.
positions.evidence: Isaiah 2:4; Hosea 6:6; Matthew 5:43–48; Luke 9:54–55; the cross.

debate.agree: All agree that these texts may never be used to justify killing anyone today, and that the Bible's own standard, 'Shouldn't the Judge of all the earth do right?', is the one by which they must be judged.

look.why: John Martin, an English painter famous for vast, apocalyptic scenes, painted a later battle of the conquest, at Gibeon, when Joshua prayed for the sun to stand still until Israel had defeated its enemies (Joshua 10:12–13). He made the war look like the end of the world.
points: A huge, dark storm fills the left of the sky, with rain slanting down and light breaking through on the right.
On a rocky ledge near the centre, a soldier with a round shield, Joshua, raises his arm towards the sky.
Beside him stand three figures in white robes with red sashes, and a fourth bows low.
On the right, a long column of soldiers and horsemen winds up a road towards a walled city with domes and temples.
In the lower left, tiny figures fight in the shadowed valley below.

music.why: Górecki's 'Symphony of Sorrowful Songs' is a lament for the innocent victims of war; its second movement sets a prayer a young woman wrote on the wall of a Gestapo cell.

think.why: Paine judged God by our moral sense; Plato asked whether good is good because God commands it. See the modern debate.

learn.why: Israel's own prophet looked to the end of war: the strongest answer the Old Testament gives to its own violence.

check.q: What did the Hebrew word herem ('devoted') mean in war?
options: Given over entirely to God: total destruction, with no plunder or slaves taken
A ceremony of anointing
A tax paid to the Temple
A treaty of peace
check.why: Nothing devoted could be kept; in war it meant destroying everything.

check.q: What is the core of Paine's objection?
options: That miracles are impossible
That Joshua never existed
That the Bible was written in Hebrew
That believing God commanded the killing of whole peoples, including infants, means giving up belief in God's justice
check.why: Paine, a believer in God, uses God's justice against the Bible.

check.q: Why is the Mesha Stele relevant to this question?
options: It records the fall of Jericho
It shows a neighbouring king using the same 'devoted to destruction' language of his own wars, suggesting a common rhetoric of ancient war
It is a Christian inscription
It proves Joshua existed
check.why: Mesha of Moab used herem of his own massacre, about 840 BC.

check.q: What do the Bible's own later chapters suggest about Joshua's 'left no one remaining'?
options: That it was exaggerated: Judges 1 says the Canaanites were still living in the land
That the Canaanites had all moved to Egypt
Nothing
That Joshua had lied
check.why: Many scholars read the language as the hyperbole of ancient war reports.

check.q: What did Kathleen Kenyon conclude from excavating Jericho?
options: That its great walls fell around 1550 BC, and there was little or no walled city in the 1200s BC
That its walls fell around 1200 BC, exactly as Joshua says
That Jericho never existed
That the city was Roman
check.why: Most archaeologists now doubt the conquest happened as described.

check.q: How did the Mishnah and Maimonides limit these commands?
options: They said the commands applied to all foreigners
They declared Joshua a false prophet
The Mishnah said the nations could no longer be identified, and Maimonides required peace to be offered first
They required them to be carried out every generation
check.why: Jewish law treated the commands as ended and hedged with conditions.

tutorial.question: 'The God of Joshua cannot be the God of Jesus.' Discuss.
tutorial.approach: State the objection at full strength, with the texts and Paine's argument. Then assess the main answers: the language of ancient war, the archaeology, the Jewish and Christian traditions of reading, and the three modern Christian views. Be honest about what each answer does and does not solve. End with your own judgement.
strong: States the objection fairly and in its strongest form, including the children.
Explains herem and the Mesha Stele.
Uses the Bible's own evidence of exaggeration (Judges 1; 1 Samuel 30).
Notes that archaeology may remove the event but not the problem.
Explains at least two traditional readings (the Mishnah, Origen, just war).
Weighs the three modern Christian answers and their weaknesses.

reading.author: Paul Copan
reading.title: Is God a Moral Monster?
reading.why: A clear defence of the Old Testament against the new atheists.

reading.author: Richard Dawkins
reading.title: The God Delusion
reading.why: Chapter 7 sets out the case against in its best-known modern form.

reading.author: Eric Seibert
reading.title: Disturbing Divine Behavior
reading.why: A Christian scholar who argues the texts show Israel's picture of God, not God himself.

reading.author: Gregory A. Boyd
reading.title: The Crucifixion of the Warrior God
reading.why: A long theological argument for reading every violent text through the cross.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: notice where you or people around you justify harming someone by appeal to a cause, a group or 'what they deserve'. Refuse it once, in word or in thought.
sessions.reflect: Which answer to this objection persuades you most, and which persuades you least? Why?
takeaways: Joshua, Deuteronomy and 1 Samuel say God commanded the destruction of whole peoples, including children; Paine and Dawkins say no good God could command it.
Answers point to the exaggerated language of ancient war (the Mesha Stele, Judges 1), archaeology that doubts the conquest, and Jewish law that ended the commands.
Christians read the texts through Jesus, who loved his enemies; some think God permitted Israel's limited picture of him. None of the answers makes the texts easy.

sessions.title: The servant who suffers
sessions.line: After the exile, a prophet sings of comfort, and of a servant who wins not by taking but by being crushed for others.
sessions.plain: In the last years of the exile in Babylon, a prophet whose words are found in the second half of the book of Isaiah announced comfort: God was coming to bring his people home. He also spoke of a mysterious 'servant of the Lord' who would be despised, beaten and killed, and whose suffering would heal others. Jews have read this servant as Israel itself; Christians, from the first century, have read him as Jesus. Six centuries later, an Ethiopian official reading this passage in his chariot asked, 'Who is the prophet talking about?' This session asks his question, and brings the journey to its verdict.
sessions.why: Session 4 left the people in exile; session 5 faced the violence at the beginning of the story. Now we reach its end. The journey began with kings who took. It ends with a servant who gives his life. This is the Old Testament's last word on power, and the bridge to the New.
answers: What is the comfort of Isaiah 40?
Who is the suffering servant?
How does the servant answer the problem of power?
Why did the first Christians read this passage as being about Jesus?
So what happens when power forgets justice?
sessions.finding: The story of kings that began with 'he will take' ends with a servant who 'poured out his soul to death' for others: the Bible's answer to power that forgets justice.

paras: Session 4 left the people of Judah in exile in Babylon after 587 BC. Jeremiah had told them to settle down; Psalm 137 had wept. Then, in the 540s BC, a new power rose in the east: Cyrus of Persia, who conquered kingdom after kingdom and, in 539 BC, took Babylon itself. To the exiles it seemed that the impossible was about to happen: they would go home.

Chapters 40–55 of Isaiah speak into exactly this moment. They name Cyrus (Isaiah 44:28; 45:1), describe Babylon's gods carried off on the backs of animals (46:1–2), and call the exiles to come out of Babylon (48:20). Their tone is completely different from the warnings of Isaiah 1, which you read in session 3: almost everything is comfort.
background.key: In the 540s BC Cyrus of Persia rose and took Babylon in 539 BC. Isaiah 40–55 speaks into that moment, naming Cyrus and promising return.

paras: Jewish and Christian tradition credits the whole book to Isaiah of Jerusalem, who lived around 740–700 BC, and the New Testament quotes these chapters as 'Isaiah'. Since the late 1700s most scholars have concluded that chapters 40–55 come from a later prophet, or a circle of prophets, living among the exiles about 550–539 BC, who carried on Isaiah's tradition. They call him 'Second Isaiah' or 'Deutero-Isaiah'. His name is not known.

Some scholars and many traditional readers still hold that Isaiah wrote it all, by prophecy. Either way, the date of the text itself is secure: the Great Isaiah Scroll, found among the Dead Sea Scrolls in 1947, contains the whole book of Isaiah, including chapter 53, and was copied around 125 BC, more than a century before Jesus.
background.key: Most scholars think Isaiah 40–55 was written by an unnamed prophet in the exile, 'Second Isaiah'; tradition credits Isaiah. The Dead Sea Isaiah Scroll (c. 125 BC) proves chapter 53 is older than Jesus.

paras: Four passages in these chapters (42:1–9; 49:1–6; 50:4–9; 52:13–53:12) speak of the 'servant of the Lord'. Scholars since Bernhard Duhm in 1892 have called them the 'servant songs'. The servant is chosen by God, brings justice to the nations, is gentle ('He won't break a bruised reed', 42:3), is beaten and humiliated, and in the last song is killed and then vindicated.

Who is he? In one song the servant is called 'Israel' (49:3), yet in the same passage he has a mission to Israel (49:5). The Ethiopian in Acts 8 asked exactly this question. The lecture sets out the main answers: Jewish, Christian and scholarly.
background.key: Four 'servant songs' in Isaiah 40–55 describe a gentle servant who brings justice, suffers, dies and is vindicated. Who he is has been debated ever since.

paras: The main reading has two parts: the comfort that opens these chapters (Isaiah 40), and the last and greatest servant song (Isaiah 52–53).
The comparison is from the New Testament: a scene from the Acts of the Apostles in which an Ethiopian official reads Isaiah 53 and asks who it is about.
background.key: The comfort of Isaiah 40 and the fourth servant song; then the Ethiopian reading Isaiah 53 in Acts 8.

before: In Isaiah 40, what is said about the people, and what about God's word?
In Isaiah 53, who is the 'we'? What did 'we' think of the servant, and what did 'we' come to see?
What does the servant do that no king in this journey did?
sessions.readWhy: Comfort after exile, and the servant who suffers for others.

paras: “Comfort, comfort my people,” says your God.
“Speak comfortably to Jerusalem; and call out to her that her warfare is accomplished, that her iniquity is pardoned, that she has received of Yahweh’s hand double for all her sins.”

The voice of one who calls out,
“Prepare the way of Yahweh in the wilderness!
Make a level highway in the desert for our God.

Every valley shall be exalted,
and every mountain and hill shall be made low.
The uneven shall be made level,
and the rough places a plain.

The voice of one saying, “Cry!”
One said, “What shall I cry?”
“All flesh is like grass,
and all its glory is like the flower of the field.

The grass withers,
the flower fades,
because Yahweh’s breath blows on it.
Surely the people are like grass.

You who tell good news to Zion, go up on a high mountain.
You who tell good news to Jerusalem, lift up your voice with strength!
Lift it up! Don’t be afraid!
Say to the cities of Judah, “Behold, your God!”

Behold, the Lord Yahweh will come as a mighty one,
and his arm will rule for him.
Behold, his reward is with him,
and his recompense before him.

He will feed his flock like a shepherd.
He will gather the lambs in his arm,
and carry them in his bosom.
He will gently lead those who have their young.

Behold, my servant will deal wisely.
He will be exalted and lifted up,
and will be very high.

Just as many were astonished at you—
his appearance was marred more than any man, and his form more than the sons of men—

Who has believed our message?
To whom has Yahweh’s arm been revealed?

For he grew up before him as a tender plant,
and as a root out of dry ground.
He has no good looks or majesty.
When we see him, there is no beauty that we should desire him.

He was despised
and rejected by men,
a man of suffering
and acquainted with disease.
He was despised as one from whom men hide their face;
and we didn’t respect him.

Surely he has borne our sickness
and carried our suffering;
yet we considered him plagued,
struck by God, and afflicted.

But he was pierced for our transgressions.
He was crushed for our iniquities.
The punishment that brought our peace was on him;
and by his wounds we are healed.

He was oppressed,
yet when he was afflicted he didn’t open his mouth.
As a lamb that is led to the slaughter,
and as a sheep that before its shearers is silent,
so he didn’t open his mouth.

He was taken away by oppression and judgment.
As for his generation,
who considered that he was cut off out of the land of the living
and stricken for the disobedience of my people?

They made his grave with the wicked,
and with a rich man in his death,
although he had done no violence,
nor was any deceit in his mouth.

Yet it pleased Yahweh to bruise him.
He has caused him to suffer.
When you make his soul an offering for sin,
he will see his offspring.
He will prolong his days
and Yahweh’s pleasure will prosper in his hand.

After the suffering of his soul,
he will see the light and be satisfied.
My righteous servant will justify many by the knowledge of himself;
and he will bear their iniquities.

parts.title: Comfort, comfort my people
parts.context: The opening of the second half of Isaiah, around 540 BC. After thirty-nine chapters dominated by warning, the tone changes completely.

commentary.on: “Comfort, comfort my people,” says your God.
commentary.text: The first words after the long silence of exile. The doubling is tender. Handel's Messiah begins with them: 'Comfort ye my people'.

commentary.on: Prepare the way of Yahweh in the wilderness!
commentary.text: A highway through the desert between Babylon and Jerusalem, for God to lead his people home: a new exodus. All four Gospels apply this verse to John the Baptist (Mark 1:3).

commentary.on: but the word of our God stands forever.
commentary.text: The empires were grass: Assyria had gone, Babylon was going. The exiles had lost everything else; what lasted was God's word. This is why the exile turned Israel into a people of the book.

commentary.on: You who tell good news to Zion
commentary.text: In the Greek translation of the Old Testament, 'tell good news' is euangelizein, from which comes 'evangelist' and the word translated 'gospel'. The early Christians took the name for their message from verses like this.

commentary.on: He will feed his flock like a shepherd.
commentary.text: The journey began with a shepherd boy anointed king. Israel's kings were meant to be shepherds of the people and mostly were not (Ezekiel 34). Now God himself will be the shepherd.

parts.title: The suffering servant
parts.context: The fourth servant song. God speaks at the beginning and end; in between, a group of people, the 'we', confess that they misjudged the servant.

commentary.on: Kings will shut their mouths at him
commentary.text: This passage is about power. The kings of the nations, who have dominated this whole journey, will be struck dumb by what God does through a despised servant.

commentary.on: He was despised and rejected by men
commentary.text: The opposite of a king. David was chosen though he did not look like a king; the servant has 'no good looks or majesty' at all.

commentary.on: yet we considered him plagued, struck by God, and afflicted.
commentary.text: The 'we' thought, as most people in the ancient world would, that his suffering proved God was against him. Then they saw the truth.

commentary.on: But he was pierced for our transgressions.
commentary.text: The centre of the song. His suffering was for others. In Israel's worship, an animal's life was offered for the sins of the people; here a person bears them. This idea, that one may suffer in the place of many, is called substitution.

commentary.on: As a lamb that is led to the slaughter
commentary.text: The servant does not resist or curse. Compare Samuel's warning: 'he will take'. The kings took others' lives; the servant gives his own.

commentary.on: My righteous servant will justify many by the knowledge of himself
commentary.text: After death, vindication: 'he will see his offspring' and 'prolong his days'. The song ends in triumph, not defeat.

commentary.on: because he poured out his soul to death
commentary.text: This is the Old Testament's last word on power. The servant is 'given a portion with the great', not for taking, but for pouring out his life for others.

paras: But an angel of the Lord spoke to Philip, saying, “Arise, and go toward the south to the way that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza. This is a desert.”
He arose and went; and behold, there was a man of Ethiopia, a eunuch of great authority under Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, who was over all her treasure, who had come to Jerusalem to worship.
He was returning and sitting in his chariot, and was reading the prophet Isaiah.
The Spirit said to Philip, “Go near, and join yourself to this chariot.”
Philip ran to him, and heard him reading Isaiah the prophet, and said, “Do you understand what you are reading?”
He said, “How can I, unless someone explains it to me?” He begged Philip to come up and sit with him.
Now the passage of the Scripture which he was reading was this,

“He was led as a sheep to the slaughter.
As a lamb before his shearer is silent,
so he doesn’t open his mouth.

In his humiliation, his judgment was taken away.
Who will declare His generation?
For his life is taken from the earth.”
The eunuch answered Philip, “Who is the prophet talking about? About himself, or about someone else?”
Philip opened his mouth, and beginning from this Scripture, preached to him about Jesus.

parts.title: The Ethiopian in the chariot
parts.context: The Acts of the Apostles, written by Luke around AD 80–90, tells of the first Christians after Jesus's death and resurrection. Philip was one of seven leaders appointed in Jerusalem. 'Ethiopia' in the Bible meant the kingdom of Kush, on the Nile in today's Sudan; 'Candace' was the title of its queens.

commentary.on: a man of Ethiopia, a eunuch of great authority under Candace, queen of the Ethiopians
commentary.text: A powerful man, the queen's treasurer, from the far edge of the known world. As a eunuch he would have been barred from the inner courts of the Temple (Deuteronomy 23:1), yet he had travelled to Jerusalem to worship. Isaiah 56:3–5 had promised eunuchs a place in God's house.

commentary.on: Do you understand what you are reading?
commentary.text: He was reading aloud, as people did in the ancient world, from a scroll of Isaiah in Greek.

commentary.on: Who is the prophet talking about? About himself, or about someone else?
commentary.text: The question scholars still ask. The Ethiopian's two options, the prophet himself or another person, are two of the answers in the lecture below.

commentary.on: beginning from this Scripture, preached to him about Jesus.
commentary.text: The first Christians read Isaiah 53 as a portrait of Jesus: the innocent man who did not open his mouth before his judges, was killed with criminals, buried in a rich man's tomb, and was vindicated. The Ethiopian was baptised on the road, and Ethiopian Christians have long honoured him as the first of their faith.

compare.why: Six centuries after these words were written, a man in a chariot asked the question this session asks.
compare.title: Who is the prophet talking about?

paras: The prophets of sessions 2 to 4 warned that power without justice would bring ruin, and it did. Isaiah 40 begins after the ruin: Jerusalem has 'received double for all her sins'. The message now is not more judgement but forgiveness and homecoming. God's justice, in the Bible, never has the last word alone; it is meant to lead to mercy.

This is why Isaiah 40 opens Handel's Messiah, and why the Gospels open with it. The early Christians believed that the comfort promised to the exiles had come in a fuller way in Jesus: a new exodus, from sin and death rather than from Babylon.
sections.key: After judgement, comfort: the exiles' homecoming. Messiah and the Gospels open with Isaiah 40, reading Jesus as a new exodus.

paras: The main Jewish reading, given its classic form by the great medieval commentator Rashi (1040–1105), is that the servant is the people of Israel, or its faithful remnant. In our words: the 'we' who speak in chapter 53 are the nations, the kings of the earth, who will one day realise that the people they despised and persecuted were suffering for the world's sins, not their own. Isaiah 49:3 explicitly calls the servant Israel.

This reading has had a terrible relevance. Jews who lived through centuries of persecution, often at Christian hands, could read Isaiah 53 as a description of their own history. Any Christian reading of the passage should be humble in the face of that.
sections.key: Rashi read the servant as Israel, despised by the nations, who will realise Israel suffered for them. Jewish history has given the reading a terrible relevance.

paras: The New Testament reads the servant as Jesus, and so has the church ever since. Jesus himself said he came 'not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many' (Mark 10:45), words that echo Isaiah 53. At his last supper, according to Luke, he quoted Isaiah 53:12, 'he was counted with transgressors' (Luke 22:37). Peter's first letter draws on Isaiah 53 to describe Jesus's suffering (1 Peter 2:22–25).

Christians point to how closely the details fit: silence before his accusers, death with criminals, a rich man's tomb (Joseph of Arimathea, Matthew 27:57–60), and vindication after death. Some ancient Jewish interpretation also read the passage as being about the Messiah; the Aramaic paraphrase known as the Targum of Jonathan names the servant 'my servant the Messiah' at 52:13, though it gives the suffering to others. Critics answer that the Gospel writers may have shaped their accounts of Jesus's death to fit Isaiah. You will weigh that question in 'Who was Jesus?'
sections.key: The New Testament reads the servant as Jesus, who 'came to serve'; the details fit closely. The Targum also linked the servant with the Messiah. Critics say the Gospels were shaped to fit.

paras: Read in the light of this whole journey, the servant song is an answer to the problem of power. Samuel warned that a king 'will take'. David took Bathsheba and Uriah's life; Ahab took Naboth's vineyard; the kings of Israel took the poor man's land; the empire of Babylon took everything. The servant takes nothing. He 'poured out his soul to death', and the kings 'shut their mouths'.

Jesus made exactly this contrast: 'The kings of the nations lord it over them... But not so with you. But one who is the greater among you, let him become as the younger, and one who is governing, as one who serves' (Luke 22:25–26). It is a startling idea, that the greatest authority is the one that serves and suffers. It has never been easy to live. But it entered the Western idea of leadership: even the Pope, the bishop of Rome, has signed himself 'servant of the servants of God' since Gregory the Great around 600, and at the British coronation of 2023, when a young chorister welcomed the king in the name of the King of kings, the king replied that he came 'not to be served but to serve'.
sections.key: The kings took; the servant gave his life. Jesus: 'the one who governs, as one who serves'. The idea entered the West, from 'servant of the servants of God' to the 2023 coronation.

paras: So what happens when power forgets justice? This journey has followed the Bible's answer. Israel asked for a king, and Samuel warned what kings do. The law put the king under God's law, and the prophets stood beside the kings to say so, from Nathan's 'You are the man' to Elijah in Naboth's vineyard and Amos at Bethel. Power forgot justice anyway: in secret crimes, in courts that sold the poor, in worship that ignored them. And the kingdoms fell, as the prophets had said.

But the story does not end in ruin. In exile Israel found God without a Temple and learned to seek the peace of its enemies' city. Its prophets looked beyond the failed kings to a different kind of ruler: a servant who suffers rather than takes. The hardest question, whether God himself commanded injustice in Joshua, has no easy answer, but even there Israel's own prophets pointed beyond war to swords beaten into ploughshares. The deepest answer the Old Testament gives to power that forgets justice is not a better king but a servant, and that is where the New Testament begins.
sections.key: Power forgot justice and the kingdoms fell, as the prophets said. But the Old Testament ends looking beyond kings to a servant who gives his life: where the New Testament begins.

debate.question: Who is the suffering servant?

positions.name: Israel
positions.who: Rashi; Ibn Ezra; most Jewish interpreters since the Middle Ages
positions.view: The servant is the people of Israel, suffering among the nations, who will one day be vindicated; the 'we' are the nations who misjudged them.
positions.evidence: Isaiah 41:8; 44:1; 49:3 call the servant Israel or Jacob.

positions.name: Jesus
positions.who: The New Testament; the church fathers; Christian tradition
positions.view: The servant is an individual who suffers for others and is vindicated after death: fulfilled in Jesus, who came to serve and give his life.
positions.evidence: Acts 8:35; Mark 10:45; Luke 22:37; 1 Peter 2:22–25; the details of the passion.

positions.name: A figure of the prophet's own time
positions.who: Many modern scholars
positions.view: The servant was the prophet himself, or a leader of the exiles, whose suffering the community came to see as meaningful. The song was later read in new ways.
positions.evidence: Isaiah 50:4–9 sounds like the prophet's own experience; the Ethiopian's first option, 'about himself'.

debate.agree: All agree that the song describes innocent suffering that brings healing to others, and that it overturns the ancient idea that the sufferer must be cursed by God.

look.why: Duccio painted this panel for the great altarpiece of Siena Cathedral, finished in 1311. He set two prophets beside the birth of Jesus: Isaiah on the left and Ezekiel on the right, each holding a scroll of his prophecy.
points: Three panels with gold backgrounds: the birth of Jesus in the centre, a standing prophet on each side.
On the left, Isaiah, an old man with a long white beard in a purple cloak, holds an unrolled scroll and raises his other hand.
On the right, Ezekiel, with a dark beard in a blue cloak, holds a scroll and raises his hand too.
In the centre, Mary, in a deep blue robe lined with red, lies in front of a wooden shelter in a cave; the baby lies in a manger behind her, with an ox and a donkey.
Angels crowd above the roof; below, Joseph sits to one side, two women bathe the baby, and shepherds with their sheep stand at the lower right.

music.why: Handel's Messiah begins with Isaiah 40, 'Comfort ye my people', and its second part sets Isaiah 53: 'He was despised', 'Surely he hath borne our griefs'. The recording here is the Hallelujah chorus that ends that part.

think.why: The first Christians read Isaiah 53 as a portrait of Jesus. Start asking who he was.

learn.why: The heart of the servant song, read in churches on Good Friday.

tutorial.question: 'The Old Testament's answer to power that forgets justice is not a better king but a servant.' Discuss.
tutorial.approach: Trace the journey: the warning of 1 Samuel 8, the law of the king, the crimes of David and Ahab, the prophets' demands, the fall and the exile. Then read Isaiah 52–53 closely and set out the main interpretations of the servant. Consider whether the claim is fair to the Old Testament, which also hopes for a just king from David's line (Isaiah 9; 11). End with your own view.
strong: Traces the argument of the whole journey with specific episodes.
Reads Isaiah 53 closely, noticing the 'we' and the vindication.
Sets out the Jewish, Christian and scholarly readings fairly.
Notes the Great Isaiah Scroll and the date of the text.
Considers the hope for a righteous king in Isaiah 9 and 11.
Connects the servant to Jesus's teaching on power (Mark 10:45; Luke 22:25–26).

closing.title: Your answer
closing.prompt: What happens when power forgets justice? In about 300 words, answer from the story of Israel's kings and prophets, using at least three of its episodes, and answer the strongest objection to your view.
closing.practice: Read the story of David in 1 and 2 Samuel over the next two weeks, two or three chapters a day, and then the book of Amos in one sitting. Notice every time someone with less power tells someone with more the truth.
synthesis: This journey asked what happens when power forgets justice, following Israel from the day it asked for a king to the exile and beyond. Here are the short answers to its questions.

Why did Israel want a king? Its judges were corrupt and its enemies strong, and it wanted to be 'like all the nations'. Samuel warned that a king would take: their sons, daughters, fields and freedom, until the people freed from Pharaoh were servants again. God let them have a king, but Deuteronomy put him under the law: he must copy it out, read it every day, and not think himself above his brothers. Unlike Egypt and Babylon, Israel's king did not make the law. God chose David, the youngest son, looking at the heart; the anointed king gave us the words Messiah and Christ. Aristotle drew the same line between a king, who rules for the common good, and a tyrant, who rules for himself.

What did kings do with power? Even David, the best of them, took another man's wife and arranged his death in secret, like Gyges with his ring. Ahab and Jezebel took Naboth's vineyard by a fake trial. But in Israel a king could be accused: Nathan told David 'You are the man', and Elijah met Ahab in the stolen field. David repented without excuse. The idea that power can be called to account by someone with no power at all runs from Nathan to Ambrose, Becket and beyond.

What did the prophets demand? Amos, Micah and Isaiah accused whole societies: courts that took bribes, the rich who sold the poor for a pair of sandals, and worship that ignored them. God hated their feasts; he wanted justice like a river that never runs dry, and 'to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God'. Hesiod warned Greek judges in the same years, but the prophets' one God took the side of the poor against his own people. Martin Luther King made their words the motto of civil rights.

What happened? The kingdoms fell: the north to Assyria in 722 BC, Jerusalem to Babylon in 587 BC, as outside records confirm. The Bible blamed Israel, not its God. In exile, the people found God without a Temple; Jeremiah told them to seek the peace of Babylon; Psalm 137 wept and raged; Lamentations found mercies new every morning. The synagogue, much of the Hebrew Bible and the diaspora grew from the ruins.

What about the God of war? Joshua, Deuteronomy and 1 Samuel say God commanded the destruction of whole peoples, children included. Paine and Dawkins say no good God could. The answers point to the exaggerated language of ancient war, to archaeology that doubts the conquest happened, to Jewish law that ended the commands and to Christian reading through Jesus, who loved his enemies. None makes the texts easy, and the Bible's own question stands over them: 'Shouldn't the Judge of all the earth do right?'

So what happens when power forgets justice? It takes, it hides, and it falls. But the Old Testament does not end with ruin, or with a better king. It ends looking towards a servant who is despised, suffers for others, and is vindicated: one who 'poured out his soul to death' instead of taking others' lives. Jews read him as Israel; Christians as Jesus, who said he came 'not to be served, but to serve'. Where the kings took, the servant gives.

One more thing. Count how much of the West comes from these chapters: the belief that no ruler is above the law; the right, and duty, to tell the powerful they are wrong; the idea that a society is judged by how it treats the widow, the orphan and the stranger; the conviction that worship without justice is hollow; and the hope that the greatest among us should be the servant of all. When people in the West say 'no one is above the law' or 'let justice roll down', they are, knowingly or not, quoting Israel's prophets.

title: Psalms and wisdom
question: How do we pray, think and live in God's world?
line: Seven sessions in the Bible's songbook and notebook: the Psalms of praise and complaint, the advice of Proverbs, the doubts of Ecclesiastes beside Tolstoy, the strongest case against, the Song of Songs, and the claim that Wisdom has a face.
why: In the middle of the Bible are books that tell almost no story. In the Psalms Israel talks to God, in every mood from joy to despair; in Proverbs, Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs it thinks about life, work, death and love. More people have prayed with these words than with any others, and they have shaped how the West grieves, loves and asks what life is for. This journey reads them with Egyptian wisdom, the Epic of Gilgamesh and Tolstoy's Confession, faces the objection that life is meaningless and God silent, and ends with the Christian claim that the Wisdom at God's side became a person. It is written at the depth of a first-year university course, for anyone.
follows: A first-year paper on Hebrew poetry and the wisdom literature of the Hebrew Bible (Introduction to the Study of the Bible), with elements of papers on the history of interpretation and on the problem of meaning.
before: kings
outcomes: Explain how the Psalter was collected and arranged, what the headings may mean, and how Hebrew parallelism works, with examples from Psalms 1, 13 and 23.

sessions.title: The songbook of the Bible
sessions.line: A hundred and fifty prayers for every mood, collected over centuries and made to be sung: what the Psalms are, who wrote them, and how Hebrew poetry works.
sessions.plain: In the middle of the Bible is a book of 150 songs and prayers called the Psalms. They were written by many people over several centuries, collected into one book, and sung aloud in the Temple in Jerusalem, in synagogues and in churches ever since. This session reads two of the most loved, Psalm 1 and Psalm 23, and one of the shortest cries of pain, Psalm 13, and shows how Hebrew poetry is built. It matters because more people have prayed with these words than with any others in history.
sessions.why: This is the first session. 'Kings and prophets' followed Israel's history from Samuel to the exile. Now we turn from the story to the prayers that grew up inside it. Before we can ask how the Bible teaches people to pray, think and live, we need to know what this songbook is.
answers: What are the Psalms, and how is the book put together?
Who wrote them? What does 'a psalm of David' mean?
How is Hebrew poetry made, if it doesn't rhyme?
How were the Psalms used, then and now?
sessions.finding: The Psalms are a book of prayers for every human mood, collected over centuries and made to be said aloud, together.

paras: If you have taken 'Kings and prophets', you have followed Israel from the day it asked for a king, about 1030 BC, to the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon in 587 BC and the return from exile after 539 BC. You met David, the shepherd who became king, and you met two psalms there: Psalm 51, the prayer linked to David's repentance, and the first verses of Psalm 137, sung by the rivers of Babylon, which you read.

If you have not, here is all you need. Israel was a small people in the land between Egypt and Mesopotamia. It believed in one God, who had freed it from slavery in Egypt and given it a law. Its second king, David, about 1010 to 970 BC, made Jerusalem the capital. His son Solomon built the Temple there, the house of God, where priests offered sacrifices and singers sang. Most of the Psalms were sung in or around that Temple.
background.key: Israel's history ran from its first kings (c. 1030 BC) to the exile and return (587–539 BC). The Psalms grew up inside that history, around the Temple in Jerusalem.

paras: The Bible is not only a story. In its middle stand five books that tell almost no story at all: Job, Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs. Christians often call them the 'wisdom' or 'poetic' books. Here Israel talks to God, and thinks about life.

This journey asks: how do we pray, think and live in God's world? Its frame is simple. The Psalms are the Bible's songbook: Israel talking to God, in every mood. The wisdom books are its notebook: Israel thinking about life. We will go from praise to complaint, from the confident advice of Proverbs to the hard questions of Ecclesiastes, then hear the strongest case against, the love poem, and the Christian claim that Wisdom has a face. (Job has a journey of its own.)

background.key: How do we pray, think and live in God's world? The Psalms are Israel's songbook, the wisdom books its notebook.

paras: The word 'psalm' comes from the Greek psalmos, a song sung to a plucked instrument such as a harp. The Hebrew title of the book is Tehillim, 'praises'. There are 150 psalms. They are divided into five 'books', perhaps to match the five books of Moses: Psalms 1 to 41, 42 to 72, 73 to 89, 90 to 106, and 107 to 150. Each of the first four ends with a short burst of praise, a doxology, such as 'Blessed be Yahweh, the God of Israel, from everlasting and to everlasting! Amen and amen' (41:13). The last psalm, 150, is all praise and closes the whole book.

A note on numbers. The ancient Greek translation, the Septuagint, joined some psalms together and split others, so from Psalm 10 to 147 its numbers usually run one behind the Hebrew. Orthodox churches and older Catholic Bibles follow the Greek; Jews, Protestants and most modern Bibles follow the Hebrew. So the Lord's my shepherd is Psalm 23 in one Bible and Psalm 22 in another. This journey uses the Hebrew numbers.
background.key: 150 psalms in five books, each closing with a doxology. Greek and Latin numbering usually runs one behind the Hebrew from Psalm 10 to 147.

paras: Many psalms have a heading. In the Hebrew, 73 name David; others name Asaph and 'the sons of Korah', both guilds of Temple singers; one names Moses (Psalm 90) and two Solomon (72 and 127). Some headings give a tune or an occasion. Jewish tradition (the Talmud, the great collection of rabbinic discussion completed around AD 500, at Bava Batra 14b–15a) says David wrote the book with the help of ten elders, among them Adam, Abraham and Moses. A scroll found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, the ancient manuscripts discovered in caves near the Dead Sea from 1947, credits David with 4,050 songs.

Most scholars think the Psalms were written over five centuries or more, from the time of the kings to after the exile; Psalm 137, sung in Babylon, cannot be earlier than 587 BC. The headings were probably added by later editors. The Hebrew phrase le-David can mean 'by David', 'for David', 'about David' or 'belonging to the David collection'. Muslims also honour the Psalms: the Qur'an calls them the Zabur, given to David (4:163).
background.key: 73 psalms name David in their headings; others name Temple singers. Most scholars think they span five centuries; 'of David' may mean by, for or about him.

paras: Psalm 1 is the doorway to the whole book: whoever put the collection together placed it first, to say what kind of life the Psalms are about. Psalm 23 is the best-known psalm in the world, prayed at bedsides and gravesides. Together they show the Psalms at their most confident.

The comparison is Psalm 13, one of the shortest prayers of complaint: four times 'How long?'. We read it so that you see from the start that the songbook holds every mood, not only the happy ones. It also lets us watch how Hebrew poetry works, line by line.
background.key: Psalm 1 opens the book; Psalm 23 is its best-loved prayer; Psalm 13 shows from the start that the Psalms hold complaint as well as trust.
