sessions.readWhy: The doorway to the Psalms, and the most loved psalm of all.

paras:
but his delight is in Yahweh’s law.
On his law he meditates day and night.

He will be like a tree planted by the streams of water,
that produces its fruit in its season,
whose leaf also does not wither.
Whatever he does shall prosper.

The wicked are not so,
but are like the chaff which the wind drives away.

Therefore the wicked shall not stand in the judgment,
nor sinners in the congregation of the righteous.

For Yahweh knows the way of the righteous,
but the way of the wicked shall perish.

Yahweh is my shepherd:
I shall lack nothing.

He makes me lie down in green pastures.
He leads me beside still waters.

He restores my soul.
He guides me in the paths of righteousness for his name’s sake.

Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death,
I will fear no evil, for you are with me.
Your rod and your staff,
they comfort me.

You prepare a table before me
in the presence of my enemies.
You anoint my head with oil.
My cup runs over.

Surely goodness and loving kindness shall follow me all the days of my life,
and I will dwell in Yahweh’s house forever.

parts.title: Two ways
parts.context: The first psalm of the book, with no heading and no named author. Most scholars think it was written late, perhaps after the exile, by the editors who arranged the collection, as an introduction. It is a wisdom psalm: it sounds more like Proverbs than like a hymn.

commentary.on: Blessed is the man who doesn't walk in the counsel of the wicked, nor stand on the path of sinners, nor sit in the seat of scoffers
commentary.text: The book of prayers begins not with a prayer but with a description of a happy life. 'Blessed' (Hebrew ashrei) means something like 'how fortunate'. Notice the three verbs: walk, stand, sit. They picture a slow slide, from going along with bad advice, to lingering, to settling down among people who sneer.

commentary.on: but his delight is in Yahweh's law. On his law he meditates day and night.
commentary.text: 'Law' is torah, which means 'teaching' or 'instruction', not only rules. 'Meditates' (hagah) is the word for a low murmur, a lion's growl or a dove's coo: in the ancient world people read aloud, even to themselves. To meditate was to mutter the words over until they sank in. 'Yahweh' is the WEB's spelling of God's personal name, which most English Bibles print as 'the LORD'.

commentary.on: He will be like a tree planted by the streams of water, that produces its fruit in its season, whose leaf also does not wither.
commentary.text: In a dry land, a tree beside an irrigation channel is the picture of life that doesn't depend on the weather. Jeremiah uses the same image (Jeremiah 17:8). Notice 'in its season': the psalm does not promise fruit every day.

commentary.on: The wicked are not so, but are like the chaff which the wind drives away.
commentary.text: Chaff is the husk left when grain is threshed and tossed in the wind: light, dry and gone. A tree has roots; chaff has none. The whole poem rests on that contrast.

commentary.on: For Yahweh knows the way of the righteous, but the way of the wicked shall perish.
commentary.text: The 'two ways' are a theme you will meet again in Proverbs. 'Knows' in Hebrew means more than 'is aware of': it means to care for, to be in relationship with. The psalm ends not with a rule but with a relationship.

parts.title: The Lord is my shepherd
parts.context: Headed 'A Psalm by David' in the Hebrew. David had been a shepherd before he was king, and kings in the ancient Near East were often called the 'shepherds' of their people. The psalm is a song of trust: no request, only confidence.

commentary.on: Yahweh is my shepherd: I shall lack nothing.
commentary.text: The king of Israel calls God his shepherd: the ruler admits he is one of the flock. A shepherd in Judah led his sheep to grass and water across dry hills, and guarded them at night. 'I shall lack nothing' is the confidence of a sheep that knows whose it is.

commentary.on: He restores my soul.
commentary.text: 'Soul' (nephesh) means the whole living self, even 'life' or 'breath'. 'Restores' can mean 'brings back': God brings the strayed or exhausted self home.

commentary.on: Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me.
commentary.text: Here the poem turns. Up to now the speaker has talked about God ('he'); now he talks to him ('you'). And the turn comes in the darkest place. The Hebrew tsalmavet can mean 'deep darkness' or 'death's shadow'. The psalm does not promise there will be no dark valley, only company in it.

commentary.on: You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies. You anoint my head with oil.
commentary.text: The picture changes from shepherd to host. In the ancient Near East a guest who ate at your table was under your protection, even from enemies watching outside. Oil on the head was a sign of welcome and of honour, the same word used of anointing kings.

commentary.on: Surely goodness and loving kindness shall follow me all the days of my life
commentary.text: 'Follow' is stronger in Hebrew: radaph means 'pursue', 'chase'. Enemies usually pursue; here goodness and loving kindness (hesed, God's faithful covenant love) run after the speaker. 'Yahweh's house' is the Temple, the place of God's presence.

paras:
How long, Yahweh?
Will you forget me forever?
How long will you hide your face from me?

How long shall I take counsel in my soul,
having sorrow in my heart every day?
How long shall my enemy triumph over me?

Behold, and answer me, Yahweh, my God.
Give light to my eyes, lest I sleep in death;

lest my enemy say, “I have prevailed against him;”
lest my adversaries rejoice when I fall.

But I trust in your loving kindness.
My heart rejoices in your salvation.

I will sing to Yahweh,
because he has been good to me.

parts.title: How long, Yahweh?
parts.context: Headed 'For the Chief Musician. A Psalm by David.' One of the shortest psalms of complaint. Nobody knows the occasion: the speaker names an enemy but no event, which is why anyone can pray it.

commentary.on: How long, Yahweh? Will you forget me forever? How long will you hide your face from me?
commentary.text: Four times 'How long?' in two verses. The speaker accuses God of forgetting him and hiding his face, the opposite of the blessing 'Yahweh make his face to shine on you' (Numbers 6:25). This is complaint, spoken directly to God.

commentary.on: How long shall I take counsel in my soul, having sorrow in my heart every day?
commentary.text: Watch the pairs: 'take counsel in my soul' and 'sorrow in my heart'. That is Hebrew poetry. It doesn't rhyme; it repeats the thought in a second line that echoes or sharpens the first. Scholars call this parallelism.

commentary.on: Behold, and answer me, Yahweh, my God. Give light to my eyes, lest I sleep in death
commentary.text: After the complaint, the plea: look, answer, give light. 'Give light to my eyes' may mean 'keep me alive', since dim eyes were a sign of approaching death.

commentary.on: But I trust in your loving kindness. My heart rejoices in your salvation.
commentary.text: Then, with one word, 'But', the psalm turns to trust. Nothing in the situation has changed: no answer has come, no enemy has gone. The turn is in the speaker. Complaint, plea, trust: you will meet this shape again and again.

commentary.on: I will sing to Yahweh, because he has been good to me.
commentary.text: The last line looks back ('has been good') to find hope for what is ahead. Many psalms do this: memory of past mercy holds the speaker up in the present.

compare.why: The songbook does not only hold confident songs. Psalm 13 is a prayer from the bottom: read it to see how a psalm of complaint is built, and how Hebrew poetry works line by line.
compare.title: How long?

sections.h: A book made of many books
paras: The Psalms were not written as a book; they were gathered into one. You can still see the seams. Psalm 72 ends: 'This ends the prayers by David, the son of Jesse' (72:20), yet more psalms of David follow later. Psalms 14 and 53 are almost the same psalm, copied into two collections. Groups of psalms belong together: the 'Songs of Ascents' (120–134), probably sung by pilgrims going up to Jerusalem; the psalms of Asaph (50, 73–83); the psalms of the sons of Korah (42–49, 84–85, 87–88).

Among the Dead Sea Scrolls, copied between about 250 BC and AD 68, there are around forty manuscripts of the Psalms, more than of any other book. Some keep a different order and add psalms not in our Bibles, including Psalm 151, which the Greek Bible and the Orthodox churches still include. So the collection was still settling in the last centuries before Christ, though the core was long fixed.

Someone then shaped the whole. It opens with Psalm 1, the happy life of the one who meditates on God's teaching, and Psalm 2, God's anointed king. It ends with five psalms of pure praise. Many scholars read the book as a journey: from obedience, through lament (complaint is commonest in the first half), to praise.
sections.key: The Psalms were gathered from older collections, still settling in the Dead Sea Scrolls, and shaped into a journey from Psalm 1's obedience to Psalm 150's praise.

paras: English poems used to rhyme. Hebrew poems don't. Their music is in the thought. In 1753 Robert Lowth, an Oxford professor of poetry who later became Bishop of London, published his lectures on the sacred poetry of the Hebrews. He showed that most lines come in pairs (sometimes threes), and that the second half answers the first. He called this parallelism, and sorted it into kinds: the second line can repeat the first in other words, or state its opposite, or carry it further.

Look at Psalm 23: 'He makes me lie down in green pastures. He leads me beside still waters.' The second line says nearly the same, with a new picture. Psalm 1: 'For Yahweh knows the way of the righteous, but the way of the wicked shall perish': the opposite.

Later scholars, among them James Kugel (1981) and Robert Alter (1985), pointed out that the second line rarely just repeats. It usually sharpens: 'A, and what's more, B'. 'How long will you forget me? How long will you hide your face?' moves from being forgotten to being turned away from. One happy result: because the poetry lives in meaning, not in sound, the Psalms survive translation better than almost any poetry in the world.
sections.key: Hebrew poetry rhymes thoughts, not sounds: the second line echoes, contrasts or sharpens the first (Lowth, 1753). That is why the Psalms translate so well.

paras: Read straight through and the Psalms swing between praise and grief, trust and fury, thanks and confession. In the 1920s the German scholar Hermann Gunkel sorted them by type: hymns of praise; laments, by one person or the whole people; songs of thanksgiving; royal psalms for the king; wisdom psalms like Psalm 1. Most scholars still use his types.

Early Christian teachers saw the same range. Athanasius of Alexandria, in his Letter to Marcellinus (fourth century), said that most of Scripture speaks to us, but the Psalms speak for us: whoever reads them finds their own feelings already written down, like looking in a mirror. John Calvin, introducing his commentary on the Psalms in 1557, called the book an anatomy of every part of the soul: there is no emotion, he said, that is not pictured there.
That is the first answer to the question of this journey. If you want to know how to pray, the Bible does not give you a method first. It gives you 150 examples, and none of them pretends.
sections.key: The Psalms hold every mood: praise, lament, thanks, confession. Athanasius said they speak for us, not only to us; Calvin called them an anatomy of the soul.

sections.h: Sung in the Temple, the synagogue and the church
paras: The Psalms were made to be sung aloud, together. The books of Chronicles describe guilds of Levite singers in the Temple, led by Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun (1 Chronicles 25). The Mishnah, the first written collection of Jewish oral law (about AD 200), lists the psalm the Levites sang for each day of the week (Tamid 7:4). In the synagogue, Psalms 113 to 118, the Hallel ('praise'), are sung at festivals and at the Passover meal. When the Gospels say that Jesus and his disciples 'sung a hymn' after the Last Supper (Mark 14:26), it was probably the Hallel.

The church kept singing. The Rule of Benedict (about 530) has monks pray all 150 psalms every week, and remarks that the early monks did it in a single day. The Book of Common Prayer (1549, 1662) sets the whole Psalter to be read every month. The Reformers in Geneva and Scotland put the psalms into rhyming verse so whole congregations could sing them: the Geneva Psalter (1562) and the Scottish Psalter (1650), whose 'The Lord's my shepherd, I'll not want' is still sung to the tune Crimond. Orthodox monasteries read the whole Psalter every week. More people have prayed with these words than with any others.
sections.key: Sung by Levites in the Temple, in the synagogue's Hallel, by monks weekly (Benedict), monthly in the Prayer Book, in metre in Geneva and Scotland.

sections.h: The Psalms in English and in the West
paras: English speakers have prayed the Psalms in three great versions. Miles Coverdale translated them for his Bible of 1535; his version went into the Book of Common Prayer and is still sung at evensong, which is why many people know 'The Lord is my shepherd: therefore can I lack nothing' rather than the King James wording. The King James Bible of 1611 gave the other familiar form, 'The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want'. The metrical psalms of Scotland and New England gave a third.

Their words run through Western culture. Psalm 23 is read at more funerals than any other text. Handel's Messiah quotes Psalms 2, 16, 22, 24 and 68. Bach, Monteverdi, Mendelssohn, Brahms and Stravinsky (Symphony of Psalms, 1930) set them. Lincoln's Second Inaugural Address (1865) answered its own hardest question with Psalm 19:9, and the astronauts of Apollo 11 left on the Moon a disc of goodwill messages, among them Pope Paul VI's, which quoted Psalm 8. Phrases like 'out of the mouths of babes', 'at their wits' end' and 'the apple of my eye' come from the Psalms.

You do not need to believe anything to see that these prayers shaped how the West speaks of grief, trust and praise. Whether they are more than that is the question the rest of this journey will put to the test.
sections.key: Coverdale (1535, the Prayer Book), the King James (1611) and the metrical psalms carried the Psalms into English; their words run through Western music, speech and funerals.

refs: Talmud, Bava Batra 14b–15a; Mishnah, Tamid 7:4; the Great Psalms Scroll from Qumran (11QPs-a), column 27 ('David's compositions').
Robert Lowth, De sacra poesi Hebraeorum (Lectures on the Sacred Poetry of the Hebrews), Oxford, 1753; James Kugel, The Idea of Biblical Poetry (1981); Robert Alter, The Art of Biblical Poetry (1985).
Hermann Gunkel, Einleitung in die Psalmen (completed by Joachim Begrich, 1933); Athanasius, Letter to Marcellinus 10–12; John Calvin, Commentary on the Psalms, author's preface (1557).
The Rule of Benedict, chapters 16–18; The Book of Common Prayer (1662), the Psalter and its table; the Geneva Psalter (1562); The Psalms of David in Metre (Scotland, 1650).

debate.question: Did David write the Psalms?

positions.name: Yes, most of them
positions.who: Jewish and Christian tradition: the Talmud (Bava Batra 14b); the New Testament writers; most readers until the 1700s; some conservative scholars today
positions.view: David was a musician and poet (1 Samuel 16:23; 2 Samuel 1:17–27; 23:1, 'the sweet psalmist of Israel'). The headings are old and name him 73 times. Jesus and the apostles quote psalms as David's (Mark 12:36; Acts 2:25).
positions.evidence: The headings; David's harp and laments in Samuel; the New Testament's use; the 11QPs-a scroll's tribute to David's songs.

positions.name: No: a library of many hands
positions.who: Most modern scholars, from Hermann Gunkel on
positions.view: The Psalms come from many poets over five or six centuries. Some are plainly later than David: Psalm 137 is set in the exile. The headings were added by editors, and their 'of David' means 'belonging to the David collection' or 'in David's style'.
positions.evidence: Psalm 137; differences of language and theme; duplicate psalms in different collections (14 and 53); the Septuagint adding headings the Hebrew lacks.

positions.name: David as the founder of a tradition
positions.who: Many scholars and theologians today, Jewish and Christian
positions.view: David may well have written some psalms and certainly founded Israel's tradition of Temple song. The collection grew around his name, as a school grows around its founder. The headings are an early way of reading the psalms: they invite us to imagine David praying them in his own life.
positions.evidence: Chronicles credits David with organising the singers; thirteen headings tie psalms to scenes from David's story (e.g. Psalm 51 to Nathan, Psalm 3 to Absalom); the growth of credit to David from the Hebrew to the Greek to the Dead Sea Scrolls.

debate.agree: All agree that the Psalms were sung and prayed by Israel over centuries, and that their value as prayer does not depend on who wrote each one.

look.why: No painting for this session. The National Gallery of Art's open collection has no painting of David as a psalmist or harpist that is free to use here, and we do not use a stand-in.

music.why: Psalm 23 in the Scottish metrical version of 1650, sung to the tune Crimond: the psalms as Reformed Scotland made them, for a whole congregation to sing.

think.why: Saying the same words day after day, as monks and synagogues have done with the Psalms: does repeated practice change who we are?

learn.why: The most prayed psalm in the world. Learn the first four verses; they were made to be said aloud.

check.q: Why does Psalm 1 come first in the book of prayers, though it contains no prayer?
options: Because the editors placed it as a doorway, to describe the life the Psalms are about: delighting in God's teaching
Because the Temple service always began with it
Because it is the oldest psalm
Because David wrote it first
check.why: Most scholars think Psalm 1 is a late wisdom psalm placed first as an introduction. Its position, not its date, is the point.

check.q: Which best describes how Hebrew poetry works?
options: Poems are always acrostics, one letter per verse
Each line has exactly the same number of syllables
The second line of a pair echoes, contrasts or sharpens the thought of the first
Lines rhyme in pairs, as in English hymns
check.why: Lowth called it parallelism; Kugel and Alter showed the second line usually intensifies. Some psalms are acrostics, but not most.

check.q: In Psalm 23 the speaker stops talking about God and starts talking to him. Where, and why does it matter?
options: Nowhere: the psalm speaks about God throughout
At 'He restores my soul', because the soul is the subject
At 'Surely goodness', because the poem ends there
At 'the valley of the shadow of death', because God's presence is felt most directly in the darkest place
check.why: 'I will fear no evil, for you are with me': the switch to 'you' comes in the dark valley, not the green pasture.

check.q: Psalm 13 ends in trust. What has changed between its opening and its close?
options: The speaker has died and gone to God
God has answered audibly
The enemy has been defeated
Nothing outside the speaker: the turn to trust comes before any rescue
check.why: No answer or rescue is described. 'But I trust' is a choice made inside the complaint, which is the pattern of many laments.

check.q: A psalm's heading says 'of David'. What is the most careful conclusion?
options: David certainly wrote it
The Hebrew can mean by, for, about or belonging to David's collection, so the heading alone doesn't settle authorship
It was written for David's funeral
David certainly did not write it
check.why: Le-David is ambiguous, and most scholars think headings were added by later editors; tradition reads them as authorship.

check.q: Why might the Psalms survive translation better than most poetry?
options: Because translators have changed them very little
Because their poetry lives in meaning and images, not in rhyme or sound
Because they were first written in English
Because they are mostly in prose
check.why: Parallelism repeats and sharpens thoughts, and thoughts carry across languages in a way rhyme and metre cannot.

tutorial.question: 'The Psalms are not a book of answers but a book of prayers.' Explain and assess, with reference to Psalms 1, 13 and 23.
tutorial.approach: Start with what the Psalms are: a collection of songs for worship, gathered over centuries. Then look at the three psalms: one teaches (Psalm 1), one trusts (Psalm 23), one complains (Psalm 13). Ask whether teaching and prayer can be separated. Use parallelism to show how the poems work on the reader. End with what it means that the Bible gives examples of prayer rather than a method.
strong: Explains how the Psalter was collected and shaped (five books, Psalm 1 as doorway).
Shows how parallelism works, with an example from each psalm.
Notes the turn to 'you' in Psalm 23:4 and the turn to trust in Psalm 13:5.
Recognises that Psalm 1 is a wisdom psalm that teaches rather than prays.
Uses Athanasius or Calvin on the Psalms as a mirror of the soul.
Mentions how the Psalms were and are used: Temple, synagogue, monastery, congregation.

reading.title: Reflections on the Psalms
reading.why: A short, honest book by a layman for laymen, including the hard psalms.

reading.author: Robert Alter
reading.title: The Book of Psalms: A Translation with Commentary
reading.why: A literary translation that keeps the Hebrew's compression, with notes on every line.

reading.author: Robert Alter
reading.title: The Art of Biblical Poetry
reading.why: How Hebrew parallelism really works, and why the second line sharpens the first.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: read one psalm aloud each morning, slowly, the way 'meditate' in Psalm 1 means: Psalms 1, 23, 13, 121, 46, 100 and 150. Notice which line stays with you, and say it again before you sleep.
sessions.reflect: Which of the three psalms sounds most like you today: the tree by the water, the sheep in the dark valley, or the voice asking 'How long?'
takeaways: The Psalms are 150 songs and prayers in five books, gathered over centuries and shaped from Psalm 1's happy obedience to Psalm 150's praise.
Hebrew poetry rhymes thoughts, not sounds: the second line echoes, contrasts or sharpens the first.
The Psalms hold every human mood, and they were made to be said aloud and together, in Temple, synagogue and church.

sessions.title: Angry with God
sessions.line: The psalm with no happy ending, the psalms that curse, and why the Bible teaches people to argue with God instead of pretending.
sessions.plain: Many people assume that you must be polite to God, or at least cheerful. The Psalms say otherwise. The most common kind of psalm is the lament: a complaint to God, sometimes furious, sometimes despairing. This session reads Psalm 88, the darkest prayer in the Bible, which ends in darkness with no comfort at all, and the 'cursing psalms', which ask God to destroy enemies. It asks whether it is all right to be angry with God, and what to do with prayers that shock us.
sessions.why: Session 1 showed that the Psalms hold every mood, and met complaint briefly in Psalm 13, which turned to trust. Now we go to the bottom: what happens when the turn never comes, and when the complaint turns to rage?
answers: Is it all right to complain to God?
Why are some psalms so dark? Is there one with no happy ending?
What do you do with the psalms that curse their enemies?
How have Jews and Christians prayed these psalms?
sessions.finding: Lament is the most common kind of psalm: the Bible teaches people to argue with God, not to pretend.

paras: In session 1 you met the shape of a lament in Psalm 13: complaint ('How long?'), plea ('answer me') and trust ('But I trust in your loving kindness'). Most laments follow that shape and end in praise or a promise to praise.

Hermann Gunkel, the scholar who sorted the psalms by type, found that laments are the largest single group: by most counts around a third of the whole book, more than the hymns of praise. Some are prayed by one person (Psalms 6, 13, 22, 88); some by the whole people after a disaster (Psalms 44, 74, 79). The Bible's songbook, in other words, is full of complaint.
background.key: Laments follow the shape complaint, plea, trust. They are the largest single type of psalm, about a third of the book.

paras: The Hebrew heading of Psalm 88 calls it a song of the sons of Korah, a guild of Temple singers, and a maskil (perhaps 'a skilful song') of Heman the Ezrahite. Heman appears among the Temple musicians in Chronicles (1 Chronicles 6:33; 15:19), and a wise man called Heman is named beside Solomon (1 Kings 4:31). The heading also gives a tune or mode, mahalath leannoth, whose meaning is lost; it may mean 'for sickness, to afflict'.

We know nothing else about the poet. The psalm itself suggests long illness from youth, and abandonment by friends. Nobody can date it. Like most laments it gives no names or events, which is what allowed later people in every kind of darkness to pray it as their own.
background.key: Psalm 88 is credited to Heman the Ezrahite of the sons of Korah. It names no event, so anyone can pray it.

paras: To read Psalm 88 you need one idea. Most of the Old Testament has little hope of life after death. The dead go down to Sheol, also called 'the pit': a shadowy place under the earth where they are 'cut off' from life, and, in most texts, from the praise of God. Clearer hope of resurrection comes late, in Daniel 12:2 (second century BC).

So when the psalmist asks 'Do the departed spirits rise up and praise you?', he is not asking a theology question. He is bargaining: if I die, you lose a worshipper. It is a bold argument to put to God, and it is in the Bible.
background.key: In most of the Old Testament the dead go to Sheol, 'the pit', cut off from life and praise. The psalmist argues from that: if I die, you lose my praise.

paras: Psalm 88 is the one lament in the Psalter that never turns to trust or praise. Its last word in Hebrew is 'darkness'. If any psalm shows whether the Bible allows despair to be spoken to God, it is this one.

The comparison is two of the 'cursing psalms': Psalm 58, against corrupt judges, and the last verses of Psalm 137, against Babylon (you read its first verses in 'Kings and prophets'). They raise the opposite problem. Psalm 88 is too sad; these seem too angry. What can a believer do with them?
background.key: Psalm 88 is the only lament with no turn to trust; Psalms 58 and 137:7–9 are cursing psalms. Too sad, and too angry: both are in the Bible.

before: Psalm 88 opens with 'the God of my salvation'. Does anything else in the psalm sound hopeful?
Count the questions in verses 10 to 12. What argument is the psalmist making?
In Psalms 58 and 137, who is cursed, and what have they done?
sessions.readWhy: The darkest prayer in the Bible, with no comfort at its end.

paras:
Yahweh, the God of my salvation,
I have cried day and night before you.

Let my prayer enter into your presence.
Turn your ear to my cry.

For my soul is full of troubles.
My life draws near to Sheol.

I am counted among those who go down into the pit.
I am like a man who has no help,

set apart among the dead,
like the slain who lie in the grave,
whom you remember no more.
They are cut off from your hand.

You have laid me in the lowest pit,
in the darkest depths.

Your wrath lies heavily on me.
You have afflicted me with all your waves.

You have taken my friends from me.
You have made me an abomination to them.
I am confined, and I can’t escape.

My eyes are dim from grief.
I have called on you daily, Yahweh.
I have spread out my hands to you.

Do you show wonders to the dead?
Do the departed spirits rise up and praise you?

Is your loving kindness declared in the grave?
Or your faithfulness in Destruction?

Are your wonders made known in the dark?
Or your righteousness in the land of forgetfulness?

But to you, Yahweh, I have cried.
In the morning, my prayer comes before you.

Yahweh, why do you reject my soul?
Why do you hide your face from me?

I am afflicted and ready to die from my youth up.
While I suffer your terrors, I am distracted.

Your fierce wrath has gone over me.
Your terrors have cut me off.

They came around me like water all day long.
They completely engulfed me.

You have put lover and friend far from me,
and my friends into darkness.

parts.title: Darkness is my closest friend
parts.context: A lament by one person, credited to Heman the Ezrahite. It is the only psalm of complaint that never turns to trust. It was probably sung, or at least kept, in the Temple: Israel chose to keep this prayer in its songbook.

commentary.on: Yahweh, the God of my salvation, I have cried day and night before you.
commentary.text: Hold on to the first line. It is the only hopeful phrase in the psalm: 'the God of my salvation'. Everything that follows is complaint, but it is all addressed to God. Even in despair the speaker has not stopped praying.

commentary.on: I am counted among those who go down into the pit. I am like a man who has no help
commentary.text: The speaker is so ill or so near death that people already count him among the dead. 'The pit' is Sheol. 'Whom you remember no more': the worst thing about death, for the psalmist, is being forgotten by God.

commentary.on: You have laid me in the lowest pit, in the darkest depths. Your wrath lies heavily on me.
commentary.text: Now he blames God directly: 'you have laid me', 'your wrath'. He does not soften it or explain it. Many readers find this shocking. The Bible keeps it.

commentary.on: You have taken my friends from me. You have made me an abomination to them.
commentary.text: Illness in the ancient world often meant isolation: those with skin diseases were put outside the camp (Leviticus 13:46). The speaker is not only sick but alone, and he says God did that too.

commentary.on: Do you show wonders to the dead? Do the departed spirits rise up and praise you?
commentary.text: Three pairs of questions, each expecting the answer no. They are an argument: you are the God of loving kindness and faithfulness, but no one in the grave can tell of it. Keep me alive, for your own sake. Arguing with God in this way has a long history in Israel: Abraham over Sodom (Genesis 18), Moses after the golden calf (Exodus 32).

commentary.on: But to you, Yahweh, I have cried. In the morning, my prayer comes before you.
commentary.text: This 'But' is where a lament usually turns to trust, as in Psalm 13. Here it turns only to more prayer. The speaker keeps showing up, every morning.

commentary.on: You have put lover and friend far from me, and my friends into darkness.
commentary.text: The psalm ends here. The Hebrew can be read 'my companions are darkness', or 'darkness is my closest friend'. There is no turn, no praise, no comfort. And yet the whole psalm, from first line to last, is spoken to God.

paras:
Do you indeed speak righteousness, silent ones?
Do you judge blamelessly, you sons of men?

No, in your heart you plot injustice.
You measure out the violence of your hands in the earth.

The wicked go astray from the womb.
They are wayward as soon as they are born, speaking lies.

Their poison is like the poison of a snake,
like a deaf cobra that stops its ear,

which doesn’t listen to the voice of charmers,
no matter how skillful the charmer may be.

Break their teeth, God, in their mouth.
Break out the great teeth of the young lions, Yahweh.

Let them vanish like water that flows away.
When they draw the bow, let their arrows be made blunt.

Let them be like a snail which melts and passes away,
like the stillborn child, who has not seen the sun.

Before your pots can feel the heat of the thorns,
he will sweep away the green and the burning alike.

The righteous shall rejoice when he sees the vengeance.
He shall wash his feet in the blood of the wicked,

so that men shall say, “Most certainly there is a reward for the righteous.
Most certainly there is a God who judges the earth.”

Remember, Yahweh, against the children of Edom in the day of Jerusalem,
who said, “Raze it!
Raze it even to its foundation!”

Daughter of Babylon, doomed to destruction,
he will be happy who repays you,
as you have done to us.

Happy shall he be,
who takes and dashes your little ones against the rock.

parts.title: Break their teeth
parts.context: Headed 'For the Chief Musician. To the tune of Do Not Destroy. A poem by David.' It is addressed first to unjust rulers or judges (the Hebrew of verse 1 is uncertain: 'silent ones' may be 'gods' or 'mighty ones'), then to God, asking him to destroy them.

commentary.on: Do you indeed speak righteousness, silent ones? Do you judge blamelessly, you sons of men?
commentary.text: The target is not a personal enemy but corrupt judges, people with power over the weak. The anger of this psalm is anger at injustice, the same anger you heard in the prophets.

commentary.on: Break their teeth, God, in their mouth.
commentary.text: Now the curse. It is violent, and it is a prayer: the speaker does not break anyone's teeth; he asks God to. Notice the pictures of the judges as lions with great teeth, a snail that melts away, water that drains off. It is the language of rage.

commentary.on: He shall wash his feet in the blood of the wicked
commentary.text: The most disturbing line. It pictures a battlefield after victory. A modern reader recoils, rightly. But read on to see what the psalmist wants above all.

commentary.on: Most certainly there is a God who judges the earth.
commentary.text: This is the point. The psalm's deepest wish is not blood but justice: that the world should be seen not to be ruled by the corrupt. It is the cry of people for whom human courts have failed.

parts.title: By the rivers of Babylon: the ending
parts.context: You may have read the first six verses in 'Kings and prophets': exiles in Babylon, after 587 BC, hang up their harps and refuse to sing the songs of Zion. These are the three verses that follow, and that churches have often left out.

commentary.on: Remember, Yahweh, against the children of Edom in the day of Jerusalem
commentary.text: Edom, Judah's neighbour to the south-east, cheered on the Babylonians as they destroyed Jerusalem (Obadiah 10–14). The exiles remember who stood by and laughed.

commentary.on: he will be happy who repays you, as you have done to us.
commentary.text: 'As you have done to us': the psalmist asks for Babylon to suffer what Jerusalem suffered. That is the old law of retaliation, measure for measure.

commentary.on: Happy shall he be, who takes and dashes your little ones against the rock.
commentary.text: The worst line in the Psalms. Ancient armies did kill children when a city fell, and the Babylonians had done it in Jerusalem (Lamentations 2:20–21). The psalmist wishes the same on them. It is honest about what grief and humiliation do to people. Whether it may be prayed is the question of this session's debate.

compare.why: Psalm 88 is too sad for many readers; these are too angry. Read two of the 'cursing psalms' and ask what they are for.
compare.title: The cursing psalms

paras: A lament usually has five parts, though not always in order: an address to God ('O God'), the complaint (what is wrong, often with 'why?' and 'how long?'), the plea (what the speaker wants God to do), a reason why God should act (his loving kindness, his reputation, past mercies), and a turn to trust or a vow to praise. Psalm 13 has them all in six verses.

The American scholar Walter Brueggemann (The Message of the Psalms, 1984) offered a simple map. Some psalms are songs of orientation: life is in order, God is good (Psalm 1). Some are songs of disorientation: the world has fallen apart (Psalm 88). Some are songs of new orientation: a surprised joy after rescue (Psalm 30). Real life, he argued, moves through all three, and the Psalms give words for each.

His sharpest point was a warning. Churches that sing only songs of orientation, he said, teach people to pretend. When disaster comes, they have no words for it, and may conclude that faith has nothing to say about the dark. The Psalter does the opposite: by giving lament so much room, it tells sufferers that their complaint already belongs inside the life of faith, not outside it. Psalm 13 shows the whole movement in miniature; Psalm 88 shows that the movement can stall, and the prayer still be kept.
sections.key: A lament: address, complaint, plea, reason, trust. Brueggemann: orientation, disorientation, new orientation. Singing only happy songs teaches people to pretend.

paras: Lament assumes something surprising: that God can be argued with. Abraham bargains over Sodom: 'Shouldn't the Judge of all the earth do right?' (Genesis 18:25). Moses talks God out of destroying Israel (Exodus 32). Job demands a hearing. Jeremiah complains that God has overpowered and tricked him (Jeremiah 20:7). The book of Lamentations, written after the fall of Jerusalem, is five laments in a row.

Jewish tradition has kept this boldness. The Talmud tells of rabbis who argued with God, and later Jewish writers, after the pogroms and the Holocaust, wrote prayers that put God on trial. Many Christians have felt less free. Yet the New Testament keeps it too: Jesus in Gethsemane asks for the cup to pass (Mark 14:36), and on the cross he prays a lament, the first line of Psalm 22: 'My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?' (Mark 15:34).

What makes it faith and not just anger? The address. A lament is said to God. The one who complains still believes there is someone to complain to, who ought to answer. The opposite of lament is not praise but silence: giving up on God altogether.
sections.key: Abraham, Moses, Job, Jeremiah and Jesus all argued with God. A lament is faith because it is addressed to God; its opposite is not praise but silence.

sections.h: Psalm 88: the prayer that doesn't resolve
paras: Why would anyone keep a prayer with no hope in it? Readers have given several answers. First, honesty: some people do not get better, and the Bible gives them words too. Second, persistence: the speaker prays 'day and night' and 'in the morning'; he has not let go. Third, its place: Psalm 88 sits next to Psalm 89, a long hymn to God's faithfulness to David that also ends in bitter complaint. The editors set darkness and promise side by side without resolving them.

Christians have long linked Psalm 88 with the death of Jesus: the Catholic night prayer, Compline, sets it for Fridays, the day of the crucifixion. People caring for the dying, and people in long depression, have said it is the one psalm that does not ask them to feel better than they do.

If you are in that darkness yourself, the psalm's example is to say so, to God and to someone near you. A doctor, a friend, a pastor or a helpline such as Samaritans (116 123 in the UK and Ireland) can help you carry it.
sections.key: Psalm 88 keeps praying with no answer; it sits beside Psalm 89's unresolved promise, and it gives words to those who do not get better.

sections.h: What to do with the cursing psalms
paras: The 'imprecatory' psalms (from Latin imprecari, to call down a curse), chiefly 35, 58, 69, 109 and 137, have troubled readers for centuries. Three main ways of reading them have emerged.

Augustine of Hippo (354–430), in his Expositions of the Psalms, read them spiritually: the 'little ones' of Babylon in Psalm 137 are our sinful desires while they are still small, to be dashed against the rock, which is Christ. Monks prayed the curses against sin and the devil. C. S. Lewis, in Reflections on the Psalms (1958), refused to soften them: he called their hatred plainly wicked, but argued that they show honestly what injustice does to its victims, and that they come from people who took right and wrong seriously, as the indifferent do not. Dietrich Bonhoeffer, in his little book on the Psalms (1940), written as the Nazi state tightened its grip, argued that the psalmist hands vengeance over to God instead of taking it himself, and that Christians pray these psalms with Christ, who bore God's judgement and prayed for his enemies.

Jewish readers have often seen the curses as a cry for justice against real oppressors, which Jews have had too much cause to pray. All these readings agree on one thing: the curses are prayers. They are given to God, not acted out.
sections.key: Augustine read the curses against sin; Lewis called their hatred wicked but honest; Bonhoeffer said they give vengeance to God. All agree they are prayed, not acted out.

paras: Israel kept lamenting long after the Psalms. The book of Lamentations mourns the fall of Jerusalem in 587 BC in five poems, four of them acrostics, one verse for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet: grief given shape, so that it can be said from A to Z. Jews still read it on Tisha B'Av, the fast that remembers the destruction of both Temples. The communal laments (Psalms 44, 74, 79) ask why God has let his people be crushed; Psalm 44 even says, 'Wake up! Why do you sleep, Lord?' (44:23).

Christians have lamented too, though less boldly in public worship. The enslaved Africans of the American South made laments of their own in the spirituals, songs of sorrow sung to God and to one another. After the twentieth century's wars and the Holocaust, theologians Jewish and Christian turned back to lament as the only honest language for faith in the face of horror.

The lesson of this session for anyone, believer or not, is practical. Grief that is spoken, in a shape and to someone, can be borne in a way that grief kept silent often cannot. The Psalms give the shape. They also insist on the someone.
sections.key: Lamentations (read at Tisha B'Av), the communal laments, the spirituals and post-Holocaust theology kept lament alive: grief given shape and spoken to someone.

debate.question: Should churches still sing the cursing psalms?

positions.name: Leave them out of worship
positions.who: The Catholic Liturgy of the Hours since 1971, which omits Psalms 58, 83 and 109 and some verses such as 137:7–9; many modern hymn books and lectionaries
positions.view: These verses express hatred that Jesus taught his followers to overcome: 'love your enemies' (Matthew 5:44). Said aloud in worship, by people with no context, they can teach the wrong thing. They remain in the Bible to be studied, not sung.
positions.evidence: The 1971 General Instruction (§131) gives pastoral reasons for the omissions; Matthew 5:44; Romans 12:19–21.

positions.name: Keep them: they are honest
positions.who: C. S. Lewis (in part); Walter Brueggemann; many Jewish and liberation theologians
positions.view: Victims of injustice need words for their rage. Praying it to God is better than acting on it or denying it. Leaving these psalms out lets comfortable people forget that others are crying out against oppressors.
positions.evidence: Psalm 58's target is corrupt judges; Psalm 137 comes from the survivors of a sacked city; Revelation 6:10, the martyrs' 'How long?'

positions.name: Keep them, read through Christ
positions.who: Augustine; Benedictine monks, who pray the whole Psalter; Dietrich Bonhoeffer
positions.view: The whole Psalter is the prayer of Christ and his church. The curses are prayed against evil itself, or handed over to God, who in Christ took judgement on himself. Cutting them out makes the church's prayer smaller than the Bible's.
positions.evidence: Rule of Benedict 18 (all 150 psalms weekly); Augustine on Psalm 137; Bonhoeffer, Prayerbook of the Bible (1940).

debate.agree: All agree that the cursing psalms must not be used to justify violence, and that they show how seriously Israel took injustice.

look.why: No painting for this session. The few mourning figures in the National Gallery of Art's open collection are already used by other journeys, and we do not use a stand-in.

music.why: Gregorio Allegri's setting of Psalm 51, a lament of confession, written for the Sistine Chapel in the 1630s and sung in Holy Week in the dark: a lament made into some of the most beautiful music ever written.

think.why: How the great teachers, from Augustine on, have spoken about suffering and the God who seems silent.

learn.why: 'Out of the depths': a lament that does turn to hope, prayed at funerals and by Luther in his hymn. Learn it as the counterpart to Psalm 88.

check.q: What makes Psalm 88 different from almost every other lament?
options: It was written in Babylon
It is the longest psalm
It never turns to trust or praise, and ends in darkness
It is addressed to the king, not to God
check.why: Most laments turn ('But I trust...'); Psalm 88's 'But' (v. 13) leads only to more prayer, and its last word is darkness.

check.q: In Psalm 88:10–12 the speaker asks whether the dead praise God. What is the best reading of these questions?
options: They are a later Christian addition
They teach that the dead certainly praise God in heaven
They are an argument to God: if I die, you lose a worshipper, so keep me alive
They show the speaker no longer believes in God
check.why: Sheol was a place cut off from praise in most Old Testament thought; the psalmist bargains with God on that basis.

check.q: Why might Psalm 88 still count as a prayer of faith?
options: Because it is entirely addressed to God, and the speaker keeps praying day and night
Because it ends with a promise to praise
Because it blames the speaker's enemies, not God
Because it was written by David
check.why: Its only hopeful phrase is 'the God of my salvation', but every line is spoken to God. Giving up would be silence.

check.q: Psalm 58 asks God to break the teeth of corrupt judges. What does its last verse suggest the psalmist most wants?
options: That the judges will become his friends
Personal revenge on a neighbour
Wealth
That people will see there is a God who judges the earth: justice, not just blood
check.why: 'Most certainly there is a God who judges the earth.' The rage is at injustice.

check.q: How did Augustine read 'dashes your little ones against the rock' (Psalm 137:9)?
options: As a prophecy of the fall of Rome
Spiritually: the 'little ones' are sinful desires while still small, dashed against the rock, which is Christ
As a mistake in the text
As a command for Christians to fight Babylon
check.why: Augustine's spiritual reading let monks pray the verse against sin; modern readers debate whether that is honest to the text.

check.q: Which of these best states the common ground of Augustine, Lewis and Bonhoeffer on the cursing psalms?
options: They are prayers handed to God, not instructions to act
They were written by Christians
They prove the God of the Old Testament is cruel
They should be deleted from the Bible
check.why: However they read them, all three treat the curses as prayer, given to God, and none treats them as a licence for violence.

tutorial.question: Why does the Bible include prayers of complaint?
tutorial.approach: Begin with how common lament is (about a third of the Psalms) and its usual shape. Use Psalm 13 as the normal case and Psalm 88 as the extreme. Bring in the tradition of arguing with God (Abraham, Moses, Jeremiah, Jesus on the cross). Then deal honestly with the cursing psalms. End with what lament says about faith: is it the opposite of trust, or a form of it?
strong: Gives the shape of a lament and shows it in Psalm 13.
Explains why Psalm 88 is unique, and why it might have been kept.
Uses the idea of Sheol to explain Psalm 88:10–12.
Places lament in the wider tradition of arguing with God, including Jesus's use of Psalm 22.
Treats the cursing psalms fairly, with at least two readings (Augustine, Lewis, Bonhoeffer).
Uses Brueggemann's orientation, disorientation and new orientation, or a similar map.

reading.why: His chapter on the cursings is still the most honest short treatment.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: write a lament of your own, in the psalm's shape: address God, say plainly what is wrong, ask for what you want, give a reason, and end where you honestly are, even if that is not yet trust. It need be no longer than Psalm 13.
sessions.reflect: Have you ever felt you had to be polite to God, or pretend to feel better than you did? What would it mean to pray as Psalm 88 does?
takeaways: Lament is the most common kind of psalm: complaint, plea and, usually, a turn to trust.
Psalm 88 never turns, and ends in darkness, yet every line is spoken to God; the Bible keeps it.
The cursing psalms are rage at injustice handed over to God; Augustine, Lewis and Bonhoeffer read them differently, but all as prayer, not action.

sessions.title: The beginning of wisdom
sessions.line: A father's advice, a woman calling in the street, and an Egyptian book of thirty chapters: what the Bible means by wisdom, and whether goodness pays.
sessions.plain: After the Psalms comes Proverbs, a book of short sayings about how to live: work, money, words, friendship, anger, sex and God. It claims that wisdom 'begins' with 'the fear of the Lord'. This session asks what the Bible means by wisdom, whether Proverbs is just common sense, who the woman called Wisdom is, and how much of the book Israel shared with its neighbours. It ends with the hardest question Proverbs raises: does being good really pay?
sessions.why: Sessions 1 and 2 heard Israel talking to God: praising, trusting and complaining. Now we open its notebook: Israel thinking about life. Psalm 1, the doorway of the Psalms, already spoke of 'two ways'; Proverbs is a whole book about them.
answers: What is 'wisdom' in the Bible?
Is Proverbs just common sense?
Who is the woman called Wisdom?
Did Israel borrow from Egypt?
Does being good really pay?
sessions.finding: Biblical wisdom is practical skill in living, and it begins with 'the fear of the Lord': reverence, not terror.

paras: Session 1 began with Psalm 1: the person who delights in God's teaching is like a tree by the water, and 'the way of the wicked shall perish'. Session 2 heard what happens when life doesn't look like that: Psalm 88 in the dark, and the cursing psalms crying out against corrupt judges.

The Psalms speak to God. Proverbs mostly speaks to us: a parent to a child, a teacher to a student. 'My son, listen to your father's instruction.' Its subject is ordinary life: how to work, what to say, whom to trust, how to treat the poor, how to stay out of trouble.
background.key: Psalm 1 spoke of two ways; Psalm 88 showed life not working out. Proverbs, a teacher talking to a student, is about the two ways in everyday life.

paras: The book opens 'The proverbs of Solomon, the son of David, king of Israel'. Solomon, who reigned about 970 to 930 BC, was remembered as the wisest of kings: he 'spoke three thousand proverbs; and his songs numbered one thousand five' (1 Kings 4:32). Jesus speaks of people travelling 'from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon' (Luke 11:31).

But the book itself names other authors. A section begins 'the words of the wise' (22:17). Another says these proverbs were copied out by 'the men of Hezekiah king of Judah' (25:1), who reigned about 715 to 686 BC. Chapter 30 is 'the words of Agur', chapter 31 'the words of King Lemuel', taught him by his mother. Most scholars think Proverbs is a collection of collections, some perhaps going back to Solomon's court, finished after the exile, with chapters 1 to 9 written last as an introduction.

timeline.text: The Egyptian Instruction of Ptahhotep, among the oldest wisdom books
The Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope is probably composed
Solomon reigns
Hezekiah reigns; his scribes copy proverbs (Proverbs 25:1)
Proverbs probably reaches its final form, chapters 1–9 added as an introduction
The papyrus of Amenemope is published; Adolf Erman points out its parallels with Proverbs

background.key: Proverbs names Solomon, 'the wise', Hezekiah's scribes, Agur and Lemuel: a collection of collections, finished after the exile.

paras: Israel was not the only people with wise sayings. Egypt had a tradition of 'instructions' going back more than a thousand years before Solomon, in which an official or king teaches his son how to succeed and live rightly. Mesopotamia had its proverbs and its sages too. Wisdom was international: the Bible itself says Solomon's wisdom 'excelled the wisdom of all the children of the east, and all the wisdom of Egypt' (1 Kings 4:30), which assumes that there was Egyptian wisdom to compare it with.

What these books share is the belief that the world has an order, and that a wise person learns to live with the grain of it. In Egypt that order was called ma'at: truth, justice and balance. What Proverbs adds is the claim that the order comes from one God, and that knowing him is where wisdom starts.
background.key: Egypt and Mesopotamia had wisdom books long before Proverbs; all assume the world has an order. Proverbs says the order comes from one God.

paras: The main reading has three parts: the opening of Proverbs, which states what the book is for and its motto, 'the fear of Yahweh'; the first speech of the woman called Wisdom, calling in the street (1:20–33); and a father's advice that includes the book's best-known lines (3:1–12).

The comparison has two parts. Proverbs 22:17–21 introduces a section that closely resembles an Egyptian book, the Instruction of Amenemope, so it lets us ask how much Israel borrowed. Psalm 73 then lets a psalmist ask what Proverbs seldom does: what if the wicked prosper?
background.key: The opening and motto, Wisdom calling in the street, a father's advice; then the Egyptian parallel and Psalm 73's question.

before: Proverbs 1:2–6 says what the book is for. Make a list of the words it uses for wisdom. Are they about knowing facts, or about living?
Wisdom in 1:20–33 is a woman. Where does she speak, and to whom?
In Psalm 73, what nearly made the psalmist slip, and what changed his mind?
sessions.readWhy: The book's purpose and motto, Wisdom calling in the street, and a father's advice.

paras: The proverbs of Solomon, the son of David, king of Israel:

to know wisdom and instruction;
to discern the words of understanding;

to receive instruction in wise dealing,
in righteousness, justice, and equity;

to give prudence to the simple,
knowledge and discretion to the young man:

that the wise man may hear, and increase in learning;
that the man of understanding may attain to sound counsel:

to understand a proverb, and parables,
the words and riddles of the wise.

The fear of Yahweh is the beginning of knowledge;
but the foolish despise wisdom and instruction.

My son, listen to your father’s instruction,
and don’t forsake your mother’s teaching:

for they will be a garland to grace your head,
and chains around your neck.

Wisdom calls aloud in the street.
She utters her voice in the public squares.

She calls at the head of noisy places.
At the entrance of the city gates, she utters her words:

“How long, you simple ones, will you love simplicity?
How long will mockers delight themselves in mockery,
and fools hate knowledge?

Turn at my reproof.
Behold, I will pour out my spirit on you.
I will make known my words to you.

Because I have called, and you have refused;
I have stretched out my hand, and no one has paid attention;

but you have ignored all my counsel,
and wanted none of my reproof;

I also will laugh at your disaster.
I will mock when calamity overtakes you,

when calamity overtakes you like a storm,
when your disaster comes on like a whirlwind,
when distress and anguish come on you.

Then they will call on me, but I will not answer.
They will seek me diligently, but they will not find me;

because they hated knowledge,
and didn’t choose the fear of Yahweh.

They wanted none of my counsel.
They despised all my reproof.

Therefore they will eat of the fruit of their own way,
and be filled with their own schemes.

For the backsliding of the simple will kill them.
The careless ease of fools will destroy them.

But whoever listens to me will dwell securely,
and will be at ease, without fear of harm.”

My son, don’t forget my teaching;
but let your heart keep my commandments:

for they will add to you length of days,
years of life, and peace.

Don’t let kindness and truth forsake you.
Bind them around your neck.
Write them on the tablet of your heart.

So you will find favor,
and good understanding in the sight of God and man.

Trust in Yahweh with all your heart,
and don’t lean on your own understanding.

In all your ways acknowledge him,
and he will make your paths straight.

Don’t be wise in your own eyes.
Fear Yahweh, and depart from evil.

It will be health to your body,
and nourishment to your bones.

Honor Yahweh with your substance,
with the first fruits of all your increase:

so your barns will be filled with plenty,
and your vats will overflow with new wine.

My son, don’t despise Yahweh’s discipline,
neither be weary of his correction;

for whom Yahweh loves, he corrects,
even as a father reproves the son in whom he delights.

parts.title: What wisdom is for
parts.context: The opening of the book. The first six verses are its title page and statement of purpose, the seventh its motto. Then the teaching begins in the voice of a parent.

commentary.on: to know wisdom and instruction; to discern the words of understanding
commentary.text: Notice how many words the opening piles up: wisdom, instruction, understanding, wise dealing, prudence, knowledge, discretion, learning, counsel. The Hebrew for wisdom, hokhmah, is used elsewhere of the skill of craftsmen who made the tabernacle (Exodus 31:3–6). Biblical wisdom is a skill: knowing how to live, as a carpenter knows how to cut wood.

commentary.on: in righteousness, justice, and equity
commentary.text: Skill in living is not just cleverness. From the start it includes justice and fairness. A con man can be shrewd; in Proverbs he is a fool.

commentary.on: to give prudence to the simple, knowledge and discretion to the young man
commentary.text: The first readers were probably young men being trained, perhaps for service at court, as in Egypt. 'The simple' are not the stupid but the inexperienced: people easily led, who could still go either way.

commentary.on: The fear of Yahweh is the beginning of knowledge
commentary.text: This is the motto of the whole book; it returns at 9:10 and is echoed in Psalm 111:10 and Job 28:28. 'Fear' here is reverence: the awe of a creature before its maker, which makes it take God seriously. 'Beginning' can mean the starting point or the first principle. Wisdom starts with knowing you are not God.

commentary.on: My son, listen to your father's instruction, and don't forsake your mother's teaching
commentary.text: Wisdom is passed down at home, by mothers as well as fathers. The word for the mother's 'teaching' is torah, the same word used for God's law in Psalm 1.

parts.title: Wisdom calls in the street
parts.context: Here, for the first time, wisdom speaks as a woman. She will speak again in chapters 8 and 9. Scholars call her 'Lady Wisdom' or 'Woman Wisdom'. She is a personification: a quality pictured as a person, as we might say Justice is blind.

commentary.on: Wisdom calls aloud in the street. She utters her voice in the public squares.
commentary.text: Wisdom is not hidden in temples or libraries. She shouts in the street, the square and the city gate, where markets were held and law cases heard. Wisdom is for ordinary life, and it is available to anyone who listens.

commentary.on: How long, you simple ones, will you love simplicity?
commentary.text: 'How long?': the same cry as Psalm 13, but now Wisdom asks it of us. She is impatient with people who prefer not to think.

commentary.on: Turn at my reproof. Behold, I will pour out my spirit on you.
commentary.text: 'Turn' is the prophets' word for repentance. Wisdom speaks like a prophet, and promises to pour out her spirit, as God does in Joel 2:28. She is more than good advice.

commentary.on: Then they will call on me, but I will not answer.
commentary.text: A hard saying. Wisdom warns that a time comes when it is too late: the consequences of folly arrive, and no cry undoes them. It is less a threat than a description of how life works.

commentary.on: Therefore they will eat of the fruit of their own way
commentary.text: Proverbs' idea of judgement is often built into the world: folly brings its own result, as a tree bears its own fruit. Compare Psalm 1's tree and chaff.

commentary.on: But whoever listens to me will dwell securely, and will be at ease, without fear of harm.
commentary.text: The promise is security. Hold on to it: it is the promise that Psalm 73, in the comparison, and Ecclesiastes, in the next session still to come, will put to the test.

parts.title: Trust in Yahweh with all your heart
parts.context: A father's teaching, one of ten 'lectures' in chapters 1 to 9. It holds the best-known verses in the book (3:5–6) and its plainest statement that goodness is rewarded.

commentary.on: Write them on the tablet of your heart.
commentary.text: The ten commandments were written on tablets of stone. Wisdom is to be written on the heart, the Hebrew seat of thinking and choosing. Jeremiah promises the same of God's law (Jeremiah 31:33).

commentary.on: Trust in Yahweh with all your heart, and don't lean on your own understanding.
commentary.text: A surprising line in a book about being wise. The wise person does not trust their own cleverness most. 'Lean on' is the word for leaning on a staff: don't put your whole weight on your own reading of things.

commentary.on: In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight.
commentary.text: 'Acknowledge' is literally 'know him': in all your ways, know God. A 'straight' path in the hills of Judah is one without obstacles, which gets you where you are going.

commentary.on: Don't be wise in your own eyes. Fear Yahweh, and depart from evil.
commentary.text: Back to the motto. The opposite of wisdom here is not ignorance but conceit.

commentary.on: so your barns will be filled with plenty, and your vats will overflow with new wine.
commentary.text: Here is Proverbs' confident promise: honour God and you will prosper. Read as a general rule it is often true; read as a guarantee it is not, as the Bible itself will say.

commentary.on: for whom Yahweh loves, he corrects, even as a father reproves the son in whom he delights.
commentary.text: But the passage ends by admitting that life is not all plenty. Hardship may be discipline, a sign of love, not of punishment. The Letter to the Hebrews quotes these lines (Hebrews 12:5–6).

paras:
Turn your ear, and listen to the words of the wise.
Apply your heart to my teaching.

For it is a pleasant thing if you keep them within you,
if all of them are ready on your lips.

I teach you today, even you,
So that your trust may be in Yahweh.

Haven’t I written to you thirty excellent things
of counsel and knowledge,

To teach you truth, reliable words,
to give sound answers to the ones who sent you?

Surely God is good to Israel,
to those who are pure in heart.

But as for me, my feet were almost gone.
My steps had nearly slipped.

For I was envious of the arrogant,
when I saw the prosperity of the wicked.

For there are no struggles in their death,
but their strength is firm.

They are free from burdens of men,
neither are they plagued like other men.

Therefore pride is like a chain around their neck.
Violence covers them like a garment.

Their eyes bulge with fat.
Their minds pass the limits of conceit.

They scoff and speak with malice.
In arrogance, they threaten oppression.

They have set their mouth in the heavens.
Their tongue walks through the earth.

Therefore their people return to them,
and they drink up waters of abundance.

They say, “How does God know?
Is there knowledge in the Most High?”

Behold, these are the wicked.
Being always at ease, they increase in riches.

Surely I have cleansed my heart in vain,
and washed my hands in innocence,

For all day long I have been plagued,
and punished every morning.

If I had said, “I will speak thus”;
behold, I would have betrayed the generation of your children.

When I tried to understand this,
it was too painful for me,

until I entered God’s sanctuary,
and considered their latter end.

Surely you set them in slippery places.
You throw them down to destruction.

How they are suddenly destroyed!
They are completely swept away with terrors.

As a dream when one wakes up,
so, Lord, when you awake, you will despise their fantasies.

For my soul was grieved.
I was embittered in my heart.

I was so senseless and ignorant.
I was a brute beast before you.

Nevertheless, I am continually with you.
You have held my right hand.

You will guide me with your counsel,
and afterward receive me to glory.

Whom do I have in heaven?
There is no one on earth whom I desire besides you.

My flesh and my heart fails,
but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever.

For, behold, those who are far from you shall perish.
You have destroyed all those who are unfaithful to you.

But it is good for me to come close to God.
I have made the Lord Yahweh my refuge,
that I may tell of all your works.

parts.title: The words of the wise
parts.context: The start of a new section of Proverbs (22:17–24:22), headed 'the words of the wise'. In 1924, the year after the British Museum published an Egyptian papyrus called the Instruction of Amenemope, the German Egyptologist Adolf Erman showed that this section closely follows it. Amenemope is a book of thirty chapters by an Egyptian official teaching his son.

commentary.on: Turn your ear, and listen to the words of the wise. Apply your heart to my teaching.
commentary.text: Amenemope's first chapter opens in much the same way: give your ears, hear what is said, set your heart to understand it, for it is good to keep it in your belly. The Egyptian 'belly' and the Hebrew 'within you' (literally 'in your belly') match.

commentary.on: I teach you today, even you, So that your trust may be in Yahweh.
commentary.text: Here Proverbs does something Amenemope does not. The goal of the teaching is trust in Israel's God, by his name. The borrowed frame is given a new centre.

commentary.on: Haven't I written to you thirty excellent things of counsel and knowledge
commentary.text: The Hebrew word here was long a puzzle; older translations read 'excellent things' or 'before'. After Amenemope was published, most scholars read it as 'thirty': Amenemope has thirty chapters. Other parallels follow: 'Don't move the ancient boundary stone' (22:28) and riches that 'sprout wings like an eagle and fly' (23:5) both have close matches in Amenemope.

commentary.on: To teach you truth, reliable words, to give sound answers to the ones who sent you?
commentary.text: Training a young man to carry messages and answer for his masters: this is a school text for officials, in Israel as in Egypt.

parts.title: When the wicked prosper
parts.context: Headed 'A Psalm by Asaph', the Temple singer. It is a wisdom psalm: it wrestles with the question of reward. It opens the third book of the Psalms.

commentary.on: Surely God is good to Israel, to those who are pure in heart.
commentary.text: The psalm begins with the confident creed of Proverbs: God rewards the good. Then the speaker confesses he nearly lost it.

commentary.on: For I was envious of the arrogant, when I saw the prosperity of the wicked.
commentary.text: The problem is simple and modern: the people who cheat seem to do best. They are healthy, rich and untroubled, and they mock God.

commentary.on: Surely I have cleansed my heart in vain
commentary.text: The speaker's crisis: if goodness doesn't pay, why be good? This is the question Proverbs 3 seemed to answer, asked from experience.

commentary.on: until I entered God's sanctuary, and considered their latter end.
commentary.text: The turning point is worship, not argument. In the Temple he sees things over a longer time: 'their latter end'. Prosperity built on wrong does not last.

commentary.on: Whom do I have in heaven? There is no one on earth whom I desire besides you.
commentary.text: And then something deeper than reward. The prize is not barns and wine but God himself. 'God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever.' The psalm moves from 'does goodness pay?' to 'God is the payment'.

compare.why: First, a passage that resembles an Egyptian book: how much did Israel share with its neighbours? Then a psalm that asks the question Proverbs' promises raise: what if the wicked prosper?
compare.title: Thirty sayings, and a question

paras: When we say someone is wise, we usually mean they know a lot, or they think deeply. The Hebrew hokhmah is more practical. It is used of sailors' skill at sea (in Psalm 107:27 the Hebrew says that in a storm their 'wisdom' is swallowed up), of weavers and metalworkers, of the women who mourned well at funerals (Jeremiah 9:17), of a king who can govern. It means knowing how to do something well. Proverbs applies it to living.

So Proverbs is full of particulars: 'A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger' (15:1). 'He becomes poor who works with a lazy hand, but the hand of the diligent brings wealth' (10:4). Debts, gossip, drink, adultery, laziness, kindness to the poor, choosing friends, the power of the tongue: almost nothing is too small. The wise person in Proverbs is not a philosopher in a study but someone who can live in the real world without wrecking it.
sections.key: Hokhmah is skill: of sailors, weavers, kings. Proverbs applies it to everyday living: words, work, money, friends, the poor.

paras: Much of Proverbs sounds like what any grandmother might say, and Proverbs would not mind. It believes that wisdom is built into the world, so anyone who pays attention can learn some of it: 'Go to the ant, you sluggard' (6:6). That is why Israel could share it with Egypt.

But three things make it more than common sense. First, it is not a set of rules. Proverbs 26:4–5 sets two sayings side by side: 'Don't answer a fool according to his folly, lest you also be like him. Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he be wise in his own eyes.' Both are true; wisdom is knowing which fits the moment. Second, it is moral: shrewdness without justice is folly. Third, it starts with God. 'The fear of Yahweh is the beginning of knowledge' means that the deepest truth about the world is that it is God's, and the wise live accordingly.
'Fear' does not mean terror. It is the reverence that takes God seriously, as a sensible person respects the sea. The wise fear God and so, Proverbs says, need fear nothing else.
sections.key: Proverbs is not a rulebook (26:4–5): it trains judgement. It is moral, and it begins with reverence for God, not terror.

paras: In chapters 1 to 9 wisdom speaks as a woman. She calls in the streets (1:20), she builds a house and sets a banquet (9:1–6), and she is set against another woman, Folly, who also calls from her doorway (9:13–18). The young man must choose whose invitation to accept. Proverbs ends, in chapter 31, with a portrait of a capable woman who runs a household and a business and 'opens her mouth with wisdom' (31:26).

Why a woman? 'Wisdom' is a feminine noun in Hebrew, as it is in Greek (sophia). The young male readers are being taught to love wisdom as they would court a bride. And in chapter 8, which we keep for the last session still to come, Wisdom goes further: she says she was with God before the world began.

Was she a goddess? Some scholars have compared her with Egyptian Ma'at or with goddesses of the ancient Near East. Most think she is a vivid personification of God's own wisdom: not a second god, but the way God's mind is at work in the world, pictured as a person who invites us in.
sections.key: Wisdom is a woman who calls in the street and sets a banquet, rival to Folly. Most scholars see a personification of God's wisdom, not a goddess.

paras: The Instruction of Amenemope survives on a papyrus in the British Museum (EA 10474), with fragments on other papyri and tablets. It was probably composed in the late New Kingdom, roughly 1300 to 1075 BC. Its author, a scribe and official, teaches his son honesty, self-control and care for the weak: do not move the boundary stones of a field, do not cheat the widow, do not mock the blind or the lame, do not chase riches, which fly away like geese into the sky.

When it was published in 1923–24, scholars quickly saw that Proverbs 22:17–24:22 follows it, sometimes almost line by line, though freely, and not in the same order. Most now think the Israelite scribes knew the Egyptian book, perhaps through the court contacts between Jerusalem and Egypt in the time of the kings, and adapted it. A minority argued that the borrowing went the other way, or that both used a common source; the dating of Amenemope makes Egyptian priority most likely.

Does this matter for faith? Jews and Christians have usually said no: all truth is God's truth. What Israel did with the borrowed wisdom is telling. It added 'so that your trust may be in Yahweh', and set it inside a book whose motto is the fear of the Lord.
sections.key: Amenemope (c. 1300–1075 BC) closely matches Proverbs 22:17–24:22. Most scholars think Israel adapted it, adding trust in Yahweh.

paras: Proverbs often promises that the wise and good will prosper and the wicked fall: 'your barns will be filled with plenty' (3:10). Read as general truths, many of these are borne out: honest, hard-working, sober, kind people often do better, and people who lie, drink and cheat often come to grief. But Proverbs offers them as tendencies, not guarantees, as all proverbs are. 'Many hands make light work' does not mean every job goes faster with more people.

Proverbs itself knows this. It says 'Better is little, with the fear of Yahweh, than great treasure with trouble' (15:16), which only makes sense if the good are sometimes poor. And the Bible does not leave Proverbs alone. Psalm 73 asks why the wicked prosper; Job's friends speak like Proverbs and are told they are wrong (Job 42:7); Ecclesiastes says flatly that the race is not to the swift. The Bible holds the rule and its exceptions together. A wise reader learns both.
sections.key: Proverbs' promises are tendencies, not guarantees. Psalm 73, Job and Ecclesiastes test them; the Bible keeps the rule and the exceptions together.

paras: Proverbs begins with Wisdom as a woman calling in the street and ends with a woman at home. Its last twenty-two verses (31:10–31) are an acrostic poem, each verse starting with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet, in praise of 'a worthy woman'. She buys a field, plants a vineyard, trades in cloth, works late, gives to the poor, and 'opens her mouth with wisdom' (31:26). Her husband is known in the city gates because of her.

Many scholars think the book is framed on purpose: Lady Wisdom at the start, the capable woman at the end, so that the young man who began by choosing Wisdom over Folly ends by seeing what wisdom looks like in a real household. Jewish husbands traditionally sing this poem, Eshet Chayil ('a woman of valour'), to their wives at the Sabbath meal on Friday evening.

The poem also answers the question of whether Proverbs is just about getting on. Its last line is the book's motto turned into a portrait: 'a woman who fears Yahweh, she shall be praised' (31:30). Wisdom, in the end, is a life.
sections.key: Proverbs ends with an acrostic portrait of a capable woman who 'opens her mouth with wisdom': Lady Wisdom in a real household, sung at the Jewish Sabbath table.

refs: E. A. Wallis Budge, Facsimiles of Egyptian Hieratic Papyri in the British Museum, Second Series (1923) and The Teaching of Amen-em-apt (1924); Adolf Erman, 'Eine ägyptische Quelle der Sprüche Salomos', Sitzungsberichte der Preussischen Akademie der Wissenschaften (1924); F. Ll. Griffith, 'The Teaching of Amenophis the Son of Kanakht', Journal of Egyptian Archaeology 12 (1926).
Miriam Lichtheim, Ancient Egyptian Literature, vol. 2 (1976), for Amenemope and the Egyptian instructions.
Michael V. Fox, Proverbs (Anchor Bible, 2000 and 2009); Gerhard von Rad, Wisdom in Israel (1970, English 1972).

debate.question: How much did Proverbs borrow from Egypt?

positions.name: A direct adaptation
positions.who: Adolf Erman (1924); most Egyptologists and biblical scholars today, e.g. Miriam Lichtheim, Michael V. Fox
positions.view: Israelite scribes had a copy of Amenemope, or knew it well, and adapted about a third of it into Proverbs 22:17–24:22, changing its order and adding Israel's God. The word 'thirty' in 22:20 points to Amenemope's thirty chapters.
positions.evidence: Close parallels in wording and images (the boundary stone, riches with wings, 'within your belly'); the 'thirty'; Amenemope's earlier date; known contacts between the courts of Israel and Egypt.

positions.name: Common stock, not copying
positions.who: Some scholars, especially in the decades after 1924 (e.g. R. O. Kevin and others who argued for Hebrew priority); some today who stress oral tradition
positions.view: The likenesses come from a shared international tradition of school sayings, passed on by word of mouth, not from one text copying another. The order differs and the parallels are loose.
positions.evidence: Many differences in detail and order; similar sayings elsewhere in the ancient Near East; the uncertain reading of 'thirty'.

positions.name: Borrowed and transformed
positions.who: Many Jewish and Christian interpreters, e.g. Gerhard von Rad
positions.view: The borrowing is real, and that is the point: Israel's wisdom was open to the world. But it was transformed by being set under 'the fear of Yahweh'. The question is not where a saying came from but what it serves.
positions.evidence: Proverbs 22:19, 'so that your trust may be in Yahweh'; 1 Kings 4:30, which praises Egyptian wisdom even as it claims Solomon surpassed it.

debate.agree: All agree that Proverbs and Amenemope are closely related, and that Israel's wisdom shared a language with its neighbours.

look.why: No painting for this session. There is no painting of Solomon or of Wisdom in the National Gallery of Art's open collection, and its scholars and philosophers are already used by other journeys.

music.why: An old Irish prayer, sung to an Irish folk tune, that asks God to be 'my wisdom': the prayer of Proverbs 3:5–6 turned into a hymn.

think.why: Israel's wisdom and Greece's philosophy both loved wisdom; see how the two met and shaped the West.

learn.why: The heart of Proverbs in two lines: the wise do not lean on their own understanding.

check.q: Which best captures what Proverbs means by 'wisdom' (hokhmah)?
options: A large store of facts about the world
Secret knowledge given only to priests
Practical skill in living well and justly, starting from reverence for God
The ability to win arguments
check.why: Hokhmah is used of craftsmen and sailors; Proverbs applies it to life, and insists it includes justice and starts with the fear of the Lord.

check.q: Proverbs 26:4 says 'Don't answer a fool according to his folly' and 26:5 says 'Answer a fool according to his folly'. What follows?
