options: Proverbs trains judgement: each saying is true in some situations, and wisdom is knowing which applies
One verse is a copying error
The book contradicts itself and can't be trusted
Only verse 5 is meant seriously
check.why: Placed side by side on purpose, the two show that proverbs are not rules but tools for judgement.

check.q: What does 'the fear of Yahweh is the beginning of knowledge' most likely mean?
options: You must be terrified of God before you can learn anything
Reverence for God, taking him seriously as creator, is the starting point and first principle of wisdom
Knowledge begins when you stop fearing God
Only religious people can know facts
check.why: 'Fear' is reverence; 'beginning' is the starting point or first principle. The opposite of wisdom in Proverbs is conceit.

check.q: Why do most scholars think the 'thirty' in Proverbs 22:20 matters?
options: It shows the passage was written in Greek
It matches the thirty chapters of the Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope, which this section closely follows
It proves Solomon wrote the passage
It is the number of Israel's tribes
check.why: The obscure Hebrew word was reread as 'thirty' after Amenemope was published; with other parallels it points to borrowing.

check.q: Proverbs adapted Egyptian wisdom. What did it change, according to 22:19?
options: It turned the sayings into laws with punishments
It removed all religious language
It made the goal of the teaching trust in Yahweh, Israel's God
It replaced the father with a priest
check.why: 'I teach you today... so that your trust may be in Yahweh': the borrowed form is given a new centre.

check.q: Psalm 73's speaker nearly gives up because the wicked prosper. What turns him around?
options: He becomes rich himself
In God's sanctuary he sees their 'latter end', and realises that God himself is his portion
The wicked are punished in front of him
Wisdom appears to him in the street
check.why: Worship gives a longer view, and the reward changes from prosperity to God himself.

tutorial.question: Is Proverbs just common sense?
tutorial.approach: Give the case for: much of it is shared with Egypt and with folk wisdom, and it assumes anyone can learn from the world. Then give the case against: it trains judgement rather than giving rules (26:4–5), it is moral, and it begins with the fear of the Lord. Use Amenemope and Proverbs 22:19 to show what Israel did with borrowed wisdom. Finish with the problem of reward: does Proverbs promise too much?
strong: Defines hokhmah as practical skill, with examples.
Uses Amenemope fairly, and notes the added 'trust in Yahweh'.
Explains 'the fear of the Lord' as reverence and first principle.
Uses 26:4–5 to show Proverbs trains judgement.
Discusses Lady Wisdom as a personification.
Recognises that Proverbs' promises are tendencies, tested by Psalm 73 and other books.

reading.author: Ellen F. Davis
reading.title: Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs
reading.why: A wise, readable commentary on all three wisdom books.

reading.author: Gerhard von Rad
reading.title: Wisdom in Israel
reading.why: The classic account of how Israel thought about the order of the world.

reading.author: Michael V. Fox
reading.title: Proverbs 1–9 and Proverbs 10–31 (Anchor Bible)
reading.why: The standard scholarly commentary, with full treatment of Amenemope.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: read one chapter of Proverbs a day, matching the date (there are 31). Choose one saying each day and test it against what you see that day: is it true here, and when would it not be?
sessions.reflect: Where in your life are you leaning on your own understanding? What would it look like to trust someone wiser?
takeaways: Biblical wisdom is practical skill in living well and justly, and it begins with 'the fear of the Lord', which is reverence, not terror.
Proverbs shares much with Egyptian wisdom, especially the Instruction of Amenemope, and sets it under trust in Israel's God.
Its promises of reward are tendencies, not guarantees; the Bible itself tests them, in Psalm 73 and beyond.

sessions.title: Vanity of vanities
sessions.line: A king who had everything says it is all breath, and still tells you to eat your bread with joy; a famous novelist hides a rope from himself.
sessions.plain: Ecclesiastes is one of the strangest books in the Bible. Its narrator, 'the Preacher', has tried everything (work, pleasure, wisdom, wealth) and concludes that all is 'vanity': breath, vapour, gone. The good and the wicked die alike, and no one remembers either. And yet he keeps telling his readers to eat, drink and enjoy their work. This session asks what the book is really saying, and reads it beside Leo Tolstoy, who at the height of his fame quoted Ecclesiastes as he hid a rope so that he would not hang himself.
sessions.why: Session 3 ended with Proverbs' confident promise that wisdom brings security, and with Psalm 73 asking why the wicked prosper. Ecclesiastes goes further: what if wisdom itself cannot save you from death?
answers: Is Ecclesiastes saying life is meaningless?
Who was 'the Preacher'?
What does 'vanity' (hevel) mean?
Why did Tolstoy quote it, and what did he hear in it?
sessions.finding: Ecclesiastes faces the worst, that death erases everything, and still tells you to eat your bread with joy: it is not despair but a cure for false hopes.

paras: Session 3 showed Proverbs' world: wisdom is a skill, it begins with the fear of the Lord, and it tends to bring a long and secure life. Psalm 73 already strained at that promise, and found its answer in God himself rather than in reward.

Ecclesiastes is wisdom examining itself. It uses Proverbs' methods (observe the world, draw conclusions) and its form (short sayings), but turns them on the biggest question: what is the point of it all, if we die?
background.key: Proverbs promised security; Psalm 73 strained at it. Ecclesiastes uses wisdom's own methods to ask what the point is, if we die.

paras: The book calls its speaker Qoheleth, a Hebrew word from the root for 'assembly'. It may mean 'one who gathers people' or 'one who gathers sayings'. The Greek translation called him Ekklesiastes, 'member of the assembly', which gives the book its English name; Luther's German Bible called him 'the Preacher', and the WEB follows. He is called 'the son of David, king in Jerusalem', so tradition took him to be Solomon. A Jewish tradition says Solomon wrote the Song of Songs in his youth, Proverbs in middle age and Ecclesiastes in old age (Song of Songs Rabbah 1:1).

Most scholars think the book is later. Its Hebrew is late, close to the Hebrew of the Mishnah, and it uses Persian loanwords such as pardes, 'park' (2:5). Most date it between about 450 and 250 BC, after the exile, when Judah was ruled by Persia and then by Alexander's Greek successors. 'Solomon' is a role: the richest and wisest king imaginable, who tried everything, is the best witness to whether everything is enough.

timeline.text: Solomon reigns: the king the Preacher speaks as
Ecclesiastes probably written, under Persian or early Greek rule
Fragments of Ecclesiastes copied among the Dead Sea Scrolls
The Mishnah records rabbis still debating whether Ecclesiastes is holy (Yadayim 3:5)
Leo Tolstoy
Tolstoy writes A Confession
Aylmer Maude's English translation

background.key: Qoheleth, 'the gatherer', speaks as Solomon; most scholars date the book c. 450–250 BC from its late Hebrew and Persian words.

paras: Leo Tolstoy (1828–1910) was a Russian count, landowner and novelist, author of War and Peace (1869) and Anna Karenina (1878), often called the greatest novels ever written. In the late 1870s, when he was about fifty, rich, famous, healthy and happily married, he fell into a crisis so deep that he thought of killing himself.

He told the story in A Confession, written between 1879 and 1882. The Russian censors banned it, and it was first printed in Geneva in 1884. The translation we read is by Aylmer Maude (1858–1938), an Englishman who knew Tolstoy well and translated him with his wife Louise; it was published in 1921. In the chapters we read, Tolstoy quotes Ecclesiastes at length, in the old English of the King James Bible that Maude used. He went on to find his way back to faith; that is a story for another journey.
background.key: Tolstoy, author of War and Peace, wrote A Confession (1879–82) about the despair that nearly killed him at fifty; Maude's translation, 1921.

paras: The main reading has two parts: the opening poem of Ecclesiastes (1:1–11), with its famous cry 'Vanity of vanities', and chapter 9:1–12, where the Preacher faces death squarely and gives his strongest advice to enjoy life.

The comparison is from Tolstoy's Confession, chapters IV and VI. We read it because it is the most famous modern reading of Ecclesiastes, by someone who took the book at its word, and because it shows what is at stake. Tolstoy hears only the 'vanity'. Watch whether he hears the joy.
background.key: Ecclesiastes 1 and 9, then Tolstoy, who quoted Ecclesiastes in his own despair: does he hear the whole book?

before: In 1:3–11, list the things that go round and round. What is the speaker's complaint about them?
In 9:1–6, why does the speaker say a living dog is better than a dead lion?
In 9:7–10, what does he tell you to do? Why does he give death as the reason?
sessions.readWhy: The opening poem, and the Preacher's advice in the face of death.

paras: The words of the Preacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem:
“Vanity of vanities,” says the Preacher; “Vanity of vanities, all is vanity.”
What does man gain from all his labor in which he labors under the sun?
One generation goes, and another generation comes; but the earth remains forever.
The sun also rises, and the sun goes down, and hurries to its place where it rises.
The wind goes toward the south, and turns around to the north. It turns around continually as it goes, and the wind returns again to its courses.
All the rivers run into the sea, yet the sea is not full. To the place where the rivers flow, there they flow again.
All things are full of weariness beyond uttering. The eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing.
That which has been is that which shall be; and that which has been done is that which shall be done: and there is no new thing under the sun.
Is there a thing of which it may be said, “Behold, this is new?” It has been long ago, in the ages which were before us.
There is no memory of the former; neither shall there be any memory of the latter that are to come, among those that shall come after.

For all this I laid to my heart, even to explore all this: that the righteous, and the wise, and their works, are in the hand of God; whether it is love or hatred, man doesn’t know it; all is before them.

All things come alike to all. There is one event to the righteous and to the wicked; to the good, to the clean, to the unclean, to him who sacrifices, and to him who doesn’t sacrifice. As is the good, so is the sinner; he who takes an oath, as he who fears an oath.

This is an evil in all that is done under the sun, that there is one event to all: yes also, the heart of the sons of men is full of evil, and madness is in their heart while they live, and after that they go to the dead.
For to him who is joined with all the living there is hope; for a living dog is better than a dead lion.
For the living know that they will die, but the dead don’t know anything, neither do they have any more a reward; for their memory is forgotten.
Also their love, their hatred, and their envy has perished long ago; neither do they any longer have a portion forever in anything that is done under the sun.
Go your way—eat your bread with joy, and drink your wine with a merry heart; for God has already accepted your works.
Let your garments be always white, and don’t let your head lack oil.

Live joyfully with the wife whom you love all the days of your life of vanity, which he has given you under the sun, all your days of vanity, for that is your portion in life, and in your labor in which you labor under the sun.
Whatever your hand finds to do, do it with your might; for there is no work, nor plan, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in Sheol, where you are going.

I returned and saw under the sun that the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, neither yet bread to the wise, nor yet riches to men of understanding, nor yet favor to men of skill; but time and chance happen to them all.

For man also doesn’t know his time. As the fish that are taken in an evil net, and as the birds that are caught in the snare, even so are the sons of men snared in an evil time, when it falls suddenly on them.

parts.title: Vanity of vanities
parts.context: The opening of the book. A frame narrator introduces 'the Preacher' and his motto; then comes a poem about the endless cycles of nature and history.

commentary.on: “Vanity of vanities,” says the Preacher; “Vanity of vanities, all is vanity.”
commentary.text: 'Vanity' translates the Hebrew hevel, which means breath, vapour, a puff of wind. It is the name of Abel, who died young (Genesis 4:2). 'Vanity of vanities' is Hebrew for 'the utmost breath'. Some translate 'meaningless', but hevel is a picture: not 'nothing matters' but 'nothing lasts, nothing can be held'. The word comes 38 times in this short book. Notice that someone else is speaking here, 'says the Preacher': a narrator is quoting him.

commentary.on: What does man gain from all his labor in which he labors under the sun?
commentary.text: The book's question. 'Gain' is a business word: profit, what is left over. 'Under the sun' is the Preacher's phrase for life as we see it, in this world: it comes about thirty times.

commentary.on: One generation goes, and another generation comes; but the earth remains forever.
commentary.text: Then a poem of circles: generations, sun, wind, rivers. In Psalm 104 the same things are signs of God's care. Here they are signs of weariness: everything moves, and nothing arrives. 'The sea is not full.'

commentary.on: The eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing.
commentary.text: The cycles are in us too. Desire never reaches its end: there is always another thing to see or hear. Every advertiser knows this verse is true.

commentary.on: there is no new thing under the sun.
commentary.text: The most quoted line. It is not quite despair: it is a refusal of the hope that the next thing, or the next age, will finally fix us.

commentary.on: There is no memory of the former; neither shall there be any memory of the latter that are to come
commentary.text: The cruellest fact for an ancient reader, who hoped to live on in a good name: you will be forgotten. Psalm 88 feared being forgotten by God; the Preacher says everyone is forgotten by everyone.

parts.title: Eat your bread with joy
parts.context: Near the end of the Preacher's reflections. He has tried pleasure, work, wisdom and wealth (chapter 2), seen injustice in the courts (3:16) and the tears of the oppressed (4:1). Now he faces death head on, and draws his conclusion.

commentary.on: the righteous, and the wise, and their works, are in the hand of God
commentary.text: He starts with faith: everything is in God's hand. But we cannot read his hand: 'whether it is love or hatred, man doesn't know it'. You cannot tell from how your life goes whether God approves of you. That cuts against a simple reading of Proverbs.

commentary.on: There is one event to the righteous and to the wicked
commentary.text: The 'one event' is death. It comes to good and bad, clean and unclean, worshipper and scoffer alike. For the Preacher this is 'an evil': it seems unfair.

commentary.on: for a living dog is better than a dead lion.
commentary.text: Dogs were despised scavengers; lions were noble. A live scavenger is better off than a dead king. It is a joke, and a serious one: life itself, however humble, is a gift the dead have lost.

commentary.on: Go your way—eat your bread with joy, and drink your wine with a merry heart; for God has already accepted your works.
commentary.text: And now the turn. Because we will die, enjoy the bread and wine you have today. 'God has already accepted your works': this is not a desperate grab at pleasure but permission from God. The Preacher says this kind of thing seven times in the book (for example 2:24, 3:12–13, 5:18).

commentary.on: Live joyfully with the wife whom you love all the days of your life of vanity
commentary.text: Joy is found in the ordinary: clean clothes, oil on the head (a sign of festivity), the person you love, your work. It is all hevel, all breath, and that is exactly why it should be enjoyed now.

commentary.on: Whatever your hand finds to do, do it with your might; for there is no work, nor plan, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in Sheol, where you are going.
commentary.text: Sheol, the shadowy place of the dead you met in session 2, gives a reason to work well now. The thought of death does not paralyse; it focuses.

commentary.on: the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, neither yet bread to the wise
commentary.text: Proverbs said the diligent prosper. The Preacher has seen otherwise: 'time and chance happen to them all'. Life is not a machine that pays out to the deserving.

paras: My life came to a standstill. I could breathe, eat, drink, and sleep, and I could not help doing these things; but there was no life, for there were no wishes the fulfillment of which I could consider reasonable. If I desired anything, I knew in advance that whether I satisfied my desire or not, nothing would come of it. Had a fairy come and offered to fulfill my desires I should not have known what to ask. If in moments of intoxication I felt something which, though not a wish, was a habit left by former wishes, in sober moments I knew this to be a delusion and that there was really nothing to wish for. I could not even wish to know the truth, for I guessed of what it consisted. The truth was that life is meaningless. I had as it were lived, lived, and walked, walked, till I had come to a precipice and saw clearly that there was nothing ahead of me but destruction. It was impossible to stop, impossible to go back, and impossible to close my eyes or avoid seeing that there was nothing ahead but suffering and real death—complete annihilation.

It had come to this, that I, a healthy, fortunate man, felt I could no longer live: some irresistible power impelled me to rid myself one way or other of life. I cannot say I wished to kill myself. The power which drew me away from life was stronger, fuller, and more widespread than any mere wish. It was a force similar to the former striving to live, only in a contrary direction. All my strength drew me away from life. The thought of self-destruction now came to me as naturally as thoughts of how to improve my life had come formerly, and it was seductive that I had to be cunning with myself lest I should carry it out too hastily. I did not wish to hurry, because I wanted to use all efforts to disentangle the matter. “If I cannot unravel matters, there will always be time.” And it was then that I, a man favoured by fortune, hid a cord from myself lest I should hang myself from the crosspiece of the partition in my room where I undressed alone every evening, and I ceased to go out shooting with a gun lest I should be tempted by so easy a way of ending my life. I did not myself know what I wanted: I feared life, desired to escape from it, yet still hoped something of it.

And all this befell me at a time when all around me I had what is considered complete good fortune. I was not yet fifty; I had a good wife who loved me and whom I loved, good children, and a large estate which without much effort on my part improved and increased. I was respected by my relations and acquaintances more than at any previous time. I was praised by others and without much self-deception could consider that my name was famous. And far from being insane or mentally diseased, I enjoyed on the contrary a strength of mind and body such as I have seldom met with among men of my kind; physically I could keep up with the peasants at mowing, and mentally I could work for eight and ten hours at a stretch without experiencing any ill results from such exertion. And in this situation I came to this—that I could not live, and, fearing death, had to employ cunning with myself to avoid taking my own life.

There is an Eastern fable, told long ago, of a traveller overtaken on a plain by an enraged beast. Escaping from the beast he gets into a dry well, but sees at the bottom of the well a dragon that has opened its jaws to swallow him. And the unfortunate man, not daring to climb out lest he should be destroyed by the enraged beast, and not daring to leap to the bottom of the well lest he should be eaten by the dragon, seizes a twig growing in a crack in the well and clings to it. His hands are growing weaker and he feels he will soon have to resign himself to the destruction that awaits him above or below, but still he clings on. Then he sees that two mice, a black one and a white one, go regularly round and round the stem of the twig to which he is clinging and gnaw at it. And soon the twig itself will snap and he will fall into the dragon’s jaws. The traveller sees this and knows that he will inevitably perish; but while still hanging he looks around, sees some drops of honey on the leaves of the twig, reaches them with his tongue and licks them. So I too clung to the twig of life, knowing that the dragon of death was inevitably awaiting me, ready to tear me to pieces; and I could not understand why I had fallen into such torment. I tried to lick the honey which formerly consoled me, but the honey no longer gave me pleasure, and the white and black mice of day and night gnawed at the branch by which I hung. I saw the dragon clearly and the honey no longer tasted sweet. I only saw the unescapable dragon and the mice, and I could not tear my gaze from them, and this is not a fable but the real unanswerable truth intelligible to all.

The deception of the joys of life which formerly allayed my terror of the dragon now no longer deceived me. No matter how often I may be told, “You cannot understand the meaning of life so do not think about it, but live,” I can no longer do it: I have already done it too long. I cannot now help seeing day and night going round and bringing me to death. That is all I see, for that alone is true. All else is false.

“Vanity of vanities,” says Solomon—“vanity of vanities—all is vanity. What profit hath a man of all his labor which he taketh under the sun? One generation passeth away, and another generation commeth: but the earth abideth forever. … The thing that hath been, is that which shall be; and that which is done is that which shall be done: and there is no new thing under the sun. Is there anything whereof it may be said, ‘See, this is new?’ It hath been already of old time, which was before us. There is no remembrance of former things; neither shall there be any remembrance of things that are to come with those that shall come after. I the Preacher was King over Israel in Jerusalem. And I gave my heart to seek and search out by wisdom concerning all that is done under heaven: this sore travail hath God given to the sons of man to be exercised therewith. I have seen all the works that are done under the sun; and behold, all is vanity and vexation of spirit. … I communed with my own heart, saying, Lo, I am come to great estate, and have gotten more wisdom than all they that have been before me over Jerusalem: yea, my heart hath great experience of wisdom and knowledge. And I gave my heart to know wisdom, and to know madness and folly: I perceived that this also is vexation of spirit. For in much wisdom is much grief: and he that increaseth knowledge increaseth sorrow.
So said Solomon, or whoever wrote those words.
“All that is in the world—folly and wisdom and riches and poverty and mirth and grief—is vanity and emptiness. Man dies and nothing is left of him. And that is stupid,” says Solomon.
And what these strong minds said has been said and thought and felt by millions upon millions of people like them. And I have thought it and felt it.
It is no good deceiving oneself. It is all—vanity! Happy is he who has not been born: death is better than life, and one must free oneself from life.

parts.author: Leo Tolstoy
parts.title: My life came to a standstill
parts.context: Tolstoy is about fifty, in the late 1870s, on his estate at Yasnaya Polyana, south of Moscow. He has finished Anna Karenina. For some years he has been troubled by the question 'Why?', and now it has stopped him living. Translated by Aylmer Maude (1921); the cuts are marked '…'.
parts.plain: Tolstoy says: my life stopped. I could still eat and sleep, but I wanted nothing, because I knew everything ended in death. I was so drawn to suicide that I hid a rope and stopped taking my gun out, though I was healthy, rich, famous and loved. He compares himself to a man in an old fable: hanging over a dragon in a well, on a twig that two mice are gnawing, licking honey from the leaves. He can no longer taste the honey.

commentary.on: The truth was that life is meaningless.
commentary.text: Tolstoy's conclusion, stated flatly. He did not reason his way to it at first; he says he 'guessed' it, and could not stop seeing it.

commentary.on: hid a cord from myself lest I should hang myself from the crosspiece of the partition in my room
commentary.text: The most famous sentence in the book. Tolstoy is not describing a theory but a danger. If these pages touch something in you, please talk to someone today: a friend, a doctor, a pastor, or Samaritans (116 123 in the UK and Ireland).

commentary.on: I was not yet fifty; I had a good wife who loved me and whom I loved, good children, and a large estate
commentary.text: This is what makes his case so strong. He is not poor, sick or alone. He has everything the Preacher had: success, love, fame, strength. Like the Preacher, he is the best possible witness that these are not enough.

commentary.on: There is an Eastern fable, told long ago, of a traveller overtaken on a plain by an enraged beast.
commentary.text: The fable comes from India and travelled west in the medieval story of Barlaam and Josaphat. The beast and the dragon are death; the mice, white and black, are day and night; the honey is the pleasures of life. It is Ecclesiastes 1 as a picture: time gnaws, and nothing lasts.

commentary.on: the honey no longer gave me pleasure
commentary.text: Here Tolstoy differs from the Preacher. The Preacher, knowing about the dragon, still says: eat your bread with joy. Tolstoy can no longer taste the honey. His two 'drops' had been his family and his writing; both now seem hevel.

commentary.on: You cannot understand the meaning of life so do not think about it, but live,
commentary.text: This is the advice of many sensible people, and Tolstoy rejects it: he has already lived without thinking 'too long'. That is his challenge to the reader: can you honestly un-see death?

parts.author: Leo Tolstoy
parts.title: So said Solomon
parts.context: In chapter VI Tolstoy surveys 'the wisest of mankind' on the meaning of life: Socrates, the philosopher Schopenhauer, Solomon (whom he takes to be the author of Ecclesiastes) and the Buddha. Here he quotes Ecclesiastes 1 and 2 in the King James wording, which Maude used; the cuts within the quotation are Tolstoy's own. A footnote marker after 'words' has been removed.
parts.plain: Tolstoy quotes the opening of Ecclesiastes: all is vanity, nothing is new, no one is remembered, and more wisdom means more grief. He sums up Solomon: everything in the world is empty, man dies and nothing is left. He says millions have felt this, and so has he. His conclusion: it is all vanity, it is better not to have been born, and one must free oneself from life.

commentary.on: One generation passeth away, and another generation commeth: but the earth abideth forever.
commentary.text: Compare the WEB you have just read: 'One generation goes, and another generation comes'. This is the King James Version of 1611. Tolstoy quotes the opening poem almost whole.

commentary.on: For in much wisdom is much grief: and he that increaseth knowledge increaseth sorrow.
commentary.text: From Ecclesiastes 1:18. For Tolstoy, a man who had read and thought more than almost anyone, this was the heart of it: the more you know, the more clearly you see the dragon.

commentary.on: So said Solomon, or whoever wrote those words.
commentary.text: Tolstoy knew scholars doubted Solomon wrote it. It does not matter to him: what matters is whether it is true.

commentary.on: Man dies and nothing is left of him. And that is stupid,
commentary.text: This is Tolstoy's summary of Solomon, not a quotation, and it is sharper than the Preacher. The Preacher says death is hevel and unfair. He never says it is 'stupid', and he never draws the conclusion Tolstoy draws next.

commentary.on: Happy is he who has not been born: death is better than life, and one must free oneself from life.
commentary.text: Ecclesiastes 4:2–3 does say the dead, and the unborn, are more fortunate than the living who see oppression. But the Preacher's conclusion is never 'free oneself from life'. It is 'eat your bread with joy', 'whatever your hand finds to do, do it with your might', and 'remember your Creator' (12:1). Tolstoy has read the book's question and missed its answer, or found that he could not believe it.

compare.author: Leo Tolstoy
compare.why: Tolstoy read Ecclesiastes as the most honest book ever written about life, and it nearly finished him. Read his account, and his quotation of the Preacher, to see the book's despair at full strength, and ask what he left out.
compare.title: A traveller in a well

paras: Everything in Ecclesiastes hangs on one word. Hevel, translated 'vanity' since the Latin Bible's vanitas, literally means breath or vapour: the mist of your breath on a cold morning. It is the name of Abel, the son of Adam who lived briefly and was killed. It can suggest three things: what is brief (it vanishes), what is insubstantial (you cannot grasp it), and what is baffling (you cannot see through it).

That is why modern translators disagree. 'Meaningless' (the New International Version) makes the book sound nihilist. 'Futility', 'absurd', 'fleeting', 'enigma', 'a chasing after wind' each catch part of it. The scholar Michael Fox argued for 'absurd', in the sense of a gap between what should be and what is: the good die like the wicked. Others prefer 'fleeting'.

Hold on to the picture. When the Preacher says 'all is hevel', he means at least: nothing under the sun lasts, and nothing under the sun can be held on to as the meaning of your life. Work, pleasure, wisdom, wealth, reputation: all breath. That is not the same as saying nothing is good.
sections.key: Hevel is breath or vapour: brief, ungraspable, baffling. 'All is hevel' means nothing under the sun lasts or can be held as life's meaning, not that nothing is good.

paras: Chapter 2 is the Preacher's experiment. Like a scientist, he tests each candidate for the meaning of life. He tries pleasure: wine, laughter, music, sex. He tries achievement: houses, vineyards, gardens and parks, pools, slaves, herds, silver and gold. He tries wisdom, and finds it better than folly, as light is better than darkness; but the wise man dies just like the fool (2:16). Each time the result is the same: hevel, a chasing after wind.

He then looks at the world. In the courts, where justice should be, there is wickedness (3:16). He sees 'the tears of those who were oppressed, and they had no comforter' (4:1). He sees the man who works alone for wealth he will never enjoy (4:8), and the rich man who cannot sleep (5:12).

Yet between these findings, seven times, comes the other refrain: 'There is nothing better for a man than that he should eat and drink, and make his soul enjoy good in his labor. This also I saw, that it is from the hand of God' (2:24). The scholar R. N. Whybray (1982) called Qoheleth 'a preacher of joy'. The question for every reader is how the two refrains fit.
sections.key: The Preacher tests pleasure, achievement and wisdom, and finds all hevel; yet seven times he says to enjoy food, drink and work as God's gift.

paras: Ecclesiastes has a frame. Most of the book is the Preacher speaking as 'I'. But at the beginning (1:2), once in the middle (7:27) and at the end (12:8), another voice speaks about him: 'says the Preacher'. Then an epilogue (12:9–14) tells us he was wise, taught the people, 'set in order many proverbs', and ends: 'This is the end of the matter... Fear God and keep his commandments; for this is the whole duty of man' (12:13).

Scholars debate the epilogue. Some think a later editor added it to make a risky book safe. Others think the frame narrator is the real author, who presents the Preacher's search, honours it, and then gives his own verdict, as a teacher might set a student a hard text and then say what to take from it. Either way, the book as we have it ends where Proverbs begins: with the fear of God. If you have taken 'Death and hope', you have read that ending there.
sections.key: A frame narrator quotes 'the Preacher' and closes with 'Fear God and keep his commandments': Ecclesiastes ends where Proverbs begins.

paras: Ecclesiastes was not the first book to ask this question. The Epic of Gilgamesh, from Mesopotamia, whose oldest versions go back to about 1800 BC, tells of a king who, after his friend Enkidu dies, sets out to find eternal life. On his journey he meets Siduri, a woman who keeps a tavern at the edge of the world. In the Old Babylonian version she tells him, in effect: the gods kept life for themselves and gave death to mankind; so fill your belly, make merry day and night, wear clean clothes, wash your head, look at the child who holds your hand, and let your wife delight in your embrace.

The likeness to Ecclesiastes 9:7–9 (bread, wine, white garments, oil on the head, the wife you love) is striking, and most scholars think the Preacher knew this old advice, which had travelled widely. The difference is in one clause: 'for God has already accepted your works'. In Gilgamesh, joy is a consolation prize from gods who hoard life. In Ecclesiastes, joy is a gift from the one God, whose purposes we cannot see but whose hand holds us.
sections.key: Siduri in Gilgamesh gives almost the same advice as Ecclesiastes 9:7–9; the Preacher adds that joy is God's gift, 'for God has already accepted your works'.

sections.h: A book that nearly wasn't in the Bible
paras: Ecclesiastes troubled ancient readers too. The Mishnah (Yadayim 3:5, about AD 200) records rabbis still debating whether it 'makes the hands unclean', their way of saying whether it was holy Scripture. The Talmud reports that the sages wanted to hide it away because it contradicts itself, and kept it because it begins and ends with words of Torah (Shabbat 30b). It was kept.

Today Jews read Ecclesiastes aloud in the synagogue at Sukkot, the autumn Feast of Booths, when families live for a week in flimsy shelters open to the sky: a festival of joy in a house of breath. Christians have read it as a preparation for the gospel: it clears away false hopes so that real hope can be heard. Jerome, the translator of the Latin Bible, wrote a commentary on it around 388, remembering how he had read the book in Rome with a young widow, Blesilla, to persuade her to leave a life of luxury for one of prayer.

So is it a book of despair? Read whole, no. It is a book against illusions: the illusion that work, pleasure, wisdom or fame can be the meaning of a life, and the illusion that life is fair. Having cleared them away, it hands you back your bread and wine, and the people you love, as gifts for today.
sections.key: Debated in the Mishnah and kept; read at Sukkot. Ecclesiastes is a book against illusions, not of despair: it gives back ordinary joys as gifts.

paras: Few books so short have left so many marks. 'There is no new thing under the sun', 'a time to be born, and a time to die', 'eat, drink and be merry', 'of making many books there is no end': all are from Ecclesiastes. Ernest Hemingway took the title of his first novel, The Sun Also Rises (1926), from 1:5, and printed 1:4–7 at its front, for a generation that had lost its illusions in the First World War. The vanitas still lifes of seventeenth-century Holland, with their skulls, guttering candles and wilting flowers, are named from its first verse in Latin: vanitas vanitatum.

Philosophers have read it too. It has been compared with the Stoics, with Epicurus, and with modern existentialists, and claimed by believers and sceptics alike. That is a sign of its honesty. A book that only comforted would not be read by the comfortless.
sections.key: Ecclesiastes gave the West 'nothing new under the sun', Hemingway's title and the vanitas painting; believers and sceptics both claim it.

refs: Leo Tolstoy, A Confession (1879–82), chapters IV and VI, tr. Aylmer Maude (Oxford: World's Classics, 1921), text from Standard Ebooks.
Mishnah, Yadayim 3:5; Talmud, Shabbat 30b; Song of Songs Rabbah 1:1:10 (Solomon's three books); Jerome, Commentary on Ecclesiastes (c. 388).
The Epic of Gilgamesh, Old Babylonian version (the 'Sippar' tablet), Siduri's advice; see A. R. George, The Babylonian Gilgamesh Epic (2003).

Michael V. Fox, Qohelet and His Contradictions (1989); R. N. Whybray, 'Qoheleth, Preacher of Joy', Journal for the Study of the Old Testament 23 (1982); Choon-Leong Seow, Ecclesiastes (Anchor Bible, 1997), on the date and the Persian loanwords.

debate.question: Is Ecclesiastes a sceptic in the Bible, or a believer who has seen through everything else?

positions.name: A sceptic, smuggled in
positions.who: Many modern critics, e.g. James Crenshaw; and, in his own way, Tolstoy
positions.view: The Preacher doubts that God's ways can be known, that justice is done or that anything lasts. His 'enjoy life' passages are resignation, making the best of a bad job. The pious epilogue was added later to get the book past the censors.
positions.evidence: 'All is vanity'; 'one event to the righteous and to the wicked' (9:2); the debate in the Mishnah; the change of voice in 12:9–14.

positions.name: A preacher of joy
positions.who: R. N. Whybray; many Jewish readers, who read it at the festival of joy, Sukkot
positions.view: The book's real message is in its seven refrains: life is fleeting, so receive its ordinary goods as God's gift now. Hevel means 'fleeting', not 'meaningless'.
positions.evidence: 2:24; 3:12–13; 5:18; 8:15; 9:7–10; 11:9: 'God has already accepted your works'.

positions.name: A believer clearing the ground
positions.who: Most Christian and Jewish commentators through history, e.g. Jerome; many today, e.g. Craig Bartholomew
positions.view: The Preacher deliberately looks at life 'under the sun', as if from below, to show that nothing in this world can bear the weight of meaning. That clears the ground for the fear of God, which is where the book ends.
positions.evidence: The repeated 'under the sun'; 'remember your Creator' (12:1); 'He has also set eternity in their hearts' (3:11); the epilogue.

debate.agree: All agree that Ecclesiastes refuses easy answers, that it faces death without flinching, and that its book-ending verdict is the fear of God, whoever wrote it.

look.why: Michel-François Dandré-Bardon painted this memento mori, 'remember that you will die', in the early 1730s. It is not a picture of Ecclesiastes, but it shows the thought the Preacher forces on us: men in tattered robes bowing before the skulls of the dead.
points: Twelve men, and perhaps a child, kneel, sit or lie face down before an altar on which three skulls are piled.
The man nearest the altar holds up a long cross so that it almost touches the skulls; he bows so deeply that his hood hides his face.
Another man rests on the broken base of a column, reaching forward with his head bowed.
In the lower right corner, two barefoot men have chains wrapped around their bodies; one reclines and looks at an open book.
To the left lie another book and a heap of glimmering objects, perhaps pieces of armour and maybe another skull.
Behind them all, a mint-green curtain hangs across a row of columns before pale walls with an arched doorway.

music.why: Brahms's German Requiem (1868) sets 'All flesh is as grass' and the psalmist's prayer to know his end and the measure of his days: the Preacher's hevel, set to music that also finds comfort.

think.why: Ecclesiastes says the dead go to Sheol and are forgotten. What did later Jews and Christians come to believe, and why?

learn.why: The Preacher's best-known poem: everything has its season. Learn it as the other half of 'vanity of vanities'.

check.q: Why do many scholars think 'meaningless' is a misleading translation of hevel?
options: Because the word only appears once
Because hevel means 'holy'
Because Ecclesiastes was written in Greek
Because hevel is a picture (breath, vapour) suggesting brief, ungraspable and baffling, not simply 'without meaning'
check.why: Hevel is breath; the book says nothing under the sun lasts or can be held, while still calling food, work and love good gifts.

check.q: In 9:7 the Preacher says 'eat your bread with joy'. What reason does he give, and what does it show?
options: Because the wicked are punished, so it shows justice
Because tomorrow you may be rich, so it shows optimism
Because God has already accepted your works: joy is permitted as God's gift, not grabbed in despair
Because bread is cheap, so it shows thrift
check.why: The clause 'for God has already accepted your works' turns resignation into gift; it is what distinguishes the Preacher from Siduri in Gilgamesh.

check.q: Tolstoy was healthy, rich, famous and loved when he hid the rope. Why does that make his case stronger?
options: It shows he was ungrateful
It rules out the reply that his despair came from poverty or sickness: he had everything, as the Preacher did, and it was not enough
It proves he was mentally ill
It shows wealth always causes despair
check.why: Like the Preacher's 'Solomon', Tolstoy is the ideal witness: he tested every good of life and found none could give it meaning.

check.q: Where does Tolstoy's reading of Ecclesiastes go beyond the book itself?
options: He denies Solomon wrote it
He quotes it inaccurately
He concludes one must free oneself from life, while the Preacher concludes one should enjoy life's gifts and fear God
He says it is a love poem
check.why: Ecclesiastes 4:2–3 praises the unborn, but its conclusions are joy and the fear of God; Tolstoy hears the question and not the answer.

check.q: What is the best evidence that Ecclesiastes was written well after Solomon?
options: Its late Hebrew and Persian loanwords such as pardes, 'park'
It is written in Aramaic throughout
It mentions Jesus
It was found in Egypt
check.why: Its language is close to the Mishnah's, and Persian words point to the Persian period or later.

check.q: Siduri in Gilgamesh gives advice very like Ecclesiastes 9:7–9. What is the most important difference?
options: There is no difference
Siduri forbids wine
In Ecclesiastes joy is the gift of the one God who accepts our works; in Gilgamesh it is consolation from gods who kept life for themselves
Gilgamesh is later than Ecclesiastes
check.why: The shared advice is old; the Preacher sets it under God's acceptance.

tutorial.question: Is Ecclesiastes a sceptical book?
tutorial.approach: Define hevel and show why translations differ. Set out the evidence for scepticism (the 'one event', injustice, the debate in the Mishnah) and for joy (the seven refrains). Use Tolstoy as the strongest sceptical reader, and ask what he left out. Consider the frame and the epilogue. End with your own view: sceptic, preacher of joy, or believer clearing the ground?
strong: Explains hevel as breath or vapour, and the effect of different translations.
Gives both refrains: 'all is hevel' and 'eat your bread with joy'.
Uses chapter 9 closely, including 'for God has already accepted your works'.
Reads Tolstoy fairly and shows where he goes beyond the text.
Discusses the frame narrator and the epilogue (12:9–14).
Uses outside evidence such as Gilgamesh or the Mishnah debate.

reading.author: Leo Tolstoy
reading.title: A Confession (tr. Aylmer Maude)
reading.why: Short and unforgettable; read it all, including the chapters on his return.

reading.author: Ellen F. Davis
reading.title: Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs
reading.why: A wise guide to the Preacher's joy as well as his doubt.

reading.author: Michael V. Fox
reading.title: A Time to Tear Down and a Time to Build Up: A Rereading of Ecclesiastes
reading.why: The case for hevel as 'absurd', argued with care.

reading.author: Choon-Leong Seow
reading.title: Ecclesiastes (Anchor Bible)
reading.why: The standard commentary on the language, date and setting.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: each evening, write down one ordinary gift you enjoyed that day (a meal, a conversation, a piece of work done well), as Ecclesiastes 9:7–10 asks. Next to it, write one thing you were chasing that turned out to be breath.
sessions.reflect: What are you counting on to make your life mean something? Would it survive the Preacher's test?
takeaways: Hevel means breath or vapour: nothing under the sun lasts or can bear the weight of a life's meaning.
Yet the Preacher tells you seven times to receive food, work and love as God's gifts now; the book ends with the fear of God.
Tolstoy heard the book's despair at full strength, but not its joy: Ecclesiastes is a cure for false hopes, not a counsel of despair.

sessions.title: The case against: does God answer?
sessions.line: What if Tolstoy was right, and life really is meaningless? What if prayer is talking to an empty sky? The objection at full strength, and the psalmist's reply.
sessions.plain: This session gives the strongest case against everything so far. If death ends everything, perhaps life has no meaning, and the Preacher's joy is just a way of not looking. And if God never answers, perhaps the psalmists were talking to no one. We read Tolstoy's own argument, the 'four ways out' of a meaningless life, and a psalm that asks God to look away. Then we ask what, if anything, the Bible says back.
sessions.why: Session 4 read Ecclesiastes beside Tolstoy and argued that the Preacher is not a counsel of despair. But that argument assumed God is there to give the gifts. The objection comes here, once you have heard the Psalms complain and the Preacher doubt, because it uses their own words against them.
answers: What if life really is meaningless?
Isn't 'enjoy life' just a way of not thinking about death?
What if prayer is talking to an empty sky?
What does the Bible say back, if anything?
sessions.finding: The objection is real and the Bible itself voices it; its answer is not an argument but a relationship that holds on through silence.

paras: Four sessions have built a picture. The Psalms let people say everything to God, even despair (Psalm 88). Proverbs says wisdom begins with reverence for God and tends to bring a good life. Ecclesiastes says nothing under the sun lasts, and still tells us to receive our bread with joy as God's gift.

Every step assumed that God is there: that someone hears the lament and gives the bread. The objection asks: what if he isn't? Then Psalm 88 is a man talking to the dark, and the Preacher's joy is honey licked in a well.
background.key: Every session so far assumed God hears the lament and gives the gifts. The objection asks what follows if he doesn't.

background.h: Why this is the hardest objection
paras: Most objections to the Bible ask whether something happened. This one asks whether anything matters, and whether anyone is listening. It is not an outsider's attack. The Bible taught people to ask it: the Preacher says the wise die like fools; Psalm 88 says God hides his face; Isaiah says, 'Most certainly you are a God who has hidden yourself' (Isaiah 45:15).

And it is not only for philosophers. Tolstoy was a novelist, not a professor, and he felt it as a pull towards death. Many people feel it in illness, grief or depression, or simply at three in the morning. A fair answer must take that seriously.
background.key: This objection is about meaning and whether God listens. The Bible itself raises it, and people feel it, not only think it.

paras: You read in session 4 how Tolstoy's life 'came to a standstill' and how he quoted Ecclesiastes. In chapter V of A Confession he looked for an answer in the sciences, and found that they answered every question but his own: 'Why should I live?' In chapter VI he turned to the wisest of mankind and found that Socrates, Schopenhauer, Solomon and the Buddha all said the same: life is an evil, and death a release.

In chapter VII, which we read now, he looks at the people of his own class and finds four ways of living with that conclusion. In chapter VIII he faces the problem that would change his life, but not yet his mind.
background.key: Science answered every question but 'Why should I live?'; the sages said life is evil. Now Tolstoy looks at how people live with that.

paras: The main reading is Tolstoy's 'four ways out' (chapter VII, with the end of chapter VIII). It is the objection in the words of its most powerful modern advocate. Notice that he quotes the Preacher's 'eat your bread with joy' as one of the ways of not facing the truth.

The comparison is Psalm 39, a prayer as stark as Psalm 88, which you read in session 2. Its speaker calls every human life a breath, hevel, the word of Ecclesiastes, and ends by asking God to look away. It is the Bible's own voice of the objection.
background.key: Tolstoy's 'four ways out', then Psalm 39, where the psalmist calls life a breath and asks God to look away.

before: What are Tolstoy's four ways out? Which do you think most people in your world take?
Why does Tolstoy reject the second way, enjoying what one has, which the Preacher recommends?
In Psalm 39, what does the speaker ask God for at the end? Is that faith or despair?
sessions.readWhy: The objection in the words of its most powerful modern advocate.

paras: Not finding an explanation in science I began to seek for it in life, hoping to find it among the people around me. And I began to observe how the people around me—people like myself—lived, and what their attitude was to this question which had brought me to despair.
And this is what I found among people who were in the same position as myself as regards education and manner of life.
I found that for people of my circle there were four ways out of the terrible position in which we are all placed.

The first was that of ignorance. It consists in not knowing, not understanding, that life is an evil and an absurdity. People of this sort—chiefly women, or very young or very dull people—have not yet understood that question of life which presented itself to Schopenhauer, Solomon, and Buddha. They see neither the dragon that awaits them nor the mice gnawing the shrub by which they are hanging, and they lick the drops of honey, but they lick those drops of honey only for a while: something will turn their attention to the dragon and the mice, and there will be an end to their licking. From them I had nothing to learn—one cannot cease to know what one does know.

The second way out is epicureanism. It consists, while knowing the hopelessness of life, in making use meanwhile of the advantages one has, disregarding the dragon and the mice, and licking the honey in the best way, especially if there is much of it within reach. Solomon expresses this way out thus: “Then I commended mirth, because a man hath no better thing under the sun, than to eat, and to drink, and to be merry: and that this should accompany him in his labour the days of his life, which God giveth him under the sun.

“Therefore eat thy bread with joy and drink thy wine with a merry heart. … Live joyfully with the wife whom thou lovest all the days of the life of thy vanity … for this is thy portion in life and in thy labours which thou takest under the sun. … Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might, for there is not work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in the grave, whither thou goest.”

That is the way in which the majority of people of our circle make life possible for themselves. Their circumstances furnish them with more of welfare than of hardship, and their moral dullness makes it possible for them to forget that the advantage of their position is accidental, and that not everyone can have a thousand wives and palaces like Solomon, that for everyone who has a thousand wives there are a thousand without a wife, and that for each palace there are a thousand people who have to build it in the sweat of their brows; and that the accident that has today made me a Solomon may tomorrow make me a Solomon’s slave. The dullness of these people’s imagination enables them to forget the things that gave Buddha no peace—the inevitability of sickness, old age, and death, which today or tomorrow will destroy all these pleasures.

The third escape is that of strength and energy. It consists in destroying life, when one has understood that it is an evil and an absurdity. A few exceptionally strong and consistent people act so. Having understood the stupidity of the joke that has been played on them, and having understood that it is better to be dead than to be alive, and that it is best of all not to exist, they act accordingly and promptly end this stupid joke, since there are means: a rope round one’s neck, water, a knife to stick into one’s heart, or the trains on the railways; and the number of those of our circle who act in this way becomes greater and greater, and for the most part they act so at the best time of their life, when the strength of their mind is in full bloom and few habits degrading to the mind have as yet been acquired.
I saw that this was the worthiest way of escape and I wished to adopt it.

The fourth way out is that of weakness. It consists in seeing the truth of the situation and yet clinging to life, knowing in advance that nothing can come of it. People of this kind know that death is better than life, but not having the strength to act rationally—to end the deception quickly and kill themselves—they seem to wait for something. This is the escape of weakness, for if I know what is best and it is within my power, why not yield to what is best? … I found myself in that category.

So people of my class evade the terrible contradiction in four ways. Strain my attention as I would, I saw no way except those four. One way was not to understand that life is senseless, vanity, and an evil, and that it is better not to live. I could not help knowing this, and when I once knew it could not shut my eyes to it. The second way was to use life such as it is without thinking of the future. And I could not do that. I, like Sakya Muni, could not ride out hunting when I knew that old age, suffering, and death exist. My imagination was too vivid. Nor could I rejoice in the momentary accidents that for an instant threw pleasure to my lot. The third way, having understood that life is evil and stupid, was to end it by killing oneself. I understood that, but somehow still did not kill myself. The fourth way was to live like Solomon and Schopenhauer—knowing that life is a stupid joke played upon us, and still to go on living, washing oneself, dressing, dining, talking, and even writing books. This was to me repulsive and tormenting, but I remained in that position.

I see now that if I did not kill myself it was due to some dim consciousness of the invalidity of my thoughts. However convincing and indubitable appeared to me the sequence of my thoughts and of those of the wise that have brought us to the admission of the senselessness of life, there remained in me a vague doubt of the justice of my conclusion.

It was like this: I, my reason, have acknowledged that life is senseless. If there is nothing higher than reason (and there is not: nothing can prove that there is), then reason is the creator of life for me. If reason did not exist there would be for me no life. How can reason deny life when it is the creator of life? Or to put it the other way: were there no life, my reason would not exist; therefore reason is life’s son. Life is all. Reason is its fruit yet reason rejects life itself! I felt that there was something wrong here.

My position was terrible. I knew I could find nothing along the path of reasonable knowledge except a denial of life; and there—in faith—was nothing but a denial of reason, which was yet more impossible for me than a denial of life. From rational knowledge it appeared that life is an evil, people know this and it is in their power to end life; yet they lived and still live, and I myself live, though I have long known that life is senseless and an evil. By faith it appears that in order to understand the meaning of life I must renounce my reason, the very thing for which alone a meaning is required.

parts.author: Leo Tolstoy
parts.title: Four ways out
parts.who: Leo Tolstoy (1828–1910), Russian novelist
parts.context: Tolstoy has found no answer in science or philosophy. Now he looks at 'people of my circle', the educated Russian upper class, and asks how they live with the knowledge that life ends in death. He is writing a few years after the crisis, looking back. Translated by Aylmer Maude (1921); the cuts are marked '…'. The '…' marks inside Tolstoy's quotation of Ecclesiastes and in the paragraph on the fourth way are in Maude's text.
parts.plain: Tolstoy says there are four ways people like him deal with the meaninglessness of life. Some simply don't see it (ignorance). Some see it but enjoy what they have while they can (epicureanism), as Solomon advised. A few strong ones see it and kill themselves (strength). Most see it and carry on anyway, without reason (weakness), and he was one of those. Then he notices something odd: his reason, which says life is senseless, is itself a product of life. Why does it reject the life that made it?

commentary.on: I found that for people of my circle there were four ways out of the terrible position in which we are all placed.
commentary.text: Tolstoy is precise: 'people of my circle'. He is describing the rich and educated. Notice the phrase 'the terrible position in which we are all placed': he takes it as proved that life has no meaning. The question is only how to live with it.

commentary.on: The first was that of ignorance.
commentary.text: The first way is not to see the dragon at all. Tolstoy's own description of who does this ('chiefly women, or very young or very dull people') is a nineteenth-century aristocrat's prejudice, and shows the limits of his view. His point, though, is fair: you cannot choose to stop knowing what you know.

commentary.on: The second way out is epicureanism.
commentary.text: Epicurus (341–270 BC) taught that the good life is a quiet pleasure free of fear. Tolstoy uses his name for the life of enjoying what you have and not thinking about the end, and he quotes Ecclesiastes 8:15 and 9:7–10 as its motto. This is the sharpest point of the objection for this journey: what session 4 called the Preacher's wisdom, Tolstoy calls looking away.

commentary.on: not everyone can have a thousand wives and palaces like Solomon
commentary.text: And a moral objection: enjoyment is a privilege. For every palace there are a thousand people who built it. 'Enjoy your bread' is easy advice for those who have bread. Tolstoy's later life, giving up his property and living like a peasant, began with this thought.

commentary.on: The third escape is that of strength and energy. It consists in destroying life
commentary.text: Here Tolstoy calls suicide the 'worthiest' and most consistent response, and says he wished to take it. We read it because it is the objection at full strength, not because it is right. If you are thinking along these lines yourself, please speak to someone today: a friend, a doctor, a pastor, or Samaritans on 116 123 (UK and Ireland). Tolstoy himself came to see this reasoning as a mistake.

commentary.on: The fourth way out is that of weakness.
commentary.text: Most people, Tolstoy says, know life is senseless and carry on anyway, 'washing oneself, dressing, dining, talking, and even writing books'. He despises it and admits it was his own position. This is the objection's sting: perhaps all of us who carry on are simply failing to follow our own logic.

commentary.on: I see now that if I did not kill myself it was due to some dim consciousness of the invalidity of my thoughts.
commentary.text: The first crack in the argument, and it comes from inside him. Something in him doubted his own conclusion before he could say why.

commentary.on: How can reason deny life when it is the creator of life?
commentary.text: Tolstoy's puzzle: reason is 'life's son', the fruit of living. If it concludes that life is worthless, it saws off the branch it sits on. He does not yet know what to do with this, but he feels 'there was something wrong here'.

commentary.on: By faith it appears that in order to understand the meaning of life I must renounce my reason
commentary.text: The trap as he saw it, at the end of chapter VIII: reason leads to the denial of life, faith seems to require the denial of reason. That is where we leave him. How he found his way out of the trap is told in the rest of A Confession, and in another journey.

read.author: Leo Tolstoy
read.who: Leo Tolstoy (1828–1910), Russian novelist

paras:
I said, “I will watch my ways, so that I don’t sin with my tongue.
I will keep my mouth with a bridle while the wicked is before me.”

I was mute with silence.
I held my peace, even from good.
My sorrow was stirred.

My heart was hot within me.
While I meditated, the fire burned.
I spoke with my tongue:

“Yahweh, show me my end,
what is the measure of my days.
Let me know how frail I am.

Behold, you have made my days hand widths.
My lifetime is as nothing before you.
Surely every man stands as a breath.”

“Surely every man walks like a shadow.
Surely they busy themselves in vain.
He heaps up, and doesn’t know who shall gather.

Now, Lord, what do I wait for?
My hope is in you.

Deliver me from all my transgressions.
Don’t make me the reproach of the foolish.

I was mute.
I didn’t open my mouth,
because you did it.

Remove your scourge away from me.
I am overcome by the blow of your hand.

When you rebuke and correct man for iniquity,
you consume his wealth like a moth.
Surely every man is but a breath.”

“Hear my prayer, Yahweh, and give ear to my cry.
Don’t be silent at my tears.
For I am a stranger with you,
a foreigner, as all my fathers were.

Oh spare me, that I may recover strength,
before I go away and exist no more.”

parts.title: Every man is but a breath
parts.context: Headed 'For the Chief Musician. For Jeduthun. A Psalm by David.' Jeduthun was one of David's Temple musicians (1 Chronicles 16:41). Like Psalm 88, it is a lament with almost no comfort, and it ends with a request no other psalm makes.

commentary.on: I said, “I will watch my ways, so that I don't sin with my tongue.
commentary.text: The speaker tried silence first. He would not complain in front of 'the wicked', perhaps so as not to give them a reason to mock his faith. But silence made it worse: 'my heart was hot within me'.

commentary.on: Yahweh, show me my end, what is the measure of my days. Let me know how frail I am.
commentary.text: When he finally speaks, it is to ask to know the worst: how short life is. Brahms set these words in his German Requiem.

commentary.on: Surely every man stands as a breath.
commentary.text: 'Breath' is hevel, the Preacher's word, which the WEB translates 'vanity' in Ecclesiastes. The psalmist and the Preacher see the same thing.

commentary.on: Surely every man walks like a shadow. Surely they busy themselves in vain. He heaps up, and doesn't know who shall gather.
commentary.text: This is Tolstoy's fourth way described from the inside: busy, heaping up, unable to keep any of it. The psalmist does not deny it.

commentary.on: Now, Lord, what do I wait for? My hope is in you.
commentary.text: And yet in the middle of the psalm, this. The psalmist does not answer the argument. He turns to someone. Having seen that everything is breath, he puts his hope in the one who is not.

commentary.on: Don't be silent at my tears.
commentary.text: The problem of divine silence, in five words. He asks God to speak, and the psalm records no answer.

commentary.on: Oh spare me, that I may recover strength, before I go away and exist no more.
commentary.text: The last verse literally asks God to look away from him, so that he can smile again before he dies. It is as dark an ending as Psalm 88's. But it is still a prayer: even 'look away' is said to God.

compare.why: The Bible does not leave the objection to its critics. Psalm 39 voices it from inside faith, using the very word of Ecclesiastes, hevel.
compare.title: Look away from me

sections.h: The objection at full strength: meaning
paras: Put Tolstoy's case as strongly as it can be put. Everything we do ends in death: ours, our children's, our civilisation's, and in the end the death of the sun. Nothing we achieve lasts. If there is no God and no life beyond this one, then every human story ends in the same nothing, and no amount of love or work changes the ending. A meaning that death erases, the argument runs, was never really a meaning at all.

The German philosopher Arthur Schopenhauer (1788–1860), whom Tolstoy read with passion, went further. In The World as Will and Representation (1818) he argued that all life is driven by a blind, endless will to live, which can never be satisfied: we suffer when we lack what we want, and are bored when we have it, so life swings like a pendulum between pain and boredom. On this view the Preacher's 'the eye is not satisfied with seeing' is not a sad observation but the law of existence.

In the twentieth century Albert Camus (The Myth of Sisyphus, 1942) began from the same place, calling suicide the one truly serious philosophical problem, though he answered it differently: live in defiance of the absurd. All three agree on the starting point: the universe gives no meaning back.
sections.key: If death ends everything, no meaning survives it (Tolstoy). Schopenhauer: life swings between pain and boredom. Camus: the universe gives no meaning back.

sections.h: The objection at full strength: silence
paras: The second half of the objection is about prayer. The Psalms are full of people crying to God. But how often does God answer? Psalm 13 asks 'How long?'; Psalm 88 ends in darkness; Psalm 39 asks God not to be silent at its tears, and he is. If God existed and loved us, the sceptic asks, why would he leave people who are seeking him in the dark?

The Canadian philosopher J. L. Schellenberg (Divine Hiddenness and Human Reason, 1993) turned this into a formal argument. A perfectly loving God would always make a relationship with himself possible for anyone who is not resisting him. But there are people who are not resisting, who would like to believe, and cannot. So, he concludes, there is no perfectly loving God.

Believers have felt this too. The letters of Mother Teresa of Calcutta, published after her death (Come Be My Light, 2007), revealed that for most of her nearly fifty years of work among the dying she felt no sense of God's presence at all. The objection is not only from outside the faith. It is in the Psalms, and in the lives of saints.
sections.key: If God loved us, why the silence? Schellenberg (1993): non-resisting unbelief shows there is no perfectly loving God. Even saints, like Mother Teresa, felt the absence.

sections.h: What the replies are, and are not
paras: Philosophers have offered replies. To the argument from meaning: perhaps meaning does not need to last for ever to be real; a kindness done today is good even if no one remembers it. To the argument from silence: perhaps a God who was always obvious would overwhelm our freedom, so that we could not love him freely (an argument found in Pascal and many since); or perhaps hiddenness is a stage, as Psalm 13's trust follows its complaint. These are serious, and each has serious critics.

But notice what the Bible does not do. It does not answer Tolstoy with an argument. Ecclesiastes concedes the premise: all is hevel. Psalm 88 concedes the silence. Psalm 39 concedes that every life is a breath. What they offer instead is a stance: to keep speaking to God in the dark. 'My hope is in you' (39:7) is not a proof. It is holding on.

Is that an evasion? A sceptic will say yes: it is Tolstoy's fourth way, carrying on without reason. A believer will say no: it is what trust is, in any relationship, when the other is silent. That is the choice this session leaves you with.
sections.key: Philosophical replies exist and are contested. The Bible itself concedes the premise and offers a stance: to keep speaking to God in the dark.

sections.h: Where the Bible goes from here
paras: Three things in the Bible bear on the objection without pretending to settle it. First, the Psalms never treat silence as the last word, even when the psalm ends in it; they were kept and sung by a community that had come through. Psalm 88 sits in the same book as Psalm 30, 'Weeping may stay for the night, but joy comes in the morning' (30:5).
Second, later Jewish faith came to hope that death is not the end (Daniel 12:2), which changes the Preacher's question: if God raises the dead, then what is done under the sun is not simply erased.

Third, the Gospels show Jesus praying a lament on the cross, 'My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?' (Psalm 22:1; Mark 15:34). Christians have seen in that cry God himself entering the silence, not explaining it. These are claims of faith, not arguments that would satisfy Tolstoy in chapter VII. The question of whether God exists at all belongs to the Great Questions hall. This journey's question is narrower: can someone honestly pray with the Psalms after hearing Tolstoy? The psalmists' answer is that they already had.
sections.key: The Psalms were kept by people who came through; later Israel hoped for resurrection; Jesus prayed Psalm 22 on the cross. These are faith's claims, not proofs.

paras: One of the most interesting replies to Tolstoy's kind of despair came from the American psychologist and philosopher William James (1842–1910), who had been through a crisis of his own as a young man. In a lecture to Harvard students in 1895, 'Is Life Worth Living?', later printed in The Will to Believe (1897), he took on the pessimists directly, Schopenhauer among them.

James did not claim to prove that life has meaning. He argued, first, that the pessimist's conclusion is not forced by the evidence: the universe as science shows it neither proves nor disproves a deeper meaning. Second, that in some questions our belief helps to make the fact. A climber who believes he can make a leap across a crevasse is more likely to make it; a person who believes life is worth living will live in a way that makes it more so. Third, that it is not irrational to act on faith where the evidence is open and the choice cannot be avoided: not to choose is itself to choose.

That is not the psalmist's answer, which is trust in a God who is there. But it is a reply in Tolstoy's own terms, by someone who had felt what Tolstoy felt, and it shows that the objection, strong as it is, is not the only rational conclusion.
sections.key: William James (1895) argued the pessimist's conclusion is not forced, that belief can help make life worth living, and that faith is rational when the choice is unavoidable.

refs: Leo Tolstoy, A Confession, chapters V–VIII, tr. Aylmer Maude (1921).
Psalms 13, 22, 30:5, 39, 88; Ecclesiastes 1:8; 8:15; 9:7–10; Isaiah 45:15; Daniel 12:2; Mark 15:34; 1 Chronicles 16:41.

J. L. Schellenberg, Divine Hiddenness and Human Reason (1993); Daniel Howard-Snyder and Paul Moser (eds.), Divine Hiddenness: New Essays (2002).
Mother Teresa, Come Be My Light, ed. Brian Kolodiejchuk (2007); Blaise Pascal, Pensées (1670), on the hidden God.

debate.question: After Tolstoy, can anyone honestly pray the Psalms?

positions.name: Tolstoy in chapter VII: no
positions.who: Leo Tolstoy (as he stood in 1879); Arthur Schopenhauer
positions.view: Reason shows that life ends in nothing and so has no meaning. Prayer and enjoyment are ways of not looking. The honest options are to end life or to admit one carries on from weakness.
positions.evidence: A Confession VI–VII; the agreement of Socrates, Schopenhauer, Solomon and the Buddha as Tolstoy read them; Ecclesiastes 1:2; 4:2–3.

positions.name: The modern sceptic: there is no one to pray to
positions.who: J. L. Schellenberg; many secular thinkers
positions.view: We need not despair, as Tolstoy did: human life can have meaning we make ourselves. But the silence of God is evidence that no loving God is there. The Psalms are moving human poetry, not conversation.
positions.evidence: The argument from hiddenness (1993); the many sincere seekers who never find faith; the unanswered endings of Psalms 39 and 88.

positions.name: The psalmist: yes, in the dark
positions.who: The writers of Psalms 13, 39 and 88; Jewish and Christian tradition; e.g. Bonhoeffer, Mother Teresa
positions.view: The Psalms already know everything Tolstoy knew: life is a breath, God is silent. They pray anyway, not because they have answered the argument, but because faith is a relationship that holds on. Praying in the dark is not the denial of the problem but the way through it.
positions.evidence: Psalm 39:7, 'My hope is in you'; Psalm 88:13, 'In the morning, my prayer comes before you'; Jesus praying Psalm 22 on the cross.

debate.agree: All three agree that Tolstoy's question is real, that easy comfort is no answer, and that death and silence must be faced honestly.

look.why: Richard Wilson painted Solitude in the 1760s. It is not a scene from the Bible or from Tolstoy, and it is daylight, not night: a man lies alone at the foot of a broken monument, with a book and a cross beside him. It is here for the stance of Psalm 39: alone, facing the end, with the book still open before him.
points: A broken stone lion stands on a tall, cracked pedestal at the edge of still water; only the back half of its body and one front paw, resting on a ball, remain.
A man lies on the ground, propped on one elbow against the pedestal, a white cloth draped over his head, hiding much of his face.
He looks down at a book propped on a rock; a wooden cross rests against the rock beside him.
Under the dark trees to the left, one robed figure sits reading a book, and an old man with a long white beard and a walking stick stands.
A willow bows over the water; across it is a low arched entrance, perhaps to a grotto, and far away smoke rises from a mountain.

music.why: Henryk Górecki's Symphony of Sorrowful Songs (1976) is three slow laments, one sung from words a young woman wrote on the wall of a Gestapo cell. It does not hurry to comfort: the right sound for the objection.

think.why: The modern debate about whether God exists, including the argument from hiddenness, stated fairly on both sides.

learn.why: The cry Jesus prayed from the cross: the Bible's own words for the silence of God.

check.q: Tolstoy quotes Ecclesiastes 9:7–10 ('eat thy bread with joy') as an example of which 'way out', and why does that matter for this journey?
options: Ignorance; it shows the Preacher was ignorant
Epicureanism; it means the advice session 4 called wisdom, Tolstoy calls looking away from the truth
Weakness; it shows the Preacher had no reasons
Strength; it shows the Preacher recommended suicide
check.why: Tolstoy makes the Preacher's joy a form of distraction; the objection turns the book's answer into part of the problem.

check.q: What is Tolstoy's moral objection to the second way, enjoying what one has?
options: That the Bible forbids wine
That it makes people lazy
That it is only open to the fortunate: for every palace a thousand people build it
That pleasure is always sinful
check.why: 'Not everyone can have a thousand wives and palaces like Solomon': enjoyment as life's answer is a privilege of the few.

check.q: What 'crack' does Tolstoy find in his own reasoning at the end of chapter VII?
options: That his family needed him financially
That Schopenhauer had changed his mind
That reason, which says life is senseless, is itself the fruit of life, so its rejection of life seems self-defeating
That science had disproved God
check.why: 'Reason is life's son... yet reason rejects life itself! I felt that there was something wrong here.'

check.q: Which best states Schellenberg's argument from divine hiddenness?
options: God is hidden because people are sinful, so he must exist
A perfectly loving God would make relationship with himself possible for anyone not resisting; non-resisting unbelievers exist; so there is no such God
Hiddenness proves God is not all-powerful
God is hidden because he does not care
check.why: The argument turns on non-resistant unbelief, people who want to believe and cannot.

check.q: Psalm 39 calls every human life 'a breath' (hevel). What does the psalmist do with that conclusion?
options: He concludes there is no God
He curses his enemies
He turns to God: 'My hope is in you', and keeps praying though no answer is recorded
He decides to enjoy life while he can
check.why: The psalm concedes the premise of the objection and responds with relationship, not argument.

check.q: Which reply to the objection does this session say the Bible itself mainly gives?
options: A stance of holding on to God in prayer through silence, with hope in resurrection and the cross in the background
The claim that suffering is an illusion

tutorial.question: 'The Psalms already knew everything Tolstoy knew.' Do you agree?
tutorial.approach: State Tolstoy's case at full strength, including his treatment of the Preacher as an epicurean. Add the argument from divine silence. Then set Psalms 39 and 88 beside him: what do they concede, and what do they do differently? Decide whether holding on to God in silence is faith or Tolstoy's 'fourth way' of weakness. Be fair to the sceptic.
strong: States the four ways out accurately, with Tolstoy's reasons.
Explains why Tolstoy puts Ecclesiastes 9 under epicureanism, and assesses it.
Presents the argument from hiddenness fairly, with Schellenberg or the psalms' own complaints.
Reads Psalm 39 closely: hevel, 'My hope is in you', 'Don't be silent at my tears'.
Distinguishes an argument from a stance, and asks whether the stance is honest.
Notes Tolstoy's own doubt about his reasoning (reason as 'life's son').

sessions.practice: Live it this week: if a question is troubling you, write it down as a psalmist would, addressed to God, without softening it. Then say it aloud once a day, and add 'My hope is in you' only if you can mean it. If the dark is heavy, tell one person this week.
