paras: Yahweh spoke to Moses after the death of the two sons of Aaron, when they came near before Yahweh, and died;

and Yahweh said to Moses, “Tell Aaron your brother not to come at just any time into the Most Holy Place within the veil, before the mercy seat which is on the ark; lest he die; for I will appear in the cloud on the mercy seat.
“Aaron shall come into the sanctuary with a young bull for a sin offering, and a ram for a burnt offering.

He shall put on the holy linen tunic. He shall have the linen trousers on his body, and shall put on the linen sash, and he shall be clothed with the linen turban. They are the holy garments. He shall bathe his body in water, and put them on.
He shall take from the congregation of the children of Israel two male goats for a sin offering, and one ram for a burnt offering.
“Aaron shall offer the bull of the sin offering, which is for himself, and make atonement for himself and for his house.
He shall take the two goats, and set them before Yahweh at the door of the Tent of Meeting.
Aaron shall cast lots for the two goats: one lot for Yahweh, and the other lot for the scapegoat.
Aaron shall present the goat on which the lot fell for Yahweh, and offer him for a sin offering.
But the goat on which the lot fell for the scapegoat shall be presented alive before Yahweh, to make atonement for him, to send him away as the scapegoat into the wilderness.
“Aaron shall present the bull of the sin offering, which is for himself, and shall make atonement for himself and for his house, and shall kill the bull of the sin offering which is for himself.
He shall take a censer full of coals of fire from off the altar before Yahweh, and two handfuls of sweet incense beaten small, and bring it within the veil.
He shall put the incense on the fire before Yahweh, that the cloud of the incense may cover the mercy seat that is on the covenant, so that he will not die.
He shall take some of the blood of the bull, and sprinkle it with his finger on the mercy seat on the east; and before the mercy seat he shall sprinkle some of the blood with his finger seven times.

“Then he shall kill the goat of the sin offering that is for the people, and bring his blood within the veil, and do with his blood as he did with the blood of the bull, and sprinkle it on the mercy seat and before the mercy seat.

He shall make atonement for the Holy Place, because of the uncleanness of the children of Israel, and because of their transgressions, even all their sins; and so he shall do for the Tent of Meeting that dwells with them in the middle of their uncleanness.

No one shall be in the Tent of Meeting when he enters to make atonement in the Holy Place, until he comes out, and has made atonement for himself and for his household, and for all the assembly of Israel.
“He shall go out to the altar that is before Yahweh and make atonement for it, and shall take some of the bull’s blood, and some of the goat’s blood, and put it around on the horns of the altar.
He shall sprinkle some of the blood on it with his finger seven times, and cleanse it, and make it holy from the uncleanness of the children of Israel.
“When he has finished atoning for the Holy Place, the Tent of Meeting, and the altar, he shall present the live goat.

Aaron shall lay both his hands on the head of the live goat, and confess over him all the iniquities of the children of Israel, and all their transgressions, even all their sins; and he shall put them on the head of the goat, and shall send him away into the wilderness by the hand of a man who is ready.
The goat shall carry all their iniquities on himself to a solitary land, and he shall release the goat in the wilderness.

parts.title: Two goats
parts.context: The setting is the wilderness after the Exodus, at the Tent of Meeting, the portable sanctuary that was the model for the later Temple in Jerusalem. Its inmost room, the Most Holy Place, held the ark of the covenant, a gold-covered chest with a gold lid called the mercy seat. It was the place of God's presence. Aaron, Moses' brother, is the high priest. Two of his sons have just died for approaching God carelessly (Leviticus 10).

commentary.on: Tell Aaron your brother not to come at just any time into the Most Holy Place within the veil
commentary.text: The first thing the passage says is that God's presence is dangerous. A curtain, the 'veil', separates the Most Holy Place from everything else. The deaths of Aaron's sons are the warning. Holiness here is like a great fire: life-giving, but not to be walked into casually.

commentary.on: for I will appear in the cloud on the mercy seat
commentary.text: The 'mercy seat' is the lid of the ark. Its Hebrew name, kapporet, comes from the same root as kippur, atonement. The Greek translation of the Old Testament calls it hilasterion, the word Paul later uses of Jesus. Remember it: this lid is where the whole ritual is aimed.

commentary.on: Aaron shall come into the sanctuary with a young bull for a sin offering
commentary.text: Before the high priest can act for anyone else, he must be cleansed himself. He bathes and puts on plain linen, not his gold robes. On this one day the greatest man in Israel dresses like a servant.

commentary.on: Aaron shall cast lots for the two goats: one lot for Yahweh, and the other lot for the scapegoat.
commentary.text: Two goats, one choice by lot. 'Scapegoat' translates the Hebrew la-azazel, 'for Azazel'. Nobody is sure what Azazel means: a place, a wilderness spirit, or 'complete removal'. William Tyndale coined 'scapegoat' (the goat that escapes) in his translation of 1530, and the word has been in English ever since.

commentary.on: to make atonement for him, to send him away as the scapegoat into the wilderness
commentary.text: The two goats show two sides of one problem. Sin pollutes the holy place where God lives with his people, and it weighs on the people themselves. The first goat deals with the pollution; the second carries the weight away.

parts.title: Behind the curtain, and out to the wilderness
parts.context: Now the ritual itself. The high priest goes behind the curtain twice, once with the blood of the bull for himself and once with the blood of the goat for the people. Then he comes out and lays the people's sins on the second goat. This was done once a year, on the tenth day of the seventh month, in early autumn.

commentary.on: that the cloud of the incense may cover the mercy seat that is on the covenant, so that he will not die
commentary.text: Even the high priest cannot look on the place of God's presence. Smoke hides it. Everything in the rite says that coming near God is not ours to take for granted.

commentary.on: sprinkle it with his finger on the mercy seat on the east; and before the mercy seat he shall sprinkle some of the blood with his finger seven times
commentary.text: Blood is put on the mercy seat itself, and seven times before it. Elsewhere Leviticus explains why: 'the life of the flesh is in the blood. I have given it to you on the altar to make atonement for your souls' (17:11). Notice who gives it. The blood is not a bribe paid to God. It is God's own gift, a way he provides for life to cleanse what sin has defiled.

commentary.on: He shall make atonement for the Holy Place, because of the uncleanness of the children of Israel
commentary.text: This surprises modern readers: it is the sanctuary that is cleansed. The Jewish scholar Jacob Milgrom argued that in Leviticus sin is like a stain that clings to the holy place, so that if it built up God could no longer live among his people. The blood cleans the house so that God can stay.

commentary.on: Aaron shall lay both his hands on the head of the live goat, and confess over him all the iniquities of the children of Israel
commentary.text: The laying on of both hands and spoken confession: the sins are named aloud and placed on the goat. Here, for the first time in the passage, we see something like substitution, one creature carrying what belongs to others.

commentary.on: The goat shall carry all their iniquities on himself to a solitary land
commentary.text: The goat is not killed. It walks out of the camp into the desert, carrying the sins as far away as possible, where they cannot come back. A psalm says it in a line: 'As far as the east is from the west, so far has he removed our transgressions from us' (Psalm 103:12). It is a picture anyone can understand: what you have done is taken away.

paras: But Christ having come as a high priest of the coming good things, through the greater and more perfect tabernacle, not made with hands, that is to say, not of this creation,
nor yet through the blood of goats and calves, but through his own blood, entered in once for all into the Holy Place, having obtained eternal redemption.
For if the blood of goats and bulls, and the ashes of a heifer sprinkling those who have been defiled, sanctify to the cleanness of the flesh,
how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without defect to God, cleanse your conscience from dead works to serve the living God?

For this reason he is the mediator of a new covenant, since a death has occurred for the redemption of the transgressions that were under the first covenant, that those who have been called may receive the promise of the eternal inheritance.
For where a last will and testament is, there must of necessity be the death of him who made it.
For a will is in force where there has been death, for it is never in force while he who made it lives.
Therefore even the first covenant has not been dedicated without blood.

For when every commandment had been spoken by Moses to all the people according to the law, he took the blood of the calves and the goats, with water and scarlet wool and hyssop, and sprinkled both the book itself and all the people,
saying, “This is the blood of the covenant which God has commanded you.”
Moreover he sprinkled the tabernacle and all the vessels of the ministry in the same way with the blood.
According to the law, nearly everything is cleansed with blood, and apart from shedding of blood there is no remission.
It was necessary therefore that the copies of the things in the heavens should be cleansed with these, but the heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices than these.
For Christ hasn’t entered into holy places made with hands, which are representations of the true, but into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God for us;
nor yet that he should offer himself often, as the high priest enters into the holy place year by year with blood not his own,
or else he must have suffered often since the foundation of the world. But now once at the end of the ages, he has been revealed to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself.
Inasmuch as it is appointed for men to die once, and after this, judgment,
so Christ also, having been offered once to bear the sins of many, will appear a second time, without sin, to those who are eagerly waiting for him for salvation.

parts.title: His own blood
parts.context: The writer has just described the Tent of Meeting and the high priest's yearly entry behind the curtain (Hebrews 9:1–10). Now he turns to Christ, whom he has already called 'a high priest' (4:15).

commentary.on: nor yet through the blood of goats and calves, but through his own blood, entered in once for all into the Holy Place
commentary.text: The whole argument is in this sentence. Christ is both the high priest and the sacrifice. And the place he enters is not a room in Jerusalem but the presence of God itself. 'Once for all' is the key phrase: this does not need repeating.

commentary.on: how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without defect to God, cleanse your conscience
commentary.text: The writer reasons 'from the lesser to the greater', a standard Jewish way of arguing. The old rite cleansed the body and the sanctuary; this one cleanses the conscience. And Christ 'offered himself': no one forces it on him.

commentary.on: apart from shedding of blood there is no remission
commentary.text: This is the line critics quote most. In context it describes the old law ('according to the law, nearly everything is cleansed with blood'). The writer's point is not that God is thirsty for blood, but that forgiveness costs a life, and in this case the life is given by the one who forgives.

parts.title: Offered once
parts.context: The writer finishes the comparison: the yearly entry of the high priest against the single entry of Christ.

commentary.on: nor yet that he should offer himself often, as the high priest enters into the holy place year by year with blood not his own
commentary.text: Year by year, with blood 'not his own': the two contrasts that matter to Hebrews. The old ritual had to be repeated because it never finished the job; a few verses later the writer says it plainly: 'it is impossible that the blood of bulls and goats should take away sins' (10:4).

commentary.on: But now once at the end of the ages, he has been revealed to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself.
commentary.text: 'The sacrifice of himself.' In Israel the priest offered something else; here the priest offers himself. That is the difference between a ritual and a self-giving, and it is the seed of almost every later account of the cross.

commentary.on: so Christ also, having been offered once to bear the sins of many
commentary.text: 'To bear the sins of many' echoes Isaiah 53:12, which you read if you took 'Kings and prophets': the servant who 'bore the sins of many'. Hebrews joins the Temple and the servant in one sentence. This is the verse to learn by heart.

compare.why: The letter to the Hebrews was written while the Day of Atonement was still kept in the Temple. It reads the ritual as a picture of what Christ did, and says that his death ended the need for it.
compare.title: Once for all

paras: The first problem for Christians was not explaining the cross but defending it. Crucifixion was so degrading that polite Romans avoided the word. Around AD 200 someone in Rome scratched a cartoon on a wall of the imperial palace on the Palatine Hill: a man raising his hand to a crucified figure with a donkey's head, and the words 'Alexamenos worships his god'. It is the oldest surviving picture of the crucifixion, and it is a joke.

Paul knew the problem. 'We preach Christ crucified: a stumbling block to Jews, and foolishness to Greeks' (1 Corinthians 1:23). To a Jew, a man hanged on a tree was under God's curse (Deuteronomy 21:23); to a Greek, a crucified god was absurd. The first Christians had to show that this death was not a defeat but the centre of God's plan. They did it by reaching for the deepest pictures in their Scriptures, and the first was the Temple.
sections.key: A crucified Messiah was a scandal to Jews and a joke to Romans; the first Christians answered by reading the cross through Israel's Scriptures.

paras: Every ancient people sacrificed. Greeks and Romans burned the bones and fat of oxen for the gods and ate the meat in a feast; Homer's heroes offer 'hecatombs', a hundred cattle. Sacrifice could be a gift, a meal shared with the gods, a way of sealing an agreement, or a way of removing pollution. Some peoples, including Israel's neighbours, sometimes sacrificed children.

Israel's sacrifices looked similar from outside, but the meaning was changed. God does not eat: 'If I were hungry, I would not tell you, for the world is mine' (Psalm 50:12). Child sacrifice is forbidden as an abomination (Deuteronomy 12:31); if you took 'Abraham and the promise', you saw the story of Isaac end with a ram in his place. And the prophets warned that sacrifice without justice was worthless: 'I desire mercy, and not sacrifice' (Hosea 6:6). In Israel, sacrifice was not a way to manage a hungry god. It was a gift God gave so that a people who had gone wrong could come home.
sections.key: All ancient peoples sacrificed; Israel's God needed no food, forbade child sacrifice and wanted mercy, so sacrifice became his gift for coming home.

sections.h: What the Day of Atonement did
paras: Scholars have argued for a century about how the sacrifices were meant to work. Two ideas stand out. The first, made famous by the Jewish scholar Jacob Milgrom in his great commentary on Leviticus (1991), is cleansing: sin pollutes the holy place like grime on a house, and the blood, as the carrier of life, is the cleaning agent. The second is substitution: a life given in place of a life, the animal standing in for the worshipper who lays a hand on it.

The Day of Atonement has both. The blood on the mercy seat cleanses the sanctuary so that God can go on living among his people. The live goat, with the sins confessed over it, carries them away. Leviticus ends the chapter with a promise: 'on this day shall atonement be made for you, to cleanse you. You shall be clean from all your sins before Yahweh' (16:30). The people did not have to earn it. They had to repent, fast and trust the rite God had given.
sections.key: Two ideas meet in the Day of Atonement: cleansing (blood purifies the sanctuary) and substitution (the goat carries the people's sins away).

paras: The Hebrew verb behind 'atonement', kipper, probably means to wipe clean or to cover. English had no single word for it. 'Atonement' was formed in the early 1500s from 'at one', meaning reconciled: two people who had quarrelled were 'set at one'. William Tyndale used it in his English Bible, in Romans 5:11 (1526) and Leviticus (1530), and the King James Bible of 1611 kept it. So when English speakers say 'atonement', they are saying 'at-one-ment': the making of peace between God and people.

This matters because it tells us what the word is about. It is not first about punishment or payment. It is about a broken relationship being mended. Every picture in this journey, the ransom, the victory, the debt, the courtroom, is an attempt to say how that mending happened, and what it cost.
sections.key: 'Atonement' means 'at-one-ment', reconciliation; Tyndale put the word into the English Bible. Every theory of the cross tries to say how the mending happened.

sections.h: The Day of Atonement without a Temple
paras: In AD 70 the Romans destroyed the Temple, and the sacrifices stopped for ever. Judaism did not die with them. A story in an early rabbinic text, Avot de-Rabbi Natan (chapter 4), tells how Rabbi Yohanan ben Zakkai comforted a disciple weeping over the ruins: Israel still had a way of atonement as good as the Temple, acts of loving-kindness, for God says 'I desire mercy, and not sacrifice'.

Yom Kippur is still the holiest day of the Jewish year: a twenty-five-hour fast, the evening prayer Kol Nidre, the book of Jonah read in the afternoon, and prayers of confession said together. The Mishnah, the Jewish law code finished around AD 200, adds a rule that has shaped Jewish ethics ever since: the Day of Atonement atones for sins against God, but for sins against another person, only when you have put things right with them (Yoma 8:9). Jews and Christians both inherited the Day of Atonement. Jews kept it through repentance, prayer and charity; Christians said it was fulfilled on the cross.
sections.key: Since AD 70 Jews have kept Yom Kippur without sacrifice, through repentance, prayer and charity; Christians said the cross fulfilled it.

paras: The Day of Atonement was not the only Temple picture the first Christians used. John the Baptist calls Jesus 'the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world' (John 1:29). Paul writes that 'Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed in our place' (1 Corinthians 5:7): if you took 'Exodus and the law', you saw the Passover lamb whose blood on the doorposts marked the houses the destroyer passed over. At the Last Supper Jesus calls the cup 'my blood of the new covenant, which is poured out for many' (Mark 14:24), recalling the blood that sealed the covenant at Sinai (Exodus 24:8).

Reading earlier events as patterns that point forward is called typology. To modern readers it can look like forcing old texts to say new things. To the first Christians, all of them Jews, it was the natural way to read: the God who had rescued Israel through blood, lamb and covenant had done it again, once for all.
sections.key: The first Christians also used the Passover lamb, the covenant blood and Isaiah's servant: typology, reading old patterns as pointing to the cross.

paras: Jews and Christians both read Leviticus 16 as Scripture, and both say it still matters. They differ over what it points to now. The table sets the two readings side by side, as each describes itself.

Neither reading needs the other to be false in order to be coherent. But the difference is real, and it is the first place in this journey where a reader has to decide: was the cross the fulfilment of Israel's way of atonement, or a new claim laid on top of it?

rows: The holiest day of the year: a day of fasting, confession and return to God
Fulfilled in Christ's death; remembered in Holy Week and at every Eucharist
Repentance, prayer and charity atone (Hosea 6:6; Avot de-Rabbi Natan 4)
No more sacrifice is needed: Christ was 'offered once' (Hebrews 9:28)
Not forgiven on Yom Kippur until you have made peace with the person wronged (Mishnah Yoma 8:9)
Jesus: 'leave your gift there before the altar, and go your way. First be reconciled to your brother' (Matthew 5:24)
A sign that God removes confessed sin
A picture of Christ, who 'suffered outside of the gate' (Hebrews 13:12)
table.note: Both traditions agree that atonement begins with God's mercy and requires real repentance.

sections.key: Jews keep the Day of Atonement through repentance, prayer and charity; Christians read it as fulfilled on the cross. Both put God's mercy first.

debate.question: Is sacrifice a primitive idea that we should outgrow?

positions.name: Yes: a relic of an older religion
positions.who: Many Enlightenment critics; much liberal Protestant theology; in part the prophets themselves
positions.view: Killing animals to deal with guilt belongs to an early stage of religion. The prophets already pointed beyond it to mercy and justice, and a mature faith should leave the language of blood behind.
positions.evidence: Hosea 6:6; Psalm 51:16–17 ('you don't delight in sacrifice'); Micah 6:6–8; Judaism's own move from sacrifice to prayer after AD 70.

positions.name: No: a deep human grammar
positions.who: Anthropologists such as Henri Hubert and Marcel Mauss (1898) and Mary Douglas; many theologians today
positions.view: Sacrifice is found in every culture because it expresses something real: that wrongs cost something to put right, that gifts bind people together, and that the holy must be approached with care. We still speak this language when we talk of sacrifice for family or country.
positions.evidence: The universality of sacrifice; Leviticus 17:11, where God gives the blood; the modern use of 'sacrifice' for self-giving.

positions.name: Fulfilled, not outgrown
positions.who: The letter to the Hebrews; the Christian tradition
positions.view: The old sacrifices were real but pointed beyond themselves. They are ended not because the idea was wrong but because Christ completed it by offering himself. Christians therefore keep the language and drop the practice.
positions.evidence: Hebrews 9:26; 10:4, 10; the end of animal sacrifice in the church; the Eucharist as a remembrance of the one sacrifice.

debate.agree: All agree that the prophets put justice and mercy above ritual, and that animal sacrifice is not coming back.

look.why: Bernardo Daddi painted this small panel in Florence around 1320–1325. It shows the crucifixion, not a Temple scene, but its angels catching the blood in cups turn it into a picture of what Hebrews says: Christ entered 'through his own blood'. Painters of the time often placed a skull beneath the cross, recalling the tradition that Golgotha, 'the place of a skull', was where Adam was buried.
points: Jesus hangs on a wooden cross against a shiny gold background, his head down and eyes closed.
Three angels with two pairs of wings catch the blood from his hands and from the wound in his side in shallow gold cups.
A woman with long, unbound blond hair, in a vibrant red cloak, wraps her arms around the foot of the cross.
On our left, two people hold up a woman in a black cloak who has fainted; others behind them look up.
On our right, three bearded men look at the cross; one wears a helmet and a red cloak over armour.
A small skull is tucked into an opening in the ground below the mound where the cross stands.

music.why: Mozart wrote this motet in 1791, months before he died. Its medieval words greet the 'true body' of Christ, 'truly suffered, sacrificed on the cross' for humankind: the Temple's language of sacrifice, sung in three minutes of stillness.

think.why: Atonement assumes something has gone wrong between God and people. See what Christians mean by the story of estrangement in Genesis.

learn.why: Hebrews' whole argument in one sentence: offered once, to bear the sins of many. It also recalls Isaiah 53:5, 'by his wounds we are healed', if you learned it in 'Kings and prophets'.

check.q: Why does the ritual of Leviticus 16 cleanse the sanctuary, and not only the people?
options: Because the priests had sinned and the people had not
Because the building was physically dirty after a year of use
Because the Romans required it
Because sin was thought to pollute the holy place where God lived among his people, so that it had to be cleansed for God to stay
check.why: In Leviticus sin defiles the sanctuary itself; the blood on the mercy seat cleans God's house so that he can go on living with his people.

check.q: Which detail best shows that, in Leviticus, sacrifice is not a bribe offered to an angry God?
options: The goat is chosen by lot
God says 'I have given it to you on the altar to make atonement' (17:11): the means of atonement is God's own gift
The ritual takes place once a year
The high priest wears linen
check.why: If God provides the blood as a way back, the rite runs from God to the people, not the other way.

check.q: What do the two goats together represent?
options: Two sides of the problem of sin: the pollution of the holy place (the slain goat) and the weight of guilt carried away (the scapegoat)
A sacrifice to God and a sacrifice to a desert spirit, equally
The two kingdoms of Israel and Judah
Two kinds of sinner, the good and the bad
check.why: The first goat's blood cleanses; the second carries the confessed sins away.

check.q: According to Hebrews 9, what is the decisive difference between the high priest's offering and Christ's?
options: Christ's was offered in Jerusalem, the high priest's in the wilderness
Christ offered himself, once for all, and entered God's presence itself; the high priest offered animal blood, not his own, every year
There is no difference; Hebrews says the old rite continues
Christ's sacrifice was bloodless
check.why: 'Through his own blood, entered in once for all'; 'the sacrifice of himself'.

check.q: How did Rabbi Yohanan ben Zakkai answer a disciple who wept that the Temple's atonement was lost?
options: He said Christians had taken it over
He said that acts of loving-kindness atone as the sacrifices did, quoting 'I desire mercy, and not sacrifice'
He said the Temple would be rebuilt within a year
He said atonement was no longer needed
check.why: Avot de-Rabbi Natan 4 has him cite Hosea 6:6: Judaism kept atonement through repentance, prayer and charity.

check.q: Which is the best reply to the claim that 'atonement' simply means 'punishment'?
options: The word means 'at-one-ment', reconciliation; punishment is one possible account of how reconciliation happened, not the meaning of the word
The word is a modern invention with no connection to the Bible
Atonement means paying money
Punishment is never mentioned in the Bible
check.why: The English word means being set 'at one'; the theories that follow are attempts to explain how.

tutorial.question: What did 'Christ died for our sins' mean to the first Christians?
tutorial.approach: Start with the scandal of crucifixion. Then explain the Day of Atonement in Leviticus 16: the two goats, the blood on the mercy seat, and what 'atonement' means. Show how Hebrews 9 reads the rite as fulfilled in Christ, and mention the Passover lamb and Isaiah's servant. End by weighing the objection that sacrifice is a primitive idea.
strong: Explains why a crucified Messiah needed explaining (1 Corinthians 1:23; the Alexamenos graffito).
Describes the Day of Atonement accurately, including both goats.
Explains that in Leviticus the means of atonement is God's gift (17:11), not a bribe.
Uses Hebrews 9's contrasts: once for all, his own blood, God's presence itself.
Mentions at least one other Temple picture: the Passover lamb, the covenant blood or the servant.
Notes how Judaism has kept the Day of Atonement without sacrifice since AD 70.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: Yom Kippur teaches that you cannot be at one with God while you are at odds with someone you have wronged. Think of one person you owe an apology. Make it this week, without excuses, in person or in writing.
sessions.reflect: Is there anything you have done that you would like to see carried 'as far as the east is from the west'? What would it take for you to believe it could be?
takeaways: 'Atonement' means 'at-one-ment': the mending of a broken relationship between God and people.
On the Day of Atonement, blood God had given cleansed the sanctuary and a goat carried the people's confessed sins into the wilderness.
Hebrews says Christ was both priest and sacrifice, offered once for all; Jews have kept the day without sacrifice since AD 70.

sessions.title: A ransom for many
sessions.line: Two friends ask Jesus for the best seats, and he tells them he has come to give his life as a ransom. To whom?
sessions.plain: On the road to Jerusalem, two of Jesus's closest followers, James and John, ask for the places of honour in his kingdom. He tells them that his kingdom turns power upside down: the greatest must be the servant, because 'the Son of Man also came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many'. A ransom was the price paid to free a slave or a prisoner. That raised a question the early Church could not leave alone: if Jesus's life was a ransom, who was paid? Some said the devil. This session reads Jesus's words, then the early writers who argued about them.
sessions.why: Session 1 read the cross through the Temple: sacrifice and cleansing. The second picture comes from the street and the slave market: a ransom, the price of freedom. It is Jesus's own word for his death, and it led to the first great argument about the cross.
answers: What did Jesus say about his own death?
What does 'redemption' mean?
Who was the ransom paid to?
Did the early Church really think God paid the devil?
Is 'ransom' a metaphor or a transaction?
sessions.finding: Jesus called his death 'a ransom for many'; early writers asked who was paid, some answered the devil, and Gregory of Nazianzus replied that the ransom was paid to no one: it names a costly rescue, not a deal.

paras: In session 1 the first Christians read Jesus's death through the Temple. But they did not invent the link between his death and others' freedom. According to the Gospels, Jesus himself spoke about why he would die, on the road to Jerusalem, in the last weeks of his life.

Mark's Gospel, probably the earliest, written around AD 65–75, tells how Jesus three times warned his followers that he would be handed over, killed and rise again (Mark 8:31; 9:31; 10:33–34). Each time they misunderstood. The third time, they had just been told that he would be mocked, spat on, flogged and killed, and two of them asked for the best seats in his kingdom.
background.key: In Mark, Jesus three times foretells his death on the road to Jerusalem, and each time his followers misunderstand.

background.h: Slaves, captives and the price of freedom
paras: In the Roman world, slavery was everywhere. Captives taken in war, debtors and abandoned children could all be sold. A slave could be freed if someone paid the price, and the Greek word for that price was lytron, a ransom. Hundreds of inscriptions from the temple of Apollo at Delphi, from about 200 BC to AD 100, record slaves freed by being 'sold' to the god. Prisoners of war, too, could be ransomed by their families.

Israel had its own story of ransom. God brought them out of slavery in Egypt: 'I will redeem you with an outstretched arm' (Exodus 6:6). The law gave every family a 'redeemer', a go'el, a next of kin who would buy back a relative sold into slavery or land lost to debt (Leviticus 25). To 'redeem' meant to set free at a cost, and to do it as family.
background.key: A ransom (lytron) was the price that freed a slave or prisoner; in Israel God 'redeemed' his people from Egypt, and a kinsman redeemer bought back family.

background.h: Who asked the question, and who answered
paras: Jesus said his life was a ransom 'for many'. He did not say to whom it was paid, and the New Testament never says. For two centuries no one seems to have asked. Then the question arrived, and with it some strange answers.

Irenaeus of Lyons, writing around AD 180, said that God bought humanity back from the 'apostasy', the power of evil that had captured it, justly and without force. Origen of Alexandria, about fifty years later, said plainly that the ransom was paid to the devil. A century after that Gregory of Nyssa told a famous story of a fish-hook. And his friend Gregory of Nazianzus asked the question outright and gave an answer that most Christians have held ever since.
background.key: The New Testament never says to whom the ransom was paid; from about AD 180 writers asked, and some said the devil.

paras: The main reading is Mark 10:35–45: the request of James and John and Jesus's answer, ending with the ransom saying. Notice that the saying comes in an argument about power, not in a lesson about theology.

The comparison has two early voices: Irenaeus, who says God redeemed us justly and by persuasion, not force; and Gregory of Nazianzus, preaching at Easter in the 380s, who asks the question directly: 'To Whom was that Blood offered?'
background.key: Mark 10, the ransom saying in an argument about power; then Irenaeus and Gregory of Nazianzus on who, if anyone, was paid.

sessions.readWhy: Jesus's own explanation of his death, given in an argument about who is greatest.

paras: James and John, the sons of Zebedee, came near to him, saying, “Teacher, we want you to do for us whatever we will ask.”
He said to them, “What do you want me to do for you?”
They said to him, “Grant to us that we may sit, one at your right hand, and one at your left hand, in your glory.”
But Jesus said to them, “You don’t know what you are asking. Are you able to drink the cup that I drink, and to be baptized with the baptism that I am baptized with?”
They said to him, “We are able.”
Jesus said to them, “You shall indeed drink the cup that I drink, and you shall be baptized with the baptism that I am baptized with;
but to sit at my right hand and at my left hand is not mine to give, but for whom it has been prepared.”
When the ten heard it, they began to be indignant toward James and John.
Jesus summoned them, and said to them, “You know that they who are recognized as rulers over the nations lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them.
But it shall not be so among you, but whoever wants to become great among you shall be your servant.
Whoever of you wants to become first among you, shall be bondservant of all.
For the Son of Man also came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.”

parts.title: The best seats
parts.context: Jesus and the twelve are walking up to Jerusalem for Passover, the feast that remembers the Exodus. He has just told them, for the third time, that he will be killed there (10:32–34). James and John, brothers and fishermen, were among his first followers and his closest friends.

commentary.on: Teacher, we want you to do for us whatever we will ask.
commentary.text: After hearing that Jesus will be mocked, flogged and killed, the brothers ask for a blank cheque. Mark lets the timing speak for itself. It is a very human moment: people hear what they want to hear.

commentary.on: Grant to us that we may sit, one at your right hand, and one at your left hand, in your glory.
commentary.text: The right and left hand of a king were the places of greatest honour. They imagine Jesus enthroned. Mark's readers knew that the next time two men are at his right and left, it will be the two criminals crucified beside him (15:27).

commentary.on: Are you able to drink the cup that I drink, and to be baptized with the baptism that I am baptized with?
commentary.text: 'The cup' in the prophets is often the cup of suffering or of God's judgement (Isaiah 51:17). 'Baptism' here means being plunged under, overwhelmed. In the garden of Gethsemane Jesus will pray, 'remove this cup from me' (14:36). He is talking about his death.

commentary.on: When the ten heard it, they began to be indignant toward James and John.
commentary.text: The others are angry, probably not because the request was wrong but because they wanted the seats too. Everyone in the story is playing the same game of rank.

parts.title: Not to be served, but to serve
parts.context: Jesus calls all twelve together and answers their quarrel about greatness. The answer ends with the only saying in Mark where he explains why he will die.

commentary.on: they who are recognized as rulers over the nations lord it over them
commentary.text: Jesus describes power as the Roman world knew it: rulers who 'lord it over' their subjects. If you took 'Kings and prophets', you heard Samuel warn that a king would take. This is the same diagnosis.

commentary.on: whoever wants to become great among you shall be your servant
commentary.text: The reversal is total. Greatness is measured by service, and the 'first' must be the 'bondservant', the slave, of all. In a society built on rank, this was not a pious platitude but a revolution.

commentary.on: For the Son of Man also came not to be served, but to serve
commentary.text: 'The Son of Man' is Jesus's favourite way of speaking of himself. It comes from Daniel 7, where 'one like a son of man' receives a kingdom and all nations serve him. Jesus turns it upside down: the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve.

commentary.on: and to give his life as a ransom for many
commentary.text: Here is the ransom. Three things are worth noticing. He gives his life: it is not taken. It is a ransom, the price of someone else's freedom. And it is 'for many', an echo of the servant in Isaiah 53 who 'bore the sins of many'. Jesus does not say who receives the price. The point of the saying, in context, is what kind of power this is: power that pays for others' freedom with its own life.

paras: 1. For in no other way could we have learned the things of God, unless our Master, existing as the Word, had become man. For no other being had the power of revealing to us the things of the Father, except His own proper Word. For what other person knew the mind of the Lord, or who else has become His counsellor? Again, we could have learned in no other way than by seeing our Teacher, and hearing His voice with our own ears, that, having become imitators of His works as well as doers of His words, we may have communion with Him, receiving increase from the perfect One, and from Him who is prior to all creation. We — who were but lately created by the only best and good Being, by Him also who has the gift of immortality, having been formed after His likeness (predestinated, according to the prescience of the Father, that we, who had as yet no existence, might come into being), and made the first-fruits of creation — have received, in the times known beforehand, [the blessings of salvation] according to the ministration of the Word, who is perfect in all things, as the mighty Word, and very man, who, redeeming us by His own blood in a manner consonant to reason, gave Himself as a redemption for those who had been led into captivity.

And since the apostasy tyrannized over us unjustly, and, though we were by nature the property of the omnipotent God, alienated us contrary to nature, rendering us its own disciples, the Word of God, powerful in all things, and not defective with regard to His own justice, did righteously turn against that apostasy, and redeem from it His own property, not by violent means, as the [apostasy] had obtained dominion over us at the beginning, when it insatiably snatched away what was not its own, but by means of persuasion, as became a God of counsel, who does not use violent means to obtain what He desires; so that neither should justice be infringed upon, nor the ancient handiwork of God go to destruction. Since the Lord thus has redeemed us through His own blood, giving His soul for our souls, and His flesh for our flesh, and has also poured out the Spirit of the Father for the union and communion of God and man, imparting indeed God to men by means of the Spirit, and, on the other hand, attaching man to God by His own incarnation, and bestowing upon us at His coming immortality durably and truly, by means of communion with God — all the doctrines of the heretics fall to ruin.

XXII. Now we are to examine another fact and dogma, neglected by most people, but in my judgment well worth enquiring into. To Whom was that Blood offered that was shed for us, and why was It shed? I mean the precious and famous Blood of our God and High priest and Sacrifice. We were detained in bondage by the Evil One, sold under sin, and receiving pleasure in exchange for wickedness. Now, since a ransom belongs only to him who holds in bondage, I ask to whom was this offered, and for what cause? If to the Evil One, fie upon the outrage! If the robber receives ransom, not only from God, but a ransom which consists of God Himself, and has such an illustrious payment for his tyranny, a payment for whose sake it would have been right for him to have left us alone altogether. But if to the Father, I ask first, how? For it was not by Him that we were being oppressed; and next, On what principle did the Blood of His Only begotten Son delight the Father, Who would not receive even Isaac, when he was being offered by his Father, but changed the sacrifice, putting a ram in the place of the human victim? Is it not evident that the Father accepts Him, but neither asked for Him nor demanded Him; but on account of the Incarnation, and because Humanity must be sanctified by the Humanity of God, that He might deliver us Himself, and overcome the tyrant, and draw us to Himself by the mediation of His Son, Who also arranged this to the honour of the Father, Whom it is manifest that He obeys in all things? So much we have said of Christ; the greater part of what we might say shall be reverenced with silence.

parts.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
parts.translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (Ante-Nicene Fathers I, 1885)
parts.title: Not by violent means
parts.context: Irenaeus (c. 130–c. 202) grew up in Asia Minor, where as a boy he heard Polycarp, who was said to have known the apostle John. He became bishop of Lyons in Gaul and wrote Against Heresies around AD 180 against the Gnostics, who taught that the material world was evil and that Christ only seemed to have a body. This is the 1885 translation by Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut. A Bible reference that the web edition inserts into the text has been removed.
parts.plain: Irenaeus says: we could only learn about God from God's own Word becoming a man we could see and hear. Evil, which he calls 'the apostasy', had captured us by force, though we belonged to God. Christ bought us back with his own blood. But he did not snatch us back by force, as evil had snatched us; he did it justly, by persuasion, so that God's justice was kept. He gave his life for ours and his flesh for our flesh, and joined God and humanity together.

commentary.on: who, redeeming us by His own blood in a manner consonant to reason, gave Himself as a redemption for those who had been led into captivity
commentary.text: Irenaeus uses the ransom picture directly: we were captives, and Christ 'gave Himself as a redemption'. 'In a manner consonant to reason' means that the rescue made sense: it was fitting, not arbitrary.

commentary.on: though we were by nature the property of the omnipotent God, alienated us contrary to nature
commentary.text: The captor has no real right to us. We belong to God; evil took us 'contrary to nature'. This matters for what comes later: if the devil has no rights, why would God owe him anything?

commentary.on: not by violent means, as the [apostasy] had obtained dominion over us at the beginning, when it insatiably snatched away what was not its own, but by means of persuasion
commentary.text: Here is Irenaeus's key idea. Evil won by force and fraud; God wins back by persuasion and justice. God does not beat the devil by being a bigger bully. The square brackets are the translators' own: they supply the word the Greek leaves understood.

commentary.on: giving His soul for our souls, and His flesh for our flesh
commentary.text: The exchange is personal and complete: his life for ours, his body for ours. Notice that there is no payment to anyone named. The ransom is the giving.

parts.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
parts.work: Oration 45, The Second Oration on Easter
parts.translator: Charles Gordon Browne and James Edward Swallow (Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers II.7, 1894)
parts.title: Fie upon the outrage
parts.context: Gregory of Nazianzus (c. 329–390) was one of the three 'Cappadocian Fathers', from what is now central Turkey, with his friends Basil the Great and Gregory of Nyssa. He was briefly archbishop of Constantinople, presided for a time over the Council of Constantinople in 381, and resigned. This sermon, his second on Easter, was preached late in his life, probably between 383 and 389, at Arianzus near his home town. This is the 1894 translation by C. G. Browne and J. E. Swallow; the passage is cut at the end of his answer.
parts.plain: Gregory asks a question he says most people ignore: if Christ's blood was a ransom, who was paid? Not the devil: it would be an outrage for the robber to be paid at all, let alone with God himself. Not the Father either: the Father was not holding us captive, and the Father who refused Isaac's death would not delight in his Son's. His answer: the Father accepts the Son's offering without having demanded it; it was needed because humanity had to be made holy by God becoming human, so that he could free us himself, defeat the tyrant, and draw us to himself. More than that, he says, should be honoured with silence.

commentary.on: To Whom was that Blood offered that was shed for us, and why was It shed?
commentary.text: Gregory asks the question Jesus's saying raises and the New Testament never answers. He calls it 'neglected by most people'. It is a sign of how seriously the early Church took the words: if 'ransom' means something, someone must have been paid.

commentary.on: If to the Evil One, fie upon the outrage!
commentary.text: 'Fie upon the outrage' is the translators' Victorian English for a cry of disgust. Gregory's friend Gregory of Nyssa had said the ransom was paid to the devil, and Origen before him. Nazianzen will not have it: the idea that the robber is paid, and paid with God, is monstrous.

commentary.on: For it was not by Him that we were being oppressed
commentary.text: The other obvious answer, the Father, fails too. A ransom is paid to whoever holds the captives, and the Father was not holding us. Gregory refuses both halves of the transaction picture.

commentary.on: Who would not receive even Isaac, when he was being offered by his Father, but changed the sacrifice, putting a ram in the place of the human victim?
commentary.text: A powerful argument from the Old Testament: the God who stopped Abraham's knife did not want human blood. If he would not take Isaac, why would he delight in the death of his own Son? If you took 'Abraham and the promise', you know the story.

commentary.on: the Father accepts Him, but neither asked for Him nor demanded Him
commentary.text: This is Gregory's answer. The Father receives the gift but did not require it. It was needed not as a payment but 'on account of the Incarnation': human nature had to be made holy by God sharing it, so that Christ might 'deliver us Himself, and overcome the tyrant, and draw us to Himself'. The ransom is real, but it is not paid to anyone. It is the cost of the rescue.

commentary.on: the greater part of what we might say shall be reverenced with silence
commentary.text: Gregory ends by admitting he cannot explain everything. That humility is part of the Eastern tradition: the cross is a mystery to be worshipped, not a mechanism to be diagrammed.

compare.author: Irenaeus of Lyons and Gregory of Nazianzus
compare.translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (Ante-Nicene Fathers I, 1885)
compare.why: Two early bishops on the question Jesus's saying raised. Irenaeus, around 180, says God redeemed us justly and without force. Gregory of Nazianzus, two centuries later, asks outright who received the ransom.
compare.title: To whom was the ransom paid?

paras: Redemption is one of the commonest words for salvation in the New Testament, and its home is not the Temple but the street. 'You were redeemed, not with corruptible things, with silver or gold … but with precious blood' (1 Peter 1:18–19). 'He gave himself as a ransom for all' (1 Timothy 2:6). Behind it lies the Exodus, when God freed slaves, and the law of the go'el, the next of kin who buys back a relative sold into slavery (Leviticus 25:47–49). The book of Ruth tells the story of one such redeemer, Boaz.

So when Jesus speaks of a ransom 'for many', he is speaking as the next of kin of the whole human family, paying the cost of their freedom. The picture says three things: that we are not free, that freedom costs, and that someone who did not have to pay has paid.
sections.key: Redemption is a family word: the next of kin who buys back a relative from slavery; Jesus pays the cost of others' freedom.

paras: Some scholars have doubted that Jesus said Mark 10:45. They point out that it sounds like the theology of the later Church, and that Luke's version of the scene (Luke 22:24–27) has the line about serving but not the ransom. Others, such as Martin Hengel and N. T. Wright, argue that it fits Jesus well: he expected to die, he chose to go to Jerusalem at Passover, and at the Last Supper he spoke of his blood 'poured out for many', using the same echo of Isaiah 53.

Either way, the saying is very early. Mark's Gospel was written within forty years of Jesus's death, and Paul, writing even earlier, speaks of Christ who 'gave himself for our sins' (Galatians 1:4). The idea that Jesus's death was for others was not added late. It is in the oldest layers of the tradition.
sections.key: Scholars debate whether Jesus spoke Mark 10:45; either way, the idea that his death was 'for many' is in the earliest sources.

paras: Around AD 240, Origen of Alexandria, the greatest Christian scholar of his age, asked in his Commentary on Matthew to whom the ransom was paid, and answered: not to God, so it must have been to the evil one, who held us captive until the price, the soul of Jesus, was given. But the devil could not hold Jesus, and lost both the price and the captives.

The idea behind this is sometimes called 'the devil's rights'. Humanity had sold itself to evil by sinning, so evil had a kind of legal claim, and God, being just, would not simply break it by force. Irenaeus had already insisted that God acts justly, 'by means of persuasion', not violence. For more than eight centuries, many Christians in East and West thought along these lines, and preachers loved the drama of it.
sections.key: Origen said the ransom was paid to the devil, who had a sort of claim on sinners; the idea, 'the devil's rights', lasted for centuries.

paras: Gregory of Nyssa, in his Great Catechism (chapters 22–26, written around 385), told the most famous version. The devil saw in Jesus a prize worth more than all his captives and took him in exchange. But the divine nature was hidden in the human nature, as a hook is hidden in bait, and when the devil swallowed the bait he was caught on the hook of the Godhead. Gregory admitted this was a deception, but said it was just: the deceiver was himself deceived, and in the end, he thought, even the devil would be healed.

Augustine, in a sermon for Ascension Day, put it more bluntly: the cross was the devil's mousetrap, baited with Christ's blood. Pope Gregory the Great used the fish-hook again around 590. These pictures were never meant as diagrams. They are preachers' stories, saying in vivid form that evil overreached itself when it killed the innocent Son of God. (No public-domain English translation of Gregory of Nyssa's passage was available to us, so it is given here in our own words.)
sections.key: Gregory of Nyssa pictured Christ's humanity as bait hiding the hook of divinity; Augustine called the cross the devil's mousetrap.

sections.h: The answer: no one was paid
paras: Gregory of Nazianzus, as you read, rejected both answers: not the devil, which was an outrage, and not the Father, who held no one captive. Six centuries later, Anselm of Canterbury began his own book on the cross by saying he could not see the force of the argument that God had to deal justly with the devil, since neither the devil nor humanity belongs to anyone but God (Why God Became Man I.7).

Most Christians since have agreed with Gregory. A ransom, in this view, is a metaphor: it tells the truth about our condition (we are captive), about the cost of freedom (a life), and about the one who pays (God himself), but it does not need a receiver. We say a parent 'paid a high price' to care for a sick child without meaning that anyone received the money.
sections.key: Gregory of Nazianzus and later Anselm rejected a payment to the devil; most Christians since treat 'ransom' as a true metaphor that needs no receiver.

paras: If the ransom is a metaphor, what were we captive to? The New Testament names several powers: sin, which Paul treats almost as a slave-master ('the wages of sin is death', Romans 6:23); death itself, and the 'fear of death' by which people are 'all their lifetime subject to bondage' (Hebrews 2:15); the law, when it only condemns; and the devil, 'the prince of this world' (John 12:31).

Many people today find the language of captivity truer than they expect: addiction, compulsion, inherited patterns of violence, a society's systems that trap people. The ransom picture says that we cannot buy ourselves out, and that freedom came at a cost to someone else. It also prepares for the next picture. If we were held by hostile powers, then the cross is not only a payment but a battle.
sections.key: The New Testament names sin, death, the law and the devil as the powers that held us; the ransom picture leads naturally to the picture of victory.

paras: Jesus says his life is a ransom 'for many'. Does that mean some people and not others? In the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, Calvinists who believed Christ died only for the chosen, a view called 'limited atonement', pointed to verses like this one. Most interpreters, Catholic, Orthodox and many Protestants, have read it differently.

Two reasons are usually given. First, in Hebrew and Aramaic idiom 'the many' can mean the whole community, everyone set against the one; the German scholar Joachim Jeremias made this argument in the 1950s. Second, the phrase echoes Isaiah 53, where the one servant bears the sins of 'many'. The point is the contrast: one gives his life, and multitudes go free. Another early Christian writer says it without the idiom: Christ 'gave himself as a ransom for all' (1 Timothy 2:6).
sections.key: 'For many' contrasts the one with the multitude, echoing Isaiah 53; most readers take it to include all, though some Calvinists read it as limited.

debate.question: Is 'ransom' a metaphor or a transaction?

positions.name: A transaction with the devil
positions.who: Origen; Gregory of Nyssa; many medieval preachers
positions.view: Humanity sold itself to the devil by sin, and God, being just, paid the price rather than seize us by force. The devil took Christ and lost everything, because he could not hold him.
positions.evidence: Mark 10:45; Hebrews 2:14–15; John 12:31; the fish-hook of Gregory of Nyssa; Augustine's mousetrap.

positions.name: A metaphor that needs no receiver
positions.who: Gregory of Nazianzus; John of Damascus; Anselm; most theologians today
positions.view: The ransom tells us that we were captive, that freedom cost a life, and that God paid it, but no one received a payment. Asking 'to whom?' presses a picture beyond what it was meant to say.
positions.evidence: Oration 45.22; the New Testament's silence about a receiver; Anselm, Why God Became Man I.7.

positions.name: A price paid to God's justice
positions.who: Many Reformed theologians, following Calvin
positions.view: There is a receiver, but it is not the devil: it is the justice of God, which must be satisfied if sin is to be forgiven. The ransom picture points towards the courtroom.
positions.evidence: Calvin speaks of Christ 'ransoming us from the justice of God' (Institutes II.16.12); Romans 3:24–26.

debate.agree: All agree that we could not free ourselves, that freedom cost Christ his life, and that he gave it willingly.

look.why: This session has no painting. The gallery's open collection has no picture of James and John's request or of captives set free that we could use without pretending it shows something else.

music.why: Bach's St Matthew Passion (1727) opens with a double choir calling the daughters of Zion to 'see' the bridegroom, who comes as a lamb: the one who gives his life for many, sung on the road to the cross.

think.why: The ransom picture came from a world full of slaves. See how the same faith later fed the long fight to end slavery.

learn.why: Jesus's own explanation of his death, and of what greatness is.

check.q: Why does Jesus give the ransom saying in Mark 10?
options: To answer an argument about rank: his kind of greatness gives itself for others, even to death
To teach a theory about payment to the devil
To predict the destruction of Jerusalem
To explain the Temple sacrifices
check.why: The saying ends his reply to the quarrel about the best seats; the ransom is the supreme example of service.

check.q: What does the Old Testament background of 'redemption' add to the ransom picture?
options: That redemption means punishment
That the ransom is paid to Pharaoh
That only priests can be redeemed
That the redeemer is family: God freeing his people from Egypt, and the next of kin buying back a relative from slavery
check.why: Exodus 6:6 and the go'el of Leviticus 25 make redemption a costly act of family loyalty.

check.q: In Against Heresies V.1, why does Irenaeus insist that God redeemed us 'by means of persuasion' and not violence?
options: Because Irenaeus was a pacifist
Because evil had taken us by force and fraud, and God's justice would not be kept if he simply did the same
Because the devil had a full legal right to us
Because God is too weak to use force
check.why: God wins back 'not by violent means, as the [apostasy] had obtained dominion over us', 'so that neither should justice be infringed upon'.

check.q: Why does Gregory of Nazianzus reject the idea that the ransom was paid to the Father?
options: Because the Father does not exist
Because Gregory thought the cross was unnecessary
Because the Father was not the one holding us captive, and the God who spared Isaac would not delight in his Son's blood
Because the ransom was paid to the devil instead
check.why: 'It was not by Him that we were being oppressed'; and he 'would not receive even Isaac'.

check.q: What did Gregory of Nyssa's fish-hook image mean to convey?
options: That fishermen were the first disciples
That God paid the Father
That Christ was not really human
That evil overreached itself: the devil took Christ's humanity as bait and was caught by the divinity hidden in it
check.why: The bait is Christ's humanity, the hook his divinity; the deceiver is deceived.

check.q: Which is the strongest reason for treating 'ransom' as a metaphor rather than a payment to someone?
options: Ransoms did not exist in the ancient world
Metaphors are never true
Jesus never mentioned his death
The New Testament never names a receiver, and the picture's point (captivity, cost, a willing payer) holds without one
check.why: The silence of the New Testament and the force of the picture without a receiver are the case Gregory of Nazianzus and Anselm make.

tutorial.question: To whom was the ransom paid?
tutorial.approach: Begin with Mark 10:45 in its setting: an argument about power. Explain redemption and ransom in the ancient world and in Israel. Then set out the early answers: Irenaeus, Origen and Gregory of Nyssa, and Gregory of Nazianzus's rejection of both the devil and the Father. Decide whether 'ransom' is a metaphor or a transaction, and say what is lost or gained either way.
strong: Reads the ransom saying in its context in Mark 10.
Explains lytron, the Exodus and the go'el.
States the 'devil's rights' view fairly, with Origen or Gregory of Nyssa.
Uses Gregory of Nazianzus's two arguments: the outrage, and the Father who held no one captive.
Distinguishes a true metaphor from a literal transaction.
Notes what the captivity was: sin, death, the fear of death.
