sessions.practice: Live it this week: Jesus answered a quarrel about rank by serving. Choose one setting this week where you usually expect to be served (at home, at work, in a shop) and quietly serve instead: do the job no one wants, without mentioning it.
sessions.reflect: What, if anything, do you feel captive to? What would freedom from it cost, and who would pay?
takeaways: Jesus called his death 'a ransom for many' while answering a quarrel about greatness: his power gives itself for others.
Some early writers said the ransom was paid to the devil; Gregory of Nyssa told the story of the fish-hook.
Gregory of Nazianzus answered that it was paid neither to the devil nor to the Father: 'ransom' names a costly rescue, not a deal.

sessions.title: Victory: Christ the conqueror
sessions.line: Death had the human race by the throat. God came down into it, and broke it from the inside: the cross as a battle won.
sessions.plain: The third picture comes from the battlefield. For the early Church, and for Orthodox Christians to this day, the cross is first of all a victory: over sin, over death and over the powers of evil. In the 300s Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, explained it like this: humanity was sliding back into nothing, and God could neither let his creation be ruined nor break his own word. So God the Son took a human body, died our death, and broke death's hold. This session reads Athanasius, Paul's picture of Christ triumphing over the powers, and Irenaeus's idea that Christ lived the human story again and won where Adam lost.
sessions.why: Session 2 ended with captives: humanity held by sin, death and the devil, and a ransom that was not a payment to anyone. If we were held by hostile powers, the natural next picture is a battle. This is the picture the early Church loved most, and the one the Christian East has kept at the centre.
answers: What is 'Christus Victor'?
Why couldn't God just tell people to repent?
How do Orthodox Christians see the cross?
What does 'he descended into hell' mean?
Are the incarnation and the cross one rescue or two?
sessions.finding: For the early Church and the Christian East the cross is first a victory over sin, death and the devil, and the incarnation, cross and resurrection are one rescue in which God enters death to undo it from inside.

paras: In session 1 the cross was a sacrifice that cleansed; in session 2, a ransom that freed. Both pictures assume that something has a hold on us. The early Christians were sure what it was. Paul says that 'death reigned from Adam' (Romans 5:14), and the letter to the Hebrews that Christ died 'that through death he might bring to nothing him who had the power of death, that is, the devil, and might deliver all of them who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage' (Hebrews 2:14–15).

So the question became: how does a death defeat death? The answer of the first Christian centuries is that God himself entered death, and death could not hold him. The cross and the empty tomb are one event: a battle and its victory.
background.key: Sacrifice and ransom assume we are held; the early Church named death and the devil, and saw the cross and resurrection as one victory over them.

paras: Athanasius was born around 296 in Alexandria, the great Greek-speaking city of Egypt, and became its bishop in 328. He spent his life defending the Council of Nicaea (325), which declared that the Son of God is 'of one being' with the Father, against the followers of Arius, who taught that the Son was the first and greatest creature. For this he was exiled five times, by four emperors, and spent years hidden among the monks of the desert.

On the Incarnation is a short book written for a friend. Scholars disagree about the date: some think he wrote it as a young man around 318, before the Arian quarrel, others during his first exile at Trier around 335. Its question is simple: why did the Word of God, through whom the world was made, become a human being and die? C. S. Lewis, introducing a modern translation in 1944, called it a masterpiece.
background.key: Athanasius (c. 296–373), bishop of Alexandria and defender of Nicaea, exiled five times; On the Incarnation asks why the Word became human and died.

paras: Athanasius builds on two older ideas. The first is Genesis: God made humans from nothing, 'in his image', and warned that if they disobeyed they would 'surely die' (Genesis 2:17). The second comes from Irenaeus of Lyons, whom you met in session 2: Christ 'recapitulated', or summed up, the human story, living it again from the beginning and getting it right where Adam went wrong.

Two words need explaining. 'The Word' translates the Greek Logos, John's name for the Son of God, through whom 'all things were made' (John 1:3). 'Corruption' is Athanasius's word for what sin set going: not just bad acts, but a decay of human nature itself, a sliding back towards the nothing it came from.
background.key: Athanasius draws on Genesis and on Irenaeus's 'recapitulation'; 'the Word' is the Son of God, 'corruption' the decay of human nature after the fall.

paras: The main reading is On the Incarnation, chapters 6 to 10, in three parts: God's dilemma, the Word taking a body, and death undone. It is the clearest early account of why God became man and died.

The comparison has two parts. First, Colossians 2:13–15, where Paul pictures Christ triumphing over the 'principalities and powers' like a Roman general in a victory parade. Then Irenaeus, Against Heresies III.18, the older source of Athanasius's thinking: Christ as the new Adam who fought and conquered.
background.key: Athanasius, On the Incarnation 6–10; then Colossians 2 and Irenaeus on Christ the victor and the new Adam.

before: What two things does Athanasius say God could not allow?
Why, in his view, would repentance not be enough?
In Colossians, what does Christ do to the 'principalities and powers'?
sessions.readWhy: The classic early account of why the Word of God became human and died: a rescue from death, not first a payment.

paras: For this cause, then, death having gained upon men, and corruption abiding upon them, the race of man was perishing; the rational man made in God's image was disappearing, and the handiwork of God was in process of dissolution. 2. For death, as I said above, gained from that time forth a legal hold over us, and it was impossible to evade the law, since it had been laid down by God because of the transgression, and the result was in truth at once monstrous and unseemly. 3. For it were monstrous, firstly, that God, having spoken, should prove false — that, when once He had ordained that man, if he transgressed the commandment, should die the death, after the transgression man should not die, but God's word should be broken. For God would not be true, if, when He had said we should die, man died not. 4. Again, it were unseemly that creatures once made rational, and having partaken of the Word, should go to ruin, and turn again toward non-existence by the way of corruption. 5. For it were not worthy of God's goodness that the things He had made should waste away, because of the deceit practised on men by the devil. 6. Especially it was unseemly to the last degree that God's handicraft among men should be done away, either because of their own carelessness, or because of the deceitfulness of evil spirits.

7. So, as the rational creatures were wasting and such works in course of ruin, what was God in His goodness to do? Suffer corruption to prevail against them and death to hold them fast? And where were the profit of their having been made, to begin with? For better were they not made, than once made, left to neglect and ruin. 8. For neglect reveals weakness, and not goodness on God's part — if, that is, He allows His own work to be ruined when once He had made it — more so than if He had never made man at all. 9. For if He had not made them, none could impute weakness; but once He had made them, and created them out of nothing, it were most monstrous for the work to be ruined, and that before the eyes of the Maker. 10. It was, then, out of the question to leave men to the current of corruption; because this would be unseemly, and unworthy of God's goodness.

But just as this consequence must needs hold, so, too, on the other side the just claims of God lie against it: that God should appear true to the law He had laid down concerning death. For it were monstrous for God, the Father of truth, to appear a liar for our profit and preservation. 2. So here, once more, what possible course was God to take? To demand repentance of men for their transgression? For this one might pronounce worthy of God; as though, just as from transgression men have become set towards corruption, so from repentance they may once more be set in the way of incorruption. 3. But repentance would, firstly, fail to guard the just claim of God. For He would still be none the more true, if men did not remain in the grasp of death; nor, secondly, does repentance call men back from what is their nature — it merely stays them from acts of sin. 4. Now, if there were merely a misdemeanour in question, and not a consequent corruption, repentance were well enough. But if, when transgression had once gained a start, men became involved in that corruption which was their nature, and were deprived of the grace which they had, being in the image of God, what further step was needed? Or what was required for such grace and such recall, but the Word of God, which had also at the beginning made everything out of nought? 5. For His it was once more both to bring the corruptible to incorruption, and to maintain intact the just claim of the Father upon all. For being Word of the Father, and above all, He alone of natural fitness was both able to recreate everything, and worthy to suffer on behalf of all and to be ambassador for all with the Father.

For this purpose, then, the incorporeal and incorruptible and immaterial Word of God comes to our realm, howbeit he was not far from us before. For no part of Creation is left void of Him: He has filled all things everywhere, remaining present with His own Father. But He comes in condescension to show loving-kindness upon us, and to visit us. 2. And seeing the race of rational creatures in the way to perish, and death reigning over them by corruption; seeing, too, that the threat against transgression gave a firm hold to the corruption which was upon us, and that it was monstrous that before the law was fulfilled it should fall through: seeing, once more, the unseemliness of what had come to pass: that the things whereof He Himself was Artificer were passing away: seeing, further, the exceeding wickedness of men, and how little by little they had increased it to an intolerable pitch against themselves: and seeing, lastly, how all men were under penalty of death: He took pity on our race, and had mercy on our infirmity, and condescended to our corruption, and, unable to bear that death should have the mastery — lest the creature should perish, and His Father's handiwork in men be spent for nought — He takes unto Himself a body, and that of no different sort from ours.

3. For He did not simply will to become embodied, or will merely to appear. For if He willed merely to appear, He was able to effect His divine appearance by some other and higher means as well. But He takes a body of our kind, and not merely so, but from a spotless and stainless virgin, knowing not a man, a body clean and in very truth pure from intercourse of men. For being Himself mighty, and Artificer of everything, He prepares the body in the Virgin as a temple unto Himself, and makes it His very own as an instrument, in it manifested, and in it dwelling. 4. And thus taking from our bodies one of like nature, because all were under penalty of the corruption of death He gave it over to death in the stead of all, and offered it to the Father — doing this, moreover, of His loving-kindness, to the end that, firstly, all being held to have died in Him, the law involving the ruin of men might be undone (inasmuch as its power was fully spent in the Lord's body, and had no longer holding-ground against men, his peers), and that, secondly, whereas men had turned toward corruption, He might turn them again toward incorruption, and quicken them from death by the appropriation of His body and by the grace of the Resurrection, banishing death from them like straw from the fire.

For the Word, perceiving that no otherwise could the corruption of men be undone save by death as a necessary condition, while it was impossible for the Word to suffer death, being immortal, and Son of the Father; to this end He takes to Himself a body capable of death, that it, by partaking of the Word Who is above all, might be worthy to die in the stead of all, and might, because of the Word which had come to dwell in it, remain incorruptible, and that thenceforth corruption might be stayed from all by the Grace of the Resurrection. Whence, by offering unto death the body He Himself had taken, as an offering and sacrifice free from any stain, straightway He put away death from all His peers by the offering of an equivalent. 2. For being over all, the Word of God naturally by offering His own temple and corporeal instrument for the life of all satisfied the debt by His death. And thus He, the incorruptible Son of God, being conjoined with all by a like nature, naturally clothed all with incorruption, by the promise of the resurrection.

For the actual corruption in death has no longer holding-ground against men, by reason of the Word, which by His one body has come to dwell among them. 3. And like as when a great king has entered into some large city and taken up his abode in one of the houses there, such city is at all events held worthy of high honour, nor does any enemy or bandit any longer descend upon it and subject it; but, on the contrary, it is thought entitled to all care, because of the king's having taken up his residence in a single house there: so, too, has it been with the Monarch of all. 4. For now that He has come to our realm, and taken up his abode in one body among His peers, henceforth the whole conspiracy of the enemy against mankind is checked, and the corruption of death which before was prevailing against them is done away. For the race of men had gone to ruin, had not the Lord and Saviour of all, the Son of God, come among us to meet the end of death.

Now in truth this great work was peculiarly suited to God's goodness. 1. For if a king, having founded a house or city, if it be beset by bandits from the carelessness of its inmates, does not by any means neglect it, but avenges and reclaims it as his own work, having regard not to the carelessness of the inhabitants, but to what beseems himself; much more did God the Word of the all-good Father not neglect the race of men, His work, going to corruption: but, while He blotted out the death which had ensued by the offering of His own body, He corrected their neglect by His own teaching, restoring all that was man's by His own power. 2. And of this one may be assured at the hands of the Saviour's own inspired writers, if one happen upon their writings, where they say: For the love of Christ constrains us; because we thus judge, that if one died for all, then all died, and He died for all that we should no longer live unto ourselves, but unto Him Who for our sakes died and rose again, our Lord Jesus Christ. And, again: But we behold Him, Who has been made a little lower than the angels, even Jesus, because of the suffering of death crowned with glory and honour, that by the grace of God He should taste of death for every man. 3. Then He also points out the reason why it was necessary for none other than God the Word Himself to become incarnate; as follows: For it became Him, for Whom are all things, and through Whom are all things, in bringing many sons unto glory, to make the Captain of their salvation perfect through suffering;

by which words He means, that it belonged to none other to bring man back from the corruption which had begun, than the Word of God, Who had also made them from the beginning. 4. And that it was in order to the sacrifice for bodies such as His own that the Word Himself also assumed a body, to this, also, they refer in these words : Forasmuch then as the children are the sharers in blood and flesh, He also Himself in like manner partook of the same, that through death He might bring to naught Him that had the power of death, that is, the devil; and might deliver them who, through fear of death, were all their lifetime subject to bondage. 5. For by the sacrifice of His own body, He both put an end to the law which was against us, and made a new beginning of life for us, by the hope of resurrection which He has given us. For since from man it was that death prevailed over men, for this cause conversely, by the Word of God being made man has come about the destruction of death and the resurrection of life; as the man which bore Christ says: For since by man came death, by man came also the resurrection of the dead. For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive: and so forth. For no longer now do we die as subject to condemnation; but as men who rise from the dead we await the general resurrection of all, which in its own times He shall show, even God, Who has also wrought it, and bestowed it upon us. 6. This then is the first cause of the Saviour's being made man. But one might see from the following reasons also, that His gracious coming among us was fitting to have taken place.

parts.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
parts.work: On the Incarnation of the Word
parts.translator: Archibald Robertson (Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers II.4, 1892)
parts.who: Athanasius (c. 296–373), bishop of Alexandria, the great defender of the Council of Nicaea
parts.title: God's dilemma
parts.context: Athanasius has explained that God made humans from nothing and gave them a share in his own Word, so that they could know him and live. But they turned away, and the threatened death took hold. Now he sets out the problem as a dilemma for God. The numbers in the text are the translator's section numbers. The web edition inserts a Bible reference into the first paragraph; it has been removed.
parts.plain: Athanasius says: after the fall, death had a legal hold on humanity, and the human race was disappearing. God was caught, as it were, between two things. He could not break his word that sin would bring death; that would make him a liar. But he could not let his own creatures be ruined either; that would be weakness, not goodness. What about repentance? It is not enough. Repentance stops us sinning, but it cannot undo the decay of our nature, and it does not keep God's word true. Only the Word who made us could remake us.

commentary.on: death, as I said above, gained from that time forth a legal hold over us
commentary.text: Death is not only a natural event here but a sentence. God had said that sin would bring death, and his word stands. Athanasius uses legal language, but the problem he describes is more like a disease.

commentary.on: For God would not be true, if, when He had said we should die, man died not.
commentary.text: The first horn of the dilemma: God's truthfulness. A God who threatens and does not mean it cannot be trusted when he promises either.

commentary.on: For it were not worthy of God's goodness that the things He had made should waste away, because of the deceit practised on men by the devil.
commentary.text: The second horn: God's goodness. A craftsman who lets his best work rot is either weak or careless. Athanasius does not imagine an angry God looking for a reason to punish. He imagines a maker who cannot bear to lose what he made.

commentary.on: For better were they not made, than once made, left to neglect and ruin.
commentary.text: A striking thought: it would have been better not to create at all than to create and then abandon. Creation commits God to his creatures.

commentary.on: But repentance would, firstly, fail to guard the just claim of God.
commentary.text: Here is Athanasius's answer to 'why couldn't God just forgive?' Telling people to repent sounds worthy of God. But it would leave God's word unkept.

commentary.on: nor, secondly, does repentance call men back from what is their nature — it merely stays them from acts of sin.
commentary.text: This is the deeper reason. Repentance changes what we do; it does not heal what we are. If sin were only a misdemeanour, repentance would do. But it has become a corruption of our nature, and a sick nature needs a cure, not an apology.

commentary.on: He alone of natural fitness was both able to recreate everything, and worthy to suffer on behalf of all and to be ambassador for all with the Father.
commentary.text: Three things only the Word can do: recreate, suffer for all, and represent all before the Father. Only the one who made us can remake us.

parts.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
parts.work: On the Incarnation of the Word
parts.translator: Archibald Robertson (Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers II.4, 1892)
parts.who: Athanasius (c. 296–373), bishop of Alexandria, the great defender of the Council of Nicaea
parts.title: The Word takes a body
parts.context: Athanasius now describes the incarnation: the Word, who was never absent from the world, comes into it in a new way, by taking a human body from the Virgin Mary. A Bible reference inserted by the web edition has been removed.
parts.plain: Athanasius says: the Word of God, who fills all things, came to us in a new way, out of kindness. He saw us dying, saw the threat of death holding us, saw his own work being ruined, and took pity on us. So he took a real human body, like ours, from the Virgin, and gave it up to death in the place of all, offering it to the Father. Because all died in him, the law of death was used up on his body; and because he raised it, he turns us back to life, 'like straw from the fire'.

commentary.on: howbeit he was not far from us before. For no part of Creation is left void of Him
commentary.text: The Word does not travel from somewhere else. He already holds the universe together. The incarnation is not God arriving from a distance but God coming close in a new way, as one of us.

commentary.on: He took pity on our race, and had mercy on our infirmity, and condescended to our corruption
commentary.text: The motive is pity and mercy. 'Condescended' here has its old meaning: came down to our level. There is no anger in this passage at all.

commentary.on: He takes unto Himself a body, and that of no different sort from ours.
commentary.text: This was the issue against the Gnostics, whom Irenaeus fought: the body is real. A rescue of human beings has to happen inside a real human life.

commentary.on: He gave it over to death in the stead of all, and offered it to the Father
commentary.text: 'In the stead of all': in our place. The victory picture does not exclude substitution and sacrifice. Athanasius uses both words. But notice the purpose: to use up death's claim, not to pay off an angry God.

commentary.on: the law involving the ruin of men might be undone (inasmuch as its power was fully spent in the Lord's body
commentary.text: The image is of death spending its whole force on one body and having nothing left. The sentence was carried out; it simply could not hold this victim.

commentary.on: banishing death from them like straw from the fire
commentary.text: A homely, vivid picture: straw put to a fire vanishes. That is what happens to death when it meets the life of God.

parts.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
parts.work: On the Incarnation of the Word
parts.translator: Archibald Robertson (Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers II.4, 1892)
parts.who: Athanasius (c. 296–373), bishop of Alexandria, the great defender of the Council of Nicaea
parts.title: Death undone
parts.context: Athanasius explains why a death was needed, and why this death could undo death for everyone. He then gives a picture, a king living in one house of a city, and a list of Scripture passages. Two Bible references inserted by the web edition have been removed.
parts.plain: Athanasius says: death could only be undone by a death, but the Word, being God, could not die. So he took a body that could. By dying in that body he paid the debt for all; by living in it he made it, and through it all of us, incorruptible. Think of a great king who comes to live in one house of a city: the whole city is safe because he is there. So the human race is protected because the King has come to live in one human body. He did this out of goodness, as a king rescues his own city from bandits, and taught us as well as dying for us.

commentary.on: no otherwise could the corruption of men be undone save by death as a necessary condition, while it was impossible for the Word to suffer death, being immortal
commentary.text: The puzzle of the incarnation in one sentence. Only death can deal with death, but God cannot die. So God takes a nature that can. The cross is the reason for the cradle.

commentary.on: satisfied the debt by His death
commentary.text: Athanasius uses the language of debt, seven centuries before Anselm made it the centre. For him the pictures sit happily together: victory, sacrifice, substitution and debt.

commentary.on: like as when a great king has entered into some large city and taken up his abode in one of the houses there
commentary.text: This is the most famous image in the book. The king lives in one house, and the whole city is safe. Christ lives one human life, and the whole human race is protected. Salvation here is not a transaction but a presence: God has moved in.

commentary.on: henceforth the whole conspiracy of the enemy against mankind is checked
commentary.text: The battlefield language returns: an enemy, a conspiracy, a king's protection. This is the Christus Victor picture: the cross as the defeat of the powers that held us.

commentary.on: He corrected their neglect by His own teaching
commentary.text: Athanasius adds a second gift: teaching. Christ dies for us and also shows us how to live. Even the 'example' picture, which we will meet with Abelard, is here in seed.

commentary.on: For no longer now do we die as subject to condemnation; but as men who rise from the dead we await the general resurrection of all
commentary.text: The end of the argument is not acquittal but resurrection. Christians still die, but death has changed its meaning: it is no longer a sentence but a sleep before waking. This is why the East preaches the cross in the light of Easter.

read.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
read.work: On the Incarnation of the Word
read.translator: Archibald Robertson (Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers II.4, 1892)
read.who: Athanasius (c. 296–373), bishop of Alexandria, the great defender of the Council of Nicaea

paras: You were dead through your trespasses and the uncircumcision of your flesh. He made you alive together with him, having forgiven us all our trespasses,
wiping out the handwriting in ordinances which was against us. He has taken it out of the way, nailing it to the cross.
Having stripped the principalities and the powers, he made a show of them openly, triumphing over them in it.

1. As it has been clearly demonstrated that the Word, who existed in the beginning with God, by whom all things were made, who was also always present with mankind, was in these last days, according to the time appointed by the Father, united to His own workmanship, inasmuch as He became a man liable to suffering, [it follows] that every objection is set aside of those who say, If our Lord was born at that time, Christ had therefore no previous existence. For I have shown that the Son of God did not then begin to exist, being with the Father from the beginning; but when He became incarnate, and was made man, He commenced afresh the long line of human beings, and furnished us, in a brief, comprehensive manner, with salvation; so that what we had lost in Adam — namely, to be according to the image and likeness of God — that we might recover in Christ Jesus.

7. Therefore, as I have already said, He caused man (human nature) to cleave to and to become, one with God. For unless man had overcome the enemy of man, the enemy would not have been legitimately vanquished. And again: unless it had been God who had freely given salvation, we could never have possessed it securely. And unless man had been joined to God, he could never have become a partaker of incorruptibility. For it was incumbent upon the Mediator between God and men, by His relationship to both, to bring both to friendship and concord, and present man to God, while He revealed God to man. For, in what way could we be partaken of the adoption of sons, unless we had received from Him through the Son that fellowship which refers to Himself, unless His Word, having been made flesh, had entered into communion with us? Wherefore also He passed through every stage of life, restoring to all communion with God. Those, therefore, who assert that He appeared putatively, and was neither born in the flesh nor truly made man, are as yet under the old condemnation, holding out patronage to sin; for, by their showing, death has not been vanquished, which reigned from Adam to Moses, even over them that had not sinned after the similitude of Adam's transgression.

But the law coming, which was given by Moses, and testifying of sin that it is a sinner, did truly take away his (death's) kingdom, showing that he was no king, but a robber; and it revealed him as a murderer. It laid, however, a weighty burden upon man, who had sin in himself, showing that he was liable to death. For as the law was spiritual, it merely made sin to stand out in relief, but did not destroy it. For sin had no dominion over the spirit, but over man. For it behooved Him who was to destroy sin, and redeem man under the power of death, that He should Himself be made that very same thing which he was, that is, man; who had been drawn by sin into bondage, but was held by death, so that sin should be destroyed by man, and man should go forth from death. For as by the disobedience of the one man who was originally moulded from virgin soil, the many were made sinners, and forfeited life; so was it necessary that, by the obedience of one man, who was originally born from a virgin, many should be justified and receive salvation. Thus, then, was the Word of God made man, as also Moses says: God, true are His works. But if, not having been made flesh, He did appear as if flesh, His work was not a true one. But what He did appear, that He also was: God recapitulated in Himself the ancient formation of man, that He might kill sin, deprive death of its power, and vivify man; and therefore His works are true.

parts.title: Triumphing over them
parts.context: Paul, or a close follower writing in his name (scholars disagree), writes to Christians in Colossae, a small town in what is now western Turkey, around AD 60. Some there were teaching that they needed special rules and the favour of spiritual powers. Paul answers that Christ has already dealt with every power.

commentary.on: wiping out the handwriting in ordinances which was against us. He has taken it out of the way, nailing it to the cross.
commentary.text: 'The handwriting' is a written record of debt, an IOU. Paul pictures it nailed to the cross, as the charge against a condemned man was nailed above his head. The debt picture and the victory picture meet here.

commentary.on: Having stripped the principalities and the powers, he made a show of them openly, triumphing over them in it.
commentary.text: This is the image of a Roman 'triumph': a victorious general paraded through Rome with his defeated enemies stripped and led in chains behind him. Paul's paradox is that it happens on the cross. What looked like Christ's defeat, stripped and paraded to execution, was in fact the defeat of the powers.

parts.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
parts.translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (Ante-Nicene Fathers I, 1885)
parts.title: He fought and conquered
parts.context: Irenaeus, bishop of Lyons around AD 180, whom you met in session 2, is arguing against teachers who said that the divine Christ left the man Jesus before the crucifixion. Against them he insists that the Son of God truly became man and truly suffered, because that is how he saves. Three Bible references that the web edition inserts into the text have been removed; the translators' square brackets are kept.
parts.plain: Irenaeus says: when the Son of God became man, he began the human story again and gave us salvation in short form, so that what we lost in Adam, the image and likeness of God, we might get back in Christ. A defeated humanity could not save itself, so God had to give salvation, but a man had to win the fight, or the enemy would not be fairly beaten. So Christ, God and man, joined us to God. As one man's disobedience made many sinners, one man's obedience made many righteous. He 'recapitulated' the old human story, to kill sin, take away death's power and give us life.

commentary.on: He commenced afresh the long line of human beings, and furnished us, in a brief, comprehensive manner, with salvation
commentary.text: This is recapitulation: Christ starts the human line again. 'In a brief, comprehensive manner' translates the idea of summing up, as a long story is summed up in one line. Christ is the human story told again, rightly.

commentary.on: For unless man had overcome the enemy of man, the enemy would not have been legitimately vanquished.
commentary.text: Why did God become man rather than simply defeat evil from heaven? Because humanity lost the fight, humanity must win it. A rescue from outside would not be a human victory. This is the same logic Anselm will use in a different key.

commentary.on: unless it had been God who had freely given salvation, we could never have possessed it securely
commentary.text: And why must the saviour be God? Because only God's gift is secure. Irenaeus gives both halves of the argument: a man must win, and God must give.

commentary.on: Wherefore also He passed through every stage of life, restoring to all communion with God.
commentary.text: Irenaeus believed Christ lived through infancy, childhood, youth and maturity, sanctifying each. The whole of his life saves, not only his death.

commentary.on: God recapitulated in Himself the ancient formation of man, that He might kill sin, deprive death of its power, and vivify man
commentary.text: Three verbs, three victories: kill sin, disarm death, give life. That is the Christus Victor picture in one line, written around 180.

compare.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
compare.why: Athanasius did not invent the victory picture. Paul had already described the cross as a triumph over the powers, and Irenaeus, a century and a half before Athanasius, had described Christ as the new Adam who fought and won.
compare.title: The powers disarmed, and a new Adam

paras: The New Testament is full of the language of conflict. Jesus casts out demons and says he has bound 'the strong man' (Mark 3:27). 'To this end the Son of God was revealed: that he might destroy the works of the devil' (1 John 3:8). On the night before he died he said, 'Now the prince of this world will be cast out' (John 12:31). And Paul ends his great chapter on the resurrection with a taunt: 'Death, where is your sting?' (1 Corinthians 15:55).

In this picture humanity is not mainly a debtor or a defendant but a prisoner of war, and God is the liberator. Sin, death and the devil are enemies, and the cross is where they were beaten. It is the most dramatic of the five pictures, and for the first thousand years of Christianity it was probably the most popular.
sections.key: The New Testament describes Christ binding the strong man and destroying the devil's works: humanity as prisoner, God as liberator.

paras: In 1930 the Swedish bishop Gustaf Aulén gave a set of lectures, published in English in 1931 as Christus Victor. He argued that Christians had held three main types of view about the cross. The 'classic' view of the early Church saw it as a drama of victory in which God himself acts. The 'Latin' view, beginning with Anselm, saw it as a satisfaction offered by Christ as man to God. The 'subjective' view, beginning with Abelard, saw it as a change in us.

Aulén thought the classic view was the oldest, the most biblical and the one Martin Luther had recovered, and that Western theology had lost it. Many scholars think he simplified: the Fathers, as you are reading, used every picture at once, and Luther used the courtroom too. But his book changed the conversation. Since Aulén, 'Christus Victor', Latin for 'Christ the victor', has been the name for this picture.
sections.key: Gustaf Aulén's Christus Victor (1930) sorted the theories into classic (victory), Latin (satisfaction) and subjective (moral influence), and revived the first.

paras: Athanasius's argument is easy to caricature and hard to dismiss. God faces two claims that seem to pull apart: his truthfulness (the warning that sin brings death must stand) and his goodness (he cannot abandon what he made). Repentance cannot resolve it, because the problem is not only what we have done but what we have become.

Modern readers often ask why God cannot simply forgive, as a good parent does. Athanasius would say we have misunderstood the problem. Forgiveness deals with guilt between persons. But humanity's trouble is also a disease: we are sliding towards death and nothingness. You do not forgive someone out of cancer. You cure them, and the cure, in Athanasius's account, is that life itself enters death and overcomes it. This is why Orthodox theologians often speak of the cross in medical terms: Christ is the physician, and salvation is healing.
sections.key: For Athanasius the problem is not only guilt but corruption, a disease of human nature: it needs a cure, not only forgiveness.

paras: If Christ really died, where did he go? The first letter of Peter says that he 'preached to the spirits in prison' (1 Peter 3:19). By about AD 400 the creed used at Aquileia in northern Italy, as Rufinus reports it, included the words 'he descended into hell', and the line passed into the Apostles' Creed said in Western churches today. 'Hell' here means the place of the dead, in Hebrew Sheol, not the place of punishment.

Later writers told the story in full. The Gospel of Nicodemus, a legendary text probably of the fifth or sixth century, describes Christ breaking the gates of the underworld and leading out Adam, Eve and the righteous of the Old Testament. In English this became 'the harrowing of hell', from an Old English word for plundering. Medieval mystery plays acted it out, and it is the scene of the painting in this session.
sections.key: 'He descended into hell' (the place of the dead) entered the creed by about AD 400; the 'harrowing of hell' tells of Christ freeing Adam, Eve and the righteous dead.

paras: In the Christian East the main image of Easter is not the empty tomb but the Anastasis, Greek for 'resurrection'. Christ, in white, stands on the broken doors of hell, which lie in the shape of a cross. Locks and keys are scattered below, and sometimes a bound figure of death. With each hand he pulls Adam and Eve out of their tombs, by the wrist, not the hand: they cannot save themselves.

The greatest example is the fresco in the side chapel of the Chora Church in Istanbul, painted around 1315–1321. Every Orthodox Easter the same idea is sung again and again, in a short hymn usually rendered in English as 'Christ is risen from the dead, trampling down death by death'. The phrase sums up this whole session: not death avoided, but death defeated by being entered.
sections.key: The Orthodox Easter icon, the Anastasis, shows Christ on the broken gates of hell pulling Adam and Eve out by the wrist: 'trampling down death by death'.

paras: For the Christian East the victory does not stop at rescue. A little later in the same book, Athanasius writes a sentence that has been quoted ever since: 'He was made man that we might be made God' (On the Incarnation 54). He does not mean that humans become gods in their own right. He means that by joining our nature to his, the Son draws us into the life of God, as iron in a fire glows with the fire's heat.

The Greek word for this is theosis, 'deification'. It explains why Orthodox Christians speak less than Western Christians about guilt and punishment and more about healing, light and transformation. Salvation is not only being let off; it is being made new. In the East the incarnation, the cross, the resurrection and the gift of the Spirit are one movement of God towards us, and the cross is its turning point rather than its whole meaning.
sections.key: Athanasius: 'He was made man that we might be made God'. Theosis, sharing God's life, is why the East speaks of healing more than punishment.

sections.h: What the victory picture leaves open
paras: The picture has great strengths. It keeps the resurrection at the centre; it is cosmic, about the whole creation and not only the individual; and it has spoken powerfully to people under oppression, from the slaves who sang spirituals about Christ's victory to the liberation theologians of twentieth-century Latin America.

But it leaves questions. Why did the victory require a death? A God who can defeat death could, it seems, do it without dying. Who exactly are 'the powers', and what does it mean today to say the devil was defeated, when evil goes on? And what does the victory do about guilt, the sense that I have done wrong and must answer for it? Athanasius touches all of these, but he does not settle them. Six centuries later, in the West, a monk named Anselm took up exactly the first question.
sections.key: The victory picture keeps the resurrection central and speaks to the oppressed, but leaves open why a death was needed and what it does about guilt.
