debate.question: Is the cross first a victory or a payment?

positions.name: First a victory
positions.who: Irenaeus and Athanasius; Gustaf Aulén; Orthodox theologians such as Vladimir Lossky; in part N. T. Wright
positions.view: The cross is God's own act, defeating the powers that held humanity, and it cannot be separated from the resurrection. Talk of payment, where it appears, serves the story of victory.
positions.evidence: Colossians 2:15; Hebrews 2:14–15; 1 John 3:8; the Anastasis icon; 'trampling down death by death'.

positions.name: First a payment
positions.who: Anselm; Reformed theologians such as John Stott
positions.view: Victory is the result, but it rests on something prior: Christ dealing with sin before God. Evil's power over us is our guilt; take away the guilt, and the powers are disarmed.
positions.evidence: Colossians 2:14, where the debt is nailed to the cross before the powers are stripped (2:15); Romans 3:25; 1 Corinthians 15:56 ('the sting of death is sin').

positions.name: Both, inseparably
positions.who: Fleming Rutledge; much recent theology across the traditions
positions.view: The New Testament holds the pictures together, and so did Athanasius, who uses victory, sacrifice and debt in the same chapter. To make one the key and the others decoration is to lose something true.
positions.evidence: On the Incarnation 8–9 ('in the stead of all'; 'satisfied the debt'; 'the conspiracy of the enemy'); Colossians 2:14–15 read together.

debate.agree: All agree that the cross and resurrection belong together, and that Christ's death defeated something that held humanity captive.

look.why: Benvenuto di Giovanni painted this scene in Siena, probably in 1491. Western painters called it 'Christ in Limbo', from the Latin limbus, 'edge': the borderland of the dead where, in medieval belief, the righteous of the Old Testament waited for Christ. It is the Western form of the Anastasis. In such scenes the first person Christ raises is usually Adam, and the hoe across the kneeling old man's knee may be the sign of the labour laid on Adam in Genesis 3.
points: Jesus, haloed and barefoot, is seen from behind, wrapped in a white cloth and carrying a white banner marked with a red cross.
He steps onto the door of a box-like structure set into the rock; the hinged door has crushed a wild-haired, red-skinned demon against the ground.
More than two dozen men and women of all ages crowd inside, their faces tipped back towards him.
He holds the wrist of a kneeling man with a long white beard, in a dark fur-like garment, with a hoe hooked across his knee.
With his other hand he holds the hand of a second kneeling man in a canary-yellow robe edged in blue, who grips his wrist.
Striated boulders and rocky cliffs surround the scene, under a sapphire-blue sky.

music.why: Rachmaninoff's All-Night Vigil (1915) sets the Russian Orthodox service sung on Saturday night before every Sunday, which the Orthodox call a little Easter. Its hymns of the resurrection celebrate Christ's victory over death: the Eastern picture of the cross, in music.

think.why: If the cross is a victory over death, what does that mean for our own deaths? See what Christians hope for.

learn.why: John Donne's sonnet talks down to death as Athanasius does: 'Death, thou shalt die'. The victory picture, in fourteen lines.

check.q: What are the two sides of 'God's dilemma' in On the Incarnation 6–7?
options: God's power and God's knowledge
God's love for Israel and for the nations
God's justice and the devil's rights
God's truthfulness (his word that sin brings death must stand) and his goodness (he cannot let his creatures be ruined)
check.why: God would not be 'true' if man did not die, but it would be unworthy of his goodness to let his work 'waste away'.

check.q: Why, according to Athanasius, was repentance not enough?
options: Because people refused to repent
Because repentance stops sinful acts but cannot heal the corruption of human nature, nor keep God's word true
Because God does not accept repentance
Because repentance was only for Jews
check.why: Repentance 'merely stays them from acts of sin'; it does not 'call men back from what is their nature'.

check.q: What is the point of Athanasius's image of the king who lives in one house of a city?
options: That God lives only in temples
That Christ was born into a royal family
That because the Word lives in one human body, the whole human race is protected and death's power is checked
That the Church should be ruled by kings
check.why: The king's presence in one house makes the whole city safe; so with the Word in one body.

check.q: In Colossians 2:15, what is the force of the image of a 'triumph'?
options: It describes the resurrection appearances
It shows that Christians should fight wars
It means the Romans were defeated in battle
It reverses appearances: what looked like Christ's defeat, stripped and paraded to death, was the public defeat of the powers
check.why: A Roman triumph paraded stripped enemies; Paul says the powers, not Christ, were stripped at the cross.

check.q: Why does Irenaeus say that a man, and not God alone, had to defeat the enemy?
options: Because angels refused to help
Because the devil was human
Because humanity had lost the fight, so a human victory was needed for the enemy to be 'legitimately vanquished'
Because God is not strong enough
check.why: 'Unless man had overcome the enemy of man, the enemy would not have been legitimately vanquished.'

check.q: Which is the strongest objection to the victory picture taken on its own?
options: It does not explain why a death was needed for God to defeat death, or what the victory does about guilt
It was invented in the twentieth century
It contradicts the Gospels
It does not mention the resurrection
check.why: If God can defeat death, why die? And victory over the powers does not obviously deal with my guilt: questions Anselm took up.

tutorial.question: 'For Athanasius, the incarnation, not the cross, saves.' Discuss.
tutorial.approach: Set out God's dilemma in On the Incarnation 6–7 and why repentance is not enough. Explain how the Word's taking a body leads to the cross (8–9). Then weigh the claim: does the incarnation do the saving, or does it exist for the sake of the death? Use Irenaeus's recapitulation and the Anastasis icon, and say what the victory picture leaves open.
strong: States both sides of the divine dilemma.
Explains why repentance cannot cure corruption.
Shows that for Athanasius the incarnation is for the sake of the death ('a body capable of death').
Notes that he also uses sacrifice, substitution and debt.
Uses Irenaeus's recapitulation and Colossians 2:15.
Concludes that incarnation, cross and resurrection form one rescue.

reading.author: Athanasius
reading.title: On the Incarnation, with an introduction by C. S. Lewis
reading.why: The whole short book in a modern translation, with Lewis's famous essay on reading old books.

reading.author: Gustaf Aulén
reading.title: Christus Victor
reading.why: The book that named this picture and set the terms of the debate.

reading.author: Vladimir Lossky
reading.title: The Mystical Theology of the Eastern Church
reading.why: The classic account of Orthodox theology, including theosis.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: Christ in the icon pulls people up by the wrist because they cannot climb out alone. This week, reach out to one person who is stuck (lonely, ill, out of work, grieving) with one concrete offer of help, and follow it through.
sessions.reflect: What does death mean to you: an end, a sentence, a sleep, or an enemy already beaten? What would change if you believed the last?
takeaways: For the early Church and the Christian East the cross is first a victory over sin, death and the devil, inseparable from the resurrection.
Athanasius argued that repentance could not cure the corruption of human nature; only the Word, taking a body that could die, could undo death from inside.
Irenaeus saw Christ as the new Adam who won the fight humanity lost; the Anastasis icon shows him pulling Adam and Eve from their tombs.

sessions.title: Satisfaction: Anselm
sessions.line: A monk asks why God could not simply forgive, and builds an answer that shaped the West for nine hundred years. A rival says the cross works by love.
sessions.plain: In 1098 Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury, finished a short book called Why God Became Man. It is a dialogue with a younger monk, Boso, who asks the question everyone asks: why couldn't God just forgive? Anselm's answer is that sin is a debt of honour owed to God, so great that no human could pay it, and that God could not simply ignore it without making sin not matter. Only someone who was both God and man could pay. A generation later Peter Abelard answered that the cross changes us, not God: it saves by showing a love that wins our love. This session reads Anselm and the passage of Paul that Abelard built on, and asks which, if either, is right.
sessions.why: Session 3 ended with a question the victory picture leaves open: why did God's victory require a death? Anselm took up exactly that question, and in answering it gave the West its most influential theory of the cross, and its most famous rival.
answers: Why couldn't God just forgive?
What did Anselm argue, step by step?
What does 'satisfaction' mean?
What did Abelard say instead?
Is Anselm's God a feudal lord obsessed with his honour?
sessions.finding: Anselm argued that sin withholds an infinite debt of honour that no human can pay and God cannot ignore, so only one who is both God and man could make satisfaction; Abelard answered that the cross saves by kindling love, and the West's great argument about the cross began.

paras: For a thousand years Christians had used all the pictures you have met so far, the sacrifice, the ransom and the victory, side by side, without needing to say which was the key. Many preachers in the West still spoke of the devil's rights, as in session 2. But no one had written a full argument for why God's way of saving had to be the cross.

By the late eleventh century two things had changed. Monks and teachers in the new schools of France were asking for reasons, not only for authorities. And Jews and Muslims, in conversation with Christians, were asking why God would stoop to be born and die at all. Anselm says in his first chapter that 'infidels' raise the question, ridiculing Christian simplicity, and that believers ponder it too.
background.key: By the late 1000s, Christian teachers wanted reasons, and Jewish and Muslim critics asked why God would need to die; Anselm set out to answer.

paras: Anselm was born in 1033 at Aosta, in the Alps of northern Italy. As a young man he crossed into France and in 1060 became a monk at the abbey of Bec in Normandy, under the great teacher Lanfranc. He became prior, then abbot. In 1093 he followed Lanfranc as Archbishop of Canterbury. He quarrelled with two English kings, William II and Henry I, over the rights of the Church, and spent years in exile.

He was a man of prayer and of rigorous argument. His motto was 'faith seeking understanding': he believed first, and then tried to understand what he believed. In an earlier book, the Proslogion, he had given his famous argument for God's existence. Why God Became Man, begun in England and finished in 1098 during his exile in southern Italy, applies the same method to the cross.
background.key: Anselm (1033–1109), from Aosta, monk and abbot of Bec, Archbishop of Canterbury from 1093; 'faith seeking understanding'.

paras: Three words need explaining. In Anselm's world 'honour' was the respect owed to a person because of their place, above all the loyalty a vassal owed his lord. To withhold it was a serious wrong. But Anselm uses the word in a deeper sense: the honour owed to God is simply that every creature should will what God wills, and so take its right place in the order of the world.

A 'debt' is what is owed. 'Satisfaction' means making amends: not only giving back what you took, but adding something to put right the insult. The word came from the Church's practice of penance, in which a sinner who had confessed did works of 'satisfaction', such as fasting or almsgiving, to make amends. Anselm asks: what satisfaction could make amends for sin against God?
background.key: Honour: the right ordering of the will under God. Satisfaction: making amends, a word from the Church's practice of penance.

paras: The main reading is Why God Became Man, in five short parts: Anselm's question, what sin is, why God cannot simply forgive, how heavy sin is, and why only a God-man can pay. It is written as a dialogue between Anselm and Boso, a monk of Bec who later became its abbot. Read it as a conversation: watch Boso push back, and see whether Anselm answers him.

Abelard's commentary on Romans, where he gave his reply, has no English translation old enough to quote, so the comparison is the passage he built on, Romans 5:6–11, with his view explained in the commentary.
background.key: Anselm's dialogue with Boso in five parts; then Romans 5, the text behind Abelard's reply.

before: How does Anselm define sin?
Boso asks why God cannot forgive as he tells us to. How does Anselm answer?
Why must the one who makes satisfaction be both God and man?
sessions.readWhy: The most influential argument about the cross ever written in the West, in the form of a dialogue that lets the objections speak.

paras: I HAVE been often and most earnestly requested by many, both personally and by letter, that I would hand down in writing the proofs of a certain doctrine of our faith, which I am accustomed to give to inquirers; for they say that these proofs gratify them, and are considered sufficient. This they ask, not for the sake of attaining to faith by means of reason, but that they may be gladdened by understanding and meditating on those things which they believe; and that, as far as possible, they may be always ready to convince any one who demands of them a reason of that hope which is in us. And this question, both infidels are accustomed to bring up against us, ridiculing Christian simplicity as absurd; and many believers ponder it in their hearts; for what cause or necessity, in sooth, God became man, and by his own death, as we believe and affirm, restored life to the world; when he might have done this, by means of some other being, angelic or human, or merely by his will.

Anselm. We must needs inquire, therefore, in what manner God puts away men’s sins; and, in order to do this more plainly, let us first consider what it is to sin, and what it is to make satisfaction for sin.
Boso. It is yours to explain and mine to listen.
Anselm. If man or angel always rendered to God his due, he would never sin.
Boso. I cannot deny that.
Anselm. Therefore to sin is nothing else than not to render to God his due.
Boso. What is the debt which we owe to God?
Anselm. Every wish of a rational creature should be subject to the will of God.
Boso. Nothing is more true.

Anselm. This is the debt which man and angel owe to God, and no one who pays this debt commits sin; but every one who does not pay it sins. This is justice, or uprightness of will, which makes a being just or upright in heart, that is, in will; and this is the sole and complete debt of honor which we owe to God, and which God requires of us. For it is such a will only, when it can be exercised, that does works pleasing to God; and when this will cannot be exercised, it is pleasing of itself alone, since without it no work is acceptable. He who does not render this honor which is due to God, robs God of his own and dishonors him; and this is sin. Moreover, so long as he does not restore what he has taken away, he remains in fault; and it will not suffice merely to restore what has been taken away, but, considering the contempt offered, he ought to restore more than he took away. For as one who imperils another’s safety does not enough by merely restoring his safety, without making some compensation for the anguish incurred; so he who violates another’s honor does not enough by merely rendering honor again, but must, according to the extent of the injury done, make restoration in some way satisfactory to the person whom he has dishonored. We must also observe that when any one pays what he has unjustly taken away, he ought to give something which could not have been demanded of him, had he not stolen what belonged to another. So then, every one who sins ought to pay back the honor of which he has robbed God; and this is the satisfaction which every sinner owes to God.
Boso. Since we have determined to follow reason in all these things, I am unable to bring any objection against them, although you somewhat startle me.
Anselm. Let us return and consider whether it were proper for God to put away sins by compassion alone, without any payment of the honor taken from him.
Boso. I do not see why it is not proper.

Anselm. To remit sin in this manner is nothing else than not to punish; and since it is not right to cancel sin without compensation or punishment; if it be not punished, then is it passed by undischarged.
Boso. What you say is reasonable.
Anselm. It is not fitting for God to pass over anything in his kingdom undischarged.
Boso. If I wish to oppose this, I fear to sin.
Anselm. There is also another thing which follows if sin be passed by unpunished, viz., that with God there will be no difference between the guilty and the not guilty; and this is unbecoming to God.
Boso. I cannot deny it.
Anselm. Observe this also. Every one knows that justice to man is regulated by law, so that, according to the requirements of law, the measure of award is bestowed by God.
Boso. This is our belief.
Anselm. But if sin is neither paid for nor punished, it is subject to no law.
Boso. I cannot conceive it to be otherwise.

Anselm. Injustice, therefore, if it is cancelled by compassion alone, is more free than justice, which seems very inconsistent. And to these is also added a further incongruity, viz., that it makes injustice like God. For as God is subject to no law, so neither is injustice.

Boso. I cannot withstand your reasoning. But when God commands us in every case to forgive those who trespass against us, it seems inconsistent to enjoin a thing upon us which it is not proper for him to do himself.

Anselm. There is no inconsistency in God’s commanding us not to take upon ourselves what belongs to Him alone. For to execute vengeance belongs to none but Him who is Lord of all; for when the powers of the world rightly accomplish this end, God himself does it who appointed them for the purpose.

Anselm. Therefore the honor taken away must be repaid, or punishment must follow; otherwise, either God will not be just to himself, or he will be weak in respect to both parties; and this it is impious even to think of.
Boso. I think that nothing more reasonable can be said.

Anselm. Suppose that you did not owe any of those things which you have brought up as possible payment for your sin, let us inquire whether they can satisfy for a sin so small as one look contrary to the will of God.
Boso. Did I not hear you question the thing, I should suppose that a single repentant feeling on my part would blot out this sin.
Anselm. You have not as yet estimated the great burden of sin.
Boso. Show it me then.

Anselm. Not to detain you too long; what if it were necessary either that the whole universe, except God himself, should perish and fall back into nothing, or else that you should do so small a thing against the will of God?

Boso. When I consider the action itself, it appears very slight; but when I view it as contrary to the will of God, I know of nothing so grievous, and of no loss that will compare with it; but sometimes we oppose another’s will without blame in order to preserve his property, so that afterwards he is glad that we opposed him.

Anselm. This is in the case of man, who often does not know what is useful for him, or cannot make up his loss; but God is in want of nothing, and, should all things perish, can restore them as easily as he created them.
Boso. I must confess that I ought not to oppose the will of God even to preserve the whole creation.
Anselm. But this cannot be effected, except the price paid to God for the sin of man be something greater than all the universe besides God.
Boso. So it appears.
Anselm. Moreover, it is necessary that he who can give God anything of his own which is more valuable than all things in the possession of God, must be greater than all else but God himself.
Boso. I cannot deny it.
Anselm. Therefore none but God can make this satisfaction.
Boso. So it appears.
Anselm. But none but a man ought to do this, other wise man does not make the satisfaction.
Boso. Nothing seems more just.

Anselm. If it be necessary, therefore, as it appears, that the heavenly kingdom be made up of men, and this cannot be effected unless the aforesaid satisfaction be made, which none but God can make and none but man ought to make, it is necessary for the God-man to make it.
Boso. Now blessed be God! we have made a great discovery with regard to our question. Go on, therefore, as you have begun. For I hope that God will assist you.

parts.author: Anselm of Canterbury
parts.work: Why God Became Man (Cur Deus Homo)
parts.translator: James Gardiner Vose (Bibliotheca Sacra, 1854–1855), reprinted by Open Court (1903)
parts.who: Anselm (1033–1109), Italian-born monk of Bec in Normandy and Archbishop of Canterbury
parts.ref: Anselm, Why God Became Man I.1
parts.title: The question
parts.context: Anselm opens the book by saying why he is writing. The translation is by James Gardiner Vose, an American minister, published in 1854–1855 and reprinted in 1903 with Sidney Norton Deane's translations of Anselm's other works. The extract stops at the end of the question.
parts.plain: Anselm says: many people, by letter and in person, have asked me to write down the reasons I give for one part of our faith. They do not want reasons in order to believe, but to enjoy understanding what they already believe, and to be able to answer anyone who asks. Unbelievers mock the question, and believers wonder about it: why did God become man and save the world by his death, when he could have done it some other way, through an angel or a human being, or simply by willing it?

commentary.on: not for the sake of attaining to faith by means of reason, but that they may be gladdened by understanding and meditating on those things which they believe
commentary.text: This is 'faith seeking understanding'. Anselm is not trying to prove Christianity to someone with no faith. He is trying to show believers that what they believe makes sense, and to equip them to answer critics.

commentary.on: infidels are accustomed to bring up against us, ridiculing Christian simplicity as absurd
commentary.text: 'Infidels' means unbelievers, probably the Jews and perhaps Muslims whom Christian writers were debating in these years. Their mockery is fair: why would the almighty need to be born and die? Anselm takes it seriously.

commentary.on: when he might have done this, by means of some other being, angelic or human, or merely by his will
commentary.text: The question is sharp. If God can do anything, why not save by a word, as he created by a word? Anselm will answer that it is not a question of what God can do, but of what is fitting for him to do.

parts.author: Anselm of Canterbury
parts.work: Why God Became Man (Cur Deus Homo)
parts.translator: James Gardiner Vose (Bibliotheca Sacra, 1854–1855), reprinted by Open Court (1903)
parts.who: Anselm (1033–1109), Italian-born monk of Bec in Normandy and Archbishop of Canterbury
parts.ref: Anselm, Why God Became Man I.11
parts.title: What sin is
parts.context: Anselm and Boso have cleared away some bad arguments, including the idea that God had to deal justly with the devil (I.7). Now Anselm starts again from the beginning: what is sin, and what is it to make satisfaction for it? The extract is the whole of chapter 11.
parts.plain: Anselm says: to sin is not to give God what we owe him. What we owe is that our will should be subject to God's will. This is what justice or uprightness is, and it is the only honour God asks of us. Anyone who withholds it robs God of his honour. And it is not enough to give it back: because of the insult, the sinner must give back more than he took, as someone who has injured another must compensate for the harm as well as stop doing it. That extra is 'satisfaction'.

commentary.on: Therefore to sin is nothing else than not to render to God his due.
commentary.text: Anselm's definition of sin is short and strong. Sin is not breaking an arbitrary rule. It is a refusal to give God what is owed, like a debt unpaid.

commentary.on: Every wish of a rational creature should be subject to the will of God.
commentary.text: And what is owed? Not money or ritual but the will. This matters for judging Anselm: the 'honour' God wants is not flattery but that we should be what we were made to be.

commentary.on: He who does not render this honor which is due to God, robs God of his own and dishonors him; and this is sin.
commentary.text: Here the language of honour appears. A medieval reader heard the vassal who withholds loyalty from his lord. But Anselm will soon say (I.15) that God's honour cannot actually be damaged. What is damaged is the order of the world, and the sinner's own place in it.

commentary.on: considering the contempt offered, he ought to restore more than he took away
commentary.text: This is satisfaction: restoring what was taken is not enough; the wrong itself needs amends. We know this from ordinary life. If I steal your car and return it a week later, I still owe you an apology and probably more.

commentary.on: Since we have determined to follow reason in all these things, I am unable to bring any objection against them, although you somewhat startle me.
commentary.text: Boso is honest: he cannot refute the argument, but it startles him. The dialogue form lets the reader's own unease speak.

parts.author: Anselm of Canterbury
parts.work: Why God Became Man (Cur Deus Homo)
parts.translator: James Gardiner Vose (Bibliotheca Sacra, 1854–1855), reprinted by Open Court (1903)
parts.who: Anselm (1033–1109), Italian-born monk of Bec in Normandy and Archbishop of Canterbury
parts.ref: Anselm, Why God Became Man I.12
parts.title: Why not simply forgive?
parts.context: Now the question everyone asks. Boso has heard that sin is a debt. Why can God not simply cancel it, out of compassion? This is chapter 12, almost complete.
parts.plain: Anselm says: to cancel sin without payment or punishment would mean not dealing with it at all, leaving it 'undischarged', and that is not fitting for God. It would make no difference between the guilty and the innocent. It would leave sin outside any law, freer than justice, and so like God, who is under no law. Boso objects: but God tells us to forgive those who wrong us; why can he not do the same? Anselm answers: we are told to forgive because vengeance is not ours but God's. What is fitting for us is not the same as what is fitting for the judge of all.

commentary.on: To remit sin in this manner is nothing else than not to punish
commentary.text: Anselm's starting point is that forgiveness without any dealing-with is really just ignoring. A world where wrongs are simply waved away is not a merciful world but an indifferent one.

commentary.on: with God there will be no difference between the guilty and the not guilty; and this is unbecoming to God
commentary.text: This is Anselm's strongest argument, and it is a moral one. If sin makes no difference to God, then goodness makes no difference either. A judge who acquits everyone without condition is not kind; he has stopped caring about the victims.

commentary.on: Injustice, therefore, if it is cancelled by compassion alone, is more free than justice, which seems very inconsistent.
commentary.text: A subtle point: if sin carries no consequence at all, it is under no law, and so in a strange way it is 'free' like God. Injustice would end up with a freedom that even justice does not have.

commentary.on: when God commands us in every case to forgive those who trespass against us, it seems inconsistent to enjoin a thing upon us which it is not proper for him to do himself
commentary.text: Boso's objection is the one most modern readers make: Jesus tells us to forgive seventy times seven. Why does God not do as he says?

commentary.on: For to execute vengeance belongs to none but Him who is Lord of all
commentary.text: Anselm's answer is that we forgive because judgement is not ours: 'Vengeance belongs to me', says God (Romans 12:19). Many readers find this the weakest moment in the book. Others reply that human forgiveness, too, is never free: the one who forgives absorbs the cost of the wrong instead of passing it on.

parts.author: Anselm of Canterbury
parts.work: Why God Became Man (Cur Deus Homo)
parts.translator: James Gardiner Vose (Bibliotheca Sacra, 1854–1855), reprinted by Open Court (1903)
parts.who: Anselm (1033–1109), Italian-born monk of Bec in Normandy and Archbishop of Canterbury
parts.ref: Anselm, Why God Became Man I.13 and I.21
parts.title: Satisfaction or punishment, and the weight of sin
parts.context: Two short extracts. At the end of chapter 13 Anselm states his conclusion: either satisfaction or punishment. Then, in chapter 21, Boso suggests that a single feeling of repentance would be enough, and Anselm shows him how heavy sin is. The cuts are marked '…'.
parts.plain: Anselm says: the honour taken from God must be repaid, or punishment must follow. Boso thinks a single sorry thought would cancel a small sin, such as one glance against God's will. Anselm replies: you have not yet weighed how heavy sin is. Would you look against God's will to save the whole world from being destroyed? Boso admits he should not, not even to save the whole creation. So even the smallest sin outweighs the whole universe, because it is against God.

commentary.on: the honor taken away must be repaid, or punishment must follow
commentary.text: This is the hinge of the whole book: aut satisfactio aut poena, either satisfaction or punishment. Notice that for Anselm these are alternatives. Christ, in his account, does not take our punishment; he makes satisfaction, so that punishment is not needed. The Reformers will change this.

commentary.on: a single repentant feeling on my part would blot out this sin
commentary.text: Boso speaks for most people: surely being sorry is enough? It is the same suggestion Athanasius considered and rejected, for a different reason.

commentary.on: You have not as yet estimated the great burden of sin.
commentary.text: One of the most quoted lines in medieval theology. In Latin it is shorter: nondum considerasti quanti ponderis sit peccatum, 'you have not yet considered how heavy sin is'. Anselm's point is that we judge sin by its size, as an act, and forget whom it is against.

commentary.on: what if it were necessary either that the whole universe, except God himself, should perish and fall back into nothing, or else that you should do so small a thing against the will of God?
commentary.text: A thought experiment. Would you disobey God to save the universe? If not, then even a small sin outweighs the universe, and nothing in the universe could pay for it. This is the step that makes the debt infinite.

commentary.on: I must confess that I ought not to oppose the will of God even to preserve the whole creation.
commentary.text: Boso concedes. Not every reader will. A modern critic might say that a God who would let the universe perish rather than tolerate one glance has a strange sense of proportion. Anselm's reply would be that the point is not God's touchiness but his goodness: nothing in creation is worth more than being in the right with the source of all good.

parts.author: Anselm of Canterbury
parts.work: Why God Became Man (Cur Deus Homo)
parts.translator: James Gardiner Vose (Bibliotheca Sacra, 1854–1855), reprinted by Open Court (1903)
parts.who: Anselm (1033–1109), Italian-born monk of Bec in Normandy and Archbishop of Canterbury
parts.ref: Anselm, Why God Became Man II.6
parts.title: Only a God-man
parts.context: In Book II Anselm draws his conclusion. Humans were made for happiness with God, and God's purpose cannot fail. But the debt is greater than the universe. This is chapter 6, complete.
parts.plain: Anselm says: the payment must be greater than everything in the universe except God. Only someone greater than everything except God could give it, so only God can pay. But humanity owes it, so only a human ought to pay. Therefore the one who pays must be both God and man. Boso is delighted: they have found the answer to the question of the book.

commentary.on: except the price paid to God for the sin of man be something greater than all the universe besides God
commentary.text: Because sin outweighs the universe, the satisfaction must outweigh it too. Nothing created will do.

commentary.on: Therefore none but God can make this satisfaction.
commentary.text: First half of the argument: only God has anything big enough to give.

commentary.on: But none but a man ought to do this, other wise man does not make the satisfaction.
commentary.text: Second half: the debt is humanity's, so a human must pay it. If God simply paid it from outside, it would be charity, not satisfaction. This is the same logic as Irenaeus: a man must win.

commentary.on: which none but God can make and none but man ought to make, it is necessary for the God-man to make it
commentary.text: The conclusion that gives the book its title: the God-man. God became man because only a God-man could do what was needed. The argument does not mention the devil, and it does not say that Christ is punished. In Anselm's account Christ, owing God nothing for himself, freely gives his life, a gift worth more than every debt, and the Father rewards him by giving him what he asks: our forgiveness (II.19).

commentary.on: Now blessed be God! we have made a great discovery with regard to our question.
commentary.text: Boso's joy is part of the point. For Anselm the argument is not cold logic but a kind of prayer: understanding what God has done leads to praise.

read.author: Anselm of Canterbury
read.work: Why God Became Man (Cur Deus Homo)
read.ref: Anselm, Why God Became Man I.1
read.translator: James Gardiner Vose (Bibliotheca Sacra, 1854–1855), reprinted by Open Court (1903)
read.who: Anselm (1033–1109), Italian-born monk of Bec in Normandy and Archbishop of Canterbury

paras: For while we were yet weak, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly.
For one will hardly die for a righteous man. Yet perhaps for a righteous person someone would even dare to die.
But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.
Much more then, being now justified by his blood, we will be saved from God’s wrath through him.
For if while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, being reconciled, we will be saved by his life.
Not only so, but we also rejoice in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received the reconciliation.

parts.title: While we were yet sinners
parts.context: Paul writes to the Christians in Rome around AD 57. In chapters 1–4 he has argued that all have sinned and that God puts people right through faith. Now he turns to what that means: peace with God, and hope.

commentary.on: For while we were yet weak, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly.
commentary.text: Christ died 'for the ungodly', not for people who had made themselves worthy. Anselm and Abelard both start here, but they draw different lessons.

commentary.on: But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.
commentary.text: This is Abelard's key verse. The cross 'commends', shows and proves, God's love. Abelard argued, in our own words, that the Son took our nature and taught us by word and example even to death, and that this supreme love binds us to God and kindles in us a love that sets us free. Redemption, he wrote, is that love. He found Anselm's necessity and the devil's rights both unworthy: how could God be pleased by the death of an innocent, let alone require it?

commentary.on: Much more then, being now justified by his blood, we will be saved from God's wrath through him.
commentary.text: Here is the verse Anselm's defenders point to. Paul speaks of 'blood' and of being saved from 'wrath': something objective happened, not only a change in us. Abelard, recent scholars have shown, also used the language of sacrifice and merit; he was not a pure 'moral influence' theorist. But his emphasis was on love's effect on us.

commentary.on: For if while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son
commentary.text: 'While we were enemies': the reconciliation begins from God's side, before any change in us. Both Anselm and Abelard agree on this. They disagree on what the death did: paid a debt that had to be paid (Anselm), or showed a love that had to be shown (Abelard).

compare.why: Peter Abelard's reply to Anselm came in his Commentary on Romans, written around 1133–1137. It has no English translation old enough to quote here, so we read the passage of Paul that his view rests on, and give Abelard's own view in our own words in the commentary.
compare.title: Love first: the text behind Abelard

sections.h: A book for people who ask why
paras: Why God Became Man is a short book, about the length of a long essay, in two parts. In the preface Anselm says that in Book I he will set Christ aside, as if nothing were known of him, and show by reason alone that no one can be saved without him; in Book II he shows that human nature was made for eternal happiness and that this requires a God-man. This method, often called remoto Christo, 'Christ set aside', is bold: it treats the incarnation as the answer to a problem anyone can see.

Historians, including Anselm's great modern biographer R. W. Southern, treat it as a turning point. It was the first full-length treatise devoted to the question of why God's way of saving was the cross. Its influence on Western theology, Catholic and Protestant, is hard to overstate.
sections.key: Why God Became Man (1098) argues from reason alone, 'Christ set aside', that only a God-man can save: the first full treatise on why the cross.

paras: Stripped to its bones, Anselm's argument runs like this. Each step depends on the one before; to reject the conclusion you must reject one of the steps.

Most critics attack step 3 (must God require satisfaction?) or step 4 (is sin's weight really infinite?). Most defenders point out that the argument never says God is angry, and never says Christ is punished.

rows: God made humans for eternal happiness with him, and his purpose cannot fail.
To sin is to withhold the honour we owe God: a will subject to his.
God cannot simply overlook sin: either satisfaction or punishment must follow.
Even the least sin outweighs the whole creation, so the debt exceeds anything created.
Only God could pay it; only a human ought to pay it.
So a God-man must pay it, by freely giving his life, which he did not owe.
table.note: Anselm adds that because Christ owed nothing, his free death merits a reward, which he gives to us (II.19).

sections.key: Purpose, sin as withheld honour, satisfaction or punishment, an infinite debt, God can but man ought, so a God-man: six steps.

sections.h: Is Anselm's God a feudal lord?
paras: The commonest objection is that Anselm made God in the image of a Norman baron, offended in his honour and demanding compensation. Anselm lived among such lords; the language of honour, debt and vassalage was the air he breathed.

But Anselm himself guards against the caricature. 'Nothing can be added to or taken from the honor of God', he says (I.15). God does not need our honour as a baron needs his tenants' rents. What sin damages is the order and beauty of the world, and our own place in it. The demand for satisfaction is not God's wounded pride but the moral seriousness of a universe in which wrongs matter. The theologian David Bentley Hart has argued that, read this way, Anselm is much closer to the Greek Fathers than Aulén thought: the God-man restores what humanity spoiled. Critics reply that, whatever Anselm meant, the picture of God as creditor is what his readers took from him.
sections.key: Critics see a feudal lord; Anselm says God's honour cannot be harmed and sin damages the order of the world. Whether that rescues him is debated.

paras: Peter Abelard (1079–1142) was the most brilliant and the most controversial teacher in the new schools of Paris. He is remembered for his love affair with his pupil Héloïse, his castration by her uncle's men, and their letters; but he was also a logician of genius and a bold theologian.

In his Commentary on Romans, written around 1133–1137, he paused at Romans 3:26 to ask how the death of Christ redeems us. He rejected the devil's rights, and he found it hard to see why God should require the blood of an innocent at all, still less be pleased by it. His answer, in our own words: the Son became man and persevered in teaching us by word and example even to death, and this supreme love binds us to God, so that we no longer fear to do anything for him. Redemption is the love kindled in us by the cross. This has come to be called the 'moral influence' or 'exemplary' view, and it is the fifth picture of this journey: the road, where someone shows the way by walking it.
sections.key: Abelard (1079–1142), commenting on Romans, said the cross redeems by showing a love that kindles love in us: the 'moral influence' view.

paras: Abelard's great opponent was Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), the most powerful churchman of his day. In a long letter of around 1140 on the errors of Abelard, Bernard protested that if the cross were only an example, Christ would have taught us love but not given us anything. In Bernard's view, such a Christ would teach us what righteousness is without giving it to us, and an example is no use to someone who is drowning.

In 1141 a church council at Sens condemned a list of propositions drawn from Abelard's works, including his view of the cross, and the pope confirmed it. Abelard appealed, fell ill, and died the next year at the priory of Saint-Marcel near Chalon, reconciled with Bernard. Modern scholars think the condemned list sometimes misrepresented him: Abelard did speak of Christ's death as a sacrifice and of his merit. But the debate he started never ended. Liberal Protestant theologians of the nineteenth century, such as Albrecht Ritschl, revived his emphasis.
sections.key: Bernard objected that an example saves no one who cannot follow it; Abelard was condemned at Sens in 1141, though scholars think he was partly misread.

paras: In the 1270s Thomas Aquinas wrote the part of his Summa Theologiae on the passion of Christ (Part III, questions 46–49). He disagreed with Anselm on one point: the cross was not strictly necessary. God could have forgiven humanity without any satisfaction, and would not have acted unjustly in doing so, since he is the one wronged and has no judge above him (III.46.2). But the cross was the most fitting way, because it showed God's love, gave us an example, freed us from sin, won for us the grace that justifies, and made satisfaction 'superabundantly', with a love that outweighed every offence (III.46.3; 48.2).

So Aquinas kept Anselm's satisfaction and Abelard's love, and added sacrifice, redemption and merit beside them. This is close to Catholic teaching today. The Council of Trent (1547) taught that Christ merited our justification by his passion and made satisfaction for us to the Father, and that the Mass makes present the one sacrifice of the cross.
sections.key: Aquinas said the cross was not strictly necessary but most fitting, and held satisfaction, love, example, sacrifice and merit together: Catholic teaching since.

sections.h: What Anselm got right, and what he did not
paras: Anselm's lasting gift is seriousness. He refused to let sin be small, or forgiveness cheap. His question to Boso, 'you have not yet considered how heavy sin is', still lands. And he saw why it mattered that Christ was both God and man: a rescue that was only divine would not be ours, and one that was only human would not be enough.

His critics point to what is missing. The argument has little to say about Jesus's life and teaching, or about the resurrection, which hardly appears in the book. It explains why someone had to die but not why it had to be crucifixion. And it frames the whole question in terms of debt and honour, which can make God sound like a creditor. Abelard's view has the opposite strengths and weaknesses: it makes love central, but it struggles to say what the cross did that a life of love, without a death, could not.
sections.key: Anselm made sin serious and the God-man necessary; critics say he neglected Jesus's life and resurrection and made God a creditor. Abelard has the opposite profile.

debate.question: Anselm or Abelard: does the cross change God's situation, or ours?

positions.name: Anselm: the cross deals with a real debt
positions.who: Anselm; in modified form Thomas Aquinas and the Reformers; many theologians today
positions.view: Sin is a real wrong that cannot simply be overlooked without making goodness meaningless. The God-man freely makes the satisfaction we could not, and so restores what we broke. Something objective happened on the cross.
positions.evidence: Why God Became Man I.12, 21; II.6; Romans 5:9 ('justified by his blood'); Hebrews 9.

positions.name: Abelard: the cross changes us
positions.who: Abelard; Albrecht Ritschl and much liberal Protestant theology; many modern Christians
positions.view: God does not need to be satisfied; he is love already. The cross shows that love so fully that it melts our hostility and wins our love. To say God required an innocent death is to make him worse than a good human father.
positions.evidence: Romans 5:8; 1 John 4:10, 19; the parable of the prodigal son, where the father forgives without payment (Luke 15).

positions.name: Both, in different measure
positions.who: Thomas Aquinas; much Catholic and Anglican theology
positions.view: The cross was not strictly necessary, but it was the most fitting way: it both satisfied for sin superabundantly and showed a love that draws us. Objective and subjective belong together.
positions.evidence: Summa Theologiae III.46.2–3; 48.2; Romans 5:8–10, read as a whole.

debate.agree: All agree that God's love comes first, that Christ gave himself freely, and that the cross must change the way we live.

look.why: Andrea di Bartolo, a painter of Siena, painted this side of a two-sided panel around 1380–1390. It shows Christ alone on the cross, with no mourners: the one figure on whom, in Anselm's argument, everything depends, God and man in one suffering body.
points: A thin, haggard, nearly nude man is nailed to a wooden cross, his body stretched between wide-spread hands.
Blood trickles from each nailed hand and from a gash over his right ribs.
Blood from the nail through his overlapping feet drips down the platform, the foot of the cross and onto the ground.
His head droops to one side, eyes closed under deeply furrowed brows, with a ring of thorns in his long, coppery-red hair.
He wears only a sheer white cloth draped low on his hips.
The background is streaked with tawny brown, burnt orange and gold.

music.why: Gregorio Allegri set Psalm 51, 'Have mercy on me, O God', in the 1630s for the Pope's choir to sing in Holy Week. It is the prayer of someone who has begun to weigh how heavy sin is, and who trusts mercy anyway.

think.why: Anselm argued that if sin made no difference to God, goodness would make no difference either. See the wider debate about whether morality needs God.

learn.why: The verse Abelard built on, and one every account of the cross must fit: the love came first.

check.q: How does Anselm define sin in Why God Became Man I.11?
options: Offending against the Church
Not rendering to God his due: withholding the will's subjection to God, which is the honour we owe
Any harm done to another person
Breaking any of the Ten Commandments
check.why: 'To sin is nothing else than not to render to God his due', and the debt is that 'every wish of a rational creature should be subject to the will of God'.

check.q: What is Anselm's strongest reason why God cannot simply forgive without satisfaction?
options: Because the devil would object
Because the Bible never mentions forgiveness
Because God would then make no difference between the guilty and the innocent, and sin would matter to no one
Because God is too angry to forgive
check.why: 'With God there will be no difference between the guilty and the not guilty; and this is unbecoming to God.'

check.q: How does Anselm answer Boso's objection that God commands us to forgive?
options: He says Boso has misread the Lord's Prayer
He agrees that God can forgive without satisfaction
He says God never commanded it
He says vengeance belongs to God alone, so what is fitting for us is not what is fitting for the judge of all
check.why: 'To execute vengeance belongs to none but Him who is Lord of all.' Many readers find this his weakest answer.

check.q: What is the point of Anselm's thought experiment about saving the universe by one glance against God's will?
options: To show that even the least sin outweighs everything in creation, so nothing created could pay for it
To show that God would destroy the world
To show that the universe is unimportant
To show that Boso was a sinner
check.why: If you should not glance against God's will to save creation, sin's weight exceeds creation; so the satisfaction must too.

check.q: In Anselm's account, which statement is true?
options: The cross is not necessary at all
Christ is punished in our place by an angry Father
The ransom is paid to the devil
Satisfaction and punishment are alternatives: Christ freely makes satisfaction so that punishment is not needed
check.why: 'The honor taken away must be repaid, or punishment must follow'. Anselm's Christ satisfies; the Reformers later spoke of him bearing the penalty.

check.q: Which is the best statement of Bernard's objection to Abelard?
options: That Romans 5 is not in the Bible
That an example of love, on its own, does not give us anything we lack: it teaches righteousness without bestowing it
That Abelard denied that Jesus died
That Abelard believed in the devil's rights
check.why: Bernard's complaint was that if the cross is only an example, it helps only those already able to follow it.

tutorial.question: Assess Anselm's argument that only a God-man could make satisfaction for sin.
tutorial.approach: Set out the argument in steps, using the passages you read. Then test the weakest steps: must God require satisfaction (I.12)? Is the debt infinite (I.21)? Consider the 'feudal' objection and Anselm's reply in I.15. Compare Abelard's alternative and Aquinas's view that the cross was fitting rather than necessary. Reach a judgement.
strong: States the argument accurately, including 'God can, man ought'.
Distinguishes satisfaction from punishment in Anselm.
Engages Boso's objection about forgiveness and Anselm's reply.
Discusses the feudal objection fairly, with I.15.
Compares Abelard's view and Bernard's criticism.
Uses Aquinas's 'fitting, not necessary' as a middle way.
