sessions.title: Witnesses
sessions.line: Forty days after the cross, a small group of Jews in Jerusalem says that Jesus is alive, and will not stop saying so.
sessions.plain: Some time around the year 30, Jesus of Nazareth was crucified by the Romans in Jerusalem. A few weeks later his followers were back in the same city, saying publicly that God had raised him from the dead and that they had seen him. They were Jews, they met in the Temple, and they shared what they owned. This session asks who these first Christians were, and why a movement that should have ended at the cross began there instead.
sessions.why: This is the first session. The question of the whole journey is how a few followers of a crucified man changed an empire. Before we can ask how the movement spread, we need to see where it began: with a handful of people in one city, and one claim.
answers: Who were the first Christians?
What happened after Easter, according to Acts?
Who wrote Acts, and can we trust it?
Why did the first Christians share what they owned?
sessions.finding: The Church began as a group of Jewish witnesses in Jerusalem who said they had seen the risen Jesus and would not stop saying so.

paras: Jesus of Nazareth was a Jewish teacher from Galilee, in the north of what is now Israel. After perhaps three years of teaching and healing, he went up to Jerusalem for the Passover festival and was arrested, tried and crucified on the orders of the Roman governor, Pontius Pilate. Most historians date his death to AD 30 or 33. Crucifixion was the Roman death for slaves and rebels. It was meant to end a movement as well as a life.

His closest followers ran away. Yet within weeks they were saying that the tomb was empty and that Jesus had appeared to them alive. If you have taken 'Who was Jesus?' and 'The last week and the cross', you have weighed that claim and the evidence for it. This journey starts the morning after: what the witnesses did next.
background.key: Jesus was crucified in Jerusalem around AD 30 or 33. Within weeks his followers were saying he was alive.

paras: By the year 300 there were perhaps six million Christians in the Roman Empire, about one person in ten, and by 400 Christianity was the empire's official faith. It had no army, no money to speak of, no state behind it, and for much of that time it was illegal. How did that happen?

We will follow the movement outwards, step by step, the way the book of Acts does: from Jerusalem, to Judea and Samaria, to the ends of the earth. At each step we ask why it spread. Then we hear what the Romans thought of it, give the strongest objection its full weight, and end with a verdict.

timeline.text: Witnesses: the first Christians in Jerusalem (Acts 1)
The first martyr and the persecutor: Stephen and Paul (Acts 7–9)
To the ends of the earth: Paul's journeys and his network (Acts 28; Romans 16)
How they lived: the Didache and the care of the sick
What Rome saw: Pliny's letter to the emperor
The case against: did Paul invent Christianity?
The verdict: how did they change an empire?

background.key: A tiny sect became the faith of the Roman Empire in under three centuries, without force. We follow it outwards and ask why.

paras: The Acts of the Apostles is the fifth book of the New Testament. It is the second volume of a two-part work: its first words, 'The first book I wrote, Theophilus', point back to the Gospel of Luke, which is addressed to the same man. The author never names himself. From about AD 180 Christian writers, beginning with Irenaeus of Lyons, name him as Luke, a doctor and a companion of Paul (Colossians 4:14). In some later chapters the story suddenly says 'we' instead of 'they', as if the writer had joined Paul on the road.

Most scholars date Acts to around AD 80 to 90. Some date it as early as the 60s, because it ends with Paul still alive in Rome; a few date it as late as 110 to 120. Luke wrote in good Greek, in the manner of the Greek historians, with speeches, journeys and named officials. He also wrote to persuade: he wanted Theophilus to know that the Christian message was true and that it was no threat to Rome.
background.key: Acts is the second volume of Luke's Gospel, probably written around AD 80–90 by a companion of Paul, as history written to persuade.

paras: The main reading is the opening of Acts (1:1–14): the risen Jesus's last words, his departure, and the first gathering of his followers. Its key verse, 'You will be witnesses', is the plan of the whole book and of this journey.
The comparison is a short scene a few weeks later (Acts 4:32–37): how the first believers in Jerusalem lived together. It answers a simple question: what did believing this message make them do?
background.key: Acts 1 gives the plan, 'you will be witnesses'; Acts 4 shows the first community living it.

before: What does Jesus tell his followers to do, and what does he refuse to tell them?
Who is in the upper room? Notice anyone you did not expect.
What do you think a 'witness' is, as opposed to a teacher or a believer?
sessions.readWhy: The first page of the Church's history: Jesus's last words, his departure, and the first gathering in Jerusalem.

paras: The first book I wrote, Theophilus, concerned all that Jesus began both to do and to teach,
until the day in which he was received up, after he had given commandment through the Holy Spirit to the apostles whom he had chosen.
To these he also showed himself alive after he suffered, by many proofs, appearing to them over a period of forty days, and speaking about God’s Kingdom.
Being assembled together with them, he commanded them, “Don’t depart from Jerusalem, but wait for the promise of the Father, which you heard from me.
For John indeed baptized in water, but you will be baptized in the Holy Spirit not many days from now.”
Therefore when they had come together, they asked him, “Lord, are you now restoring the kingdom to Israel?”
He said to them, “It isn’t for you to know times or seasons which the Father has set within his own authority.
But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you. You will be witnesses to me in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the uttermost parts of the earth.”
When he had said these things, as they were looking, he was taken up, and a cloud received him out of their sight.
While they were looking steadfastly into the sky as he went, behold, two men stood by them in white clothing,
who also said, “You men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into the sky? This Jesus, who was received up from you into the sky, will come back in the same way as you saw him going into the sky.”
Then they returned to Jerusalem from the mountain called Olivet, which is near Jerusalem, a Sabbath day’s journey away.

When they had come in, they went up into the upper room where they were staying; that is Peter, John, James, Andrew, Philip, Thomas, Bartholomew, Matthew, James the son of Alphaeus, Simon the Zealot, and Judas the son of James.
All these with one accord continued steadfastly in prayer and supplication, along with the women, and Mary the mother of Jesus, and with his brothers.

parts.title: You will be witnesses
parts.context: Jerusalem, some weeks after the crucifixion, perhaps AD 30 or 33. Luke opens his second volume by recalling the end of the first: the risen Jesus has been appearing to his followers. Now he meets them for the last time on the Mount of Olives, just east of the city.

commentary.on: The first book I wrote, Theophilus, concerned all that Jesus began both to do and to teach
commentary.text: Notice 'began'. The Gospel told what Jesus began to do. Acts will tell what he goes on doing through his followers. Theophilus ('friend of God') may be a real patron, perhaps a Roman official, or a name for any reader who loves God; scholars are divided.

commentary.on: he also showed himself alive after he suffered, by many proofs, appearing to them over a period of forty days
commentary.text: Luke states the claim at once, as a historian would state his evidence: 'many proofs', over forty days. Forty is a biblical number of preparation (Israel's forty years in the desert, Jesus's forty days of fasting), but Luke means a real period between Easter and the Ascension. Christians still keep the Ascension forty days after Easter.

commentary.on: Lord, are you now restoring the kingdom to Israel?
commentary.text: The disciples are still thinking as Jews of their time did: the Messiah would free Israel from Rome. Jesus does not mock the question. He changes it. The kingdom will come, but not as a revolt, and not on a timetable they can know.

commentary.on: You will be witnesses to me in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the uttermost parts of the earth.
commentary.text: This is the plan of Acts. Chapters 1 to 7 take place in Jerusalem; chapters 8 to 12 in Judea and Samaria; chapters 13 to 28 follow Paul across the empire to Rome. A witness, in a law court, does not make up a story; he tells what he has seen. The Greek word is martys, from which we get 'martyr': within a generation, witnesses would die for their testimony.

commentary.on: he was taken up, and a cloud received him out of their sight
commentary.text: This is the Ascension. In the Bible a cloud often means God's presence, as on Mount Sinai. Luke is saying that Jesus has gone into God's presence, not into the upper atmosphere. Christians have always read it as a change of the way Jesus is present, not as an absence.

commentary.on: You men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into the sky?
commentary.text: A gentle rebuke with a touch of humour. Staring upwards is not the task. The two men in white send them back to the city, with a promise: 'This Jesus' will come back. The first Christians lived between a departure and a return.

commentary.on: Peter, John, James, Andrew, Philip, Thomas, Bartholomew, Matthew, James the son of Alphaeus, Simon the Zealot, and Judas the son of James
commentary.text: Eleven names: the Twelve without Judas Iscariot, who had betrayed Jesus. Twelve stood for the twelve tribes of Israel, so in the verses after our reading they choose a replacement, Matthias. These are ordinary men: fishermen, a tax collector, a 'Zealot', which may mean a former anti-Roman militant.

commentary.on: along with the women, and Mary the mother of Jesus, and with his brothers
commentary.text: Women are named among the first believers, as they were the first witnesses at the tomb in Luke's Gospel. Mary is mentioned here for the last time in the New Testament. And Jesus's brothers are there, who in the Gospels did not believe in him (John 7:5). One of them, James, will soon lead the church in Jerusalem. Something changed their minds.

paras: The multitude of those who believed were of one heart and soul. Not one of them claimed that anything of the things which he possessed was his own, but they had all things in common.
With great power, the apostles gave their testimony of the resurrection of the Lord Jesus. Great grace was on them all.
For neither was there among them any who lacked, for as many as were owners of lands or houses sold them, and brought the proceeds of the things that were sold,
and laid them at the apostles’ feet, and distribution was made to each, according as anyone had need.
Joses, who by the apostles was also called Barnabas (which is, being interpreted, Son of Encouragement), a Levite, a man of Cyprus by race,
having a field, sold it and brought the money and laid it at the apostles’ feet.

parts.title: One heart and soul
parts.context: Jerusalem, perhaps a year or less after the crucifixion. Luke says the believers now number in the thousands. Peter and John have just been arrested and released after being ordered to stop speaking about Jesus. They have refused.

commentary.on: The multitude of those who believed were of one heart and soul.
commentary.text: 'One heart and soul' echoes a Greek proverb about friendship: friends have all things in common. Luke's educated readers would hear in it the ideal community the philosophers dreamed of, here made real among fishermen and widows.

commentary.on: With great power, the apostles gave their testimony of the resurrection of the Lord Jesus.
commentary.text: Notice what sits at the centre of the paragraph about money: the testimony to the resurrection. For Luke the two belong together. People who believe death has been beaten can afford to let go of property.

commentary.on: For neither was there among them any who lacked
commentary.text: This echoes the law of Moses: 'there will be no poor with you' (Deuteronomy 15:4). Luke is saying that the new community has kept the old promise to Israel. It was voluntary: in the next chapter Peter tells a man that his land was his own to keep or sell (Acts 5:4).

commentary.on: Joses, who by the apostles was also called Barnabas (which is, being interpreted, Son of Encouragement)
commentary.text: The first named convert who gives his property is a Jew from Cyprus, a Levite (from the priestly tribe), with a nickname. Barnabas matters: soon he will vouch for a dangerous new convert called Saul when no one else will trust him.

compare.why: A few weeks later, after the festival of Pentecost, the believers have grown in number. Luke describes how they lived. Read it as an answer to the question: what did believing make them do?
compare.title: All things in common

paras: The first Christians did not call themselves Christians. They were Jews who believed that Jesus was Israel's Messiah, the anointed king God had promised, and that God had raised him from the dead. They kept the Jewish law, prayed in the Temple and met in each other's homes. Outsiders called them 'the sect of the Nazarenes' (Acts 24:5); they called their faith 'the Way' (Acts 9:2). The name 'Christians', 'Christ's people', was first used at Antioch in Syria, perhaps ten years later (Acts 11:26), probably by outsiders.

This matters for the whole journey. Christianity did not begin as a new religion founded by a philosopher. It began as a claim inside Judaism: that the long story of Israel, from Abraham to the prophets, had reached its turning point in a crucified and risen man. Everything that follows, including the arguments with other Jews and the decision to welcome non-Jews, grows from that root.
sections.key: The first Christians were Jews who believed Jesus was the Messiah, raised from the dead. 'Christians' was a later name, first used at Antioch.

paras: Luke opens his Gospel like a Greek historian: he says he has 'traced the course of all things accurately from the first', using eyewitnesses (Luke 1:1–4; you read these lines if you have taken 'Can I trust the Bible?'). Acts keeps that manner. It names more than a hundred people, and many of its small details can be checked.

Some have been confirmed by inscriptions. Luke calls the rulers of Thessalonica 'politarchs' (Acts 17:6, 'rulers of the city'), a rare title once doubted and now found on inscriptions from the city. He names Gallio as governor of Achaia when Paul was in Corinth; an inscription at Delphi dates Gallio's year in office to about AD 51–52. He calls the leading man of Malta the 'first man' of the island (28:7), a title also found there in inscriptions.
None of this proves that Luke's account of miracles is true. It shows that he knew the world he described, and that he wrote as a historian, not as a teller of fables.
sections.key: Luke writes as an ancient historian; inscriptions confirm details such as the 'politarchs' of Thessalonica and Gallio's year in Corinth, about AD 51–52.

sections.h: The Twelve, Mary and the brothers
paras: The upper room holds three groups. The Twelve were the inner circle Jesus had chosen, a deliberate sign: twelve, for the twelve tribes of Israel, the people being gathered again. Peter, a fisherman from Galilee, leads them in the first half of Acts. Then there are the women who had followed Jesus from Galilee and stood near the cross. Then there are Mary and Jesus's brothers.

The brothers are a surprise. The Gospels say they did not believe in Jesus during his life (Mark 3:21; John 7:5). Paul, writing in the 50s, lists James among those to whom the risen Jesus appeared (1 Corinthians 15:7). James went on to lead the church in Jerusalem for about thirty years; the Jewish historian Josephus records his execution in AD 62. A sceptical brother who becomes the leader of his brother's movement, and dies for it, is one of the facts historians have to explain.
Christians differ over who these 'brothers' were. The table shows the three main views.

rows: Mary remained a virgin all her life. Jerome (about 383) argued that 'brother' could mean any kinsman, as in Genesis 13:8, where Abraham calls his nephew Lot a brother.
Sons of Joseph by an earlier marriage
Also holds Mary's lifelong virginity. This view is older than Jerome's; it appears in the second-century Protevangelium of James.
Usually, younger children of Mary and Joseph
Many Protestants take 'brother' in its plain sense. Luther and Calvin themselves held Mary's lifelong virginity; the view became common among Protestants later.
table.note: All agree that James 'the Lord's brother' (Galatians 1:19) led the Jerusalem church.

sections.key: The Twelve, the women, Mary and Jesus's once-sceptical brothers formed the first church. James, a brother, led it for thirty years; traditions differ on who the brothers were.

paras: Between our two readings comes the day Christians call the birthday of the Church. Pentecost was a Jewish harvest festival, the Feast of Weeks, fifty days after Passover, when Jerusalem was full of pilgrims from across the Jewish world. Acts 2 tells how the Holy Spirit came on the believers 'like the rushing of a mighty wind', how they spoke in other languages, and how Peter preached to the crowd. If you have taken 'The whole story' or 'Time made holy', you have read it.

Two things in that chapter matter here. First, the crowd was international: Luke lists people from Parthia in the east to Rome in the west. The message was heard on its first public day by Jews who would carry it home. Second, Luke gives a number: about three thousand were baptised that day (Acts 2:41), and soon 'about five thousand' men (4:4). Most historians think these numbers are rounded up, as ancient writers often did. Even so, the movement grew fast in the city where its founder had just been executed.
sections.key: At Pentecost, a pilgrim festival, the message was first preached publicly to Jews from across the world. Luke's numbers are probably rounded, but the movement grew in the very city of the cross.

paras: The first community shared its property. Was this communism? Not in the modern sense. It was voluntary: Peter tells Ananias that his land was his own (Acts 5:4). There was no rule that everyone must sell everything, and it did not last as a system; later Paul organised collections for the 'poor among the saints' in Jerusalem (Romans 15:26), which suggests the Jerusalem church stayed poor.

What did last was the principle. No one in the community should go without. That principle is the seed of something we will see again and again in this journey: Christians caring for widows, orphans and the sick, their own first and then others. The Greek philosophers had praised friendship in which 'friends share all things'. Luke shows it practised by ordinary people because of something they believed about Jesus.

Plato, in the Republic, imagined a ruling class sharing all property; if you take 'Plato' in Hall III, you will compare the two. The difference is that Plato's scheme was imposed from above, and Luke's grew from below.
sections.key: The Jerusalem believers shared property voluntarily so that no one lacked: not a system, but a principle that became the Christian care of the poor.

paras: Ordered by the Temple authorities to stop speaking about Jesus, Peter and the apostles answered: 'We must obey God rather than men' (Acts 5:29). Within a generation several of them had died for it. James the son of Zebedee was beheaded by King Herod Agrippa I around AD 44 (Acts 12:2). James the Lord's brother was stoned in AD 62, according to Josephus. Early Christian writers, beginning with the letter known as 1 Clement (about AD 96), say that Peter and Paul died in Rome under the emperor Nero in the 60s.

People die for false beliefs all the time; martyrdom does not prove a belief true. But it does show sincerity. These were not people repeating something they had heard; they claimed to have seen it themselves. As historians from every side agree, something convinced Jesus's followers, very soon after his death, that they had seen him alive. Whatever it was, it turned frightened men into public witnesses, and it is where the whole story of this journey begins.
sections.key: Threatened, the apostles said 'We must obey God rather than men'; several died for their testimony. Martyrdom shows sincerity, not truth, but it shows they believed they had seen.

refs: Acts 1–5; 11:26; 12:2; 17:6; 18:12; 24:5; 28:7; Luke 1:1–4; Mark 3:21; John 7:5; 1 Corinthians 15:3–7; Galatians 1:19; Romans 15:26; Deuteronomy 15:4.
Irenaeus, Against Heresies III.1.1 and III.14.1 (about AD 180), on Luke as author.
Josephus, Antiquities XX.9.1 (XX.200), the death of James; 1 Clement 5, Peter and Paul.
The Gallio inscription at Delphi (published 1905); the politarch inscriptions of Thessalonica; Colin Hemer, The Book of Acts in the Setting of Hellenistic History (1989).
Jerome, Against Helvidius (about 383); the Protevangelium of James (second century).
Richard Pervo, Dating Acts (2006); Craig Keener, Acts: An Exegetical Commentary (2012–2015).

debate.question: How reliable is Acts?

positions.name: A careful ancient historian
positions.who: William Ramsay (1851–1939); Colin Hemer; Martin Hengel; Craig Keener
positions.view: Luke knew the geography, officials and customs of the eastern empire in detail and wrote within living memory, probably with Paul's own companions as sources. Where he can be checked, he is usually right. His speeches are summaries in his own words, as all ancient historians wrote them, but the events are real.
positions.evidence: Politarchs, Gallio, the 'first man' of Malta; the 'we' passages; the sea voyage of Acts 27, which experts in ancient sailing have found accurate.

positions.name: Theology in the form of history
positions.who: Ernst Haenchen; Hans Conzelmann; Richard Pervo
positions.view: Luke shaped his story to make a point: that the Church spread smoothly from Jerusalem to Rome, united and harmless to the empire. He smooths over conflicts that Paul's letters show were sharp, and he may be writing as late as the early second century.
positions.evidence: Differences from Paul's own letters (for example, when Paul first visited Jerusalem, compare Acts 9:26 with Galatians 1:17–18); the neat pattern of the book; the idealised picture of the first church.

positions.name: Both: a historian with a purpose
positions.who: Loveday Alexander; James Dunn; many scholars today
positions.view: All ancient history was written with a purpose, Thucydides' included. Luke selects and shapes, but within the limits of what his readers, some of whom remembered the events, would accept. Read Acts critically, beside Paul's letters, and it is a valuable source.
positions.evidence: Luke's preface compared with other Greek historians'; the broad agreement of Acts with the letters on people, places and order of events.

debate.agree: All agree that Acts is our only narrative of the first Christian generation, that it was written to persuade, and that it should be checked against Paul's letters wherever possible.

look.why: Johann Koerbecke painted the Ascension in 1456–57 for an altarpiece in Westphalia, in Germany. It shows the moment in our reading when Jesus is 'taken up' before his followers. The painter adds figures Luke does not mention; the gallery identifies the woman as Mary.
points: Twelve men and a woman kneel on the ground on either side of a moss-green rock, looking or gesturing upwards.
Jesus sits on a black cloud at the top, wrapped in a red robe, his right hand raised with two fingers lifted in blessing.
He holds a thin staff topped with a cross and a red pennant; the wounds show on his hands and side.
Two footprints are pressed into the top of the rock, where he last stood.
Closest to us on the left, the woman in a cobalt-blue mantle, with a gold halo, looks up with her hands together in prayer.
Rays of light, cut into the gold background, run down from Jesus and up from the heads of the people below.

music.why: 'Come, Creator Spirit', a Latin hymn of the ninth century, prays for the Spirit Jesus promised in Acts 1:8. It is still sung at ordinations and coronations.

think.why: The first Christians' whole message rested on one claim: that death had been beaten. See what Christians believe about death and resurrection.

learn.why: The plan of the book of Acts, and of this journey, in one verse.

check.q: Why does it matter that Luke calls the first volume what Jesus 'began' to do and teach?
options: It means Jesus did not finish his teaching before he died
It means the apostles completed teaching that Jesus left unfinished
It presents Acts as the continuation of Jesus's work through his followers
It shows Luke had not finished the Gospel
check.why: The Gospel tells what Jesus began; Acts tells what he continues to do through the witnesses.

check.q: How does Acts 1:8 work as a plan for the book?
options: It predicts the date of Jesus's return
It tells the disciples to stay in Jerusalem for ever
It names the places the book moves through: Jerusalem, then Judea and Samaria, then the ends of the earth
It lists the apostles in the order they will die
check.why: Chapters 1–7, 8–12 and 13–28 follow exactly that outward movement.

check.q: Which fact about the people in the upper room do historians find hardest to explain without something having happened after the crucifixion?
options: That there were eleven apostles
That they met in an upper room
That Jesus's brothers, who had not believed in him, were now among the believers, and James later led the church
That women were present
check.why: A sceptical brother who becomes the leader of the movement, and dies for it, needs an explanation; Paul says the risen Jesus appeared to James.

check.q: What do inscriptions such as those naming the politarchs of Thessalonica show about Acts?
options: That Luke knew the officials and places of the world he described in accurate detail
That Acts was written in the fourth century
That every event in Acts happened as told
That Luke was a politarch himself
check.why: They show Luke's accuracy on checkable details; they cannot by themselves prove the miracles.

check.q: Which is the best description of the sharing of property in Acts 4?
options: A voluntary sharing so that no one lacked, rooted in belief in the resurrection
A tax paid to the Temple
A Roman law for religious groups
A compulsory system abolishing private property
check.why: Peter tells Ananias his land was his own (5:4); the principle, not a system, was that no one should go without.

check.q: Does the willingness of the apostles to die prove that the resurrection happened?
options: Yes, because Luke says so
No, but it shows they sincerely believed they had seen it, which historians must explain
No, and it tells us nothing at all
Yes: no one dies for something false
check.why: Martyrdom shows sincerity, not truth. But these were eyewitnesses, not repeaters of a story, and their conviction needs explaining.

tutorial.question: Who were the first Christians, and what did they believe that made them different?
tutorial.approach: Describe the people in the upper room and the community of Acts 4. Explain why they were still Jews, and what single claim set them apart. Weigh how far Acts can be trusted as a source, using the debate. End with why their claim made them 'witnesses' rather than simply followers of a teacher.
strong: Identifies them as Jews in Jerusalem who believed Jesus was the Messiah, raised from the dead.
Uses Acts 1:8 to explain what a 'witness' is.
Notices the women and Jesus's brothers, and what James's change of mind implies.
Explains the voluntary sharing of Acts 4 and its link to the resurrection.
Weighs the reliability of Acts fairly, with at least one confirmed detail and one problem.
Notes that martyrdom shows sincerity, not truth.

reading.author: N. T. Wright
reading.title: Acts for Everyone (2 vols)
reading.why: A clear, short commentary on every passage, for anyone.

reading.author: Martin Hengel
reading.title: Acts and the History of Earliest Christianity
reading.why: A great German historian argues that Acts is a reliable source, and shows how to use it.

reading.author: Richard Pervo
reading.title: Dating Acts
reading.why: The case for a late Acts, to read against Hengel.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: the first Christians made sure that 'no one lacked'. Find one person near you who is short of something you have (time, a meal, a lift, a tool) and give it without being asked.
sessions.reflect: What have you seen with your own eyes that you would keep saying even if you were told to stop?
takeaways: The first Christians were Jews in Jerusalem, including the Twelve, women, Mary and Jesus's once-sceptical brothers, who said the crucified Jesus was alive.
Acts, written by Luke as history with a purpose, follows their witness outwards from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth; its checkable details are usually right.
Believing that death had been beaten, they shared what they owned so that no one lacked, and would not stop speaking even under threat.

sessions.title: The first martyr and the persecutor
sessions.line: A young man holds the coats while Stephen is stoned. A few years later, on the road to Damascus, he is stopped by the man he is persecuting.
sessions.plain: Stephen, one of the first Christian leaders in Jerusalem, was stoned to death for what he said about Jesus and the Temple. A young Pharisee named Saul watched and approved, then hunted down Christians from house to house. Soon after, on his way to Damascus to arrest more of them, Saul saw a blinding light and heard Jesus speak to him. He became Paul, the greatest missionary the Church has known. This session asks who Stephen and Paul were, what happened on the Damascus road, and why it mattered so much for the spread of the faith.
sessions.why: Session 1 left the witnesses in Jerusalem. Acts 1:8 said they would go on to Judea and Samaria, but they did not go of their own accord. This session shows what drove them out: a death, a persecution, and a persecutor who changed sides.
answers: Who was Stephen, and why was he killed?
Who was Paul before he became a Christian?
What happened on the road to Damascus?
Was it a conversion, or a calling?
sessions.finding: The first martyr's death scattered the Church, and its fiercest persecutor became its greatest missionary.

paras: Session 1 showed the first believers in Jerusalem: Jews who said Jesus was risen, met in the Temple and shared what they had. As the community grew it included two kinds of Jews: 'Hebrews', who spoke Aramaic and were at home in Judea, and 'Hellenists', Greek-speaking Jews who had come to Jerusalem from cities around the Mediterranean.

When the Hellenist widows were being overlooked in the daily sharing of food (Acts 6:1), the apostles appointed seven men to look after them. One was Stephen, 'full of faith and of the Holy Spirit'. He was soon preaching as well as serving, and arguing with other Greek-speaking Jews in their synagogues. They accused him before the Jewish council of speaking against the Temple and the law of Moses. Acts 7 gives his long defence: a retelling of Israel's history, ending with the charge that Israel had always resisted its prophets.
background.key: Stephen was a Greek-speaking Jewish believer, chosen to care for widows, who was accused of speaking against the Temple and the law.

paras: Saul was born in Tarsus, a large Greek-speaking city in Cilicia, in the south-east of modern Turkey. He was a Jew of the tribe of Benjamin, named after Israel's first king, who was from that tribe. He was also, Acts says, a Roman citizen from birth (22:28), a rare privilege for a provincial Jew. His Roman name was Paulus, Paul. He learned a trade, tent-making or leather-working (18:3), and studied the law in Jerusalem 'at the feet of Gamaliel', a famous rabbi (22:3).

He was a Pharisee: a member of a lay movement devoted to keeping God's law in every part of daily life. In his own words, he was 'concerning zeal, persecuting the assembly; concerning the righteousness which is in the law, found blameless' (Philippians 3:6). He was probably in his twenties when Stephen died.
background.key: Saul of Tarsus was a Greek-speaking Jew, a Roman citizen, a Pharisee trained in Jerusalem and a zealous persecutor of the believers.

paras: The dates can be worked out roughly from Paul's own letters. He says he went to Jerusalem three years after his conversion (Galatians 1:18) and again fourteen years later (2:1). He also says that he escaped from Damascus while it was under the governor of King Aretas (2 Corinthians 11:32), a Nabataean king who died around AD 40. Most scholars place Stephen's death and Paul's conversion between AD 31 and 36, only a few years after the crucifixion.

timeline.text: Saul born in Tarsus
Crucifixion of Jesus
Stephen stoned; Saul persecutes the church
Saul's experience on the Damascus road
Arabia, Damascus, then a first visit to Peter in Jerusalem
Paul in Tarsus and Antioch

background.key: Stephen's death and Paul's conversion both happened within about six years of the crucifixion, probably between AD 31 and 36.

paras: The main reading has two parts: the death of Stephen and the persecution that followed (Acts 7:54–8:3), and Saul on the road to Damascus (Acts 9:1–22). The first explains how the Church left Jerusalem. The second explains how it gained the man who would carry it furthest.

The comparison is Paul's own account, written about twenty years later in his letter to the Galatians. Acts tells the story from outside; Galatians tells it from inside. Reading them side by side lets us test Luke against Paul.
background.key: Acts tells how Stephen died and Saul was stopped on the road; Paul's own letter to the Galatians tells it from inside.

before: What does Stephen say as he dies? Whose words does he echo?
In Acts 9, what does the voice say Saul is persecuting? Why is that surprising?
In Galatians, what does Paul insist on most strongly about how he received his message?
sessions.readWhy: The first martyr, and the persecutor who became the apostle: the events that drove the Church out of Jerusalem and gave it its greatest missionary.

paras: Now when they heard these things, they were cut to the heart, and they gnashed at him with their teeth.
But he, being full of the Holy Spirit, looked up steadfastly into heaven and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing on the right hand of God,
and said, “Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God!”
But they cried out with a loud voice and stopped their ears, then rushed at him with one accord.
They threw him out of the city and stoned him. The witnesses placed their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul.
They stoned Stephen as he called out, saying, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit!”
He kneeled down, and cried with a loud voice, “Lord, don’t hold this sin against them!” When he had said this, he fell asleep.

Saul was consenting to his death. A great persecution arose against the assembly which was in Jerusalem in that day. They were all scattered abroad throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria, except for the apostles.
Devout men buried Stephen and lamented greatly over him.
But Saul ravaged the assembly, entering into every house and dragged both men and women off to prison.
But Saul, still breathing threats and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord, went to the high priest
and asked for letters from him to the synagogues of Damascus, that if he found any who were of the Way, whether men or women, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem.
As he traveled, he got close to Damascus, and suddenly a light from the sky shone around him.
He fell on the earth, and heard a voice saying to him, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?”
He said, “Who are you, Lord?”
The Lord said, “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.
But rise up and enter into the city, then you will be told what you must do.”
The men who traveled with him stood speechless, hearing the sound, but seeing no one.
Saul arose from the ground, and when his eyes were opened, he saw no one. They led him by the hand, and brought him into Damascus.
He was without sight for three days, and neither ate nor drank.
Now there was a certain disciple at Damascus named Ananias. The Lord said to him in a vision, “Ananias!”
He said, “Behold, it’s me, Lord.”
The Lord said to him, “Arise, and go to the street which is called Straight, and inquire in the house of Judah for one named Saul, a man of Tarsus. For behold, he is praying,
and in a vision he has seen a man named Ananias coming in and laying his hands on him, that he might receive his sight.”
But Ananias answered, “Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he did to your saints at Jerusalem.
Here he has authority from the chief priests to bind all who call on your name.”
But the Lord said to him, “Go your way, for he is my chosen vessel to bear my name before the nations and kings, and the children of Israel.
For I will show him how many things he must suffer for my name’s sake.”

Ananias departed and entered into the house. Laying his hands on him, he said, “Brother Saul, the Lord, who appeared to you on the road by which you came, has sent me that you may receive your sight and be filled with the Holy Spirit.”
Immediately something like scales fell from his eyes, and he received his sight. He arose and was baptized.
He took food and was strengthened. Saul stayed several days with the disciples who were at Damascus.
Immediately in the synagogues he proclaimed the Christ, that he is the Son of God.
All who heard him were amazed, and said, “Isn’t this he who in Jerusalem made havoc of those who called on this name? And he had come here intending to bring them bound before the chief priests!”
But Saul increased more in strength, and confounded the Jews who lived at Damascus, proving that this is the Christ.

parts.title: The death of Stephen
parts.context: Jerusalem, about AD 31–36. Stephen has just finished his defence before the council, the Sanhedrin, the highest Jewish court. He has ended by accusing his hearers of resisting the Holy Spirit and killing the Righteous One, as their fathers killed the prophets.

commentary.on: I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God!
commentary.text: 'Son of Man' was Jesus's own favourite name for himself, from the vision in Daniel 7 of a human figure given authority by God. This is the only time anyone else uses it of him in the New Testament outside the Gospels. Usually Jesus 'sits' at God's right hand; here he stands, perhaps to welcome Stephen, or as a witness rising in court for the defence.

commentary.on: They threw him out of the city and stoned him.
commentary.text: Stoning was the law's penalty for blasphemy (Leviticus 24:16). Under Roman rule the Jewish council was not normally allowed to carry out executions (John 18:31), so this looks like a lynching, a mob acting in fury rather than a formal sentence. Historians debate it.

commentary.on: The witnesses placed their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul.
commentary.text: Luke introduces the hero of the second half of his book in passing, as a young man minding coats. The witnesses, who by law threw the first stones (Deuteronomy 17:7), took off their cloaks to do it. Saul is close enough to see everything.

commentary.on: Lord Jesus, receive my spirit!
commentary.text: Stephen dies as Jesus died in Luke's Gospel, with two prayers. Jesus prayed 'Father, into your hands I commit my spirit' (Luke 23:46); Stephen prays to Jesus. Within a few years of the cross, a Jew is praying to Jesus as one prays to God. That is one of the most important facts in this whole journey.

commentary.on: Lord, don't hold this sin against them!
commentary.text: And his second prayer echoes Jesus's prayer for his executioners, 'Father, forgive them' (Luke 23:34). This is the first Christian martyrdom, and it sets the pattern: the witness dies forgiving.

commentary.on: He kneeled down, and cried with a loud voice
commentary.text: Then Luke says that Stephen 'fell asleep'. Christians used 'sleep' for death because they expected to wake. Our word 'cemetery' comes from the Greek koimeterion, a sleeping place.

commentary.on: They were all scattered abroad throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria, except for the apostles.
commentary.text: This is the turning point. Acts 1:8 said 'Judea and Samaria'; now persecution makes it happen. The believers who fled were mostly Greek-speaking Jews like Stephen, and they preached wherever they went (8:4). The scattering became a sowing.

commentary.on: But Saul ravaged the assembly, entering into every house and dragged both men and women off to prison.
commentary.text: The WEB translates the Greek ekklesia as 'assembly'; older Bibles say 'church'. Notice 'every house': the church met in homes. Notice 'men and women': women were counted as full members, worth arresting.

parts.title: On the road to Damascus
parts.context: A year or two later. The believers have fled as far as Damascus, the great city of Syria, about 135 miles (220 kilometres) north-east of Jerusalem, which had a large Jewish community. Saul sets out with letters of authority from the high priest to arrest them.

commentary.on: if he found any who were of the Way, whether men or women, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem
commentary.text: 'The Way' is the earliest name for the movement. The high priest had no power over Damascus under Roman law, but synagogues could discipline their own members. Saul means to bring the believers back for trial.

commentary.on: Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?
commentary.text: Not 'my followers', but 'me'. The voice identifies itself with the people Saul is hunting. Paul never forgot it: his later teaching that believers are 'the body of Christ' (1 Corinthians 12:27) may begin here.

commentary.on: I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.
commentary.text: For Saul this was a catastrophe. He believed Jesus was a false Messiah, rightly crucified: the law says 'cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree' (Deuteronomy 21:23, quoted by Paul in Galatians 3:13). If Jesus was alive and speaking from heaven, then God had vindicated the man Saul thought God had cursed. Everything had to be rethought.

commentary.on: The men who traveled with him stood speechless, hearing the sound, but seeing no one.
commentary.text: Acts tells this story three times (chapters 9, 22 and 26), with small differences. Here the companions hear a sound but see no one; in 22:9 they see the light but do not understand the voice. Ancient historians retold events with varied details. The core never changes: a light, a voice, the words 'why do you persecute me?'.

commentary.on: He was without sight for three days, and neither ate nor drank.
commentary.text: The proud persecutor is led by the hand, blind and fasting. Three days is a quiet echo of the three days between Jesus's death and resurrection: Saul is going through a death of his own.

commentary.on: Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he did to your saints at Jerusalem.
commentary.text: Ananias's fear is entirely reasonable. One of the most moving things in the story is that an ordinary believer, whose name we know only from this scene, is asked to go and lay hands on the man who came to arrest him.

commentary.on: he is my chosen vessel to bear my name before the nations and kings, and the children of Israel
commentary.text: 'The nations' means the Gentiles, the non-Jewish peoples. In Paul's own account it is the heart of the call: he was sent to the Gentiles. The rest of Acts shows him before governors and kings, and finally on his way to the emperor.

commentary.on: Brother Saul
commentary.text: Ananias's first words are 'Brother Saul'. The enemy is greeted as family before he has done anything to deserve it.

commentary.on: Immediately in the synagogues he proclaimed the Christ, that he is the Son of God.
commentary.text: Saul goes straight back to the synagogues he came to purge, now preaching what he came to stamp out. The listeners' astonishment, 'Isn't this he who in Jerusalem made havoc', is the reaction of everyone who knew him.

paras: But I make known to you, brothers, concerning the Good News which was preached by me, that it is not according to man.
For I didn’t receive it from man, nor was I taught it, but it came to me through revelation of Jesus Christ.
For you have heard of my way of living in time past in the Jews’ religion, how that beyond measure I persecuted the assembly of God and ravaged it.
I advanced in the Jews’ religion beyond many of my own age among my countrymen, being more exceedingly zealous for the traditions of my fathers.
But when it was the good pleasure of God, who separated me from my mother’s womb and called me through his grace
to reveal his Son in me, that I might preach him among the Gentiles, I didn’t immediately confer with flesh and blood,
nor did I go up to Jerusalem to those who were apostles before me, but I went away into Arabia. Then I returned to Damascus.

parts.title: It came to me through revelation
parts.context: Paul writes, probably between AD 48 and 55, to churches he founded in Galatia. Visiting teachers have told the Gentile believers there that they must be circumcised and keep the Jewish law, and have said that Paul is not a real apostle. He defends his calling. (The next verses, 1:18–24, tell of his first visit to Peter in Jerusalem; if you have taken 'Can I trust the Bible?', you read them there.)

commentary.on: For I didn't receive it from man, nor was I taught it, but it came to me through revelation of Jesus Christ.
commentary.text: Paul's claim is strong: his message came directly from the risen Jesus, not from the apostles. He says this because his opponents were using the Jerusalem leaders against him. Hold on to this sentence; it will matter when we ask, as the journey will later on, whether Paul invented Christianity.

commentary.on: beyond measure I persecuted the assembly of God and ravaged it
commentary.text: Paul uses the same word as Acts 8:3, 'ravaged'. On the fact of the persecution, Acts and Paul agree exactly. Paul never hides it; elsewhere he calls himself 'the least of the apostles', because he persecuted the church (1 Corinthians 15:9).

commentary.on: being more exceedingly zealous for the traditions of my fathers
commentary.text: 'Zeal' was a word with a history. The great heroes of zeal in the Bible, Phinehas and Elijah, used force against those they thought were leading Israel away from God. Saul saw himself in that line.

commentary.on: who separated me from my mother's womb and called me through his grace
commentary.text: Paul describes his experience in the language of the prophets' calls: 'Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you... I have appointed you a prophet to the nations' (Jeremiah 1:5). He sees it less as changing religion than as being called, like Jeremiah, to a task within Israel's story.

commentary.on: to reveal his Son in me, that I might preach him among the Gentiles
commentary.text: Notice 'in me', not only 'to me'. And notice the purpose: the Gentiles. For Paul the vision and the mission came together.

commentary.on: but I went away into Arabia. Then I returned to Damascus.
commentary.text: 'Arabia' here means the Nabataean kingdom, east and south of Damascus, in modern Jordan. Acts does not mention this. We do not know what he did there, preach or pray. Elijah, the great zealot, had gone into the desert to Mount Horeb after a crisis (1 Kings 19); some scholars think Paul, the zealot, did the same.

compare.why: About twenty years later, writing to churches he had founded in Galatia (central Turkey), Paul told the story himself. Some there were saying he had learned his message second-hand from the apostles in Jerusalem. Read how he answers.
compare.title: Paul in his own words

paras: Why was Stephen killed, when the apostles had only been flogged and released? The charge tells us: he was accused of saying that Jesus would destroy the Temple and change the customs Moses had given (Acts 6:14). The Temple in Jerusalem was the centre of Jewish life, the one place where sacrifice was offered to God. To question it was to question everything.

Stephen's speech in Acts 7 retells Israel's history to show that God was never confined to one building or one land. God spoke to Abraham in Mesopotamia and to Moses in the desert; the Most High 'doesn't dwell in temples made with hands' (7:48). Greek-speaking Jews like Stephen, who had grown up far from Jerusalem, may have been the first believers to see that faith in Jesus pointed beyond the Temple.

That idea would carry the Church out of Jerusalem. If God could be worshipped anywhere through Jesus, then the message could go anywhere. Stephen died for the idea that made the rest of this journey possible.
sections.key: Stephen was killed for saying God was not confined to the Temple: the idea that would let the faith go anywhere.

sections.h: Persecution as the engine of mission
paras: Luke tells the story so that the persecution after Stephen's death is not a defeat but a turning point. The believers who scattered 'went around preaching the word' (8:4). Philip, another of the seven, went to Samaria, whose people the Jews regarded as half-outsiders, and many believed (8:5–8). Others went as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus and Antioch, where, for the first time, they spoke to Greeks who were not Jews at all (11:19–21).

This pattern recurs through the history of the Church. The second-century writer Tertullian would tell the Roman authorities that 'the blood of Christians is seed': if you take 'The martyrs and the empire' in Hall IV, you will read his words. In the twentieth century, the church in China grew most quickly after missionaries were expelled in 1949.

Persecution does not always help a faith. In parts of North Africa and Asia, Christian communities were wiped out by persecution. But in the first generation, scattering a movement of preachers spread it.
sections.key: The persecution after Stephen's death scattered the believers to Samaria, Cyprus and Antioch, where they first preached to non-Jews.

paras: Acts tells the story three times: in Luke's own words (chapter 9), and twice in speeches by Paul, to a Jewish crowd (chapter 22) and to King Agrippa (chapter 26). The table compares them. Paul's own letters say less, but say it plainly: 'Haven't I seen Jesus Christ, our Lord?' (1 Corinthians 9:1); he appeared 'to me also', 'last of all' (15:8).

Historians cannot test a vision. What they can say is that Paul believed he had seen the risen Jesus, that he lists his experience with the earlier appearances to Peter and James, and that it turned his life around. Explanations offered range from a real encounter with the risen Jesus, as Christians believe, to a psychological crisis or an epileptic seizure, as some sceptics have suggested. The psychological explanations have a difficulty: Paul shows no sign of doubting his old faith before the event; he was 'blameless' and zealous.

rows: Hear a sound, see no one
Ananias's vision and visit; Saul's blindness and baptism
Paul, to a crowd in Jerusalem
See the light, do not understand the voice
Ananias, 'a devout man according to the law'; Paul's call to the Gentiles comes later, in the Temple
The voice speaks 'in the Hebrew language' and adds 'It is hard for you to kick against the goads'; the commission is given on the road
table.note: The core is the same each time: a light at midday, a voice, 'Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?' and 'I am Jesus'.

sections.key: Acts tells the Damascus road story three times with differences of detail; the core is constant, and Paul himself says simply that he saw the risen Lord.

paras: Saul was not a brute. He was a devout and learned man who believed he was defending God. What made the followers of Jesus so offensive to him?

Part of the answer is the cross. Paul later calls the preaching of a crucified Messiah 'a stumbling block to Jews' (1 Corinthians 1:23). The Messiah was supposed to defeat Israel's enemies, not be executed by them, and the law said a man hanged on a tree was cursed by God. To proclaim such a man as Messiah looked like blasphemy.

Part of it may be what the believers were doing. Stephen and the Hellenists questioned the Temple. Some may already have been eating with non-Jews and loosening the food laws. And they were praying to Jesus, as Stephen did as he died. For a zealous Pharisee, defending the one God and his law, all of this was dangerous. That is why the vision was so shattering: the man Saul believed God had cursed was alive, and God had raised him. The curse had been turned upside down: 'Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us' (Galatians 3:13).
sections.key: Saul persecuted out of zeal: a crucified Messiah seemed cursed by God, and the believers questioned the Temple and prayed to Jesus.

paras: The result of the Damascus road was not only a changed man but a changed mission. Paul came to believe that God had sent him to the Gentiles, the non-Jewish nations. Over the next thirty years he would travel thousands of miles, found churches in the great cities of the eastern empire, and write the letters that make up nearly half of the books of the New Testament: thirteen letters bear his name, of which seven are accepted by nearly all scholars as his own (Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians, 1 Thessalonians and Philemon).

He paid for it. He lists what it cost him: 'Five times I received forty stripes minus one from the Jews. Three times I was beaten with rods. Once I was stoned. Three times I suffered shipwreck' (2 Corinthians 11:24–25). The once-zealous persecutor was now on the receiving end. Paul did not stop being a Jew. He still called himself an Israelite (Romans 11:1), and he believed that what had happened in Jesus was the fulfilment of Israel's own hope, now opened to the whole world.
sections.key: Paul became the apostle to the Gentiles; seven of his thirteen letters are accepted by nearly all scholars; he suffered for his mission and remained a Jew.

paras: There is a thread through this session that is easy to miss. Stephen dies praying, 'Lord, don't hold this sin against them!' Saul is standing there. Then Jesus does not destroy the persecutor but calls him. Ananias, risking everything, calls him 'Brother Saul'. Barnabas, the generous Levite from session 1, later takes the frightening new convert to the apostles when everyone else is afraid of him (Acts 9:27).

Paul never got over it. 'Grace', undeserved love, became the centre of his teaching. He wrote that 'by the grace of God I am what I am' (1 Corinthians 15:10). When he later insists that God welcomes people not because of what they have done but because of what Christ has done, he is describing his own life.

Christians have seen in Stephen and Paul the first proof that the enemy can become a brother. Augustine, preaching in the fifth century, said that if Stephen had not prayed, the Church would not have had Paul.
sections.key: Stephen prayed for his killers, Jesus called his persecutor, Ananias called him 'brother': Paul's teaching on grace grew from his own story.

debate.question: Was Paul converted, or called?

positions.name: A conversion
positions.who: Augustine; the long Christian tradition; Alan Segal (a Jewish scholar)
positions.view: Paul's life was turned upside down: from persecutor to apostle, from one understanding of God's law to another. Segal argued that Paul shows all the marks of a convert, who reinterprets his whole past in the light of the new faith.
positions.evidence: Philippians 3:7–8 ('I count all things to be a loss'); the reversal from persecuting to preaching; his rethinking of the law.

positions.name: A calling
positions.who: Krister Stendahl (1976); many scholars of 'Paul within Judaism'
positions.view: Paul did not change religion; 'Christianity' did not yet exist as a separate religion. He was called, like Jeremiah, to a new task within Israel's story: to bring the nations to Israel's God. Reading him as a convert from Judaism projects later history back onto him.
positions.evidence: Galatians 1:15 echoes the prophets' calls; Paul still calls himself an Israelite (Romans 11:1); he never uses the word 'convert' of himself.

positions.name: Both
positions.who: James Dunn; N. T. Wright
positions.view: Paul was called within Israel's story, as he says, but the call converted his understanding of that story: of the Messiah, the law and who belongs to God's people. The two words describe different sides of one event.
positions.evidence: Galatians 1 combines prophetic call language with a sharp break from his 'former way of life'.

debate.agree: All agree that Paul believed he had seen the risen Jesus, that it reversed his attitude to Jesus's followers, and that it sent him to the Gentiles.

look.why: Jacopo Tintoretto painted the Conversion of Saint Paul in Venice about 1544. He turns the road to Damascus into a scene of chaos: a whole troop of riders and horses thrown into confusion by a figure in the sky. Acts mentions no horse; painters added it.
points: At the bottom centre Saul lies sprawled across a short set of grey stone steps, arms raised, palms facing out, looking back and up.
He wears a gold chain and a sword at his belt; a round gold shield lies on the steps and pieces of armour are scattered in the grass.
To the left a rider on a rearing white horse clutches his head with both hands.
To the right, men and horses flail in a river, and more riders with billowing flags push across a low arched bridge.
In the upper left corner a bearded figure stretches out across a bank of white clouds, gesturing with an open palm to the scene below.

music.why: Mendelssohn's oratorio Elijah (1846) tells the story of the Bible's great zealot, who fled to the desert and heard God in 'a still small voice'. Paul saw himself as zealous like Elijah, and he too went into the desert after his crisis. (Mendelssohn also wrote an oratorio on Paul himself, St Paul, in 1836.)

think.why: A single persecutor's change of heart changed history, and his teaching that each person is loved by God helped make the West believe that every individual counts.

learn.why: Paul's own summary of what happened to him: 'it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me'.

check.q: Why was Stephen's teaching more dangerous to the authorities than the apostles' preaching had been?
options: Because he was a Roman citizen
Because he refused to care for widows
Because he spoke Aramaic
Because he was accused of saying Jesus would destroy the Temple and change the law of Moses
check.why: The Temple was the centre of Jewish life; questioning it was a threat to everything.

check.q: What does Stephen's prayer 'Lord Jesus, receive my spirit!' tell historians about the earliest Christians?
options: That within a few years of the cross a Jew prayed to Jesus as one prays to God
That Stephen did not believe in the resurrection
That the prayer was added in the fourth century
That they thought Jesus was a prophet like Elijah
check.why: Jesus prayed 'Father, into your hands'; Stephen prays to Jesus. Very early devotion to Jesus is a key fact.

check.q: How does Luke present the persecution after Stephen's death?
options: As a Roman campaign
As the end of the Jerusalem church
As the moment the message spread to Judea and Samaria, fulfilling Acts 1:8
As a punishment for Stephen's errors
check.why: The scattered believers preached wherever they went; the scattering became a sowing.

check.q: Why was a crucified Messiah such an offence to a Pharisee like Saul?
options: Because the law said a man hanged on a tree was cursed by God, and the Messiah was expected to defeat Israel's enemies
Because the Romans had forbidden talk of Messiahs
Because Jesus had been a Pharisee too
Because the Messiah was meant to come from Tarsus
check.why: Deuteronomy 21:23; Paul later says Christ 'became a curse for us'.

check.q: The three accounts of the Damascus road in Acts differ on what Saul's companions experienced. What is the best conclusion?
options: The story is invented
Only one account can be from Luke
Ancient historians retold events with varied details; the core of all three is the same
Luke was careless and the event cannot have happened
check.why: The light, the voice and 'why do you persecute me?' are constant; ancient historians varied their retellings.

check.q: Why does Paul insist in Galatians that he did not receive his message 'from man'?
options: Because he wanted to show that he alone had seen the risen Jesus
Because he wanted to start a new religion
Because he had never met any apostle
Because his opponents in Galatia were saying he was only a second-hand apostle, dependent on Jerusalem
check.why: He is defending his calling against teachers who used the Jerusalem leaders against him.

tutorial.question: Why did the death of Stephen and the conversion of Paul matter so much for the spread of the Church?
tutorial.approach: Explain who Stephen was, why he was killed, and what the scattering after his death achieved. Then explain who Saul was, why he persecuted, and what happened on the road, comparing Acts with Galatians. End by weighing whether 'conversion' or 'calling' better describes what happened, and why it sent Paul to the Gentiles.
strong: Explains Stephen's teaching about the Temple and why it was dangerous.
Shows how the persecution spread the message (Acts 8:1–4; 11:19–21).
Describes Saul's background and his reasons for persecuting.
Compares the Acts accounts with Paul's own words, noting agreements and differences.
Weighs 'conversion' against 'calling' with evidence.
Notices the thread of grace to the enemy: Stephen's prayer, Ananias's 'Brother Saul'.
