reading.why: Paul as a Jew to the end, sent to the Gentiles.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: Paul and Peter disagreed openly and still called each other brother. If you are at odds with someone, say plainly what you disagree about, once, and then do one thing that shows you are still on the same side.
sessions.reflect: When you pass on something you were taught, how do you know whether you are keeping it or changing it?
takeaways: The case against says Paul, who never knew Jesus, turned a Jewish teacher of the kingdom into a divine saviour for the Gentiles: Nietzsche, Wrede and Maccoby made it in different ways.
Against it, Paul says he 'received' the core of the faith, the Jerusalem pillars gave him the right hand of fellowship, and Jesus was worshipped as Lord by Aramaic-speaking believers before him.
Paul did shift the emphasis and open the faith to Gentiles; the real question is whether that was faithful development or a new religion.

sessions.title: The verdict
sessions.line: A letter to a port city in Greece, about the year 50, and a North African lawyer's defence, about 197. So how did they change an empire?
sessions.plain: Here is the verdict. A message about a crucified and risen Lord, carried by small communities that lived by it, grew for three centuries without power, money or force, until it became the faith of the Roman Empire and spread far beyond it. Historians still argue about why. This session reads the oldest Christian writing we have, Paul's first letter to the Thessalonians, and a Christian lawyer's answer to Rome a century and a half later, and weighs the explanations.
sessions.why: Session 6 tested the strongest objection and found that Paul handed on a faith he had received, though the debate about how far he changed it goes on. Now we can answer the journey's question: how did a few followers of a crucified man change an empire?
answers: So how did they change an empire?
Did Christianity spread only within the Roman Empire?
What changed because they did?
Why do historians still disagree?
sessions.finding: A message about a crucified and risen Lord, carried by small communities that lived it, spread without power, money or force: historians still argue why.

paras: The first Christians changed an empire because they believed something had happened, that God had raised Jesus from the dead, and built communities that lived as if it were true. They had no army and no state behind them, and for long periods they were illegal. They grew slowly, steadily and through relationships, perhaps 40 per cent a decade, until by AD 300 about one in ten people in the empire was a Christian.

They spread along roads, in Greek, through synagogues and households. They were known for what they did: caring for widows, orphans, prisoners and the sick; refusing to kill infants; sharing one table across the lines of class. Romans thought them stubborn and superstitious, and executed some of them, which made their witness more visible. The strongest objection, that Paul invented the faith, fails on its main point: he handed on what he received. But why the growth was so steady remains debated, and each explanation leaves something out.
background.key: The verdict: a message about a risen Lord, lived by small communities, grew without force to a tenth of the empire by 300; why exactly is still debated.

paras: We have walked the path of Acts 1:8. Witnesses in Jerusalem (session 1). The first martyr and the converted persecutor, as the movement spread through Judea and Samaria (session 2). Paul's network across the empire to Rome (session 3). The way of life that drew people in (session 4). The Roman view: obstinate superstition, suspected of crimes, yet admired for its discipline (session 5). And the case that Paul invented it all (session 6).

Stephen stoned; Paul's conversion
1 Thessalonians, the earliest surviving Christian writing
Nero's persecution in Rome; Peter and Paul die there, by tradition, in the 60s
Pliny's letter to Trajan
Tertullian's Apology
The house church at Dura-Europos

paras: The main reading is the opening of Paul's first letter to the Thessalonians, written about AD 50, probably the oldest Christian document that survives. In ten verses it shows the whole pattern: a message, a community, a way of life, suffering, and a reputation spreading by word of mouth.

The comparison is from Tertullian's Apology, written in Carthage in North Africa about AD 197. It shows the same pattern a century and a half later, described by a Christian to Roman rulers: what the Christian community is and does.
background.key: The oldest Christian writing, about AD 50, and Tertullian's defence of about 197: the same pattern, a century and a half apart.

before: What three things does Paul remember about the Thessalonians in verse 3?
How has news of them spread, according to Paul?
What does Tertullian say the church's money is spent on?
sessions.readWhy: The oldest Christian writing that survives: how a new church in a Greek port was born, and how its story spread.

paras: Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy, to the assembly of the Thessalonians in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
We always give thanks to God for all of you, mentioning you in our prayers,
remembering without ceasing your work of faith and labor of love and perseverance of hope in our Lord Jesus Christ, before our God and Father.
We know, brothers loved by God, that you are chosen,
and that our Good News came to you not in word only, but also in power, and in the Holy Spirit, and with much assurance. You know what kind of men we showed ourselves to be among you for your sake.
You became imitators of us and of the Lord, having received the word in much affliction, with joy of the Holy Spirit,
so that you became an example to all who believe in Macedonia and in Achaia.
For from you the word of the Lord has been declared, not only in Macedonia and Achaia, but also in every place your faith toward God has gone out, so that we need not to say anything.
For they themselves report concerning us what kind of a reception we had from you, and how you turned to God from idols, to serve a living and true God,
and to wait for his Son from heaven, whom he raised from the dead: Jesus, who delivers us from the wrath to come.

parts.title: You turned to God from idols
parts.context: About AD 50, from Corinth. Paul, with his co-workers Silvanus (Silas) and Timothy, had founded a church in Thessalonica, the chief city of Macedonia, a port on the Via Egnatia, only a few months before. Opposition had forced them to leave suddenly (Acts 17:1–10). Paul has just heard from Timothy that the new believers are holding firm.

commentary.on: to the assembly of the Thessalonians in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ
commentary.text: Within twenty years of the cross, in the oldest Christian writing we have, Paul puts 'God the Father' and 'the Lord Jesus Christ' side by side, as the source of grace and peace. The worship of Jesus that session 6 discussed is here from the first line.

commentary.on: your work of faith and labor of love and perseverance of hope
commentary.text: Faith, love and hope: the same three Paul names at the end of 1 Corinthians 13. Notice that each one is active: faith works, love labours, hope endures. This is the way of life of session 4 in a phrase.

commentary.on: our Good News came to you not in word only, but also in power, and in the Holy Spirit, and with much assurance
commentary.text: Paul says the message came with more than argument. Early Christians spoke of healings and other signs, and Gibbon counted the claim of miracles among the causes of growth. Paul also points to his own conduct: 'you know what kind of men we showed ourselves to be'.

commentary.on: having received the word in much affliction, with joy of the Holy Spirit
commentary.text: Suffering and joy together, from the start. The Thessalonians had been attacked by their neighbours for joining the movement. That is the pattern Pliny will find sixty years later.

commentary.on: so that you became an example to all who believe in Macedonia and in Achaia
commentary.text: A few months old, and already an example. Macedonia is northern Greece; Achaia is southern Greece, with Corinth and Athens. The network of session 3 at work.

commentary.on: For from you the word of the Lord has been declared, not only in Macedonia and Achaia, but also in every place
commentary.text: Paul did not need to advertise: people were already talking about the Thessalonians. The message spread less by preachers than by reputation.

commentary.on: how you turned to God from idols, to serve a living and true God
commentary.text: These converts were Gentiles, not Jews. Turning from idols meant leaving the gods of the city, its festivals and sacrifices, and often family and friends. That is what made Romans call Christians atheists.

commentary.on: and to wait for his Son from heaven, whom he raised from the dead
commentary.text: And here is the centre: the resurrection. Everything rests on the claim the first witnesses made in session 1. The Thessalonians did not join a philosophy; they joined people waiting for someone who had been raised.

paras: I shall at once go on, then, to exhibit the peculiarities of the Christian society, that, as I have refuted the evil charged against it, I may point out its positive good. We are a body knit together as such by a common religious profession, by unity of discipline, and by the bond of a common hope. We meet together as an assembly and congregation, that, offering up prayer to God as with united force, we may wrestle with Him in our supplications. This violence God delights in. We pray, too, for the emperors, for their ministers and for all in authority, for the welfare of the world, for the prevalence of peace, for the delay of the final consummation. We assemble to read our sacred writings, if any peculiarity of the times makes either forewarning or reminiscence needful. However it be in that respect, with the sacred words we nourish our faith, we animate our hope, we make our confidence more steadfast;

and no less by inculcations of God's precepts we confirm good habits. In the same place also exhortations are made, rebukes and sacred censures are administered. For with a great gravity is the work of judging carried on among us, as befits those who feel assured that they are in the sight of God; and you have the most notable example of judgment to come when any one has sinned so grievously as to require his severance from us in prayer, in the congregation and in all sacred intercourse. The tried men of our elders preside over us, obtaining that honour not by purchase, but by established character. There is no buying and selling of any sort in the things of God. Though we have our treasure chest, it is not made up of purchase-money, as of a religion that has its price. On the monthly day, if he likes, each puts in a small donation; but only if it be his pleasure, and only if he be able: for there is no compulsion;

all is voluntary. These gifts are, as it were, piety's deposit fund. For they are not taken thence and spent on feasts, and drinking-bouts, and eating-houses, but to support and bury poor people, to supply the wants of boys and girls destitute of means and parents, and of old persons confined now to the house; such, too, as have suffered shipwreck; and if there happen to be any in the mines, or banished to the islands, or shut up in the prisons, for nothing but their fidelity to the cause of God's Church, they become the nurslings of their confession. But it is mainly the deeds of a love so noble that lead many to put a brand upon us. See, they say, how they love one another, for themselves are animated by mutual hatred; how they are ready even to die for one another, for they themselves will sooner put to death. And they are angry with us, too, because we call each other brethren;

for no other reason, as I think, than because among themselves names of consanguinity are assumed in mere pretence of affection. But we are your brethren as well, by the law of our common mother nature, though you are hardly men, because brothers so unkind. At the same time, how much more fittingly they are called and counted brothers who have been led to the knowledge of God as their common Father, who have drunk in one spirit of holiness, who from the same womb of a common ignorance have agonized into the same light of truth! But on this very account, perhaps, we are regarded as having less claim to be held true brothers, that no tragedy makes a noise about our brotherhood, or that the family possessions, which generally destroy brotherhood among you, create fraternal bonds among us. One in mind and soul, we do not hesitate to share our earthly goods with one another. All things are common among us but our wives.

Our feast explains itself by its name. The Greeks call it agapè, i.e., affection. Whatever it costs, our outlay in the name of piety is gain, since with the good things of the feast we benefit the needy; not as it is with you, do parasites aspire to the glory of satisfying their licentious propensities, selling themselves for a belly-feast to all disgraceful treatment — but as it is with God himself, a peculiar respect is shown to the lowly. If the object of our feast be good, in the light of that consider its further regulations. As it is an act of religious service, it permits no vileness or immodesty. The participants, before reclining, taste first of prayer to God. As much is eaten as satisfies the cravings of hunger; as much is drunk as befits the chaste. They say it is enough, as those who remember that even during the night they have to worship God; they talk as those who know that the Lord is one of their auditors.

After manual ablution, and the bringing in of lights, each is asked to stand forth and sing, as he can, a hymn to God, either one from the holy Scriptures or one of his own composing — a proof of the measure of our drinking. As the feast commenced with prayer, so with prayer it is closed. We go from it, not like troops of mischief-doers, nor bands of vagabonds, nor to break out into licentious acts, but to have as much care of our modesty and chastity as if we had been at a school of virtue rather than a banquet. Give the congregation of the Christians its due, and hold it unlawful, if it is like assemblies of the illicit sort: by all means let it be condemned, if any complaint can be validly laid against it, such as lies against secret factions. But who has ever suffered harm from our assemblies? We are in our congregations just what we are when separated from each other; we are as a community what we are individuals; we injure nobody, we trouble nobody. When the upright, when the virtuous meet together, when the pious, when the pure assemble in congregation, you ought not to call that a faction, but a curia

parts.author: Tertullian
parts.title: What the Christian society is
parts.context: Tertullian (about 155 to about 220) was a brilliant, sharp-tongued Christian writer of Carthage, in what is now Tunisia, probably trained in law and rhetoric. His Apology, about AD 197, is addressed to the governors of the Roman provinces. Having answered the charges against Christians, he now describes what they actually do. A passage mocking pagan morals and feasts is cut, marked '…'. Translated by S. Thelwall, 1885; New Advent's lightly revised text.
parts.plain: Tertullian says: we are one body, joined by faith, discipline and hope. We meet to pray, even for the emperors and for peace; to read our Scriptures; to encourage and correct each other. Our leaders are tested elders who earn respect, not buy it. Once a month anyone who can puts a gift in the common chest, if they wish. The money goes not on feasts but to feed and bury the poor, to support orphans and the old, the shipwrecked, and Christians in the mines, on islands or in prison for their faith. That is why people say, 'See how they love one another', though they mean it as a sneer. We call each other brothers and share everything except our wives. Our feast is called agape, love: we pray before eating, eat modestly, sing, and pray again. We harm nobody.

commentary.on: We are a body knit together as such by a common religious profession, by unity of discipline, and by the bond of a common hope.
commentary.text: Faith, discipline and hope: Tertullian's version of Paul's faith, love and hope. A body, as in Romans 12. The idea of the Church as one body runs from Paul to Tertullian unchanged.

commentary.on: We pray, too, for the emperors, for their ministers and for all in authority
commentary.text: This answers the charge of disloyalty. Christians would not offer incense to the emperor, but they prayed for him, as 1 Timothy 2:1–2 told them to. Their loyalty was real; it simply had a limit.

commentary.on: The tried men of our elders preside over us, obtaining that honour not by purchase, but by established character.
commentary.text: In Rome, priesthoods and offices were often bought or inherited. Tertullian says Christian leaders are chosen for character. It was not always so in practice, but it was the ideal.

commentary.on: On the monthly day, if he likes, each puts in a small donation; but only if it be his pleasure, and only if he be able
commentary.text: Voluntary giving, as in Acts 4. There was no fee to belong: one reason the poor could join.

commentary.on: to support and bury poor people, to supply the wants of boys and girls destitute of means and parents, and of old persons confined now to the house
commentary.text: Here is the welfare system of the early Church: the poor fed and given decent burial (which mattered greatly to Romans), orphans supported, the housebound elderly cared for. No ancient state did this for ordinary people.

commentary.on: See, they say, how they love one another
commentary.text: The most famous line in the book. Tertullian reports it as something pagans said, half in mockery. It became the Church's own motto for what it should be.

commentary.on: One in mind and soul, we do not hesitate to share our earthly goods with one another.
commentary.text: Almost the words of Acts 4:32, 'of one heart and soul'. A century and a half later, in a different continent, the first community's ideal is still being claimed.

commentary.on: The Greeks call it agapè, i.e., affection.
commentary.text: The love feast, the agape. Tertullian insists it is modest and generous: 'with the good things of the feast we benefit the needy'. He is answering the rumours of drunken orgies we met in Minucius Felix.

commentary.on: We are in our congregations just what we are when separated from each other
commentary.text: A claim about integrity: the Christian is the same in church and outside it. That consistency, more than any argument, was what outsiders were asked to judge.

compare.author: Tertullian
compare.why: A century and a half later, a Christian lawyer in Carthage describes the Christian community to Rome's rulers. Compare it with Paul's church in Thessalonica.
compare.title: See how they love one another

paras: The first thing to say about the growth of Christianity is what it lacked. For nearly three centuries it had no support from the state; for much of that time it was liable to persecution, and twice, under Decius in 250 and Diocletian from 303, the state tried to destroy it. It had no great wealth: Tertullian's monthly collection was voluntary and spent on the poor. It used no force: its members refused the arena, and its writers urged non-violence. It had no ancient pedigree, which Romans prized. It worshipped a man executed as a criminal.

Few movements in history have grown so far from such a start. Most religions that spread widely did so with the help of rulers or conquest. Christianity did gain an emperor in 312, but by then it was already perhaps a tenth of the empire and strong in the cities. Constantine did not create its success; he backed it. If you take 'The martyrs and the empire' in Hall IV, you will follow that story, and its cost.
Whatever explanation we give must account for growth under those conditions.
sections.key: For three centuries Christianity grew with no state, no wealth, no force and no pedigree; Constantine backed a movement already strong.

paras: Christianity did not spread only westwards. Acts' 'ends of the earth' pointed in every direction. Edessa, in upper Mesopotamia, outside the empire until the third century, had Christians by the late second century and became a great centre of Syriac-speaking Christianity. A tradition that the apostle Thomas preached in India is held by the Thomas Christians of Kerala to this day; historians cannot confirm it, but there were Christians in India by the fourth century or earlier.

Armenia became the first kingdom to adopt Christianity, when King Tiridates III was baptised by Gregory the Illuminator; the traditional date is 301, and many historians prefer about 314. In the 330s, Ezana, king of Aksum in what is now Ethiopia and Eritrea, became a Christian through Frumentius, a Syrian who had been shipwrecked there as a boy; his coins changed from the sun and moon to the cross. There were Christians in Persia, Rome's great enemy, persecuted there for being on the wrong side.
So the first Christian kingdoms were not Roman. The faith was never only the religion of the West. 'The world church' in Hall VII follows that wider story.
sections.key: Christianity spread east and south too: Edessa, India, Persia, Armenia (the first Christian kingdom, about 301–314) and Aksum (the 330s).

paras: What did the Christians change? Not everything, and not quickly. Slavery continued in the Christian empire. Women did not become equal citizens. But some things changed because of them.

The exposure of infants was made a crime by Christian emperors in 374. Gladiatorial games ended in the early fifth century. Care for the poor became a public duty of the bishops, whom the historian Peter Brown calls 'lovers of the poor'; in the 360s and 370s Basil of Caesarea built a complex for the sick and poor outside his city, often called the first hospital. The week with its day of rest became the week of the empire when Constantine made Sunday a holiday in 321.

Above all, an idea changed. Paul wrote that in Christ 'there is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free man, there is neither male nor female' (Galatians 3:28). The Roman world was built on rank. The Christians claimed that every person, the slave, the widow, the unwanted baby, had infinite worth before God. That idea took centuries to work out, and Christians often betrayed it. But it is one root of what the West came to believe about human dignity.
sections.key: Christian emperors banned infant exposure (374), the games ended, bishops became 'lovers of the poor' and Sunday became a holiday; above all the idea that every person has worth before God took root.

paras: We have met several explanations in this journey: the conditions of the Roman world in session 3, the networks and care of sessions 3 and 4, the distinctiveness that Romans complained of in session 5, Gibbon's five causes, and the claim of the first witnesses in session 1. None of them is simply wrong, and most historians now combine several. The useful question is what each explains well and what it leaves out. An explanation from conditions, for example, tells us how a message could travel fast, but many cults travelled the same roads and did not conquer the empire. An explanation from networks tells us how growth could be steady, but not why people stayed when staying could cost them their lives. The table sets them side by side.

rows: Favourable conditions: roads, peace, Greek, synagogues
How the message could travel fast
Why this message, and not others that travelled the same roads, won
Steady growth; care in plagues; the role of women
Why people stayed under persecution, when the costs were high
A distinctive new kind of religion
The oddness Romans complained of, and the strong identity it gave
Why oddness attracted rather than repelled
Zeal, discipline and the hope of a future life
Gibbon's irony sets aside the believers' own reason
Why the movement began at all, and why its first witnesses would not stop
Historians cannot test it as they test the others
table.note: Most historians combine several explanations. Believers do not deny the others; they add one.

sections.key: Each explanation, conditions, networks, distinctiveness, Gibbon's causes, the resurrection, explains part of the growth; most historians combine them.

paras: In Acts 5, when the council in Jerusalem wanted to kill the apostles, a respected Pharisee named Gamaliel, Paul's teacher, advised caution. He reminded them that other movements had risen and collapsed when their leaders died. 'If this counsel or this work is of men, it will be overthrown. But if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow it' (Acts 5:38–39).

It is not a proof. Many movements have lasted for centuries; lasting does not make a thing true. But Gamaliel's test is the one historians are still applying. Every other first-century Jewish movement around a would-be Messiah ended when its leader died. This one began when its leader died.

That is why the explanations, however good, keep returning to the same starting point. The growth is explained by roads and networks and care and discipline. But the roads carried a claim, the networks gathered round it, the care was done in its name, and the discipline was kept by people who would die rather than deny it. The claim was the one Paul repeated to the Thessalonians: that God had raised Jesus from the dead. Whether it is true, history alone cannot say. That it was believed, and what it did, history can.
sections.key: Gamaliel's test: other messianic movements ended when their leader died; this one began then. History can show the claim was believed and what it did, not whether it is true.

paras: The first Christians are often invoked today, by believers who want to return to the simplicity of the early Church and by critics who want to show how far the Church has fallen from it. Both should look at what the evidence shows.

It shows small communities, not mass movements: thirty or fifty people in a house. It shows ordinary people, slaves and women prominent among them, doing the work of mission by how they lived and whom they invited. It shows a faith that was costly: it meant leaving the gods of the city and accepting suspicion. And it shows a care for the weak that even enemies admitted.

It also shows quarrels, freeloaders, false teachers and failures: the Didache warns against them and Paul rebuked them. The first Christians were not perfect. What they had was a conviction and a way of life that went together. In many parts of the world today, in China, in Africa, in Iran, Christianity is again growing as it grew then: through households, under pressure, without power. And in the West, where churches are shrinking, many are asking what the first Christians knew.
sections.key: The evidence shows small, costly, caring communities of ordinary people, imperfect but convinced; in many places today the faith grows the same way.

refs: 1 Thessalonians 1–2; Acts 5:33–39; 17:1–10; Galatians 3:28; 1 Corinthians 13:13; 1 Timothy 2:1–2.
Tertullian, Apology 39 and 40, tr. S. Thelwall, ANF III (1885).
On Armenia: Agathangelos, History of the Armenians; on Aksum: Rufinus, Church History I.9; the coins of Ezana; on Edessa: Eusebius, Church History I.13 and the Chronicle of Edessa.
Codex Theodosianus 9.14.1 (374, infanticide); Codex Justinianus 3.12.2 (321, Sunday); Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 43.63 (Basil's foundation).

Peter Brown, Poverty and Leadership in the Later Roman Empire (2002); Rodney Stark, The Rise of Christianity (1996); Larry Hurtado, Destroyer of the Gods (2016); Bart Ehrman, The Triumph of Christianity (2018); Robin Lane Fox, Pagans and Christians (1986).
Philip Jenkins, The Lost History of Christianity (2008), on the churches of the East.

debate.question: How did the first Christians change an empire?

positions.name: A social movement, explained by social causes
positions.who: Rodney Stark; Bart Ehrman; Keith Hopkins
positions.view: No miracle is needed. Steady growth through networks, care in crises, the attraction of an exclusive faith with a strong community, and finally imperial support, are enough to explain it. Christianity won because it offered more than its rivals.
positions.evidence: The growth model; Christian care in plagues; the role of women and households; Constantine's patronage after 312.

positions.name: A message and a community that were new
positions.who: Larry Hurtado; N. T. Wright; Alan Kreider
positions.view: The social causes are real, but they depend on what Christians believed: that a crucified Jew had been raised and was Lord. That belief created a new kind of community, and gave people a reason to stay in it under persecution.
positions.evidence: The resurrection at the centre of every early text, from 1 Thessalonians to Tertullian; the worship of Jesus from the first years; the willingness to die.

positions.name: The hand of God
positions.who: Eusebius; Origen; Christian believers ever since
positions.view: God prepared the world (the roads, the peace, the language), raised Jesus and sent his Spirit, and the Church grew because it was 'of God', as Gamaliel said. The human causes are the means God used.
positions.evidence: Acts 5:38–39; the movement beginning, not ending, with its founder's death; its survival of every attempt to destroy it.

debate.agree: All agree that Christianity grew steadily for three centuries without power or force, through small communities known for their care, and that belief in Jesus's resurrection was at its centre.

look.why: Giovanni Paolo Pannini painted the inside of Saint Peter's, Rome, about 1754. The bronze canopy at the crossing stands over the place where, by ancient tradition, Peter, the fisherman who said 'We must obey God rather than men', was buried after his execution under Nero. The greatest church of Christendom rose over the grave of one of the first witnesses.
points: The soaring gilded vault of the nave, lined with gold-decorated coffers, curves away like a tunnel.
White stone pillars, carved with winged cherubs holding portraits, line the nave; pink marble columns flank altars in the side chapels.
At the far end the nave opens into the light-filled crossing.
There four twisting bronze columns hold up a canopy, marking where the long hall of the church meets the shorter arm.
Tiny men and women pray or gather along the nave; some wear tattered clothing, others are elegantly dressed.

music.why: 'For all the saints, who from their labours rest': William Walsham How's hymn of 1864, to Vaughan Williams's tune, is a procession of witnesses down the centuries, from the first to the last.

think.why: 'Neither slave nor free': the first Christians did not abolish slavery, but planted an idea that, centuries later, helped end it.

learn.why: From the oldest Christian writing we have: what conversion meant, in one sentence.

check.q: Why does the timing of Constantine's support matter for explaining Christian growth?
options: Because he persecuted the Christians
Because by 312 Christianity was already perhaps a tenth of the empire; he backed a movement that had grown without state support
Because he made Christianity the majority religion overnight
Because he founded the church in Rome
check.why: Constantine's support came after three centuries of growth without it.

check.q: What does 1 Thessalonians 1 show about how the message spread?
options: That Paul relied on paid preachers
That the church faced no opposition
That news of the converts' change of life spread by word of mouth, 'in every place', so that Paul 'need not say anything'
That the Thessalonians were all Jews
check.why: Reputation, not advertising: the community's example carried the message.

check.q: What does 'you turned to God from idols' tell us about the Thessalonian converts?
options: That they were Gentiles who left the gods of their city, which is why Romans called Christians 'atheists'
That they had destroyed the temples
That they had been Jews
That they had been philosophers
check.why: Gentile converts abandoned the city's gods; to outsiders this looked like atheism.

check.q: How does Tertullian's description of the church, about 197, compare with Acts 4 and 1 Thessalonians?
options: It shows the Church had abandoned its first ideals
It describes a wealthy church that charged fees
It has nothing in common with them
It shows the same pattern: one body, voluntary sharing, care for the poor, orphans, the old and prisoners, and love that outsiders noticed
check.why: 'One in mind and soul' echoes Acts 4:32; the pattern held for a century and a half.

check.q: Which statement about the spread of Christianity beyond Rome is correct?
options: Armenia became a Christian kingdom (about 301–314) and Aksum's king became Christian in the 330s, before the empire made it official in 380
India had no Christians until the sixteenth century
Christianity reached Ethiopia only after the empire made it official in 380
It reached nowhere outside the empire before 400
check.why: The first Christian kingdoms were outside, or on the edge of, the Roman Empire.

check.q: Why can history show that the resurrection was believed and what it did, but not whether it happened?
options: Because historians can test beliefs and their effects, but a unique act of God is outside what historical method can confirm or rule out
Because Gibbon proved it false
Because there is no evidence of any kind
Because the first Christians did not claim it
check.why: The belief and its effects are historical facts; the event itself is where history meets faith.

tutorial.question: How did a few followers of a crucified man change an empire?
tutorial.approach: Set out the conditions, the networks, the way of life and the Roman response, using the evidence from each session. Use 1 Thessalonians and Tertullian to show the pattern over 150 years. Weigh the explanations in the table, saying what each explains and what it leaves out. Then give your own answer, and say how much of it history can establish.
strong: Uses evidence from at least four of the sessions.
Uses 1 Thessalonians 1 and Tertullian, Apology 39 to show continuity.
Notes what the movement lacked: power, money, force, pedigree.
Weighs at least three explanations fairly, with their weaknesses.
Mentions the spread beyond the empire.
Distinguishes what history can and cannot establish about the resurrection.

reading.title: Destroyer of the Gods
reading.why: Why early Christianity was so distinctive, and why it mattered.

reading.author: Bart Ehrman
reading.title: The Triumph of Christianity
reading.why: An agnostic historian's clear account of how a forbidden religion swept the world.

reading.author: Peter Brown
reading.title: The Rise of Western Christendom
reading.why: The great historian of late antiquity on how the faith spread from 200 to 1000, east and west.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: 'See how they love one another.' Choose one person in a community you belong to who is overlooked, old, alone or new, and do one concrete thing for them this week.
sessions.reflect: The first Christians changed the world through small groups who lived what they believed. What small group could you belong to, or begin?
takeaways: The first Christians grew steadily for three centuries without power, money or force, to about a tenth of the empire by 300, and spread beyond it to Armenia, Aksum and the East.
From 1 Thessalonians (about AD 50) to Tertullian (about 197), the pattern was the same: a message about a risen Lord, a community, care for the weak, and a reputation spread by example.
Historians combine several explanations; at the centre of all of them is a claim the first witnesses would not stop making, which history can show was believed, but cannot by itself prove.

closing.title: Your answer
closing.prompt: How did a few followers of a crucified man change an empire? In about 300 words, make the case for the explanation you find most convincing, using evidence from at least three sessions, and answer the strongest objection to it.
closing.practice: Read the Acts of the Apostles from beginning to end over the next two weeks, two chapters a day. As you read, mark each place where the message moves outwards, and ask each time: why did it spread here?
synthesis: This journey asked how a few followers of a crucified man changed an empire. It followed them outwards, as the book of Acts does, and asked at each step why they spread. Here are the short answers.

Who were the first Christians? Jews in Jerusalem: the Twelve, women who had followed Jesus from Galilee, Mary his mother and his brothers, who had not believed in him before. Within weeks of his crucifixion, around AD 30 or 33, they were saying publicly that God had raised him from the dead and that they had seen him. They kept the law, prayed in the Temple and shared their property so that no one lacked. Ordered to stop, they said 'We must obey God rather than men', and several died for it. They called themselves 'the Way'; the name 'Christians' came later, at Antioch.

How reliable is Acts? Luke wrote as an ancient historian, probably around AD 80 to 90, with a purpose: to show the message spreading from Jerusalem to Rome and to show that it was no threat to the empire. Where he can be checked, by inscriptions naming politarchs in Thessalonica or Gallio in Corinth, he is usually right. He also smooths over conflicts that Paul's letters show were sharp. Read beside the letters, Acts is a valuable source, not a neutral one.

Who was Paul, and what happened to him? A Greek-speaking Jew from Tarsus, a Roman citizen, a Pharisee and a zealous persecutor of the believers. He watched Stephen, the first martyr, die praying for his killers. A few years later, on the road to Damascus, he believed he saw the risen Jesus, who asked him 'why do you persecute me?' He became the apostle to the Gentiles, travelled thousands of miles, founded churches across Turkey and Greece, and wrote the oldest Christian writings we have. Whether to call it a conversion or a calling is debated; it was something of both.

Why did Christianity spread so fast? The conditions helped: one empire at peace, Roman roads and ships, a common Greek language, and Jewish synagogues in every city with their circle of non-Jewish 'God-fearers'. Paul's method used them: he began at the synagogue, gathered households, and held them together by letters and co-workers. Romans 16 shows the result in Rome: house churches of slaves, freed slaves and householders, Jews and Gentiles, with ten women among those Paul greets, including Phoebe the deacon and Junia, 'notable among the apostles'. Rodney Stark's estimate of growth at about 40 per cent a decade would take a thousand believers in AD 40 to six million, a tenth of the empire, by 300. The growth was steady rather than sudden.

What did early Christians actually do? The Didache, a manual for new believers from perhaps AD 50 to 120, teaches 'two ways', one of life and one of death. The way of life is love of God and neighbour, generosity without conditions, and no murder, magic, abortion or infanticide. Christians shared a meal of thanksgiving, prayed the Lord's Prayer three times a day, and fasted on Wednesdays and Fridays. Their Aramaic prayer, 'Maranatha', 'Our Lord, come', shows that Jesus was worshipped as Lord from the first. In plagues they nursed the sick when others fled; in Rome in 251 the church supported fifteen hundred widows and needy people. They kept away from the arena. They were known for what they did.

What did Romans think of them? To Pliny, governor of Bithynia about AD 112, they were 'an absurd and extravagant superstition', guilty of no crime he could find, but punishable for their 'inflexible obstinacy' in refusing to offer incense to the gods and the emperor. Trajan told him not to hunt them, but to execute those who were accused and refused to sacrifice. Popular rumour charged them with atheism, cannibalism and incest, twisted versions of their refusal of the gods, their meal of 'body' and 'blood' and their 'brothers and sisters'. Yet hostile witnesses, Lucian, Galen and Pliny himself, noticed their discipline, mutual care and contempt of death.

Did Paul invent Christianity? The case against him is serious. Paul never knew Jesus during his life, insisted on his independence, quarrelled publicly with Peter, and preached a heavenly Christ more than the Galilean teacher of the kingdom. Nietzsche, Wrede and Maccoby, in different ways, called him the real founder. But Paul says he 'received' and 'delivered' the core of the faith: that Christ died for our sins, was buried and was raised on the third day, a summary most scholars date to within a few years of the cross. The Jerusalem pillars, James, Peter and John, gave him the right hand of fellowship. Jesus was already worshipped as Lord by Aramaic-speaking believers. Paul cites Jesus's teaching and carefully separates it from his own. He shifted the emphasis and opened the faith to Gentiles without the law. The fair question is whether that was faithful development or a new religion, and the evidence leans towards the first.

So how did they change an empire? Without power, money or force. For nearly three centuries the faith had no state support and was often persecuted, yet it grew steadily through small communities that lived what they believed, until by the time Constantine backed it, in 312, it was already strong. It spread beyond the empire too: Armenia and Aksum became Christian kingdoms in the fourth century. It changed things: infant exposure was outlawed, the gladiatorial games ended, care for the poor became a public duty, and the idea that every person, slave, widow or unwanted child, has worth before God took root in the West.

Historians still argue why. Favourable conditions explain how it could travel, Stark's networks explain the steadiness, Hurtado's distinctiveness explains the strong identity, Gibbon's causes explain the discipline. Each leaves something out. All of them, followed back, reach the same place: a claim made by witnesses in Jerusalem, repeated to Gentiles in Thessalonica, and held by people who would die rather than deny it. Gamaliel told the council that if the movement was of men it would fail, and if it was of God it could not be stopped. History can show that the claim was believed, and what it did. Whether it is true is the question this journey leaves with you.
exam: 'Acts is theology, not history.' Discuss.
Compare the accounts of Paul's conversion in Acts and in Galatians. What do the differences show?
Why did Christianity spread so rapidly in the first three centuries? Assess at least two explanations.
What does Romans 16 reveal about the early Church, and about the place of women in it?
How distinctive was the early Christian way of life? Discuss with reference to the Didache.
What does Pliny's letter to Trajan tell us about Christians and about Roman attitudes to them?
'Paul, not Jesus, was the founder of Christianity.' Discuss.
'Without power, money or force.' How far is this an adequate account of the growth of early Christianity?

title: The Sermon on the Mount
question: What did Jesus teach about how to live?
line: Seven sessions on the most famous teaching in the world: a new Sinai and its blessings, the law taken to the heart, the other cheek and love of enemies, faith in secret, the house on the rock, Nietzsche's case against it, and whether anyone can live it.
why: Turn the other cheek, love your enemies, do not judge, the golden rule, the Lord's Prayer, the house built on rock: more of the West's moral language comes from these three chapters of Matthew than from almost anywhere else. Tolstoy, Gandhi and Martin Luther King built movements on them; Nietzsche called them the revenge of the weak. This journey reads the Sermon block by block with Augustine, the rabbis of the Mishnah, Tolstoy and the first Christians, hears Nietzsche's charge at full strength, and asks whether anyone can actually live it. It is written at the depth of a first-year university course, for anyone.
follows: A first-year paper on the ethics of the New Testament, with elements of papers on the Synoptic Gospels, Christian ethics (war and nonviolence) and the reception of Jesus's teaching in Christian and modern thought.
before: who-was-jesus
outcomes: Explain how Matthew frames the Sermon as a new teaching on a mountain, compare it with Luke's sermon on the plain, and interpret the Beatitudes, with Augustine's reading.
Explain what Jesus meant by fulfilling the law, analyse the six antitheses, and compare them fairly with Jewish teaching of the time.
Set out the main Christian readings of 'turn the other cheek' and 'love your enemies': pacifism, just war, two kingdoms and nonviolent resistance.
Explain the teaching on giving, prayer and fasting in secret, the place of the Lord's Prayer, and the call not to worry, with the Didache as evidence of early practice.
Explain 'do not judge', the golden rule and its parallels across cultures, and the meaning of the two houses.

State Nietzsche's charge that Christian ethics is a 'slave morality' at full strength, and assess the replies of Scheler, Holland and King, reaching a reasoned verdict on whether the Sermon can be lived.

sessions.title: A new Sinai
sessions.line: A teacher goes up a mountain, as Moses did, and begins not with a command but with a blessing on the poor.
sessions.plain: The Sermon on the Mount is the longest stretch of Jesus's teaching in the Bible: three chapters of Matthew's Gospel (5 to 7), with a shorter version in Luke. It contains many of the most famous sayings in the world: 'turn the other cheek', 'love your enemies', the Lord's Prayer, 'do not judge', the golden rule. Matthew tells it so that it echoes Moses receiving the law on Mount Sinai, and it opens with eight blessings, the Beatitudes, on people the world does not usually call lucky. This session asks what the Sermon is, where it comes from and why it begins as it does.
sessions.why: This is the first session. 'Who was Jesus?' met the man from Nazareth through the Gospels and outside witnesses. Now we listen to what he taught about how to live, starting with the frame Matthew gives it: a new teaching on a mountain, like the law given at Sinai.
answers: What is the Sermon on the Mount, and where is it in the Bible?
Where, when and to whom was it given?
Why does Matthew make it sound like Moses on Sinai?
Why are there two versions, in Matthew and in Luke?
What are the Beatitudes, and what do they mean?
sessions.finding: Matthew presents Jesus as a new Moses giving the law on a mountain, and the new law opens with blessing, not command.

paras: Jesus of Nazareth was a Jewish teacher from Galilee, in the north of what is now Israel, in the early first century AD. If you have taken 'Who was Jesus?', you met him in Mark's Gospel and in Roman and Jewish writers. He was baptised by John in the river Jordan, called fishermen to follow him, healed the sick, taught in parables, was crucified in Jerusalem around AD 30 under the Roman governor Pontius Pilate, and his followers said he rose from the dead.

The four Gospels, Matthew, Mark, Luke and John, are the four accounts of his life in the New Testament. Each was written for a community of his followers within about seventy years of his death. Each arranges his words and deeds in its own way. Matthew collects a great deal of his teaching into long speeches, and the first and most famous of them is the Sermon on the Mount.
background.key: Jesus was a Jewish teacher from Galilee, crucified around AD 30. Matthew's Gospel gathers his teaching into long speeches; the Sermon on the Mount is the first.

paras: The question of this journey is simple: what did Jesus teach about how to live? The Sermon on the Mount is the place to ask it. It has been called the heart of Christian ethics. Tolstoy, Gandhi and Martin Luther King built movements on it. Nietzsche thought it the most dangerous idea in history. Many people who have never opened a Bible can quote it.

We follow the Sermon in order, block by block, as Matthew tells it: who is blessed; how the old law is fulfilled; the hardest commands, to turn the other cheek and love your enemies; how to pray and give in secret; and the choice between building on rock or sand. Then we hear the strongest case against it, and end with a verdict: can anyone actually live this?

timeline.text: A new Sinai: the setting and the Beatitudes (Matthew 4; Luke 6)
You have heard it said: the law fulfilled (Matthew 5:17–37)
The other cheek: non-retaliation and love of enemies (Matthew 5:38–48)
In secret: giving, prayer, fasting and worry (Matthew 6)
Rock and sand: judging, the golden rule and the two ways (Matthew 7)
The case against: a morality for slaves? (Nietzsche)
Can anyone live this? The verdict

background.key: What did Jesus teach about how to live? We follow the Sermon block by block, hear the case against it, then give a verdict.

paras: The Gospel of Matthew does not name its author. Early Christian tradition gave it to Matthew, a tax collector who became one of Jesus's twelve disciples (Matthew 9:9). The earliest witness is Papias, a bishop in Asia Minor around AD 110–130, whom the historian Eusebius quotes as saying that Matthew put Jesus's sayings in order in the Hebrew language. Most modern scholars think the Gospel as we have it was written in Greek, around AD 80–90, by a Jewish Christian teacher who used Mark's Gospel and a collection of Jesus's sayings that Luke also used. Some scholars still defend an earlier date and a closer link to the apostle.

Whoever he was, the writer was steeped in the Jewish Scriptures. He quotes them more than any other Gospel writer, and he writes for a community that was arguing with other Jews about what it meant to be faithful to God's law. That matters for everything in the Sermon.
background.key: Tradition credits the apostle Matthew; most scholars date the Gospel to about AD 80–90 and think it was written by a Jewish Christian who used Mark and a sayings source.

paras: If you have taken 'A good life', you have already read the opening of the Sermon, Matthew 5:1–16, with its eight Beatitudes and the sayings about salt and light. We will not reprint it. Instead, the main reading sets the scene Matthew gives just before it (4:23–25), and then gives Luke's version of the same sermon (6:17–26), which is shorter, sharper and has four woes as well as four blessings. Seeing the two side by side shows how the Gospel writers shaped what Jesus said.

The comparison is from Augustine of Hippo, the most influential thinker of the early Western Church, whose book on the Sermon, written around AD 394, gave it its name. He reads the Beatitudes as seven steps up a mountain, from humility to wisdom.
background.key: Matthew's setting and Luke's sermon on the plain (the Beatitudes themselves are in 'A good life'); then Augustine's steps.

sessions.readWhy: Matthew's setting for the Sermon, then Luke's version of the same teaching, with its blessings and woes.

paras: Jesus went about in all Galilee, teaching in their synagogues, preaching the Good News of the Kingdom, and healing every disease and every sickness among the people.

The report about him went out into all Syria. They brought to him all who were sick, afflicted with various diseases and torments, possessed with demons, epileptics, and paralytics; and he healed them.
Great multitudes from Galilee, Decapolis, Jerusalem, Judea and from beyond the Jordan followed him.

He came down with them, and stood on a level place, with a crowd of his disciples, and a great number of the people from all Judea and Jerusalem, and the sea coast of Tyre and Sidon, who came to hear him and to be healed of their diseases;
as well as those who were troubled by unclean spirits, and they were being healed.
All the multitude sought to touch him, for power came out of him and healed them all.
He lifted up his eyes to his disciples, and said,

“Blessed are you who are poor,
God’s Kingdom is yours.

Blessed are you who hunger now,
for you will be filled.
Blessed are you who weep now,
for you will laugh.
Blessed are you when men hate you, and when they exclude and mock you, and throw out your name as evil, for the Son of Man’s sake.
Rejoice in that day, and leap for joy, for behold, your reward is great in heaven, for their fathers did the same thing to the prophets.

“But woe to you who are rich!
For you have received your consolation.

Woe to you, you who are full now,
for you will be hungry.
Woe to you who laugh now,
for you will mourn and weep.

Woe, when men speak well of you,
for their fathers did the same thing to the false prophets.

parts.title: The crowds
parts.context: Galilee, around AD 28. Jesus has been baptised, has been tested in the wilderness for forty days, and has called his first disciples, four fishermen from the Sea of Galilee. These three verses are Matthew's summary of what came next, just before the Sermon begins.

commentary.on: teaching in their synagogues, preaching the Good News of the Kingdom, and healing every disease
commentary.text: Three verbs sum up the work of Jesus: teaching, preaching and healing. The 'Kingdom' is the kingdom of God (Matthew, out of Jewish reverence, usually says 'Kingdom of Heaven'): God's rule, coming into the world. The Sermon is the teaching that belongs to that kingdom.

commentary.on: They brought to him all who were sick
commentary.text: Notice who comes first: the sick, the tormented, people with epilepsy and paralysis. Before Jesus says a word about how to live, he has already been with people the world pushed aside. When the Sermon blesses the poor and the mourning, the people in front of him are exactly those.

commentary.on: Great multitudes from Galilee, Decapolis, Jerusalem, Judea and from beyond the Jordan followed him.
commentary.text: The crowd comes from every direction, including the Decapolis, a league of ten largely Greek-speaking cities east of the Jordan. Matthew then says (5:1) that Jesus 'saw the multitudes' and 'went up onto the mountain', sat down, and taught his disciples. Sitting was the posture of a Jewish teacher; the mountain is the first echo of Moses.

parts.title: The sermon on the plain
parts.context: Luke's Gospel, written around the same time as Matthew's, tells a shorter version of the same sermon (6:20–49). Jesus has spent a night in prayer on a mountain and chosen the twelve apostles. Now he comes down and teaches on 'a level place'.

commentary.on: He came down with them, and stood on a level place
commentary.text: In Matthew Jesus goes up; in Luke he comes down. That is why this is called the 'sermon on the plain'. Many scholars think Luke did not have Matthew's Moses pattern in mind; others think he chose a level place to show Jesus standing among the people. Either way, the two writers framed one tradition differently.

commentary.on: Blessed are you who are poor, God’s Kingdom is yours.
commentary.text: Matthew has 'poor in spirit'. Luke has simply 'you who are poor'. 'Blessed' translates the Greek makarios: not 'happy' in a passing sense, but fortunate, in the right place, favoured by God. To call the poor fortunate made no sense by the world's standards. That is the point.

commentary.on: Blessed are you who hunger now, for you will be filled.
commentary.text: Again Luke is concrete: hungry now, not 'hungry for righteousness' as in Matthew. The blessing is a promise about the future: God will reverse things. Jesus is announcing a world turned the right way up.

commentary.on: for their fathers did the same thing to the prophets.
commentary.text: Those who are hated for following Jesus stand in a long line: Israel's prophets, like Jeremiah and Elijah, were mocked and persecuted too. To be rejected for doing right is a sign of being in good company.

commentary.on: But woe to you who are rich! For you have received your consolation.
commentary.text: Luke adds four woes, a mirror of the four blessings. 'Woe' is the prophets' word of grief and warning (Isaiah 5:8, Amos 6:1). The rich are not cursed for having money, but warned: if comfort now is all they want, they have already had it.

commentary.on: Woe, when men speak well of you, for their fathers did the same thing to the false prophets.
commentary.text: The last woe is for the popular. Being praised by everyone is a danger sign. Luke's sermon makes the reversal sharp: the people the world envies are the ones to worry about.

paras: 1. If any one will piously and soberly consider the sermon which our Lord Jesus Christ spoke on the mount, as we read it in the Gospel according to Matthew, I think that he will find in it, so far as regards the highest morals, a perfect standard of the Christian life: and this we do not rashly venture to promise, but gather it from the very words of the Lord Himself. For the sermon itself is brought to a close in such a way, that it is clear there are in it all the precepts which go to mould the life. For thus He speaks: Therefore, whosoever hears these words of mine, and does them, I will liken him unto a wise man, which built his house upon a rock: and the rain descended, and the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat upon that house; and it fell not: for it was founded upon a rock. And every one that hears these words of mine, and does them not, I will liken unto a foolish man, which built his house upon the sand: and the rain descended, and the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat upon that house; and it fell: and great was the fall of it. Since, therefore, He has not simply said, Whosoever hears my words, but has made an addition, saying, Whosoever hears these words of mine, He has sufficiently indicated, as I think, that these sayings which He uttered on the mount so perfectly guide the life of those who may be willing to live according to them, that they may justly be compared to one building upon a rock. I have said this merely that it may be clear that the sermon before us is perfect in all the precepts by which the Christian life is moulded; for as regards this particular section a more careful treatment will be given in its own place.

For this reason the number of sentences before us is to be carefully considered. For the beatitudes begin with humility: Blessed are the poor in spirit, i.e. those not puffed up, while the soul submits itself to divine authority, fearing lest after this life it go away to punishment, although perhaps in this life it might seem to itself to be happy. Then it (the soul) comes to the knowledge of the divine Scriptures, where it must show itself meek in its piety, lest it should venture to condemn that which seems absurd to the unlearned, and should itself be rendered unteachable by obstinate disputations. After that, it now begins to know in what entanglements of this world it is held by reason of carnal custom and sins: and so in this third stage, in which there is knowledge, the loss of the highest good is mourned over, because it sticks fast in what is lowest. Then, in the fourth stage there is labour, where vehement exertion is put forth, in order that the mind may wrench itself away from those things in which, by reason of their pestilential sweetness, it is entangled: here therefore righteousness is hungered and thirsted after, and fortitude is very necessary; because what is retained with delight is not abandoned without pain. Then, at the fifth stage, to those persevering in labour, counsel for getting rid of it is given; for unless each one is assisted by a superior, in no way is he fit in his own case to extricate himself from so great entanglements of miseries.

But it is a just counsel, that he who wishes to be assisted by a stronger should assist him who is weaker in that in which he himself is stronger: therefore blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy. At the sixth stage there is purity of heart, able from a good conscience of good works to contemplate that highest good, which can be discerned by the pure and tranquil intellect alone. Lastly is the seventh, wisdom itself — i.e. the contemplation of the truth, tranquillizing the whole man, and assuming the likeness of God, which is thus summed up: Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called the children of God. The eighth, as it were, returns to the starting-point, because it shows and commends what is complete and perfect: therefore in the first and in the eighth the kingdom of heaven is named, Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven; and, Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven: as it is now said, Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword? Seven in number, therefore, are the things which bring perfection: for the eighth brings into light and shows what is perfect, so that starting, as it were, from the beginning again, the others also are perfected by means of these stages.

parts.author: Augustine
parts.work: Our Lord's Sermon on the Mount, Book I
parts.ref: Augustine, Our Lord's Sermon on the Mount I.1 and I.3
parts.title: A perfect standard of the Christian life
parts.context: Augustine (354–430) was a teacher of rhetoric from North Africa who became a Christian in 386 and a priest at Hippo, in what is now Algeria, in 391. He wrote this commentary there around AD 394, while still a young priest. He quotes the Latin Bible of his day, so his wording of the Beatitudes ('the meek ... shall by inheritance possess the earth') differs a little from the World English Bible. Translated by William Findlay (1888), as revised for New Advent. The first paragraph opens the book; the second comes from chapter 3.
parts.plain: Augustine says: anyone who studies the Sermon carefully will find in it a complete pattern for the Christian life, and Jesus himself says so at the end, where he compares those who hear and do his words to a man who builds on rock. Then he reads the Beatitudes as steps. They begin with humility, go on through gentleness, grief over sin, hunger for goodness, mercy and purity of heart, and reach wisdom and peace. The eighth blessing, for the persecuted, returns to the start and shows the whole is complete.

commentary.on: a perfect standard of the Christian life
commentary.text: Augustine's first claim is bold: the Sermon is not a few nice sayings but a complete pattern for how to live. Most Christian traditions since have agreed, though they have argued fiercely over what kind of pattern it is, as we will see.

commentary.on: Whosoever hears these words of mine
commentary.text: He proves it from the Sermon's own ending. Jesus says 'these words of mine', meaning the Sermon itself, are the foundation for a whole life. Augustine reads the Sermon from its end.

commentary.on: For the beatitudes begin with humility: Blessed are the poor in spirit, i.e. those not puffed up
commentary.text: For Augustine, 'poor in spirit' means humble: not puffed up, willing to be taught by God. Humility is the first step because pride, in his view, is the root of every other sin.

commentary.on: what is retained with delight is not abandoned without pain
commentary.text: A deeply human line. Augustine knew from his own life, told in his Confessions, how hard it is to let go of what we enjoy even when we know it harms us. Hunger for righteousness, the fourth step, is the hard labour of breaking free.

commentary.on: he who wishes to be assisted by a stronger should assist him who is weaker
commentary.text: The fifth step is mercy. Augustine's logic: we cannot climb alone; we need God's help, and the fair condition of being helped by the stronger is to help the weaker. Mercy given and mercy received belong together.

commentary.on: Seven in number, therefore, are the things which bring perfection
commentary.text: Augustine counts seven steps, with the eighth returning to the first, because both promise 'the kingdom of heaven'. In the next chapter he links the seven to the seven gifts of the Spirit in Isaiah 11. Many modern scholars think the Beatitudes are a list of the kinds of people God favours rather than a ladder. But Augustine's reading shaped a thousand years of Christian thinking about the spiritual life.

compare.author: Augustine
compare.work: Our Lord's Sermon on the Mount, Book I
compare.ref: Augustine, Our Lord's Sermon on the Mount I.1 and I.3
compare.why: Augustine wrote one of the first books devoted to the Sermon alone. Read how he sees the Beatitudes not as a list but as a ladder, the stages of a life turning towards God.
compare.title: Seven steps up the mountain

paras: The name 'Sermon on the Mount' comes from Augustine's book, De sermone Domini in monte. Matthew does not call it a sermon. It runs to three chapters and 111 verses, and can be read aloud in about fifteen minutes.

Did Jesus deliver it in one go? Most scholars think not, at least not in this form. Matthew gathers Jesus's teaching into five great speeches (chapters 5–7, 10, 13, 18 and 24–25), each ending with the same formula: 'When Jesus had finished saying these things' (7:28, 11:1, 13:53, 19:1, 26:1). Many of the Sermon's sayings turn up elsewhere in Luke, scattered across his Gospel: the Lord's Prayer in Luke 11, the birds and lilies in Luke 12. So the Sermon is probably Matthew's arrangement of things Jesus taught on many occasions. That does not make it less his: a travelling teacher repeats his best sayings, and his disciples remember them.
sections.key: The Sermon is the first of Matthew's five great speeches; most scholars think Matthew gathered sayings Jesus gave on many occasions.

paras: Matthew tells the story of Jesus's early life so that it echoes Moses. A wicked king orders baby boys killed, as Pharaoh did (Matthew 2:16; Exodus 1:22). The child is saved and comes 'out of Egypt' (2:15). He passes through water at his baptism, then spends forty days in the wilderness, as Israel spent forty years. Then he goes up a mountain and gives teaching about the law.

If you took 'Exodus and the law', you read how God gave Israel the Ten Commandments on Mount Sinai. Matthew's first readers, steeped in that story, would have heard the echo at once. The American scholar Dale Allison set out the pattern in detail in The New Moses (1993). But Matthew's Jesus is more than a second Moses. Moses carried God's words down the mountain. Jesus sits on the mountain and speaks in his own name: 'But I tell you'.
sections.key: Matthew shapes Jesus's story to echo Moses: the massacre, Egypt, the water, the wilderness, the mountain. But Jesus teaches in his own name.

paras: Luke's sermon on the plain is about a quarter the length of Matthew's. Its core is the same: blessings, love of enemies, the golden rule, not judging, the tree and its fruit, the house on the rock. Most scholars explain the overlap by a lost collection of Jesus's sayings that both used, called Q (from the German Quelle, 'source'). A minority, following Austin Farrer and Mark Goodacre, think Luke simply used Matthew.

The differences tell us what each writer cared about. Matthew has eight blessings, often more spiritual ('poor in spirit', 'hunger and thirst for righteousness'); Luke has four, blunt and economic ('you who are poor', 'you who hunger now'), with four woes. Scholars argue over which is closer to Jesus's own words. Many think Luke's are closer in form, and that Matthew draws out their meaning; others think Matthew preserves Jesus's echo of Isaiah 61, where good news is for the 'poor' and 'broken-hearted'.

rows: On a level place; Jesus stands
Eight, in the third person ('Blessed are the poor in spirit')
Four, in the second person ('Blessed are you who are poor')
The law fulfilled, the Lord's Prayer, worry, the narrow gate
Most of these elsewhere in Luke
table.note: Both end with the house built on rock.

sections.key: Luke's shorter sermon shares Matthew's core. Most scholars think both used a sayings source called Q; Luke's blessings are blunter and come with woes.

paras: The eight Beatitudes in Matthew bless the poor in spirit, those who mourn, the gentle (or meek), those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, the merciful, the pure in heart, the peacemakers, and those persecuted for righteousness. 'Beatitude' comes from the Latin beatus, 'blessed'.

There are two main ways of reading them. One sees them as virtues to aim at, as Augustine did: be humble, be merciful, be pure. The other, stressed by many modern scholars, sees them first as announcements: God is on the side of people in these conditions, and his kingdom is coming to them. The two readings need not compete. The first Beatitude is good news to people who have nothing; and the fifth, 'blessed are the merciful', is plainly a call to become something. Either way, Jesus starts with gift before demand. Sinai began with 'I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage' before a single command; the Sermon begins with blessing.
sections.key: The Beatitudes can be read as virtues to grow into or as God's announcement of favour; both start with gift before demand, as Sinai did.

sections.h: The world turned the right way up
paras: In the ancient world, blessedness belonged to the fortunate: the gods' favourites, the rich, the strong, the well-born. The Greek word makarios was used of the gods themselves, and of the dead heroes on the Isles of the Blessed. To call the poor, the grieving and the persecuted blessed was to turn that picture upside down.

It was not entirely new. Israel's Psalms and prophets had long said God hears the poor and lifts the humble (Psalm 34:18; Isaiah 57:15; 1 Samuel 2:8). What was new was to put this at the very start of a teaching about how to live, as its foundation. Session 6, still to come, will hear the philosopher who thought this reversal was the greatest revolution in history, and a disaster. For now, notice how it begins: not with what you must do, but with who God is for.
sections.key: Blessing the poor and grieving reversed the ancient world's idea of who was fortunate, building on Israel's psalms and prophets.

paras: Matthew does not name the mountain. Since at least the Byzantine period, pilgrims have remembered it on the hills above the north-west shore of the Sea of Galilee, near Capernaum, the fishing town where Jesus based himself. Remains of a small fourth-century church have been found on the slope near Tabgha. Today the Church of the Beatitudes, built in 1938 to designs by the Italian architect Antonio Barluzzi, stands on the hill: an eight-sided building, one side for each Beatitude.

The setting matters less than the shape Matthew gives it, but it is worth knowing that the hills there form natural slopes where a crowd can sit and hear a speaker below. The Sermon belongs to a real place: farming villages and fishing towns under Roman rule, where most people were poor, taxes were heavy, and soldiers could press a man into service. Those details will matter in the sessions that follow.
sections.key: Tradition places the Sermon on the hills above the Sea of Galilee near Capernaum; the Church of the Beatitudes (1938) stands there today.

debate.question: Did Jesus preach the Sermon on the Mount as one sermon?

positions.name: A collection made by Matthew
positions.who: Most modern scholars, e.g. Ulrich Luz, W. D. Davies and Dale Allison
positions.view: Matthew gathered sayings Jesus gave on many occasions into one carefully built speech, as he did with the other four great speeches in his Gospel.
positions.evidence: The same sayings are scattered across Luke's Gospel (11:2–4; 12:22–31; 16:17–18); Matthew's five speeches all end with the same formula; the Sermon is tightly structured.

positions.name: One sermon, remembered
positions.who: Many traditional readers, from Augustine to John Wesley; some modern conservative scholars
positions.view: Jesus did preach a long sermon on a hillside, and his disciples remembered its substance. He may also have repeated parts of it elsewhere, which explains Luke.
positions.evidence: Both Matthew and Luke place a sermon with the same beginning and ending at the same point in Jesus's ministry; teachers in an oral culture repeated their teaching and pupils memorised it.

positions.name: A summary of a typical sermon
positions.who: Some scholars, such as Craig Keener
positions.view: The Sermon is a faithful summary of what Jesus taught again and again, set in one typical occasion. Ancient writers often presented speeches this way.
positions.evidence: Ancient historians like Thucydides openly gave the gist of speeches in their own arrangement (History I.22).

debate.agree: All agree that the Sermon gives the heart of Jesus's moral teaching, and that Matthew has arranged it with great care.

look.why: There is no painting of the Sermon itself in the gallery's open collection. This small panel by the Florentine painter Grifo di Tancredi, around 1310, shows Christ raising his hand in blessing: the gesture the Sermon begins with.
points: Christ is shown from the waist up against a gold background, with long, honey-blond hair and a beard.
His right hand is raised, with the index and middle fingers extended upwards: a gesture of blessing.
In his other hand he holds an open book whose pages face us, inscribed in gold: 'ECO SUM LUX MUNDI', Latin for 'I am the light of the world'.
He wears a rose-pink robe under a spruce-blue mantle, both trimmed with gold.
A halo is incised into the gold, with clusters of five dots in dark red, blue and black.
The panel's top is a five-sided, angular arch framing his head.

music.why: John Greenleaf Whittier, an American Quaker poet, wrote these words in 1872. They picture the calm of the hills of Galilee where Jesus taught and ask for 'simple trust' like that of the first disciples.

think.why: The Sermon shows a teacher who speaks with his own authority. See what Christians believe about who he was.

learn.why: The opening of the Sermon: eight blessings worth carrying for life.

check.q: Why do many scholars think the Sermon on the Mount was arranged by Matthew rather than preached in exactly this form?
options: Because Matthew says it was a collection
Because many of its sayings appear scattered across different scenes in Luke, and Matthew arranges all his teaching into five speeches with the same ending
Because Augustine said so
Because no one could listen to a sermon of fifteen minutes
check.why: The scattered parallels in Luke and Matthew's repeated formula point to a careful arrangement. Matthew himself does not say.

check.q: What is the main point of Matthew's echoes of Moses (the massacre, Egypt, the wilderness, the mountain)?
options: To present Jesus as a new Moses giving God's teaching to his people, while speaking with an authority of his own
To replace the Jewish law with Greek philosophy
To show that Jesus was born in Egypt
To prove that Moses wrote Matthew's Gospel
check.why: The pattern invites readers to hear Sinai behind the Sermon; 'But I tell you' shows Jesus is more than a messenger.

check.q: Luke's blessings say 'you who are poor' and 'you who hunger now'. What does that tell us compared with Matthew's 'poor in spirit'?
options: Matthew and Luke describe two unrelated sermons
Luke stresses people in real need, and pairs blessings with woes for the rich, while Matthew draws out the inner meaning
Luke's version is a later mistranslation of Matthew
Luke did not believe in spiritual poverty
check.why: The two writers shape one tradition: Luke concrete and economic, Matthew more inward. Neither cancels the other.

check.q: Why does it matter that the Sermon begins with blessings rather than commands?
options: Because the Beatitudes were added later
Like Sinai, which began with what God had done before giving the commandments, it puts God's gift before his demand
Because blessings are easier to remember
It shows that commands do not matter
check.why: 'I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt' came before the Ten Commandments; the Beatitudes come before the Sermon's demands.

check.q: In Augustine's reading, why is humility ('poor in spirit') the first step?
options: Because the soul must stop being 'puffed up' and submit to God before it can learn and grow
Because the poor were the largest group in the crowd
Because Isaiah lists humility first
Because poverty is the only virtue
check.why: For Augustine pride is the root of sin, so humility, being teachable, is where the climb begins.

check.q: Which is the strongest objection to Augustine's 'seven steps' reading?
options: There are only four Beatitudes
Augustine could not read Latin
The Beatitudes may be a list of the kinds of people God favours, not a ladder of stages; Matthew gives no sign of a sequence
Augustine ignored the eighth Beatitude
check.why: Many modern scholars read them as announcements of God's favour. Augustine did discuss the eighth: it returns to the first.

tutorial.question: Why does Matthew present Jesus as a new Moses, and what difference does it make to how we read the Sermon on the Mount?
tutorial.approach: Set out the parallels between Jesus's early life and Moses's, and the Sinai echo of the mountain. Then compare Matthew with Luke's sermon on the plain. Ask what the Moses frame tells a reader to expect, and where Jesus goes beyond Moses. End with what it means that the new teaching begins with blessing.
strong: Lists at least three Moses parallels in Matthew 1–5.
Explains why Matthew's Jewish readers would hear Sinai behind the mountain.
Compares Matthew's setting and Beatitudes with Luke's, and suggests why they differ.
Notices 'But I tell you': Jesus speaks in his own name.
Explains the significance of beginning with blessing.
Mentions the scholarly debate over whether it was one sermon.
