reading.title: Strength to Love
reading.why: King's sermons, including 'Loving Your Enemies' and 'Pilgrimage to Nonviolence'.

reading.author: Leo Tolstoy
reading.title: The Kingdom of God Is Within You
reading.why: The classic case for taking 'resist not evil' literally, still in print.

reading.author: Walter Wink
reading.title: Engaging the Powers
reading.why: The 'third way' reading of the Sermon's examples.

reading.author: Richard B. Hays
reading.title: The Moral Vision of the New Testament
reading.why: A leading New Testament scholar's argument that the New Testament as a whole calls for nonviolence, with the other views stated fairly.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: pray each day, by name, for one person who has hurt you or whom you find hard to bear. Ask for something good for them. Once this week, do them one small good turn they will not expect.
sessions.reflect: Who is your enemy? What would it mean to want their good?
takeaways: 'An eye for an eye' limited revenge; Jesus asks his followers not to retaliate at all, even for what a fair law allowed.
Love of enemies is shown in blessing, doing good and praying, because God loves the just and the unjust.
Christians have read these words as pacifism (Tolstoy, the peace churches), as forbidding revenge in the heart (Augustine, just war) and as nonviolent resistance (Gandhi, King).

sessions.title: In secret
sessions.line: Give, pray and fast where only God can see; store treasure in heaven; and look at the birds and the lilies before you worry about tomorrow.
sessions.plain: In chapter 6 Jesus turns from how we treat others to how we practise our faith. Three practices every Jew knew, giving to the poor, prayer and fasting, are to be done in secret, for God alone, not to be admired. Then he talks about money and worry: you cannot serve both God and wealth; look at the birds and the wild flowers, which do not worry, and trust your Father for tomorrow. This session asks what it means to live for an audience of one, and whether 'do not worry' is realistic.
sessions.why: Sessions 2 and 3 took the law inwards, from deed to heart, in how we treat others. Chapter 6 does the same for religion itself: it moves faith from the stage to the inner room, and then asks what we really trust.
answers: How should we give, pray and fast, according to Jesus?
What is a 'hypocrite', and why does Jesus keep using the word?
Where does the Lord's Prayer fit in the Sermon?
Why does Jesus say not to worry, and is that realistic?
sessions.finding: Chapter 6 moves religion from the stage to the inner room: give, pray and fast for God alone, and trust him for tomorrow.

paras: So far the Sermon has blessed the poor and the grieving (session 1), pressed the law from the deed to the heart (session 2), and asked for no revenge and love of enemies (session 3). All of that was about how we treat other people. Now Jesus turns to something closer to home: how we practise our religion, and what we trust.
background.key: After the antitheses on how we treat others, the Sermon turns to religious practice and trust.

paras: In Jewish life, three practices stood together: giving to the poor, prayer and fasting. The book of Tobit, written a century or two before Jesus, puts it in one line: 'Good is prayer with fasting and alms and righteousness' (Tobit 12:8). Giving was called tsedakah, which also means justice: in Jewish thought, helping the poor is not optional kindness but what is owed. Faithful Jews prayed at set times each day (Daniel prayed three times a day, Daniel 6:10) and recited the Shema, 'Hear, O Israel', morning and evening. Many devout Jews fasted on Mondays and Thursdays; the Pharisee in one of Jesus's parables says 'I fast twice a week' (Luke 18:12).
Jesus assumes his followers will do all three. He never says 'if you give', only 'when you give'. His concern is how, and for whom.
background.key: Giving (tsedakah, also 'justice'), prayer and fasting were the three pillars of Jewish practice; Jesus assumes all three and asks how and for whom.

paras: The word 'hypocrite' first appears in the Bible here. In Greek, a hypokritēs was an actor on the stage, someone who wore a mask and played a part. There was a large Greek theatre at Sepphoris, a city a few miles from Nazareth, rebuilt in Jesus's lifetime, though when the theatre itself was built is debated.

Jesus uses the word for people whose religion is a performance: done to be seen by an audience. It is a warning for anyone, not a label for one group. Christians have often used it against Jews, which is unfair: the Jewish teachers of the time also warned against showy piety, and the warning applies first to Jesus's own disciples.
background.key: A hypokritēs was a stage actor; Jesus warns against religion as performance, a warning for anyone, including his own followers.

paras: The main reading is the whole of Matthew 6, in two parts: giving, prayer and fasting in secret, with the Lord's Prayer at its centre (6:1–18); then treasure, the two masters and worry (6:19–34). If you have taken 'How to pray', you have already studied the Lord's Prayer phrase by phrase; here we look only at its place in the Sermon.

The comparison is from the Didache, or 'Teaching of the Twelve Apostles', a short Christian handbook from around AD 100, rediscovered in 1873. Its eighth chapter shows the first Christians putting this part of the Sermon into practice: when to fast, and how often to pray the Lord's Prayer.
background.key: Matthew 6, in two parts; then the Didache, showing the earliest Christians living this chapter.

before: Count how often Jesus says 'in secret'. Who sees?
What reward do the hypocrites get?
What reasons does Jesus give for not worrying?
sessions.readWhy: The three practices in secret, and the call to trust God instead of wealth and worry.

paras: “Be careful that you don’t do your charitable giving before men, to be seen by them, or else you have no reward from your Father who is in heaven.

Therefore when you do merciful deeds, don’t sound a trumpet before yourself, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and in the streets, that they may get glory from men. Most certainly I tell you, they have received their reward.
But when you do merciful deeds, don’t let your left hand know what your right hand does,
so that your merciful deeds may be in secret, then your Father who sees in secret will reward you openly.

“When you pray, you shall not be as the hypocrites, for they love to stand and pray in the synagogues and in the corners of the streets, that they may be seen by men. Most certainly, I tell you, they have received their reward.
But you, when you pray, enter into your inner room, and having shut your door, pray to your Father who is in secret, and your Father who sees in secret will reward you openly.
In praying, don’t use vain repetitions, as the Gentiles do; for they think that they will be heard for their much speaking.
Therefore don’t be like them, for your Father knows what things you need, before you ask him.
Pray like this: ‘Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy.
Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.
Give us today our daily bread.
Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.
Bring us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one. For yours is the Kingdom, the power, and the glory forever. Amen.’
“For if you forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you.
But if you don’t forgive men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.

“Moreover when you fast, don’t be like the hypocrites, with sad faces. For they disfigure their faces, that they may be seen by men to be fasting. Most certainly I tell you, they have received their reward.
But you, when you fast, anoint your head, and wash your face;
so that you are not seen by men to be fasting, but by your Father who is in secret, and your Father, who sees in secret, will reward you.
“Don’t lay up treasures for yourselves on the earth, where moth and rust consume, and where thieves break through and steal;
but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust consume, and where thieves don’t break through and steal;
for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.
“The lamp of the body is the eye. If therefore your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light.
But if your eye is evil, your whole body will be full of darkness. If therefore the light that is in you is darkness, how great is the darkness!
“No one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other; or else he will be devoted to one and despise the other. You can’t serve both God and Mammon.
Therefore I tell you, don’t be anxious for your life: what you will eat, or what you will drink; nor yet for your body, what you will wear. Isn’t life more than food, and the body more than clothing?
See the birds of the sky, that they don’t sow, neither do they reap, nor gather into barns. Your heavenly Father feeds them. Aren’t you of much more value than they?
“Which of you, by being anxious, can add one moment to his lifespan?
Why are you anxious about clothing? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow. They don’t toil, neither do they spin,
yet I tell you that even Solomon in all his glory was not dressed like one of these.
But if God so clothes the grass of the field, which today exists, and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, won’t he much more clothe you, you of little faith?
“Therefore don’t be anxious, saying, ‘What will we eat?’, ‘What will we drink?’ or, ‘With what will we be clothed?’
For the Gentiles seek after all these things; for your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things.
But seek first God’s Kingdom, and his righteousness; and all these things will be given to you as well.
Therefore don’t be anxious for tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Each day’s own evil is sufficient.

parts.title: Give, pray and fast in secret
parts.context: The Sermon continues on the mountain. Jesus takes the three great practices of Jewish piety in turn, with the same pattern each time: do not do it like the hypocrites, to be seen; do it in secret, and your Father who sees in secret will reward you.

commentary.on: Be careful that you don’t do your charitable giving before men, to be seen by them
commentary.text: The heading for the whole section. The danger is not doing good in public, which the Sermon has already asked for ('let your light shine', 5:16), but doing it in order to be seen. The question is who your audience is.

commentary.on: don’t sound a trumpet before yourself
commentary.text: Probably a vivid picture rather than a real custom: no one has found evidence that donors blew trumpets. The point is plain: do not advertise your generosity.

commentary.on: Most certainly I tell you, they have received their reward.
commentary.text: The Greek word for 'received' was used on receipts: 'paid in full'. They wanted to be admired, and they were. That is all they will get.

commentary.on: don’t let your left hand know what your right hand does
commentary.text: Another deliberate exaggeration: give so quietly that you hardly notice yourself. Jewish tradition prized the same thing: the Temple had a 'chamber of secrets' where the devout left gifts and the poor took them, with neither seeing the other (Mishnah Shekalim 5:6).

commentary.on: enter into your inner room, and having shut your door, pray to your Father who is in secret
commentary.text: The 'inner room' was the storeroom of a village house, often the only room with a door. Prayer is first of all a private meeting with God, not a public display.

commentary.on: don’t use vain repetitions, as the Gentiles do; for they think that they will be heard for their much speaking
commentary.text: 'Gentiles' are non-Jews. Many ancient prayers piled up the names and titles of a god to be sure of getting his attention. Jesus's reason for brevity is trust: 'your Father knows what things you need, before you ask him'.

commentary.on: Pray like this: ‘Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy.
commentary.text: The Lord's Prayer sits at the very centre of the Sermon. Ulrich Luz and other scholars have noticed that the Sermon is built around it, with matching sections before and after. It is the model of prayer 'in secret': short, trusting, and about God's kingdom before our needs. (The closing words 'For yours is the Kingdom, the power, and the glory' are missing from the oldest manuscripts of Matthew; most scholars think they were added from early Christian worship, as the Didache, the comparison, shows.)

commentary.on: But if you don’t forgive men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.
commentary.text: Of all the prayer's lines, Jesus comments on only one: forgiveness. It links back to the antitheses: be reconciled to your brother, love your enemy. We cannot ask God for what we refuse to give.

commentary.on: anoint your head, and wash your face; so that you are not seen by men to be fasting
commentary.text: People fasting often left their hair unwashed and put ashes on their heads, as a sign of grief or repentance. Jesus says: look as you would on any normal day. Fasting is between you and God.

parts.title: Treasure, two masters and worry
parts.context: The second half of chapter 6 moves from religious practice to money and anxiety. The link is the same question: what do you really live for, and whom do you trust?

commentary.on: for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also
commentary.text: A simple test of what we love: watch where our thoughts go when nothing else claims them. Wealth stored on earth can be eaten by moths (fine clothes were a form of wealth), rusted or stolen.

commentary.on: The lamp of the body is the eye. If therefore your eye is sound
commentary.text: A puzzling saying. In Jewish idiom, a 'good eye' meant generosity and an 'evil eye' meant meanness or envy (Proverbs 22:9; 28:22). Between sayings about money, it probably means: a generous outlook fills a life with light; a grasping one darkens it.

commentary.on: You can’t serve both God and Mammon.
commentary.text: Mammon is an Aramaic word for wealth or property. Jesus speaks of it almost as a rival god, a master who demands service. Note 'serve': you may have money; the danger is when money has you.

commentary.on: See the birds of the sky, that they don’t sow, neither do they reap, nor gather into barns.
commentary.text: Jesus does not tell people to stop working: men sowed and reaped. The birds are an argument from the lesser to the greater, a favourite rabbinic form: if God feeds birds, how much more will he care for you?

commentary.on: Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow. They don’t toil, neither do they spin
commentary.text: Toiling and spinning were women's work, as sowing and reaping were men's: between them, Jesus covers the daily labour of a whole household. The 'lilies' were probably the bright wild flowers that cover the Galilean hills in spring, perhaps red anemones; no one is sure.

commentary.on: But seek first God’s Kingdom, and his righteousness; and all these things will be given to you as well.
commentary.text: The key to the whole passage. Jesus does not say food and clothes do not matter: 'your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things'. He gives them a place: second. Put God's kingdom first, and the rest falls into its proper place.

commentary.on: Therefore don’t be anxious for tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Each day’s own evil is sufficient.
commentary.text: The last line is not naive. It admits that each day has its own trouble. What it forbids is borrowing tomorrow's trouble today. Live one day at a time: the same wisdom that runs through the Lord's Prayer's 'give us today our daily bread'.

paras: And let not your fastings be with the hypocrites, for they fast on the second and the fifth day of the week; but do ye keep your fast on the fourth and on the preparation (the sixth) day.
Neither pray ye as the hypocrites, but as the Lord commanded in His Gospel, thus pray ye:
Our Father, which art in heaven,
hallowed be Thy name;
Thy kingdom come;
Thy will be done,
as in heaven, so also on earth;
give us this day our daily bread;
and forgive us our debt,
as we forgive our debtors;
and lead us not into temptation,
but deliver us from the evil one;
for Thine is the power and the glory for ever and ever.
Three times in the day pray ye so.

parts.author: The Didache
parts.work: The Didache (The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles)
parts.translator: J. B. Lightfoot, ed. J. R. Harmer (1891)
parts.title: Fasting and the Lord's Prayer
parts.context: The Didache is a short manual of Christian life and worship, probably from Syria or Palestine. Scholars date it anywhere between AD 50 and 150; many place it around AD 100. It was lost for centuries until Philotheos Bryennios, a Greek Orthodox metropolitan, found it in a manuscript of 1056 in a library in Constantinople in 1873, and published it in 1883. Translated by J. B. Lightfoot, in The Apostolic Fathers (1891). The 'second and fifth day' are Monday and Thursday; the 'fourth' and 'preparation' days are Wednesday and Friday.
parts.plain: The Didache tells Christians not to fast on the same days as the 'hypocrites', Monday and Thursday, but on Wednesday and Friday. They are not to pray like the hypocrites either, but as the Lord commanded in the Gospel, and it gives the Lord's Prayer, ending with 'for Thine is the power and the glory for ever and ever'. They are to pray it three times a day.

commentary.on: And let not your fastings be with the hypocrites, for they fast on the second and the fifth day of the week
commentary.text: The Didache takes Jesus's word 'hypocrites' and applies it to other Jews, who fasted on Mondays and Thursdays. That is a long way from Matthew, where the warning is about showing off, not about which days. It is an early sign of Christians and Jews drawing apart, and of an unfair use of the word that would last for centuries.

commentary.on: but do ye keep your fast on the fourth and on the preparation (the sixth) day.
commentary.text: Wednesday and Friday: Friday because Jesus died on a Friday, the 'preparation' for the Sabbath; Wednesday perhaps because the plot against him was said to have begun then. Orthodox Christians still fast on Wednesdays and Fridays; the Catholic custom of not eating meat on Fridays comes from the same root.

commentary.on: Neither pray ye as the hypocrites, but as the Lord commanded in His Gospel
commentary.text: One of the earliest references outside the New Testament to a written 'Gospel'. The prayer given is Matthew's, almost word for word, which shows how early and how widely Matthew's Gospel was used.

commentary.on: for Thine is the power and the glory for ever and ever.
commentary.text: Here is the closing praise that later copyists added to Matthew 6:13. The Didache has a shorter form, without 'the Kingdom'. It shows the line being used in worship before it entered the Bible's manuscripts.

commentary.on: Three times in the day pray ye so.
commentary.text: Three times a day, like Daniel and like Jewish practice. The first Christians kept the Jewish rhythm of prayer, with Jesus's words in it. Many Christians still say the Lord's Prayer morning, midday and evening.

compare.author: The Didache
compare.work: The Didache (The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles)
compare.translator: J. B. Lightfoot, ed. J. R. Harmer (1891)
compare.why: The Didache shows the generation after the apostles putting Matthew 6 into practice. Notice what they took from it, and what they added.
compare.title: How the first Christians kept it

paras: Chapter 6 opens with a simple test: who is watching? The same act, giving money, praying or going without food, can be done for God or for an audience. Jesus does not ban public religion; he asks what it is for.

This is one of the most psychologically acute passages in the Bible. It sees that the desire to be admired can creep into the best things we do, and that the cure is secrecy: do good where no one will know. Søren Kierkegaard, the Danish philosopher, spoke of living 'before God' as the only true audience. The Christian tradition calls the opposite vice vainglory: wanting the glory of a good act for yourself.
sections.key: The same act can be done for God or for an audience; Jesus's cure for the craving to be admired is secrecy.

sections.h: Giving, prayer and fasting in the early Church
paras: The first Christians kept all three. The Didache shows them fasting twice a week and praying three times a day. In Acts, believers sell property to give to the poor (Acts 4:34–35). By the fourth century, fasting before Easter had become the forty days of Lent, and the Church calendar was built around feasts and fasts.

The traditions still differ in practice. Orthodox Christians keep Wednesday and Friday fasts and four long fasting seasons each year. Catholics fast on Ash Wednesday and Good Friday and abstain from meat on the Fridays of Lent. Many Protestants, after the Reformation's suspicion of 'works', let fasting lapse, though Anglicans kept Lent and many evangelicals and Pentecostals have returned to fasting. Giving in secret shaped the Western idea of anonymous charity.

rows: Wednesdays and Fridays, and four long fasts (Lent, the Apostles', the Dormition, the Nativity), usually without meat, dairy, wine or oil
Fast on Ash Wednesday and Good Friday; no meat on the Fridays of Lent (and, in some countries, every Friday)
Varies: Anglicans keep Lent; many churches leave fasting to personal choice; some call corporate fasts
Yom Kippur and Tisha B'Av, with minor fasts; Monday and Thursday fasts are kept by some devout Jews
table.note: All draw on the same roots: Jewish practice, and Jesus's 'when you fast'.

sections.key: The first Christians kept fasting and prayer at set times; Orthodox, Catholics and Protestants still differ in practice.

sections.h: The Lord's Prayer at the centre
paras: Look at the shape of the Sermon. It opens with blessings and ends with a warning to build on rock. In between come the law fulfilled and the three practices. At the heart of the three practices, and roughly at the centre of the whole Sermon, is the Lord's Prayer. Some scholars, such as Ulrich Luz, think Matthew built the Sermon around it on purpose.

If so, the prayer is the key to the rest. Its first half is about God: his name, his kingdom, his will. Its second half is about us: bread for today, forgiveness, protection. That is the order of the whole Sermon: God's kingdom first, and everything else after. And the line Jesus comments on, forgiveness, binds prayer to the way we treat others. The Sermon's ethics and its prayer cannot be separated.
sections.key: The Lord's Prayer sits at the centre of the Sermon; its order, God's kingdom first and our needs after, is the order of the whole.

paras: The second half of chapter 6 is about money. It does not say money is evil. It says money can become a master, a rival to God. 'Mammon' gave English a word for wealth as an idol.

The ancient world knew the danger. Plato's Republic warns that a city that honours wealth will dishonour virtue (Book VIII, 550e–551a). The Stoic Seneca wrote that wealth should be in the wise man's house, not in his heart (On the Happy Life 26). What Jesus adds is the either-or: you cannot serve both. Christian tradition has read this in different ways: as a call for some to give up everything, which shaped monasticism; and as a call for everyone to hold possessions loosely and give generously. John Wesley's rule, 'gain all you can, save all you can, give all you can' (sermon 'The Use of Money', 1760), is one Protestant attempt.
sections.key: Money is not evil, but it can become a master; you cannot serve both God and Mammon. Plato and Seneca warned too; Jesus adds the either-or.

paras: 'Do not worry' is one of the most loved and most doubted lines in the Sermon. Jesus's argument has three steps. Worry does not work: no one adds an hour to their life by it. God cares: he feeds the birds and clothes the flowers, and you matter more. And there is a better use of your attention: seek first his kingdom.

The Danish philosopher Søren Kierkegaard (1813–1855) wrote a series of discourses on this passage, The Lily of the Field and the Bird of the Air (1849). He saw the birds and lilies as teachers of silence, obedience and joy: they live wholly in today. Worry, for Kierkegaard, is living in tomorrow, where God has not yet given us strength to live. Paul says the same in a line you can learn this session: 'In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer... let your requests be made known to God' (Philippians 4:6).
sections.key: Jesus argues that worry does not help, God cares, and his kingdom deserves our attention; Kierkegaard read the birds and lilies as teachers of living in today.

paras: The objection is obvious. It is easy to tell people not to worry if you have food and a roof. Jesus's hearers often had neither. Christians who have trusted God have still gone hungry. And modern anxiety is often not a choice but a condition that needs care and sometimes treatment.

Three things can be said in reply. First, Jesus is not forbidding planning: Joseph stored grain for the famine (Genesis 41), and the farmers he spoke to sowed and reaped. The Greek word (merimnaō) means being pulled apart by anxious care. Second, the command comes with a community: the same Gospel tells his followers to feed the hungry and clothe the naked (Matthew 25:35–36), so that trust in God is meant to be answered through other people. Third, it is an invitation as much as a command: to learn, by practice, to hand tomorrow over. People who suffer from anxiety should seek real help; faith and good care are not rivals.
sections.key: 'Do not worry' forbids being torn apart by anxiety, not planning; it comes with a community that shares, and it is learned by practice. Real anxiety needs real help.

refs: Didache 8, tr. J. B. Lightfoot, The Apostolic Fathers (1891); Mishnah Shekalim 5:6.
Ulrich Luz, Matthew 1–7 (rev. ed. 2007), on the structure of the Sermon.
Plato, Republic VIII, 550e–551a; Seneca, On the Happy Life 26; John Wesley, Sermon 50, 'The Use of Money' (1760).
Søren Kierkegaard, The Lily of the Field and the Bird of the Air (1849); Upbuilding Discourses in Various Spirits (1847).

debate.question: Is 'do not worry' realistic?

positions.name: Yes: trust frees
positions.who: Søren Kierkegaard; much of the Christian spiritual tradition, from the desert monks to Jean-Pierre de Caussade's Abandonment to Divine Providence
positions.view: Worry is living in tomorrow. Trust in God's care is not naive but realistic: it accepts what we cannot control and frees us to act well today.
positions.evidence: Matthew 6:25–34; Philippians 4:6–7; the lives of people who have lived this way under great hardship.

positions.name: It is a call to priorities, not a cure
positions.who: Many modern commentators, e.g. John Stott
positions.view: Jesus forbids letting anxiety rule us and putting possessions first; he does not promise that believers will never lack, or forbid prudent planning.
positions.evidence: 'Seek first God's Kingdom'; 'each day's own evil is sufficient'; Jesus's own followers went hungry and were persecuted (2 Corinthians 11:27).

positions.name: Too easy for the comfortable
positions.who: Critics of religion; some liberation theologians on how the verse is misused
positions.view: Telling the poor not to worry can excuse the rich from helping them, and telling anxious people to trust more can add guilt to suffering.
positions.evidence: The history of 'pie in the sky' preaching; the need to read 6:25–34 with 25:35–36 and with Luke's woes on the rich.

debate.agree: All agree that the passage forbids putting wealth before God, and that trust in God is meant to be lived together with generosity to those in need.

look.why: 'See the birds of the sky': an unknown American painter of around 1840 filled a canvas with birds of every kind on and around one small tree. None of them is sowing, reaping or storing anything.
points: Many birds of different colours and sizes gather on and around a small, leafy tree.
They include birds that look like hawks, blue jays, hummingbirds, magpies and kestrels.
They are black, white, brown, grey, red, yellow and pale blue.
The birds perch at various heights on the tree and on the ground below, all facing different directions.
The ground is green with small grasses and ferns, and the sky behind the tree is pale yellow.

music.why: William Byrd, a Catholic in Elizabethan England, wrote this Mass in the 1590s for worship held in secret in country houses, behind closed doors: prayer in the inner room, at real risk.

think.why: Jesus speaks to worry and trust. See what the research says, and does not say, about faith, prayer and well-being.

learn.why: Paul's answer to worry, close to the Sermon's: bring everything to God in prayer, and his peace will guard your heart.

check.q: What is Jesus's main concern about giving, prayer and fasting?
options: That they be done for God, not to be seen and admired by others
That they be done only on certain days
That his followers should stop doing them
That they be done only in the Temple
check.why: 'When you give... when you pray... when you fast': he assumes all three and asks for whom they are done.

check.q: What does 'they have received their reward' mean?
options: They received money for praying
Their reward is waiting in heaven
They wanted to be admired, they were, and that is all they will get: 'paid in full'
God will reward them later
check.why: The verb was used on receipts. Applause was the payment, and it is complete.

check.q: Why does the Lord's Prayer's place in the Sermon matter?
options: It was added to the Sermon in the Middle Ages
It shows that the Sermon was written by Luke
It replaces the Ten Commandments
It sits near the centre; its order, God's kingdom first and our needs second, is the order of the whole Sermon
check.why: Many scholars think Matthew built the Sermon around it; 'seek first God's Kingdom' says the same.

check.q: How does the Didache's use of 'hypocrites' differ from Matthew's?
options: It does not use the word
They mean exactly the same
Matthew warns anyone against showy piety; the Didache applies the word to Jews who fasted on Monday and Thursday
The Didache uses it of pagans
check.why: The Didache turns a warning about motive into a label for another group: an early sign of the parting of ways.

check.q: What does the Didache's ending to the Lord's Prayer suggest about Matthew 6:13?
options: That Jesus said it in the Sermon
That the closing praise was used in early Christian worship and later copied into some manuscripts of Matthew
That the prayer had no ending
That the Didache was copied from the King James Bible
check.why: The oldest manuscripts of Matthew lack the doxology; the Didache shows it in worship around AD 100.

check.q: Which reply best answers the objection that 'do not worry' is unrealistic for the poor?
options: Jesus forbids being ruled by anxiety, not planning, and the same Gospel tells his followers to feed the hungry: trust in God is meant to be answered through others
The poor should simply have more faith
Worry is always a sin
Jesus never meant it seriously
check.why: Read with Matthew 25 and 'seek first', the command is about priorities and community, not denial of need.

tutorial.question: 'Your Father who sees in secret.' What is the place of secrecy in the Sermon on the Mount's picture of the religious life?
tutorial.approach: Work through the three practices in 6:1–18 and the pattern they share. Explain 'hypocrite' and the reward. Consider the Lord's Prayer's place at the centre. Then ask how secrecy fits with 'let your light shine' (5:16), and with the Didache's public rules. End with the move from religion to trust in 6:19–34.
strong: Explains the repeated pattern: not like the hypocrites; in secret; the Father who sees.
Defines hypokritēs and the 'paid in full' reward.
Reconciles 'in secret' with 'let your light shine' (motive, not visibility).
Places the Lord's Prayer at the centre and explains its order.
Uses the Didache to show early practice, fairly noting its polemic.
Links secret religion to trust over wealth and worry.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: do one good thing each day that no one will ever know about: a gift, a kindness, a prayer for someone. Tell no one, not even at the end of the week.
sessions.reflect: If no one ever knew, what good would you still do?
takeaways: Jesus assumes his followers will give, pray and fast, and asks them to do it in secret, for God alone, not for applause.
The Lord's Prayer sits at the centre of the Sermon: God's kingdom first, our needs after, and forgiveness binding prayer to how we treat others.
You cannot serve God and wealth; 'do not worry' is a call to seek first God's kingdom, live one day at a time, and trust him for tomorrow.

sessions.title: Rock and sand
sessions.line: Do not judge; ask and you will receive; treat others as you want to be treated; and build your life on these words by doing them.
sessions.plain: The last chapter of the Sermon gathers short, famous sayings: do not judge, or you will be judged; take the beam out of your own eye first; ask, seek, knock; and the golden rule, 'whatever you desire for men to do to you, you shall also do to them'. Then it ends with a choice between two gates, two trees and two houses. The wise man builds on rock and the foolish on sand, and the difference is not hearing Jesus's words but doing them. This session asks what 'do not judge' really means, whether the golden rule is unique to Christianity, and why the Sermon ends with a storm.
sessions.why: Session 4 moved religion from the stage to the inner room and asked whom we trust. Chapter 7 brings the Sermon to its end: how to treat others without condemning them, the rule that sums up the law, and the decision every hearer must make.
answers: What does 'do not judge' mean? Does it forbid all judgement?
What is the golden rule, and is it unique to Christianity?
What are the narrow gate and the two ways?
Why does the Sermon end with the house on the rock?
sessions.finding: The Sermon ends with a choice between two ways and two houses: hearing is not enough, only doing.

paras: The Sermon opened with blessings (session 1), fulfilled the law by taking it to the heart (session 2), asked for no revenge and love of enemies (session 3), and moved giving, prayer and fasting into secret, with trust in God instead of wealth and worry (session 4). Chapter 7 is the last. It is looser in structure, a string of sayings, and then a strong ending.
background.key: Chapter 7 is the Sermon's last: a string of sayings, then a strong ending.

paras: The Sermon's ending uses a picture that runs right through the Bible: two ways, one leading to life and one to death. Moses sets it before Israel: 'I have set before you life and death, the blessing and the curse. Therefore choose life' (Deuteronomy 30:19). The first psalm contrasts the righteous, 'like a tree planted by the streams of water', with the wicked, 'like the chaff which the wind drives away' (Psalm 1:3–4). Jeremiah speaks of 'the way of life and the way of death' (Jeremiah 21:8).

Early Christians used the same frame. The Didache, which you met in session 4, opens with the words 'There are two ways, one of life and one of death'. Greek moralists had a similar story: Prodicus's fable, retold by Xenophon, of the young Heracles at a crossroads choosing between Virtue and Vice (Memorabilia II.1.21–34). Jesus's hearers would have known exactly what was being asked of them.
background.key: The 'two ways', life and death, runs from Moses, Psalm 1 and Jeremiah to the Didache; the Greeks told of Heracles choosing between Virtue and Vice.

paras: If you have taken 'Exodus and the law', you read the story from the Talmud (Shabbat 31a) of a Gentile who asked Hillel to teach him the whole law while he stood on one leg. Hillel replied: 'That which is hateful to thyself, do not do to thy neighbor. This is the whole law, and the rest is its commentary.' Hillel taught a generation before Jesus. Jesus says almost the same thing in positive form, and adds: 'for this is the law and the prophets.'

Hillel's school of Pharisees was known for its gentleness. The Mishnah's Avot preserves other sayings of his, and of his descendant Simeon. Two of them are this session's comparison, because they are close parallels to the beginning and end of Matthew 7.
background.key: Hillel, a generation before Jesus, summed up the law as 'what is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbour'; Avot preserves more of his sayings.

paras: The main reading is the whole of Matthew 7, in four parts: judging (7:1–6); asking and the golden rule (7:7–12); the two ways, false prophets and their fruits (7:13–23); and the two houses, with the crowd's reaction (7:24–29).

The comparison sets two sayings from Avot beside it: Hillel's 'Judge not thy neighbour until thou comest into his place', and Simeon's 'Not the study but the carrying-out is the essential thing'. They show how close Jesus stood to the best Jewish teaching of his time, and help us see what he added.
background.key: Matthew 7 in four parts; then Hillel on judging and Simeon on doing, from the Mishnah.

before: What does Jesus tell someone to do before they correct their brother?
Why does Jesus say God will give good things to those who ask?
In the last story, what is the only difference between the two builders?
sessions.readWhy: The last chapter of the Sermon: judging, the golden rule, and the choice between two ways and two houses.

paras: “Don’t judge, so that you won’t be judged.
For with whatever judgment you judge, you will be judged; and with whatever measure you measure, it will be measured to you.
Why do you see the speck that is in your brother’s eye, but don’t consider the beam that is in your own eye?
Or how will you tell your brother, ‘Let me remove the speck from your eye;’ and behold, the beam is in your own eye?
You hypocrite! First remove the beam out of your own eye, and then you can see clearly to remove the speck out of your brother’s eye.
“Don’t give that which is holy to the dogs, neither throw your pearls before the pigs, lest perhaps they trample them under their feet, and turn and tear you to pieces.
“Ask, and it will be given you. Seek, and you will find. Knock, and it will be opened for you.
For everyone who asks receives. He who seeks finds. To him who knocks it will be opened.
Or who is there among you, who, if his son asks him for bread, will give him a stone?
Or if he asks for a fish, who will give him a serpent?
If you then, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him!
Therefore whatever you desire for men to do to you, you shall also do to them; for this is the law and the prophets.
“Enter in by the narrow gate; for wide is the gate and broad is the way that leads to destruction, and many are those who enter in by it.
How narrow is the gate, and restricted is the way that leads to life! Few are those who find it.
“Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravening wolves.
By their fruits you will know them. Do you gather grapes from thorns, or figs from thistles?
Even so, every good tree produces good fruit; but the corrupt tree produces evil fruit.
A good tree can’t produce evil fruit, neither can a corrupt tree produce good fruit.
Every tree that doesn’t grow good fruit is cut down, and thrown into the fire.
Therefore by their fruits you will know them.
Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter into the Kingdom of Heaven; but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven.
Many will tell me in that day, ‘Lord, Lord, didn’t we prophesy in your name, in your name cast out demons, and in your name do many mighty works?’
Then I will tell them, ‘I never knew you. Depart from me, you who work iniquity.’
“Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine, and does them, I will liken him to a wise man, who built his house on a rock.
The rain came down, the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat on that house; and it didn’t fall, for it was founded on the rock.
Everyone who hears these words of mine, and doesn’t do them will be like a foolish man, who built his house on the sand.
The rain came down, the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat on that house; and it fell—and great was its fall.”
When Jesus had finished saying these things, the multitudes were astonished at his teaching,
for he taught them with authority, and not like the scribes.

parts.title: Do not judge
parts.context: The opening of the last chapter. 'Judge' here (Greek krinō) can mean to assess, but also to condemn or pass sentence.

commentary.on: Don’t judge, so that you won’t be judged.
commentary.text: This may be the most quoted verse in the Bible today, often to mean 'no one may say anything is wrong'. That cannot be what it means: within a few verses Jesus calls people 'dogs', 'pigs' and 'false prophets', and tells his hearers to know them 'by their fruits'. What he forbids is condemning: setting yourself up as another person's final judge. 'You won't be judged' means by God.

commentary.on: with whatever measure you measure, it will be measured to you
commentary.text: A market picture: a trader measuring grain. The standard you use on others will be used on you. Harsh judges of others invite God's strictness on themselves; merciful ones receive mercy, as the Beatitudes promised.

commentary.on: Why do you see the speck that is in your brother’s eye, but don’t consider the beam that is in your own eye?
commentary.text: A comic exaggeration, perhaps from the carpenter's shop: a man with a plank in his eye offering to remove a splinter from his friend's. We see others' faults clearly and our own hardly at all.

commentary.on: First remove the beam out of your own eye, and then you can see clearly to remove the speck out of your brother’s eye.
commentary.text: Note the end: Jesus does not say leave your brother's speck alone. Helping someone with a fault is good, but only after honest self-examination, and with the humility that comes from it.

commentary.on: Don’t give that which is holy to the dogs, neither throw your pearls before the pigs
commentary.text: A puzzling verse, set straight after 'do not judge' as if to balance it. Dogs and pigs were unclean animals in Jewish law. The point seems to be: some judgement is needed. Do not force what is precious on people who will trample it. The Didache uses this verse to keep the Lord's Supper for the baptised (Didache 9).

parts.title: Ask, seek, knock; and the golden rule
parts.context: Sayings about prayer, then the golden rule. The 'therefore' in verse 12 links the two: God gives good gifts generously, so treat others as generously.

commentary.on: Ask, and it will be given you. Seek, and you will find. Knock, and it will be opened for you.
commentary.text: Three verbs, in a tense that means 'keep asking, keep seeking, keep knocking'. This is not a promise that every wish will be granted, but an invitation to persistent trust.

commentary.on: If you then, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him!
commentary.text: Another argument from the lesser to the greater, as with the birds and lilies. Even flawed parents do not trick their children with a stone for bread. God's goodness is greater still. Luke's version (11:13) says God gives 'the Holy Spirit'.

commentary.on: Therefore whatever you desire for men to do to you, you shall also do to them; for this is the law and the prophets.
commentary.text: The golden rule, so called in English since the seventeenth century. 'The law and the prophets' takes us back to 5:17: this is what the law was for. The Sermon's teaching on the law begins and ends with that phrase. Notice the form: not 'do not do what you would hate', but 'do what you would want'. It asks for action, not only restraint.

parts.title: Two ways and their fruits
parts.context: The Sermon's conclusion begins: three pictures of a choice. Two gates, two trees, and two kinds of follower.

commentary.on: Enter in by the narrow gate; for wide is the gate and broad is the way that leads to destruction
commentary.text: The old picture of the two ways. The broad road is easy and crowded; the narrow one is hard and few find it. The point is not that God wants few to be saved, but that the way of the Sermon goes against the crowd.

commentary.on: Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravening wolves.
commentary.text: Here is a judgement the disciples must make. The test is not what a teacher says or how impressive they are, but what their life produces.

commentary.on: By their fruits you will know them.
commentary.text: A farmer's test: you know a tree by its fruit. Character shows in conduct over time. It is the same principle Jesus applies to his own followers next.

commentary.on: Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter into the Kingdom of Heaven; but he who does the will of my Father
commentary.text: The most sobering lines in the Sermon. Even prophesying and miracles in Jesus's name are not enough. Notice also the claim: Jesus speaks of himself as the judge 'in that day', the last judgement. A teacher of ethics would not say this; Matthew presents Jesus as more.

commentary.on: I never knew you.
commentary.text: The opposite of being known by God is not ignorance of doctrine but a life that never let him in. Knowing, in the Bible, is a relationship.

parts.title: The two houses
parts.context: The Sermon's last words, and Matthew's account of how the crowd reacted. In Galilee, dry stream beds (wadis) could become torrents within minutes in a winter storm.

commentary.on: Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine, and does them, I will liken him to a wise man, who built his house on a rock.
commentary.text: 'These words of mine': the whole Sermon. Both builders hear; only one does. This is the verse Augustine quoted at the very start of his commentary, in session 1, to show that the Sermon is a complete pattern for life.

commentary.on: The rain came down, the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat on that house; and it didn’t fall
commentary.text: From the outside, the two houses look the same in fine weather. The difference shows only in the storm. In the Bible, the storm can mean any test of life, and finally God's judgement.

commentary.on: and it fell—and great was its fall.
commentary.text: The Sermon does not end with comfort but with a crash. After the gentle blessings of the beginning, the end is a warning. Grace and demand belong together.

commentary.on: for he taught them with authority, and not like the scribes.
commentary.text: The scribes taught by quoting earlier teachers. Jesus said 'But I tell you' and 'these words of mine'. The crowd noticed. Matthew's last word on the Sermon is about the authority of the one who gave it, which brings us back to the mountain and to Moses.

paras: Hillel said: "Separate thyself not from the congregation, and trust not thyself until the day of thy death"; and "Judge not thy neighbour until thou comest into his place".

Simeon, his son, said: "All my days have I grown up amongst the wise, and I have not found aught good for man but silence"; and "Not the study (of the Law), but the carrying-out (of it) is the essential thing".

parts.author: The rabbis of the Mishnah
parts.work: Mishnah Avot (The Sayings of the Jewish Fathers)
parts.title: Judge not thy neighbour
parts.context: Hillel the Elder taught in Jerusalem in the generation before Jesus, roughly 30 BC to AD 10. He was born in Babylon and was remembered for his gentleness and for milder readings of the law than his rival Shammai. Translated by W. O. E. Oesterley (1919), from a scanned copy; the translator's footnote markers have been removed, and his verse numbers differ from today's standard ones.
parts.plain: Hillel gives two pieces of advice. Do not cut yourself off from the community, and never be too sure of yourself as long as you live. And do not judge another person until you have been in their position.

commentary.on: trust not thyself until the day of thy death
commentary.text: A warning against spiritual pride: no one is safe from falling while they live. It is close to the beam in your own eye: the first danger is in yourself.

commentary.on: Judge not thy neighbour until thou comest into his place
commentary.text: Strikingly close to 'Don't judge'. Hillel's reason is understanding: you do not know what you would have done in their place. Jesus's reason is God's judgement and your own faults. Both forbid the quick condemnation of others.

parts.author: The rabbis of the Mishnah
parts.work: Mishnah Avot (The Sayings of the Jewish Fathers)
parts.title: Not the study, but the doing
parts.context: Simeon was the son of Rabban Gamaliel, Hillel's grandson, and led the Pharisees in Jerusalem during the war with Rome (AD 66–70); some scholars think the saying belongs to another Simeon of Hillel's family. Gamaliel appears in Acts as Paul's teacher (Acts 22:3). Same translation and editing as above; the brackets are Oesterley's.
parts.plain: Simeon says he grew up among wise men and found nothing better for a person than silence. And the most important thing is not studying the law but carrying it out.

commentary.on: I have not found aught good for man but silence
commentary.text: A rabbi's warning against too many words, close to Jesus's 'let your yes be yes' and his warning against long prayers.

commentary.on: Not the study (of the Law), but the carrying-out (of it) is the essential thing
commentary.text: This is the house on the rock in a single line. Jewish teaching, like Jesus, put doing above hearing. Where Jesus goes further is in what must be done: 'these words of mine'. The rock is not only the law but his teaching of it.

compare.author: The rabbis of the Mishnah
compare.work: Mishnah Avot (The Sayings of the Jewish Fathers)
compare.why: Two sayings from the house of Hillel, close to the beginning and the end of Matthew 7. Read them and ask how near Jesus is to them, and where he goes further.
compare.title: Judging and doing in the Mishnah

paras: 'Do not judge' does not forbid moral judgement. The same chapter requires it: recognise false prophets by their fruits, do not throw pearls to pigs. Elsewhere Matthew tells the disciples how to confront someone who has wronged them (18:15–17). Jesus himself called things evil.

What it forbids is three things. Condemning: passing final sentence on a person, which belongs to God. Hypocrisy: correcting others while blind to yourself. And harshness: a measure without mercy. Paul says the same: 'For you who judge practice the same things' (Romans 2:1). Hillel's saying adds understanding: you do not know what you would have done in their place. The verse is a call to humility, not to having no views.
sections.key: 'Do not judge' forbids condemnation, hypocrisy and harshness, not moral judgement, which the same chapter requires.

paras: Between the warning about judging and the golden rule comes a short passage on prayer. It can look out of place, but it carries the argument. The Sermon has asked for things no one can do by effort alone: no anger, no lust, love of enemies, no worry. Here Jesus tells his hearers to keep asking, keep seeking, keep knocking, because the Father gives good things to those who ask.

The picture is of a parent. No father gives his hungry child a stone that looks like a loaf, or a snake that looks like a fish. If flawed parents give good gifts, God gives better ones. This is not a promise that every request will be granted as asked. It is a promise about God's character: he can be trusted to give what is good. The golden rule then follows with a 'therefore': because God is generous with you, be generous with others. The Sermon's ethics rest on its picture of God.
sections.key: Ask, seek, knock: the Sermon's demands are met by asking a generous Father; and because he is generous, we are to treat others as we would be treated.

sections.h: The golden rule around the world
paras: Versions of the golden rule appear in many cultures, which is part of why it has been called the closest thing humanity has to a shared ethic. Most of the older ones are negative in form: do not do to others what you would not want done to you.
In 1993 the Parliament of the World's Religions in Chicago made the golden rule the centre of its 'Declaration toward a Global Ethic', drafted by the Catholic theologian Hans Küng.

rows: Negative: what you do not want for yourself, do not do to others
Negative: do not do to others what angers you when others do it to you
Negative, with a positive sense: do not do to others what would be hurtful to yourself
Negative: what you hate, do not do to anyone
Positive in sense: as you wish no evil to happen to you, act the same way towards others
Negative: what is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbour
Positive: whatever you want others to do to you, do to them
table.note: Dates for the Mahabharata and some sayings are approximate; wording paraphrased in our own words.

sections.key: Versions of the golden rule appear in Confucius, Isocrates, the Mahabharata, Tobit and Hillel; most are negative in form.

sections.h: What is new in Jesus's form?
paras: Christian writers have often claimed that the positive form is a great advance: the negative form asks only for restraint (do no harm), the positive asks for active love (do good). There is something to this. 'Do not hurt your neighbour' can be kept by staying home; 'do for your neighbour what you would want' sends you out of the door.

But fairness requires caution. Positive versions exist before Jesus, as in the Letter of Aristeas. Hillel's negative form, in context, is meant as a summary of the whole law, which includes many positive commands, such as leaving grain for the poor. And many scholars think the difference between the two forms is less important than it looks. What is most distinctive in Jesus is the setting: in Luke, the golden rule sits in the middle of 'love your enemies' (6:27–36), and in Matthew it follows 'how much more will your Father give good things'. The rule is not only about fair exchange; it is about imitating God's generosity, even towards enemies.
sections.key: The positive form asks for active good, not only restraint, but it is not unique; what is most distinctive is its setting beside love of enemies and God's generosity.

paras: 'By their fruits you will know them' gave the West a lasting test: judge people, and ideas, by what they produce over time. The American philosopher William James quoted it in The Varieties of Religious Experience (1902) as the right way to assess religion: not by its origins but by its fruits in life.

The warning that follows is aimed at Jesus's own followers. Saying 'Lord, Lord', even doing miracles in his name, is no substitute for doing the Father's will. Christianity has often been at its worst when it forgot this verse: when profession was enough and practice did not matter. Its reformers, from Francis of Assisi to the Methodists, have usually begun by reading it again.
sections.key: 'By their fruits' became the West's test of people and ideas; the warning against 'Lord, Lord' is aimed at Christians who profess without practising.

paras: The Sermon ends with a parable anyone could picture. In Galilee, a house built on the sandy floor of a dry valley might stand all summer; in the first winter storm, a flash flood could sweep it away. The wise builder digs down to rock, as Luke's version says (6:48). It takes longer, and no one sees the foundations.

Two lessons follow. The first is the one Matthew states: hearing is not enough, only doing. James puts it bluntly: 'be doers of the word, and not only hearers' (James 1:22). The second is the authority behind it: 'these words of mine'. The crowd's amazement in the last verse is not at the moral wisdom alone, but at the one who claims that a life stands or falls on what he says. The Sermon, from beginning to end, is a claim about Jesus as well as a teaching about life.
sections.key: Only doing builds a life that stands; and the Sermon ends with a claim about Jesus's own authority: 'these words of mine'.

refs: Matthew 7:1–29; 18:15–17; Luke 6:27–49; 11:9–13; Romans 2:1; James 1:22; Deuteronomy 30:15–19; Psalm 1; Jeremiah 21:8; Tobit 4:15.
Mishnah Avot 1:17; 2:4, tr. W. O. E. Oesterley (1919); Talmud, Shabbat 31a, tr. P. I. Hershon (1880), as read in 'Exodus and the law'; Didache 1, 9.
Confucius, Analects 15.24; Isocrates, Nicocles 61; Mahabharata, Anushasana Parva 113; Letter of Aristeas 207; Xenophon, Memorabilia II.1.21–34.
William James, The Varieties of Religious Experience (1902), lecture I; Hans Küng and the Parliament of the World's Religions, Declaration toward a Global Ethic (Chicago, 1993).
Jeffrey Wattles, The Golden Rule (1996); Dale C. Allison, The Sermon on the Mount: Inspiring the Moral Imagination (1999).

debate.question: Is the golden rule unique to Christianity?

positions.name: No: it is humanity's common ethic
positions.who: Hans Küng; the Parliament of the World's Religions (1993); historians of ethics such as Jeffrey Wattles
positions.view: The golden rule appears in nearly every moral tradition. That is not a problem for Christianity but a sign of a shared human conscience, which Christians themselves call the natural law.
positions.evidence: Confucius, Isocrates, the Mahabharata, Tobit, Hillel; Paul's 'the work of the law written in their hearts' (Romans 2:15).

positions.name: Yes: the positive form is new
positions.who: Many Christian writers, especially in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries
positions.view: The older versions ask us not to harm; Jesus asks us to do good, actively. That turns a rule of fairness into a rule of love.
positions.evidence: The positive form of Matthew 7:12; the contrast with Tobit 4:15 and Hillel.

positions.name: The rule is shared; its setting is distinctive
positions.who: Many New Testament scholars
positions.view: Positive and negative forms both existed and often meant much the same. What is distinctive is that Jesus sets the rule beside love of enemies and grounds it in God's generosity, so that it goes beyond fair exchange.
positions.evidence: The Letter of Aristeas 207; Luke 6:27–36, where the rule sits among the commands to love enemies; Matthew 7:11–12.

debate.agree: All agree that the golden rule is found far beyond Christianity, and that in Jesus's teaching it sums up 'the law and the prophets'.

look.why: There is no painting of the wise and foolish builders in the gallery's collection. In 1872 Alfred Sisley painted a real flood: the Seine had risen and covered the streets of Port-Marly, west of Paris. The houses stand in the water; the people go about by boat. It is the Sermon's last picture in modern dress: 'the floods came... and beat on that house'.
points: Clouds hang over a waterlogged street that separates us from the end of a row of buildings.
The building across from us has an apricot-orange ground floor and a pale peach second storey, with the letters 'AS' NICOLAS' painted near the top.
Two women in long skirts stand at a dark, open doorway at the front corner of the building.
Three men are in and near a shallow boat, pushed along by a man standing in the stern with a long stick.
Only the dashes of mauve, pink and grey on the left show that this is a flooded cobblestone road, not a canal.
The scene is loosely painted, especially the sky and water; the artist signed and dated it 'Sisley 72'.

music.why: The Swedish pastor Carl Boberg wrote the poem behind this hymn in 1885; the usual story is that he wrote it after a sudden thunderstorm gave way to calm. It is the song of someone whose house stood in the storm.

think.why: The golden rule appears in Athens and in Jerusalem alike. See how the two traditions met and shaped the West.

learn.why: The Sermon's last words: the test of everything that came before.

check.q: Why can 'do not judge' not mean 'never make any moral judgement'?
options: Because it applies only to judges in court
Because Jesus did not say it
Because the same chapter tells the disciples to recognise false prophets by their fruits and not to throw pearls to pigs
Because the Pharisees disagreed
check.why: Jesus requires discernment; what he forbids is condemnation, hypocrisy and harshness.

check.q: What is the point of the speck and the beam?
options: That carpenters make poor judges
That we see others' faults clearly and our own hardly at all; examine yourself first, then you can help your brother
That we should never help anyone with their faults
That only priests may correct others
check.why: 'First remove the beam... and then you can see clearly to remove the speck.' Helping is good, after honesty.

check.q: What does 'for this is the law and the prophets' after the golden rule show?
options: That the prophets wrote the golden rule
That the golden rule replaces the Old Testament
That the rule sums up what the law was for, closing the section that began at 5:17
That only Jews should keep it
check.why: The phrase brackets the Sermon's teaching on the law: 5:17 and 7:12.

check.q: Which statement about the golden rule is most accurate?
options: The negative form is found only in China
Versions appear in Confucius, Isocrates, Tobit and Hillel; Jesus's positive form is not unique, but its setting beside love of enemies is distinctive
It appears only in the Bible
Jesus was the first person to teach it
check.why: The rule is widespread; the Letter of Aristeas even has a positive version. The setting is what stands out.

check.q: In the parable of the two houses, what is the only difference between the builders?
options: One heard Jesus and the other did not
One built in summer and one in winter
Both heard; one did what he heard and the other did not
One was richer
check.why: 'Everyone who hears these words of mine, and does them' versus 'and doesn't do them'.

check.q: Why were the crowds astonished at the end of the Sermon?
options: Because he performed a miracle
Because it was very long
Because he told them to leave the law
Because Jesus taught with authority, in his own name, not by quoting earlier teachers like the scribes
check.why: 'These words of mine': Matthew ends with the authority of the teacher.

tutorial.question: Is the golden rule unique to Christianity? What, if anything, is distinctive about Jesus's version?
tutorial.approach: Set out the parallels across cultures, with dates, and Hillel's saying. Weigh the claim that the positive form is new, fairly, using the Letter of Aristeas. Then look at the setting of the rule in Matthew 7 and Luke 6. End with what follows for Christians in a world of many traditions.
strong: Gives at least three parallels from different traditions, with approximate dates.
Explains the difference between negative and positive forms.
Notes that positive forms existed before Jesus.
Uses the setting in Luke 6 and Matthew 7:11–12.
Relates the rule to 'the law and the prophets'.
Reaches a balanced conclusion.
