sessions.practice: Live it this week: before you criticise anyone, aloud or in your head, stop and name one fault of your own. Then, once a day, do one thing for someone that you would be glad to have done for you.
sessions.reflect: What are you building your life on? How would you know before the storm?
takeaways: 'Do not judge' forbids condemnation, hypocrisy and harshness, not moral judgement, which the same chapter requires.
The golden rule appears across many traditions; Jesus's positive form and its setting beside love of enemies give it a distinctive edge.
The Sermon ends with two ways, two trees and two houses: hearing is not enough, only doing, and the rock is 'these words of mine'.

sessions.title: The case against: a morality for slaves?
sessions.line: Nietzsche said the Sermon was a revolt of the weak, revenge disguised as love. Hear him at full strength.
sessions.plain: Friedrich Nietzsche, the German philosopher, admired the ancient Greeks and Romans: strong, proud, healthy people who called themselves 'good' and the weak 'bad'. He argued that the Jews, and then the Christians, turned this upside down. They called the poor, the meek and the suffering 'blessed' and the strong 'evil'. He called this the 'slave revolt in morals', driven by resentment, the secret hatred of the weak for the strong. The Sermon on the Mount is exactly what he meant. This session lets him make his case, then asks whether he was right, and what kind of strength love needs.
sessions.why: Sessions 1 to 5 read the Sermon block by block: the blessings, the law fulfilled, the other cheek, the inner room and the two houses. Now we hear the strongest case against it, from someone who understood how radical it was and hated it.
answers: What did Nietzsche mean by 'slave morality'?
Is Christianity a morality of resentment?
Does the Sermon make people weak?
Was Nietzsche right that Christianity overturned ancient values?
sessions.finding: Nietzsche saw clearly that the Sermon overturned the ancient world's values; whether that was a sickness or a liberation is the question.

paras: The Sermon blesses the poor in spirit, the meek and the persecuted. It tells its hearers not to hit back, to love their enemies, to give in secret, not to worry, not to judge. Most people today, believers or not, admire at least some of this. Nietzsche thought it was the most dangerous idea in history, and that our admiration for it was a sign of how completely it had won.
background.key: The Sermon blesses the meek and forbids revenge; Nietzsche thought our admiration for it showed how completely it had won.

paras: Friedrich Nietzsche (1844–1900) was the son of a Lutheran pastor in Saxony. A brilliant classical scholar, he became professor of Greek at the University of Basel at twenty-four, in 1869. Ill health made him give up the post ten years later, and he spent the next decade wandering between Switzerland and Italy, writing books few people read. In January 1889 he collapsed in Turin and never recovered his mind. He died in Weimar in 1900.

In The Gay Science (1882) he had a madman announce that 'God is dead': Europe no longer truly believed in God, and had not yet faced what that meant. If God is dead, Nietzsche argued, Christian morality has lost its foundation too, and we must ask where our values came from. The Genealogy of Morals (1887) is his answer: a history, or 'genealogy', of how 'good' and 'evil' were invented.
background.key: Nietzsche (1844–1900), a classicist and pastor's son, said 'God is dead' (1882) and in the Genealogy (1887) asked where Christian values came from.

paras: To feel the force of Nietzsche's case, picture the world he loved. In Homer's Iliad, the hero Achilles lives for honour and glory; the ideal is to be always the best, and to excel others. The aristocrats of Greece called themselves the 'good' and the 'beautiful', and the common people 'bad' or 'wretched'. Aristotle's 'great-souled man' (Nicomachean Ethics IV.3) is proud, rightly aware of his own worth, ashamed to be in anyone's debt. Humility was not a virtue; it was the condition of slaves.

Into that world came a religion whose founder was a crucified provincial, who blessed the meek and told people to turn the other cheek. Nietzsche was right that this was a shock. Early critics of Christianity, such as the Greek philosopher Celsus around AD 175, mocked it as a religion for slaves, women and children (Origen, Against Celsus III.44).
background.key: The Greek and Roman ideal prized honour, excellence and pride; humility was for slaves. Celsus mocked Christianity as a religion for slaves around AD 175.

paras: The main reading is from the First Essay of the Genealogy, sections 7, 8 and 10, translated by Horace B. Samuel in 1913. In them Nietzsche sets out the 'slave revolt in morals' and its root in resentment. His language is fierce, and in places about the Jews it is ugly; the lecture explains its context.

The comparison is Mary's song in Luke's Gospel, the Magnificat: 'He has put down princes from their thrones, and has exalted the lowly.' It is the reversal Nietzsche describes, in the Bible's own words. Read the two together and ask: is this resentment, or something else?
background.key: Nietzsche's Genealogy, First Essay 7, 8 and 10; then the Magnificat, the Bible's own song of reversal.

before: What two 'modes of valuation' does Nietzsche contrast?
What does Nietzsche say the 'new love' grew from?
How, according to Nietzsche, does the 'aristocratic man' treat his enemies, and how does the 'resentful man'?
sessions.readWhy: The strongest case against the Sermon's morality, in Nietzsche's own words.

paras: The reader will have already surmised with what ease the priestly mode of valuation can branch off from the knightly aristocratic mode, and then develop into the very antithesis of the latter: special impetus is given to this opposition, by every occasion when the castes of the priests and warriors confront each other with mutual jealousy and cannot agree over the prize. The knightly-aristocratic "values" are based on a careful cult of the physical, on a flowering, rich, and even effervescing healthiness, that goes considerably beyond what is necessary for maintaining life, on war, adventure, the chase, the dance, the tourney--on everything, in fact, which is contained in strong, free, and joyous action. The priestly-aristocratic mode of valuation is--we have seen--based on other hypotheses: it is bad enough for this class when it is a question of war! Yet the priests are, as is notorious, the worst enemies--why? Because they are the weakest. Their weakness causes their hate to expand into a monstrous and sinister shape, a shape which is most crafty and most poisonous. The really great haters in the history of the world have always been priests, who are also the cleverest haters--in comparison with the cleverness of priestly revenge, every other piece of cleverness is practically negligible. Human history would be too fatuous for anything were it not for the cleverness imported into it by the weak--take at once the most important instance. All the world's efforts against the "aristocrats," the "mighty," the "masters," the "holders of power," are negligible by comparison with what has been accomplished against those classes by the Jews--the Jews, that priestly nation which eventually realised that the one method of effecting satisfaction on its enemies and tyrants was by means of a radical transvaluation of values, which was at the same time an act of the cleverest revenge.

Yet the method was only appropriate to a nation of priests, to a nation of the most jealously nursed priestly revengefulness. It was the Jews who, in opposition to the aristocratic equation (good = aristocratic = beautiful = happy = loved by the gods), dared with a terrifying logic to suggest the contrary equation, and indeed to maintain with the teeth of the most profound hatred (the hatred of weakness) this contrary equation, namely, "the wretched are alone the good; the poor, the weak, the lowly, are alone the good; the suffering, the needy, the sick, the loathsome, are the only ones who are pious, the only ones who are blessed, for them alone is salvation--but you, on the other hand, you aristocrats, you men of power, you are to all eternity the evil, the horrible, the covetous, the insatiate, the godless; eternally also shall you be the unblessed, the cursed, the damned!" We know who it was who reaped the heritage of this Jewish transvaluation. In the context of the monstrous and inordinately fateful initiative which the Jews have exhibited in connection with this most fundamental of all declarations of war, I remember the passage which came to my pen on another occasion (Beyond Good and Evil, Aph. 195)--that it was, in fact, with the Jews that the revolt of the slaves begins in the sphere of morals; that revolt which has behind it a history of two millennia, and which at the present day has only moved out of our sight, because it--has achieved victory.

But you understand this not? You have no eyes for a force which has taken two thousand years to achieve victory?--There is nothing wonderful in this: all lengthy processes are hard to see and to realise. But this is what took place: from the trunk of that tree of revenge and hate, Jewish hate,--that most profound and sublime hate, which creates ideals and changes old values to new creations, the like of which has never been on earth,--there grew a phenomenon which was equally incomparable, a new love, the most profound and sublime of all kinds of love;--and from what other trunk could it have grown? But beware of supposing that this love has soared on its upward growth, as in any way a real negation of that thirst for revenge, as an antithesis to the Jewish hate! No, the contrary is the truth! This love grew out of that hate, as its crown, as its triumphant crown, circling wider and wider amid the clarity and fulness of the sun, and pursuing in the very kingdom of light and height its goal of hatred, its victory, its spoil, its strategy, with the same intensity with which the roots of that tree of hate sank into everything which was deep and evil with increasing stability and increasing desire.

This Jesus of Nazareth, the incarnate gospel of love, this "Redeemer" bringing salvation and victory to the poor, the sick, the sinful--was he not really temptation in its most sinister and irresistible form, temptation to take the tortuous path to those very Jewish values and those very Jewish ideals? Has not Israel really obtained the final goal of its sublime revenge, by the tortuous paths of this "Redeemer," for all that he might pose as Israel's adversary and Israel's destroyer? Is it not due to the black magic of a really great policy of revenge, of a far-seeing, burrowing revenge, both acting and calculating with slowness, that Israel himself must repudiate before all the world the actual instrument of his own revenge and nail it to the cross, so that all the world--that is, all the enemies of Israel--could nibble without suspicion at this very bait? Could, moreover, any human mind with all its elaborate ingenuity invent a bait that was more truly dangerous? Anything that was even equivalent in the power of its seductive, intoxicating, defiling, and corrupting influence to that symbol of the holy cross, to that awful paradox of a "god on the cross," to that mystery of the unthinkable, supreme, and utter horror of the self-crucifixion of a god for the salvation of man? It is at least certain that sub hoc signo Israel, with its revenge and transvaluation of all values, has up to the present always triumphed again over all other ideals, over all more aristocratic ideals.

The revolt of the slaves in morals begins in the very principle of resentment becoming creative and giving birth to values--a resentment experienced by creatures who, deprived as they are of the proper outlet of action, are forced to find their compensation in an imaginary revenge. While every aristocratic morality springs from a triumphant affirmation of its own demands, the slave morality says "no" from the very outset to what is "outside itself," "different from itself," and "not itself": and this "no" is its creative deed. This volte-face of the valuing standpoint--this inevitable gravitation to the objective instead of back to the subjective--is typical of "resentment": the slave-morality requires as the condition of its existence an external and objective world, to employ physiological terminology, it requires objective stimuli to be capable of action at all--its action is fundamentally a reaction. The contrary is the case when we come to the aristocrat's system of values: it acts and grows spontaneously, it merely seeks its antithesis in order to pronounce a more grateful and exultant "yes" to its own self;--its negative conception, "low," "vulgar," "bad," is merely a pale late-born foil in comparison with its positive and fundamental conception (saturated as it is with life and passion), of "we aristocrats, we good ones, we beautiful ones, we happy ones."

When the resentment of the aristocratic man manifests itself, it fulfils and exhausts itself in an immediate reaction, and consequently instills no venom: on the other hand, it never manifests itself at all in countless instances, when in the case of the feeble and weak it would be inevitable. An inability to take seriously for any length of time their enemies, their disasters, their misdeeds--that is the sign of the full strong natures who possess a superfluity of moulding plastic force, that heals completely and produces forgetfulness: a good example of this in the modern world is Mirabeau, who had no memory for any insults and meannesses which were practised on him, and who was only incapable of forgiving because he forgot. Such a man indeed shakes off with a shrug many a worm which would have buried itself in another; it is only in characters like these that we see the possibility (supposing, of course, that there is such a possibility in the world) of the real "love of one's enemies." What respect for his enemies is found, forsooth, in an aristocratic man--and such a reverence is already a bridge to love! He insists on having his enemy to himself as his distinction. He tolerates no other enemy but a man in whose character there is nothing to despise and much to honour! On the other hand, imagine the "enemy" as the resentful man conceives him--and it is here exactly that we see his work, his creativeness; he has conceived "the evil enemy," the "evil one," and indeed that is the root idea from which he now evolves as a contrasting and corresponding figure a "good one," himself--his very self!

parts.author: Friedrich Nietzsche
parts.work: The Genealogy of Morals, First Essay
parts.ref: Nietzsche, The Genealogy of Morals, First Essay §7
parts.title: The revolt of the slaves
parts.context: Nietzsche wrote the Genealogy in the summer of 1887, in Sils-Maria in the Swiss Alps. In the sections before this one, he argues that 'good' first meant 'noble, powerful, happy': the word of the ruling class for itself. Here he describes how a priestly class turned this upside down. Translated by Horace B. Samuel (1913); the translation's italics are not shown.
parts.plain: Nietzsche says there are two kinds of aristocratic values. Warriors value strength, health, war, adventure and joyful action. Priests, who are weaker, come to hate the warriors, and their hatred is clever. The Jews, a nation of priests, took revenge on their powerful enemies by reversing values: only the poor, weak and suffering are good and blessed, and the powerful are evil and damned. This was the start of the 'revolt of the slaves' in morality, which has lasted two thousand years and has won.

commentary.on: The knightly-aristocratic "values" are based on a careful cult of the physical
commentary.text: Nietzsche's ideal: the Homeric warrior, strong, healthy, overflowing with life, delighting in war, the hunt and the dance. His 'good' means flourishing, not kindness.

commentary.on: Because they are the weakest. Their weakness causes their hate to expand into a monstrous and sinister shape
commentary.text: The heart of his psychology. The weak cannot fight, so their hatred goes underground and becomes clever. Revenge that cannot act openly finds another way.

commentary.on: "the wretched are alone the good; the poor, the weak, the lowly, are alone the good; the suffering, the needy, the sick, the loathsome, are the only ones who are pious, the only ones who are blessed
commentary.text: Read this beside the Beatitudes and Luke's blessings and woes from session 1. Nietzsche has put the Sermon's reversal in its harshest form: blessed are the poor, woe to the rich. He thinks it is a curse disguised as a blessing.

commentary.on: the Jews, that priestly nation
commentary.text: Nietzsche's language about the Jews here is dangerous, and was later abused. He means the Jewish priests and prophets as the authors of the reversal, which he half admires as a feat of genius. The lecture explains his own contempt for the antisemites of his day.

commentary.on: with the Jews that the revolt of the slaves begins in the sphere of morals
commentary.text: The phrase that gave the whole idea its name: the 'slave revolt in morals'. It has a history of two millennia, he says, and we no longer see it 'because it has achieved victory'. Our own sense that the meek should be protected is, for him, the proof.

parts.author: Friedrich Nietzsche
parts.work: The Genealogy of Morals, First Essay
parts.ref: Nietzsche, The Genealogy of Morals, First Essay §8
parts.title: A new love grown from hate
parts.context: The next section. Nietzsche now turns to Jesus and the cross. (Section 9, the voice of an imagined freethinker who replies to him, is left out.)
parts.plain: Nietzsche says: you cannot see it because it took two thousand years. From the tree of Jewish hatred grew a new love, the deepest ever. But this love was not the opposite of the hatred; it was its crown, its way of winning. Jesus, the gospel of love bringing salvation to the poor and sick, was the most seductive bait of all, and the image of 'God on the cross' has triumphed over every nobler ideal.

commentary.on: there grew a phenomenon which was equally incomparable, a new love, the most profound and sublime of all kinds of love
commentary.text: Nietzsche does not deny that Christian love is real, or even sublime. He grants its greatness. His claim is about its root.

commentary.on: This love grew out of that hate, as its crown
commentary.text: This is the charge in a sentence: Christian love is revenge in disguise. Loving your enemies, blessing those who curse you, is how the weak defeat the strong, by making strength itself look evil.

commentary.on: This Jesus of Nazareth, the incarnate gospel of love, this "Redeemer" bringing salvation and victory to the poor, the sick, the sinful
commentary.text: Note who Jesus is for, in Nietzsche's description: the poor, the sick, the sinful. He has read the Gospels accurately. He just values what he reads the other way round.

commentary.on: that awful paradox of a "god on the cross
commentary.text: For an ancient Greek or Roman, crucifixion was the death of slaves and rebels: the most shameful of all. To worship a crucified God was to turn every ancient value upside down. Paul knew it: 'Christ crucified: a stumbling block to Jews, and foolishness to Greeks' (1 Corinthians 1:23). On this, Nietzsche and Paul agree.

parts.author: Friedrich Nietzsche
parts.work: The Genealogy of Morals, First Essay
parts.ref: Nietzsche, The Genealogy of Morals, First Essay §10
parts.title: Resentment becomes creative
parts.context: Section 10, the centre of the argument. The cut in the middle, marked '…', leaves out a long passage on Greek words for the common people. Samuel translates Nietzsche's French word ressentiment as 'resentment'.
parts.plain: Nietzsche says the slave revolt begins when resentment becomes creative and makes values. The noble say 'yes' to themselves first; the slave morality starts by saying 'no' to others, to what is different. The strong man does not nurse grudges: he reacts at once and forgets. Only such a man can really respect, and even love, his enemy. The resentful man invents 'the evil enemy', and then makes himself 'the good one' by contrast.

commentary.on: The revolt of the slaves in morals begins in the very principle of resentment becoming creative and giving birth to values
commentary.text: Resentment (ressentiment) is the key term: a lasting, bitter hatred felt by those who cannot act on it. Nietzsche's claim is that values like humility, patience and love of enemies are not virtues discovered but weapons invented by the powerless.

commentary.on: the slave morality says "no" from the very outset to what is "outside itself,"
commentary.text: Noble morality starts with 'we are good'; 'bad' is an afterthought. Slave morality starts with 'they are evil'; 'good' is just 'not them'. Its action is 'fundamentally a reaction'.

commentary.on: it is only in characters like these that we see the possibility (supposing, of course, that there is such a possibility in the world) of the real "love of one's enemies."
commentary.text: A brilliant twist. Nietzsche quotes the Sermon against itself: only the strong, who can forget insults, could really love their enemies. The weak who claim to love their enemies are secretly waiting for God to punish them.

commentary.on: he has conceived "the evil enemy," the "evil one," and indeed that is the root idea from which he now evolves as a contrasting and corresponding figure a "good one," himself
commentary.text: This is the deepest point of the charge, and the hardest to dismiss: a morality can make us feel good about ourselves by making others evil. Every honest Christian can recognise the temptation. The question is whether the Sermon gives in to it, or warns against it.

read.work: The Genealogy of Morals, First Essay

paras: Mary said,
“My soul magnifies the Lord.
My spirit has rejoiced in God my Savior,

for he has looked at the humble state of his servant.
For behold, from now on, all generations will call me blessed.

For he who is mighty has done great things for me.
Holy is his name.
His mercy is for generations of generations on those who fear him.

He has shown strength with his arm.
He has scattered the proud in the imagination of their hearts.

He has put down princes from their thrones,
and has exalted the lowly.

He has filled the hungry with good things.
He has sent the rich away empty.
He has given help to Israel, his servant, that he might remember mercy,

as he spoke to our fathers,
to Abraham and his offspring forever.”

parts.title: Mary's song
parts.context: Luke's Gospel, chapter 1. Mary, a young woman from Nazareth, has been told she will bear the Messiah. She visits her relative Elizabeth and sings this song. It echoes the song of Hannah in 1 Samuel 2:1–10. It has been sung at evening prayer in churches every day for more than a thousand years.

commentary.on: for he has looked at the humble state of his servant
commentary.text: The song begins with God noticing a poor, unimportant woman: 'servant' is the word for a slave girl. This is the reversal from below, but its first note is not hatred; it is joy and wonder.

commentary.on: He has scattered the proud in the imagination of their hearts. He has put down princes from their thrones, and has exalted the lowly.
commentary.text: Here is Nietzsche's 'transvaluation' in the Bible's own words. It is a revolutionary song: some governments have banned its public singing. Nietzsche is right that the Bible takes the side of the lowly against the proud.

commentary.on: He has filled the hungry with good things. He has sent the rich away empty.
commentary.text: The same pairing as Luke's blessings and woes. But notice who acts: God, not the lowly. Mary does not plan revenge. She trusts God to judge, which is what Paul means by 'give place to God's wrath' (Romans 12:19). Nietzsche would call that revenge postponed; others call it the end of revenge.

commentary.on: that he might remember mercy, as he spoke to our fathers, to Abraham and his offspring forever.
commentary.text: The song ends with mercy and promise, not with the enemy's ruin. That is a key point in the reply to Nietzsche: the reversal is grounded in God's faithfulness, not in hatred of the strong.

compare.why: The Magnificat is the song Luke gives to Mary when she is expecting Jesus. It celebrates the very reversal Nietzsche describes. Is it resentment, or something else?
compare.title: He has put down princes

paras: Nietzsche's case can be put in four steps. First, values have a history: 'good' and 'evil' were not handed down from heaven but made by people, for reasons. Second, the original 'good' was the self-affirmation of the strong: health, pride, excellence. Third, the weak, unable to beat the strong, took revenge in the only way they could: by calling strength evil and weakness good. Meekness, patience, humility, love of enemies and pity are the virtues of people who cannot fight, dressed up as moral superiority. Fourth, this 'slave morality' won, through Christianity, and now shapes even atheists and democrats, who still believe the weak have special worth.

The cost, he thought, was enormous. A morality that blesses weakness keeps humanity small, sick and guilty, suspicious of its own strength and joy. In The Antichrist (written 1888, published 1895) he calls pity the practice of nihilism, because it preserves what life itself would discard, and calls Christianity the one great curse on humanity.
sections.key: Values have a history; 'good' first meant strong; the weak took revenge by calling strength evil; their 'slave morality' won through Christianity, and keeps humanity small.

paras: This is not a cheap objection. It fits the evidence surprisingly well. Christianity did grow first among the poor, slaves and women, as its critic Celsus and its own apostle Paul both said (1 Corinthians 1:26). The Beatitudes and the Magnificat do bless the lowly and humble the proud. And Christians have often been exactly what Nietzsche described: resentful, self-righteous, delighting in the thought of their enemies' punishment. The early Christian writer Tertullian, around 200, looked forward to watching his persecutors burn on the last day (On the Spectacles 30).

Nietzsche's psychology also contains a real insight that Christians should take seriously: humility and love can be faked. 'Love your enemies' can be a mask for helpless hatred. Jesus himself warned against religion done to be seen (session 4), and against the hypocrite with a beam in his own eye (session 5).
sections.key: The charge fits real evidence: Christianity grew among the weak, blesses the lowly, and Christians have often been resentful. Love can be faked.

sections.h: Nietzsche was right about the revolution
paras: The historian Tom Holland, in Dominion (2019), argues that Nietzsche saw something most modern people miss. Holland began as a lover of the classical world, like Nietzsche, and came to see how alien its values were: the casual cruelty, the exposure of unwanted babies, the contempt for the weak. Our instinct that every person has equal worth, that the victim deserves sympathy, that the powerful should serve, did not come from Greece or Rome. In Holland's account, it came from Christianity, and above all from the cross.

So Nietzsche was right that a revolution happened, and that it won so completely that we take it for granted. Even secular human rights, Holland argues, are Christian values that have forgotten their origin. On the facts, Holland and Nietzsche agree. They disagree on the verdict: Nietzsche thought it a disaster; Holland, and most people who think about it, find it hard to wish the old world back.
sections.key: Tom Holland's Dominion (2019) agrees with Nietzsche that Christianity overturned ancient values so completely we take it for granted; he judges the change differently.

paras: The German philosopher Max Scheler (1874–1928), in his essay Ressentiment (1912, revised 1915), took Nietzsche more seriously than most of his critics. He agreed that resentment is real and has shaped much of modern morality: the levelling-down kind of humanitarianism that hates excellence. But he argued that Nietzsche got Christian love exactly wrong.

Ancient love, Scheler said, was a striving upwards: the lower loving the higher, wanting what it lacked. Christian love reverses the direction. It is the higher bending down to the lower, out of fullness, not need: God becoming man, the master washing his servants' feet. That is not the reflex of the weak; it is the generosity of the strong. Resentment cannot love its enemy; it can only pretend. Real love of enemies requires the very security Nietzsche admired. On this reading, the Sermon does not ask the weak to hide their hatred, but asks everyone to love from a strength that comes from God.
sections.key: Max Scheler (1912) agreed resentment is real, but argued Christian love is the strong bending down from fullness, not the weak reacting from need.

paras: Martin Luther King, whom you met in session 3, read Nietzsche as a young theology student. In 'Pilgrimage to Nonviolence' he says Nietzsche's glorification of power, and his scorn for Christian love as weakness, nearly persuaded him that love could only work between individuals, never between groups facing injustice. Gandhi changed his mind.

King's answer was his life. The title of his book of sermons, Strength to Love (1963), is a reply to Nietzsche in three words. Nonviolent resistance in Montgomery and Birmingham was not the slave's secret resentment but open, disciplined, costly courage: facing dogs, fire hoses and prison without striking back and without hating. The French thinker René Girard added another angle in I See Satan Fall Like Lightning (1999): Nietzsche saw, more clearly than most Christians, that the Bible takes the side of the victim against the crowd, and he chose the crowd.
sections.key: King, tempted by Nietzsche as a student, answered with 'strength to love': open, costly, nonviolent courage. Girard said Nietzsche saw the Bible takes the victim's side.

paras: Nietzsche's language about 'Jewish hate' in these sections needs a word. He was not an antisemite in the political sense; he despised the antisemitic movement of his day, broke with his publisher partly over it, and was appalled when his sister married the antisemitic agitator Bernhard Förster. In other books he praised the Jews highly. Here he is describing what he sees as the Jewish priests' and prophets' genius for revaluing values, which he credits, with mixed horror and admiration, to Judaism and Christianity alike.

But words like these were later twisted. After his death, his sister Elisabeth Förster-Nietzsche controlled his papers and promoted him to German nationalists, and the Nazis claimed him. Reading him fairly means neither excusing his rhetoric nor letting his abusers define him. And it means noticing that the values he attacks, the dignity of the weak and the stranger, are the ones that stood against what was later done in his name.
sections.key: Nietzsche despised the antisemites of his day, but his rhetoric was later twisted by his sister and the Nazis; the values he attacked are those that resisted them.

refs: Friedrich Nietzsche, The Genealogy of Morals (1887), First Essay §§7–10, tr. Horace B. Samuel (1913); The Gay Science (1882) §125; Beyond Good and Evil (1886) §195; The Antichrist (1888, published 1895) §§5–7, 62.
Luke 1:46–55; 1 Samuel 2:1–10; 1 Corinthians 1:23–28; Romans 12:19; Origen, Against Celsus III.44; Tertullian, On the Spectacles 30; Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.3.
Max Scheler, Ressentiment (Das Ressentiment im Aufbau der Moralen, 1912; rev. 1915).
Tom Holland, Dominion: The Making of the Western Mind (2019); René Girard, I See Satan Fall Like Lightning (1999).

Martin Luther King Jr., Stride Toward Freedom (1958), 'Pilgrimage to Nonviolence'; Strength to Love (1963). On Nietzsche and antisemitism: Walter Kaufmann, Nietzsche: Philosopher, Psychologist, Antichrist (1950; 4th ed. 1974).

debate.question: Is the Sermon on the Mount a morality of the weak?

positions.name: Yes: it is resentment made holy
positions.who: Friedrich Nietzsche; in a different way, the ancient critic Celsus
positions.view: The Sermon blesses weakness and condemns strength. Its love of enemies is revenge postponed to the last judgement. It has kept humanity small, guilty and sick, and we should move 'beyond good and evil' to values that affirm life and strength.
positions.evidence: The Beatitudes and woes; the Magnificat; the early Church's social make-up (1 Corinthians 1:26); Christian delight in the damnation of enemies (Tertullian).

positions.name: Nietzsche was right about the revolution, wrong about its value
positions.who: Tom Holland; many historians
positions.view: Christianity did overturn the values of Greece and Rome, so completely that even secular people now share them. But the new values (the dignity of the weak, care for the sick, the equal worth of every person) were a liberation, not a sickness.
positions.evidence: The ancient acceptance of infanticide and slavery; the Christian invention of hospitals and care for the poor; the Christian roots of human rights.

positions.name: It is the morality of the strongest
positions.who: Max Scheler; Martin Luther King Jr.; René Girard
positions.view: Real love of enemies requires great strength: it flows from fullness, not need. The Sermon asks not for hidden resentment but for open, costly, nonviolent courage. Resentment is what it warns against.
positions.evidence: Scheler's analysis of love bending down; the civil rights movement; Jesus's own conduct before Pilate; the Sermon's warnings against hypocrisy and judging.

debate.agree: All agree that the Sermon overturned the values of the ancient world, and that a love that is really hidden hatred is a counterfeit.

look.why: No painting in the gallery's free collection sets a classical hero beside a humble saint. Instead, here is the world Nietzsche admired. Peter Paul Rubens painted the Roman general Germanicus (15 BC–AD 19) and his wife Agrippina around 1614, side by side in profile: a noble Roman pair, the kind of people the ancient world called 'good'. Put it beside the crucified God of Nietzsche's §8, and the 'transvaluation' becomes visible.
points: A man and a woman are shown from the shoulders up, both in profile facing our left, against a dark background.
The woman, closer to us, overlaps the man; she has pale skin, faintly blushed cheeks and a straight nose.
Her reddish-gold hair is braided across the crown and circled with a string of pearls, with a red jewel over her forehead.
The man behind her has a tan complexion, a long, bumped nose and auburn hair, and wears a burgundy-red robe.
They sit behind a stone ledge; light from the front makes a halo-like glow on the midnight-blue background.
The number '19' is painted in the lower left corner.

music.why: Bach set Mary's song in Leipzig in the 1720s. Listen for 'Deposuit potentes', 'He has put down the mighty': the reversal Nietzsche feared, sung with joy, not resentment.

think.why: Nietzsche thought Christianity made people weak; Holland that it gave every individual infinite worth. See the debate.

learn.why: Thomas à Kempis's line is everything Nietzsche despised, and everything the Sermon asks: humility that does not need to be seen. Ask whether it is weakness or freedom.

check.q: What does Nietzsche mean by the 'slave revolt in morals'?
options: The abolition of slavery in the nineteenth century
A real uprising of slaves in the Roman empire
Christianity's support for slavery
The reversal by which the weak, unable to defeat the strong, called strength evil and weakness good, through Judaism and then Christianity
check.why: It is a revolt of values, not of arms: 'the poor, the weak, the lowly, are alone the good'.

check.q: What is 'resentment' (ressentiment) in Nietzsche's argument?
options: A virtue of the strong
The lasting, hidden hatred of those who cannot act on it, which becomes creative and invents values
Ordinary anger that passes quickly
Christian forgiveness
check.why: The strong react and forget; the weak brood, and their brooding 'gives birth to values'.

check.q: Why does Nietzsche say only the strong can really love their enemies?
options: Because the strong forget insults and respect worthy enemies, while the weak who claim to love their enemies secretly want them punished
Because the strong have no enemies
Because the Sermon says so
Because love is a weakness
check.why: He turns 'love your enemies' against the Christians who preach it.

check.q: On what point do Nietzsche and the historian Tom Holland agree?
options: That Rome was kinder than Christianity
That Christianity overturned the values of the ancient world so thoroughly that even modern secular people take its values for granted
That Christianity is a curse
That the Sermon was never preached
check.why: They agree on the facts of the revolution, and disagree on whether it was good.

check.q: What is Max Scheler's main reply to Nietzsche?
options: That resentment does not exist
That the Beatitudes were added later
That Nietzsche was not a real philosopher
That Christian love is the strong bending down to the weak from fullness, not the weak reacting from need; real love of enemies is impossible for resentment
check.why: Scheler grants that resentment shapes much modern morality, but not Christian love.

check.q: Which detail in the Magnificat best answers the charge that it is resentment?
options: Mary was rich
It mentions Abraham
God, not the lowly, acts; and the song begins in joy and ends in mercy and promise, not in the enemy's ruin
It is sung in Latin
check.why: Nietzsche would call this revenge postponed; but its tone and its ending point to trust and mercy rather than hatred.

tutorial.question: Assess Nietzsche's charge that Christian ethics is a 'slave morality'.
tutorial.approach: State the charge at full strength, in Nietzsche's own terms: the two modes of valuation, resentment, the revolt that won. Show where it fits the evidence. Then weigh the replies: Holland on the revolution, Scheler on love from strength, King's nonviolence. Use the Beatitudes and the Magnificat. End with your own verdict.
strong: States the charge accurately, with quotations from §§7, 8 and 10.
Explains ressentiment and the reversal of 'good and bad' into 'good and evil'.
Admits where the charge fits: early Christian membership, Christian resentment, faked love.
Uses Holland and Scheler fairly.
Uses the Magnificat or the Beatitudes as a test case.
Notes the misuse of Nietzsche and his own view of antisemitism.

reading.author: Tom Holland
reading.title: Dominion: The Making of the Western Mind
reading.why: A historian's account of how Christianity overturned ancient values, starting from Nietzsche's insight.

reading.author: Walter Kaufmann
reading.title: Nietzsche: Philosopher, Psychologist, Antichrist
reading.why: The book that rescued Nietzsche from his Nazi misreaders.

reading.author: Max Scheler
reading.title: Ressentiment
reading.why: The classic philosophical reply to Nietzsche's charge.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: notice one moment when you feel quietly superior to someone, morally or otherwise. Ask honestly whether it is love or resentment. Then do one generous thing for that person, from strength, not duty.
sessions.reflect: Is your kindness ever a disguise? What would love from strength look like for you?
takeaways: Nietzsche argued that the Sermon's values were a 'slave revolt': the weak, driven by resentment, called strength evil and weakness good, and won.
He was right that Christianity overturned the ancient world's values; Holland argues that even secular modern morality inherits that revolution.
Scheler, King and Girard reply that real love of enemies flows from strength and fullness, not resentment, and that the Bible takes the victim's side.

sessions.title: Can anyone live this? The verdict
sessions.line: A rich young man asks what he still lacks and goes away sad. 'Who then can be saved?' 'With God all things are possible.'
sessions.plain: The verdict first: the Sermon on the Mount is meant to be lived, not admired from a distance, and no one lives it alone. Christians have read it as a law to obey, an ideal to aim at, a mirror that shows our need of grace, and the life of God's kingdom breaking in. They agree that it is lived by God's help, in a community, over a lifetime. This session reads a story in which Jesus tells a good man exactly what perfection would cost, sets beside it a letter about love in deed and Augustine's prayer for grace, and gives the journey's answer.
sessions.why: Six sessions have read the Sermon and heard Nietzsche's case against it. One question remains, the one everyone asks: can anyone actually live this? Matthew's own Gospel answers it in a story later in the book.
answers: Is the Sermon meant literally?
Can anyone actually live it?
How do the Christian traditions read it differently?
Can the Sermon guide a state, or only a person?
sessions.finding: The traditions read the Sermon as law, as ideal, as mirror and as the life of the kingdom; all agree it is meant to be lived with grace, not achieved alone.

paras: Here is the answer this journey reaches, so that you can test it as you read. The Sermon on the Mount is meant to be lived: Jesus ends it by saying that only those who do his words build on rock. It is also beyond anyone's unaided strength: 'be perfect, as your Father in heaven is perfect.' Both are true at once. The Christian traditions differ on how to hold them together, but all say the same thing at the root: the Sermon is lived by grace, God's help given freely, within a community, and over a lifetime of practice and failure and starting again.
background.key: The verdict: the Sermon is meant to be lived, and is beyond unaided strength; it is lived by grace, in community, over a lifetime.

paras: The Sermon opened with blessing (session 1), took the law to the heart (session 2), forbade revenge and commanded love of enemies (session 3), moved religion into the secret place and asked for trust (session 4), and ended with the choice between two houses (session 5). Nietzsche called it the revenge of the weak; his critics answered that it asks for the strongest love there is (session 6).

Through it all one question has kept returning. No one, it seems, has ever fully kept the Sermon: never angry, never lustful, never anxious, loving every enemy. Gandhi, who loved it, said it went straight to his heart, but he never became a Christian. If no one keeps it, what is it for?
background.key: Six sessions have read the Sermon and its critic; the remaining question is whether anyone can live it, and if not, what it is for.

paras: The main reading is not from the Sermon but from later in Matthew (19:16–26): a rich young man asks Jesus what good thing he must do. He has kept the commandments; Jesus tells him what 'perfect' would mean for him. When the disciples ask 'Who then can be saved?', Jesus gives the answer that underlies every Christian reading of the Sermon.

The comparison has two parts. The First Letter of John, written to early Christians around AD 100, says love is shown 'in deed and truth'. And Augustine, whose commentary on the Sermon you read in sessions 1 and 3, prays in his Confessions (around 400): 'Give what Thou enjoinest, and enjoin what Thou wilt.'
background.key: The rich young man (Matthew 19) and 'with God all things are possible'; then 1 John on love in deed, and Augustine's prayer for grace.

before: What does the young man say he has already done? What does he still lack?
What does 'perfect' mean here? Compare Matthew 5:48.
What is the disciples' reaction, and Jesus's answer?
sessions.readWhy: A good man asks how far he must go, and Jesus answers the question behind the whole Sermon.

paras: Behold, one came to him and said, “Good teacher, what good thing shall I do, that I may have eternal life?”
He said to him, “Why do you call me good? No one is good but one, that is, God. But if you want to enter into life, keep the commandments.”
He said to him, “Which ones?”
Jesus said, “ ‘You shall not murder.’ ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ ‘You shall not steal.’ ‘You shall not offer false testimony.’
‘Honor your father and your mother.’ And, ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ ”
The young man said to him, “All these things I have observed from my youth. What do I still lack?”
Jesus said to him, “If you want to be perfect, go, sell what you have, and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.”
But when the young man heard the saying, he went away sad, for he was one who had great possessions.
Jesus said to his disciples, “Most certainly I say to you, a rich man will enter into the Kingdom of Heaven with difficulty.
Again I tell you, it is easier for a camel to go through a needle’s eye, than for a rich man to enter into God’s Kingdom.”
When the disciples heard it, they were exceedingly astonished, saying, “Who then can be saved?”
Looking at them, Jesus said, “With men this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.”

parts.title: What do I still lack?
parts.context: Matthew 19. Jesus has left Galilee and is travelling towards Jerusalem, where he will be crucified. A young man, rich and devout, comes to him with a question about eternal life: the life of the age to come, of God's kingdom.

commentary.on: Good teacher, what good thing shall I do, that I may have eternal life?
commentary.text: The young man asks the Sermon's question: what must I do? He is sincere. He wants to build on rock.

commentary.on: But if you want to enter into life, keep the commandments.
commentary.text: Jesus's first answer is the law, as in 5:17: not a letter of it passes away. He lists commandments about other people from the Ten Commandments, and adds Leviticus 19:18, 'love your neighbour as yourself'.

commentary.on: All these things I have observed from my youth. What do I still lack?
commentary.text: A remarkable answer, and probably honest by the standards of the law. Yet he senses something missing. That is exactly the gap the Sermon opens between keeping the commandments and the 'righteousness that exceeds'.

commentary.on: If you want to be perfect, go, sell what you have, and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.
commentary.text: 'Perfect' is the same word as in 5:48, teleios: whole, complete. For this man, completeness means giving up the thing that holds his heart ('where your treasure is', 6:21) and following Jesus. The final command is not 'sell' but 'follow me': the Sermon is lived in company with its teacher.

commentary.on: he went away sad, for he was one who had great possessions.
commentary.text: He does not argue. He simply cannot. 'You can't serve both God and Mammon' (6:24) has become a real choice in a real life, and he chooses the other master, sadly.

commentary.on: Who then can be saved?
commentary.text: The disciples are 'exceedingly astonished'. In their world, wealth was often seen as a sign of God's blessing. If this good, rich man cannot make it, who can? It is the question every honest reader of the Sermon eventually asks.

commentary.on: With men this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.
commentary.text: The heart of the verdict. Jesus does not lower the bar. He says that what human beings cannot do, God can do in them. Every Christian reading of the Sermon turns on this sentence.

paras: For this is the message which you heard from the beginning, that we should love one another;
unlike Cain, who was of the evil one, and killed his brother. Why did he kill him? Because his deeds were evil, and his brother’s righteous.
Don’t be surprised, my brothers, if the world hates you.
We know that we have passed out of death into life, because we love the brothers. He who doesn’t love his brother remains in death.
Whoever hates his brother is a murderer, and you know that no murderer has eternal life remaining in him.
By this we know love, because he laid down his life for us. And we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers.
But whoever has the world’s goods and sees his brother in need, then closes his heart of compassion against him, how does God’s love remain in him?
My little children, let’s not love in word only, or with the tongue only, but in deed and truth.

And all my hope is no where but in Thy exceeding great mercy. Give what Thou enjoinest, and enjoin what Thou wilt. Thou enjoinest us continency; and when I knew, saith one, that no man can be continent, unless God give it, this also was a part of wisdom to know whose gift she is. By continency verily are we bound up and brought back into One, whence we were dissipated into many. For too little doth he love Thee, who loves any thing with Thee, which he loveth not for Thee. O love, who ever burnest and never consumest! O charity, my God, kindle me. Thou enjoinest continency: give me what Thou enjoinest, and enjoin what Thou wilt.

parts.title: Love in deed and truth
parts.context: The First Letter of John was written around AD 100, probably in Ephesus, to Christian communities troubled by division. Tradition links it to the apostle John; many scholars think it comes from a circle of his followers.

commentary.on: Whoever hates his brother is a murderer
commentary.text: The first antithesis of the Sermon in one sentence: hatred is murder in the heart (Matthew 5:21–22).

commentary.on: By this we know love, because he laid down his life for us.
commentary.text: John defines love not by a feeling or a rule but by an act: Jesus's death. The Sermon's demand is answered by the one who gave it, who lived it to the end.

commentary.on: But whoever has the world’s goods and sees his brother in need, then closes his heart of compassion against him, how does God’s love remain in him?
commentary.text: Love has an address. It is tested by a brother or sister in need, as the rich young man was tested. John is as concrete as the Sermon.

commentary.on: let’s not love in word only, or with the tongue only, but in deed and truth.
commentary.text: The house on the rock, again: not hearing but doing. This line is this session's words to learn.

parts.author: Augustine
parts.title: Give what Thou enjoinest
parts.context: Augustine wrote his Confessions around AD 397–400, as bishop of Hippo, a few years after his commentary on the Sermon. Book X looks honestly at his present struggles. 'Continency' means self-control. 'Saith one' refers to Wisdom 8:21, which Augustine's Bible read as 'no one can be continent, unless God give it'. Translated by E. B. Pusey (1838).
parts.plain: Augustine says all his hope is in God's mercy. God commands self-control, and no one has it unless God gives it. So he prays: give me what you command, and then command whatever you like. He asks God's love to set him on fire.

commentary.on: Give what Thou enjoinest, and enjoin what Thou wilt.
commentary.text: The most famous prayer in the Confessions. Augustine does not ask God to lower his commands. He asks God to give the power to keep them. Around 405, a British monk in Rome, Pelagius, was outraged when he heard it: surely, he thought, if God commands something, we must be able to do it ourselves. The great argument between them, about grace and human effort, shaped Western Christianity.

commentary.on: no man can be continent, unless God give it
commentary.text: This is the logic of 'with God all things are possible'. What the Sermon asks is God's gift before it is our achievement.

commentary.on: O love, who ever burnest and never consumest! O charity, my God, kindle me.
commentary.text: For Augustine, living the Sermon is not a matter of willpower but of love: when God's love catches fire in a person, they begin to want what he commands.

compare.author: Augustine
compare.why: Two short texts that hold together the Sermon's demand and the grace to meet it: John on love in action, and Augustine's prayer.
compare.title: In deed and truth, and by grace

sections.h: Five ways of reading the Sermon
paras: Christians agree that the Sermon matters. They have disagreed for two thousand years about how it applies. The main readings are set out below. Many Christians hold more than one.

None of them says the Sermon does not matter, or that it is only for saints. They differ on whether it is a law for everyone, a call for some, a mirror for all, a guide for the forgiven, or the shape of a life being made new.

rows: Commands for all (precepts), and a call to some to go further (counsels of poverty, chastity and obedience), as in the religious orders
God's law at full strength, showing that no one can keep it and driving us to Christ for forgiveness; then a guide for life in the 'kingdom' of the heart
The law's true meaning, restored by Christ, as the rule of life for those already saved by grace (the 'third use' of the law)
A way of life to be followed literally by every disciple, in a community set apart: no oaths, no violence, shared goods
The way of being transformed into God's likeness by grace (theosis); the Beatitudes are sung at the Divine Liturgy
table.note: A sixth view, Albert Schweitzer's 'interim ethic' (1906), held that Jesus expected the world to end soon, so the Sermon was meant for a short time only; few scholars now hold it in that form.

sections.key: Catholics read precepts and counsels; Lutherans a mirror; the Reformed a guide for the forgiven; Anabaptists a literal way; the Orthodox the way of theosis.

paras: The rich young man's story shaped one of the oldest readings. Around AD 270, a young Egyptian called Antony heard Matthew 19:21 read in church: 'If you want to be perfect, go, sell what you have.' He took it as addressed to him, gave away his family's land and went into the desert. His life, written by Athanasius around 360, inspired the monastic movement.

From this grew the Catholic distinction, set out by Thomas Aquinas in the thirteenth century (Summa Theologiae I-II, question 108, article 4): some commands are 'precepts', binding on everyone, such as loving God and neighbour; others are 'counsels', invitations to a fuller way, such as poverty, chastity and obedience, taken up in the religious orders. Protestant critics objected that this created two classes of Christian. The Second Vatican Council (Lumen Gentium 40, 1964) stressed that all Christians are called to holiness.
sections.key: Antony heard Matthew 19:21 and went into the desert; Aquinas distinguished precepts for all and counsels for some; Vatican II called all to holiness.

paras: Martin Luther (1483–1546) preached on the Sermon in Wittenberg in 1530–32. For him, one main purpose of God's law is to show us our sin, like a mirror: the Sermon's demands, taken seriously, convince everyone that they cannot be saved by their own goodness, and drive them to Christ, who forgives freely. This is the 'second use' of the law in Lutheran theology.

Luther also insisted, against the Anabaptists, that the Sermon speaks to a Christian as a person, not to the state: a Christian may suffer wrong himself, but a judge or prince must protect others (session 3). Critics, including Lutherans like Dietrich Bonhoeffer, worried that this could let Christians admire the Sermon and never live it. Defenders reply that Luther meant the forgiven to live it gladly, not to earn anything by it.
sections.key: Luther read the Sermon as a mirror showing our need of grace, and as speaking to persons rather than the state; critics feared it excused not living it.

paras: Dietrich Bonhoeffer (1906–1945), a German Lutheran pastor and theologian, wrote Discipleship (Nachfolge) in 1937, while running an underground seminary for the Confessing Church, which opposed Nazi control of the churches. Most of the book is a commentary on the Sermon on the Mount.

Its most famous idea, in our own words, is the difference between 'cheap grace' and 'costly grace'. Cheap grace is forgiveness without repentance, grace without following Jesus: a comfortable doctrine that asks nothing. Costly grace is the call to follow Jesus, which costs a person their life and gives them true life. Bonhoeffer argued that only those who believe obey, and only those who obey truly believe: faith and doing cannot be separated. He was arrested in 1943 for links to the plot against Hitler, and hanged at Flossenbürg on 9 April 1945, weeks before the war ended.
sections.key: Bonhoeffer's Discipleship (1937), a commentary on the Sermon, attacked 'cheap grace' without following; he was hanged by the Nazis in April 1945.

sections.h: Can the Sermon guide a state?
paras: Tolstoy said yes, and that the state's violence must be abandoned. Luther said no: the Sermon is for persons, and the state must bear the sword. The German sociologist Max Weber, in his lecture 'Politics as a Vocation' (1919), put the dilemma sharply: the ethic of the Sermon is an absolute ethic, which asks only whether an act is right; politics requires an ethic of responsibility, which must answer for consequences, including the use of force.

Most Christians have taken a middle path. A state cannot turn the other cheek on behalf of its citizens. But the Sermon has shaped states anyway: through Christians who brought mercy into law, from the abolition of gladiatorial games to modern prison reform; through movements that used its methods, in India and in the American South; and through the idea, now built into law, that power is for service. The Sermon is not a constitution. It has been a conscience.
sections.key: Tolstoy said the Sermon rules out state force; Luther and Weber said politics needs another ethic. In practice it has worked on states as a conscience, not a constitution.

paras: So, can anyone live this? Not perfectly, and not alone: on that the traditions agree, and so does the Sermon, which begins with blessing on the poor in spirit and puts the prayer 'forgive us our debts' at its centre. Christianity has always said that the person who prays the Sermon's prayer is someone who has not yet kept the Sermon's law.

But it is meant to be lived, not admired. Its demands are concrete: make peace before you worship, give in secret, pray for an enemy by name, do not judge. Each can be started today. Christians have lived them, imperfectly but really: monks and Quakers, Wesley's Methodists and Bonhoeffer's seminarians, King's marchers and countless ordinary people. They have done it by grace ('with God all things are possible'), together ('come, follow me') and by practice, day by day ('give us today our daily bread'). That is the journey's answer: the Sermon is not a ladder to heaven, but the shape of a life made new.
sections.key: No one lives the Sermon perfectly or alone; but it is meant to be lived, by grace, together and by daily practice, as many have: the shape of a life made new.

refs: Augustine, Confessions X.29 (tr. E. B. Pusey, 1838); On the Gift of Perseverance 20.53 (Pelagius's reaction); Athanasius, Life of Antony 2.

Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I-II q. 108 a. 4; Second Vatican Council, Lumen Gentium 40 (1964); Martin Luther, Sermons on Matthew 5–7 (1530–32); John Calvin, Institutes of the Christian Religion II.7.12 (the third use of the law); Schleitheim Confession (1527).
Albert Schweitzer, The Quest of the Historical Jesus (1906); Dietrich Bonhoeffer, Discipleship (1937); Max Weber, 'Politics as a Vocation' (1919).
Mohandas K. Gandhi, An Autobiography (1927–29), part I, chapter 20; Clarence Bauman, The Sermon on the Mount: The Modern Quest for Its Meaning (1985).

debate.question: What is the Sermon on the Mount for?

positions.name: A law to be obeyed, literally
positions.who: Anabaptists, Mennonites and Quakers; Tolstoy
positions.view: Jesus meant his words to be done. Every disciple should refuse oaths and violence, give freely and love enemies, in a community that lives differently from the world. To call it impossible is to excuse disobedience.
positions.evidence: 'Everyone who hears these words of mine, and does them'; the Amish forgiveness of the gunman at Nickel Mines (2006); centuries of peace-church witness.

positions.name: A mirror that shows our need
positions.who: Martin Luther and much Lutheran tradition
positions.view: The Sermon shows God's will at full strength. No one keeps it, so it drives us to Christ for forgiveness; then the forgiven begin to live it gladly, without trying to earn anything.
positions.evidence: 'Be perfect, as your Father is perfect'; the Lord's Prayer's 'forgive us our debts'; Augustine's 'give what Thou enjoinest'.

positions.name: The life of the kingdom, by grace
positions.who: Catholic and Orthodox tradition; Bonhoeffer; many modern scholars such as Dale Allison
positions.view: The Sermon describes the life of God's kingdom, which begins now in those who follow Jesus. It is neither a law kept by willpower nor an impossible ideal, but a way of life God makes possible, learned in community over a lifetime.
positions.evidence: 'With God all things are possible'; 'come, follow me'; the Orthodox singing of the Beatitudes in the liturgy; Bonhoeffer's costly grace.

debate.agree: All agree that the Sermon is Jesus's own teaching, that no one keeps it perfectly, and that it is meant to change how Christians actually live.

look.why: Antony of Egypt heard the words of today's reading, 'If you want to be perfect, go, sell what you have', and did it: around 270 he gave away his land and went into the desert. The Sienese painter known as the Master of the Osservanza painted this panel of his later life around 1430–35: the old hermit, travelling to meet Paul, another hermit. It shows the Sermon's demand lived for a lifetime, slowly, on foot.
points: Saint Antony appears three times along a path that winds from the lower right around hills and trees into the distance.
Each time he has a long white beard, a halo, bare feet and a black monk's robe, with a coral-pink cloak.
Closest to us, at the mouth of a dark cave, he embraces a bearded man with long, curly blond hair in cream-white robes, also with a halo; two walking sticks lie at their feet.
Further along the path, on a ridge, he meets a centaur holding a palm frond, and raises one hand.
In the distance on the left he walks with a stick, his pink robe hanging over a second stick on his shoulder.
A sliver of sky is painted gold above the trees, and pale red shapes in the distance could be a building, perhaps a church.

music.why: 'Where charity and love are, God is there': an ancient chant sung on Maundy Thursday as feet are washed. It is the Sermon lived, by grace, in a community.

think.why: The verdict says the Sermon is learned by practice. See what Christians and researchers say about whether practice changes us.

learn.why: One line that sums up the whole journey: love is something done.

check.q: Why does the rich young man's story matter for reading the Sermon?
options: Because it shows a sincere law-keeper meeting the Sermon's call to be 'perfect', failing, and Jesus answering 'with God all things are possible'
Because it shows Jesus rejecting the commandments
Because it proves that only the poor can be saved
Because it is part of the Sermon
check.why: It dramatises the gap between keeping the commandments and the Sermon's 'more', and gives the answer: God's power.

check.q: What does Jesus mean by 'If you want to be perfect' in Matthew 19:21?
options: Someone who has memorised the law
A member of the priesthood
Whole or complete (teleios, as in 5:48): for this man, freeing his heart from his wealth and following Jesus
Flawless in every action

check.q: What is the difference between 'precepts' and 'counsels' in Catholic teaching?
options: Counsels are older than precepts
Precepts bind everyone (such as love of God and neighbour); counsels (poverty, chastity, obedience) invite some to a fuller way, as in religious orders
There is no difference
Precepts are for priests, counsels for lay people
check.why: Aquinas, Summa I-II q. 108 a. 4; Vatican II adds that all are called to holiness.

check.q: Why did Pelagius object to Augustine's prayer 'Give what Thou enjoinest, and enjoin what Thou wilt'?
options: He disliked the Latin
He thought prayer was useless
He thought God never commanded anything
He believed that if God commands something, human beings must be able to do it by their own effort, so asking for grace to obey seemed to excuse moral laziness
check.why: The dispute over grace and effort shaped Western Christianity; Augustine held that God gives what he commands.

check.q: What did Bonhoeffer mean by 'cheap grace'?
options: The grace given in the sacraments
A Catholic error
Grace that is free of charge
Forgiveness without repentance or discipleship: a comfortable doctrine that asks nothing
check.why: Against it he set costly grace, the call to follow Jesus, which he found in the Sermon.

check.q: Which answer best states the journey's verdict on 'Can anyone live this?'
options: Only monks can live it
No: it is an impossible ideal and should not be tried
Not perfectly and not alone; but it is meant to be lived, by grace, together and by daily practice
Yes: anyone can keep it perfectly by trying hard
check.why: It holds together the Sermon's demand ('does them') and its grace ('with God all things are possible').

tutorial.question: Can the Sermon on the Mount guide a state, or only a person?
tutorial.approach: Set out the positions of Tolstoy, Luther and Weber. Consider what the Sermon itself addresses: personal injuries, the heart, a community of disciples. Then give examples where it has shaped public life without becoming its constitution. End with your own answer, and test it on one hard case: a state's response to a terrorist attack.

Notes that the Sermon's examples are mostly personal.
Distinguishes the Sermon as constitution from the Sermon as conscience.
Gives at least two historical examples of its public influence.
Engages with the objection that it is irresponsible in politics.
Tests the answer on a hard case.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: choose one command from the Sermon that you have read in this journey and do it each day for seven days. Each morning pray Augustine's prayer: 'Give what you command, and command what you will.'
sessions.reflect: What would you still lack? What is your 'great possession'?
takeaways: The rich young man's story shows the Sermon's call to be 'perfect', and Jesus's answer: 'with God all things are possible'.
Christians read the Sermon as precepts and counsels, as a mirror, as a guide for the forgiven, as literal discipleship and as the way of theosis.
The verdict: no one lives it perfectly or alone, but it is meant to be lived, by grace, together and by daily practice.

closing.title: Your answer
closing.prompt: What did Jesus teach about how to live? In about 300 words, answer from the Sermon on the Mount, using at least three of its passages, and answer the strongest objection to your view.
closing.practice: Read the whole Sermon on the Mount, Matthew 5 to 7, aloud, once a week for the next month: it takes about fifteen minutes. Each time, choose one sentence and live it until the next reading.
synthesis: This journey asked what Jesus taught about how to live, by reading the Sermon on the Mount block by block. Here are the short answers to its questions.

What is the Sermon on the Mount? It is the first and longest of the five great speeches in Matthew's Gospel, chapters 5 to 7, with a shorter version in Luke 6, the 'sermon on the plain'. Most scholars think Matthew gathered sayings Jesus gave on many occasions; Luke's shorter version, and the same sayings scattered elsewhere in his Gospel, point that way. Matthew frames it as a new Sinai: Jesus, like Moses, goes up a mountain and gives God's teaching. But he speaks in his own name, 'But I tell you', and the crowds are astonished at his authority. And it begins not with command but with blessing.

What are the Beatitudes? Eight blessings on people the world does not call fortunate: the poor in spirit, the grieving, the gentle, the hungry for justice, the merciful, the pure in heart, the peacemakers, the persecuted. Luke's four blessings are blunter, and come with four woes on the rich and the comfortable. Augustine read them as seven steps up a mountain, from humility to wisdom; many modern scholars read them first as God's announcement of favour. Both readings agree that God's gift comes before his demand, as it did at Sinai.

Did Jesus abolish the law? No. He said he came to fulfil it, and that not a letter would pass away. His six 'antitheses' press the commandments from the deed to the heart: from murder to anger and contempt, from adultery to the lustful look, from oaths to plain truth. Three forbid what the law permitted: divorce, revenge and hatred of enemies. None tells anyone to break a commandment. Other Jewish teachers, as the Mishnah shows, shared his concern with the heart and built 'fences' around the law; what stood out was the authority with which he spoke.

Does 'turn the other cheek' mean never resisting evil? The four examples in Matthew 5 are personal injuries: an insult, a lawsuit, a soldier's demand, a request for money. Jesus forbids retaliation, even the fair retaliation the old law allowed, and commands love of enemies, because God sends rain on the just and the unjust. Christians have read this three ways: as pacifism, from the early Church to the Quakers and Tolstoy; as forbidding revenge in the heart while allowing lawful force to protect the innocent, from Augustine to the just-war tradition and Luther's two kingdoms; and as active nonviolent resistance, as Gandhi and Martin Luther King practised it. All agree it forbids hatred and asks for love that acts.

How should we pray, give and fast? In secret, for God alone, not for an audience. The hypocrite, the actor, has already been paid in applause. The Lord's Prayer sits at the Sermon's centre, God's kingdom first and our needs after, with forgiveness binding prayer to how we treat others. The first Christians, as the Didache shows, fasted twice a week and prayed it three times a day. Why not worry? Because worry adds nothing, because God cares for the birds and the lilies and for us, and because God's kingdom deserves our first attention. It is a call to priorities and trust, lived in a community that shares, not a denial of real need.

What does 'do not judge' mean? Not that nothing is wrong, since the same chapter tells us to know false prophets by their fruits, but that we must not condemn others, ignore the beam in our own eye, or measure without mercy. The golden rule, 'do to others what you would want them to do to you', sums up the law and the prophets. Versions of it appear in Confucius, Isocrates, Tobit and Hillel; Jesus's positive form, set beside love of enemies, asks for more than restraint. And the Sermon ends with two houses: both builders hear; only one does. Hearing is not enough.

Is Christianity a 'slave morality'? Nietzsche argued that the weak, unable to beat the strong, took revenge by calling strength evil and meekness good, and that the Sermon is that revenge disguised as love. He was right that it overturned the values of Greece and Rome, so completely that we now take its values for granted, as Tom Holland argues. He was right that love can be faked. But Max Scheler replied that Christian love is the strong bending down from fullness, not the weak reacting from need; King showed that loving enemies can be the hardest courage there is; and the Magnificat's reversal is grounded in God's mercy, not hatred.

Can anyone live this? Not perfectly, and not alone. The rich young man kept the commandments and went away sad when Jesus showed him what 'perfect' would mean. 'Who then can be saved?' 'With God all things are possible.' The traditions read the Sermon differently: as precepts for all and counsels for some, as a mirror that shows our need of grace, as a guide for the forgiven, as literal discipleship, as the way of becoming like God. All agree that it is meant to be lived, by grace, in company, and by daily practice. Augustine prayed it in one line: 'Give what Thou enjoinest, and enjoin what Thou wilt.'

One more thing. Notice how much of the West's moral language comes from these three chapters: going the extra mile, turning the other cheek, salt of the earth, a city on a hill, the golden rule, the narrow way, wolves in sheep's clothing, building on sand, judging by fruits. Notice, too, how many of its convictions do: that the poor and the grieving matter to God; that an inner life counts as much as outward conduct; that the powerful are to serve; that an enemy is still a person. Whether or not you believe in the teacher, you have probably been living, a little, in the house he built.

title: How to read the Bible
question: How do you read a text so that it reads you?
line: Seven sessions on reading the Bible for life: where to start and which translation; then four rungs of a ladder (the plain sense, the one story, reading with others, and prayer); the strongest case against, from a book used to defend slavery; and a practice you can keep.
why: Most people who try to read the Bible give up, and many who read it are told it can be made to say anything. For two thousand years Jews and Christians developed ways of reading it: rules for the plain sense, the four senses of the medieval schools, the Church's tradition and the rabbis' commentary, and the slow, prayerful reading the monks called lectio divina. This journey teaches them from the sources (Augustine, Origen, Aquinas, the Jewish Fathers, Thomas à Kempis and the King James translators), tests them against Frederick Douglass's account of a Bible quoted to justify the whip, and ends with a daily practice. It closes the Old Testament hall, at the depth of a first-year university course in biblical interpretation, for anyone.
follows: A first-year paper in biblical interpretation (hermeneutics): genre and the literal sense, the history of interpretation from Origen to the Reformation, Scripture and tradition, the ethics of interpretation, with the practice of lectio divina.

glossary.def: Reading a text, or a story, as standing for something else; in Christian reading, especially for Christ and the Church.
The early Christian teachers of Alexandria, such as Origen, who sought spiritual meanings beneath the words.
The sense of Scripture that points to our final hope: heaven and the life to come.
The early Christian teachers of Antioch, such as John Chrysostom, who insisted on the historical sense.
A kind of writing that reveals the hidden meaning of history in vivid symbols, as in Daniel and Revelation.
The list of books a community accepts as Scripture.
The old word for love (Latin caritas): love of God, and of neighbour for God's sake.
In lectio divina, the fourth rung: resting in God, beyond words, which Guigo II calls God's gift.
Translating 'thought for thought', putting the meaning into natural modern language.
Language that says one thing by means of another, as a metaphor does.
Translating 'word for word', keeping close to the wording of the original.
A kind of writing, such as law, poetry, narrative, prophecy or letter, each with its own rules.
The modern scholarly study of a text's origins: who wrote it, when, from what sources and why.
A modern critic's term for a group whose shared assumptions shape how its members read.
'Divine reading': slow, prayerful reading of Scripture in four steps: reading, meditation, prayer and contemplation.
A fixed list of Bible readings for each Sunday or day of the year.
What the writer meant by his words, including his figures of speech.
Taking every word at face value regardless of genre; a modern approach, not the old 'literal sense'.
In Catholic teaching, the authority of the bishops in union with the Pope to interpret Scripture and tradition.
In the Bible, turning words over and murmuring them until they become part of you; in lectio divina, the second rung.
The first written collection of the Jewish oral law, compiled about AD 200.
The sense of Scripture that shows how we should live; also called the tropological sense.
In Jewish belief, the teaching given with the written Torah and handed down by word of mouth, later written in the Mishnah and Talmud.
In Jewish interpretation, the plain meaning of a verse.
Jewish interpretation of Scripture that searches out further meanings, often through stories and questions.
The modern view that meaning is made by readers, not simply found in texts.
The early Church's short summary of its belief, used as a guide for reading Scripture.
'Hear': Deuteronomy 6:4–9, the Jewish confession of faith said morning and evening.
'Scripture alone': the Reformation teaching that Scripture is the supreme authority for faith.
The meanings beyond the literal: allegorical, moral and anagogical.
The vast collection of rabbinic discussion of the Mishnah, completed about 500–600.
The Jewish name for the Hebrew Bible, from the first letters of Torah, Nevi'im (Prophets) and Ketuvim (Writings).
'Teaching': the five books of Moses; more broadly, all of God's teaching.
What the Church or the Jewish people have handed down, alongside and around the written text.
Reading earlier people and events as 'types', patterns that later ones fulfil, as Adam is a type of Christ.
Jerome's Latin translation of the Bible, the Western Church's Bible for a thousand years.
