debate.question: Is lectio divina a method anyone can learn, or a gift?

positions.name: A method
positions.who: Guigo II for the first three rungs; modern teachers of lectio, such as the Trappist M. Basil Pennington
positions.view: Lectio is a practice with clear steps that anyone can learn and repeat, like any discipline; faithfulness to the method opens a person to God.
positions.evidence: Benedict's fixed hours; Guigo's clear definitions; the experience of many who have learned it in groups.

positions.name: A gift
positions.who: Guigo II on contemplation; Luther; many Reformed teachers
positions.view: Understanding Scripture and meeting God in it come from the Holy Spirit, not from technique; methods can become a way of trying to control God.
positions.evidence: Guigo's insistence that contemplation is given; Luther's stress on the Spirit and the preached word; Jesus's 'to you it is given to know the mysteries' (Matthew 13:11).

positions.name: Study is prayer
positions.who: The rabbinic tradition; many Christian scholars
positions.view: Careful study of the text, arguing over its words, is itself a way of loving God with the mind; there need be no sharp line between understanding and devotion.
positions.evidence: Mishnah Peah 1:1; Jewish chavruta study; Augustine's view that all knowledge serves love.

debate.agree: All agree that reading Scripture should change the reader, and that it needs both effort and openness.

look.why: Giovanni Bellini painted this in Venice in 1505. Jerome, who lived as a monk in Bethlehem, is shown alone at the mouth of a cave, reading. It is here because it shows lectio as the monks practised it: solitude, attention, and a book read slowly.
points: A bearded, balding man with deeply tanned skin, wearing only a strip of robin's-egg-blue cloth, sits on a rock at the mouth of a craggy cave.
He faces left in profile, his head bowed over an open book propped on the rock by his knee.
A lion lies beside him in the lower right corner, its mouth open.
Around him are other animals: a lizard by a rectangular pool, a squirrel on the cave's grassy top, a black bird in a bare tree, and two rabbits touching noses on a low wall.
In the distance, stone buildings, some in ruins, run down a hillside to the water, under a vivid azure sky.

music.why: Gregorio Allegri's setting of Psalm 51 (1630s), sung slowly, verse by verse, in the Sistine Chapel in Holy Week: Scripture turned into prayer, which is what lectio teaches.

think.why: What the research and the great teachers say about whether daily practices like slow reading change who we are.

learn.why: A one-line prayer to say before you begin: the wonders are in the text; what you ask for is eyes to see them.

check.q: In Guigo's image, which rung 'chews' the food?
options: Contemplation
Prayer
Reading
Meditation
check.why: Reading puts it in the mouth, meditation chews it, prayer tastes it, contemplation is the sweetness.

check.q: Why does Guigo insist that contemplation is different from the other three rungs?
options: Because it is a technique for emptying the mind
Because it is God's gift, which comes to meet the reader's prayer, rather than something the reader does
Because it is only for monks
Because it requires no reading
check.why: The first three are ours to climb; the fourth is given.

check.q: Thomas à Kempis says our curiosity hinders us 'when we seek to understand and discuss, where we should pass simply on'. What follows for the way lectio differs from study?
options: That only the simple can read Scripture
That we should never ask questions
That there is a time to analyse and a time to let the words work, and lectio is the second
That study is wrong
check.why: He also says 'ask freely': the point is the purpose of the reading, not a ban on thinking.

check.q: Why did Benedict set fixed hours for reading?
options: Because he thought reading less important than work and wanted it limited
Because books were rare
Because 'idleness is the enemy of the soul', and attention left to mood tends to drift
Because books were shared and each monk had only a short turn
check.why: Reading had its hours, like work and prayer, and elders guarded them.

check.q: What is the main difference between Ignatius's imaginative contemplation and Guigo's lectio?
options: Guigo was a Protestant
Lectio is done in groups only
Ignatius has you picture a Gospel scene and enter it; Guigo has you turn over a word or phrase
Ignatius uses no Bible
check.why: Both pray Scripture; one through the imagination, one through words chewed slowly.

check.q: Someone says: 'I tried lectio divina for a week and felt nothing, so it doesn't work.' What is the best reply from this session?
options: Lectio asks for faithfulness, not feelings; Guigo expected dry days, and the change is usually slow
They should switch to reading more quickly
Only monks can do it
They did it wrong
check.why: The fourth rung is given, not achieved; the first three are climbed faithfully.

tutorial.question: Explain lectio divina to someone who has never prayed, and say what you think it can and cannot do.
tutorial.approach: Describe Guigo's four rungs and his images, and walk through an example (his own, Matthew 5:8, or another). Use Thomas à Kempis and Benedict to show the attitude and the discipline. Compare one other way of praying Scripture. Then weigh the debate: method or gift?
strong: Explains the four rungs accurately with Guigo's food image.
Works through an example verse step by step.
Uses Thomas à Kempis on reading humbly and Benedict on fixed times.
Compares lectio with Ignatius, Luther or Jewish study.
Weighs whether it is a method or a gift, fairly.
Is honest about dry days.

reading.author: Eugene Peterson
reading.title: Eat This Book: A Conversation in the Art of Spiritual Reading
reading.why: A pastor's lively introduction to lectio divina.

reading.author: M. Basil Pennington
reading.title: Lectio Divina: Renewing the Ancient Practice of Praying the Scriptures
reading.why: A Trappist monk's practical guide.

reading.author: Guigo II
reading.title: The Ladder of Monks and Twelve Meditations (tr. Edmund Colledge and James Walsh)
reading.why: Guigo's letter in a modern translation.

reading.author: Jean Leclercq
reading.title: The Love of Learning and the Desire for God
reading.why: The classic study of how medieval monks read.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: each morning, take Luke 10:38–42 or Matthew 5:8. Read it twice, slowly and aloud. Stop at the phrase that catches you and turn it over for two minutes. Say one sentence to God about it. Then sit in silence for one minute before you get up.
sessions.reflect: What would it mean for you to let a passage read you, rather than reading it?
takeaways: Lectio divina climbs four rungs: reading, meditation, prayer and contemplation; Guigo pictures them as eating.
It grew from the desert monks' murmured memorising and Benedict's fixed hours; Ignatius, Luther, the Puritans and Jewish study offer other ways of praying Scripture.
It asks for faithfulness, not feelings: the first three rungs are climbed, the fourth is given, and readers are changed slowly.

sessions.title: The verdict, and a practice for life
sessions.line: Read it plainly, as one story, with the Church and on your knees.
sessions.plain: Here is the verdict of this journey: read the Bible plainly, as one story, with others and in prayer, and it begins to read you. The last session reads the Bible's own image for this, a mirror, and the story of a young Egyptian who heard one verse read in church and did what it said. Then it gives a daily practice and a plan for a year.
sessions.why: Six sessions have built the ladder and tested it against the strongest objection. Now we put it together, and turn it into a habit.
answers: So how should I read the Bible?
What do I do tomorrow morning?
How do I keep going for a year?
What is the point, if I don't change?
sessions.finding: Read it plainly, as one story, with the Church and on your knees, and then do what it says: that is how a text begins to read you.

paras: The question of this journey was: how do you read a text so that it reads you? The answer has four rungs. Read it as it was written: the plain sense, in its own kind of writing, as the writer meant it. Read it as one story, in which the Old Testament points to Christ, without letting allegory float free of the literal sense. Read it with others: with a community, with the tradition, and with readers unlike yourself. And let it read you, in slow and prayerful reading.

The objection showed that none of these rungs works alone. The slaveholders had the letter without the whole story or the rule of love. The answer was not to throw the Bible away but to read it better, and above all to read it as Lawson did, to be changed by it rather than to control others with it. That is where the last rung ends: in doing.
background.key: Read plainly, as one story, with others and in prayer; the rungs work together, and they end in doing.

paras: The Letter of James is the most practical book in the New Testament. By tradition it was written by James, the brother of Jesus, leader of the church in Jerusalem until his execution in AD 62 (the Jewish historian Josephus records his death). Some scholars think a later writer used his name. It has been called a book of wisdom, like Proverbs, written for Christians.

Antony of Egypt (about 251–356) is counted the father of Christian monks. His life was written soon after his death by Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, and it spread across the Roman world; Augustine, in his Confessions, says that hearing it helped bring him to faith. Its most famous scene is the moment Antony heard a Gospel read in church.
background.key: James is the New Testament's most practical book; Antony is the reader who heard one verse and did it.

paras: The main reading is James 1:19–27, with its picture of a man who looks in a mirror and forgets what he saw. It is the Bible's own verdict on reading without doing.

The comparison is Athanasius's account of Antony hearing Matthew 19:21 read in church, 'as though the passage had been read on his account', and going out to do it. It shows what it looks like when a text reads someone.
background.key: James's mirror is the verdict; Antony is the example.

before: What is the difference, in James, between a hearer and a doer?
What does the mirror show, and why does the man forget?
In the comparison, what did Antony do when he heard the Gospel, and how quickly?
sessions.readWhy: The Bible's own verdict on reading: James's picture of the mirror, and what it means to be a doer of the word.

paras: So, then, my beloved brothers, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger;
for the anger of man doesn’t produce the righteousness of God.
Therefore, putting away all filthiness and overflowing of wickedness, receive with humility the implanted word, which is able to save your souls.
But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.
For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he is like a man looking at his natural face in a mirror;
for he sees himself, and goes away, and immediately forgets what kind of man he was.
But he who looks into the perfect law of freedom and continues, not being a hearer who forgets, but a doer of the work, this man will be blessed in what he does.
If anyone among you thinks himself to be religious while he doesn’t bridle his tongue, but deceives his heart, this man’s religion is worthless.
Pure religion and undefiled before our God and Father is this: to visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep oneself unstained by the world.

parts.title: Receive the implanted word
parts.context: The letter is addressed 'to the twelve tribes which are in the Dispersion', probably Jewish Christians scattered outside the land of Israel, in the first century AD. Its first chapter is about trials, temptation and the word of God.

commentary.on: let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger
commentary.text: The first rule of reading, as of conversation: listen first. Augustine's reader who 'feels more angry with Scripture than he is with himself' broke all three.

commentary.on: receive with humility the implanted word, which is able to save your souls
commentary.text: The word is 'implanted', like a seed: the parable of the sower again. It is received with humility, as Thomas à Kempis said.

parts.title: The mirror
parts.context: The centre of the passage.

commentary.on: But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.
commentary.text: James's verdict. To hear without doing is not neutral; it is self-deception. A person can read the Bible every day and use it to avoid changing.

commentary.on: he is like a man looking at his natural face in a mirror; for he sees himself, and goes away, and immediately forgets what kind of man he was
commentary.text: Scripture is a mirror: you see yourself in it. The fourth rung of the ladder is exactly this, the text reading you. But a mirror is useless if you walk away and forget.

commentary.on: But he who looks into the perfect law of freedom and continues
commentary.text: 'Looks into' is a strong word in Greek: to stoop and peer closely, the word used of the disciples looking into the empty tomb (John 20:5). 'Continues' means he keeps looking, day after day. 'The law of freedom' is a striking phrase: God's teaching sets people free, as the Exodus story you read in this hall showed.

commentary.on: this man will be blessed in what he does.
commentary.text: The blessing is in the doing. The Bible's first psalm began with the blessed man who meditates on God's law day and night; James finishes the thought: blessed in what he does.

parts.title: Pure religion
parts.context: James gives two tests of real religion.

commentary.on: If anyone among you thinks himself to be religious while he doesn't bridle his tongue
commentary.text: The first test is speech. A reader who uses Scripture as a weapon in arguments has not yet been read by it.

commentary.on: to visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep oneself unstained by the world
commentary.text: The second test is care for the most vulnerable. It is the prophets' test, which you met in Kings and prophets, and it is the test Douglass applied to the slaveholders' Christianity.

paras: 2. After the death of his father and mother he was left alone with one little sister: his age was about eighteen or twenty, and on him the care both of home and sister rested. Now it was not six months after the death of his parents, and going according to custom into the Lord's House, he communed with himself and reflected as he walked how the Apostles left all and followed the Saviour; and how they in the Acts sold their possessions and brought and laid them at the Apostles' feet for distribution to the needy, and what and how great a hope was laid up for them in heaven. Pondering over these things he entered the church, and it happened the Gospel was being read, and he heard the Lord saying to the rich man, 'If you would be perfect, go and sell that you have and give to the poor; and come follow Me and you shall have treasure in heaven.' Antony, as though God had put him in mind of the Saints, and the passage had been read on his account, went out immediately from the church, and gave the possessions of his forefathers to the villagers — they were three hundred acres, productive and very fair — that they should be no more a clog upon himself and his sister. And all the rest that was movable he sold, and having got together much money he gave it to the poor, reserving a little however for his sister's sake.

3. And again as he went into the church, hearing the Lord say in the Gospel, 'be not anxious for the morrow,' he could stay no longer, but went out and gave those things also to the poor. Having committed his sister to known and faithful virgins, and put her into a convent to be brought up, he henceforth devoted himself outside his house to discipline, taking heed to himself and training himself with patience. For there were not yet so many monasteries in Egypt, and no monk at all knew of the distant desert; but all who wished to give heed to themselves practised the discipline in solitude near their own village. Now there was then in the next village an old man who had lived the life of a hermit from his youth up. Antony, after he had seen this man, imitated him in piety. And at first he began to abide in places outside the village: then if he heard of a good man anywhere, like the prudent bee, he went forth and sought him, nor turned back to his own palace until he had seen him; and he returned, having got from the good man as it were supplies for his journey in the way of virtue. So dwelling there at first, he confirmed his purpose not to return to the abode of his fathers nor to the remembrance of his kinsfolk; but to keep all his desire and energy for perfecting his discipline. He worked, however, with his hands, having heard, 'he who is idle let him not eat,' and part he spent on bread and part he gave to the needy. And he was constant in prayer, knowing that a man ought to pray in secret unceasingly. For he had given such heed to what was read that none of the things that were written fell from him to the ground, but he remembered all, and afterwards his memory served him for books.

parts.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
parts.translator: H. Ellershaw, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 4 (1892)
parts.title: As though the passage had been read on his account
parts.context: Egypt, about 270. Antony, born about 251 to a well-off Christian family in a village of Middle Egypt, has lost both parents. He has a younger sister to care for and inherited land. The scene is the village church, where the Gospel is read aloud, as in every service.
parts.plain: Athanasius says: Antony was about eighteen or twenty when his parents died, leaving him to look after his sister and the household. Six months later, walking to church, he was thinking about how the apostles left everything to follow Jesus, and how the first Christians sold their property for the poor. As he went in, the Gospel being read was Jesus's word to the rich young man: 'If you would be perfect, go and sell what you have and give to the poor, and come follow me.' Antony felt it had been read for him. He went straight out, gave his family's land to the villagers, sold everything else and gave the money to the poor, keeping a little for his sister.

commentary.on: he communed with himself and reflected as he walked how the Apostles left all and followed the Saviour
commentary.text: Antony was already meditating on Scripture as he walked, as Deuteronomy said to do: 'when you walk by the way'. The verse that changed him fell on prepared ground.

commentary.on: it happened the Gospel was being read, and he heard the Lord saying to the rich man
commentary.text: He heard it read aloud in church, in the regular reading. Not alone, not by searching: in the community's reading, the third rung.

commentary.on: as though God had put him in mind of the Saints, and the passage had been read on his account
commentary.text: This is what it means for a text to read you. Antony did not think the verse was only about a rich man in Galilee long ago. The plain sense addressed him.

commentary.on: went out immediately from the church, and gave the possessions of his forefathers to the villagers
commentary.text: And he did it. Immediately. James's 'doer of the word'. Antony's response is not the only faithful one; most Christians are not called to give away everything. But it is the clearest picture of reading that ends in doing.

parts.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
parts.translator: H. Ellershaw, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 4 (1892)
parts.title: His memory served him for books
parts.context: Soon afterwards. Antony begins to live as an ascetic, a person of disciplined prayer and simplicity, near his village. There are as yet no monasteries in the desert.
parts.plain: Athanasius says: another time Antony heard in church 'do not be anxious about tomorrow', and gave away what he had kept. He put his sister in the care of a community of women, and began a life of discipline near his village, learning from an old hermit and from any good person he heard of. He worked with his hands, gave to the poor, and prayed constantly. He listened so carefully to Scripture that he forgot nothing, and his memory served him for books.

commentary.on: hearing the Lord say in the Gospel, 'be not anxious for the morrow,' he could stay no longer
commentary.text: A second verse, a second act. Reading that ends in doing is not one dramatic moment but a habit.

commentary.on: like the prudent bee, he went forth and sought him
commentary.text: Antony learned from others, gathering a little from each, as a bee gathers from many flowers. Even the father of hermits did not read alone.

commentary.on: He worked, however, with his hands
commentary.text: Work and reading, as in Benedict's Rule two centuries later.

commentary.on: afterwards his memory served him for books
commentary.text: Antony probably could not read, or not well; he heard Scripture read aloud. He carried it in memory, as Deuteronomy asked: 'on your heart'. This is why this journey asks you to learn words by heart.

compare.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
compare.translator: H. Ellershaw, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 4 (1892)
compare.why: The most famous example in Christian history of a person read by a text: a young man who heard one verse in church and did what it said, that same day.
compare.title: Antony hears the Gospel

paras: Put the four rungs side by side and you can see why each needs the others. The plain sense without the whole story can be used, verse by verse, to defend slavery. The whole story without the plain sense floats off into allegory. Both without a community become private eccentricity; a community without the plain sense becomes an echo chamber. And all three without prayer become an academic exercise, or a weapon.

Together, they make a way of reading that Christians of every tradition, and in large part Jews too, would recognise. The emphasis differs: Protestants stress the plain sense, Catholics and Orthodox the tradition and the liturgy, monks the prayer. But no tradition has given up any of the four.

rows: Where does this fit in the whole, and what does it show of Christ?
Origen's body, soul and spirit; Aquinas's four senses
Verses torn from their story, as the slaveholders did
How have others read it, and who corrects me?
Augustine's rule of love; Avot's chain of teachers
Private eccentricity or an echo chamber
What is it saying to me, and what will I do?
Guigo's ladder; Thomas à Kempis; James's mirror

sections.key: Each rung guards against the failures of the others; every tradition keeps all four, with different emphases.

paras: Here is a daily pattern built from the whole journey. It takes about fifteen minutes. It can be done on a bus or at a kitchen table; it needs a Bible, a notebook and a little quiet.

Begin with a one-line prayer, such as Psalm 119:18: 'Open my eyes, that I may see wondrous things out of your law.' Read the day's passage once, at normal speed, asking only: what kind of writing is this, and what happens? Read it again slowly, aloud if you can, and stop at the phrase that catches you. Turn it over: what does it mean, where else does the Bible say something like it, what does it ask of me? Say one or two sentences to God about it. Sit quietly for a minute. Then write down one thing to do today, however small.

rows: Read the passage through: what kind of writing, what happens?
Read slowly, aloud; stop at the phrase that catches you
Meditate: what it means, where else, what it asks
Speak to God about it; then a minute of silence
Write one thing to do today

sections.key: A fifteen-minute pattern: ask, read, read again, turn it over, pray, and write one thing to do.

paras: A daily pattern needs a plan, or you will spend each morning deciding what to read. Choose one and keep it for a year.

For beginners: one Gospel and one psalm a day. Read Mark, then Luke, then John, then Matthew, a chapter a day, with a psalm each day; then Acts, Genesis and Exodus. That covers the heart of the Bible in about nine months. For those who want the whole Bible: M'Cheyne's four chapters a day, or two of them, which takes two years. For those who want to read with the Church: the daily lectionary of the Catholic Church or the Church of England, which pairs an Old Testament reading, a psalm and a New Testament reading, and is used by millions on the same day.

Whatever plan you choose, keep two kinds of reading going: the daily slow reading, and once in a while a whole book in one sitting, so that you hear it as its first readers did. Mark, Ruth, Jonah, Philippians and James can each be read in under an hour.
sections.key: Choose a plan and keep it for a year: a Gospel and a psalm a day, M'Cheyne's calendar, or the Church's lectionary; and sometimes read a whole book at once.

paras: You will miss days. Everyone does. The Bible's picture of reading is a relationship, not a performance: Mary sitting at Jesus's feet, the Beroeans asking questions, Lawson praying at his work. Augustine said that a reader who aims at love can come to the Bible 'with an easy mind'. If you miss a day, do not try to catch up; simply begin again with today's reading.

Two things help most. A fixed time and place, as Benedict knew: the same chair, the same hour. And another person: a friend, a group or a congregation, who will ask what you are reading and tell you what they are. Reading with others, the third rung, is also the best way to keep going.
sections.key: Missed days are normal: begin again with today, keep a fixed time and place, and read with someone.

sections.h: The Old Testament hall, looking back
paras: This journey closes the first hall, the Old Testament. Look back at what you have read. The whole story gave you the map, seven acts from creation to new creation. What is the Bible? showed you how the library was gathered and handed down, and that it can be trusted as ancient and faithfully copied. In the beginning read Genesis 1–11 beside the myths of Babylon. Abraham and the promise followed one family and its faith. Exodus and the law heard the cry of slaves and the ten words at Sinai. Kings and prophets watched power forget justice and the prophets call it to account. Psalms and wisdom gave the Bible's prayer book and its wisdom.

Now you have the ladder for reading all of it. The next hall begins with Jesus himself, and with the Gospels, where Christians believe the Old Testament's story reaches its centre. Read them plainly, as the end of one story, with others, and on your knees.
sections.key: The Old Testament hall gave the story and its books; this journey gives the way to read them; the next hall turns to Jesus and the Gospels.

paras: This journey has asked you to learn a few words by heart: 'Your word is a lamp to my feet'; 'Every Scripture is God-breathed'; 'Weren't our hearts burning within us?'; the double commandment of love; Micah's 'act justly, love mercy, walk humbly'; 'Open my eyes'; and now 'Be doers of the word'. Together they are a short summary of everything you have read.

Antony's memory 'served him for books'. Most of us will never memorise as the desert monks did, but a handful of verses known by heart change how the Bible works in a life. They come back unbidden in the moments when you need them: in the night, in a hospital, in an argument, at a graveside. Keep adding one a week. In a year you will have fifty, and they will have begun to read you.
sections.key: The verses learned in this journey summarise it; a verse a week, known by heart, lets Scripture go with you.

paras: The hall ends with a short essay: you defend one idea from the Old Testament hall in about 300 words, and answer the strongest objection to it. Here is how to use this journey to write it.

Choose an idea you think is true and important. Find the passage it rests on, and read it by the four rungs: what does it plainly say, in its own kind of writing? Where does it sit in the one story? How have Jews and Christians read it, and is there a reading from someone unlike you that you need to hear? What does it ask of you? Then state the strongest objection fairly, in the terms its best advocate would use, as Aquinas did at the start of every article. Answer it as honestly as you can, admitting what it gets right. That is the method of this whole hall, and of every good argument.
sections.key: To make the case: choose an idea, read its passage by the four rungs, state the strongest objection fairly as Aquinas did, and answer it honestly.

refs: James 1:19–27; Matthew 19:21; Matthew 6:34; Psalm 119:18; Psalm 1:1–3; John 20:5.
Athanasius, Life of Antony 2–3 (tr. H. Ellershaw, 1892); Augustine, Confessions VIII.6.

debate.question: What is lost when the Bible is read only critically, or only devotionally?

positions.name: Only critically
positions.who: The concern of Brevard Childs and of the Pontifical Biblical Commission (1993)
positions.view: Read only as an ancient text to be explained by its history and sources, the Bible's claims on the reader go unheard; you learn a great deal about it and never ask whether it is true or what it asks of you.
positions.evidence: Jowett's hope that honest reading would show the Bible unique; the critique that historical criticism 'stops too soon'.

positions.name: Only devotionally
positions.who: The concern of critical scholars such as James Barr, and of Augustine and Origen before them
positions.view: Read only for personal comfort, the Bible becomes a mirror of the reader's own feelings; its strangeness, its history and its hard sayings are lost, and it can be made to say what we want.
positions.evidence: The slaveholders' use of single verses; Augustine's warning about custom; Origen's insistence that the text is work.

positions.name: Both, in order
positions.who: Augustine, Aquinas, Guigo; most teachers of reading today
positions.view: Study and prayer belong together: the plain sense and the history first, then meditation and prayer, so that understanding feeds devotion and devotion keeps study honest.
positions.evidence: Guigo's warning that prayer without meditation is lukewarm and meditation without reading goes astray; the four rungs of this journey.

debate.agree: All agree that the Bible can be read badly in either way, and that it asks for both mind and heart.

look.why: Martino di Bartolomeo of Siena painted this panel about 1415–20. The main figure is a young deacon saint whom the gallery does not name. Saint Antony appears only small, at the very top, holding a book. He is here because the gallery identifies him, and because he is shown as Athanasius describes him: a man of the book he heard read.
points: A pale-skinned, clean-shaven young man, shown from the hips up against a gold background, holds a palm frond in one hand and a book in the other.
The book has a slate-blue cover and canary-yellow pages.
He wears a red robe edged with gold, with rectangular gold patches on the sleeves, and a white ruffled collar.
In the tip of the panel, tiny in scale, a balding man with a long grey beard, in a muted purple robe under a black cloak, holds a red book in one hand and a crutch in the other: Saint Antony.
Both have halos punched into the gold, under a pointed gilded arch.

music.why: Bach's chorale from a cantata of 1723, his first year in Leipzig, flows on steadily over a gentle triplet melody: a picture of a daily habit, unhurried and joyful.

think.why: James asks for doers of the word: why do Christians think goodness is something God calls us to, not just something we choose?

learn.why: James's verdict on all reading, and the last words of this journey: be doers of the word, and not only hearers.

check.q: Why does each rung of the ladder need the others?
options: Because the four rungs come from four different churches, each holding one

Because each guards against the failures of the others: the plain sense alone can tear verses from their story, the one story alone floats off into allegory, a community alone can become an echo chamber, and all without prayer leave the reader unchanged
Because no single rung is true
Because the churches require all four
check.why: The objection showed what happens when one rung is used alone.

check.q: In James's picture, what is the problem with the man who looks in the mirror?
options: He looks too long
The mirror is distorted
He studies his face too critically
He sees himself and then goes away and forgets: he hears without doing
check.why: Hearing without doing is self-deception.

check.q: What made Antony's hearing of Matthew 19:21 an example of a text 'reading' someone?
options: He took the plain sense as addressed to him, 'as though the passage had been read on his account', and did it at once
He allegorised it
He studied the Greek carefully
He read it alone in the desert
check.why: The plain sense, heard in the community's reading, applied to himself, and done.

That memorising is only for those who cannot read

closing.title: Your answer, and make the case
closing.prompt: Make the case (the end of the Old Testament hall). Choose one idea you have met in this hall, for example that every human being bears God's image, that God hears the cry of slaves, that power must answer to justice, or that the Bible can be trusted as an ancient witness. In about 300 words, defend it from the passages it rests on, read by the four rungs (the plain sense, the one story, the reading of others, and what it asks of you), and answer the strongest objection to it.
closing.practice: Keep the fifteen-minute pattern for forty days, with a Gospel and a psalm a day. At the end, read back through your notebook and write down the three things the Bible asked you to do that you actually did.
synthesis: This journey asked how to read a text so that it reads you. Its answer is a ladder of four rungs, tested against the strongest objection and ending in a daily practice. Here are the short answers to the questions it set out to answer, in order.

Where do I start? Not at Genesis 1, reading straight through: the Bible is a library, not a novel. Begin with a Gospel (Mark is the shortest), a psalm a day and Genesis; then Acts, a short letter and Exodus. The Bible's own picture of reading is little, often, aloud and slow: Joshua murmuring the book day and night, the Shema talked over at home and on the road, the Beroeans examining the Scriptures daily. Fifteen minutes a day is a good beginning.

Which translation? One you understand and will read. Translations range from formal equivalence, close to the original wording, to dynamic equivalence, which puts the meaning into natural speech. The King James translators said in 1611 that translation opens the window to let in the light, and admitted no translation is perfect. A study Bible helps a beginner; read the text before the notes, and know whose notes they are.

Do I have to take it literally? You must take it in its literal sense, which in the old meaning of the word is what the writer meant, figures of speech included. Aquinas said the literal sense of 'God's arm' is God's power. That depends on genre: poetry as poetry, law as law, letters as letters. Augustine's rules bind both ways: read plainly first and look for a figure only when the plain reading cannot teach love or true belief; and never call a passage figurative merely because your own culture dislikes it. Literalism, taking every word at face value regardless of genre, is a modern approach, not the tradition's.

Why did the old writers find Christ everywhere? Because Jesus and Paul read the Old Testament as one story pointing to him. Origen taught that Scripture, like a person, has body, soul and spirit, and that its difficulties are signposts to deeper reading; but he insisted most of its history happened. The Middle Ages read every passage on four levels: what happened, what it shows of Christ, how to live and what to hope for, with Jerusalem as city, Church, soul and heaven. Aquinas tied them together: God can make things as well as words signify, so a real event can carry a further meaning; but every sense rests on the literal, and no doctrine may be proved from allegory alone. Jews, too, read on several levels, but their deeper meanings point to Torah and Israel. The Reformers rejected free allegory and kept typology.

Why do Christians disagree about what it says, and how do Jews read it? Because the Bible is read within communities, and they differ on who decides. Jews read the written Torah with the oral Torah, handed down from Moses in a chain of teachers and gathered in the Mishnah and Talmud, and they study it together, turning it over 'for all things are in it'. Catholics read Scripture with Tradition and the bishops' teaching office; the Orthodox within the life of the Church, its Fathers, councils and liturgy; Protestants by Scripture alone, but never alone with Scripture, keeping the creeds and confessions. All the large churches share the core the creeds state. And Augustine's rule cuts across them all: a reading that does not build up love of God and neighbour has not yet understood, however accurate its words.

What about the bits I find shocking, and hasn't the Bible been used to justify terrible things? Yes. In America it was quoted, verse by verse and sincerely, to defend slavery; Frederick Douglass watched a converted slaveholder whip his disabled cousin while quoting Luke 12:47. Readers do find what they bring, and modern critics argue that meaning is made by interpretive communities. The honest reply admits that the Bible regulates slavery without explicitly abolishing it, and that Christians long defended it. But the pro-slavery readings tore verses from their stories, ignored their plain sense and passed over the texts that judged them. The tradition's own rules, the whole story from Genesis 1:27 to Philemon's 'beloved brother', and above all the readings of the enslaved themselves exposed them. Douglass never stopped reading the Bible; he claimed it against his enslavers: 'That which is inhuman cannot be divine.' The parable of the sower puts the problem in the soil, not the seed, and makes fruit the test.

What is lectio divina, and how do I pray with the Bible? It is the monks' slow reading in four steps, as the Carthusian Guigo II described it: reading puts the food in the mouth, meditation chews it, prayer tastes it, and contemplation is its sweetness, which is God's gift rather than our achievement. Benedict gave it fixed hours, because idleness is the enemy of the soul; Thomas à Kempis said to read humbly, simply and honestly, in the spirit in which Scripture was written. Ignatius pictured the Gospel scenes, Luther wove each verse into a garland of instruction, thanks, confession and prayer, and Jews hold the study of Torah itself to be worship. Most days nothing dramatic happens; lectio asks for faithfulness, not feelings.

So how should I read it? Plainly, as one story, with others and on your knees. Each rung guards against the failures of the others. And then do what it says. James's man who looks in the mirror and walks away has heard without being read; Antony, hearing one verse read in church 'as though the passage had been read on his account', went out and did it. A fifteen-minute pattern (ask, read, read again, turn it over, pray, do), a plan for the year, a fixed time and someone to read with will keep you going.

Can a text have more than one true meaning? The tradition says yes, within limits: Augustine thought a great text holds more truth than one reader sees, and Aquinas that God signifies by things as well as words. But it also says no reading is true that contradicts the plain sense or fails to build up love. That balance is the heart of this journey.

One more thing. Notice how much of the West grew from the ways of reading in this journey. Universities began in the cathedral schools where monks and scholars argued over the senses of Scripture, and the very method of the Summa, objections stated fairly before an answer, became the method of disputation and debate. The demand to read what an ancient author actually meant, in his own language and time, which Jerome, the Antiochenes and the Reformers pressed, grew into modern historical scholarship. The conviction that every ploughman and milkmaid should be able to read the Bible for themselves did more than anything else to spread literacy across Protestant Europe and beyond, and drove the translation of the Bible into thousands of languages. And the habit of slow, daily attention to a text, learned in monasteries, is still what every serious reader of anything practises. Whatever you conclude about the Bible, you have learned the way the West learned to read.
